# Build: A/B Layer Ping-Pong

A double buffer for DOM content. Incoming content is written into whichever of two absolutely-positioned layers is currently invisible, then the two swap opacity. Because the outgoing content is still on screen, every change is a real crossfade rather than a swap with a fade bolted on — and running two of these at different durations is how a hover preview gets its lag between thumbnail and full-bleed background.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Two stacked layers alternate so any change crossfades, however fast you move between rows.

- Category: transition
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. Two absolutely positioned layers share a stacking context. A `front` slot (`"a"` or `"b"`) records which one is currently visible; the other is always at opacity 0.
2. When `contentKey` changes, the new children are written into the BACK slot and `front` flips. The back layer is already transparent, so the new content mounts invisibly — writing into the front layer instead would replace the outgoing content before it had faded.
3. `gsap.killTweensOf([inEl, outEl])` runs before every transition. Moving across a list faster than the duration otherwise leaves an unfinished fade-out driving the same node a fade-in is now driving up, and the layers flicker.
4. Two symmetric tweens — `opacity: 1` on the incoming layer, `opacity: 0` on the outgoing — with `power2.inOut`, which keeps the midpoint of the fade at roughly equal luminance instead of dipping through a visible trough.
5. The first commit is a `gsap.set`, not a tween, so the initial content is simply present; only subsequent key changes animate.
6. The last `contentKey` acted on is held in a ref, so a parent re-rendering with the same key (new inline children, a hover on the row that is already active) does not restart the fade.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `duration (background) = 1`
  Seconds. A full-bleed area needs a long fade or the whole frame appears to jump brightness; at 0.5s a large gradient change reads as a cut.
- `duration (thumbnail) = 0.6`
  The small element under the cursor answers first. Both at 1s and the interface feels unresponsive; both at 0.6s and the background flickers on fast passes. The 0.4s difference is the effect.
- `ease = 'power2.inOut'`
  Symmetric ease on both halves keeps their crossover near 50/50. With `power2.out` on the way in and `power2.in` on the way out, both layers are dim at the midpoint and the panel visibly darkens mid-fade.

## API

```ts
function ABLayerCrossfade(props: { contentKey: string; children: ReactNode; duration?: number; ease?: string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `contentKey: string`
  Identity of the current content. A change starts a crossfade.
- `children: ReactNode`
  Content for the current key. Captured into a layer at the moment the key changes.
- `duration: number` — default `1`
  Crossfade length in seconds. Use a shorter one for the smaller element in a pair.
- `ease: string` — default `'power2.inOut'`
  GSAP ease applied to both halves.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the positioned wrapper. Give it a size — the layers are absolute.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function ABLayerCrossfade({
  contentKey,
  children,
  duration = 1,
  ease = 'power2.inOut',
  className,
}: ABLayerCrossfadeProps) {
  const aRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const bRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  const [front, setFront] = useState<Slot>('a');
  const [layers, setLayers] = useState<{ a: ReactNode; b: ReactNode }>({
    a: children,
    b: null,
  });

  const shownKey = useRef(contentKey);
  const frontRef = useRef<Slot>('a');
  const first = useRef(true);

  // Write into the BACK layer, then flip. The back layer is already at
  // opacity 0, so the new content mounts invisibly — no flash of it at full
  // strength before the tween starts.
  useEffect(() => {
    if (shownKey.current === contentKey) return;
    shownKey.current = contentKey;
    const next: Slot = frontRef.current === 'a' ? 'b' : 'a';
    frontRef.current = next;
    setLayers((l) => ({ ...l, [next]: children }));
    setFront(next);
  }, [contentKey, children]);

  useEffect(() => {
    const inEl = front === 'a' ? aRef.current : bRef.current;
    const outEl = front === 'a' ? bRef.current : aRef.current;
    if (!inEl || !outEl) return;

    if (first.current) {
      first.current = false;
      gsap.set(inEl, { opacity: 1 });
      gsap.set(outEl, { opacity: 0 });
      return;
    }

    // Kill first, always. Two rapid changes otherwise leave an old fade-out
    // running on the layer the new fade-in is driving up.
    gsap.killTweensOf([inEl, outEl]);

    if (reduced) {
      gsap.set(inEl, { opacity: 1 });
      gsap.set(outEl, { opacity: 0 });
      return;
    }

    gsap.to(inEl, { opacity: 1, duration, ease });
    gsap.to(outEl, { opacity: 0, duration, ease });
  }, [front, duration, ease, reduced]);

  useEffect(
    () => () => {
      gsap.killTweensOf([aRef.current, bRef.current]);
    },
    [],
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** An unmount effect calls `gsap.killTweensOf` on both layer elements, so an in-flight fade cannot write opacity to a detached node after React has removed it.

**Reduced motion.** The layers still ping-pong, but the swap is a `gsap.set` rather than a tween: content changes instantly with no fade. The double-buffer structure is unchanged, so nothing else in the component behaves differently.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Crossfading one element by swapping its content at opacity 0. There is nothing to fade out of, so it reads as a blink; the two-layer buffer is the whole point.
- Writing incoming content into the front layer. The old content is replaced before it has faded, which is a hard cut with a pointless fade on top.
- Skipping `killTweensOf`. Hovering four rows in a second stacks eight opacity tweens across two nodes, and the layers end up at whatever the last-finishing pair leaves behind — usually both partly transparent.
- Giving both layers the same duration in a paired preview. The lag between the small element and the full-bleed one is what makes the interaction feel like it is answering you; without it the whole frame changes at once and reads as a page change.
- Restarting the fade when the parent re-renders. Any inline `children` array is a new object every render, so the effect must compare `contentKey`, not identity, or a hover crossfades continuously.
- Leaving tweens running past unmount. They keep writing opacity onto detached nodes; the unmount cleanup kills both layers.

## Notes

- Layers hold whatever you give them — a gradient, a canvas, a `<video>`, an image. Nothing here is image-specific.
- Content is captured per key, so if the same key needs to show new children you must change the key. That is deliberate: it is the only way to know when a transition is warranted.
- App Router wiring: pass `contentKey={usePathname()}` and render the route content as children for a whole-page crossfade with no layout thrash.

## Definition of done

Move down a list at a normal pace and each change is a smooth blend with no dip in brightness at the midpoint. Sweep the cursor across every row as fast as you can and the layers never flicker or settle half-faded. In a paired setup, the small preview visibly finishes before the background does.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Analytic Disc Picking

A slow ring of camera-facing discs that answers "what is under the pointer" without a raycaster. Because every disc is parallel to the image plane, the pick reduces to intersecting the pointer ray with one plane per disc and comparing the hit against the radius — four arithmetic operations, no traversal, no allocation, and exact rather than approximate. It is also the only correct answer here: the billboard happens in the vertex shader, so `Raycaster` intersects a square that is not on screen.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Hit-test camera-facing discs by intersecting the pointer ray with their plane. Exact, allocation-free, and correct for shader billboards.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1

## How it works

1. The vertex shader billboards in view space: `vec4 mv = modelViewMatrix * vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0); mv.xy += position.xy * uScale;` takes only the translation out of the model-view matrix and adds the quad offset afterwards. The mesh's rotation and scale never reach a vertex, so the disc is always exactly parallel to the image plane and its view-space radius is exactly `uRadius * uScale`.
2. Because the disc is parallel to the image plane, its plane normal is the camera's view direction for every disc in the scene. `camera.getWorldDirection(viewDir)` is called once per frame and `plane.setFromNormalAndCoplanarPoint(viewDir, disc.position)` then differs only in its constant.
3. `raycaster.setFromCamera(ndc, camera)` builds the pointer ray and nothing else is used from the Raycaster — `intersectObjects` is never called. Constructing the ray is the cheap half of raycasting; the traversal, the per-object matrix inverse, and the per-triangle intersection are the half being skipped.
4. `ray.intersectPlane(plane, hit)` returns `Vector3 | null`, and the null case is a free depth rejection: `Ray.distanceToPlane` returns null for `t < 0`, so anything behind the camera drops out before any distance work.
5. The winner is the nearest hit along the ray whose distance from the disc centre is within the radius, both compared squared. Depth is tested FIRST — `if (along >= bestAlong) continue;` — so a disc that cannot beat the incumbent never runs its own radius test.
6. The pick radius is `uRadius * uScale`, the same two numbers the vertex shader multiplies. Hover eases `uScale` from 1 to 1.14, and the pick reads the eased value in the same frame, so a disc is never clickable over area it has not grown into and never stops being clickable over area it still occupies.
7. Every scratch object — ray, plane, hit vector, view direction, NDC vector — is allocated once into the stage object and reused. A pick loop that allocates a `Vector3` per disc per frame produces 780 garbage vectors a second at 60 Hz on a ring of thirteen.
8. Rendering is gated on a dirty flag. The flag is set by the spin, by pointer movement, by a hover easing that is still in flight, and by resize. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the spin never sets it, so the renderer idles at zero draw calls until the pointer moves.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `FOV = 42`
  Camera vertical field of view in degrees. Wide enough that the near discs are visibly larger than the far ones — which is what makes an analytic test worth having — and narrow enough that the ring does not distort into an oval at preview aspect ratios.
- `CAM_Z / ringRadius = 5.6 / 2.15`
  A ratio of about 2.6. Closer and the front disc overruns the frame at preview width; further and the perspective flattens until a cheap screen-space approximation would have been good enough, which defeats the demonstration.
- `discRadius = 0.46`
  World units, and simultaneously the pick radius. A single source for both is the entire point: two constants that mean "how big is this disc" is how a hit region drifts away from the pixels it is supposed to cover.
- `WAVE = 0.34`
  Vertical amplitude of the sin(2a) offset. Enough that the ring reads as a ribbon rather than a flat carousel; past ~0.6 the discs at the crossings overlap and the nearest-along-the-ray tie-break starts doing visible work the user has no way to predict.
- `HOVER_SMOOTHING = 0.0006`
  Fraction of the hover gap remaining after one second, as `damp` defines it — about 12% of the gap per frame at 60 Hz, settling in roughly 0.2 s. A per-frame constant instead would converge twice as fast on a 120 Hz display and the growth would feel like a different component.
- `HOVER_GROWTH = 0.14`
  A hovered disc grows 14%. Large enough to read at the back of the ring where a disc is a third of its front size, small enough that the grown disc does not swallow its neighbours and make the pick ambiguous.
- `FEATHER = 0.035`
  Rim gradient width in units of the radius — roughly 1.5 px at preview scale. This is why the renderer is built with `antialias: false`: MSAA would pay for an entire extra sample buffer to solve a problem one smoothstep already solved.

## API

```ts
function AnalyticDiscPicking(props: { count?: number; period?: number; discRadius?: number; ringRadius?: number; color?: string; accent?: string; seed?: number | string; compare?: boolean; onPick?: (index: number) => void; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `count: number` — default `13`
  Discs around the ring.
- `period: number` — default `30`
  Seconds for one revolution.
- `discRadius: number` — default `0.46`
  Disc radius in world units. Also the pick radius — the two cannot drift apart.
- `ringRadius: number` — default `2.15`
  Ring radius in world units.
- `color: string` — default `'#7d848e'`
  Base plate colour. Any value `THREE.Color` accepts.
- `accent: string` — default `'#e8e4dc'`
  Colour of the picked disc.
- `seed: number | string` — default `'analytic-disc-picking'`
  Seeds the per-disc plate pattern. Same seed, same ring every reload.
- `compare: boolean` — default `false`
  Also run a real `Raycaster` each frame and report what it thinks was hit.
- `onPick: (index: number) => void`
  Fired when a disc is clicked, with its index.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
useRaf((dt) => {
  const s = stage.current;
  if (!s) return;

  // The ring phase is integrated from dt, not read from a wall clock, so
  // freezing it for reduced motion is a matter of not adding anything.
  if (!reduced) {
    spin.current = (spin.current + (TAU / period) * dt) % TAU;
    dirty.current = true;
  }

  // -- place the discs -----------------------------------------------------
  for (const disc of s.discs) {
    const a = disc.phase + spin.current;
    disc.mesh.position.set(
      Math.sin(a) * ringRadius,
      Math.sin(a * 2) * WAVE,
      Math.cos(a) * ringRadius,
    );
    // `cos(a)` is +1 at the front of the ring and -1 at the back. Remapped
    // to 0..1 it is the depth fade, and it costs nothing extra here.
    disc.uniforms.uDepth.value = Math.cos(a) * 0.5 + 0.5;
  }
  // No `updateMatrixWorld` here on purpose. The discs are direct children of
  // the scene at identity, so `mesh.position` IS the world position, and the
  // camera's matrix was made current in `resize`. The only consumer of the
  // full matrix graph is `render`, which updates it itself.

  // -- the analytic pick ---------------------------------------------------
  let best = -1;
  const p = pointer.current;
  if (p) {
    s.ndc.set(p.x, p.y);
    // The Raycaster is used for its RAY and nothing else. Building an
    // NDC-to-world ray by hand means duplicating `unproject`; the expensive
    // half of raycasting is `intersectObjects`, which is never called.
    s.raycaster.setFromCamera(s.ndc, s.camera);
    const ray = s.raycaster.ray;
    // Every disc is parallel to the image plane, so they all share one
    // normal — the camera's view direction, already unit length. Only the
    // plane's constant differs from disc to disc.
    s.camera.getWorldDirection(s.viewDir);

    let bestAlong = Infinity;
    for (let i = 0; i < s.discs.length; i += 1) {
      const disc = s.discs[i];
      if (!disc) continue;

      s.plane.setFromNormalAndCoplanarPoint(s.viewDir, disc.mesh.position);
      // `intersectPlane` returns null when the plane is behind the ray
      // origin, which rejects anything behind the camera for free. Note that
      // `Ray.distanceToPlane` returns null too but is TYPED `number` in
      // @types/three — the honest signature is on this method.
      if (ray.intersectPlane(s.plane, s.hit) === null) continue;

      // Nearest along the ray wins. Checked first so a disc that cannot
      // beat the incumbent skips its own radius test.
      const along = s.hit.distanceToSquared(ray.origin);
      if (along >= bestAlong) continue;

      // The drawn radius, hover growth included. `uScale` was eased last
      // frame and is applied by the vertex shader this frame, so the region
      // tested is the region rasterised.
      const r = disc.uniforms.uRadius.value * disc.uniforms.uScale.value;
      if (s.hit.distanceToSquared(disc.mesh.position) > r * r) continue;

      bestAlong = along;
      best = i;
    }
  }

  // -- ease the hover, which the next frame's pick will read ---------------
  for (let i = 0; i < s.discs.length; i += 1) {
    const disc = s.discs[i];
    if (!disc) continue;
    const target = i === best ? 1 : 0;
    const next = damp(disc.hover, target, HOVER_SMOOTHING, dt);
    if (Math.abs(next - disc.hover) > 0.0005) dirty.current = true;
    disc.hover = next;
    disc.uniforms.uHover.value = next;
    disc.uniforms.uScale.value = 1 + HOVER_GROWTH * next;
    disc.uniforms.uPicked.value = i === pickedRef.current ? 1 : 0;
  }

  if (best !== hovered.current) {
    hovered.current = best;
    setHover(best);
    dirty.current = true;
  }

  // -- what a real raycaster would have said -------------------------------
  if (compare) {
    let g = -1;
    if (p) {
      // The raycaster reads `matrixWorld`, which `render` would not refresh
      // until the end of this frame. The analytic path needed no such call —
      // it reads `position` directly — so this traversal is a cost the
      // comparison introduces, not one it inherits.
      s.scene.updateMatrixWorld();
      // Reused array, cleared by hand: `intersectObjects` pushes into the
      // target and sorts it, but never empties it.
      s.intersects.length = 0;
      s.raycaster.intersectObjects(s.meshes, false, s.intersects);
      const first = s.intersects[0];
      if (first) g = s.meshes.indexOf(first.object as THREE.Mesh);
    }
    if (g !== ghost) setGhost(g);
  }

  if (dirty.current) {
    dirty.current = false;
    s.renderer.render(s.scene, s.camera);
  }
}, ready && !unsupported);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The effect removes every disc from the scene and disposes its `ShaderMaterial`, disposes the one shared `PlaneGeometry`, then calls `disposeRenderer` — which stops the animation loop, disposes the renderer, calls `forceContextLoss()`, and zeroes the drawing buffer — and finally removes the canvas it appended. The canvas is created by the renderer inside the effect and never handed to React, so a StrictMode double-invoke rebuilds a fresh context rather than reusing a killed one. The frame loop unsubscribes with `useRaf`; the shared rAF parks once nothing is subscribed. The `ResizeObserver` unobserves with its hook.

**Reduced motion.** The ring holds still: the phase is integrated from delta time, so freezing it is a matter of adding nothing. The dirty flag is then only set by the pointer, which means the renderer draws zero frames until the pointer moves. Picking, hover growth and selection are unaffected — the technique is about where things are, not about them moving.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Reaching for `THREE.Raycaster` against a shader billboard. The vertex shader runs on the GPU; the `BufferGeometry` in main memory is an unrotated square lying in world XY. The raycast intersects that square and reports hits on a shape nobody can see — turn on `compare` and the two readouts disagree the moment the camera is not staring down the world Z axis.
- Using `Ray.distanceToPlane` and testing its result for null. It does return null at runtime for a plane behind the ray origin, but `@types/three` declares it as `number`, so the null check is a type error and removing the null check is a crash. `intersectPlane` has the honest `Vector3 | null` signature; use it.
- Approximating the disc as a screen-space circle whose NDC radius is `halfDiagonal / (tanHalfFov * camDist)`. That is only correct for a sphere. For a flat disc it over-reports near the edges of frame, where perspective stretches the footprint, so the hover boundary is visibly not the disc boundary. The plane intersection is exact for the same cost.
- Deriving the pick radius from a second constant. Hover growth then applies to the pixels but not the hit region, and the disc becomes clickable on a ring of its own body it has already grown past.
- Leaving `frustumCulled` on. The culler tests the geometry bounding sphere at the mesh transform, but the vertices are moved by the shader, so a disc vanishes the instant the untransformed square leaves the frustum.
- Allocating in the pick loop. `new THREE.Vector3()` per disc per frame is invisible in a profile and unmistakable in a GC trace; reuse a scratch object on the stage.
- Enabling depth test on the discs. They are square quads with the corners discarded, so the depth buffer records the quad, not the disc, and neighbouring rims punch holes in each other. Painter's-algorithm sorting is correct here because the billboard leaves the object position — the key three sorts on — untouched.
- Handing three's renderer a React-rendered `<canvas ref>`. StrictMode double-invokes the effect, the first cleanup calls `forceContextLoss()`, and the second run is given the same permanently dead element. Let the renderer make its own canvas inside the effect and remove it in cleanup.

## Notes

- The same reduction works for any primitive with a closed-form ray test: a sphere is `ray.intersectSphere`, an axis-aligned card is `ray.intersectBox`, a ground plane is one `intersectPlane`. Raycasting against triangles is the fallback for arbitrary meshes, not the default for known shapes.
- A square quad plus `discard` beats a `CircleGeometry` fan on both counts — two triangles instead of thirty-two, and a rim anti-aliased by a smoothstep instead of a polygon approximated by segments.
- The `compare` prop exists to be switched on once. Leave it on in production and you pay for the traversal you set out to avoid, plus an `intersectObjects` call whose result you throw away.

## Definition of done

Hover a disc at the front of the ring and it brightens and grows, and the readout says `plane hit NN`. Follow one disc as it travels to the back: it stays pickable over exactly its drawn silhouette, smaller but never offset. Set `compare` and hover a disc anywhere off the centre of frame — the `raycast` readout says something different, usually nothing, because it is testing an unrotated square in world XY. Click and the disc under the pointer takes the accent colour. With reduced motion the ring is static and every one of those behaviours still works.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Anti-Aliased Point Discs

A point sprite is a square; this is the pair of shader tricks that makes it a dot. The fragment shader carves a disc with one smoothstep across the outer few percent of the sprite and discards everything below a visibility threshold, and the vertex shader clamps the point size to the hardware floor and then divides the alpha by the area that clamp invented. The field is laid out as a phyllotaxis spiral with a size ramp so both ends of the problem — sub-pixel dots and twenty-pixel dots — are on screen at once.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A phyllotaxis field of dots that stay the same weight at every pixel ratio, with no MSAA and no texture.

- Category: webgl
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1

## How it works

1. Dots are placed by golden-angle phyllotaxis: `t = sqrt((i + 0.5) / count)` for the normalised radius and `i * 137.507°` for the angle, so spacing is even rather than crowded at the centre. A seeded jitter of ±0.06 rad is added to break the moiré a pure spiral shows at small radii.
2. The vertex shader rotates differentially — `angle + uElapsed * uSpin * (0.6 + t)` — so the rim turns 1.6x faster than the core and the arms shear instead of the field spinning rigidly.
3. Point size ramps as `mix(uMinRadius, uMaxRadius, t * t)`, quadratic so most of the field stays small and the large discs are confined to the rim where the anti-aliasing is easiest to inspect.
4. The size is then clamped: `clamped = max(2.0, radius * 2.0 * uPixelRatio)` against `unclamped = max(1.0, …)`, and `vAlphaScale = unclamped² / clamped²` is passed to the fragment shader. A dot the driver forced to be twice as wide comes out four times fainter, so total emitted light is unchanged.
5. The fragment shader computes `d = length(gl_PointCoord - 0.5)` and `disc = 1.0 - smoothstep(uEdgeInner, 0.5, d)` where `uEdgeInner = 0.5 - softness`, so the falloff always ends exactly at the sprite edge and the disc stays inscribed in its square.
6. Anything whose final alpha lands below 0.003 is discarded rather than blended, which removes a framebuffer read-modify-write per pixel across the sparse outer field.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `GOLDEN_ANGLE = Math.PI * (3 - Math.sqrt(5)) ≈ 2.39996 rad`
  The only angle whose successive multiples never repeat a rational fraction of a turn. Any nearby value produces visible spokes within a few hundred points.
- `softness = 0.07`
  Anti-aliased band as a fraction of the sprite radius, giving `smoothstep(0.43, 0.5, d)`. Below ~0.05 a 2px dot aliases back into a square; above ~0.15 every dot reads as blurred rather than small.
- `MIN_POINT_SIZE = 2.0`
  Hardware floor in device pixels. Below roughly 1px most GPUs rasterise nothing, so the smallest dots would be absent on some machines and present on others.
- `ALPHA_EPSILON = 0.003`
  Discard threshold, just under 1/255. Anything fainter cannot be shown by an 8-bit framebuffer, so blending it is pure fill cost.
- `radius ramp exponent = t * t`
  Quadratic rather than linear. Linear puts mid-size discs everywhere and the field turns into a solid disc; quadratic keeps the interesting large sprites at the rim.
- `count = 4000`
  One buffer, one draw call, and about 4000 sprites of up to 20px — roughly the point where fill rate rather than vertex count starts to dominate on integrated graphics.
- `differential spin factor = (0.6 + 1.0 * t)`
  Rim-to-core angular speed ratio of 1.6. At 1.0 the field spins rigidly and reads as a rotating image; past ~2.5 the arms wind into a solid ring within a minute.

## API

```ts
function AntialiasedDiscFragment(props: { count?: number; minRadius?: number; maxRadius?: number; fieldRadius?: number; spin?: number; softness?: number; opacity?: number; colorInner?: string; colorOuter?: string; seed?: number | string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `count: number` — default `4000`
  Number of discs. One draw call regardless.
- `minRadius: number` — default `0.5`
  Disc radius in CSS pixels at the centre — deliberately sub-pixel at DPR 1.
- `maxRadius: number` — default `10`
  Disc radius in CSS pixels at the rim.
- `fieldRadius: number` — default `0.92`
  Field diameter as a fraction of the container short side.
- `spin: number` — default `0.08`
  Base angular speed in radians per second; the rim runs 1.6x faster.
- `softness: number` — default `0.07`
  Anti-aliased band width as a fraction of the sprite radius.
- `opacity: number` — default `1`
  Multiplier applied before the area compensation.
- `colorInner: string` — default `'#ffffff'`
  Tint at the centre of the field.
- `colorOuter: string` — default `'#6f7680'`
  Tint at the rim.
- `seed: number | string` — default `'antialiased-disc-fragment'`
  Seeds the angular jitter so the layout is stable across reloads and matches on the server.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function AntialiasedDiscFragment({
  count = 4000,
  minRadius = 0.5,
  maxRadius = 10,
  fieldRadius = 0.92,
  spin = 0.08,
  softness = 0.07,
  opacity = 1,
  colorInner = '#ffffff',
  colorOuter = '#6f7680',
  seed = 'antialiased-disc-fragment',
  className,
}: AntialiasedDiscFragmentProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const stage = useRef<Stage | null>(null);
  const [unsupported, setUnsupported] = useState(false);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const size = useRef({ width, height });
  size.current = { width, height };

  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const ready = width > 0 && height > 0;

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = host.current;
    if (!el || !ready) return;

    if (!hasWebGL()) {
      setUnsupported(true);
      return;
    }

    const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: false, alpha: true });
    renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio());
    renderer.setClearAlpha(0);

    const scene = new THREE.Scene();
    const camera = new THREE.OrthographicCamera(-1, 1, 1, -1, 0.1, 10);
    camera.position.z = 1;

    const rng = createRng(seed);
    const positions = new Float32Array(count * 3); // all zeros; the shader places them
    const disc = new Float32Array(count * 2);

    for (let i = 0; i < count; i += 1) {
      // sqrt spacing, not linear: linear spacing crowds the centre, which is
      // exactly where the sub-pixel dots are and where crowding is least
      // forgiving.
      const t = Math.sqrt((i + 0.5) / count);
      // A little seeded angular jitter breaks the moiré that a pure golden
      // spiral shows at small radii on a low-DPR screen.
      disc[i * 2] = t;
      disc[i * 2 + 1] = i * GOLDEN_ANGLE + (rng() - 0.5) * 0.12;
    }

    const geometry = new THREE.BufferGeometry();
    geometry.setAttribute('position', new THREE.BufferAttribute(positions, 3));
    geometry.setAttribute('aDisc', new THREE.BufferAttribute(disc, 2));

    const uniforms: Uniforms = {
      uElapsed: { value: 0 },
      uExtent: { value: 1 },
      uPixelRatio: { value: renderer.getPixelRatio() },
      uSpin: { value: spin },
      uFieldRadius: { value: fieldRadius },
      uMinRadius: { value: minRadius },
      uMaxRadius: { value: maxRadius },
      uOpacity: { value: opacity },
      uColorInner: { value: new THREE.Color(colorInner) },
      uColorOuter: { value: new THREE.Color(colorOuter) },
      // The band always ENDS at 0.5 — the sprite's own edge. Softening inward
      // keeps the disc inscribed in the sprite; softening outward would clip
      // the falloff square at the corners.
      uEdgeInner: { value: 0.5 - softness },
    };

    const material = new THREE.ShaderMaterial({
      vertexShader: ANTIALIASED_DISC_VERT,
      fragmentShader: ANTIALIASED_DISC_FRAG,
      uniforms,
      transparent: true,
      depthTest: false,
      depthWrite: false,
      // Additive would blow the overlapping core to white. Normal blending
      // with a discard keeps the density readable where the dots overlap.
      blending: THREE.NormalBlending,
    });

    const points = new THREE.Points(geometry, material);
    points.frustumCulled = false;
    scene.add(points);

    el.appendChild(renderer.domElement);
    renderer.domElement.style.display = 'block';
    renderer.domElement.style.width = '100%';
    renderer.domElement.style.height = '100%';

    const resize = (w: number, h: number) => {
      renderer.setSize(w, h, false);
      camera.left = -w / 2;
      camera.right = w / 2;
      camera.top = h / 2;
      camera.bottom = -h / 2;
      camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
      uniforms.uExtent.value = Math.min(w, h);
      // Re-read rather than assume: moving a window between a retina and a
      // non-retina display changes devicePixelRatio without changing the
      // canvas size, and a stale value breaks the whole compensation.
      uniforms.uPixelRatio.value = renderer.getPixelRatio();
    };

    const draw = (elapsed: number) => {
      uniforms.uElapsed.value = elapsed;
      renderer.render(scene, camera);
    };

    resize(size.current.width, size.current.height);
    stage.current = { resize, draw };
    draw(STATIC_ELAPSED);

    return () => {
      stage.current = null;
      disposeObject(scene);
      material.dispose();
      disposeRenderer(renderer);
      renderer.domElement.remove();
    };
  }, [
    ready,
    count,
    minRadius,
    maxRadius,
    fieldRadius,
    spin,
    softness,
    opacity,
    colorInner,
    colorOuter,
    seed,
  ]);

  useEffect(() => {
    stage.current?.resize(width, height);
    if (reduced) stage.current?.draw(STATIC_ELAPSED);
  }, [width, height, reduced]);

  useRaf((_dt, elapsed) => stage.current?.draw(elapsed), ready && !reduced && !unsupported);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nulls the stage ref, disposes the geometry and material via `disposeObject` plus an explicit `material.dispose()`, calls `disposeRenderer` for `dispose` + `forceContextLoss` + a zeroed drawing buffer, then removes the canvas. `useRaf` releases the frame subscription itself.

**Reduced motion.** No rAF subscription is opened. A single frame is drawn at `uElapsed = 6`, which is far enough into the rotation that the arms are already sheared, so the composition is the interesting one rather than the unrotated starting pose. The field is fully visible; only the spin stops.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Softening the disc outward from 0.5 instead of inward to it. The sprite has no pixels past 0.5, so the outer half of the falloff is clipped by the sprite boundary and the dot shows four square corners.
- Clamping `gl_PointSize` and leaving the alpha alone. The clamp does nothing at DPR 3 and doubles the covered area at DPR 1, so the identical component looks twice as heavy on a non-retina monitor — a bug that is invisible on the machine most people develop on.
- Caching the pixel ratio at construction. Dragging the window from a retina to a non-retina display changes `devicePixelRatio` without changing the canvas size, so the compensation silently goes stale; it is re-read on every resize.
- Reaching for `antialias: true` when the dots look jagged. MSAA allocates a multisample buffer the size of the canvas and does not help a point sprite whose edge is defined by alpha — the smoothstep is the fix.
- Blending fully transparent fragments instead of discarding them. At 4000 sprites with a 20px radius the outer field is mostly empty pixels, and each one still costs a read-modify-write of the framebuffer.
- Linear radial spacing instead of `sqrt`. It crowds the centre, which is precisely where the sub-pixel dots live, and the core turns into an undifferentiated smear.

## Notes

- The camera is orthographic and 1:1 with CSS pixels, so `uMinRadius` and `uMaxRadius` are literal pixel radii rather than scene units.
- The same two tricks apply to any `THREE.Points` material. The spiral is only a way to show the whole size range at once.

## Definition of done

A spiral of dots that grows from barely-visible at the centre to clearly round discs at the rim, with soft edges and no square corners at any size. Zoom the browser between 100% and 200% and the field keeps the same apparent weight instead of getting denser or lighter. Nothing shimmers along the arms as they turn. With reduced motion the spiral renders in full and holds still.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Asymmetric In/Out Staggers

A list whose entrance and exit are deliberately different animations. In: 24px up, 0.5s each, 0.06s apart, after a 0.25s hold that lets the outgoing view clear. Out: 16px up, 0.3s each, 0.03s apart, running from the last item back to the first. The exit is roughly half the total time of the entrance, which is what makes a view swap feel responsive without making the arrival feel rushed.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A list that arrives item by item after a hold and leaves twice as fast, from the last row backwards.

- Category: transition
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. Every direct child is wrapped in a `[data-stagger-item]` div, so the caller writes ordinary list markup and the component owns the animated node — no cloneElement, no required ref forwarding.
2. Entering runs `gsap.fromTo(items, { autoAlpha: 0, y: 24 }, { autoAlpha: 1, y: 0, duration: 0.5, ease: "power2.out", stagger: 0.06, delay: 0.25 })`. The delay is not decoration: it is the window in which whatever this list replaces finishes leaving.
3. Leaving runs `gsap.to(items, { autoAlpha: 0, y: -16, duration: 0.3, ease: "power2.in", stagger: { each: 0.03, from: "end" } })`. Halving the stagger and reversing its origin is what stops the exit from reading as the entrance rewound.
4. `autoAlpha` rather than `opacity`: at zero it also writes `visibility: hidden`, so a faded row cannot swallow a click aimed at the view underneath it.
5. Both tweens carry `overwrite: "auto"`, and the whole thing lives in a `useGsap` context keyed on `show`, so toggling twice in quick succession cancels the in-flight direction instead of layering two opposing tweens on the same nodes.
6. A layout effect hides the items before first paint when the component mounts closed, and an internal `hasShown` flag makes sure `onExited` can only fire after a real entrance.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `inStagger = 0.06`
  Seconds between arriving items. Below ~0.04 a five-item list reads as one block; above ~0.1 the last row lands well after the eye has moved on and the list feels slow to load.
- `outStagger = 0.03`
  Half the entrance value. Exits are acknowledgement, not presentation — the wave still reads as a direction, but the whole list is gone in under 200ms.
- `inDelay = 0.25`
  Seconds of hold before the first item arrives. Sized to the outgoing view's own fade (~0.3-0.4s) so the two never overlap; at 0 both views are half-opaque at the same time and the frame looks like a rendering bug.
- `inDuration / outDuration = 0.5 / 0.3`
  Per-item. The exit is shorter for the same reason its stagger is: nobody is reading rows that are leaving.
- `inDistance / outDistance = 24 / 16`
  Pixels. The entrance comes up from below (from where the content is arriving); the exit continues upward and travels less, because a long exit path is time spent watching nothing.
- `stagger.from = 'end'`
  Reverses the exit wave. Same-direction staggers make the exit look like a backwards entrance; from the end it looks like the list is being pulled off the screen.

## API

```ts
function AsymmetricStagger(props: { children: ReactNode; show: boolean; inStagger?: number; outStagger?: number; inDelay?: number; inDuration?: number; outDuration?: number; inDistance?: number; outDistance?: number; onExited?: () => void; className?: string; itemClassName?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  List items. Each direct child is wrapped and animated on its own.
- `show: boolean`
  True enters, false exits. The component stays mounted through both.
- `inStagger: number` — default `0.06`
  Seconds between entering items.
- `outStagger: number` — default `0.03`
  Seconds between leaving items.
- `inDelay: number` — default `0.25`
  Hold before the entrance, sized to the outgoing view.
- `inDuration: number` — default `0.5`
  Per-item entrance length in seconds.
- `outDuration: number` — default `0.3`
  Per-item exit length in seconds.
- `inDistance: number` — default `24`
  Pixels travelled on the way in.
- `outDistance: number` — default `16`
  Pixels travelled on the way out.
- `onExited: () => void`
  Called once the last item has left. Safe place to unmount the data.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the flex column wrapper.
- `itemClassName: string`
  Merged onto every generated item wrapper.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function AsymmetricStagger({
  children,
  show,
  inStagger = 0.06,
  outStagger = 0.03,
  inDelay = 0.25,
  inDuration = 0.5,
  outDuration = 0.3,
  inDistance = 24,
  outDistance = 16,
  onExited,
  className,
  itemClassName,
}: AsymmetricStaggerProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  const exited = useRef(onExited);
  exited.current = onExited;

  const startedHidden = useRef(!show);
  /* An exit only makes sense after an entrance. Without this, mounting with
     `show={false}` plays an invisible exit and fires `onExited` — and under
     StrictMode the double-invoked effect fires it a second time. */
  const hasShown = useRef(show);

  // Before paint, not after. A passive effect can land on the far side of the
  // first frame, so a list that starts closed would flash its items once.
  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    const el = root.current;
    if (!el || !startedHidden.current) return;
    gsap.set(el.querySelectorAll('[data-stagger-item]'), { autoAlpha: 0 });
  }, []);

  useGsap(
    gsap,
    () => {
      const el = root.current;
      if (!el) return;
      const items = Array.from(el.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-stagger-item]'));
      if (items.length === 0) return;

      if (!show && !hasShown.current) return;

      if (reduced) {
        // No travel and no stagger, but the state change still has to happen
        // or the list is stuck in whichever position it was left in.
        gsap.set(items, { autoAlpha: show ? 1 : 0, y: 0 });
        if (show) hasShown.current = true;
        else exited.current?.();
        return;
      }

      if (show) {
        hasShown.current = true;
        // autoAlpha, not opacity: at 0 it also sets visibility:hidden, so a
        // faded-out row cannot still swallow a click meant for what is
        // underneath it.
        gsap.fromTo(
          items,
          { autoAlpha: 0, y: inDistance },
          {
            autoAlpha: 1,
            y: 0,
            duration: inDuration,
            ease: 'power2.out',
            stagger: inStagger,
            delay: inDelay,
            overwrite: 'auto',
          },
        );
        return;
      }

      gsap.to(items, {
        autoAlpha: 0,
        y: -outDistance,
        duration: outDuration,
        ease: 'power2.in',
        // `from: 'end'` reverses the wave. Same-direction staggers on the way
        // out read as the list re-entering backwards.
        stagger: { each: outStagger, from: 'end' },
        overwrite: 'auto',
        onComplete: () => exited.current?.(),
      });
    },
    root,
    [show, reduced],
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useGsap` reverts the context on unmount and on every `show` change, killing both tweens and restoring the inline styles GSAP wrote. `onExited` is held in a ref so a completion callback cannot reach a stale closure after the parent has re-rendered.

**Reduced motion.** No travel and no stagger. Items are set to their visible or hidden state in one `gsap.set`, and `onExited` still fires, so the surrounding state machine behaves identically — only the choreography is dropped.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Reusing the entrance timeline with `reverse()`. That gives you power2.out played backwards (so it decelerates into nothing), the entrance delay stranded at the end, and the same stagger direction — three separate reasons the exit feels heavy.
- Unmounting the list when `show` flips false. React removes the nodes on the same frame, so the exit never runs; the component stays mounted and reports completion through `onExited`.
- Animating `opacity` alone. A finished row sits at opacity 0 with full hit area and eats clicks intended for the view underneath. `autoAlpha` writes `visibility: hidden` at zero.
- Omitting `overwrite: "auto"`. Toggling twice inside 300ms leaves the entrance tween running under the exit tween, and the rows settle at whatever opacity the two happen to agree on.
- Setting the initial hidden state in a passive effect. Mounting with `show={false}` paints the list once, then hides it — a visible flash of content that was never meant to be seen. It is set in `useLayoutEffect` instead.
- Firing `onExited` on mount. With `show={false}` at mount there is nothing to exit, and under StrictMode the double-invoked effect would call it twice; a `hasShown` flag gates it.

## Notes

- The same numbers apply outside lists — modals, drawers, route content. Any pair of entrance/exit values that are equal is worth questioning.
- App Router wiring: drive `show` from a pathname comparison in a layout, and do the actual `router.push` from `onExited` if you want the route to change only once the list has gone.

## Definition of done

Switch to the list: the previous view fades, a quarter-second of nothing, then rows arrive top to bottom. Switch back: the bottom row leaves first and the whole list is gone in about half the time it took to arrive. Toggle rapidly and rows never settle at a partial opacity.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Asymmetric Typewriter

A phrase erases itself and a new one is typed in its place, cycling forever. Deleting runs at exactly half the interval of typing, because backspacing is a held key with a mechanical auto-repeat while typing is composition — give both phases the same interval and the result reads as a ticker tape rather than as somebody at a keyboard. A quarter-second pause at the empty string turns the turnaround from a dropped frame into a decision.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Rotating phrases that delete at twice the speed they type, with a beat of nothing at the empty string.

- Category: text
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. Timing is a chain of `setTimeout` calls, not a `setInterval`: the four phases (type, hold, delete, empty) each have their own interval, and the boundaries between them are pauses that a fixed interval cannot express without a counter and a modulo.
2. The state machine is four closures over a `text` local — `type` slices one more character off the target and reschedules at `typeMs`; on reaching full length it schedules `beginErase` at `holdMs`. `erase` slices one character off and reschedules at `deleteMs`; at length zero it schedules `advance` at `emptyMs`. `advance` moves the phrase index modulo the list length and re-enters `type`.
3. Typing slices the *target* string (`target.slice(0, text.length + 1)`) rather than concatenating a looked-up character. Under `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` an index read is `string | undefined`, and slicing also means the visible text can never desync from the source phrase.
4. A single `timer` ref holds the one outstanding timeout id, so cleanup is a single `clearTimeout` regardless of which phase was in flight.
5. The effect is keyed on `phrases.join("\u0000")` rather than on the array itself. An array prop is a fresh reference every parent render, which would tear the machine down and restart it, pinning the typewriter to its first character forever. NUL is the delimiter because real phrases contain spaces and commas.
6. The caret is the `step-end-caret` component, driven with `paused={busy}`: while characters are being added or removed the caret holds solid, and it resumes blinking only during the hold and empty beats.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `TYPE_MS = 70`
  Milliseconds per character while typing. Around 14 characters a second — brisk human typing. Below ~45ms the reader cannot follow the word forming; above ~110ms the phrase takes longer to appear than anyone will wait for.
- `DELETE_MS = 35`
  Exactly half of `TYPE_MS`. This ratio is the whole component: deleting is a held key on auto-repeat, typing is composition. Equal intervals make both directions read as machine output.
- `HOLD_MS = 1500`
  How long a completed phrase stays up. It has to exceed the time to read four or five words. Under ~900ms the phrase is gone before it has been parsed and the component reads as flickering.
- `EMPTY_MS = 250`
  The beat at zero characters. Without it the string bottoms out and immediately rebounds, which the eye reads as a dropped frame rather than as a turnaround.
- `START_DELAY_MS = 1500`
  Longer than a normal hold, so the first phrase is legible while the rest of the page is still settling. Starting the erase immediately makes the component look like it is correcting a mistake.

## API

```ts
function AsymmetricTypewriter(props: { phrases: string[]; typeMs?: number; deleteMs?: number; holdMs?: number; emptyMs?: number; startDelayMs?: number; caret?: boolean; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `phrases: string[]`
  Cycled in order, forever. Index 0 is also the server-rendered string.
- `typeMs: number` — default `70`
  Milliseconds between characters while typing.
- `deleteMs: number` — default `35`
  Milliseconds between characters while deleting.
- `holdMs: number` — default `1500`
  Milliseconds a completed phrase is held.
- `emptyMs: number` — default `250`
  Milliseconds held at the empty string.
- `startDelayMs: number` — default `1500`
  Milliseconds before the very first deletion.
- `caret: boolean` — default `true`
  Render the blinking caret after the text.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the outer span via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const TYPE_MS = 70;
const DELETE_MS = 35;
const HOLD_MS = 1500;
const EMPTY_MS = 250;
const START_DELAY_MS = 1500;

export function AsymmetricTypewriter({
  phrases,
  typeMs = TYPE_MS,
  deleteMs = DELETE_MS,
  holdMs = HOLD_MS,
  emptyMs = EMPTY_MS,
  startDelayMs = START_DELAY_MS,
  caret = true,
  className,
}: AsymmetricTypewriterProps) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  // An array prop is a fresh reference on every parent render. Keying on the
  // joined string is what stops the effect tearing down and restarting each
  // time — which would pin the typewriter to its first character forever.
  // NUL is the delimiter because real phrases contain spaces and commas, and
  // a separator that occurs in the data silently splits one phrase into two.
  const key = phrases.join('\u0000');
  const list = useMemo(() => key.split('\u0000'), [key]);

  const [shown, setShown] = useState(() => list[0] ?? '');
  const [busy, setBusy] = useState(false);
  const timer = useRef(0);

  useEffect(() => {
    const first = list[0] ?? '';
    if (reduced || list.length < 2) {
      setShown(first);
      setBusy(false);
      return;
    }

    let index = 0;
    let text = first;
    setShown(text);

    const at = (fn: () => void, ms: number) => {
      timer.current = window.setTimeout(fn, ms);
    };

    const erase = () => {
      if (text.length === 0) {
        // The beat. Caret goes back to blinking because nothing is happening.
        setBusy(false);
        at(advance, emptyMs);
        return;
      }
      text = text.slice(0, -1);
      setShown(text);
      at(erase, deleteMs);
    };

    const advance = () => {
      index = (index + 1) % list.length;
      setBusy(true);
      at(type, typeMs);
    };

    const type = () => {
      const target = list[index] ?? '';
      if (text.length >= target.length) {
        setBusy(false);
        at(beginErase, holdMs);
        return;
      }
      // Slice the target rather than concatenating a looked-up character:
      // `target[i]` is `string | undefined` and the slice cannot desync from
      // the source string if the phrase list changes underneath.
      text = target.slice(0, text.length + 1);
      setShown(text);
      at(type, typeMs);
    };

    const beginErase = () => {
      setBusy(true);
      erase();
    };

    at(beginErase, startDelayMs);

    return () => {
      window.clearTimeout(timer.current);
    };
  }, [list, reduced, typeMs, deleteMs, holdMs, emptyMs, startDelayMs]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** A single `window.clearTimeout(timer.current)` in the effect teardown. Only one timeout is ever outstanding, so no phase can survive unmount and call `setState` on a dead component.

**Reduced motion.** The machine never starts. The first phrase is rendered in full and stays — the final text state, immediately, rather than an empty slot or a sped-up cycle. The caret is still rendered but its own reduced-motion rule holds it solid.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Driving the whole cycle from one `setInterval`. Hold and empty pauses then have to be faked with a frame counter, and every change to a phase length becomes an arithmetic edit rather than a constant.
- Depending on the `phrases` array identity in the effect. Every parent render gives a new array, the effect restarts, and the typewriter is stuck showing the first character of the first phrase.
- Joining phrases with a comma or a pipe as the effect key. Both occur in real copy, so one phrase silently becomes two.
- Letting the element size itself from the current string. It grows and shrinks by tens of pixels several times a second and drags every neighbouring element with it — a transparent copy of the longest phrase reserves the box instead.
- Using normal whitespace collapsing. A phrase erased back to "Product " loses its trailing space, so the caret jumps one character left and then right again on the next tick.
- Blinking the caret while characters are being typed. Real cursors hold solid during input; a caret blinking mid-word makes the text look like it is being deleted by something else.

## Notes

- No text-splitting library is involved: the component owns a single string in React state and never mutates the DOM. Adding a split dependency here would buy nothing, since there are no per-character targets to animate.
- React state at ~14 updates a second is a deliberate tradeoff. The subtree is one span, and holding the string in state is what keeps the server-rendered first phrase and the client in agreement.
- A list of fewer than two phrases renders the first one statically and never starts the machine.

## Definition of done

Watch one full cycle: the phrase erases visibly faster than the next one types — time it and the ratio is 2:1. At the empty string there is a perceptible pause before the next phrase starts. The caret holds solid while characters move and blinks while the phrase is held. Nothing to the right of the component moves at any point during the cycle. With reduced motion enabled the first phrase is present on first paint and never changes.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Auto-Advance Filmstrip

Panels are a fixed number of container-width units wide and the whole track is one `translateX`. The active panel sits centred, its neighbours are dimmed and scaled down, and the strip steps every few seconds until you touch it. All motion is a CSS transition on a value React already recomputes when the index changes — there is no tween and no animation loop.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A centred strip that steps one panel every few seconds, neighbours dimmed and shrunk, on one CSS transition.

- Category: layout
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. Every panel is `W` container-width units wide (`width: 46cqw`) and the track is translated to `(100 - W) / 2 - W * index` of the same unit. The first term centres one panel — `(100 - 46) / 2 = 27` — and the second steps exactly one panel per index. It is one expression with no measurement and no resize handler, because both terms are already relative to the container.
2. `cqw` rather than `vw`: the strip is sized against its own container, so it stays centred inside a card, a modal or a split layout instead of only when it happens to be full-bleed. The root sets `container-type: inline-size` to establish that container.
3. The transition is `transform 500ms cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)` on the track. For a component where React already re-renders on index change, a CSS transition is fewer moving parts than a tween and it interpolates on the compositor.
4. Inactive panels get `opacity: 0.35` **and** `scale(0.8)`, transitioning on the same curve and duration as the track so the three properties land together.
5. Auto-advance is `setTimeout` re-armed on every index change, not `setInterval`. Manual navigation therefore restarts the dwell rather than inheriting whatever was left of the current tick.
6. The timer is gated on four conditions — `autoPlay`, not reduced-motion, `document.visibilityState === "visible"`, and not currently hovered or focused within — so it never advances behind the user's back or in a background tab.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `panelWidth = 46`
  Panel width in `cqw`. Under 50 means two neighbours are partly visible, which is what makes it a filmstrip rather than a slideshow. At 46 the centred panel leaves 27 units of peek on each side — enough to read the neighbour as a real panel, not a sliver.
- `interval = 3000`
  Milliseconds per panel. Below ~2500 a caption cannot be read before it leaves; above ~5000 the strip looks broken rather than paced on a page where nothing else is moving.
- `duration = 500`
  Slide transition. Roughly a sixth of the dwell, which keeps the strip reading as a series of held frames with a transition between them rather than as continuous motion.
- `EASE = cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)`
  Expo-out. It covers about 80% of the distance in the first 30% of the duration, so the strip appears to arrive early and settle — the same reason it is the default curve for interface movement that should feel decided rather than mechanical.
- `inactiveOpacity / inactiveScale = 0.35 / 0.8`
  Both, together. 0.35 alone reads as a loading state; 0.8 alone reads as a layout bug. Applied together they read as depth, which is the only interpretation a viewer will land on.

## API

```ts
function AutoAdvanceFilmstrip(props: { children: ReactNode; panelWidth?: number; interval?: number; duration?: number; autoPlay?: boolean; inactiveOpacity?: number; inactiveScale?: number; className?: string; panelClassName?: string; 'aria-label'?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  One panel per child.
- `panelWidth: number` — default `46`
  Panel width in container-width units (`cqw`).
- `interval: number` — default `3000`
  Milliseconds a panel is held before the strip advances.
- `duration: number` — default `500`
  Slide transition duration in milliseconds.
- `autoPlay: boolean` — default `true`
  Whether the strip advances on its own.
- `inactiveOpacity: number` — default `0.35`
  Opacity applied to every panel that is not active.
- `inactiveScale: number` — default `0.8`
  Scale applied to every panel that is not active.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root, which is also the query container.
- `panelClassName: string`
  Merged onto each panel cell.
- `aria-label: string` — default `'Filmstrip'`
  Label for the carousel group.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
// (100 - W) / 2 centres a panel of width W; W * index steps one panel per
// index. Both terms are in the same unit as the panel width, so the strip
// stays centred at every container size with no measurement at all.
const offset = (100 - panelWidth) / 2 - panelWidth * index;

const running = autoPlay && !reduced && visible && !held && count > 1;

useEffect(() => {
  if (!running) return;
  // setTimeout keyed on `index`, not setInterval: any manual navigation
  // re-arms a full dwell. With an interval, tapping "next" one tick before
  // it fires advances twice in a row.
  const id = window.setTimeout(() => {
    setIndex((current) => wrapIndex(current + 1, count));
  }, interval);
  return () => window.clearTimeout(id);
}, [running, index, interval, count]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The pending `setTimeout` is cleared by the effect's own teardown, which also runs on every index change and whenever the strip pauses. `useVisibility` and `useReducedMotion` unsubscribe their listeners. There is nothing else to release: all motion is CSS on nodes React owns.

**Reduced motion.** Auto-advance never starts, so nothing moves unless the user presses a control. When they do, `transition` is set to `none` on both the track and the panels, so the strip cuts to the new panel in one frame instead of sliding. The dot pager and arrows behave identically; only the interpolation is gone.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Using a percentage in the track's `translateX`. Percentages on `transform` resolve against the *element's own* width, and the track is as wide as all its panels — so `translateX(-46%)` moves it by 46% of the whole strip, not of one panel. The arithmetic only works in a unit that refers to the container: `cqw` here, `vw` if the strip is genuinely full-bleed.
- Using `setInterval` for the auto-advance. Tap "next" a hundred milliseconds before the tick fires and the strip advances twice; the second jump has no cause the user can see. A `setTimeout` keyed on the index gives every panel a full dwell.
- Leaving the timer running while the tab is hidden. The user comes back to a strip that has silently walked eleven panels forward, and every intervening transition ran on a throttled timer.
- Not pausing on hover or focus. A pointer resting on a panel and a keyboard user tabbing into a control both mean "I am reading this"; advancing underneath either one is the single most common complaint about auto-advancing carousels.
- Only setting `containerType` on an ancestor that has no definite inline size. `cqw` then resolves against the viewport-sized fallback and the arithmetic silently reverts to the `vw` behaviour it was meant to replace.
- Fading inactive panels to `opacity: 0`. They are still in the layout and still hit-testable, so a click intended for the active panel can land on an invisible neighbour that happens to be under the cursor.

## Notes

- Cheapest of the three carousels here and the right default when the set is short and each panel needs a moment on screen. Unlike `wrapping-drum-carousel` it does not wrap continuously — it jumps from the last index back to the first, and that jump is a full-width slide, which is visible. Keep the set small enough that the loop point is rare.
- Every panel stays mounted and in the layout at all times. For twenty panels that is twenty subtrees painting; virtualise or switch technique past roughly a dozen.

## Definition of done

The strip steps one panel roughly every three seconds with the neighbours visible, dimmed and smaller on both sides. Hovering anywhere over it stops the advance and moving away resumes it with a full dwell. Switch tabs for ten seconds and come back: it is on the panel it was on, not ten further along. Resize the container from 320 px to full width and the active panel stays exactly centred.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
