# Build: Banded Scrollspy Rail

A section rail that never flickers, because only one section can be "active" at a time by construction. The IntersectionObserver root is shrunk to a 7%-tall band across the middle of the scroller, so a section registers only while it crosses that line. The active tick grows from 16 to 32 pixels — a size change, legible in peripheral vision, rather than a tint change that is not. No animation library: one observer, one CSS width transition.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A tick rail whose active mark widens as a section crosses a 7% band through the middle of the screen.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. One IntersectionObserver watches every `[data-scrollspy]` element with `rootMargin: "-38% 0px -55% 0px"`. Trimming 38% off the top and 55% off the bottom leaves a 7%-tall detection band (100 − 38 − 55), positioned just below centre so a section becomes active while you are reading it rather than while it is still arriving.
2. Entries maintain a `Set` of ids currently inside the band. The active id is resolved by scanning the authored `sections` order for the first member of that set — not by reading `entries[0]`, whose order depends on how the observer batched the callback and therefore on scroll direction.
3. When the set is empty — a gap between sections, or a header taller than the band — the previous answer is held rather than cleared, so the rail never blanks between sections.
4. A second observer watches the element named by `endId` with `rootMargin: "0px 0px -25% 0px"`, which makes "intersecting" mean exactly "its top has climbed above 75% of the root". That retires the whole rail, so it is not hovering over a footer with nothing left to navigate.
5. The indicator itself is a `<span>` whose inline `width` flips between 16 and 32 px with a 260 ms CSS transition. The only JavaScript per scroll event is a `Set` mutation and at most one `setState`.
6. Section elements are collected into an id → element `Map` by walking the attribute once, rather than running a `[data-scrollspy="id"]` selector per section — that form needs escaping for any id containing punctuation and silently matches nothing when the escaping is wrong.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `bandTop / bandBottom = 38 / 55`
  Leaves a 7% band. Widen it and two sections are inside at once on a tall screen, which is the flicker this design exists to remove. Narrow it below about 4% and a fast flick can jump the band entirely between two observer callbacks, leaving the rail on the previous section. The asymmetry (38 vs 55) puts the band below centre, where the eye is while reading.
- `ACTIVE_WIDTH / IDLE_WIDTH = 32 / 16`
  A 2x length change is detectable without looking directly at it. Equal widths with only a colour change is invisible in peripheral vision, which defeats the point of a rail you are not supposed to be looking at.
- `TRANSITION_MS = 260`
  Long enough that the width change reads as movement and draws the eye, short enough that it has finished before the next section can reach the band during normal scrolling.
- `hideAt = 0.75`
  Fraction of the root the end marker must pass before the rail retires. At 1.0 the rail is still on screen while the footer is being read; below about 0.6 it disappears while the last section is still active.

## API

```ts
function BandedScrollspyRail(props: { sections: { id: string; label: string }[]; rootRef?: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>; bandTop?: number; bandBottom?: number; endId?: string; hideAt?: number; attribute?: string; onActiveChange?: (id: string | null) => void; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `sections: { id: string; label: string }[]`
  Ordered list. Each `id` must match a `data-scrollspy` attribute inside the root.
- `rootRef: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>`
  The scroll container holding the sections. Omit for the document.
- `bandTop: number` — default `38`
  Percent of the root trimmed from the top to form the band.
- `bandBottom: number` — default `55`
  Percent trimmed from the bottom. The two must sum to under 100.
- `endId: string`
  Section after which the rail retires. Usually the footer.
- `hideAt: number` — default `0.75`
  Fraction down the root the end marker must pass before the rail hides.
- `attribute: string` — default `'data-scrollspy'`
  Attribute used to find sections inside the root.
- `onActiveChange: (id: string | null) => void`
  Fires once per active-section change. Held in a ref, so it needs no memo.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the nav element via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const ACTIVE_WIDTH = 32;
const IDLE_WIDTH = 16;
const TRANSITION_MS = 260;

export function BandedScrollspyRail({
  sections,
  rootRef,
  bandTop = 38,
  bandBottom = 55,
  endId,
  hideAt = 0.75,
  attribute = 'data-scrollspy',
  onActiveChange,
  className,
}: BandedScrollspyRailProps) {
  const [active, setActive] = useState<string | null>(null);
  const [retired, setRetired] = useState(false);
  const [expanded, setExpanded] = useState(false);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  // Held in refs so a new array literal or a fresh callback on every parent
  // render does not tear down and rebuild the observers.
  const sectionsRef = useRef(sections);
  sectionsRef.current = sections;
  const notify = useRef(onActiveChange);
  notify.current = onActiveChange;

  const order = sections.map((s) => s.id).join('|');

  useEffect(() => {
    const root = rootRef?.current ?? null;
    const scope: ParentNode = root ?? document;

    // Build id -> element by walking the attribute once, rather than running a
    // `[attr="id"]` selector per section: that needs escaping for any id with
    // punctuation in it, and silently matches nothing when the escaping is
    // wrong.
    const elements = new Map<string, Element>();
    for (const el of Array.from(scope.querySelectorAll(`[${attribute}]`))) {
      const id = el.getAttribute(attribute);
      if (id) elements.set(id, el);
    }
    if (elements.size === 0) return;

    const inBand = new Set<string>();

    const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
      (entries) => {
        for (const entry of entries) {
          const id = entry.target.getAttribute(attribute);
          if (!id) continue;
          if (entry.isIntersecting) inBand.add(id);
          else inBand.delete(id);
        }

        // Resolve in authored order, not entry order: callbacks arrive in
        // whatever order the observer batched them, so picking `entries[0]`
        // makes the active section depend on scroll direction.
        const next = sectionsRef.current.find((s) => inBand.has(s.id))?.id;

        // Nothing in the band — a gap between sections, or a header taller
        // than the band. Hold the last answer instead of blanking the rail,
        // which would read as the nav breaking.
        if (next === undefined) return;

        setActive((prev) => {
          if (prev === next) return prev;
          notify.current?.(next);
          return next;
        });
      },
      {
        root,
        // The band. 100 - bandTop - bandBottom percent of the root's height,
        // centred low enough that a section is "active" while you are reading
        // it rather than while it is still arriving.
        rootMargin: `-${bandTop}% 0px -${bandBottom}% 0px`,
        threshold: 0,
      },
    );

    for (const el of elements.values()) observer.observe(el);

    // Second observer: retire the rail once the end marker has climbed past
    // `hideAt`, so it is not hovering over a footer with nothing left to
    // navigate. Shrinking the bottom margin by (1 - hideAt) makes
    // "intersecting" mean exactly "its top is above hideAt of the root".
    let endObserver: IntersectionObserver | null = null;
    const endEl = endId === undefined ? undefined : elements.get(endId);
    if (endEl) {
      endObserver = new IntersectionObserver(
        (entries) => {
          const entry = entries[entries.length - 1];
          if (entry) setRetired(entry.isIntersecting);
        },
        { root, rootMargin: `0px 0px -${Math.round((1 - hideAt) * 100)}% 0px`, threshold: 0 },
      );
      endObserver.observe(endEl);
    }

    return () => {
      observer.disconnect();
      endObserver?.disconnect();
    };
  }, [rootRef, attribute, bandTop, bandBottom, endId, hideAt, order]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Both IntersectionObservers are disconnected on unmount and on any option change. An observer holds a strong reference to every element it watches, so skipping this pins the unmounted section tree in memory and keeps firing `setState` on a dead component.

**Reduced motion.** The rail still tracks the active section and still changes width — that is state, not decoration. Every `transition` is set to `none`, so the tick snaps between widths and the labels appear instantly, and click-to-navigate uses `behavior: "auto"` rather than a smooth scroll.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Observing with the default full-height root. Three sections intersect at once on a tall screen and the active tick flickers between them on every callback. Debouncing hides the symptom and adds lag; shrinking the root removes the ambiguity.
- Taking the active section from `entries[0]`. The callback batches entries in an order that depends on which boundaries were crossed, so the same scroll direction can yield a different winner between two frames. Resolve against the authored order instead.
- Clearing the active state when nothing is intersecting. Any gap taller than the band — a spacer, a full-bleed image, a header — blanks the rail mid-scroll and it reads as broken.
- Signalling the active section with colour only. On a hairline tick in the corner of the eye a tint change is imperceptible; a width change is not, and it also survives a monochrome or high-contrast rendering.
- Rebuilding the observers on every render. `sections` is usually a fresh array literal from the parent, so keying the effect on it disconnects and reconnects two observers on every keystroke elsewhere in the page. Key on the joined id list and read the array from a ref.
- Forgetting `observer.disconnect()`. IntersectionObserver keeps a strong reference to every observed element, so an undisconnected observer pins the whole unmounted section tree in memory and keeps calling `setState` on a dead component.
- Scrolling with `window.scrollTo` on click when the sections live in a container. `scrollIntoView` walks up and scrolls whichever ancestor actually holds the overflow, which is the only version that works in both cases.

## Notes

- No GSAP and no ScrollTrigger: the whole component is two IntersectionObservers and a CSS transition, which is why it is classed `css` cost and can be used dozens of times on a page.
- The labels are always in the DOM at `opacity: 0` and reveal on hover or keyboard focus, so the rail is operable and readable without a pointer.

## Definition of done

Scroll slowly: the active tick changes exactly once as each section crosses the middle of the screen, with no flicker at the boundary and no blank state in the gaps. The active tick is visibly twice as long as the others. Scroll to the end and the whole rail fades out. Hover it and the labels appear; tab into it and they appear too. With reduced motion on, the tick still moves but snaps rather than eases.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Batched Blur Reveal

A page-wide entrance that reveals elements in groups rather than one at a time. Everything that crosses the start line inside the same 100 ms window is handed to one tween, so a real stagger runs across a row of cards that entered simultaneously. Opacity, rise, scale and blur move together, which reads as the content focusing rather than sliding.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Cards that enter together focus in as one staggered group instead of arriving as a slab.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. On mount, every `[data-reveal]` descendant of the container — queried from the container element, never from `document` — is set to `{ opacity: 0, y: 90, scale: 0.94, filter: "blur(12px)" }` plus a `will-change` hint for transform, filter and opacity.
2. `ScrollTrigger.batch(targets, { start: "top 88%", interval: 0.1, batchMax: 6 })` replaces the usual one-trigger-per-element loop. Elements that cross the start line within `interval` seconds of each other are collected and delivered to `onEnter` as a single array.
3. That array is animated by one `gsap.to` with `stagger: 0.14`, so the offset is computed across the whole group. Individual triggers cannot do this: each one starts at its own t=0 and knows nothing about its neighbours.
4. The tween carries `overwrite: true` so a fast flick that re-enters an element mid-reveal restarts it cleanly instead of interpolating from a half-finished state.
5. `onComplete` calls `gsap.set(batch, { clearProps: "filter,willChange" })`. A `filter` that survives the animation keeps the node on its own composited layer for the life of the page, which is exactly the cost the reveal was supposed to pay once.
6. Under `prefers-reduced-motion`, no trigger is created at all: the targets are `gsap.set` to their final values and the content is already correct on first paint.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `start = 'top 88%'`
  The element begins revealing when its top reaches 88% down the scroller — a sliver above the fold. At `top bottom` the reveal happens off-screen and the user sees nothing; below about 80% the element is already well into view before it starts, which reads as a late load.
- `BATCH_INTERVAL = 0.1`
  Seconds of grace before a batch is flushed. Too small and a row of three cards splits into three batches with no stagger between them — the exact failure this component exists to avoid. Too large and the first element visibly waits before anything moves.
- `batchMax = 6`
  Cap on group size. With `stagger: 0.14`, a batch of 20 puts 2.7 s between the first and last element, so the tail is still blurred long after the user has read the head. Six keeps the whole group inside roughly a second.
- `stagger = 0.14`
  Offset within a batch. Below ~0.08 the group reads as simultaneous and the batching is invisible; above ~0.2 it reads as a queue rather than a wave.
- `blur = 12`
  Starting blur in pixels. This is the expensive property — it forces a full repaint of the layer every frame — and it is what turns a slide into a focus-pull. Past ~20px the text is unreadable for long enough that the reveal feels broken.
- `distance = 90`
  Pixels of rise. Paired with `scale: 0.94` it reads as depth. Much more and the element travels further than its own height, which looks like a layout jump rather than an entrance.
- `duration = 1.1`
  Long for an entrance, and deliberately so: the blur needs time to resolve or the focus-pull reads as a flicker.

## API

```ts
function BatchedBlurReveal(props: { children: ReactNode; selector?: string; start?: string; distance?: number; blur?: number; scale?: number; duration?: number; stagger?: number; once?: boolean; batchMax?: number; scrollerRef?: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Section content. Anything matching `selector` inside it is revealed.
- `selector: string` — default `'[data-reveal]'`
  Which descendants reveal. Queried against the container, not the document.
- `start: string` — default `'top 88%'`
  ScrollTrigger start position for every batched element.
- `distance: number` — default `90`
  Pixels the element rises through.
- `blur: number` — default `12`
  Starting blur radius. Set 0 to drop the focus-pull and keep the rise.
- `scale: number` — default `0.94`
  Starting scale.
- `duration: number` — default `1.1`
  Seconds per element.
- `stagger: number` — default `0.14`
  Seconds between elements within one batch.
- `once: boolean` — default `true`
  Reveal once and never replay.
- `batchMax: number` — default `6`
  Largest group a single callback may receive.
- `scrollerRef: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>`
  The scroll container that owns the scroll position. Omit for the document.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the container via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const BATCH_INTERVAL = 0.1;

export function BatchedBlurReveal({
  children,
  selector = '[data-reveal]',
  start = 'top 88%',
  distance = 90,
  blur = 12,
  scale = 0.94,
  duration = 1.1,
  stagger = 0.14,
  once = true,
  batchMax = 6,
  scrollerRef,
  className,
}: BatchedBlurRevealProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  useGsap(
    gsap,
    () => {
      const el = root.current;
      if (!el) return;

      // Query from the container, never `document`. Two instances of this
      // component on one page would otherwise each claim the other's targets
      // and fight over the same tweens.
      const targets = Array.from(el.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>(selector));
      if (targets.length === 0) return;

      if (reduced) {
        // Not "duration 0" — no trigger at all. The content is simply already
        // in its final state on first paint.
        gsap.set(targets, { opacity: 1, y: 0, scale: 1, filter: 'none' });
        return;
      }

      gsap.set(targets, {
        opacity: 0,
        y: distance,
        scale,
        filter: `blur(${blur}px)`,
        // Promoting up front matters more than usual here: an animated
        // `filter` repaints the layer every frame, and without the hint the
        // first two or three frames of every batch are the browser deciding
        // whether to promote at all.
        willChange: 'transform, filter, opacity',
      });

      ScrollTrigger.batch(targets, {
        start,
        once,
        batchMax,
        interval: BATCH_INTERVAL,
        scroller: scrollerRef?.current ?? undefined,
        onEnter: (batch) => {
          gsap.to(batch, {
            opacity: 1,
            y: 0,
            scale: 1,
            filter: 'blur(0px)',
            duration,
            ease: 'power3.out',
            stagger,
            // A fast flick can re-enter an element while its own reveal is
            // still running. Without overwrite the second tween interpolates
            // from wherever the first had got to and the two fight.
            overwrite: true,
            onComplete: () => {
              // A permanent `filter` keeps the element on its own composited
              // layer for the life of the page. Drop both hints once settled.
              gsap.set(batch, { clearProps: 'filter,willChange' });
            },
          });
        },
      });
    },
    root,
    [selector, start, distance, blur, scale, duration, stagger, once, batchMax, reduced],
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useGsap` runs the whole setup inside a `gsap.context` and calls `ctx.revert()` on unmount and on any prop change. That kills every batched ScrollTrigger and every in-flight tween, and restores the inline styles the initial `gsap.set` wrote, so an unmount mid-reveal leaves no opacity or blur behind on a node React may reuse.

**Reduced motion.** No ScrollTrigger is created. The targets are set to their final state — full opacity, no offset, no blur — during the first effect, so the section renders as finished content and never moves.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Creating one ScrollTrigger per element. Sixty targets means sixty sets of start/end calculations on every refresh, and — the visible part — two cards entering in the same frame both begin at t=0, so the row lands flat. `stagger` cannot cross independent triggers.
- Querying targets with `document.querySelectorAll`. Two instances of the component on one page each claim the other's elements, so both apply the initial state and both tween it, and elements reveal twice at different speeds.
- Leaving `filter` on the node after the reveal. A non-`none` filter keeps the element on its own composited layer permanently; on a page with sixty of them the compositor memory cost outlives the animation by the whole session. Clear it in `onComplete`.
- Omitting `overwrite: true`. Flick-scrolling re-enters an element while its reveal is running and the second tween starts from the partial state, so opacity and blur end up somewhere between the two.
- Animating `filter: blur()` without a `will-change` hint. The first frames go to the browser deciding whether to promote the layer, so every reveal starts with a visible hitch.
- Registering ScrollTrigger inside the component body. It runs on every render and touches `document`, which throws during server rendering. Register once at module scope behind a `typeof window` guard.

## Notes

- Pass `scrollerRef` when the content scrolls inside a container rather than the document — ScrollTrigger measures against the window by default and every start position will be wrong.
- `once: true` is the default because these are entrances, not a narrative. Set it false when the section is something the user is expected to scroll back through.

## Definition of done

Scroll a grid of cards into view: the cards in the same row lift and focus one after another with a visible offset, not all at once. Scroll back up and they stay revealed. Inspect a settled card and it has no `filter` or `will-change` left in its inline style. With reduced motion enabled the section is fully visible before any scrolling happens.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Bayer-Quantised Plasma

A full-screen plasma built from sixteen passes of iterated domain warping, then reduced to eleven grey levels through an 8x8 ordered dither matrix. The quantisation is the whole point: a smooth plasma is a screensaver, and the same plasma printed in eleven tones is a texture that type can sit on. The pointer displaces the plasma's own coordinate space so the field leans into the cursor rather than growing a highlight under it.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

An iterated domain-warped plasma crushed to eleven grey levels, so the hero reads as a dot-matrix proof.

- Category: webgl
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. Each of the `iterations` passes rotates the sample point by `rotate` radians, then folds it: `p += warp * sin(p.yx * 1.31 + t + i*0.7) / (1 + i*0.35)`. The `p.yx` swap is what couples the two axes into marbling — with `p.xy` the same code produces stripes.
2. Each pass also accumulates `amp * sin(p.x + p.y + t*0.6)` with `amp` decaying by 0.86, and the sum is divided by the amplitude actually accumulated rather than by a constant, so lowering `iterations` for a weak GPU changes the detail without changing the exposure.
3. The result is remapped to 0..1, pushed through `clamp((lum - 0.5) * contrast + 0.5, 0, 1)`, then multiplied by an elliptical vignette centred at `(0.5, 0.4)` — the optical centre, not the geometric one; at 0.5 a hero reads bottom-heavy.
4. Quantisation happens on a gamma-spaced ramp: `encode = pow(lum, 1/gamma)`, add the dither offset, `round` to one of `levels-1` steps, `decode = pow(q, gamma)`. The reference implementation carried an eleven-entry grey table and found the nearest entry with a branchless ladder of ten mix/step pairs; a monotone ramp collapses that search into encode, round, decode.
5. The dither offset `(bayer8(fragCoord / cell) - 0.5) / (levels - 1)` is added in the ENCODED space. Applied after decoding it would be the wrong physical size in the shadows, where the ramp is compressed, and the dark half of the frame would band anyway.
6. `iterations` is a uniform read against a constant `MAX_ITERATIONS = 48` loop bound with a `break`, so quality can be lowered at runtime without relinking a program or triggering a driver recompile.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `MAX_ITERATIONS = 48`
  Compile-time loop ceiling. A fully dynamic bound is legal in ES 3.00 but stops the compiler bounding register pressure, and some mobile drivers recompile the shader when the uniform changes — a visible hitch at exactly the moment you were trying to avoid one.
- `iterations = 16`
  Runtime pass count. Below about 6 the field is a plain ripple with no interference; past about 24 each extra pass adds detail finer than one dither cell, so it is thrown away by the quantiser and costs a full sin/rot per fragment for nothing.
- `warp = 1.5`
  How far each pass folds the coordinate. Under ~0.5 the passes barely disturb each other and the plasma is concentric; over ~2.5 the folding self-intersects and produces hard creases that survive quantisation as jagged black shapes.
- `amplitude decay = 0.86`
  Per-pass amplitude falloff. At 1.0 the late passes carry as much weight as the first and the field turns to grey mush; below ~0.6 only the first three passes contribute and the iteration count stops mattering.
- `phase offset = float(i) * 0.7`
  Decorrelates the passes. Without it every pass warps in lockstep and sixteen iterations look identical to one.
- `levels = 11`
  Grey steps. Eleven is the count that still reads as print: enough to hold the shape of the plasma, few enough that every transition is visibly dots rather than a ramp. Past ~20 the dither becomes invisible and you have paid for it anyway.
- `gamma = 1.49`
  Exponent the levels are spaced on. At 1.0 the steps are uniform in code and non-uniform to the eye, so the shadows show obvious banding while the highlights look smooth.
- `vignette centre = (0.5, 0.4)`
  The optical centre. Vignetting around the geometric centre makes a hero read as bottom-heavy, because the eye already places the middle of a frame slightly above halfway.
- `cellSize = 2`
  CSS pixels per dither cell, so the 8x8 tile is 16 CSS px. Indexing the matrix by device pixels instead makes the texture twice as coarse on a 1x monitor as on a 2x one.

## API

```ts
function BayerPlasmaHero(props: { iterations?: number; warp?: number; frequency?: number; rotate?: number; contrast?: number; gamma?: number; levels?: number; cellSize?: number; vignette?: number; ink?: readonly [number, number, number]; paper?: readonly [number, number, number]; speed?: number; maxDpr?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `iterations: number` — default `16`
  Plasma warp passes. Clamped to 1..48, the shader's compiled ceiling.
- `warp: number` — default `1.5`
  How far each pass folds the coordinate through its own sine.
- `frequency: number` — default `2.2`
  Base spatial frequency of the plasma.
- `rotate: number` — default `-0.1`
  Radians of rotation applied to the coordinate each pass.
- `contrast: number` — default `1.35`
  Contrast pivoted on mid grey, applied before quantisation.
- `gamma: number` — default `1.49`
  Exponent the output levels are spaced on.
- `levels: number` — default `11`
  Output grey levels, both ends included.
- `cellSize: number` — default `2`
  CSS pixels per dither cell. Multiplied by DPR internally.
- `vignette: number` — default `0.55`
  Strength of the elliptical vignette at the optical centre.
- `ink: readonly [number, number, number]` — default `[0.03, 0.032, 0.038]`
  Darkest output colour, linear 0..1 RGB.
- `paper: readonly [number, number, number]` — default `[0.88, 0.92, 0.9]`
  Lightest output colour, linear 0..1 RGB.
- `speed: number` — default `1`
  Multiplier on plasma evolution.
- `maxDpr: number` — default `2`
  Upper bound on device pixel ratio.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const TRIANGLE = new Float32Array([-1, -1, 3, -1, -1, 3]);
const MAX_ITERATIONS = 48;
const ITERATIONS = 16;
const WARP = 1.5;
const FREQUENCY = 2.2;
const ROTATE = -0.1;
const CONTRAST = 1.35;
const GAMMA = 1.49;
const LEVELS = 11;
const CELL_SIZE = 2;
const VIGNETTE = 0.55;
const INK: readonly [number, number, number] = [0.03, 0.032, 0.038];
const PAPER: readonly [number, number, number] = [0.88, 0.92, 0.9];

interface Gpu {
  gl: WebGL2RenderingContext;
  program: WebGLProgram;
  vao: WebGLVertexArrayObject;
  buffer: WebGLBuffer;
  locations: Map<string, WebGLUniformLocation | null>;
}

function build(gl: WebGL2RenderingContext): Gpu | null {
  const compile = (type: number, src: string): WebGLShader | null => {
    const shader = gl.createShader(type);
    if (!shader) return null;
    gl.shaderSource(shader, src);
    gl.compileShader(shader);
    if (gl.getShaderParameter(shader, gl.COMPILE_STATUS)) return shader;
    console.error('[bayer-plasma-hero]', gl.getShaderInfoLog(shader));
    gl.deleteShader(shader);
    return null;
  };

  const vert = compile(gl.VERTEX_SHADER, BAYER_PLASMA_VERT);
  const frag = compile(gl.FRAGMENT_SHADER, BAYER_PLASMA_FRAG);
  const program = gl.createProgram();
  const vao = gl.createVertexArray();
  const buffer = gl.createBuffer();
  if (!vert || !frag || !program || !vao || !buffer) return null;

  gl.attachShader(program, vert);
  gl.attachShader(program, frag);
  gl.linkProgram(program);
  gl.deleteShader(vert);
  gl.deleteShader(frag);
  if (!gl.getProgramParameter(program, gl.LINK_STATUS)) {
    console.error('[bayer-plasma-hero]', gl.getProgramInfoLog(program));
    gl.deleteProgram(program);
    return null;
  }

  gl.bindVertexArray(vao);
  gl.bindBuffer(gl.ARRAY_BUFFER, buffer);
  gl.bufferData(gl.ARRAY_BUFFER, TRIANGLE, gl.STATIC_DRAW);
  const attrib = gl.getAttribLocation(program, 'a_pos');
  if (attrib >= 0) {
    gl.enableVertexAttribArray(attrib);
    gl.vertexAttribPointer(attrib, 2, gl.FLOAT, false, 0, 0);
  }
  gl.bindVertexArray(null);

  return { gl, program, vao, buffer, locations: new Map() };
}

function loc(gpu: Gpu, name: string): WebGLUniformLocation | null {
  const cached = gpu.locations.get(name);
  if (cached !== undefined) return cached;
  const found = gpu.gl.getUniformLocation(gpu.program, name);
  gpu.locations.set(name, found);
  return found;
}

export function BayerPlasmaHero({
  iterations = ITERATIONS,
  warp = WARP,
  frequency = FREQUENCY,
  rotate = ROTATE,
  contrast = CONTRAST,
  gamma = GAMMA,
  levels = LEVELS,
  cellSize = CELL_SIZE,
  vignette = VIGNETTE,
  ink = INK,
  paper = PAPER,
  speed = 1,
  maxDpr = 2,
  className,
}: BayerPlasmaHeroProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const canvasRef = useRef<HTMLCanvasElement>(null);
  const gpuRef = useRef<Gpu | null>(null);
  const dprRef = useRef(1);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const visible = useVisibility();
  const pointer = useSmoothPointer({ target: host, smoothing: 0.03 });
  const [supported, setSupported] = useState(true);

  const paramsRef = useRef({
    iterations, warp, frequency, rotate, contrast, gamma,
    levels, cellSize, vignette, ink, paper, speed,
  });
  paramsRef.current = {
    iterations, warp, frequency, rotate, contrast, gamma,
    levels, cellSize, vignette, ink, paper, speed,
  };

  const drawRef = useRef<(elapsed: number) => void>(() => {});
  drawRef.current = (elapsed: number) => {
    const gpu = gpuRef.current;
    if (!gpu) return;
    const { gl } = gpu;
    const q = paramsRef.current;
    const p = pointer.current;

    gl.useProgram(gpu.program);
    gl.uniform2f(loc(gpu, 'u_resolution'), gl.drawingBufferWidth, gl.drawingBufferHeight);
    gl.uniform1f(loc(gpu, 'u_time'), elapsed * q.speed);
    gl.uniform2f(loc(gpu, 'u_pointer'), p.nx, 1 - p.ny);
    // Clamped to the shader's compiled ceiling: a value above MAX_ITERATIONS
    // would silently do nothing, which is worse than being clamped.
    gl.uniform1i(
      loc(gpu, 'u_iterations'),
      Math.max(1, Math.min(MAX_ITERATIONS, Math.round(q.iterations))),
    );
    gl.uniform1f(loc(gpu, 'u_warp'), q.warp);
    gl.uniform1f(loc(gpu, 'u_freq'), q.frequency);
    gl.uniform1f(loc(gpu, 'u_rotate'), q.rotate);
    gl.uniform1f(loc(gpu, 'u_contrast'), q.contrast);
    gl.uniform1f(loc(gpu, 'u_gamma'), Math.max(0.05, q.gamma));
    gl.uniform1f(loc(gpu, 'u_levels'), Math.max(2, Math.round(q.levels)));
    gl.uniform1f(loc(gpu, 'u_cell'), Math.max(1, q.cellSize * dprRef.current));
    gl.uniform1f(loc(gpu, 'u_vignette'), q.vignette);
    gl.uniform3f(loc(gpu, 'u_ink'), q.ink[0], q.ink[1], q.ink[2]);
    gl.uniform3f(loc(gpu, 'u_paper'), q.paper[0], q.paper[1], q.paper[2]);

    gl.bindVertexArray(gpu.vao);
    gl.drawArrays(gl.TRIANGLES, 0, 3);
    gl.bindVertexArray(null);
  };

  useEffect(() => {
    const canvas = canvasRef.current;
    if (!canvas) return;
    if (!hasWebGL()) {
      setSupported(false);
      return;
    }

    const gl = canvas.getContext('webgl2', {
      antialias: false,
      alpha: false,
      depth: false,
      stencil: false,
      powerPreference: 'high-performance',
    });
    if (!gl) {
      setSupported(false);
      return;
    }

    const gpu = build(gl);
    if (!gpu) {
      loseContext(gl);
      setSupported(false);
      return;
    }
    gpuRef.current = gpu;
    setSupported(true);

    return () => {
      gpuRef.current = null;
      gl.deleteVertexArray(gpu.vao);
      gl.deleteBuffer(gpu.buffer);
      gl.deleteProgram(gpu.program);
      loseContext(gl);
    };
  }, []);

  useEffect(() => {
    const canvas = canvasRef.current;
    const gpu = gpuRef.current;
    if (!canvas || !gpu || width === 0 || height === 0) return;

    const dpr = pixelRatio(maxDpr);
    dprRef.current = dpr;
    const w = Math.max(1, Math.round(width * dpr));
    const h = Math.max(1, Math.round(height * dpr));
    if (canvas.width !== w || canvas.height !== h) {
      canvas.width = w;
      canvas.height = h;
    }
    gpu.gl.viewport(0, 0, w, h);
    // At t = 0 every sine in the warp chain is in phase and the plasma is a
    // near-flat field, so the still frame is taken from a developed moment.
    drawRef.current(reduced ? 7.5 : 0);
  }, [width, height, maxDpr, supported, reduced]);

  const running = supported && visible && !reduced && width > 0 && height > 0;
  useRaf((_dt, elapsed) => drawRef.current(elapsed), running);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Deletes the VAO, vertex buffer and program, then `loseContext(gl)` to hand the context back. The rAF subscription and the pointer listener unsubscribe with their hooks.

**Reduced motion.** No rAF subscription. A single frame is drawn at a fixed `u_time` of 7.5 seconds and redrawn on resize — not at t=0, where every sine in the warp chain is still in phase and the plasma is a nearly flat field. The dithered texture, the vignette and the level structure are all fully present; only the evolution stops.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Dividing the plasma sum by a hard-coded normaliser. Drop from 16 iterations to 8 on a weak GPU and the whole image gets darker, so the low-quality path looks like a different component rather than the same one with less detail.
- Applying the dither offset after decoding the gamma ramp. In the shadows the ramp is compressed, so a fixed offset spans much less than one output step there and the dark half of the frame bands exactly as if there were no dither at all.
- Writing `sin(p.xy * ...)` instead of `sin(p.yx * ...)`. The axes stop being coupled, every pass warps x by a function of x, and the marbling degenerates into diagonal stripes.
- Making the iteration count a `const int`. Every quality level then needs its own compiled program, and switching between them stalls the pipeline; a uniform plus a constant loop bound with `break` costs one comparison per pass.
- Centring the vignette at (0.5, 0.5). It is subtle and it is real — the frame reads as sagging, and the usual reaction is to reduce the vignette strength instead of moving it.
- Rendering at native DPR. This shader is 16 iterations of transcendentals per fragment; at DPR 3 that is 2.25x the fragments of DPR 2 for no perceptible gain, and it is the difference between 60fps and 25 on a phone.
- Leaving the context alive on unmount. Raw GL has no `dispose()` — the VAO, buffer and program are deleted explicitly and `loseContext(gl)` returns the context, or the page starts blanking its oldest canvases after roughly sixteen mounts.

## Notes

- The 8x8 matrix is derived from `gl_FragCoord` with six integer operations rather than sampled from a texture. The derivation is documented in full in `bayer8-ordered-dither`; the function is duplicated here so this component installs standalone.
- The entire look is data: `iterations`, `warp`, `frequency`, `contrast`, `gamma` and `levels` are the only things separating newsprint from oil-slick.

## Definition of done

Every tonal transition is made of visible ordered dots — put your eye close and there is no smooth ramp anywhere in the frame. Set `iterations={6}` and the field simplifies without getting darker. Move the cursor and the plasma shears toward it rather than a bright spot appearing under it. The frame is darkest at the corners and brightest slightly above the middle.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Bit-Math Bayer8 Dither

Ordered dithering with the threshold matrix computed from the fragment coordinate instead of sampled from a texture. Six integer operations reproduce the classic 8x8 Bayer matrix exactly, which turns a banding-prone gradient into a stable newsprint texture that holds at any zoom and costs less than the texture fetch it replaces.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A smooth gradient crushed to five levels through an 8x8 ordered matrix derived from six integer ops.

- Category: webgl
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The Bayer matrix is defined recursively as `M2 = [[0,2],[3,1]]` and `M2n(x,y) = 4*Mn(x mod n, y mod n) + M2(x div n, y div n)`. Writing M2 in binary (0=00, 2=10, 3=11, 1=01) collapses it to the closed form `M2(a,b) = 2*(a^b) + b`.
2. Unrolling that recursion three times gives `M8(x,y) = 16*M2(x0,y0) + 4*M2(x1,y1) + M2(x2,y2)` where xN is bit N of x, and substituting the closed form yields the whole matrix as one expression: `32*(x0^y0) + 16*y0 + 8*(x1^y1) + 4*y1 + 2*(x2^y2) + y2`.
3. Read as bits that is the low three bits of `x ^ y` and of `y`, interleaved and reversed — the LEAST significant coordinate bit drives the MOST significant threshold bit, which is precisely what makes the pattern maximally dispersed instead of clustered. In GLSL it is `int x = c.x & 7; int y = c.y & 7;` followed by those six terms, divided by 64.
4. `gl_FragCoord.xy` is divided by `cellSize * dpr` before the matrix lookup, so the dither cell is a fixed physical size and the texture does not get four times finer on a retina display.
5. Quantisation is `floor(clamp(c + (threshold - 0.5) / steps, 0, 1) * steps + 0.5) / steps` with `steps = levels - 1`. Centring the threshold on zero and scaling it to exactly one output step is what makes the perturbation cancel out on average.
6. A `pow(g, 1.35)` gamma is applied before quantisation, because the output levels are evenly spaced in the encoded value while the eye is not — quantising the linear value alone dumps all the visible banding into the shadows.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `divisor = 64.0`
  The matrix holds 0..63, so dividing by 64 keeps the thresholds in [0, 1). Dividing by 63 puts the top cell at exactly 1.0, which pushes one cell in every 8x8 tile a full step brighter and stamps a visible dot grid across flat areas.
- `levels = 5`
  Output steps per channel. At 2 it is a pure 1-bit print and the gradient becomes texture only. Above about 12 the eye can no longer see the individual steps and the dither is doing nothing but adding noise — use it to fix banding, not as a look.
- `cellSize = 2`
  CSS pixels per dither cell, so the 8x8 tile is 16 CSS px. At 1 the pattern is at the Nyquist limit of most displays and shimmers when the page scrolls; above about 6 it stops reading as print texture and starts reading as a deliberate checkerboard.
- `threshold scale = (t - 0.5) / (levels - 1)`
  The perturbation must span exactly one output step. Larger and the dither adds contrast of its own — flat areas visibly sparkle. Smaller and it cannot push a value across a level boundary, so the bands survive untouched.
- `gamma = 1.35`
  Applied before quantisation. Without it the evenly spaced levels bunch perceptually in the highlights and spread in the shadows, so the dark half of the frame shows obvious steps while the bright half looks smooth.

## API

```ts
function Bayer8OrderedDither(props: { levels?: number; cellSize?: number; speed?: number; dark?: readonly [number, number, number]; light?: readonly [number, number, number]; maxDpr?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `levels: number` — default `5`
  Output steps per channel, both ends included. 2 is pure 1-bit.
- `cellSize: number` — default `2`
  CSS pixels per dither cell. Multiplied by DPR internally.
- `speed: number` — default `1`
  Multiplier on the sweep that animates the underlying gradient.
- `dark: readonly [number, number, number]` — default `[0.035, 0.038, 0.045]`
  Darkest output colour, linear 0..1 RGB.
- `light: readonly [number, number, number]` — default `[0.9, 0.94, 0.92]`
  Lightest output colour, linear 0..1 RGB.
- `maxDpr: number` — default `2`
  Upper bound on device pixel ratio.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const TRIANGLE = new Float32Array([-1, -1, 3, -1, -1, 3]);
const LEVELS = 5;
const CELL_SIZE = 2;
const DARK: readonly [number, number, number] = [0.035, 0.038, 0.045];
const LIGHT: readonly [number, number, number] = [0.9, 0.94, 0.92];

interface Gpu {
  gl: WebGL2RenderingContext;
  program: WebGLProgram;
  vao: WebGLVertexArrayObject;
  buffer: WebGLBuffer;
  locations: Map<string, WebGLUniformLocation | null>;
}

function build(gl: WebGL2RenderingContext): Gpu | null {
  const compile = (type: number, src: string): WebGLShader | null => {
    const shader = gl.createShader(type);
    if (!shader) return null;
    gl.shaderSource(shader, src);
    gl.compileShader(shader);
    if (gl.getShaderParameter(shader, gl.COMPILE_STATUS)) return shader;
    console.error('[bayer8-ordered-dither]', gl.getShaderInfoLog(shader));
    gl.deleteShader(shader);
    return null;
  };

  const vert = compile(gl.VERTEX_SHADER, BAYER8_DITHER_VERT);
  const frag = compile(gl.FRAGMENT_SHADER, BAYER8_DITHER_FRAG);
  const program = gl.createProgram();
  const vao = gl.createVertexArray();
  const buffer = gl.createBuffer();
  if (!vert || !frag || !program || !vao || !buffer) return null;

  gl.attachShader(program, vert);
  gl.attachShader(program, frag);
  gl.linkProgram(program);
  gl.deleteShader(vert);
  gl.deleteShader(frag);
  if (!gl.getProgramParameter(program, gl.LINK_STATUS)) {
    console.error('[bayer8-ordered-dither]', gl.getProgramInfoLog(program));
    gl.deleteProgram(program);
    return null;
  }

  gl.bindVertexArray(vao);
  gl.bindBuffer(gl.ARRAY_BUFFER, buffer);
  gl.bufferData(gl.ARRAY_BUFFER, TRIANGLE, gl.STATIC_DRAW);
  const attrib = gl.getAttribLocation(program, 'a_pos');
  if (attrib >= 0) {
    gl.enableVertexAttribArray(attrib);
    gl.vertexAttribPointer(attrib, 2, gl.FLOAT, false, 0, 0);
  }
  gl.bindVertexArray(null);

  return { gl, program, vao, buffer, locations: new Map() };
}

function loc(gpu: Gpu, name: string): WebGLUniformLocation | null {
  const cached = gpu.locations.get(name);
  if (cached !== undefined) return cached;
  const found = gpu.gl.getUniformLocation(gpu.program, name);
  gpu.locations.set(name, found);
  return found;
}

export function Bayer8OrderedDither({
  levels = LEVELS,
  cellSize = CELL_SIZE,
  speed = 1,
  dark = DARK,
  light = LIGHT,
  maxDpr = 2,
  className,
}: Bayer8OrderedDitherProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const canvasRef = useRef<HTMLCanvasElement>(null);
  const gpuRef = useRef<Gpu | null>(null);
  const dprRef = useRef(1);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const visible = useVisibility();
  const pointer = useSmoothPointer({ target: host, smoothing: 0.004 });
  const [supported, setSupported] = useState(true);

  const paramsRef = useRef({ levels, cellSize, speed, dark, light });
  paramsRef.current = { levels, cellSize, speed, dark, light };

  const drawRef = useRef<(elapsed: number) => void>(() => {});
  drawRef.current = (elapsed: number) => {
    const gpu = gpuRef.current;
    if (!gpu) return;
    const { gl } = gpu;
    const params = paramsRef.current;
    const p = pointer.current;

    gl.useProgram(gpu.program);
    gl.uniform2f(loc(gpu, 'u_resolution'), gl.drawingBufferWidth, gl.drawingBufferHeight);
    gl.uniform1f(loc(gpu, 'u_time'), elapsed * params.speed);
    gl.uniform2f(loc(gpu, 'u_pointer'), p.nx, 1 - p.ny);
    gl.uniform1f(loc(gpu, 'u_levels'), Math.max(2, Math.round(params.levels)));
    // Cell size is authored in CSS pixels and converted here, so the dither
    // grain is the same physical size on a 1x monitor and a 3x phone.
    gl.uniform1f(loc(gpu, 'u_cell'), Math.max(1, params.cellSize * dprRef.current));
    gl.uniform3f(loc(gpu, 'u_dark'), params.dark[0], params.dark[1], params.dark[2]);
    gl.uniform3f(loc(gpu, 'u_light'), params.light[0], params.light[1], params.light[2]);

    gl.bindVertexArray(gpu.vao);
    gl.drawArrays(gl.TRIANGLES, 0, 3);
    gl.bindVertexArray(null);
  };

  useEffect(() => {
    const canvas = canvasRef.current;
    if (!canvas) return;
    if (!hasWebGL()) {
      setSupported(false);
      return;
    }

    const gl = canvas.getContext('webgl2', {
      antialias: false,
      alpha: false,
      depth: false,
      stencil: false,
      powerPreference: 'high-performance',
    });
    if (!gl) {
      setSupported(false);
      return;
    }

    const gpu = build(gl);
    if (!gpu) {
      loseContext(gl);
      setSupported(false);
      return;
    }
    gpuRef.current = gpu;
    setSupported(true);

    return () => {
      gpuRef.current = null;
      gl.deleteVertexArray(gpu.vao);
      gl.deleteBuffer(gpu.buffer);
      gl.deleteProgram(gpu.program);
      loseContext(gl);
    };
  }, []);

  useEffect(() => {
    const canvas = canvasRef.current;
    const gpu = gpuRef.current;
    if (!canvas || !gpu || width === 0 || height === 0) return;

    const dpr = pixelRatio(maxDpr);
    dprRef.current = dpr;
    const w = Math.max(1, Math.round(width * dpr));
    const h = Math.max(1, Math.round(height * dpr));
    if (canvas.width !== w || canvas.height !== h) {
      canvas.width = w;
      canvas.height = h;
    }
    gpu.gl.viewport(0, 0, w, h);
    drawRef.current(0);
  }, [width, height, maxDpr, supported, reduced]);

  const running = supported && visible && !reduced && width > 0 && height > 0;
  useRaf((_dt, elapsed) => drawRef.current(elapsed), running);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Deletes the VAO, vertex buffer and program, then `loseContext(gl)`. The rAF subscription and pointer listener are removed by their hooks.

**Reduced motion.** The rAF loop never subscribes; the sweep is frozen at t=0 and the pointer light sits at its seeded centre. One frame is drawn on mount and on every resize, so the dithered gradient is fully rendered — the texture is the point, and it is static.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Uploading the matrix as an 8x8 texture. It needs a texture unit, a sampler uniform, GL_NEAREST filtering and CLAMP wrapping set correctly on a non-power-of-two-safe path, and a resource to dispose — all to replace six integer instructions that are cheaper than the fetch.
- Dividing the matrix by 63 instead of 64. The top cell lands on exactly 1.0, that one cell per tile is pushed a full level brighter than its neighbours, and flat regions grow a faint regular dot grid that only shows up on a real screen.
- Comparing against the raw matrix value with `step(0.0, x)`. The matrix contains a genuine zero cell, so the comparison passes there even when it should not, and every 8x8 tile gets one stuck pixel. Bias the comparison by about 0.001 if you use a threshold form rather than the quantise form here.
- Indexing the matrix with `gl_FragCoord` directly. The cell then measures one device pixel, so the same component looks twice as coarse on a 1x monitor as on a 2x one. Divide by `cellSize * dpr` and the texture is stable.
- Quantising the linear value with no gamma. The steps are uniform in code and non-uniform to the eye, so the shadows band visibly while the highlights look fine and the fix gets misdiagnosed as "not enough levels".
- Leaving the raw GL objects behind on unmount. There is no `dispose()` here — the VAO, buffer and program are deleted by hand and `loseContext(gl)` returns the context, without which a page that mounts this repeatedly starts blanking its oldest canvases.

## Notes

- The alternative implementation, a nested `mix`/`step` ladder, is branchless and works on WebGL1. This one needs WebGL2 for integer bit operators but is roughly half the instruction count.
- The same six lines dither any signal — swap the gradient in `main` for a scene texture and this becomes a post-process.

## Definition of done

The gradient shows no smooth ramp anywhere — every transition is a field of ordered dots resolving between five flat levels. Zoom the browser to 200% and the dot pitch doubles with the page instead of staying at one device pixel. Screenshot two consecutive frames with the pointer still: the dot pattern is byte-identical, because the matrix depends only on position.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Blend-Difference Cursor

A white circle replaces the pointer and inverts everything under it via `mix-blend-mode: difference`, so it is legible over any background without a single contrast rule. It has three sizes — 16px idle, 44px over a link, 150px over a `data-cursor="view"` target, the last carrying a text label — and the size change is CSS while the position is GSAP, deliberately kept on different properties.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A white dot in difference blend mode inverts whatever it crosses, growing 16 to 44 to 150px on hover.

- Category: cursor
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. Difference blending subtracts the backdrop from the source per channel. A pure white source therefore outputs `1 - backdrop`: black over white, white over black, the complement over any colour. That is the entire contrast strategy — no theme awareness, no luminance sampling, no per-section overrides.
2. Position is two `gsap.quickTo` setters created once, each backed by a single tween whose end value is mutated per event. At 0.32s with `power3` the dot trails the pointer by a few frames — enough to read as a physical object, short enough that clicking still feels direct.
3. `xPercent: -50, yPercent: -50` centres the dot on its own box once at mount, so the handler can pass raw pointer coordinates and, critically, the centring survives the width and height changing from 16px to 150px. A pixel offset would have to be recomputed for every size.
4. Size transitions list `width`, `height` and `background-color` explicitly. `transform` is excluded because GSAP writes it every frame; a CSS transition on the same property would interpolate toward a value GSAP has already replaced, and the result is a cursor that lags by a constant distance no tween duration accounts for.
5. Hover state is resolved by hit-testing `e.target.closest(...)` on each move rather than binding listeners to interactive children. React can add, remove and reorder those children freely and the cursor keeps working, with no subscription bookkeeping.
6. The dot is `display: none` in markup and only switched to `flex` after the `(pointer: fine)` check passes, so nothing renders before JS confirms there is a cursor to replace — no stray blob flashes during hydration on a phone.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `SIZE_IDLE / SIZE_HOVER / SIZE_VIEW = 16 / 44 / 150`
  16px reads as a cursor rather than a dot of dust. 44px is roughly the tap-target minimum and clearly signals "this is interactive" without hiding the word underneath. 150px is enormous on purpose: it has to hold a 15px label with breathing room, and at that size the inverted region becomes a design element rather than a pointer.
- `FOLLOW_DURATION = 0.32`
  Seconds of catch-up. Below ~0.15 the dot is welded to the pointer and the blend looks like a rendering artefact; above ~0.5 clicking feels disconnected because the visual lands after the press.
- `ease: 'power3' = power3 (in-out)`
  In-out rather than `.out`. quickTo remutates the end value continuously, so the tween is always restarting mid-flight; the symmetric curve absorbs direction changes instead of snapping into a fresh outward ramp on every event.
- `size transition timing = 0.4s cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)`
  A strong ease-out. The dot reaches most of its new size in the first ~120ms so the hover feels instant, then settles. Linear at this scale looks mechanical; a longer duration means the dot is still growing when the pointer has left the target.
- `label scale = 0.5 -> 1`
  The label grows with the dot rather than fading in at full size, so at the halfway point of the transition the text is proportionate to the circle around it instead of overflowing it.

## API

```ts
function BlendDifferenceCursor(props: { children?: ReactNode; label?: string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Content the cursor inverts. Mark targets with `data-cursor="view"` or use plain `a`/`button`.
- `label: string` — default `'View'`
  Text shown inside the 150px state. Must fit at 15px inside the circle.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root container via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** The three states. Diameters in px, not scales — see the note above. */
const SIZE_IDLE = 16;
const SIZE_HOVER = 44;
const SIZE_VIEW = 150;

const FOLLOW_DURATION = 0.32;

export function BlendDifferenceCursor({
  children,
  label = 'View',
  className,
}: BlendDifferenceCursorProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const dot = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const text = useRef<HTMLSpanElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = root.current;
    const node = dot.current;
    const caption = text.current;
    if (!el || !node || !caption) return;

    // Never on touch: there is no hover state to grow into, and `pointermove`
    // only fires mid-drag, so the dot would appear under the finger already
    // covering it and then be stranded on lift.
    if (!window.matchMedia('(pointer: fine)').matches) return;
    const reduced = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;

    /* The dot is `display: none` until JS confirms a fine pointer, so nothing
       renders before this line — no stray blob flashes during hydration. */
    node.style.display = 'flex';
    /* Hiding the native cursor from JS, not CSS, for the same reason: a
       stylesheet rule would blank the cursor on touch devices too, where this
       component draws nothing to replace it. */
    const previousCursor = el.style.cursor;
    el.style.cursor = 'none';

    gsap.set(node, { xPercent: -50, yPercent: -50, autoAlpha: 0 });

    const duration = reduced ? 0 : FOLLOW_DURATION;
    // Two tweens for the lifetime of the component, end values mutated in
    // place. `gsap.to` per event would allocate ~120 tweens a second, each one
    // overwriting a tween that had not finished.
    const xTo = gsap.quickTo(node, 'x', { duration, ease: 'power3' });
    const yTo = gsap.quickTo(node, 'y', { duration, ease: 'power3' });

    let entered = false;
    let state: 'idle' | 'hover' | 'view' = 'idle';

    const apply = (next: typeof state) => {
      if (next === state) return;
      state = next;
      const size = next === 'view' ? SIZE_VIEW : next === 'hover' ? SIZE_HOVER : SIZE_IDLE;
      // Width and height only. `transform` is GSAP's.
      node.style.width = `${size}px`;
      node.style.height = `${size}px`;
      caption.style.opacity = next === 'view' ? '1' : '0';
      caption.style.transform = next === 'view' ? 'scale(1)' : 'scale(0.5)';
    };

    const onMove = (e: PointerEvent) => {
      const rect = el.getBoundingClientRect();
      const x = e.clientX - rect.left;
      const y = e.clientY - rect.top;

      if (!entered) {
        entered = true;
        // Second argument is quickTo's START value: this teleports instead of
        // easing, so the dot does not sail across the panel on every entry.
        xTo(x, x);
        yTo(y, y);
        gsap.to(node, { autoAlpha: 1, duration: reduced ? 0 : 0.2, overwrite: 'auto' });
      } else {
        xTo(x);
        yTo(y);
      }

      // Hit-testing the event target beats a listener per interactive child:
      // it survives children being added, removed or re-rendered by React.
      const target = e.target instanceof Element ? e.target : null;
      if (target?.closest('[data-cursor="view"]')) apply('view');
      else if (target?.closest('a, button, [data-cursor="hover"]')) apply('hover');
      else apply('idle');
    };

    const onLeave = () => {
      entered = false;
      apply('idle');
      gsap.to(node, { autoAlpha: 0, duration: reduced ? 0 : 0.2, overwrite: 'auto' });
    };

    /* Listening on the container, not the dot. A listener on the dot would see
       its own `pointerleave` as it slides out from under the pointer and chase
       itself. `pointer-events: none` on the dot is the other half of that. */
    el.addEventListener('pointermove', onMove, { passive: true });
    el.addEventListener('pointerleave', onLeave);

    return () => {
      el.removeEventListener('pointermove', onMove);
      el.removeEventListener('pointerleave', onLeave);
      el.style.cursor = previousCursor;
      node.style.display = '';
      gsap.killTweensOf(node);
      gsap.set(node, { clearProps: 'all' });
    };
  }, []);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Removes both container listeners, restores the container's original inline `cursor` value, resets the dot to `display: none`, then `gsap.killTweensOf` and `clearProps: "all"` to drop the two quickTo tweens and the centring transform. Nothing is left on the element for a remount to inherit.

**Reduced motion.** The cursor still appears, still inverts and still changes size — those are affordances, not motion. Both quickTo durations drop to 0 so the dot is welded to the pointer, and the fade in and out is instant. The CSS size transition is left in place; it is a 400ms state change, not continuous movement.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- An ancestor that creates a stacking context. A `transform`, `filter`, `opacity` below 1, `will-change`, `isolation: isolate`, `contain: paint`, a `position: fixed` parent or a `backdrop-filter` anywhere between the intended blend root and the dot silently confines the blend to that subtree — the dot inverts its immediate parent and nothing else. This is the single most common reason this effect "does not work", and it produces no error, no warning and no console output.
- Transitioning `all` on the dot. It catches `transform`, which GSAP is writing at 60-120fps, and CSS interpolates toward values that are already stale. The cursor then trails the pointer by a fixed distance that changing the tween duration does not fix, because the tween is not the thing lagging.
- Scaling instead of resizing. `scale()` is a transform, so it collides with the follow tween AND it scales the label's stroke weight and letter-spacing along with the circle. Animating `width`/`height` keeps typography at its designed size.
- Listening for `pointermove` on the dot itself. It sits under the pointer, so it receives its own `pointerleave` as it slides, and the cursor chases itself out of the panel. Listen on the container and keep `pointer-events: none` on the dot.
- Hiding the native cursor from CSS. A `cursor: none` rule applies on touch devices too, where this component renders nothing to replace it, so links become untappable-looking with no visible affordance. Set it from JS after the `(pointer: fine)` check and restore it on cleanup.
- Centring with a negative margin instead of `xPercent`/`yPercent`. The margin is a fixed pixel value and the dot changes size by a factor of nine, so it visibly slides off the pointer as it grows.
- Leaving the effect on over navigation. A 150px inverted blob over link text is genuinely worse than an arrow; a real deployment needs an escape hatch that restores the native cursor over the nav.
- Using a theme token for the dot colour. Difference blending only produces a clean inversion from pure white; a near-white token yields a muddy tint over mid-greys.

## Notes

- Gated on `(pointer: fine)`. On touch nothing mounts, the native cursor is never hidden, and the markup stays `display: none` — there is no hover to grow into and `pointermove` only exists mid-drag, which would put the dot under the finger already covering it.
- Scoped to its own container with `position: absolute` inside a `relative isolate` root rather than `position: fixed`. A production site-level cursor is `fixed` at the document root; the isolate here is what makes the blend stop at the component edge instead of inverting the whole page.
- Reduced motion keeps the cursor but sets every duration to 0, so the affordance and the inversion survive while the drift does not.
- The label is `#000` and the dot `#fff` as raw literals, not tokens. Difference blending is defined on the actual channel values; a token would break the inversion the moment the theme shifted.

## Definition of done

Move across the panel and a white dot follows a few frames behind, inverting the text and background under it — dark text goes light where the dot crosses it. Hover a link and it grows to 44px; hover a `data-cursor="view"` target and it grows to 150px with a label that scales up inside it. During the growth the dot stays centred on the pointer and never lags further behind than it did at rest. Leave the panel and it fades out. On touch there is no dot at all and the native cursor is untouched.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Browser Chrome Frame

A title bar plus a content well, drawn entirely in CSS, wrapped around anything you want to present as a live site rather than a picture of one. The address pill copies the URL and confirms with a checkmark that draws along its own path and holds for 1600 ms. Every state change happens inside a fixed-width pill, so nothing in the bar ever reflows.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A macOS window frame with hover-revealed traffic lights and an address pill whose check draws itself on copy.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The frame is a flex column: a `shrink-0` title bar and a `min-h-0 flex-1` content well. `min-h-0` is what lets the well actually shrink inside a flex parent — without it a tall child pushes the frame past its container and the rounded bottom corners leave the viewport.
2. The three window buttons are `11px` circles filled with the real macOS values (`#ff5f57`, `#febc2e`, `#28c840`) holding a `7px` SVG glyph at `opacity: 0`. The cluster is one Tailwind `group`, so hovering anywhere in the title bar fades all three glyphs in together — which is how the system chrome behaves, and hovering one button to reveal only that button is the tell of a reimplementation.
3. Copying goes through `navigator.clipboard?.writeText?.(url)`. That returns `undefined` outside a secure context and a rejecting promise when the document is not focused, so both branches resolve to an explicit `failed` state rather than a swallowed catch. A pill that silently does nothing reads as a broken button.
4. The confirmation checkmark carries `pathLength="1"` and `strokeDasharray="1"`, so `strokeDashoffset` moves between exactly `1` and `0` regardless of the path coordinates, and a single 320 ms `cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)` transition draws it. The link icon it replaces crossfades over 180 ms in an absolutely-positioned 12 px box, so the icon slot never changes size.
5. Both text labels — the URL and the confirmation — sit in the same CSS grid cell (`col-start-1 row-start-1`) and swap by opacity. The pill therefore cannot resize between states, so the URL never shifts sideways under the cursor that just clicked it.
6. A single `setTimeout` ref holds the return to idle. Every entry point clears it first, so clicking the pill three times in a row extends one confirmation rather than queuing three overlapping ones.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `COPIED_MS = 1600`
  How long the confirmed state holds. Deliberately long: at the 600-800 ms most implementations use, a user who looks back at the pill after moving their eyes to the clipboard target has already missed it, and clicks again. 1600 ms survives a glance away and back.
- `DRAW_MS = 320`
  Stroke-draw duration for the check. Below ~200 ms the draw is indistinguishable from a hard appear, which throws away the only cue that says "this just happened now"; past ~450 ms the confirmation is still arriving after the user has moved on.
- `FADE_MS = 180`
  Crossfade for the icon and label swap, and the traffic-light glyph reveal. Shorter than the draw on purpose — the check should finish last, so the eye lands on the completed mark rather than on a half-drawn one under settled text.
- `traffic light fills = #ff5f57 / #febc2e / #28c840`
  The actual macOS window-button values. This component reproduces a specific piece of system chrome, so these are content, not theme: recolouring them to the site palette turns the frame from "a browser" into "a diagram of a browser" and the recognition is gone.
- `dot size = 11px`
  Matches the system button diameter at 1x. At 8px the glyphs are unreadable; past ~14px the bar starts to read as a toy illustration rather than chrome.

## API

```ts
function BrowserChromeFrame(props: { url: string; children: ReactNode; label?: string; onCopy?: (url: string) => void; copiedDurationMs?: number; className?: string; bodyClassName?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `url: string`
  Shown in the address pill and written to the clipboard on click.
- `children: ReactNode`
  The framed content. Sized by the frame, not by itself.
- `label: string`
  Display text for the pill. Defaults to `url` with the scheme stripped, which is what a browser shows.
- `onCopy: (url: string) => void`
  Fires after a successful clipboard write, never on failure.
- `copiedDurationMs: number` — default `1600`
  How long the confirmed state holds before returning to idle.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the outer frame.
- `bodyClassName: string`
  Merged onto the content well below the title bar.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const COPIED_MS = 1600;
const DRAW_MS = 320;
const FADE_MS = 180;

type CopyState = 'idle' | 'copied' | 'failed';

export function BrowserChromeFrame({
  url,
  children,
  label,
  onCopy,
  copiedDurationMs = COPIED_MS,
  className,
  bodyClassName,
}: BrowserChromeFrameProps) {
  const [state, setState] = useState<CopyState>('idle');
  const timer = useRef<ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | null>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  const notify = useRef(onCopy);
  notify.current = onCopy;

  const reset = useCallback(() => {
    if (timer.current !== null) {
      clearTimeout(timer.current);
      timer.current = null;
    }
  }, []);

  // A pending timer outlives the component unless it is cleared. Left alone it
  // calls setState on an unmounted tree — React 19 no longer warns about that,
  // which makes it quieter, not less of a leak.
  useEffect(() => reset, [reset]);

  const copy = useCallback(() => {
    // `navigator.clipboard` is undefined outside a secure context and its
    // promise rejects when the document is not focused. Both are ordinary, so
    // the failure has a state of its own rather than a swallowed catch: a pill
    // that silently does nothing reads as a broken button.
    const write = navigator.clipboard?.writeText?.(url);
    if (!write) {
      reset();
      setState('failed');
      timer.current = setTimeout(() => setState('idle'), copiedDurationMs);
      return;
    }

    void write.then(
      () => {
        reset();
        setState('copied');
        notify.current?.(url);
        timer.current = setTimeout(() => setState('idle'), copiedDurationMs);
      },
      () => {
        reset();
        setState('failed');
        timer.current = setTimeout(() => setState('idle'), copiedDurationMs);
      },
    );
  }, [url, copiedDurationMs, reset]);

  const copied = state === 'copied';
  const failed = state === 'failed';

  // Reduced motion keeps the state change and drops only the tweening: the
  // check is already fully drawn on the frame it appears, and the two labels
  // hard-swap instead of crossfading. The confirmation is still legible for
  // the same 1600 ms — the information was never the animation.
  const drawMs = reduced ? 0 : DRAW_MS;
  const fadeMs = reduced ? 0 : FADE_MS;
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** One `clearTimeout` on the single pending reset timer, via an effect that returns the same `reset` callback every entry point already uses. There are no listeners, no rAF and no tweens — all motion is CSS transitions on mounted nodes, which the browser discards with the node.

**Reduced motion.** The state machine is untouched: clicking still copies, the check still replaces the link icon, and the confirmation still holds for the full 1600 ms. What goes to zero is `DRAW_MS` and `FADE_MS`, so the check appears already fully drawn and the labels hard-swap instead of crossfading. The traffic-light glyphs still reveal on hover, without the fade.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Swapping the icon element instead of stacking both. Replacing a link icon with a check changes the rendered width by a pixel or two, the flex row re-solves, and the URL text jumps sideways at the exact moment the user is reading the confirmation.
- Letting the label change the pill width. If the URL and "Copied" are the same node with different text, the pill resizes and the whole title bar reflows. Stacking them in one grid cell keeps the width pinned to the longer of the two, permanently.
- Hard-coding the measured path length for the dash animation. The first time anyone nudges a coordinate in the checkmark, the offset no longer matches the path and the stroke either starts partly drawn or never completes. `pathLength="1"` renormalises so the animation is coordinate-independent.
- Assuming `navigator.clipboard` exists. On `http://` origins and inside some embedded webviews it is `undefined`, and calling it throws a TypeError that takes the click handler down with it. On a secure origin it still rejects if the document is not focused — a case that happens constantly in dev tools.
- Not clearing the reset timer before starting a new one. Rapid clicks queue several timeouts and the confirmation flickers off at the first one's deadline rather than the last one's, so the state disappears while the user is still clicking.
- Leaving the timer pending on unmount. It fires into a disposed tree; React 19 no longer warns, which makes it quieter, not less of a leak.
- Reading the reduced-motion state and disabling the confirmation itself. The check is information, not decoration. Only the tweening is dropped.

## Notes

- The `group-hover` glyph reveal has no touch equivalent, and correctly so: there is no hover on touch, and firing the reveal on press would light up three buttons the user cannot click.
- The content well sets `overflow-hidden` and `bg-bg`, which is what gives the embed its edge. Framing exists as much to bound the content as to decorate it.

## Definition of done

Hover the title bar and all three glyphs fade in together. Click the pill: the link icon fades out, a checkmark draws itself left to right, "Copied" replaces the URL, the pill does not change width by a single pixel, and the state returns to the URL 1600 ms later. Click three times quickly and you get one confirmation that ends 1600 ms after the last click. On an `http://` origin the pill shows "Press to copy" instead of a silent no-op. With reduced motion the check is fully drawn on the first frame it appears.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
