# Build: Chord-Synced Particle Burst

A burst is N notes a fixed interval apart, each with a visual flare that has to appear on the same beat as its note. Audio is scheduled on `AudioContext.currentTime`, which is sample-accurate; the flares are driven by a rAF loop, which is not. This hook schedules both from one set of offsets and converts the audio times into wall-clock times via `getOutputTimestamp()`, so a flare is never more than one frame from its note however long the burst runs.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Fires an arpeggio and its visual flares off one schedule, so each flash lands on its own note.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. Notes are scheduled ahead of time on the audio clock: for step `i`, `at = ctx.currentTime + LEAD + step * i`, then `gain.setValueAtTime(peak, at)` and `gain.exponentialRampToValueAtTime(0.001, at + decay)`. Nothing is timed by `setTimeout`, so a busy main thread cannot skew a note.
2. `audibleAt(ctx, at)` converts that audio time into a `performance.now()` millisecond value. `ctx.getOutputTimestamp()` returns a matched pair — the sample frame currently leaving the output device and the wall-clock instant it left — so the mapping is `ts.performanceTime + (at - ts.contextTime) * 1000`. Hardware output latency is already inside that pair; adding `outputLatency` on top double-counts it.
3. When `getOutputTimestamp` is unavailable, or has not rendered a frame yet and returns `contextTime: 0`, the fallback is `performance.now() + (at - ctx.currentTime) * 1000 + min(outputLatency, 0.05) * 1000`. `currentTime` is the write head, not the speaker, so the latency has to be added back in this branch only.
4. Each step is pushed onto a queue sorted by wall-clock time, and a rAF loop pops every entry whose time has passed and calls `onStep(index, total)`. Overlapping bursts merge into one sorted queue rather than one loop per burst.
5. The loop is subscribed only while the queue is non-empty — `useRaf(tick, running)` — and unsubscribes itself on the frame it drains the last step, so an idle instrument holds no animation frame.
6. The `AudioContext` is constructed inside `fire()`, which the caller invokes from a click handler, and `resume()` is called if the browser still hands it back suspended. Constructing it at mount produces a suspended context whose scheduled notes are silently discarded.
7. `fire(steps)` caps at `chord.length` and returns the count actually scheduled, so a caller that has fewer flares available than the chord has notes hears exactly as many notes as it shows.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `step = 0.46`
  Seconds between notes, and the same number the visuals use. Around 130 bpm in eighths — fast enough to read as one gesture rather than four separate events, slow enough that each flare is individually visible. Below ~0.2s the flares smear into one flash; above ~0.7s the burst stops sounding like a chord and starts sounding like four taps.
- `gain = 0.15`
  Peak amplitude of a single sine. Four notes overlapping at 1.0 would sum past full scale and hard-clip the destination; 0.15 leaves headroom for the tails of earlier notes still decaying under later ones.
- `SILENCE = 0.001`
  -60 dB, the ramp target. `exponentialRampToValueAtTime` is mathematically undefined at 0 and throws; ramping to a literal 0 is the single most common Web Audio error. -60 dB is inaudible.
- `decay = 0.4`
  Seconds from peak to silence. Slightly shorter than the 0.46s step so a note has essentially finished before the next arrives — overlap past about 0.6s turns the arpeggio into a chord and the individual attacks stop being audible.
- `TAIL = 0.1`
  Extra seconds before `osc.stop()`. Stopping an oscillator exactly at the end of its ramp truncates the last samples and can produce a faint click; 0.1s of -60 dB signal costs nothing and guarantees the stop is inaudible.
- `LEAD = 0.02`
  Seconds of lead before the first note. One render quantum at 44.1 kHz is 128 samples, about 2.9 ms; 20 ms covers several quanta plus the jitter in getting from the click to the scheduling call. Scheduling at exactly `currentTime` means the first note is already partly in the past and its attack is clipped.
- `MAX_LATENCY = 0.05`
  Ceiling on the fallback latency compensation, in seconds. Bluetooth output can report 150-300 ms; delaying the visual by that much to match makes the click itself feel broken. Capping trades exact sync on pathological hardware for a UI that still responds.

## API

```ts
function useBurstAudioSync(options?: { chord?: readonly number[]; step?: number; gain?: number; decay?: number; onStep?: (index: number, total: number) => void; muted?: boolean }): { fire: (steps?: number) => number; unlocked: boolean }
```

- `chord: readonly number[]` — default `[261.63, 329.63, 392, 523.25]`
  One frequency in Hz per step. Caps how many notes a single `fire` can schedule.
- `step: number` — default `0.46`
  Seconds between steps. Shared by the audio schedule and the visual queue.
- `gain: number` — default `0.15`
  Peak gain of one note. Divided by the note count when the stagger collapses.
- `decay: number` — default `0.4`
  Seconds for the exponential ramp from `gain` down to -60 dB.
- `onStep: (index: number, total: number) => void`
  Called on the frame nearest each note. `index` is the position in the chord.
- `muted: boolean` — default `false`
  Skips audio entirely. Visual steps still fire on the same schedule, so the UI is unchanged.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** `exponentialRampToValueAtTime` is undefined at 0, so silence is -60 dB. */
const SILENCE = 0.001;
/** Seconds of dead air after the ramp before the oscillator is stopped. */
const TAIL = 0.1;
/** Seconds of lead before the first note. Absorbs one graph render quantum. */
const LEAD = 0.02;
/** Ceiling on latency compensation, in seconds. */
const MAX_LATENCY = 0.05;

/**
 * Wall-clock time at which a sample scheduled at `contextTime` is heard.
 *
 * The `getOutputTimestamp()` pair is measured *at the output device*, so the
 * hardware latency is already folded into it — adding `outputLatency` on top
 * would double-count it and push every flare late.
 */
function audibleAt(ctx: AudioContext, contextTime: number): number {
  if (typeof ctx.getOutputTimestamp === 'function') {
    const ts = ctx.getOutputTimestamp();
    // Before the graph has rendered anything both fields are 0. Trusting that
    // pair maps every future note to wall-clock zero, and the whole burst
    // flashes at once on the very next frame.
    if (
      ts.contextTime !== undefined &&
      ts.performanceTime !== undefined &&
      ts.contextTime > 0
    ) {
      return ts.performanceTime + (contextTime - ts.contextTime) * 1000;
    }
  }
  // Fallback. `currentTime` is the time of the sample being *written*, which
  // runs ahead of the speaker by roughly the output latency, so add it back.
  const reported = Number.isFinite(ctx.outputLatency)
    ? ctx.outputLatency
    : ctx.baseLatency;
  const latency = Number.isFinite(reported) ? Math.min(reported, MAX_LATENCY) : 0;
  return performance.now() + (contextTime - ctx.currentTime) * 1000 + latency * 1000;
}

export function useBurstAudioSync(options: UseBurstAudioSyncOptions = {}): BurstAudioSync {
  const { chord = C_MAJOR, step = 0.46, gain = 0.15, decay = 0.4 } = options;
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  const [unlocked, setUnlocked] = useState(false);
  const [running, setRunning] = useState(false);

  const ctxRef = useRef<AudioContext | null>(null);
  const queue = useRef<QueuedStep[]>([]);

  // Everything `fire` reads lives in one ref, so `fire` keeps a stable
  // identity and can be handed to a memoised child without re-binding it on
  // every render.
  const config = useRef({ chord, step, gain, decay, reduced, options });
  config.current = { chord, step, gain, decay, reduced, options };

  const fire = useCallback((steps?: number): number => {
    const cfg = config.current;
    const wanted = steps ?? cfg.chord.length;
    const total = Math.min(Math.max(Math.trunc(wanted), 0), cfg.chord.length);
    if (total === 0) return 0;

    // Reduced motion collapses the arpeggio into a single chord: the feedback
    // survives — it was asked for by a click, so it is not decoration — but
    // nothing travels across the screen.
    const stagger = cfg.reduced ? 0 : cfg.step;

    let ctx: AudioContext | null = null;
    if (!cfg.options.muted) {
      ctx = ctxRef.current;
      if (!ctx) {
        // Constructed here and only here: we are inside the gesture handler
        // that called `fire`, which is the one moment the autoplay policy
        // lets a context start.
        ctx = new AudioContext();
        ctxRef.current = ctx;
        setUnlocked(true);
      }
      if (ctx.state === 'suspended') void ctx.resume();
    }

    let baseMs = performance.now();

    if (ctx) {
      const start = ctx.currentTime + LEAD;
      // Four sines at full gain sum to 4x the peak and clip the destination.
      // They only ever overlap when the stagger is gone, so divide then.
      const peak = stagger === 0 ? cfg.gain / total : cfg.gain;

      for (let i = 0; i < total; i++) {
        const freq = cfg.chord[i];
        if (freq === undefined) continue;
        const at = start + stagger * i;

        const osc = ctx.createOscillator();
        const env = ctx.createGain();
        osc.type = 'sine';
        osc.frequency.value = freq;
        env.gain.setValueAtTime(peak, at);
        env.gain.exponentialRampToValueAtTime(SILENCE, at + decay);
        osc.connect(env);
        env.connect(ctx.destination);
        osc.start(at);
        osc.stop(at + decay + TAIL);
        // Without this every burst leaves two live nodes attached to the
        // destination. A few hundred bursts and the graph audibly degrades.
        osc.onended = () => {
          osc.disconnect();
          env.disconnect();
        };
      }

      baseMs = audibleAt(ctx, start);
    }

    const q = queue.current;
    for (let i = 0; i < total; i++) {
      q.push({ at: baseMs + stagger * i * 1000, index: i, total });
    }
    // Two bursts can overlap; the drain below assumes the head is the
    // earliest step, so keep the queue sorted rather than scanning it.
    q.sort((a, b) => a.at - b.at);
    setRunning(true);

    return total;
  }, []);

  // The loop only exists while something is queued. An always-on rAF for a
  // widget that fires twice a minute keeps the browser's animation frame
  // pipeline alive for nothing.
  useRaf(() => {
    const q = queue.current;
    const now = performance.now();
    while (q.length > 0) {
      const head = q[0];
      if (head === undefined || head.at > now) break;
      q.shift();
      config.current.options.onStep?.(head.index, head.total);
    }
    if (q.length === 0) setRunning(false);
  }, running);

  useEffect(
    () => () => {
      queue.current.length = 0;
      const ctx = ctxRef.current;
      ctxRef.current = null;
      // close() stops every scheduled note and releases the hardware. Chrome
      // caps a document at ~6 live contexts and throws on the seventh.
      if (ctx && ctx.state !== 'closed') void ctx.close();
    },
    [],
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The unmount cleanup empties the pending-step queue and calls `ctx.close()`, which cancels every note still scheduled in the future and releases the hardware. The rAF subscription is owned by `useRaf` and released when `running` goes false or the component unmounts. Each oscillator disconnects itself and its gain node in `onended`.

**Reduced motion.** The stagger collapses to zero: all notes are scheduled at the same audio time and every `onStep` fires on one frame, so the burst is a chord rather than a sequence travelling across the screen. Audio is not muted — it is direct feedback for a click, not ambient motion — but the per-note gain is divided by the note count because the notes now overlap.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Constructing the `AudioContext` at mount. Outside a user gesture the browser hands back a `suspended` context; `osc.start(at)` on it neither throws nor plays, so the bug presents as "audio just does not work" with a clean console.
- Ramping the gain to 0. `exponentialRampToValueAtTime(0, t)` throws a `RangeError` — the target must be strictly positive. Ramp to 0.001 instead.
- Using `setTimeout` for the notes so audio and visuals share a timer. Both then inherit the main thread's jitter, and on a frame that takes 80 ms the note lands 80 ms late while the sample-accurate alternative would not have moved.
- Adding `outputLatency` on top of a `getOutputTimestamp()` mapping. That pair is measured at the output device and already contains the latency, so adding it again pushes every flare a full hardware buffer behind its note — the exact defect the conversion exists to prevent.
- Trusting `getOutputTimestamp()` immediately after construction. Before the graph has rendered a quantum both fields read 0, which maps every future note to wall-clock zero and dumps the entire burst onto the next frame.
- Never disconnecting the oscillator and gain. Both stay attached to the destination after the note ends; a few hundred bursts in one session and the graph is carrying hundreds of dead nodes, which shows up as rising CPU and eventually distortion.
- Keeping a rAF loop running so the flare queue can be polled. The queue is empty almost all the time — subscribe on `fire`, unsubscribe on the frame the last step drains.
- Letting the notes overlap at full gain when reduced motion collapses the stagger. Four sines at 0.15 sum to 0.6 and the summed peak clips; the per-note gain has to be divided by the note count in the collapsed case.
- Forgetting `ctx.close()` on unmount. Chrome allows roughly six live `AudioContext` objects per document and throws on the next one, so a page that mounts this in a list silently stops producing sound after the sixth item.

## Notes

- The hook deliberately exposes no `play()` that can be called from an effect. `fire` is the only entry point and its contract is "call me from a gesture handler" — encoding the autoplay policy in the API rather than in a comment.
- Two clocks, two policies. Reduced motion collapses the stagger but does not mute anything: the sound is feedback for a click the user made, not ambient decoration, and silencing it removes information.
- `chord` is any frequency list. A minor triad is `[261.63, 311.13, 392]`; a single frequency makes it a one-shot tick with the same scheduling guarantees.

## Definition of done

Click a string: four flares appear 0.46s apart and each one coincides with a note — watch the fourth flare and hear the fourth note land together, not a beat apart. Click a string at either end and only one flare appears and only one note sounds. Nothing plays before the first click. Toggle sound off and the flares keep exactly the same timing. With reduced motion on, all four strings light in the same frame and you hear a chord. Unmount mid-burst and the remaining notes do not play.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Canvas Handoff Transition

The usual way to put a shader on more than one page is to mount it on each of them, and the price is a new context, a new compile and a new first frame every time the route changes. No easing hides that: a field restarting from t = 0 is visibly a different object. Here one canvas is created imperatively, outside React's ownership, and moved into the destination page with `appendChild` during the layout phase — no paint happens in between, so the context never blinks. What the viewer sees is the surface they were already looking at, travelling from one rectangle to another.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

The live WebGL canvas is handed to the next page and flies to its new slot, instead of being destroyed and rebuilt.

- Category: transition
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1, gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. Four steps in a fixed order. MEASURE first, inside the click handler, because one `setState` later the outgoing rectangle no longer exists. FLUSH one frame, so the pixels about to travel are current. MOVE in a `useLayoutEffect`, which shares its task with React's DOM mutations and therefore straddles no paint. RESIZE last, on the tween's completion.
2. The move is a plain `target.appendChild(canvas)`. `appendChild` on a node that already has a parent relocates it rather than copying it, and a WebGL context belongs to the canvas element, not to its position in the document — so the context, the compiled program and the drawing buffer all survive being detached and re-attached.
3. The flight is FLIP: `scaleX = first.width / last.width`, `scaleY = first.height / last.height`, and the translation is the difference between the two centre points. Scale, never `width`/`height` — a width tween is 0.72 s of continuous reflow, and writing the canvas's width attribute would reallocate the drawing buffer on every frame of it.
4. The buffer resize is deferred to `onComplete` and the `ResizeObserver` is muted for the duration by a `flying` flag. Assigning `canvas.width` is what reallocates and CLEARS the backing store; do it while the element is mid-flight and the object being animated goes black for a frame. During the flight the old buffer is simply scaled by CSS, which is slightly soft and completely invisible at this duration.
5. Measuring inside the handler also makes interruption correct for free. If a flight is already running, `getBoundingClientRect()` returns the TRANSFORMED rect — where the canvas visually is, mid-air — so a second click continues from that point instead of snapping back to the slot it was heading for.
6. The destination slot has its `overflow` forced to `visible` inline for the length of the flight and restored afterwards. Inline, because the clipping usually comes from a utility class on the consumer's own markup that a rule in our stylesheet would lose to.
7. A `uHandoff` uniform is tweened 0 to 1 and back on the same timeline, shearing the field's sampling coordinate. It disturbs the picture rather than fading it: a fade would hide precisely the frames that prove the surface is the same one.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `HANDOFF_DURATION = 0.72`
  Seconds for the flight. It is long for a page transition, deliberately — the whole point is that you can watch a specific fold of the field travel and see that it never restarts. Under about 0.45 s the eye cannot track it and the effect degrades to a cut; over about 1 s the route change starts to feel withheld.
- `HANDOFF_EASE = 'power3.inOut'`
  Symmetric, because the two rectangles are equally important — the canvas is not leaving somewhere for somewhere, it is the same object being re-placed. An `out` ease would put the acceleration at the origin and imply the old page was the one that mattered.
- `SURGE_EASE = 'sine.inOut'`
  The `uHandoff` shear runs half the flight forward and half back (`yoyo: true, repeat: 1`). Sine, because it is the only common ease with zero slope at both ends, so the disturbance grows out of stillness and returns to it with no visible corner at the turnaround.
- `LEVELS = 6`
  Tones the field is crushed to. Low enough that the quantisation edges are hard and locked to the drawing buffer, which is what makes the mid-flight scaling legible as "these are the pixels that were already there". Above about ten the picture is a smooth gradient again and the proof is lost.
- `CELL = 2`
  Dither cell size in DRAWING-BUFFER pixels, so on a 2x display the pattern is one CSS pixel per cell — fine enough to read as tone, coarse enough to survive the scaling. Measured in buffer pixels rather than CSS pixels on purpose: it is the buffer that stretches during the flight.
- `MAX_DPR = 2`
  Device pixel ratio ceiling. Above 2 the visual gain on a quantised field is nil and the fill-rate cost is quadratic — and this surface is on screen on every page rather than on one hero, so its cost is paid continuously.
- `INK / PAPER = [0.42, 0.65, 1] / [0.035, 0.037, 0.045]`
  The two ends of the quantisation ramp, as raw 0..1 RGB. Passed as `THREE.Vector3` rather than `THREE.Color` because three applies working-colour-space conversion to a Color and none to a Vector3, and a `ShaderMaterial` emits `gl_FragColor` without the output-encoding chunk — Vector3 is the only pairing where the numbers written in the source are the numbers that reach the screen.

## API

```ts
function CanvasHandoffTransition(props: { controller: CanvasHandoff; children: ReactNode; duration?: number; ease?: string; ink?: readonly [number, number, number]; paper?: readonly [number, number, number]; levels?: number; cell?: number; maxDpr?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
function CanvasHandoffSlot(props: { controller: CanvasHandoff; id: string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
function useCanvasHandoff(initialId: string): { active: string; fallback: boolean; handoff: (id: string, commit?: () => void) => void }
```

- `controller: CanvasHandoff`
  From `useCanvasHandoff(initialSlotId)`. Shared by the host and every slot.
- `children: ReactNode`
  The pages. Each renders one `CanvasHandoffSlot` for its own landing place.
- `duration: number` — default `0.72`
  Seconds for the flight. `0` moves the canvas instantly with no tween.
- `ease: string` — default `'power3.inOut'`
  Easing for the flight.
- `ink: readonly [number, number, number]` — default `[0.42, 0.65, 1]`
  Bright end of the quantisation ramp, raw 0..1 RGB.
- `paper: readonly [number, number, number]` — default `[0.035, 0.037, 0.045]`
  Dark end of the quantisation ramp, raw 0..1 RGB.
- `levels: number` — default `6`
  How many tones the field is crushed to.
- `cell: number` — default `2`
  Dither cell size in drawing-buffer pixels.
- `maxDpr: number` — default `2`
  Device pixel ratio ceiling.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host root via `cn`.
- `id: string`
  `CanvasHandoffSlot` only. Stable identity for this landing place, unique within one controller.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/* ------------------------------------------------------------------------
   BUILD. Depends on the motion preference and the DPR ceiling and nothing
   else — emphatically not on the active slot, or a route change would tear
   down the very context the component exists to preserve.
   ------------------------------------------------------------------------ */
useEffect(() => {
  const rootEl = root.current;
  if (!rootEl) return;

  /* Probed in an effect, never during render: `hasWebGL()` needs `document`,
     and branching the markup on it would be a hydration mismatch rather than
     a graceful degradation. */
  if (!hasWebGL()) {
    setFallback(true);
    return;
  }
  setFallback(false);

  const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({
    antialias: false,
    alpha: false,
    powerPreference: 'low-power',
  });
  renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio(maxDpr));

  /* three constructs the canvas; React never sees it. This is the whole
     strict-mode story: the second invocation gets a brand new element and a
     brand new context, because the first invocation's cleanup removed and
     released its own. */
  const canvas = renderer.domElement;
  canvas.className = 'kx-handoff-canvas';
  canvas.setAttribute('aria-hidden', 'true');

  const l = look.current;
  const uniforms: HandoffUniforms = {
    uResolution: { value: new THREE.Vector2(1, 1) },
    uTime: { value: 0 },
    uHandoff: { value: 0 },
    uLevels: { value: l.levels },
    uCell: { value: l.cell },
    /* Vector3, not Color: three applies working-colour-space conversion to a
       Color and none to a Vector3, and a `ShaderMaterial` emits `gl_FragColor`
       without the output-encoding chunk. Vector3 is the only pair of ends
       where the numbers written here are the numbers that reach the screen. */
    uInk: { value: new THREE.Vector3(l.ink0, l.ink1, l.ink2) },
    uPaper: { value: new THREE.Vector3(l.paper0, l.paper1, l.paper2) },
  };

  const material = new THREE.ShaderMaterial({
    vertexShader: canvasHandoffVertexShader,
    fragmentShader: canvasHandoffFragmentShader,
    uniforms,
  });
  // A 2x2 plane under an identity ortho camera is a full-screen quad with no
  // projection maths and no camera to keep in sync on resize.
  const geometry = new THREE.PlaneGeometry(2, 2);
  const scene = new THREE.Scene();
  scene.add(new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material));
  const camera = new THREE.OrthographicCamera(-1, 1, 1, -1, 0, 1);

  const render = () => renderer.render(scene, camera);

  const resize = () => {
    const host = canvas.parentElement;
    if (!host) return;
    const w = host.clientWidth;
    const h = host.clientHeight;
    if (w === 0 || h === 0) return;
    // `false` leaves the CSS size alone; the stylesheet's 100%/100% is what
    // keeps the canvas glued to whichever slot currently owns it.
    renderer.setSize(w, h, false);
    uniforms.uResolution.value.set(w, h);
    render();
  };

  // Whatever slot is active right now. `rootEl` is the safety net for a
  // controller whose slots have not registered — the canvas is visible and
  // full-bleed rather than orphaned.
  const home = slots.current.get(activeRef.current) ?? rootEl;
  home.appendChild(canvas);
  resize();

  /* Observed on the CANVAS, not the slot: the observation follows the node
     across the handoff, so one observer covers every slot it will ever live
     in. `setSize(..., false)` never writes the CSS box, so this cannot feed
     back on itself. */
  const observer = new ResizeObserver(() => {
    // The flight deliberately runs at the OLD buffer size, scaled. Honouring
    // the resize here is the black frame the deferral exists to prevent.
    if (engine.current?.flying) return;
    resize();
  });
  observer.observe(canvas);

  if (reduced) {
    // One frame, then nothing. A field that drifts forever is motion, and
    // motion is what was asked not to happen.
    render();
  } else {
    // The timestamp is absolute, so elapsed time survives the handoff with
    // no accumulator to carry across and nothing to reset.
    renderer.setAnimationLoop((time) => {
      uniforms.uTime.value = time / 1000;
      render();
    });
  }

  engine.current = { canvas, uniforms, render, resize, flying: false };

  return () => {
    observer.disconnect();
    gsap.killTweensOf(canvas);
    gsap.killTweensOf(uniforms.uHandoff);
    // Stops the loop before releasing the context; a queued frame rendering
    // into a lost context throws out of the cleanup.
    disposeRenderer(renderer);
    material.dispose();
    geometry.dispose();
    // The effect appended it, the effect removes it. React has no idea this
    // node was ever here and will not try to reconcile it.
    canvas.remove();
    engine.current = null;
  };
}, [reduced, maxDpr, slots, engine, activeRef, setFallback]);

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------------
   HAND OVER. A LAYOUT effect, because React's mutations and its layout
   effects share one task: the canvas leaves the old parent and arrives at
   the new one with no paint in between. The same code in `useEffect` shows a
   frame with a hole where the canvas used to be.
   ------------------------------------------------------------------------ */
useLayoutEffect(() => {
  const e = engine.current;
  const target = slots.current.get(active);
  if (!e || !target) return;

  const from = first.current;
  first.current = null;

  // First run after the build already parked it correctly.
  if (e.canvas.parentElement === target) return;

  // `appendChild` on a node that already has a parent MOVES it. No clone, no
  // re-creation, and the WebGL context rides along untouched.
  target.appendChild(e.canvas);

  /* An interrupted flight leaves an inline transform behind. Clear it before
     measuring or Last is read through the previous flight's scale, and the
     inversion comes out compounded — the canvas leaps somewhere neither slot
     has ever been. `clearProps` rather than a set to identity so the instant
     paths below leave the element genuinely untouched. */
  gsap.killTweensOf(e.canvas);
  gsap.set(e.canvas, { clearProps: 'transform' });

  if (!from || reduced || duration <= 0) {
    e.resize();
    return;
  }

  const to = e.canvas.getBoundingClientRect();
  if (to.width === 0 || to.height === 0) {
    e.resize();
    return;
  }

  // FLIP: invert the measured difference, then animate the inversion away.
  // Scale rather than width/height — width is a layout property and a layout
  // property tweened for 0.7 s is 0.7 s of reflow.
  const scaleX = from.width / to.width;
  const scaleY = from.height / to.height;
  const x = from.left + from.width / 2 - (to.left + to.width / 2);
  const y = from.top + from.height / 2 - (to.top + to.height / 2);

  /* For the length of the flight the canvas is bigger than, and outside, the
     slot it now lives in — so the slot must not clip. Written INLINE and
     restored afterwards, because the thing being overridden is usually a
     utility class on the consumer's own markup, and a rule in our stylesheet
     would lose to it. Skip this and the transition is invisible: the canvas
     is cropped to its destination rectangle from the first frame, which
     looks exactly like no transition at all. */
  const clipped = target.style.overflow;
  target.style.overflow = 'visible';
  const unclip = () => {
    target.style.overflow = clipped;
  };

  e.flying = true;
  const tl = gsap.timeline({
    onComplete: () => {
      e.flying = false;
      unclip();
      gsap.set(e.canvas, { clearProps: 'transform' });
      // The ONE buffer resize, now that nothing is moving.
      e.resize();
    },
  });

  tl.fromTo(
    e.canvas,
    { x, y, scaleX, scaleY, transformOrigin: '50% 50%' },
    { x: 0, y: 0, scaleX: 1, scaleY: 1, duration, ease },
    0,
  ).fromTo(
    e.uniforms.uHandoff,
    { value: 0 },
    { value: 1, duration: duration / 2, ease: SURGE_EASE, yoyo: true, repeat: 1 },
    0,
  );

  return () => {
    tl.kill();
    unclip();
    e.flying = false;
  };
}, [active, duration, ease, reduced, engine, slots, first]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `disposeRenderer` stops the animation loop before releasing the context, so a queued frame cannot render into a lost one and throw out of the cleanup; it then calls `dispose()`, `forceContextLoss()` and zeroes the canvas dimensions to release the backing store immediately. The `ResizeObserver` is disconnected, both the canvas transform tweens and the `uHandoff` tween are killed, the material and geometry are disposed, and the canvas element is removed by the same effect that appended it. The flight effect's own cleanup kills its timeline and restores the destination slot's original `overflow`, so an unmount mid-flight cannot leave a slot permanently unclipped.

**Reduced motion.** No animation loop is started: one frame is drawn when the context is built, and one more after each move and each resize, so the field is a still image rather than a drifting one. The handoff still moves the canvas — that is a DOM relocation, not motion — but the FLIP tween and the `uHandoff` surge are both skipped, and the drawing buffer is resized immediately instead of on a completion that will never fire. `prefers-reduced-motion` is read by the component through `useReducedMotion`, never inferred from the page.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Rendering the canvas from JSX. React unmounts the outgoing page's subtree on a route change, and a `<canvas ref>` inside it is destroyed with it — context, program, buffer and all. That is the exact failure this component exists to avoid, and it cannot be worked around from inside the page: the canvas has to be created by the effect and owned by nobody React can see.
- A React-owned canvas under `reactStrictMode`. The strict-mode remount reuses the SAME element across both effect invocations, so the first cleanup's `forceContextLoss()` hands the second invocation a dead context and the component renders permanently blank — in development only, which is a genuinely expensive way to lose an afternoon. Creating the element inside the effect gives the second run a clean one.
- Doing the move in `useEffect` instead of `useLayoutEffect`. Passive effects run after the browser has painted, so there is one composited frame in which the outgoing page is gone and the canvas has not arrived. It reads as a flash of empty box at exactly the moment the component is supposed to be proving continuity.
- Measuring First inside the layout effect. By then React has already removed the outgoing subtree, so there is nothing left to measure and the FLIP either animates from the wrong rectangle or is skipped. The measurement has to happen in the handler, before `setState`.
- Calling `renderer.setSize()` during the flight. Writing the canvas's width or height reallocates and clears the drawing buffer, so the object mid-animation flashes black for a frame. The `ResizeObserver` fires exactly then, because moving into a differently sized slot changes the border box — which is why it is muted by a `flying` flag rather than trusted.
- A destination slot that clips. `overflow: hidden` on the slot crops the inbound canvas to its final rectangle from the first frame, so the flight is invisible and the result looks identical to no transition. Forcing `overflow: visible` inline for the duration is the only override that reliably beats a utility class.
- Cloning instead of moving. `cloneNode(true)` on a canvas copies the element and NOT its bitmap or its context; `outerHTML` round-trips have the same effect. The clone is blank and the original is gone, so the page shows an empty box with no error anywhere.
- Tweening `width` and `height` instead of `scale`. Besides reflowing on every frame, they are the two properties that reset the drawing buffer, so the animation would clear the surface sixty times a second.
- Mounting the host inside the routed subtree. If the host unmounts on navigation the context goes with it and there is nothing left to hand over — the component silently degrades to the mount-a-new-one behaviour it replaces. It belongs in the layout, above the router outlet.
- Assuming the canvas paints where you expect. It is `position: absolute; z-index: 1` so it can lift over static page content on the way past, which means anything meant to sit ON TOP of the field needs its own stacking context. Text without `relative z-10` disappears under the canvas for the length of the flight.
- Letting the shader carry any state that could reset. Everything visible is a function of the absolute `setAnimationLoop` timestamp, so there is no accumulator to hand over. Drive the field from a per-frame increment instead and it will still restart on the handoff — the exact artefact the component was built to eliminate, hidden one layer deeper.

## Notes

- In Next.js App Router: mount `CanvasHandoffTransition` in `app/layout.tsx`, put a `CanvasHandoffSlot` in each page with an id of its own, and replace `<Link>` with a button calling `handoff(slotId, () => router.push(href))`. The component imports nothing from `next/navigation` — the route change is a callback, so the same host works under React Router or, as in the preview, plain `useState`.
- The slot renders no children while WebGL is live. That is not cosmetic: React only reconciles children it created, so an empty child list is the guarantee that it will never touch the canvas sitting inside. Content that belongs over the field goes in a sibling, not inside the slot.
- One context for the whole site is the real prize. Chromium allows roughly sixteen live WebGL contexts per renderer process and evicts the oldest without warning when you exceed it — a per-page canvas on a site with a persistent background is how an unrelated component three routes away turns black.
- The field is deliberately slow, about eight seconds per visible cycle. Anything faster and the eye cannot hold a specific fold across the transition, which is the only direct evidence the viewer gets that the surface was not rebuilt.
- Under reduced motion there is no animation loop at all — a single frame is drawn on build and again after each move — so the component costs nothing per frame for the people most likely to be on the weakest hardware.

## Definition of done

Watch one bright fold of the field and click a nav item: the same fold is still there when the canvas lands, offset only by the time the flight took. Nothing blanks, blinks, or restarts. The canvas visibly changes proportion in flight — wide banner to tall column — with the dither cells stretching along with it, then snapping to square at the end when the buffer is finally resized. Click twice in quick succession and the second flight starts from wherever the canvas is in the air rather than jumping to the first destination. In React DevTools the canvas element has no owner. Under `reactStrictMode` in development the preview renders on first load, not blank. With reduced motion the field is a still image and the canvas relocates without a flight.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Capture-Phase Click Swallow

Throw a drag carousel and let go over a card, and the browser dispatches a `click` on it — `mousedown` and `mouseup` landed in the same subtree, so that is exactly what the spec asks for. The result is that flinging the track navigates somewhere. One listener on the drag surface in the capture phase, which runs before any descendant handler, calls `stopPropagation` and `preventDefault` and the click is gone. The work is in the two edges: it has to swallow exactly one, and it has to let keyboard activation through, because Enter and Space fire a click with no pointer sequence behind it.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Cancels the single click a finished drag would fire, in the capture phase, without eating the next real click or keyboard activation.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The listener is registered with `addEventListener('click', handler, true)` on the drag surface. The third argument is the technique: capture runs root-down, so this handler sees the click before the card's own `onClick` and before a router's link interception. In the bubble phase the navigation has already happened.
2. It calls both `stopPropagation()` and `preventDefault()`. They do different jobs and neither covers the other: propagation stops listeners deeper in the path, while the default action — following an `<a href>`, submitting a form, toggling a `<label>` — is not a listener and is only cancelled by `preventDefault`. A swallow with only `stopPropagation` still navigates.
3. `arm()` is called by the gesture when it ends *having moved*, which `drag-deadzone-capture` reports as `onDragEnd(state, { moved })`. Arming on a stationary press is how the click a user actually meant gets eaten.
4. The arm is consumed inside the handler before the event is cancelled, so exactly one click is swallowed. A flag that stays set is the bug this replaces: the drag is suppressed, and so is the deliberate click that follows it.
5. Two independent stand-downs cover the drag that produces no click at all — one that ends over empty space, or that the browser cancelled. A `pointerdown` on the surface disarms, because a fresh press means the awaited click never came; and a 250 ms timer disarms as a backstop, since the click that follows a `pointerup` is dispatched in the same turn and anything later is not it.
6. `event.detail` is the keyboard test. For a pointer click it is the click count, 1 or more; for Enter, Space, and `element.click()` it is 0. Those return early and pass through untouched, so the widget stays operable from the keyboard.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `TIMEOUT_MS = 250`
  How long an arm survives with no click. The click after a `pointerup` arrives in the same turn, so one frame would do for a mouse; the margin is for the delayed synthetic click some touch browsers still emit. The ceiling is the time a person needs to press and release again — go much past ~400 ms and the arm can outlive its own gesture and reach into the next one, which is exactly the bug the expiry exists to prevent.
- `event.detail threshold = 0`
  Not a tuned number but a specified one: `UIEvent.detail` is the click count for a pointer-driven click and exactly 0 for a keyboard-driven or scripted one. Testing `detail === 0` is the only cross-browser tell available on the click event itself — `pointerId === -1` is only present where `click` is a `PointerEvent`, and the `screenX === 0 && screenY === 0` heuristic misfires on a genuine click in the top-left corner of the screen.

## API

```ts
function useClickSwallow(ref: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>, options?: { timeoutMs?: number; enabled?: boolean; onSwallow?: (event: MouseEvent) => void }): { arm: () => void; disarm: () => void; armed: RefObject<boolean>; swallowed: RefObject<number> }
```

- `timeoutMs: number` — default `250`
  How long an arm survives with no click arriving. Backstop for a drag that ends over nothing clickable.
- `enabled: boolean` — default `true`
  Detach the listeners and stand down when false.
- `onSwallow: (event: MouseEvent) => void`
  The click that was cancelled. Already stopped and prevented by the time this runs.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * Milliseconds an arm survives if no click follows. The click that follows a
 * `pointerup` is dispatched in the same turn, so anything over one frame is
 * already generous; the margin is for the delayed click some touch browsers
 * still emit. It has to stay well under the time a person needs to press and
 * release again, or the arm outlives its own gesture.
 */
const TIMEOUT_MS = 250;

/**
 * Suppress the one `click` that a finished drag is about to produce.
 *
 * Pairs with any gesture that reports whether it moved — `drag-deadzone-capture`
 * exposes exactly that as `onDragEnd(state, { moved })`. Arm on `moved`, and
 * only on `moved`: arming after a stationary press is how the click a user
 * meant gets eaten.
 */
export function useClickSwallow(
  ref: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>,
  options: UseClickSwallowOptions = {},
): ClickSwallowHandle {
  const { timeoutMs = TIMEOUT_MS, enabled = true } = options;

  const armed = useRef(false);
  const swallowed = useRef(0);
  const timer = useRef<number | null>(null);

  const config = useRef({ timeoutMs, options });
  config.current = { timeoutMs, options };

  const disarm = useCallback(() => {
    armed.current = false;
    if (timer.current !== null) {
      window.clearTimeout(timer.current);
      timer.current = null;
    }
  }, []);

  const arm = useCallback(() => {
    disarm();
    armed.current = true;
    // An expiry, not a standing flag. A drag that ends over empty space, or
    // one the browser cancelled, produces no click at all — and an arm left
    // standing swallows the user's next real click, whenever that arrives.
    timer.current = window.setTimeout(() => {
      armed.current = false;
      timer.current = null;
    }, config.current.timeoutMs);
  }, [disarm]);

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = ref.current;
    if (!el || !enabled) return;

    const onClickCapture = (e: MouseEvent) => {
      if (!armed.current) return;

      // Enter and Space on a focused link or button dispatch a click with
      // `detail === 0` and no pointer sequence behind it, as does
      // `element.click()`. There is no drag for those to be the tail of, and
      // swallowing them is what makes a drag carousel keyboard-inoperable.
      if (e.detail === 0) return;

      // Consumed here, so exactly one click is swallowed per arm.
      disarm();
      swallowed.current += 1;

      // Both, always. stopPropagation keeps it from the card's own handler and
      // from the router's link interception; preventDefault cancels the
      // default action, which is the part that actually follows an href.
      e.stopPropagation();
      e.preventDefault();

      config.current.options.onSwallow?.(e);
    };

    // A fresh press means the previous gesture is finished and the click it
    // was going to produce never arrived. Second safety net under the timer,
    // and the one that matters — it is deterministic rather than timed.
    const onPointerDown = () => disarm();

    // The third argument is the entire technique. In the bubble phase the
    // card's own handler has already run and the link has already navigated.
    el.addEventListener('click', onClickCapture, true);
    el.addEventListener('pointerdown', onPointerDown);

    return () => {
      el.removeEventListener('click', onClickCapture, true);
      el.removeEventListener('pointerdown', onPointerDown);
      // Without this the timer can fire after unmount and write to a ref that
      // nothing reads, and on a remount the widget starts life armed.
      disarm();
    };
  }, [ref, enabled, disarm]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The effect removes the capture-phase `click` listener with the same capture flag it was added with — passing `true` on the way out is required, since a listener added with capture is a different registration from one added without — removes the `pointerdown` listener, and calls `disarm()`, which clears the pending timeout and resets the flag so a remount does not start armed. No rAF, no pointer capture, nothing else held.

**Reduced motion.** Nothing changes, and the omission is deliberate rather than an oversight: this hook cancels an event, it does not animate anything, and there is no duration, distance, or easing in it to reduce. Behaviour identical under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`. Note that the keyboard path is unconditional for the same reason it matters here — the pass-through for `detail === 0` is an accessibility guarantee, not a motion setting, and it is not something a preference should be able to switch off.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Registering in the bubble phase. The card's own `onClick` runs first and the link has already navigated by the time the handler sees the event — the listener is correct and completely useless. The third argument to `addEventListener` is the whole fix.
- Calling `stopPropagation()` without `preventDefault()`. Every JavaScript handler is silenced and the `<a href>` still navigates, because following a link is a default action rather than a listener. The failure is confusing precisely because the swallow visibly "works" on buttons and does nothing on links.
- Leaving the flag set after the swallow. It eats the click after the drag as well, so the user drags, then clicks a card deliberately, and nothing happens. Consuming it inside the handler is one line and is the difference between a fix and a new bug.
- Setting the flag with no expiry at all. A drag that ends over empty space never produces a click, so the arm just sits there — and swallows a genuine click a minute later, at which point nobody will connect the two events.
- Swallowing keyboard activation. Enter and Space on a focused card dispatch a click with `detail === 0`, and if the flag happens to be armed the widget silently stops responding to the keyboard. It never shows up in testing because a carousel is tested by dragging it.
- Arming on every gesture instead of only on ones that moved. Without a dead zone upstream reporting `moved`, a two-pixel wobble during a click arms the swallow and the click is cancelled — the exact behaviour that makes drag carousels feel unreliable.
- Assuming the click lands on the element the pointer is over. Click targets the nearest common ancestor of the `mousedown` and `mouseup` targets, and while a pointer is captured the compatibility mouse events are retargeted to the capturing element. Scoping the listener to the drag surface is what makes it see the click at all.
- Reaching for `stopImmediatePropagation()` by default. It also silences capture-phase listeners registered earlier on the same node, which can include analytics or a focus manager that had nothing to do with the drag. Escalate to it only when a library has attached its own capture listener to the same element.
- Leaving the timer running at unmount. It fires against a ref nothing reads, and on remount the widget can start life armed and swallow the first click a user makes.

## Notes

- Designed to pair with `drag-deadzone-capture`: that hook decides whether the gesture moved, this one suppresses the consequence. They are separate because the classification is useful on its own, and because the swallow has edge cases — one click and no more, keyboard passes through — that have nothing to do with dragging.
- A component that activates on `pointerup` rather than on `click` cannot be helped by this; there is no click to cancel. That is a good argument for activating on `click` in a draggable surface, since `click` is also what the keyboard produces.
- `preventDefault` on the click does not undo focus. Focus was moved by `mousedown`, earlier in the sequence, so a swallowed drag can leave the card under the pointer focused. It is invisible in practice because focus from a pointer does not match `:focus-visible`.
- A `dblclick` is dispatched independently of the clicks that preceded it, so a component listening for double-click needs the same treatment applied to `dblclick`.

## Definition of done

Click a card: it opens, and the on-screen counter shows one activation and no swallow. Drag the row and release over a card: the row moves, the card does not open, and the swallow counter goes up by exactly one. Immediately click that same card: it opens — the swallow was consumed by the drag and did not carry over. Drag and release over the gap between cards, then click a card: it opens, because the arm expired instead of waiting for a click that never came. Tab to a card and press Enter, then Space: it opens both times, including immediately after a drag, and the swallow counter does not move. Put a real `<a href>` in the row and drag onto it: the page does not navigate.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Char Stagger Then Scale-Up

The headline is on screen from the first frame — small and ghosted, reading as a label. Characters resolve one at a time from left to right, and just before the last one lands the whole word scales to full size with a `back.out` overshoot. It assembles itself, then it asserts itself. Supporting copy fades up a quarter of a second into the scale, so the page is never doing only one thing at a time.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Characters resolve left to right, then the whole word scales up with an overshoot as the last one lands.

- Category: text
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. The text is split in JSX, not in the DOM: `text.split(" ")` gives word boxes, `Array.from(word)` gives one `inline-block` span per character. React owns every node, so no library mutates the tree and no `revert()` is needed to restore it.
2. The idle state — `opacity: dimOpacity` per character and `transform: scale(scaleFrom)` on the word — is written as inline JSX styles, not by GSAP. That makes the server-rendered markup and the no-JS render identical to the pre-animation frame, and it means a parent re-render cannot wipe out what GSAP wrote, because React only ever diffs props against props.
3. A `gsap.timeline` first tweens `[data-char]` to `opacity: 1` with `stagger: 0.07` and `duration: 0.28` on `power1.out`.
4. The word scale is appended at position `">-0.05"` — 50 ms *before* the character stagger ends. The overlap is what fuses two phases into one gesture; at `">"` they read as two separate animations queued back to back.
5. Supporting copy (`[data-fade]`) is appended at `"<0.25"` — 250 ms after the *scale started*, not after it finished. Relative-to-previous-start positioning is what keeps the choreography overlapping rather than sequential.
6. `transformOrigin: "50% 50%"` is set explicitly on the scale tween even though it is the default: a heading inside a flex column can inherit an origin from an earlier transform on an ancestor, and the word then grows out of one corner.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `SCALE_FROM = 0.42`
  Starting scale of the word. Around 0.4 the text reads as a caption; past ~0.65 the growth is not large enough to register as a change of role, and below ~0.3 the characters are illegible while they stagger, so the first half of the animation is wasted.
- `DIM_OPACITY = 0.24`
  Resting strength of an unresolved character, as opacity on `currentColor`. Zero would make the reveal a pop-in and lose the ghosted-label reading; above ~0.4 there is not enough contrast between resolved and unresolved for the sweep to be visible.
- `CHAR_STAGGER = 0.07`
  Seconds between adjacent characters. A ten-character word takes 0.7s to sweep. Below ~0.04 the characters resolve as a block; above ~0.12 a long headline outlasts the reader's patience.
- `CHAR_DURATION = 0.28`
  Seconds for one character. Deliberately four times the stagger, so several characters are always mid-resolve — that overlap is what makes it a sweep rather than a sequence of individual pops.
- `SCALE_DURATION = 0.9`
  Seconds for the scale-up. `back.out` spends most of its curve on the settle, so a shorter duration compresses the overshoot into something that reads as a bounce artefact.
- `OVERSHOOT = 1.3`
  The `back.out(n)` parameter. Around 1.3 the word passes a few percent beyond full size and returns. At 1.7 (GSAP's default) the overshoot on large type is tens of pixels and reads as a wobble.
- `FADE_STAGGER / FADE_DURATION / FADE_Y = 0.12 / 0.7 / 18`
  Supporting copy rises 18px over 0.7s, 0.12s apart. The travel is small on purpose — body copy that moves as far as the headline competes with it.
- `VIEW_THRESHOLD = 0.35`
  Fraction visible before the timeline runs. A headline is tall; requiring more than about a third means it has to be nearly centred before anything happens, and requiring less starts it while it is still a sliver at the bottom edge.

## API

```ts
function CharStaggerScaleUp(props: { text: string; children?: ReactNode; scaleFrom?: number; dimOpacity?: number; charStagger?: number; charDuration?: number; scaleDuration?: number; overshoot?: number; delay?: number; startOnView?: boolean; className?: string; textClassName?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `text: string`
  The headline. Split per word and per character in JSX.
- `children: ReactNode`
  Supporting copy. Fades up after the scale has begun.
- `scaleFrom: number` — default `0.42`
  Starting scale of the whole word.
- `dimOpacity: number` — default `0.24`
  Starting opacity of each character.
- `charStagger: number` — default `0.07`
  Seconds between character reveals.
- `charDuration: number` — default `0.28`
  Seconds for one character to resolve.
- `scaleDuration: number` — default `0.9`
  Seconds for the scale-up.
- `overshoot: number` — default `1.3`
  The `back.out(n)` parameter — how far past 100% the word travels.
- `delay: number` — default `0`
  Seconds before the timeline starts.
- `startOnView: boolean` — default `true`
  Run when scrolled into view rather than on mount.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the wrapper via `cn`.
- `textClassName: string`
  Merged onto the headline span — this is where type size and tracking go.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const SCALE_FROM = 0.42;
const DIM_OPACITY = 0.24;
const CHAR_STAGGER = 0.07;
const CHAR_DURATION = 0.28;
const SCALE_DURATION = 0.9;
const OVERSHOOT = 1.3;
const FADE_DURATION = 0.7;
const FADE_STAGGER = 0.12;
const FADE_Y = 18;
const VIEW_THRESHOLD = 0.35;

export function CharStaggerScaleUp({
  text,
  children,
  scaleFrom = SCALE_FROM,
  dimOpacity = DIM_OPACITY,
  charStagger = CHAR_STAGGER,
  charDuration = CHAR_DURATION,
  scaleDuration = SCALE_DURATION,
  overshoot = OVERSHOOT,
  delay = 0,
  startOnView = true,
  className,
  textClassName,
}: CharStaggerScaleUpProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const word = useRef<HTMLSpanElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const { inView } = useInView(root, { threshold: VIEW_THRESHOLD, once: true });

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = root.current;
    const wordEl = word.current;
    // Reduced motion needs no branch here: the idle state written into the
    // JSX below is already the finished state, so doing nothing is correct.
    if (!el || !wordEl || reduced) return;
    if (startOnView && !inView) return;

    const chars = Array.from(el.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-char]'));
    const fades = Array.from(el.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-fade]'));

    const ctx = gsap.context(() => {
      const tl = gsap.timeline({ delay });

      tl.to(chars, {
        opacity: 1,
        duration: charDuration,
        ease: 'power1.out',
        stagger: charStagger,
      }).to(
        wordEl,
        {
          scale: 1,
          duration: scaleDuration,
          ease: `back.out(${overshoot})`,
          // Set explicitly even though it is the default: a block-level
          // heading inside a flex column can inherit an origin from an
          // earlier transform, and the word then grows out of one corner.
          transformOrigin: '50% 50%',
        },
        '>-0.05',
      );

      if (fades.length > 0) {
        tl.to(
          fades,
          {
            opacity: 1,
            y: 0,
            duration: FADE_DURATION,
            ease: 'power3.out',
            stagger: FADE_STAGGER,
          },
          '<0.25',
        );
      }
    }, el);

    // revert(), not kill(): it also strips the inline transform and opacity
    // GSAP wrote, handing the nodes back in exactly the state React rendered.
    return () => ctx.revert();
  }, [
    text,
    reduced,
    inView,
    startOnView,
    delay,
    charDuration,
    charStagger,
    scaleDuration,
    overshoot,
  ]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The timeline is built inside a `gsap.context` scoped to the root, and teardown calls `ctx.revert()`. That kills the tweens and strips the inline `transform` and `opacity` GSAP wrote, handing the nodes back in exactly the state React rendered — which matters under React 19 StrictMode, where the effect runs twice on mount.

**Reduced motion.** The idle inline styles collapse to the finished state (`scale(1)`, `opacity: 1`, no translate) and the effect returns before building a timeline. The headline and its supporting copy are fully rendered at full size on first paint — nothing is hidden and nothing waits for a trigger.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Splitting text before the webfont has loaded. Character and word boxes are measured against the fallback face, so widths and line breaks are wrong and never re-flow once the real font arrives — see `font-safe-text-split` for the gating and re-split lifecycle this class of component needs.
- Letting a splitting library mutate the DOM under React. React has no record of the injected spans, so the next parent render replaces the whole subtree and the animation targets nodes that are no longer in the document. Splitting in JSX avoids the problem entirely.
- Writing the idle state with `gsap.set` in the effect. The first paint then shows the finished headline at full size before the effect runs, and it visibly snaps down before animating up.
- Splitting straight to characters without word boxes. A line break can then land between two letters of the same word.
- Hardcoding the dim colour as a hex value. `#3d3d3d` is invisible on a light background; opacity on `currentColor` composites correctly against any theme.
- Queuing the scale at `">"` instead of `">-0.05"`. The two phases stop overlapping and the headline reads as "characters appear… then a separate thing happens".
- Cleaning up with `kill()` rather than `revert()`. `kill()` stops the tweens but leaves GSAP's inline `transform` and `opacity` on the nodes, so a remount starts from the finished state.

## Notes

- No text-splitting dependency: the split is declarative JSX. GSAP `SplitText` is reserved for the two components whose subject *is* SplitText (`nested-splittext-restore`, `font-safe-text-split`); everything else here splits in React so consumers are not forced to adopt a DOM-mutating splitter for a per-character stagger.
- Each word is one `inline-block whitespace-nowrap` box with a real text node for the space between words, so lines still wrap normally between words.

## Definition of done

On entering the viewport the characters brighten one at a time from left to right, and the word begins growing before the last character has finished. The word overshoots full size once and settles. Supporting copy starts rising while the word is still growing, not after. Unmount mid-animation and the nodes carry no inline `transform` or `opacity`. With reduced motion enabled the finished headline is present on first paint.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
