# Build: CSS Variable Clip-Path Tween

A panel reveal that tweens a CSS custom property instead of a CSS property. The stage clips itself with `inset(var(--kx-clip))`, and because custom properties inherit, any descendant carrying `.kx-clip-follow` clips with the same value in its own box — one tween, several clip boxes, no possible drift. The media pushes from 1.4 to 1 over half again the clip duration and the lines slide up on a stagger; the exit is the same timeline reversed, which turns the positive stagger into a last-line-first peel and the scale-down back into a push.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

One tweened custom property drives every clip-path on the panel, and reversing the timeline is the exit.

- Category: transition
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. GSAP's CSSPlugin special-cases any property whose name starts with `--`: it reads the start value with `getComputedStyle(target).getPropertyValue(prop)` and writes with `style.setProperty(prop, value)`. Because neither end is a plain number, the tween routes through the complex-string interpolator, which walks both strings and interpolates every number it finds pairwise — `100% 0% 0% 0%` to `0% 0% 0% 0%` is four independent number tweens in one string.
2. The tweened value feeds `clip-path: inset(var(--kx-clip))` on the stage. `inset()` takes `top right bottom left`, so a top inset of 100% collapses the box to nothing and 0% leaves it whole: the reveal is the top edge travelling down.
3. The reason to tween a variable rather than `clipPath` itself is inheritance. `.kx-clip-follow` on any descendant re-uses the same inherited value against its own border box, so a caption reveals in proportion with the panel without a second tween. Tweening `clipPath` on each element instead means N tweens that agree only until someone edits one.
4. The initial `--kx-clip` is declared in the injected stylesheet, not in React's inline style. GSAP writes the tweened value inline, and a React re-render owning that same inline property would reset it mid-tween. It also has to be declared somewhere: an undeclared custom property computes to the empty string, and a tween with no readable start value snaps to its end.
5. One paused timeline is built and then `play()`ed or `reverse()`d. Reversing is not a shortcut — it is the exit the source had: a reversed positive stagger runs last-element-first, and a reversed `scale: 1.4 -> 1` runs `1 -> 1.4`, so the panel leaves with its lines peeling off in reverse while the media is still pushing in.
6. The timeline is built inside `gsap.context()` with `open` deliberately absent from its dependencies. Rebuilding per state change would call `context.revert()`, which strips the inline value GSAP wrote — the closing tween would then read the stylesheet default, fully shut, as its start and animate from nowhere to nowhere.
7. Media and line timings are ratios of the clip duration (1.5x, 0.6x, offset 0.35x) rather than independent numbers, so retuning the reveal cannot desynchronise the three groups.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `duration = 1.2`
  Seconds for the clip. The source ran 2 s, but that timeline was scrubbed against scroll where duration is only a proportion of the scroll range. Played back at real time, 2 s is a panel you wait for; below ~0.8 s the `power3.inOut` has no room for its slow start and the edge appears to jump.
- `mediaScale = 1.4`
  Start scale of the media. Big enough that the settle is legible for the full duration, small enough that a 1x asset is not visibly softened. Also the reason the media needs an `overflow: hidden` wrapper: at 1.4 it is 40% wider than its box.
- `lineStagger = 0.125`
  Seconds between lines. Exactly the source value. At 0 the block arrives as one slab; past ~0.2 s the last line is still climbing after the clip has finished and the reveal appears to have two endings.
- `MEDIA_DURATION_RATIO = 1.5`
  The push outlives the clip by half again. The clip is the event; the scale still resolving after it is what stops the panel feeling like it stopped dead on arrival.
- `LINE_OFFSET_RATIO = 0.35`
  Fraction of the clip before the lines start. Any earlier and they climb inside a box that is still mostly clipped, so the first thing the eye catches is text being cut in half.
- `CLIP_SHUT = '100% 0% 0% 0%'`
  Four percentages, matching the four in `CLIP_OPEN`. The complex-string interpolator pairs numbers positionally, so `inset(100%)` against `inset(0% 0% 0% 0%)` would interpolate one number and leave the other three as literal text.

## API

```ts
function ClipPathVariableTween(props: { open: boolean; children: ReactNode; duration?: number; mediaScale?: number; lineStagger?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `open: boolean`
  `true` plays the reveal, `false` reverses it. Every change re-drives the same timeline.
- `children: ReactNode`
  Content. `[data-clip-media]` is pushed from `mediaScale` to 1; `[data-clip-line]` slides up from 120%.
- `duration: number` — default `1.2`
  Seconds for the clip. Media and line timings are ratios of it.
- `mediaScale: number` — default `1.4`
  Scale the media starts at. 1 disables the push.
- `lineStagger: number` — default `0.125`
  Seconds between lines. Reversed on exit, so the last line leaves first.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the stage, which is the element that carries the clip.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** `inset(top right bottom left)`. Top at 100% collapses the box entirely. */
const CLIP_SHUT = '100% 0% 0% 0%';
const CLIP_OPEN = '0% 0% 0% 0%';

/**
 * Media scale outlives the clip by half again. The clip is the event; the push
 * continuing past it is what stops the panel feeling like it stopped dead.
 */
const MEDIA_DURATION_RATIO = 1.5;
const LINE_DURATION_RATIO = 0.6;
/** Lines start when the clip is a third open — before that they are hidden. */
const LINE_OFFSET_RATIO = 0.35;

const CLIP_CSS = `
.kx-clip-stage {
  /* Declared in CSS, never in React's inline style: GSAP writes the tweened
     value to the inline style, and a React re-render would reset it mid-tween.
     It also has to be declared SOMEWHERE — an undeclared custom property
     computes to the empty string, and a tween with no start value snaps. */
  --kx-clip: ${CLIP_SHUT};
  clip-path: inset(var(--kx-clip));
}
/* Any descendant clipped by the same inherited variable. */
.kx-clip-follow {
  clip-path: inset(var(--kx-clip));
}
`;

export interface ClipPathVariableTweenProps {
  /** `true` reveals, `false` clips away. Every change plays or reverses. */
  open: boolean;
  /**
   * Content. Two opt-in hooks:
   * `[data-clip-media]` is pushed from `mediaScale` to 1, and
   * `[data-clip-line]` slides up from 120% with a stagger.
   */
  children: ReactNode;
  /** Seconds for the clip itself. Media and lines are derived ratios of it. */
  duration?: number;
  /** Scale the media starts at. 1 disables the push. */
  mediaScale?: number;
  /** Seconds between lines. Reversed on exit, so the last line leaves first. */
  lineStagger?: number;
  className?: string;
}

export function ClipPathVariableTween({
  open,
  children,
  duration = 1.2,
  mediaScale = 1.4,
  lineStagger = 0.125,
  className,
}: ClipPathVariableTweenProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const timeline = useRef<ReturnType<typeof gsap.timeline> | null>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  // Built once and held paused. Rebuilding it per `open` change would be
  // wrong twice over: `gsap.context().revert()` strips the inline value GSAP
  // wrote, so a closing tween would read the CSS default — fully shut — as its
  // start and animate from nowhere to nowhere.
  useGsap(
    gsap,
    () => {
      const el = root.current;
      if (!el) return;

      const media = el.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-clip-media]');
      const lines = el.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-clip-line]');

      const tl = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });

      tl.fromTo(
        el,
        { '--kx-clip': CLIP_SHUT },
        { '--kx-clip': CLIP_OPEN, duration, ease: 'power3.inOut' },
        0,
      );

      if (media.length > 0) {
        tl.fromTo(
          media,
          { scale: mediaScale },
          {
            scale: 1,
            duration: duration * MEDIA_DURATION_RATIO,
            ease: 'power2.out',
          },
          0,
        );
      }

      if (lines.length > 0) {
        tl.fromTo(
          lines,
          { yPercent: 120 },
          {
            yPercent: 0,
            duration: duration * LINE_DURATION_RATIO,
            ease: 'power3.out',
            stagger: lineStagger,
          },
          duration * LINE_OFFSET_RATIO,
        );
      }

      timeline.current = tl;
      return () => {
        timeline.current = null;
      };
    },
    root,
    [duration, mediaScale, lineStagger],
  );

  // Same dependency list plus `open`, so this always runs after the effect
  // above has rebuilt the timeline rather than driving a stale one.
  useEffect(() => {
    const tl = timeline.current;
    if (!tl) return;

    if (reduced) {
      // A jump, not a zero-duration tween: the timeline is seeked to the
      // correct end state and stays paused there. Clip, scale and line offsets
      // all land correctly because they are all on this one timeline.
      tl.progress(open ? 1 : 0).pause();
      return;
    }

    if (open) tl.play();
    else tl.reverse();
  }, [open, reduced, duration, mediaScale, lineStagger]);

  return (
    <div ref={root} className={cn('kx-clip-stage', className)}>
      <style href="kinetic-clip-path-variable-tween" precedence="medium">
        {CLIP_CSS}
      </style>
      {children}
    </div>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useGsap` runs everything inside `gsap.context()` and calls `revert()` on unmount, which kills the timeline and removes the inline `--kx-clip`, `transform` and `scale` GSAP wrote so React never inherits a stray style. The context callback also nulls the timeline ref, so the effect that plays it cannot touch a reverted timeline.

**Reduced motion.** The timeline is seeked with `tl.progress(open ? 1 : 0).pause()` — a jump to the correct end state, not a zero-duration tween. Because the clip, the media scale and every line offset all live on that one timeline, one seek lands all of them correctly, which is the practical argument for putting them there in the first place.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Writing the custom property through React's inline `style` as well. React owns that attribute and GSAP writes to it; the first re-render during a tween resets the value and the clip snaps back.
- Never declaring the custom property. An undeclared custom property computes to the empty string, so GSAP has nothing to parse as a start value and the tween jumps straight to its end on the first frame.
- Mismatching the number count between the two clip strings. The interpolator pairs numbers positionally, so `inset(100%)` to `inset(0% 0% 0% 0%)` animates the first number and carries the rest through as text.
- Rebuilding the timeline whenever the open state changes. `gsap.context().revert()` removes the inline value GSAP wrote, so the reverse tween reads the stylesheet default as its start and animates from the closed state to the closed state — the exit silently does nothing.
- Tweening `clipPath` on each element instead of one shared variable. It works on the day you write it and drifts the first time one of the durations is tuned, because nothing structural keeps them equal.
- Forgetting `overflow: hidden` on the media wrapper and on each line. A 1.4x scale overflows its box by 40%, and a line entering from `yPercent: 120` is visible below its own box the entire way up.
- Assuming a clipped-away panel is inert. `clip-path` does clip hit-testing, but anything positioned outside the clip region — a fixed-position child, a focusable control — can still be reached by the keyboard, so the panel also needs its interactive state driven from the same flag.
- Tweening `--kx-clip` with a scrubbed ScrollTrigger and expecting sub-pixel smoothness. Custom property writes invalidate style for the whole inheritance subtree, so a stage with hundreds of descendants pays for it on every frame. The technique earns its keep with a handful of followers, not hundreds.

## Notes

- The `open` flag is the API surface, so a faked route change, a real router, an `IntersectionObserver` or a click all drive it identically. Nothing here imports a router.
- Registering the property with `@property { syntax: "<percentage>+" }` is not needed: GSAP interpolates the string itself and never asks the browser to. Register it only if you also want CSS transitions or keyframes to animate the same variable.
- `inset()` is the only basic shape whose numbers interpolate this cleanly. `polygon()` works the same way as long as both sides have the same vertex count, which is the same constraint stated differently.
- For a full-page version, put the stage on the layout wrapper and the follower class on the header rule and the footer — one tween, three clip boxes, and the whole chrome resolves together.

## Definition of done

Click an index row: the panel's top edge travels down over 1.2 s, the media resolves from a 1.4x push, the three lines climb into place 0.125 s apart, and the meta rule at the bottom clips itself in step without a tween of its own. Click Close: the panel clips back up, the last line leaves first, and the media pushes in again — the index underneath is revealed, not covered by a second animation. With reduced motion the panel is simply present or absent with the media at 1x and the lines in place.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Compound Group Hover Card

A content card that answers a hover with a short sequence rather than a single state flip: it lifts, its icon tilts and overshoots its scale, a corner blob brightens, and the affordance arrow slides in — each on its own duration and delay. The trigger is `:hover, :has(:focus-visible)`, so a keyboard user tabbing to the link inside gets exactly the same four changes.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

One hover drives four changes on three elements, each with its own duration and curve. Keyboard gets all four.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The card owns `translate` and `border-color` on a 260ms `cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)`. It is the fastest change in the set because it is the one that acknowledges the pointer — anything slower and the card feels like it is deciding whether to respond.
2. The icon animates `rotate` over 320ms on the same ease and `scale` over 420ms on `cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1)`, both delayed 40ms. Two curves on one element is only possible because `rotate` and `scale` are independent properties; packed into `transform` they would share a single duration and a single easing, and the overshoot would drag the rotation with it.
3. The corner blob is a radial gradient that is blurred once at paint time (`filter: blur(2rem)`) and thereafter only changes `opacity` 0.12 to 0.4 over 500ms and `scale` 1 to 1.15 over 700ms. It is the slowest element in the group, which is what makes it read as lighting rather than as a moving object.
4. `z-index: -1` on the blob places it above the card background and below the card content with no extra wrapper, and `isolation: isolate` on the card stops that negative index from escaping into the page stacking context and sliding behind an ancestor background.
5. The arrow translates 4px and goes from 0.4 to 1 opacity after an 80ms delay — last in the sequence, so the eye arrives at the call to action after the card has already committed to the hover.
6. The whole card is clickable through a stretched pseudo-element on the anchor (`::after { position: absolute; inset: 0 }`), so there is exactly one focusable, screen-reader-announced target. The card responds to that anchor's focus through `:has(:focus-visible)`, which is what gives keyboard parity without a single line of JavaScript.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `lift = -6px`
  Card travel on hover. Under 3px it is not distinguishable from a rendering shift; over about 10px the card visibly overlaps its neighbour in a tight grid and the shadow it does not have becomes conspicuous.
- `durations = 260 / 320 / 420 / 500 / 700 ms`
  Ascending by element weight: card, icon rotation, icon scale, blob opacity, blob scale. Equal durations collapse the sequence into a single snap; the spread is the entire effect. The 260ms floor is roughly the shortest a positional change can be and still be perceived as movement rather than a jump.
- `delays = 40ms icon, 80ms arrow`
  Small enough to feel like consequence rather than queueing. Past about 120ms the arrow reads as a second, separate event and a fast pointer pass leaves it half-animated.
- `icon scale = 1.1 with cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1)`
  The 1.56 control point overshoots to roughly 1.13 before settling. Overshoot on a small element reads as physical; on the card itself it would read as a bug, which is why only the icon gets it.
- `blob opacity range = 0.12 to 0.40`
  It must be visible at rest — a blob that appears only on hover reads as a new object arriving, not as a light coming up. 0.12 is enough to establish it; past about 0.5 the accent starts tinting the body copy.
- `icon rotation = -6deg`
  Anticlockwise, because the arrow moves right and the two would otherwise both push the same direction and read as a shear. Past about 10deg a glyph-based icon starts to look misaligned rather than tilted.

## API

```ts
function CompoundGroupHover(props: { title: string; description: string; eyebrow?: string; icon?: ReactNode; href?: string; accent?: string; action?: string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `title: string`
  Card heading, rendered as an `h3`.
- `description: string`
  Body copy under the heading.
- `eyebrow: string`
  Small uppercase label above the title.
- `icon: ReactNode`
  Rendered inside the tilting badge. An inline SVG or a single character.
- `href: string`
  Renders the affordance link and stretches it over the whole card.
- `accent: string` — default `'var(--color-accent, currentColor)'`
  Drives the blob, the icon border and the link colour.
- `action: string` — default `'Read more'`
  Text of the affordance link.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the card via `cn`. Use it for sizing inside a grid.

## Reference implementation of the core

the component as fixed.


## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to clean up. No listeners, no timers, no animation frames; the hover state lives entirely in the cascade. React removes the hoisted `<style>` when the last card unmounts.

**Reduced motion.** A `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block cancels the three positional changes — the card no longer lifts, the icon no longer tilts or scales, the arrow no longer slides — while keeping every non-positional one. The border still brightens, the blob still comes up from 0.12 to 0.4 opacity, and the arrow still reaches full opacity, so hover and keyboard focus remain visibly acknowledged.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Packing the icon lift into `transform: rotate(-6deg) scale(1.1)`. It works, but both halves are now one property with one duration — the moment you want the scale to overshoot and the rotation not to, you have to split them, and splitting `transform` mid-project means rewriting every rule that touches it.
- Transitioning `filter: blur()` on the blob instead of `opacity`. Every frame re-runs a 2rem blur over a 14rem box; on a grid of six cards a single pointer sweep drops the page into the teens.
- Making the card itself a `<div role="link" tabindex="0">` to get a focus state. It is not announced as a link, it does not middle-click, it does not open in a new tab, and it needs a keydown handler. The stretched `::after` on a real anchor gives all of that for one pseudo-element.
- Using `:focus-within` instead of `:has(:focus-visible)`. `:focus-within` fires on mouse clicks too, so the card sticks in its hover state after every click and only releases when something else is focused.
- Omitting `isolation: isolate` on the card. The blob's `z-index: -1` then resolves against whichever ancestor last created a stacking context and the blob disappears behind a section background — intermittently, depending on what else is on the page.
- Leaving all four changes in place under reduced motion. Lift, tilt and slide are motion; the border, the blob and the arrow opacity are not. Disabling the whole hover state is over-correction and leaves the card with no feedback at all.
- Forgetting `overflow: hidden` on the card. The blob is positioned 4rem outside the card on two sides and paints over the neighbouring card in a grid.

## Notes

- `:has()` needs Safari 15.4+, Chrome 105+ and Firefox 121+. Where it is unsupported the pointer hover still works exactly as written and the keyboard path degrades to the browser's own focus ring on the link.
- Independent `translate` / `rotate` / `scale` need Chrome 104+, Safari 14.1+, Firefox 72+. In older engines the properties are dropped and the card still changes colour and opacity on hover.
- The accent is one custom property, `--kx-hcard-accent`, read by the blob, the icon and the link. A grid of these differs only by that value.

## Definition of done

Hover the card and four things change on four different timings — you can see the arrow arrive after the card has already lifted. Tab to the link with the keyboard and the identical four changes happen. Click the card anywhere, including on the description text, and the link activates. Turn reduced motion on: nothing moves, but the border, blob and arrow still respond.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Conic @property Border

A rounded box wearing an animated conic-gradient border. Two bright stops travel around the ring in opposite quadrants, so the ring reads as rotating rather than blinking. The whole thing is one element and one keyframe — the only moving part is a registered custom property holding an angle, which the browser interpolates for you.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A gradient ring that rotates around a rounded box. Two highlights chase each other; no JavaScript runs.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. `@property --kx-conic-angle { syntax: "<angle>"; inherits: false; initial-value: 0deg }` registers the custom property so the browser knows its value is an angle. An unregistered custom property is an untyped token stream: a keyframe from `0deg` to `360deg` has no interpolation rule and the value flips at the 50% mark instead of sweeping.
2. A single keyframe block, `@keyframes kx-conic-spin { to { --kx-conic-angle: 360deg } }`, drives that property from its `initial-value` to a full turn over `--kx-conic-duration` with `linear` timing. Linear is required: any ease makes the highlights visibly hesitate once per revolution.
3. The element carries two backgrounds. `linear-gradient(fill, fill) padding-box` paints the interior flat; `conic-gradient(from var(--kx-conic-angle), …) border-box` paints under the border. With `border: 1.5px solid transparent`, the conic layer survives the clip only in the ring, which is how the gradient follows `border-radius` — `border-image` cannot round corners.
4. The gradient has six stops with the glow colour at 55deg and 305deg and the rest colour everywhere else. Two highlights roughly opposite each other read as rotation; a single highlight reads as a light blinking on and off once per cycle.
5. `inherits: false` on the registration stops descendants from picking up the animating value. With inheritance on, every element in the subtree re-resolves its computed style on every frame of the animation, which turns a one-element repaint into a whole-subtree style recalculation.
6. Every colour is read through `var(--name, fallback)`, so the component renders correctly with no props and can be re-themed by setting `--conic-glow` or `--conic-fill` on any ancestor.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `glow stop positions = 55deg and 305deg`
  Two highlights, not one, and not diametrically opposite. 250 degrees apart means one is entering the top edge as the other leaves the bottom, so there is always motion somewhere on the ring. At 180 degrees apart the pair reads as a symmetric pulse; with one stop it reads as a blinking dot.
- `durationMs = 4000`
  One revolution. Below ~2500 ms the ring reads as a loading spinner and demands attention; above ~7000 ms the highlight barely appears to move and the border looks like a static gradient someone got wrong.
- `thickness = 1.5px`
  Sub-pixel on a 1x display, which is what keeps it a hairline rather than a stripe. At 1px the highlight is too thin to read colour; at 3px or more the conic banding between stops becomes visible as facets.
- `rest colour alpha = currentColor at 10%`
  The dim majority of the ring. At 0% the border disappears between highlights and the box appears to lose its outline; above ~20% the contrast against the glow collapses and the rotation stops reading.
- `reduced-motion parked angle = 132deg`
  Puts one highlight past the top-left shoulder rather than exactly on an edge or a corner. At the `initial-value` of 0deg the highlight sits dead centre on the right edge, which looks like a rendering artefact rather than a decision.

## API

```ts
function ConicBorder(props: { children: ReactNode; durationMs?: number; thickness?: string; radius?: string; glow?: string; rest?: string; fill?: string; paused?: boolean; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Content rendered inside the ring. The element is `inline-flex`, centred.
- `durationMs: number` — default `4000`
  Milliseconds for one full revolution.
- `thickness: string` — default `'1.5px'`
  Ring thickness. Becomes the transparent border width.
- `radius: string` — default `'9999px'`
  Corner radius. The gradient follows it, unlike `border-image`.
- `glow: string`
  Colour of the two travelling highlights. Defaults to `currentColor`.
- `rest: string`
  Colour of the dim ring between highlights. Defaults to `currentColor` at 10%.
- `fill: string`
  Interior fill. Must be opaque or the gradient shows through the middle.
- `paused: boolean` — default `false`
  Sets `animation-play-state: paused`, freezing the ring at its current angle.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the ring element via `cn`. Use it for padding and typography.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/* Injected once per document. React 19 hoists `<style href precedence>` into
   <head> and de-duplicates by `href`, so a hundred rings ship one rule set —
   and `@property` registration is global anyway, so re-declaring it per
   instance would be pure waste. */
const CONIC_BORDER_CSS = `
@property --kx-conic-angle {
  syntax: "<angle>";
  inherits: false;
  initial-value: 0deg;
}

@keyframes kx-conic-spin {
  to { --kx-conic-angle: 360deg; }
}

.kx-conic {
  position: relative;
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  isolation: isolate;

  border: var(--kx-conic-width, 1.5px) solid transparent;
  border-radius: var(--kx-conic-radius, 9999px);

  /* padding-box layer paints the interior, border-box layer paints under the
     ring. Order matters: the first background listed is the topmost. */
  background:
    linear-gradient(var(--kx-conic-fill), var(--kx-conic-fill)) padding-box,
    conic-gradient(
      from var(--kx-conic-angle),
      var(--kx-conic-rest)   0deg,
      var(--kx-conic-glow)  55deg,
      var(--kx-conic-rest) 130deg,
      var(--kx-conic-rest) 230deg,
      var(--kx-conic-glow) 305deg,
      var(--kx-conic-rest) 360deg
    ) border-box;

  animation: kx-conic-spin var(--kx-conic-duration, 4s) linear infinite;
}

.kx-conic[data-paused='true'] {
  animation-play-state: paused;
}

/* No motion: keep the ring, stop the revolution, and park a highlight
   off-axis so the border still reads as decorated rather than broken. */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .kx-conic {
    animation: none;
    --kx-conic-angle: 132deg;
  }
}
`;

export function ConicBorder({
  children,
  durationMs = 4000,
  thickness = '1.5px',
  radius = '9999px',
  glow,
  rest,
  fill,
  paused = false,
  className,
}: ConicBorderProps) {
  /* Every colour resolves through a `var(..., fallback)` chain, so the
     component works with zero configuration and is themeable by setting one
     property on any ancestor. `Canvas` is the system background keyword — a
     last resort that is at least the right polarity in both colour schemes. */
  const style: StyleWithVars = {
    '--kx-conic-duration': `${durationMs}ms`,
    '--kx-conic-width': thickness,
    '--kx-conic-radius': radius,
    '--kx-conic-glow': glow ?? 'var(--conic-glow, currentColor)',
    '--kx-conic-rest':
      rest ?? 'var(--conic-rest, color-mix(in oklab, currentColor 10%, transparent))',
    '--kx-conic-fill': fill ?? 'var(--conic-fill, var(--color-bg, Canvas))',
  };

  return (
    <>
      <style href="kinetic-conic-property-border" precedence="medium">
        {CONIC_BORDER_CSS}
      </style>
      <div
        className={cn('kx-conic', className)}
        style={style}
        data-paused={paused ? 'true' : undefined}
      >
        {children}
      </div>
    </>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to clean up. There is no listener, no timer and no animation frame; unmounting the element removes the only thing that was running. The hoisted `<style>` is reference-counted by React and removed when the last instance unmounts.

**Reduced motion.** A `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block sets `animation: none` and pins `--kx-conic-angle` to 132deg. The gradient border stays — same colours, same thickness — it simply does not revolve. Nothing is removed from the layout and no size changes.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Animating the custom property without registering it with `@property`. The animation runs — `getComputedStyle` even reports it — but the gradient snaps from its start angle to its end angle at the halfway point, because an unregistered custom property interpolates as a discrete token stream. This is the single most common way this effect is reported "broken".
- Writing `border: 1.5px solid` with no colour, or omitting the border entirely. With no border there is no border-box area outside the padding box, the conic layer is fully covered by the fill layer, and the ring is invisible. The border must exist and must be transparent.
- Putting the fill layer second in the `background` list. Backgrounds paint first-listed on top; with the order reversed the flat fill is painted underneath and the conic gradient covers the entire box, not just the ring.
- Leaving `inherits` at its default of `true`. Descendants then inherit an animating value, so the browser recomputes styles for the whole subtree every frame. On a card with 40 children this shows up as a steady 3-5 ms of style recalculation per frame in a performance profile.
- Assuming the animation is compositor-driven and reaching for `will-change: transform`. It is not: animating a registered property repaints the element background on the main thread every frame. That is cheap on a button and expensive on a full-width hero — scale the element, not the hint.
- Using a semi-transparent interior fill. The conic layer extends under the whole border box, so anything less than opaque lets the gradient bleed through the middle of the card.

## Notes

- `@property` needs Safari 16.4+, Chrome 85+, Firefox 128+. Where it is unsupported the `@property` rule is dropped, the keyframe cannot animate the custom property, and `from var(--kx-conic-angle)` falls back to the guaranteed-invalid initial value — the conic gradient still paints from 0deg. The degradation is a static two-highlight ring, which is an acceptable border on its own.
- The CSS ships inside the component as a `<style href precedence>` element. React 19 hoists it into `<head>` and de-duplicates by `href`, so any number of instances contribute one rule set and one `@property` registration.
- The class name is prefixed `kx-` rather than scoped per instance on purpose: `@property` registration is document-global, so per-instance scoping would buy nothing and cost a style element per mount.

## Definition of done

Two bright arcs travel continuously around the border and pass the corners without pausing or jumping — in particular, nothing snaps at the halfway point of the cycle. The interior stays fully opaque. Set `paused` and the arcs freeze where they are. Enable reduced motion at the OS level and the ring is still coloured but completely still.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: One Reveal Engine, Two Axes

Lines rise out of a clipping box and fade up as their group enters. The interesting part is that the same builder serves a vertical page section and a panel riding a pinned horizontal strip — handed the strip's tween as `containerAnimation`, ScrollTrigger measures against that timeline's progress instead of scroll position. One set of numbers, two directions, nothing to keep in sync by hand.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

The same staggered line reveal fires for vertical sections and for panels on a horizontal track.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. The subtree is scanned for `[data-reveal-group]` elements; each becomes one ScrollTrigger. A subtree with no groups reveals as a single group rooted on the component itself.
2. Inside a group, every `[data-reveal]` element is a target of one `gsap.fromTo` running `{ yPercent: 110, opacity: 0.15 }` to `{ yPercent: 0, opacity: 1 }` on `power3.out` with a 0.12 s stagger — so the group is one tween, not one tween per line, and the stagger is real rather than simulated with delays.
3. When a `containerAnimation` is supplied it is spread into the trigger vars and the position keywords flip from `top 88% / top 45%` to `left 85% / left 45%`, because a trigger attached to a container animation measures along that container's axis.
4. The `containerAnimation` prop is tri-state: `undefined` means vertical flow, an animation means horizontal, and `null` means "a sibling owns the timeline and has not built it yet" — in which case nothing is built at all this commit.
5. `scrub: 0.4` ties the reveal to scroll position with a short catch-up, so reversing direction reverses the reveal instead of replaying it.
6. Everything is created inside a `gsap.context` scoped to the root, so `ctx.revert()` kills the triggers and restores the inline `transform` and `opacity` the tween wrote.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `lift = 110`
  Start offset as a percentage of the element's own height. 100 puts the line exactly at the bottom edge of its clipping box; 110 adds a sliver of overshoot so descenders are hidden through the whole travel rather than peeking under the mask on the first frame.
- `START_OPACITY = 0.15`
  Not 0. A line that fades from fully transparent reads as two separate events — a fade and a move. Starting at 0.15 makes the movement the thing you notice and the fade a supporting detail.
- `stagger = 0.12`
  Seconds between lines within a group. Below ~0.06 the lines read as one block; above ~0.2 the last line arrives after the eye has already moved on, which reads as lag rather than rhythm.
- `scrub = 0.4`
  Short catch-up so the reveal follows the scrollbar but survives a wheel step. At 0 the tween inherits every input spike; above ~1 the lines are still arriving after the section has left.
- `start / end (horizontal) = 'left 85%' / 'left 45%'`
  With `containerAnimation` the trigger is measured along the container's axis. Vertical keywords resolve to a position the element never occupies on that axis, so the tween simply never runs.

## API

```ts
function AxisReveals(props: { children: ReactNode; scroller?: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>; containerAnimation?: gsap.core.Animation | null; scrub?: number; lift?: number; stagger?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Markup containing `[data-reveal-group]` scopes and `[data-reveal]` targets.
- `scroller: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>`
  Scroll container the triggers read. Omit for the document.
- `containerAnimation: gsap.core.Animation | null`
  Omit for vertical flow, pass a horizontal tween to measure against it, pass `null` to hold off until that tween exists.
- `scrub: number` — default `0.4`
  Seconds of catch-up on the reveal.
- `lift: number` — default `110`
  Start offset as a percentage of the element height.
- `stagger: number` — default `0.12`
  Seconds between elements inside a group.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the wrapper. Use `contents` when the wrapper must not affect layout.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function AxisReveals({
  children,
  scroller,
  containerAnimation,
  scrub = 0.4,
  lift = 110,
  stagger = 0.12,
  className,
}: AxisRevealsProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  useEffect(() => {
    const rootEl = root.current;
    if (!rootEl || reduced) return;
    // Explicit "not ready": a sibling owns the timeline and has not built it.
    if (containerAnimation === null) return;

    const scrollerEl = scroller?.current ?? undefined;
    const horizontal = containerAnimation !== undefined;

    const ctx = gsap.context(() => {
      const groups = Array.from(rootEl.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-reveal-group]'));
      // A subtree with no explicit groups reveals as one group.
      const scopes = groups.length > 0 ? groups : [rootEl];

      for (const group of scopes) {
        const targets = Array.from(group.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-reveal]'));
        if (targets.length === 0) continue;

        gsap.fromTo(
          targets,
          { yPercent: lift, opacity: START_OPACITY },
          {
            yPercent: 0,
            opacity: 1,
            ease: 'power3.out',
            duration: 1,
            stagger,
            scrollTrigger: {
              trigger: group,
              scroller: scrollerEl,
              // The line everyone gets wrong. With `containerAnimation` the
              // trigger measures along the container's axis, so the position
              // keywords must be horizontal. "top 85%" against a horizontal
              // container resolves to a position the element never occupies,
              // and the reveal silently never fires.
              start: horizontal ? 'left 85%' : 'top 88%',
              end: horizontal ? 'left 45%' : 'top 45%',
              scrub,
              // Spreading rather than passing `undefined`: ScrollTrigger
              // branches on the key's presence, not on its value.
              ...(containerAnimation ? { containerAnimation } : {}),
            },
          },
        );
      }
    }, rootEl);

    return () => ctx.revert();
  }, [scroller, containerAnimation, scrub, lift, stagger, reduced]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `ctx.revert()` on unmount and on every dependency change: it kills each group's tween and ScrollTrigger and restores the inline `transform` and `opacity` GSAP wrote, so a re-mount measures clean markup rather than the last run's end state.

**Reduced motion.** No triggers are created and no `fromTo` runs, so every line renders at its final position and full opacity on first paint. The clipping boxes stay in the markup and do nothing, so the layout is byte-for-byte the finished state.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Keeping vertical keywords when passing `containerAnimation`. `start: "top 85%"` produces no error, no warning and no animation — the panels simply arrive already revealed, and the bug survives review because nothing is broken, only absent.
- Passing `containerAnimation: undefined` explicitly. ScrollTrigger branches on whether the key exists, so an `undefined` value is not the same as an absent key; the code spreads the object conditionally for exactly this reason.
- Treating a not-yet-built timeline as the vertical case. The strip's tween is created in a sibling effect and arrives one render later, so a naive `containerAnimation ?? undefined` builds a full set of vertical triggers on horizontal content and tears them down on the next commit — visible as a flash of pre-revealed panels.
- Writing a second reveal system for the horizontal section. Two systems mean two staggers, two easings and two sets of position keywords, and they diverge the first time someone tunes one of them.
- Building one tween per line instead of one tween per group. Stagger stops being a property of the group and becomes a pile of hand-computed delays, which no longer reverse correctly when the user scrolls back up.

## Notes

- Combine with `pinned-horizontal-track`: pass its `onTrack` payload's `animation` straight into `containerAnimation`.
- ScrollTrigger forbids `pin` on a trigger that has a `containerAnimation`. Pin the strip's section, never the panels riding it.

## Definition of done

Scroll the vertical section: the three lines rise out of their masks in sequence and reverse cleanly when you scroll back up. Keep scrolling into the pinned strip: each panel's lines rise with the same rhythm as it crosses the container, not as it crosses the viewport. With reduced motion on, every line is already in place.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Converging Flow Steps

A process diagram that assembles itself as you scroll. The two outer cards converge toward the middle from opposite ends while the connectors between them pop in at 35% through the timeline — after the cards are already moving. That ordering is the entire effect: connectors that arrive first read as "boxes with arrows", connectors that arrive during the movement read as "these things connect".

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A process diagram that closes from both ends while the connectors pop in a third of the way through.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. One `gsap.timeline` on a `scrollTrigger` with `start: "top 92%"`, `end: "center 52%"` and `scrub: 1.2` — deliberately the slowest scrub in the set, because a diagram should settle rather than track the wheel.
2. The first and last cards get `fromTo` tweens at position 0 with `±14` on the layout axis, so they close toward the centre from opposite ends. Cards in between have nowhere to converge from and only fade; giving them a direction too makes the row look shuffled rather than closing.
3. The connectors get `fromTo({ autoAlpha: 0, scale: 0.6 }, { autoAlpha: 1, scale: 1, stagger: 0.2 })` placed at absolute timeline position `0.35`. The card tweens run 0 → 1, so 0.35 is a third of the way into their travel.
4. The convergence axis is chosen from the measured container width, not the viewport: under `stackBelow` px the row becomes a column and the tweens switch from `xPercent` to `yPercent`. A stacked column with horizontal convergence has cards sliding past each other sideways.
5. The single-step case is handled explicitly — `first === last` would otherwise mean two `fromTo` tweens fighting over one element, one pulling it from -14 and one from +14.
6. `ease: "none"` throughout. Under a scrub the ease applies to timeline time, so easing here desynchronises the two converging cards from each other.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `scrub = 1.2`
  Over a second of catch-up — very slow. Right for a diagram, which you want to see settle; wrong for a hero, which would feel unresponsive. Below ~0.6 the diagram snaps together as fast as you scroll and the assembly reads as a jump.
- `connectorAt = 0.35`
  Absolute timeline position, in seconds, where the connectors start. The cards run 0 → 1, so this is a third of the way into their travel. At 0 the arrows are present before there is anything to connect; past ~0.6 they arrive after everything has stopped and read as an afterthought.
- `converge = 14`
  Percent of the card's own size. Small on purpose: this is a settling gesture, not an entrance. Past ~25% the outer cards start visibly outside the tinted wrapper and the diagram looks broken at the start of the scrub.
- `CONNECTOR_SCALE = 0.6`
  Starting scale for the pop. Below ~0.4 the arrow is a dot for the first half of its tween; above ~0.8 there is no pop left to see.
- `connectorStagger = 0.2`
  Seconds between connectors. Long enough that a three-step flow reads left to right rather than all at once, which is what tells the reader the diagram has a direction.
- `stackBelow = 420`
  Container width in px below which three cards in a row are too narrow to hold a title and a line of body. Measured from the element, not the window, because this component is usually inside a column that is narrow while the window is wide.

## API

```ts
function ConvergingFlowSteps(props: { steps: { title: string; body?: string; kicker?: string }[]; converge?: number; scrub?: number; connectorAt?: number; connectorStagger?: number; stackBelow?: number; start?: string; end?: string; scrollerRef?: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `steps: { title: string; body?: string; kicker?: string }[]`
  Ordered steps. Connectors are inserted between consecutive pairs.
- `converge: number` — default `14`
  Outer-card travel as a percentage of its own size, along the layout axis.
- `scrub: number` — default `1.2`
  Seconds of catch-up behind the scroll position.
- `connectorAt: number` — default `0.35`
  Timeline position, in seconds, at which the connectors begin.
- `connectorStagger: number` — default `0.2`
  Seconds between connectors.
- `stackBelow: number` — default `420`
  Container width in px below which the row becomes a column and the axis flips.
- `start: string` — default `'top 92%'`
  ScrollTrigger start.
- `end: string` — default `'center 52%'`
  ScrollTrigger end.
- `scrollerRef: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>`
  The scroll container that owns the scroll position. Omit for the document.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the wrapper via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const CONNECTOR_SCALE = 0.6;

export function ConvergingFlowSteps({
  steps,
  converge = 14,
  scrub = 1.2,
  connectorAt = 0.35,
  connectorStagger = 0.2,
  stackBelow = 420,
  start = 'top 92%',
  end = 'center 52%',
  scrollerRef,
  className,
}: ConvergingFlowStepsProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const { width } = useResizeObserver(root);

  // The convergence axis has to follow the layout axis, or a stacked column
  // gets cards sliding in sideways past each other. Measured from the element
  // rather than the viewport: this component is often inside a panel that is
  // narrow while the window is wide.
  const stacked = width > 0 && width < stackBelow;

  useGsap(
    gsap,
    () => {
      const container = root.current;
      if (!container || reduced) return;

      const cards = Array.from(container.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-flow-card]'));
      const connectors = Array.from(
        container.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-flow-connector]'),
      );
      const first = cards[0];
      const last = cards[cards.length - 1];
      if (!first || !last) return;

      const axis = stacked ? 'yPercent' : 'xPercent';
      const tl = gsap.timeline({
        scrollTrigger: {
          trigger: container,
          scroller: scrollerRef?.current ?? undefined,
          start,
          end,
          scrub,
          invalidateOnRefresh: true,
        },
      });

      // Outer cards travel toward the centre from opposite ends. When there is
      // only one card, `first === last` and the two tweens would fight over
      // the same target, so it takes the middle treatment instead.
      if (first === last) {
        tl.fromTo(first, { autoAlpha: 0 }, { autoAlpha: 1, ease: 'none', duration: 1 }, 0);
      } else {
        tl.fromTo(
          first,
          { autoAlpha: 0, [axis]: -converge },
          { autoAlpha: 1, [axis]: 0, ease: 'none', duration: 1 },
          0,
        );
        tl.fromTo(
          last,
          { autoAlpha: 0, [axis]: converge },
          { autoAlpha: 1, [axis]: 0, ease: 'none', duration: 1 },
          0,
        );
      }

      // Everything between the ends has nowhere to converge from, so it only
      // fades. Giving it a direction too would make the row look like it was
      // being shuffled rather than closing.
      const middle = cards.slice(1, -1);
      if (middle.length > 0) {
        tl.fromTo(middle, { autoAlpha: 0 }, { autoAlpha: 1, ease: 'none', duration: 1 }, 0);
      }

      if (connectors.length > 0) {
        tl.fromTo(
          connectors,
          { autoAlpha: 0, scale: CONNECTOR_SCALE },
          {
            autoAlpha: 1,
            scale: 1,
            ease: 'none',
            duration: 1 - connectorAt,
            stagger: connectorStagger,
          },
          // Absolute timeline position in seconds. The cards occupy 0 -> 1, so
          // 0.35 puts the first connector a third of the way into their
          // travel: they are already moving when the link appears.
          connectorAt,
        );
      }
    },
    root,
    [converge, scrub, connectorAt, connectorStagger, start, end, stacked, reduced, steps.length],
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useGsap` reverts the `gsap.context` on unmount and whenever the layout axis or any timing prop changes. That kills the ScrollTrigger and strips the inline transform and opacity from every card and connector, which matters here because the axis flip rebuilds the whole timeline on resize and a stale trigger would keep writing `xPercent` to elements now laid out in a column.

**Reduced motion.** No timeline is built, so the diagram renders assembled: cards at their layout positions, connectors at full opacity and scale. The layout still responds to container width, because that is layout rather than motion.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Animating the connectors at position 0 alongside the cards. Everything arriving together reads as a set of boxes that happen to have arrows between them; the whole point is that the link appears while the boxes are still closing.
- Giving the middle cards a convergence direction too. With every card sliding, the row reads as being reshuffled rather than closing, and the two outer cards stop being the subject.
- Not handling the one-step case. `cards[0]` and `cards[cards.length - 1]` are the same element, so it receives two `fromTo` tweens with opposite start values and ends up wherever the second one decided.
- Choosing the layout axis from `window.innerWidth`. The component is usually inside a content column; a wide window with a narrow column stacks the cards visually while the tweens still converge horizontally, so they cross each other on the way in.
- Using `opacity` rather than `autoAlpha` on the connectors. An invisible SVG still takes hit-testing area between two cards, which quietly swallows clicks aimed at the card edges.
- Assuming `stagger` inside a scrubbed timeline behaves like duration. Each connector's start is offset in timeline seconds, so a large stagger pushes the timeline total past the card tweens and the cards finish before the scroll range ends — which is intended here, but is a surprise if you assumed the total was 1.

## Notes

- The wrapper tint is derived from the accent token rather than a second hard-coded colour, so re-theming the accent moves the panel with it.
- Connectors are inline SVG paths, so they inherit `currentColor` and need no asset.

## Definition of done

Scroll the diagram into view: the leftmost and rightmost cards slide toward the middle, and only once they are moving do the arrows between them scale up one after the other. Stop scrolling mid-way and the diagram keeps settling for more than a second. Narrow the container below 420px and the same sequence plays vertically with the arrows rotated. With reduced motion on, the diagram is complete before it scrolls into view.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Converging Headline Words

A stacked headline assembles out of the margins as you approach it. Odd lines enter from the right, even lines from the left, and both land on zero at the same scrub position, so they cross the frame in opposite directions and lock into a sentence. Because the tween is scrubbed, scrolling back up disassembles it — the headline is a function of scroll position, not a playback that has happened or not happened.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Headline words slide in from opposite margins and lock into a sentence, pinned to scroll position.

- Category: text
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. Each word is a block-level span with `data-word`. A single `gsap.timeline` with a `scrollTrigger` holds one `fromTo` per word, all inserted at position `0`, so every word shares the timeline's full length and therefore the full scroll range.
2. The travel is `xPercent`, not `x`: percent of *the element's own width*, so a short word and a long word both start entirely outside the frame and neither needs a hand-tuned pixel value.
3. Direction alternates on index parity — `i % 2 === 0 ? -travel : travel` — and the text alignment alternates with it, so each word enters from the side it is aligned to and travels the shortest distance to its resting place.
4. `ease: "none"` on every tween. Under `scrub` the scroll position *is* the easing curve; layering `power2.out` on top means the words accelerate away from the scrollbar and then wait for it, which is precisely the sensation people describe as the scroll feeling sticky.
5. `fromTo`, not `to`. A bare `to` reads its start value from the DOM, and the DOM already says `xPercent: 0` because the rendered markup is the assembled headline — that is what the no-JS and reduced-motion renders show.
6. `gsap.registerPlugin(ScrollTrigger)` is called inside the effect rather than at module scope, because `registerPlugin` touches `window` and this module is still evaluated during server rendering.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `TRAVEL = 120`
  Percent of each word's own width. At exactly 100 the word starts flush against the frame edge and is already peeking in on the first pixel of scroll; the extra 20% buys a moment of empty margin before it arrives.
- `SCRUB = 1`
  One second of catch-up between the scrollbar and the words. `scrub: true` welds them exactly, which on a trackpad exposes every jitter in the input; past ~1.5s the headline is still assembling well after the reader has stopped scrolling.
- `START = 'top bottom'`
  The scrub begins the instant the headline's top edge enters the viewport. Starting later means the words are still outside the frame when the headline is already half on screen, which reads as missing content rather than as an entrance.
- `END = 'top 25%'`
  Assembly completes when the headline top reaches the upper quarter of the viewport. Ending at centre leaves the headline unresolved while it is the dominant thing on screen; ending earlier compresses the whole effect into the bottom sliver of the viewport.

## API

```ts
function ConvergingScrubWords(props: { words: string[]; travel?: number; scrub?: number; start?: string; end?: string; scroller?: Element | null; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `words: string[]`
  One per line. Even indices enter from the left, odd from the right.
- `travel: number` — default `120`
  Percent of each word's own width that it starts offset by.
- `scrub: number` — default `1`
  Seconds of catch-up between the scrollbar and the words.
- `start: string` — default `'top bottom'`
  ScrollTrigger `start`.
- `end: string` — default `'top 25%'`
  ScrollTrigger `end`.
- `scroller: Element | null` — default `null`
  Scroll container, when the headline is not in the document scroller.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the wrapper via `cn` — type size and tracking go here.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const TRAVEL = 120;
const SCRUB = 1;
const START = 'top bottom';
const END = 'top 25%';

export function ConvergingScrubWords({
  words,
  travel = TRAVEL,
  scrub = SCRUB,
  start = START,
  end = END,
  scroller = null,
  className,
}: ConvergingScrubWordsProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = root.current;
    // Reduced motion: the JSX below already renders the assembled headline at
    // its final position, so declining to attach the trigger is the whole
    // implementation. Nothing is hidden and nothing is left off-screen.
    if (!el || reduced) return;

    // Registered here rather than at module scope: registerPlugin touches
    // window, and this file is still evaluated during server rendering.
    gsap.registerPlugin(ScrollTrigger);

    const wordEls = Array.from(el.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-word]'));
    if (wordEls.length === 0) return;

    const ctx = gsap.context(() => {
      const tl = gsap.timeline({
        scrollTrigger: {
          trigger: el,
          scroller: scroller ?? undefined,
          start,
          end,
          scrub,
        },
      });

      wordEls.forEach((w, i) => {
        // fromTo, not to. A bare `to` would read the start value off the DOM,
        // and the DOM already says 0 because the inline style below is the
        // final position for the no-JS and reduced-motion renders.
        tl.fromTo(
          w,
          { xPercent: i % 2 === 0 ? -travel : travel },
          { xPercent: 0, ease: 'none' },
          0,
        );
      });
    }, el);

    return () => ctx.revert();
  }, [words, travel, scrub, start, end, scroller, reduced]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `ctx.revert()` on the `gsap.context` scoped to the root. That kills the timeline, disposes the ScrollTrigger instance (so it stops measuring a detached element and stops contributing to `ScrollTrigger.refresh()`), and strips the inline transforms GSAP wrote.

**Reduced motion.** No ScrollTrigger is attached and no tween is created. The markup React renders is already the assembled headline at `xPercent: 0`, so the finished sentence is on screen from first paint — nothing is off-screen waiting for a scroll that will not drive it.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Using an ease other than `none` under `scrub`. The words lead or lag the scrollbar and the page feels like it is fighting the input — the single most common complaint about scrubbed animation.
- Using `to` instead of `fromTo`. GSAP samples the current DOM value as the start, which is the resting position, so nothing moves — or worse, it moves only after a resize invalidates the cached start.
- Animating `x` in pixels. A word that is 400px wide and one that is 120px wide need different offsets to clear the frame; `xPercent` is self-scaling and survives a font-size change.
- Setting `overflow: hidden` on the container. It stops the horizontal scrollbar, but CSS forces `overflow-y` to `auto` when one axis is `hidden`, which silently breaks any sticky ancestor and clips descenders. `overflow-x: clip` does the same job without that side effect.
- Omitting the `scroller` option when the headline lives inside a scrolling panel rather than the document. ScrollTrigger measures against the window, so the trigger fires at the wrong time or never.
- Registering ScrollTrigger at module scope. `registerPlugin` reaches for `window` and throws during server rendering.
- Cleaning up with `kill()` on the timeline only. The ScrollTrigger instance survives and keeps measuring a detached element; `ctx.revert()` disposes both and strips the inline transforms.

## Notes

- No text-splitting library: the words arrive as an array prop and are rendered as spans by React. A splitter would add a dependency and a DOM-mutation lifecycle for something the caller already has as data.
- If you feed this component text you split elsewhere, gate the split on `document.fonts.ready` — measuring before the webfont lands gives fallback-font line breaks that never re-flow. See `font-safe-text-split`.
- The `scroller` prop exists so the component can be demoed and used inside an `overflow-y-auto` panel rather than only in the document scroller.

## Definition of done

Scroll down slowly: the words travel inward from alternating sides and are exactly aligned when the headline top reaches the upper quarter of the viewport. Scroll back up and they separate again, tracking the scrollbar. No horizontal scrollbar appears on the document at any point. With reduced motion enabled the assembled headline is present on first paint and does not move.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
