# Build: Dataset-Driven Parallax

Depth is declared in the markup: any descendant carrying `data-parallax="0.3"` drifts at that rate. One effect walks the container, parses the attribute and builds a scrubbed tween per layer, so adding a new plane to a hero is an attribute rather than a code change. Travel is expressed as a percentage of the element's own height, which keeps the effect proportional at every breakpoint.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Layers drift at a rate written on the element itself, over the widest possible scroll window.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. The container is walked once for `[data-parallax]` descendants. The depth is read with a double fallback — `parseFloat(el.getAttribute(attr) ?? "") || fallback` — so a missing value, an empty value and a non-numeric value all land on the same default.
2. Each layer gets `gsap.to(layer, { yPercent: -(100 * depth), ease: "none" })`. `yPercent` is a percentage of the element's own height, so a 2000px hero and a 400px mobile hero travel proportionally with no media query.
3. `ease: "none"` is required, not stylistic. Any easing on a scrubbed tween means the layer accelerates and decelerates independently of the wheel, so two layers at different depths drift out of sync mid-scroll and snap back at the ends.
4. The trigger window is `start: "top bottom"` to `end: "bottom top"` — the full travel range, from the instant the element enters the scroller to the instant it leaves. That is the widest window available, which spreads the same travel across the most scroll distance.
5. `invalidateOnRefresh: true` makes ScrollTrigger recompute start and end on resize; percentage-based travel is derived from element height and a stale measurement leaves every layer offset.
6. Under reduced motion the effect returns before creating anything, so the layers render at their authored positions.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `DEFAULT_DEPTH = 0.15`
  Fallback drift: 15% of the element's height across the whole window. Below ~0.05 the layer looks static next to its neighbours; above ~0.4 it visibly separates from the content it belongs to and reads as a rendering fault.
- `start / end = 'top bottom' / 'bottom top'`
  The maximum-length window. Narrowing it (say `top 80%` to `bottom 20%`) forces the same travel through less scroll, which is the difference between drift and the page appearing to come apart.
- `yPercent multiplier = -100`
  Negative so layers move against the scroll — the direction that reads as distance. A positive multiplier moves them with the scroll, which reads as the layer being dragged.
- `scrub = true`
  Locked to scroll position with no lag. Parallax is a spatial relationship: a numeric scrub adds lag, and lagging layers cross each other during a fast flick.

## API

```ts
function DatasetParallax(props: { children: ReactNode; attribute?: string; fallback?: number; scrub?: boolean | number; scrollerRef?: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Section content. Any descendant with the depth attribute becomes a layer.
- `attribute: string` — default `'data-parallax'`
  Attribute carrying the depth. Its value is parsed as a float.
- `fallback: number` — default `0.15`
  Depth used when the attribute is missing, empty or not a number.
- `scrub: boolean | number` — default `true`
  ScrollTrigger scrub. A number adds that many seconds of lag.
- `scrollerRef: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>`
  The scroll container that owns the scroll position. Omit for the document.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the container via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const DEFAULT_DEPTH = 0.15;

export function DatasetParallax({
  children,
  attribute = 'data-parallax',
  fallback = DEFAULT_DEPTH,
  scrub = true,
  scrollerRef,
  className,
}: DatasetParallaxProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  useGsap(
    gsap,
    () => {
      const el = root.current;
      if (!el || reduced) return;

      const scroller = scrollerRef?.current ?? undefined;

      for (const layer of Array.from(el.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>(`[${attribute}]`))) {
        // Double fallback, and both halves are load-bearing. `?? ''` handles a
        // bare `data-parallax` with no value; `|| fallback` handles
        // `parseFloat` returning NaN on anything non-numeric. A NaN reaching
        // `yPercent` does not throw — it silently pins the layer at its
        // untransformed position, which looks like the effect simply not
        // working on that one element.
        const raw = layer.getAttribute(attribute) ?? '';
        const depth = parseFloat(raw) || fallback;

        gsap.to(layer, {
          yPercent: -(100 * depth),
          ease: 'none',
          scrollTrigger: {
            trigger: layer,
            scroller,
            // The widest possible window: begins the instant the layer's top
            // touches the bottom of the scroller and ends when its bottom
            // leaves the top. Any narrower range concentrates the same travel
            // into less scroll, which is what makes cheap parallax feel like
            // the page is sliding apart.
            start: 'top bottom',
            end: 'bottom top',
            scrub,
            // Percent-based travel is recomputed from element height; without
            // this a resize leaves every layer measured against the old one.
            invalidateOnRefresh: true,
          },
        });
      }
    },
    root,
    [attribute, fallback, scrub, reduced],
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useGsap` wraps the whole walk in a `gsap.context`; `ctx.revert()` on unmount kills every tween and its ScrollTrigger and strips the inline `transform` GSAP wrote. Without the revert the triggers survive the unmount and keep scrubbing detached nodes on the next page.

**Reduced motion.** The effect returns before creating any tween, so every layer stays exactly where the stylesheet put it. The layout is authored to be correct at rest, so nothing is missing — the planes simply do not separate.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Using `y` in pixels instead of `yPercent`. It looks correct at the breakpoint you tuned and wrong at every other one — on a short viewport a fixed 300px offset can push the layer entirely out of its own container.
- A single `|| 0.15` fallback. `el.dataset.parallax || "0.15"` covers the missing attribute, but `parseFloat("fast")` returns `NaN` and `NaN` reaching `yPercent` does not throw — the layer just silently stops moving, which is a bug you find by eye weeks later.
- Adding an ease to a scrubbed tween. The layer then accelerates on its own schedule rather than the wheel's, so layers at different depths drift out of relative order and snap at each end of the range.
- Omitting `invalidateOnRefresh`. Rotating a phone or opening a sidebar changes element height; the tween keeps using the height measured on mount and every layer sits at the wrong offset until reload.
- Leaving the scroller as the document when the content lives in an `overflow-y-auto` container. Every start and end is then measured against the window, so nothing moves at the right time — or at all.
- Building one giant timeline for all layers. Independent triggers per layer are correct here: a layer must respond to its own position in the scroller, not to a shared progress value.

## Notes

- The attribute name is configurable so the component can coexist with an existing convention rather than forcing `data-parallax` onto a codebase that already has one.
- Depths above 1 are legal and useful for a single foreground element that should outrun everything, but two such layers next to each other stop reading as depth.

## Definition of done

Scroll the section: layers with a larger `data-parallax` value visibly outrun the ones with smaller values, and every layer is back in its authored position when it leaves the scroller. Change an attribute value in devtools and reload — the rate changes with no code edit. Resize the window mid-scroll and the layers stay aligned with their content.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Delayed-Unmount Loader

An inverted full-cover loading panel that fades out on a plain CSS transition. The mechanism is the timing of its own removal: when `loading` goes false the element sets `data-exit` and starts a 600ms fade, and a matching 600ms timeout is what finally unmounts it. Nothing is animated in JavaScript — one boolean, one timeout, one transition.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A loading overlay that stays mounted 600ms past the signal so its fade can actually play before it leaves.

- Category: transition
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. Internal `mounted` state starts true so the overlay is present in the very first paint, before any effect has run. Deriving visibility from the `loading` prop alone is what makes the exit impossible to animate.
2. When `loading` flips false, `data-exit="true"` lands on the element and the CSS rule `.k-dul[data-exit="true"] { opacity: 0; pointer-events: none }` takes over the transition declared on `.k-dul`.
3. In the same effect a `setTimeout(() => setMounted(false), exitMs)` is armed. The timeout and the transition read the same `exitMs`, passed to CSS as the custom property `--k-dul-exit`, so they cannot drift apart.
4. If `loading` goes true again — a second route, a refetch — the effect clears the pending timeout and re-arms the overlay. Because the exit is a CSS transition rather than a keyframe, an interruption mid-fade reverses from wherever the opacity had got to instead of jumping to 1.
5. The panel is drawn with the foreground colour as its background and the background colour as its text, so the reveal reads as a tonal inversion rather than a curtain, and a single pulsing dot between two brackets is the only moving part.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `exitMs = 600`
  Drives both the CSS transition and the unmount timeout. Under ~350ms a full-bleed tonal flip reads as a flicker; over ~800ms the page is legible behind a veil that is still technically covering it. Whatever value you pick, the timeout must be >= the transition or the node disappears mid-fade.
- `pulse period = 1s`
  One cycle per second is close to a resting heart rate and reads as "alive, waiting". Faster reads as urgency and makes a slow load feel worse than it is.
- `pulse scale range = 0.86 -> 1`
  Small enough that the dot never appears to change its typographic size between the brackets; a larger range makes the bracket pair look mis-set.

## API

```ts
function DelayedUnmountLoader(props: { loading: boolean; exitMs?: number; label?: string; hint?: string; position?: 'fixed' | 'absolute'; className?: string }): JSX.Element | null
```

- `loading: boolean`
  While true the overlay is opaque. False starts the reveal.
- `exitMs: number` — default `600`
  Fade length and unmount delay. One number drives both.
- `label: string` — default `'Loading experience'`
  Left-hand text.
- `hint: string` — default `'it won’t be long'`
  Right-hand text.
- `position: 'fixed' | 'absolute'` — default `'fixed'`
  Viewport cover, or cover of the nearest positioned ancestor.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the overlay.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function DelayedUnmountLoader({
  loading,
  exitMs = 600,
  label = 'Loading experience',
  hint = 'it won’t be long',
  position = 'fixed',
  className,
}: DelayedUnmountLoaderProps) {
  // Starts true so the overlay is in the very first paint. Deriving it from
  // `loading` alone is what makes the exit un-animatable.
  const [mounted, setMounted] = useState(true);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (loading) {
      // A second load (route change, refetch) re-arms the overlay.
      setMounted(true);
      return;
    }
    const t = setTimeout(() => setMounted(false), exitMs);
    return () => clearTimeout(t);
  }, [loading, exitMs]);

  if (!mounted && !loading) return null;

  return (
    <div
      // `data-exit` is the only thing that changes on the element. The
      // transition is declarative, so an interrupted reveal (loading goes
      // true again mid-fade) reverses from wherever it got to instead of
      // jumping.
      data-exit={!loading}
      aria-hidden={!loading}
      className={cn(
        'k-dul z-50 flex items-center justify-center',
        // Inverted: the loader is the page's negative, so the reveal reads as
        // a tonal flip rather than a curtain being pulled aside.
        'bg-fg text-bg',
        position === 'fixed' ? 'fixed inset-0' : 'absolute inset-0',
        className,
      )}
      style={{ ['--k-dul-exit' as string]: `${exitMs}ms` }}
    >
      <style>{CSS}</style>
      <div className="flex w-full items-center justify-between gap-2 px-4">
        <p className="w-1/3 font-mono text-[0.6875rem] uppercase leading-none tracking-[0.08em]">
          {label}
        </p>
        <p className="flex w-1/3 justify-center font-mono text-2xl leading-none tracking-[0.1em]">
          <span aria-hidden>[</span>
          <span className="k-dul-dot inline-block px-[0.15em]" aria-hidden>
            &middot;
          </span>
          <span aria-hidden>]</span>
        </p>
        <p className="w-1/3 text-right font-mono text-[0.6875rem] uppercase leading-none tracking-[0.08em]">
          {hint}
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The single timeout is cleared in the effect's cleanup, so a route change or an unmount during the fade cannot call `setMounted` on a component React has already released.

**Reduced motion.** The dot stops pulsing and sits at a fixed opacity, and the fade collapses to 1ms so the overlay simply disappears. The unmount delay is unchanged, and the exiting overlay is `pointer-events: none` throughout, so nothing is blocked while it waits.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Rendering `{loading && <Loader />}`. React removes the node on the same commit that flips the flag, so the transition has no element to run on and the loader disappears on a cut. The component owns its own removal.
- Using a keyframe animation with `forwards` for the exit. Interrupt it by starting a second load and it snaps to the start; a transition on a class/attribute is interruptible in both directions for free.
- Letting the timeout and the transition duration live in different files. They drift, and either the loader is cut off mid-fade or a fully transparent overlay sits on top of the page eating clicks. One `exitMs` feeds both, and the CSS reads it from a custom property.
- Forgetting `pointer-events: none` in the exit state. For the whole fade the page is visible but not clickable, which reads as the site having frozen just as it finished loading.
- Not clearing the timeout when `loading` goes true again. The stale timer unmounts the re-armed overlay mid-load and the page flashes through underneath.
- Leaving the pulse running under `prefers-reduced-motion`. An indefinitely looping animation is exactly what that preference exists to stop; the media query drops it to a static dot.

## Notes

- App Router wiring: render this in `app/layout.tsx` above `{children}` and drive `loading` from your own readiness state — `document.fonts.ready`, a data promise, or a route-change flag from `usePathname()`. For a first-load preloader that must never hang, use `safe-preloader` instead: this component trusts whoever owns the boolean.
- `position="absolute"` covers the nearest positioned ancestor instead of the viewport, which is what makes it embeddable in a card or a preview frame.
- The delayed-unmount pattern generalises: any exit animation on a conditionally rendered node needs the node to outlive the condition by at least the animation duration.

## Definition of done

Load the page and the inverted panel is in the first paint with its dot pulsing. When loading ends the panel fades over 600ms and the node is gone from the DOM immediately afterwards — not before. Trigger a second load mid-fade and the panel returns from its current opacity rather than snapping to full.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Depth Fade And Travelling Pulse

A lattice of dots bent around a shallow arc and lit by a pulse that travels across it. Depth is faked entirely from model-space z, which drives alpha and point size at the same time, so the arc reads as curved with no depth buffer and no perspective camera. The pulse is a cosine whose phase varies per column, and its crest also pushes dots toward the viewer, so the two techniques compound: the wave arrives as a moving band of brighter, larger dots.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A dot lattice on an arc: z drives alpha and point size together, and a per-column phase sweeps the pulse across the field.

- Category: webgl
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1

## How it works

1. Columns are placed by angle across `arcSpan`, then z is renormalised so the centre column lands at exactly `+arcDepth` and both edges at `-arcDepth`, independent of the span. Without that renormalisation the usable z range shrinks with the span and the depth cue silently weakens whenever the arc is flattened.
2. The depth cue is `depthT = clamp((z + 0.55) / 1.1, 0, 1)`, which drives alpha from 0.25 to 1.0 *and* point size from 0.65 to 1.0. Both together are the point: alpha alone reads as a grey copy of the near dots, size alone reads as a resolution change, and only the pair reads as distance.
3. The pulse is `raw = 0.65 + 0.35 * cos(2π * (uElapsed / pulseCycle - phase))`, with `phase = columnT * waveTurns + rowT * 0.12` baked into an attribute. Subtracting the phase inside the cosine is what makes the crest move *along* the lattice rather than the whole field breathing in unison.
4. The crest, renormalised to 0..1, is added to z as `p.z += crest * uWaveDepth`, so the wave feeds the depth cue. A dot at the crest is pushed nearer, and the depth fade then brightens and enlarges it — one displacement drives three visible changes.
5. The pulse ramps in over the first second (`clamp(uElapsed / 1.0, 0, 1)`), so the first frame does not land on an arbitrary point of the cosine and flash. Yaw is `sin(elapsed * yawSpeed * 2π) * yawAmplitude` degrees, applied in the shader after the wave so the lattice rocks through its own depth range.
6. `gl_PointSize` is clamped to a 2px floor and alpha is compensated by `unclamped² / clamped²`, so the field keeps the same apparent density at DPR 1 and DPR 2 instead of getting heavier on retina.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `PULSE_BASE / PULSE_SWING = 0.65 / 0.35`
  The pulse rides between 0.30 and 1.00 of nominal size and alpha. A trough at 0 would make dots vanish entirely and the lattice would look like it is dropping frames rather than breathing.
- `DEFAULT_CYCLE / pulseCycle = 3.0 seconds`
  Under ~2s the crest outruns the eye following it across the lattice; over ~5s it stops reading as a wave and becomes an idle shimmer.
- `INTRO_SECONDS = 1.0`
  Ramps the pulse amplitude from 0. Without it the first rendered frame samples the cosine at an arbitrary phase and the whole field flashes on mount.
- `DEPTH_HALF_RANGE = 0.55`
  The arc spans ±0.34 and the wave adds up to +0.18, so normalising over ±0.55 leaves headroom at both ends — no dot sits at exactly 0 or 1 and the falloff never visibly clips.
- `DEPTH_MIN_SIZE / DEPTH_MAX_SIZE = 0.65 / 1.0`
  Far dots at 65% of near ones. Paired with the 0.25→1.0 alpha ramp; either cue on its own is ambiguous, and this ratio is the smallest that still reads as depth at preview-card sizes.
- `waveTurns = 1.4`
  Wavelengths visible across the lattice at any instant. At 1 the crest and trough sit at opposite edges and it reads as a tilt; past ~2.5 the bands are too narrow to track and the field just shimmers.
- `ROW_PHASE_LEAN = 0.12`
  Small row contribution to the phase, so the crest leans instead of arriving as a perfectly vertical bar. Bigger than ~0.3 and the wave starts reading as diagonal stripes.
- `yawAmplitude / yawSpeed = 16 degrees / 0.25 Hz`
  The lattice rocks rather than spins. A full rotation would carry columns through the arc's entire depth range and destroy the near/far reading the crest depends on.
- `crest tint threshold = smoothstep(0.65, 1.0, crest)`
  Only the top third of the crest picks up `crestColor`. Tinting the whole cosine spreads the accent across the field and the wave stops having a location.

## API

```ts
function DepthPulseTravellingWave(props: { columns?: number; rows?: number; arcSpan?: number; arcDepth?: number; fieldHeight?: number; pulseCycle?: number; waveTurns?: number; waveDepth?: number; yawAmplitude?: number; yawSpeed?: number; dotScale?: number; viewScale?: number; opacity?: number; color?: string; crestColor?: string; seed?: number | string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `columns: number` — default `110`
  Columns across the arc.
- `rows: number` — default `44`
  Rows down each column.
- `arcSpan: number` — default `110`
  Arc the lattice is bent around, in degrees.
- `arcDepth: number` — default `0.34`
  Half-depth of the arc in model units — how far the edges recede.
- `fieldHeight: number` — default `1.1`
  Lattice height in model units.
- `pulseCycle: number` — default `3`
  Seconds per pulse.
- `waveTurns: number` — default `1.4`
  Wavelengths visible across the lattice at any instant.
- `waveDepth: number` — default `0.18`
  How far a crest pushes a dot toward the viewer, in model units.
- `yawAmplitude: number` — default `16`
  Peak yaw of the whole lattice, in degrees.
- `yawSpeed: number` — default `0.25`
  Yaw oscillations per second.
- `dotScale: number` — default `1`
  Dot radius multiplier in CSS pixels.
- `viewScale: number` — default `0.46`
  Model-to-pixel scale as a fraction of the container short side.
- `opacity: number` — default `1`
  Multiplier applied to every dot.
- `color: string` — default `'#6f757e'`
  Base dot colour.
- `crestColor: string` — default `'#ffffff'`
  Colour mixed in at the top of the crest.
- `seed: number | string` — default `'depth-pulse-travelling-wave'`
  Seeds the sub-cell jitter for a stable, hydration-safe lattice.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function DepthPulseTravellingWave({
  columns = 110,
  rows = 44,
  arcSpan = 110,
  arcDepth = 0.34,
  fieldHeight = 1.1,
  pulseCycle = 3,
  waveTurns = 1.4,
  waveDepth = 0.18,
  yawAmplitude = 16,
  yawSpeed = 0.25,
  dotScale = 1,
  viewScale = 0.46,
  opacity = 1,
  color = '#6f757e',
  crestColor = '#ffffff',
  seed = 'depth-pulse-travelling-wave',
  className,
}: DepthPulseTravellingWaveProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const stage = useRef<Stage | null>(null);
  const [unsupported, setUnsupported] = useState(false);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const size = useRef({ width, height });
  size.current = { width, height };

  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const ready = width > 0 && height > 0;

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = host.current;
    if (!el || !ready) return;

    if (!hasWebGL()) {
      setUnsupported(true);
      return;
    }

    const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: false, alpha: true });
    renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio());
    renderer.setClearAlpha(0);

    const scene = new THREE.Scene();
    const camera = new THREE.OrthographicCamera(-1, 1, 1, -1, 0.1, 10);
    camera.position.z = 1;

    const rng = createRng(seed);

    const total = columns * rows;
    const positions = new Float32Array(total * 3);
    const wave = new Float32Array(total * 2);

    /* ------------------------------------------------------------------
       The arc. Columns are placed by angle, then z is renormalised so the
       centre column sits at +arcDepth and the two edges at -arcDepth
       exactly. Without the renormalisation the usable z range depends on
       arcSpan, and the depth fade would get weaker every time the arc was
       flattened — the cue would silently stop working at shallow spans.
       ------------------------------------------------------------------ */
    const halfSpan = (arcSpan * Math.PI) / 360;
    const cosEdge = Math.cos(halfSpan);
    // Guard the degenerate case: a 0 degree span has no depth to normalise.
    const depthSpan = Math.max(1e-4, 1 - cosEdge);

    let cursor = 0;
    for (let c = 0; c < columns; c += 1) {
      const colT = columns === 1 ? 0.5 : c / (columns - 1);
      const angle = (colT - 0.5) * 2 * halfSpan;
      const x = Math.sin(angle);
      const z = ((Math.cos(angle) - cosEdge) / depthSpan) * 2 * arcDepth - arcDepth;

      for (let r = 0; r < rows; r += 1) {
        const rowT = rows === 1 ? 0.5 : r / (rows - 1);
        // Sub-cell jitter, seeded. A perfect lattice moirés against the pixel
        // grid and shows banding as the field yaws.
        const jx = (rng() - 0.5) * (1 / columns) * 0.9;
        const jy = (rng() - 0.5) * (1 / rows) * 0.9;

        positions[cursor * 3] = x + jx;
        positions[cursor * 3 + 1] = (rowT - 0.5 + jy) * fieldHeight;
        positions[cursor * 3 + 2] = z;

        // Phase is what makes it travel. Constant phase across the lattice
        // would give a field that breathes in unison.
        wave[cursor * 2] = colT * waveTurns + rowT * ROW_PHASE_LEAN;
        wave[cursor * 2 + 1] = rng() - 0.5;
        cursor += 1;
      }
    }

    const geometry = new THREE.BufferGeometry();
    geometry.setAttribute('position', new THREE.BufferAttribute(positions, 3));
    geometry.setAttribute('aWave', new THREE.BufferAttribute(wave, 2));

    const uniforms: Uniforms = {
      uElapsed: { value: 0 },
      uViewScale: { value: 1 },
      uPixelRatio: { value: renderer.getPixelRatio() },
      uDotScale: { value: dotScale },
      uOpacity: { value: opacity },
      uPulseCycle: { value: pulseCycle },
      uWaveDepth: { value: waveDepth },
      uYaw: { value: 0 },
      uColor: { value: new THREE.Color(color) },
      uCrestColor: { value: new THREE.Color(crestColor) },
    };

    const material = new THREE.ShaderMaterial({
      vertexShader: DEPTH_PULSE_WAVE_VERT,
      fragmentShader: DEPTH_PULSE_WAVE_FRAG,
      uniforms,
      transparent: true,
      // Every dot is projected at z = 0; the depth cue is alpha and size, not
      // the depth buffer. Leaving these on would let near dots reject far ones
      // that were rasterised first and punch holes through the lattice.
      depthTest: false,
      depthWrite: false,
    });

    const points = new THREE.Points(geometry, material);
    // Positions are unit-scale around the origin and the real placement happens
    // in the shader, so three's bounding sphere does not describe what is on
    // screen and culling against it would blank the field at some sizes.
    points.frustumCulled = false;
    scene.add(points);

    el.appendChild(renderer.domElement);
    renderer.domElement.style.display = 'block';
    renderer.domElement.style.width = '100%';
    renderer.domElement.style.height = '100%';

    const resize = (w: number, h: number) => {
      renderer.setSize(w, h, false);
      camera.left = -w / 2;
      camera.right = w / 2;
      camera.top = h / 2;
      camera.bottom = -h / 2;
      camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
      uniforms.uViewScale.value = Math.min(w, h) * viewScale;
      uniforms.uPixelRatio.value = renderer.getPixelRatio();
    };

    const draw = (elapsed: number) => {
      uniforms.uElapsed.value = elapsed;
      // Yaw oscillates rather than spins. A full rotation would carry columns
      // through the arc's own depth range and the travelling crest would stop
      // being readable as a wave.
      uniforms.uYaw.value = Math.sin(elapsed * yawSpeed * Math.PI * 2) * yawAmplitude;
      renderer.render(scene, camera);
    };

    resize(size.current.width, size.current.height);
    stage.current = { resize, draw };
    draw(STATIC_ELAPSED);

    return () => {
      stage.current = null;
      disposeObject(scene);
      material.dispose();
      disposeRenderer(renderer);
      renderer.domElement.remove();
    };
  }, [
    ready,
    columns,
    rows,
    arcSpan,
    arcDepth,
    fieldHeight,
    pulseCycle,
    waveTurns,
    waveDepth,
    yawAmplitude,
    yawSpeed,
    dotScale,
    viewScale,
    opacity,
    color,
    crestColor,
    seed,
  ]);

  useEffect(() => {
    stage.current?.resize(width, height);
    if (reduced) stage.current?.draw(STATIC_ELAPSED);
  }, [width, height, reduced]);

  useRaf((_dt, elapsed) => stage.current?.draw(elapsed), ready && !reduced && !unsupported);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nulls the stage ref so a queued frame cannot touch a dead renderer, disposes the geometry through `disposeObject(scene)`, disposes the material, calls `disposeRenderer` for `dispose` + `forceContextLoss` + a zeroed backing store, and removes the canvas. `useRaf` unsubscribes on unmount, so a StrictMode double-invoke leaves no orphaned context.

**Reduced motion.** No frame loop is opened. A single frame is drawn at `uElapsed = 1.9` — past the one-second amplitude ramp, and a third of the way through the default cycle, so the crest sits inside the lattice rather than off its edge. Both the depth falloff and the wave band are visible in that still; neither advances.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Giving every dot the same phase. The field then pulses in unison, which reads as a loading state rather than as something moving through the lattice — the per-column phase offset *is* the effect.
- Fading alpha with depth but leaving point size constant. The far edge of the arc becomes a grey copy of the near edge instead of receding, because size is the cue the eye actually uses for distance at these scales.
- Leaving `depthTest` on. Every dot is projected at z = 0, so whichever dot rasterises first wins the pixel and the lattice develops holes wherever it folds back on itself.
- Starting the pulse at full amplitude. The first frame samples the cosine at whatever phase `elapsed` happens to be, and the field flashes on mount — hence the one-second amplitude ramp.
- Placing columns by angle without renormalising z. The depth range then scales with `cos(arcSpan/2)`, so flattening the arc quietly kills the depth fade and the component looks broken at shallow spans while working at wide ones.
- A perfectly regular lattice. It moirés against the pixel grid and shows banding as the field yaws; the seeded sub-cell jitter costs nothing and removes it.
- Rebuilding the buffer on resize. Model space is size-independent — only `uViewScale` and `uPixelRatio` change, so a container reflow costs two uniform writes rather than a dropped GL context.

## Notes

- Dot count is `columns * rows`, 4840 at the defaults, in one draw call with one attribute beyond position.
- The wave is purely a function of `uElapsed` and a baked per-dot phase, so there is no simulation state and no drift — pausing and resuming lands exactly where the clock says it should.

## Definition of done

A curved lattice of dots is visibly dimmer and smaller toward its left and right edges than at its centre. A band of brighter, larger dots sweeps repeatedly across the field, roughly once every three seconds, rather than the whole field brightening at once. The lattice rocks gently side to side. Nothing flashes on mount. Resize the container and the field rescales without a flicker or a dropped context. With reduced motion it holds a single frame showing both the depth falloff and the crest.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Dither Trail Image Reveal

The image rests dimmed and near-monochrome; dragging across it restores it through a trail of 5px blocks, each block either lit or not according to an 8x8 Bayer threshold. Twenty-four pointer samples live about a second and ride in two flat uniform arrays, so the whole trail is one fullscreen quad with no geometry and no render targets. Samples are spawned on distance travelled by a damped follower rather than per event, and each carries the velocity it was born with, so the reveal smears the way the hand moved.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A dimmed image restored through a trail of Bayer-thresholded blocks that smear in the direction the pointer moved.

- Category: cursor
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1

## How it works

1. The trail is state, not geometry. Twenty-four samples sit in a ring buffer as `vec4(u, v, life, speed)` plus a parallel `vec2` of velocity, uploaded as two flat uniform arrays every frame. The fragment shader loops all twenty-four and takes `max()` of their contributions, so a full trail costs one quad and twenty-four `length()` calls per fragment — no instanced sprites, no ping-pong feedback buffer, nothing to resize.
2. A sample is released when the FOLLOWER has travelled `spawnDistance`, or after `spawnInterval` with no movement. Spawning per pointer event instead clumps on a slow drag — events fire on sub-pixel movement — and leaves gaps on a flick, because the ring is short and a fast sweep can consume all of it between two frames. The time floor is what keeps a stationary hover from decaying to nothing under the cursor.
3. The Bayer threshold is sampled at the CENTRE of the 5px block the fragment sits in, not at the fragment itself. Per-fragment sampling lets the disc edge cut through a block, which puts a soft antialiased boundary on an effect whose entire argument is that it has none. Per-block, a block is wholly lit or wholly absent and the reveal has a dither vocabulary.
4. The 8x8 matrix is built recursively — `bayer4(a) = bayer2(a * 0.5) * 0.25 + bayer2(a)`, and again for 8 — because GLSL ES 1.00 has no integer bitwise operators and the usual derivation is bit-twiddled. Three multiplies and a `fract` produce the same 64-value ordering with no lookup texture and no GLSL3 upgrade.
5. Each sample contributes its stored velocity to a flow vector, weighted by how much it contributed to the mask, and the sum is clamped. The image is then sampled at `uv - flow`, with the flow SNAPPED to the same 5px grid as the dither: a smooth sub-pixel offset is a directional blur laid on top of the picture, while a snapped one moves whole blocks and belongs to the same rendering as the dots.
6. Colour is quantised twice at two different frequencies — the reveal mask against a per-block threshold, the tone against a per-pixel one — so the shape of the trail and the banding of the image do not moire against each other.
7. `object-fit: cover` is reproduced in uv space from the intrinsic aspect of the decoded texture, so the shader crops exactly the way the equivalent CSS would and a resize is two uniform writes rather than a re-layout.
8. The pointer state updates every frame while the DRAW is throttled to 30fps. The trail geometry is smooth because the samples are, and 30fps is invisible through 5px blocks; halving the draw rate halves the fill, which is the only real cost here.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `TRAIL_POINTS = 24`
  Ring length, and a compile-time `#define` because GLSL ES 1.00 needs a constant loop bound. At the default spacing this is roughly a second of trail. Past ~48 the shader is doing more work than the image is worth, and the far end of the trail is below the first dither level anyway.
- `MAX_BUFFER_WIDTH = 1100`
  Absolute cap on drawing-buffer width in device pixels, applied on top of the dpr cap. The output is 5px blocks quantised to four levels, so a wider buffer resolves nothing: a 2560px hero at dpr 2 would shade 26 million fragments per draw for a picture with no detail above the block size.
- `fps = 30`
  Draw ceiling. This is an overlay, not the subject, and the block size hides the difference between 30 and 120. The accumulator subtracts the budget rather than zeroing, so the long-run rate is exact instead of quietly losing the remainder each frame.
- `smoothing = 0.0002`
  Fraction of the pointer gap still remaining after one second — an ~80ms half-life. Tighter than a glow needs, because the trail has a visible head: lag past ~150ms and the reveal is drawing where the pointer was, which reads as dropped frames.
- `spawnDistance / spawnInterval = 0.012 / 0.042`
  Roughly 1.2% of the container per sample, or one every 42ms if the pointer is still. Below ~0.006 a slow drag exhausts the ring in a few centimetres; above ~0.03 a fast sweep is visibly a string of beads.
- `trail radius = 0.055 -> 0.115`
  A sample GROWS as it ages, so the trail widens and softens behind the head instead of fading as a constant-width stripe. Equal radii read as a paint stroke; the taper is what makes it a wake.
- `FLOW_MAX / FLOW_CLAMP = 0.04 / 0.055`
  Per-sample and total displacement ceilings in uv units. Uncapped, a flick tears the image into unrecognisable stripes; the total clamp also stops overlapping samples from summing into a displacement several times either individual one.
- `levels = 4`
  Quantisation steps per channel inside the reveal. Two is a duotone stencil that loses the photograph; past ~8 the dither is too fine to read as one and the effect looks like a slightly noisy image.
- `Bayer epsilon = 0.001`
  The matrix contains a zero cell, so `step(threshold, soft)` lights that cell in every block on the canvas — a permanent sparse grid of stray pixels everywhere the trail has never been. Biasing the threshold is what keeps the untouched area untouched.

## API

```ts
function DitherTrailImageReveal(props: { src: string; alt?: string; levels?: number; blockSize?: number; trailLife?: number; spawnDistance?: number; spawnInterval?: number; flowGain?: number; smoothing?: number; restBrightness?: number; restSaturation?: number; fps?: number; maxDpr?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `src: string`
  Required. Image URL — http(s), blob: or data:. Never a bundled asset.
- `alt: string` — default `''`
  Accessible name for the panel. Empty marks it decorative.
- `levels: number` — default `4`
  Quantisation steps per channel inside the reveal.
- `blockSize: number` — default `5`
  Dither block size in CSS pixels.
- `trailLife: number` — default `1.05`
  Life of one trail sample in seconds.
- `spawnDistance: number` — default `0.012`
  Follower travel in uv units that releases the next sample.
- `spawnInterval: number` — default `0.042`
  Seconds after which a sample is released even with no movement.
- `flowGain: number` — default `0.03`
  uv offset stored per uv/second of pointer velocity.
- `smoothing: number` — default `0.0002`
  Fraction of the pointer gap still remaining after one second.
- `restBrightness: number` — default `0.5`
  Brightness of the untouched image, 0 to 1.
- `restSaturation: number` — default `0.16`
  Saturation of the untouched image, 0 to 1.
- `fps: number` — default `30`
  Draw rate ceiling. Pointer state still updates every frame.
- `maxDpr: number` — default `1.5`
  Device pixel ratio cap, before the 1100px absolute buffer cap.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root container via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** Samples in the ring. Must match TRAIL_POINTS in the fragment shader. */
const TRAIL_POINTS = 24;
/**
 * Hard cap on drawing-buffer width in device pixels. An overlay of 5px blocks
 * carries no detail a wider buffer could resolve, and fill is the whole cost:
 * a 2560px hero at dpr 2 would shade 26 million fragments per draw for a
 * picture that is quantised to four levels.
 */
const MAX_BUFFER_WIDTH = 1100;
/** uv units per second at which the speed term saturates. */
const SPEED_FULL_SCALE = 1.6;
/** Fraction of the velocity gap left after a second. Fast: speed must track. */
const VELOCITY_SMOOTHING = 0.001;
/** Ceiling on a single sample's stored flow, in uv units. */
const FLOW_MAX = 0.04;
/** Ceiling on the SUM of all samples' flow, applied in the shader. */
const FLOW_CLAMP = 0.055;

/** The reduced-motion still: a frozen swipe with a plausible velocity. */
const STILL_POINTS = 9;
const STILL_FLOW: readonly [number, number] = [0.02, 0.008];

interface RevealUniforms {
  /** three types `uniforms` as an open record; the index signature matches it. */
  [name: string]: THREE.IUniform;
  uResolution: THREE.IUniform<THREE.Vector2>;
  uImage: THREE.IUniform<THREE.Texture | null>;
  uHasImage: THREE.IUniform<number>;
  uUvScale: THREE.IUniform<THREE.Vector2>;
  uUvOffset: THREE.IUniform<THREE.Vector2>;
  /** Flat vec4 array: three's uniform setters take a typed array unchanged. */
  uTrail: THREE.IUniform<Float32Array>;
  uFlow: THREE.IUniform<Float32Array>;
  uBlock: THREE.IUniform<number>;
  uLevels: THREE.IUniform<number>;
  uFlowClamp: THREE.IUniform<number>;
  uRestBrightness: THREE.IUniform<number>;
  uRestSaturation: THREE.IUniform<number>;
}

interface Stage {
  renderer: THREE.WebGLRenderer;
  scene: THREE.Scene;
  camera: THREE.OrthographicCamera;
  geometry: THREE.PlaneGeometry;
  material: THREE.ShaderMaterial;
  uniforms: RevealUniforms;
  placeholder: THREE.DataTexture;
  render: () => void;
}

interface TrailSample {
  x: number;
  y: number;
  /** Elapsed seconds at spawn. Negative means the slot has never been used. */
  born: number;
  flowX: number;
  flowY: number;
  speed: number;
}

/**
 * A 1x1 opaque texture, bound before anything has loaded. Sampling an unbound
 * sampler2D is undefined behaviour: some drivers return black, some warn on
 * every draw, and one of them will be the reviewer's.
 */
function createPlaceholder(): THREE.DataTexture {
  const texture = new THREE.DataTexture(new Uint8Array([16, 17, 21, 255]), 1, 1);
  texture.needsUpdate = true;
  return texture;
}

export function DitherTrailImageReveal({
  src,
  alt = '',
  levels = 4,
  blockSize = 5,
  trailLife = 1.05,
  spawnDistance = 0.012,
  spawnInterval = 0.042,
  flowGain = 0.03,
  smoothing = 0.0002,
  restBrightness = 0.5,
  restSaturation = 0.16,
  fps = 30,
  maxDpr = 1.5,
  className,
}: DitherTrailImageRevealProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const mount = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const stage = useRef<Stage | null>(null);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const { inView } = useInView(host, { rootMargin: '10%' });
  const visible = useVisibility();
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  /* A trail needs a pointer that exists while no button is held. On touch
     `pointermove` only fires mid-drag, so the reveal would appear under the
     finger that is covering it and then be stranded on lift. */
  const finePointer = useMediaQuery('(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)');

  const [supported, setSupported] = useState(true);
  useEffect(() => setSupported(hasWebGL()), []);
  const [failed, setFailed] = useState(false);

  /** The decoded image, kept across renderer rebuilds so a resize never refetches. */
  const image = useRef<THREE.Texture | null>(null);
  /** Intrinsic aspect of that image; 0 until one has decoded. */
  const imageAspect = useRef(0);

  const target = useRef<{ x: number; y: number } | null>(null);
  const inside = useRef(false);
  const follow = useRef({ x: 0.5, y: 0.5 });
  const velocity = useRef({ x: 0, y: 0 });
  const lastSpawn = useRef({ x: 0.5, y: 0.5, at: -1 });
  const writeIndex = useRef(0);
  const budget = useRef(0);

  const trail = useRef<TrailSample[]>(
    Array.from({ length: TRAIL_POINTS }, () => ({
      x: 0,
      y: 0,
      born: -1,
      flowX: 0,
      flowY: 0,
      speed: 0,
    })),
  );

  const live = useRef({
    levels,
    blockSize,
    trailLife,
    spawnDistance,
    spawnInterval,
    flowGain,
    smoothing,
    restBrightness,
    restSaturation,
    fps,
  });
  live.current = {
    levels,
    blockSize,
    trailLife,
    spawnDistance,
    spawnInterval,
    flowGain,
    smoothing,
    restBrightness,
    restSaturation,
    fps,
  };

  const ready = supported && width > 1 && height > 1;

  /** object-fit: cover, replicated in uv space so the shader matches the CSS. */
  const applyCover = (w: number, h: number) => {
    const s = stage.current;
    if (!s || w < 1 || h < 1) return;
    const ia = imageAspect.current;
    if (ia <= 0) {
      s.uniforms.uUvScale.value.set(1, 1);
      s.uniforms.uUvOffset.value.set(0, 0);
      return;
    }
    const canvasAspect = w / h;
    if (ia > canvasAspect) {
      // Image is wider than the box: crop the sides.
      const scale = canvasAspect / ia;
      s.uniforms.uUvScale.value.set(scale, 1);
      s.uniforms.uUvOffset.value.set((1 - scale) * 0.5, 0);
    } else {
      const scale = ia / canvasAspect;
      s.uniforms.uUvScale.value.set(1, scale);
      s.uniforms.uUvOffset.value.set(0, (1 - scale) * 0.5);
    }
  };

  useEffect(() => {
    const slot = mount.current;
    if (!slot || !ready) return;

    /* The canvas is created here rather than owned by React. `reactStrictMode`
       double-invokes this effect; the first cleanup calls `forceContextLoss()`,
       and `getContext` on that same element afterwards returns the DEAD context
       instead of a fresh one — blank in development, fine in production, which
       is the worst way for a bug to behave. */
    const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({
      antialias: false,
      alpha: false,
      powerPreference: 'low-power',
    });
    // Two caps, and the lower wins: a ratio cap for sane machines and an
    // absolute width cap so a 4K hero cannot ask for a 7680px buffer.
    const ratio = Math.min(pixelRatio(maxDpr), MAX_BUFFER_WIDTH / Math.max(width, 1));
    renderer.setPixelRatio(Math.max(ratio, 0.5));
    renderer.setSize(width, height, false);
    const canvas = renderer.domElement;
    canvas.style.display = 'block';
    canvas.style.width = '100%';
    canvas.style.height = '100%';
    slot.appendChild(canvas);

    const placeholder = createPlaceholder();

    const uniforms: RevealUniforms = {
      uResolution: { value: new THREE.Vector2(width, height) },
      uImage: { value: image.current ?? placeholder },
      uHasImage: { value: image.current ? 1 : 0 },
      uUvScale: { value: new THREE.Vector2(1, 1) },
      uUvOffset: { value: new THREE.Vector2(0, 0) },
      uTrail: { value: new Float32Array(TRAIL_POINTS * 4) },
      uFlow: { value: new Float32Array(TRAIL_POINTS * 2) },
      uBlock: { value: blockSize },
      uLevels: { value: levels },
      uFlowClamp: { value: FLOW_CLAMP },
      uRestBrightness: { value: restBrightness },
      uRestSaturation: { value: restSaturation },
    };

    const material = new THREE.ShaderMaterial({
      vertexShader: ditherTrailImageRevealVertexShader,
      fragmentShader: ditherTrailImageRevealFragmentShader,
      uniforms,
    });

    const geometry = new THREE.PlaneGeometry(2, 2);
    const scene = new THREE.Scene();
    scene.add(new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material));
    const camera = new THREE.OrthographicCamera(-1, 1, 1, -1, 0, 1);
    const render = () => renderer.render(scene, camera);

    /* Listeners on the CANVAS, not the window: a document-level handler
       outlives the renderer it drives, and the rect it measures is not the rect
       being drawn into. Passive, because nothing calls preventDefault here and
       a non-passive move handler stalls the compositor on every event. */
    const onMove = (event: PointerEvent) => {
      const rect = canvas.getBoundingClientRect();
      if (rect.width === 0 || rect.height === 0) return;
      target.current = {
        x: (event.clientX - rect.left) / rect.width,
        // Flipped: uv y is up, client y is down.
        y: 1 - (event.clientY - rect.top) / rect.height,
      };
      if (!inside.current) {
        // Entering: teleport the follower rather than damping to it, or the
        // trail draws a stripe from wherever the pointer was last seen.
        follow.current.x = target.current.x;
        follow.current.y = target.current.y;
        lastSpawn.current.x = target.current.x;
        lastSpawn.current.y = target.current.y;
        velocity.current.x = 0;
        velocity.current.y = 0;
      }
      inside.current = true;
    };
    const onLeave = () => {
      inside.current = false;
      // Samples already in the ring keep ageing out on their own, so the trail
      // finishes its life instead of vanishing the instant the pointer leaves.
    };

    canvas.addEventListener('pointermove', onMove, { passive: true });
    canvas.addEventListener('pointerleave', onLeave, { passive: true });
    canvas.addEventListener('pointercancel', onLeave, { passive: true });

    stage.current = {
      renderer,
      scene,
      camera,
      geometry,
      material,
      uniforms,
      placeholder,
      render,
    };
    applyCover(width, height);
    render();

    return () => {
      stage.current = null;
      canvas.removeEventListener('pointermove', onMove);
      canvas.removeEventListener('pointerleave', onLeave);
      canvas.removeEventListener('pointercancel', onLeave);
      // `dispose()` frees GPU objects but leaves the context alive until GC
      // decides otherwise. `disposeRenderer` is the one that force-loses it,
      // and the per-process budget is about sixteen contexts.
      disposeRenderer(renderer);
      geometry.dispose();
      material.dispose();
      placeholder.dispose();
      canvas.remove();
    };
    // Everything else is pushed through `live` or the uniforms from the loop.
    // Rebuilding on a prop change would churn WebGL contexts.
    // eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps
  }, [ready, maxDpr]);

  /* Loading is its own effect and its own lifetime. It never throws: a 404
     leaves `uHasImage` at 0 and the shader keeps drawing its stand-in. */
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!ready || !src) return;
    let cancelled = false;
    setFailed(false);

    const loader = new THREE.TextureLoader();
    loader.load(
      src,
      (texture) => {
        if (cancelled) {
          // The component unmounted, or `src` changed, mid-decode. Without this
          // the texture is uploaded to a dead context and then leaked.
          texture.dispose();
          return;
        }
        texture.colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace;
        // No mipmaps: the quad is screen-filling, the image is never minified
        // past 1:1, and mipmapping a non-power-of-two texture silently fails.
        texture.generateMipmaps = false;
        texture.minFilter = THREE.LinearFilter;
        texture.magFilter = THREE.LinearFilter;
        texture.wrapS = THREE.ClampToEdgeWrapping;
        texture.wrapT = THREE.ClampToEdgeWrapping;

        image.current?.dispose();
        image.current = texture;

        const source = texture.image as { width?: number; height?: number } | null;
        const w = source?.width ?? 0;
        const h = source?.height ?? 0;
        imageAspect.current = w > 0 && h > 0 ? w / h : 0;

        const s = stage.current;
        if (!s) return;
        s.uniforms.uImage.value = texture;
        s.uniforms.uHasImage.value = 1;
        applyCover(width, height);
        s.render();
      },
      undefined,
      () => {
        if (cancelled) return;
        // A missing image is a content problem, not a crash. The stand-in field
        // keeps the panel legible and the trail keeps working on top of it.
        setFailed(true);
        imageAspect.current = 0;
        const s = stage.current;
        if (!s) return;
        s.uniforms.uHasImage.value = 0;
        s.render();
      },
    );

    return () => {
      cancelled = true;
    };
    // `width`/`height` are read for the cover fit but must not retrigger a
    // fetch; the resize effect re-applies the fit on its own.
    // eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps
  }, [src, ready]);

  // The decoded texture outlives the renderer, so it is released on unmount
  // rather than in the loader effect, which reruns whenever `src` changes.
  useEffect(() => {
    return () => {
      image.current?.dispose();
      image.current = null;
    };
  }, []);

  useEffect(() => {
    const s = stage.current;
    if (!s || width < 1 || height < 1) return;
    const ratio = Math.min(pixelRatio(maxDpr), MAX_BUFFER_WIDTH / width);
    s.renderer.setPixelRatio(Math.max(ratio, 0.5));
    s.renderer.setSize(width, height, false);
    s.uniforms.uResolution.value.set(width, height);
    applyCover(width, height);
    // Redraw once, or a resize while the loop is paused leaves the previous
    // framebuffer stretched across the new size.
    s.render();
    // eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps
  }, [width, height, maxDpr]);

  const writeTrailUniforms = (elapsed: number, life: number) => {
    const s = stage.current;
    if (!s) return;
    const points = s.uniforms.uTrail.value;
    const flows = s.uniforms.uFlow.value;
    let i = 0;
    for (const sample of trail.current) {
      const age = sample.born < 0 ? Infinity : elapsed - sample.born;
      const remaining = clamp(1 - age / life, 0, 1);
      points[i * 4] = sample.x;
      points[i * 4 + 1] = sample.y;
      points[i * 4 + 2] = remaining;
      points[i * 4 + 3] = sample.speed;
      flows[i * 2] = sample.flowX;
      flows[i * 2 + 1] = sample.flowY;
      i += 1;
    }
  };

  useRaf(
    (dt, elapsed) => {
      const s = stage.current;
      if (!s) return;
      const cfg = live.current;

      const previousX = follow.current.x;
      const previousY = follow.current.y;

      const aim = target.current;
      if (aim) {
        follow.current.x = damp(follow.current.x, aim.x, cfg.smoothing, dt);
        follow.current.y = damp(follow.current.y, aim.y, cfg.smoothing, dt);
      }

      // Velocity of the FOLLOWER, in uv units per second. Dividing by dt is
      // what makes it a velocity rather than a per-frame delta that measures
      // twice as large at 60Hz as at 120Hz for the same hand movement.
      const step = Math.max(dt, 0.0001);
      velocity.current.x = damp(
        velocity.current.x,
        (follow.current.x - previousX) / step,
        VELOCITY_SMOOTHING,
        dt,
      );
      velocity.current.y = damp(
        velocity.current.y,
        (follow.current.y - previousY) / step,
        VELOCITY_SMOOTHING,
        dt,
      );

      /* Spawn on DISTANCE travelled, or on a time floor. Distance alone gives
         an evenly spaced trail but lets the reveal decay to nothing under a
         pointer that has stopped; the time floor keeps a stationary hover
         alive. Spawning per event instead would clump on a slow drag and smear
         on a flick, because events fire on sub-pixel movement. */
      if (inside.current && aim) {
        const moved = Math.hypot(
          follow.current.x - lastSpawn.current.x,
          follow.current.y - lastSpawn.current.y,
        );
        const waited = elapsed - lastSpawn.current.at;
        if (moved >= cfg.spawnDistance || waited >= cfg.spawnInterval) {
          const slot = trail.current[writeIndex.current % TRAIL_POINTS];
          if (slot) {
            writeIndex.current = (writeIndex.current + 1) % TRAIL_POINTS;
            slot.x = follow.current.x;
            slot.y = follow.current.y;
            slot.born = elapsed;
            slot.flowX = clamp(velocity.current.x * cfg.flowGain, -FLOW_MAX, FLOW_MAX);
            slot.flowY = clamp(velocity.current.y * cfg.flowGain, -FLOW_MAX, FLOW_MAX);
            slot.speed = clamp(
              Math.hypot(velocity.current.x, velocity.current.y) / SPEED_FULL_SCALE,
              0,
              1,
            );
          }
          lastSpawn.current.x = follow.current.x;
          lastSpawn.current.y = follow.current.y;
          lastSpawn.current.at = elapsed;
        }
      }

      const life = Math.max(cfg.trailLife, 0.05);
      writeTrailUniforms(elapsed, life);

      const u = s.uniforms;
      u.uBlock.value = Math.max(cfg.blockSize, 1);
      u.uLevels.value = Math.max(cfg.levels, 2);
      u.uRestBrightness.value = cfg.restBrightness;
      u.uRestSaturation.value = cfg.restSaturation;

      /* Draw-rate throttle. The state above updates every frame — a trail
         sampled at 30Hz has visible corners — but the DRAW is the expensive
         half and 30fps is indistinguishable through 5px blocks. Subtracting
         the budget rather than zeroing the accumulator keeps the long-run rate
         exact instead of quietly losing the remainder every frame. */
      const frameBudget = 1 / clamp(cfg.fps, 10, 120);
      budget.current += dt;
      if (budget.current < frameBudget) return;
      budget.current = Math.min(budget.current - frameBudget, frameBudget);

      s.render();
    },
    ready && inView && visible && !reduced && finePointer,
  );

  /* Reduced motion, and coarse pointers, get a composed still: a short frozen
     swipe baked into the ring so the panel shows what the effect produces. The
     listeners stay attached and their target is never consumed. */
  useEffect(() => {
    const s = stage.current;
    if (!s || !ready) return;
    if (!reduced && finePointer) return;

    const [flowX = 0.02, flowY = 0.008] = STILL_FLOW;
    let i = 0;
    for (const sample of trail.current) {
      const t = i / (STILL_POINTS - 1);
      const inSwipe = i < STILL_POINTS;
      sample.x = 0.3 + t * 0.42;
      sample.y = 0.4 + Math.sin(t * 2.2) * 0.12;
      sample.flowX = flowX;
      sample.flowY = flowY;
      sample.speed = inSwipe ? 0.45 : 0;
      // `born` is unused by the still: lives are written straight below.
      sample.born = -1;
      i += 1;
    }

    const points = s.uniforms.uTrail.value;
    const flows = s.uniforms.uFlow.value;
    let j = 0;
    for (const sample of trail.current) {
      const remaining = j < STILL_POINTS ? 1 - j / STILL_POINTS : 0;
      points[j * 4] = sample.x;
      points[j * 4 + 1] = sample.y;
      points[j * 4 + 2] = remaining;
      points[j * 4 + 3] = sample.speed;
      flows[j * 2] = sample.flowX;
      flows[j * 2 + 1] = sample.flowY;
      j += 1;
    }
    s.render();
  }, [reduced, finePointer, ready, width, height]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Removes the three pointer listeners from the canvas, nulls the stage ref so an in-flight frame cannot touch a dead renderer, then `disposeRenderer(renderer)` — which force-loses the context, not just `dispose()`, since Chromium keeps roughly sixteen per process and drops the oldest — followed by the geometry, the material and the 1x1 placeholder texture, and finally removes the canvas from the DOM. The decoded image texture is disposed in a separate unmount effect, and an in-flight decode is cancelled by a flag so its callback disposes the result instead of binding it.

**Reduced motion.** The loop never starts. A short frozen swipe — nine samples with descending life and a plausible velocity — is baked into the ring and one frame is drawn, so the panel shows what the effect produces rather than a flat dimmed image. Coarse pointers get the same still, for the same reason. The listeners stay attached but their target is never consumed, so moving the pointer changes nothing.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Pushing pointer events straight into the trail. Event positions are not a path: they arrive at whatever rate the device chooses, cluster on slow movement and stop dead when the hand pauses. The handler records a target only; the loop damps a follower toward it and samples the follower.
- Damping with a per-frame constant (`x += (t - x) * 0.1`) instead of `damp(..., dt)`. The trail is visibly tighter at 120Hz than at 60Hz, so the feel is tuned to whichever machine it was authored on.
- Measuring velocity as a per-frame delta rather than dividing by `dt`. The same hand movement then reads as half the speed at 120Hz, and the smear strength — and with it the whole character of the effect — depends on the display.
- Sampling the Bayer threshold per fragment instead of per block. The reveal edge becomes smooth, which is precisely the thing a dither is supposed to replace, and the block grid stops being legible.
- Comparing against the Bayer matrix without an epsilon. Its zero cell passes `step()` everywhere, so one pixel in every 5x5 block is lit across the entire canvas, including areas the pointer has never visited.
- Dividing the 8x8 matrix by 63 instead of 64. A threshold of exactly 1.0 means the brightest level can never be selected, and the whitest part of the image clips one step down.
- Assuming `src` is decoded. A `TextureLoader` result arrives asynchronously and may never arrive at all. Leaving the sampler unbound until then is undefined behaviour — black on some drivers, a console warning per draw on others. A 1x1 placeholder is bound from the first frame and a `uHasImage` float selects a procedural stand-in.
- Letting a 404 throw or blank the panel. A component that cannot survive a missing image cannot be dropped into a CMS-backed page. The error callback leaves `uHasImage` at 0 and the trail keeps working over the stand-in field.
- Not cancelling an in-flight decode. If `src` changes or the component unmounts mid-load, the callback fires against a dead renderer and the texture is uploaded and then leaked. A `cancelled` flag disposes it instead.
- Rendering at full device pixel ratio. Fill is the entire cost of a fullscreen quad and it scales with the square of the ratio, for an image whose smallest feature is deliberately five pixels wide.
- Owning the canvas in React while calling `forceContextLoss()` on cleanup. Under `reactStrictMode` the effect runs twice and the second `getContext` on that same element returns the DEAD context: blank in development, fine in production, which is the worst way for a bug to behave.
- Shipping the demo image as a committed asset. The image is a prop; the demo paints its own canvas and passes a data URL, so the registry carries no binary.

## Notes

- `src` is required and is never bundled. Anything a browser can fetch works: an http(s) URL, a `blob:` from an upload, or a `data:` URL.
- Coarse pointers get the composed still rather than the live effect. `pointermove` only fires mid-drag on touch, so the reveal would appear under the finger covering it and then be stranded on lift.
- Without WebGL the component renders the image plainly with `object-fit: cover`. The picture is the content; the dither is decoration on top of it.
- The decoded texture is held across renderer rebuilds, so a resize or a dpr change re-uploads it rather than refetching. It is disposed in its own unmount effect, separate from the loader effect that reruns on every `src` change.
- Leaving the panel does not clear the trail. Samples keep ageing out on their own, so the reveal finishes its life instead of vanishing on `pointerleave`.
- The root carries `role="img"` and the `alt` text; an empty `alt` marks the whole panel decorative with `aria-hidden` instead.

## Definition of done

At rest the image is visible but dimmed and nearly grey. Drag across it and full colour appears in a trail of hard-edged square blocks that widens and fades behind the pointer, with the blocks smeared along the direction of travel — more on a flick, less on a slow drag. The untouched area contains no stray lit pixels anywhere. Stop moving and the reveal stays alive under the cursor instead of dying. Leave the panel and the trail finishes ageing out where it stands. The follow lag is identical on a 60Hz and a 120Hz display. Point at a `src` that 404s: the panel shows a banded stand-in field, the trail still works, and the console carries no exception. Resize wide and the image stays cover-cropped with no stretching, and the trail discs stay round.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
