# Build: Domain-Warped FBM Fog

A full-screen fragment shader on a single triangle. Two octaves of value-noise fbm are sampled twice to build a 2D offset, and that offset is fed back into a third sample — the result flows instead of cross-fading. The pointer enters the warp three times with different weights and a sign flip, so the fog leans toward the cursor without following it.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Slow, low-contrast fog that flows rather than fades, with a faint light that trails the cursor.

- Category: webgl
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. `fbm(p)` sums two octaves of 3D value noise with amplitudes 0.6 and 0.3 and lacunarity 1.93. The third dimension is time, so the field evolves continuously instead of scrolling.
2. The domain warp is `q = vec2(fbm(sp + m*0.20, t), fbm(sp + vec2(2.3,1.1) - m*0.20, t))`, then `n = fbm(sp + q*0.4 + m*0.12, t*0.8) * 0.5 + 0.5`. The `vec2(2.3, 1.1)` offset decorrelates the second channel from the first; without it both return the same number and the warp collapses into a diagonal translation.
3. Both the sample point and the pointer are multiplied by `aspect` on x before use, so the noise stays isotropic and the cursor glow stays circular on a wide screen.
4. `shade = smoothstep(0.25, 0.85, n)` crushes the noise into a soft two-tone field, and the final colour is `base + tint * (gain * shade + lift)` where `lift = (pointerY - 0.5) * 0.03` tilts the whole frame slightly as the cursor moves up and down.
5. The cursor light is `smoothstep(0.85, 0.0, d)` — arguments deliberately reversed to produce a falling ramp, 1 at the cursor and 0 at distance 0.85, without the extra `1.0 -`.
6. A vignette `smoothstep(1.25, 0.5, distance(uv, 0.5))` multiplies the result rather than subtracting from it, so the cursor glow dims with the corners instead of punching through them.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `scale = 0.7`
  Multiplier on the sample coordinate. Below 1.0 the noise features are LARGER than the screen, so you get a handful of slow masses. At 3.0 the same shader is television static.
- `warp = 0.4`
  How far `q` displaces the final sample. Under ~0.15 the warp is invisible and you are looking at plain fbm; over ~0.9 the field folds back on itself and produces hard creases that read as compression artefacts.
- `octaves = 2`
  Textbook fbm uses 4-6. Two is enough because the output goes straight through `smoothstep(0.25, 0.85, n)`, which discards the fine detail anyway. fbm is essentially the whole cost of this shader, so halving the octaves halves the frame time.
- `lacunarity = 1.93`
  Frequency step between octaves. Exactly 2.0 makes the two lattices coincide on every other cell boundary and stamps a faint axis-aligned cross into the field; an off-integer step decorrelates them.
- `amplitude schedule = 0.6 then 0.3`
  Starting below 1.0 keeps the two-octave sum inside roughly -0.9..0.9, so `n * 0.5 + 0.5` lands in 0..1 without clipping and the smoothstep window sits where the data actually is.
- `time scale = 0.03`
  The field advances 0.0005 units per frame at 60 Hz. It has to read as weather, not animation — at 0.3 it becomes a lava lamp and starts competing with the content on top of it.
- `gain = 0.22`
  Peak brightness above the base. The reference site sits at 0.08, which keeps the entire image inside the bottom 17% of the value range so white type sits on it perfectly. 0.22 is the standalone default; drop it toward 0.08 the moment you put text on top.
- `pointer smoothing = 0.02`
  Fraction of the gap left after one second. The pointer displaces a noise domain, so raw values make the whole field jump between pointer events rather than drift.

## API

```ts
function DomainWarpedFbm(props: { scale?: number; warp?: number; gain?: number; speed?: number; base?: readonly [number, number, number]; tint?: readonly [number, number, number]; maxDpr?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `scale: number` — default `0.7`
  Noise frequency. Below 1.0 the features are larger than the screen.
- `warp: number` — default `0.4`
  How far the first two fbm samples displace the third.
- `gain: number` — default `0.22`
  Peak brightness added above the base colour.
- `speed: number` — default `1`
  Multiplier on the drift, which is already very slow.
- `base: readonly [number, number, number]` — default `[0.03, 0.032, 0.042]`
  Base colour, linear 0..1 RGB, straight into the shader.
- `tint: readonly [number, number, number]` — default `[0.86, 0.9, 1]`
  Colour of the lit fog and the cursor glow.
- `maxDpr: number` — default `2`
  Upper bound on device pixel ratio.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const TRIANGLE = new Float32Array([-1, -1, 3, -1, -1, 3]);
const SCALE = 0.7;
const WARP = 0.4;
const GAIN = 0.22;
const BASE: readonly [number, number, number] = [0.03, 0.032, 0.042];
const TINT: readonly [number, number, number] = [0.86, 0.9, 1];

interface Gpu {
  gl: WebGL2RenderingContext;
  program: WebGLProgram;
  vao: WebGLVertexArrayObject;
  buffer: WebGLBuffer;
  locations: Map<string, WebGLUniformLocation | null>;
}

/* A local 60-line bootstrap rather than three.js or ogl. This component draws
   three vertices; a framework would be 100x its own weight in dependency. */
function build(gl: WebGL2RenderingContext, vertSrc: string, fragSrc: string): Gpu | null {
  const compile = (type: number, src: string): WebGLShader | null => {
    const shader = gl.createShader(type);
    if (!shader) return null;
    gl.shaderSource(shader, src);
    gl.compileShader(shader);
    if (gl.getShaderParameter(shader, gl.COMPILE_STATUS)) return shader;
    console.error('[domain-warped-fbm]', gl.getShaderInfoLog(shader));
    gl.deleteShader(shader);
    return null;
  };

  const vert = compile(gl.VERTEX_SHADER, vertSrc);
  const frag = compile(gl.FRAGMENT_SHADER, fragSrc);
  const program = gl.createProgram();
  const vao = gl.createVertexArray();
  const buffer = gl.createBuffer();
  if (!vert || !frag || !program || !vao || !buffer) return null;

  gl.attachShader(program, vert);
  gl.attachShader(program, frag);
  gl.linkProgram(program);
  gl.deleteShader(vert);
  gl.deleteShader(frag);
  if (!gl.getProgramParameter(program, gl.LINK_STATUS)) {
    console.error('[domain-warped-fbm]', gl.getProgramInfoLog(program));
    gl.deleteProgram(program);
    return null;
  }

  gl.bindVertexArray(vao);
  gl.bindBuffer(gl.ARRAY_BUFFER, buffer);
  gl.bufferData(gl.ARRAY_BUFFER, TRIANGLE, gl.STATIC_DRAW);
  const attrib = gl.getAttribLocation(program, 'a_pos');
  if (attrib >= 0) {
    gl.enableVertexAttribArray(attrib);
    gl.vertexAttribPointer(attrib, 2, gl.FLOAT, false, 0, 0);
  }
  gl.bindVertexArray(null);

  return { gl, program, vao, buffer, locations: new Map() };
}

function loc(gpu: Gpu, name: string): WebGLUniformLocation | null {
  const cached = gpu.locations.get(name);
  if (cached !== undefined) return cached;
  const found = gpu.gl.getUniformLocation(gpu.program, name);
  gpu.locations.set(name, found);
  return found;
}

export function DomainWarpedFbm({
  scale = SCALE,
  warp = WARP,
  gain = GAIN,
  speed = 1,
  base = BASE,
  tint = TINT,
  maxDpr = 2,
  className,
}: DomainWarpedFbmProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const canvasRef = useRef<HTMLCanvasElement>(null);
  const gpuRef = useRef<Gpu | null>(null);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const visible = useVisibility();
  // Heavy smoothing: the pointer drives a warp offset, and an unsmoothed
  // pointer makes the whole field snap between frames rather than drift.
  const pointer = useSmoothPointer({ target: host, smoothing: 0.02 });
  const [supported, setSupported] = useState(true);

  const paramsRef = useRef({ scale, warp, gain, speed, base, tint });
  paramsRef.current = { scale, warp, gain, speed, base, tint };

  const drawRef = useRef<(elapsed: number) => void>(() => {});
  drawRef.current = (elapsed: number) => {
    const gpu = gpuRef.current;
    if (!gpu) return;
    const { gl } = gpu;
    const params = paramsRef.current;
    const p = pointer.current;

    gl.useProgram(gpu.program);
    gl.uniform2f(
      loc(gpu, 'u_resolution'),
      gl.drawingBufferWidth,
      gl.drawingBufferHeight,
    );
    gl.uniform1f(loc(gpu, 'u_time'), elapsed * params.speed);
    gl.uniform2f(loc(gpu, 'u_pointer'), p.nx, 1 - p.ny);
    gl.uniform1f(loc(gpu, 'u_scale'), params.scale);
    gl.uniform1f(loc(gpu, 'u_warp'), params.warp);
    gl.uniform1f(loc(gpu, 'u_gain'), params.gain);
    gl.uniform3f(loc(gpu, 'u_base'), params.base[0], params.base[1], params.base[2]);
    gl.uniform3f(loc(gpu, 'u_tint'), params.tint[0], params.tint[1], params.tint[2]);

    gl.bindVertexArray(gpu.vao);
    gl.drawArrays(gl.TRIANGLES, 0, 3);
    gl.bindVertexArray(null);
  };

  useEffect(() => {
    const canvas = canvasRef.current;
    if (!canvas) return;
    if (!hasWebGL()) {
      setSupported(false);
      return;
    }

    const gl = canvas.getContext('webgl2', {
      antialias: false,
      alpha: false,
      depth: false,
      stencil: false,
      powerPreference: 'high-performance',
    });
    if (!gl) {
      setSupported(false);
      return;
    }

    const gpu = build(gl, DOMAIN_WARPED_FBM_VERT, DOMAIN_WARPED_FBM_FRAG);
    if (!gpu) {
      loseContext(gl);
      setSupported(false);
      return;
    }
    gpuRef.current = gpu;
    setSupported(true);

    return () => {
      gpuRef.current = null;
      gl.deleteVertexArray(gpu.vao);
      gl.deleteBuffer(gpu.buffer);
      gl.deleteProgram(gpu.program);
      loseContext(gl);
    };
  }, []);

  useEffect(() => {
    const canvas = canvasRef.current;
    const gpu = gpuRef.current;
    if (!canvas || !gpu || width === 0 || height === 0) return;

    const dpr = pixelRatio(maxDpr);
    const w = Math.max(1, Math.round(width * dpr));
    const h = Math.max(1, Math.round(height * dpr));
    if (canvas.width !== w || canvas.height !== h) {
      canvas.width = w;
      canvas.height = h;
    }
    gpu.gl.viewport(0, 0, w, h);
    // One frame here covers both the first paint and the reduced-motion path.
    drawRef.current(reduced ? 12 : 0);
  }, [width, height, maxDpr, supported, reduced]);

  const running = supported && visible && !reduced && width > 0 && height > 0;
  useRaf((_dt, elapsed) => drawRef.current(elapsed), running);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Deletes the VAO, the vertex buffer and the program, then `loseContext(gl)`. The rAF subscription and the pointer listener are removed by their hooks.

**Reduced motion.** The rAF loop never subscribes. One frame is drawn at a fixed `u_time` of 12 seconds — far enough into the sequence that the field is fully developed rather than at its symmetric t=0 state — and redrawn on resize. The cursor light does not track.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Aspect-correcting the sample space but not the pointer. The noise looks right and the cursor glow becomes an ellipse that stretches further the wider the window gets — the two must live in the same coordinate system.
- Using the same offset for both warp channels. `fbm(sp)` and `fbm(sp)` are the same number, so `q` becomes a scalar along the diagonal and the "warp" is a plain translation; you get sliding blobs with none of the folding.
- Feeding `sin()` a large argument inside the hash. `fract(sin(dot(p, ...)))` degrades badly once `p` is in the thousands: the noise develops repeating bands, and it fails on mobile GPUs at scales where the desktop still looks fine. Fold the input with `fract()` first.
- Running 5 octaves because that is what the tutorial did. The output is immediately crushed by a smoothstep, so octaves 3-5 cost real milliseconds and change nothing you can see.
- Letting the shader run in a hidden tab. `useVisibility` gates the loop; without it a backgrounded page keeps a GPU-bound fragment shader resident and the laptop fan tells the user about it.
- Relying on `dispose()`-style cleanup. Raw GL has none — the VAO, buffer and program are deleted explicitly and `loseContext(gl)` hands the context back, without which mounting this component twenty times kills the oldest contexts on the page.

## Notes

- Value noise rather than simplex: after `smoothstep(0.25, 0.85, n)` the two are indistinguishable, and value noise is eight hash calls and seven mixes with no permutation polynomial.
- Total brightness at the defaults runs roughly 0.03 to 0.30. Set `gain={0.08}` for the original hero behaviour, where the whole field stays under 0.18 and white type needs no scrim.

## Definition of done

Watch for ten seconds: the masses should visibly fold and stretch, not just brighten and dim in place. Move the cursor and a faint circular light follows it a beat late while the fog around it shears. Resize from 320px to full width and the noise features stay the same shape rather than stretching horizontally.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Dotted Notepad Surface

A panel textured with a dot grid drawn by a single tiled radial gradient, masked so the pattern dissolves toward the edges instead of ending on a rectangle. An optional turned-down corner is one hard-stopped linear gradient. Nothing is an image, nothing animates, and the whole surface costs one background layer.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A tiled dot grid that dissolves at the panel edges, with a hard-stopped folded corner.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. One `radial-gradient(circle, dot 1.1px, transparent 1.3px)` is tiled by `background-size: 26px 26px`, so `background-size` alone controls the pitch of the grid and the gradient controls the dot. Changing pitch never requires touching the gradient.
2. The 0.2px between the coloured stop and the transparent stop is the antialiasing ramp. With both stops at the same offset the dot edge quantises to the device pixel grid and the dots render as squares at fractional zoom; wider than about 0.4px and they visibly blur.
3. `background-position: center` rather than `0 0` keeps the lattice symmetric about the panel as it resizes. Pinned to the top-left, a resize crops the pattern on one side only and the grid appears to slide.
4. `mask-image` takes two axis gradients — one vertical, one horizontal — each opaque in the middle and transparent for `--kx-pad-fade` at both ends, combined with `mask-composite: intersect`. Intersecting two linear masks fades all four edges while keeping the interior perfectly flat; a single radial mask would instead darken the corners more than the edges and make a rectangular panel read as a lens.
5. `background-attachment` decides what the tile origin is anchored to, and only matters once the dotted element is itself a scroll container. `scroll` anchors to the element border box so the grid holds still while content slides over it; `local` anchors to the scrolled content so the grid travels with the text and the panel reads as one continuous sheet.
6. The fold is a single absolutely-positioned square carrying `linear-gradient(225deg, void 0 43%, crease 43% 48%, under 48% 100%)`. Hard stops (a stop pair at the same offset) mean no interpolation, so the boundary is a crease and not a shadow. The 225deg gradient line points down-left, which puts the void band at the top-right corner where the paper is turned back.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `pitch = 26px`
  Tile size, therefore dot spacing. Below ~18px the grid starts to read as a flat tone rather than a texture and interferes with body text; above ~34px the dots read as individual objects on the page and compete with content.
- `dotSize = 1.1px`
  Dot radius. At exactly 1px the dot lands on a whole device pixel and hardens; the fractional value is what keeps it soft on 1x displays. Above ~1.6px the surface reads as polka dots rather than paper grain.
- `antialias gap = 0.2px`
  Distance from the colour stop to the transparent stop. This is the only softening the dot gets. At 0 the edge quantises and the dots go square at fractional zoom levels; at 0.5px and above the dot loses its centre and the grid looks smudged.
- `fade = 10%`
  How far the edge mask reaches in. Below ~6% the dissolve is too abrupt to read as intentional and looks like a clipping bug; above ~18% the usable flat area of a small panel disappears and content near the edge visibly ghosts.
- `fold stop positions = 43% / 48%`
  The crease is a 5% sliver. Thinner than ~3% and it drops below a pixel on a small fold and disappears; wider than ~8% and it stops reading as a lit edge and becomes a grey stripe. The 43% start places the crease off-centre so the flap looks lifted rather than symmetrically folded.
- `shadow = 0 34px 70px -34px`
  Negative spread equal to the Y offset. It shrinks the shadow box by exactly the amount the offset moved it, so the blur only escapes below the panel. Without the negative spread a 70px blur haloes all four sides and the sheet looks lit from nowhere.

## API

```ts
function DottedNotepadSurface(props: { children?: ReactNode; pitch?: number; dotSize?: number; fade?: string; scrollable?: boolean; attachment?: 'scroll' | 'local' | 'fixed'; fold?: boolean; radius?: string; className?: string; contentClassName?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Panel content. Rendered above the dot layer.
- `pitch: number` — default `26`
  Grid pitch in pixels. Becomes `background-size`.
- `dotSize: number` — default `1.1`
  Dot radius in pixels. The transparent stop lands 0.2px further out.
- `fade: string` — default `'10%'`
  How far the edge mask reaches in from each side.
- `scrollable: boolean` — default `false`
  Makes the dotted layer the scroll container, which is what gives `attachment` meaning.
- `attachment: 'scroll' | 'local' | 'fixed'` — default `'scroll'`
  Tile origin. `scroll` holds the grid still under scrolling content; `local` scrolls the grid with it.
- `fold: boolean` — default `false`
  Draws the turned-down top-right corner.
- `radius: string` — default `'20px'`
  Panel corner radius. The fold inherits it on its own corner.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the panel. Use for sizing and border.
- `contentClassName: string`
  Merged onto the content wrapper. Put padding here so text clears the mask.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const NOTEPAD_CSS = `
.kx-notepad {
  position: relative;
  isolation: isolate;
  border-radius: var(--kx-pad-radius, 20px);
  overflow: hidden;

  /* Negative spread equal to the Y offset pulls the blur back inside the
     footprint, so the shadow only escapes below the panel. Without it a
     70px blur haloes all four sides and the sheet looks lit from nowhere. */
  box-shadow: 0 34px 70px -34px var(--kx-pad-shadow, rgb(0 0 0 / 0.55));
}

.kx-notepad-sheet {
  height: 100%;
  background-color: var(--kx-pad-bg, var(--color-bg-subtle, Canvas));

  /* One dot per tile. The 0.2px between the colour stop and the transparent
     stop IS the antialiasing — with the stops coincident the dot edge snaps
     to the device pixel grid and the dots go square at odd zoom levels. */
  background-image: radial-gradient(
    circle,
    var(--kx-pad-dot, color-mix(in oklab, currentColor 12%, transparent))
      var(--kx-pad-dot-size, 1.1px),
    transparent calc(var(--kx-pad-dot-size, 1.1px) + 0.2px)
  );
  background-size: var(--kx-pad-pitch, 26px) var(--kx-pad-pitch, 26px);

  /* Centred, not 0 0: the pattern then stays symmetric about the panel as it
     resizes instead of being pinned to the top-left and cropped on one side. */
  background-position: center;
  background-repeat: repeat;
  background-attachment: var(--kx-pad-attachment, scroll);

  /* Two axis gradients intersected. Mask reads alpha only, so the colour
     keyword here is arbitrary — 'black' means "keep", 'transparent' means
     "drop". A single radial mask would round the corners of the fade and
     make a rectangular panel look like a lens. */
  mask-image:
    linear-gradient(
      to bottom,
      transparent 0,
      black var(--kx-pad-fade, 10%),
      black calc(100% - var(--kx-pad-fade, 10%)),
      transparent 100%
    ),
    linear-gradient(
      to right,
      transparent 0,
      black var(--kx-pad-fade, 10%),
      black calc(100% - var(--kx-pad-fade, 10%)),
      transparent 100%
    );
  mask-composite: intersect;
}

.kx-notepad-sheet[data-scrollable='true'] {
  overflow-y: auto;
  overscroll-behavior: contain;
}

/* The turned corner: one hard-stopped gradient, no blur, no extra element.
   Band one is the void the fold reveals and must match whatever sits behind
   the panel; band two is a 5% sliver of highlight along the crease; band
   three is the underside of the flap. Hard stops ('0 43%', '43% 48%') are
   what make it read as a crease rather than a soft shadow. */
.kx-notepad-fold {
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0 0 auto auto;
  width: var(--kx-pad-fold, 52px);
  height: var(--kx-pad-fold, 52px);
  border-top-right-radius: var(--kx-pad-radius, 20px);
  pointer-events: none;
  background: linear-gradient(
    225deg,
    var(--kx-pad-void, var(--color-bg, Canvas)) 0 43%,
    var(--kx-pad-crease, color-mix(in oklab, currentColor 20%, transparent)) 43% 48%,
    var(--kx-pad-under, var(--color-surface, Canvas)) 48% 100%
  );
}

.kx-notepad-body {
  position: relative;
  z-index: 1;
}

/* Nothing here animates, so reduced motion has nothing to switch off. The
   surface is identical in both states by construction. */
`;

export function DottedNotepadSurface({
  children,
  pitch = 26,
  dotSize = 1.1,
  fade = '10%',
  scrollable = false,
  attachment = 'scroll',
  fold = false,
  radius = '20px',
  className,
  contentClassName,
}: DottedNotepadSurfaceProps) {
  const style: StyleWithVars = {
    '--kx-pad-pitch': `${pitch}px`,
    '--kx-pad-dot-size': `${dotSize}px`,
    '--kx-pad-fade': fade,
    '--kx-pad-radius': radius,
    '--kx-pad-attachment': attachment,
  };

  return (
    <>
      <style href="kinetic-dotted-notepad-surface" precedence="medium">
        {NOTEPAD_CSS}
      </style>
      <div className={cn('kx-notepad', className)} style={style}>
        <div className="kx-notepad-sheet" data-scrollable={scrollable ? 'true' : undefined}>
          <div className={cn('kx-notepad-body', contentClassName)}>{children}</div>
        </div>
        {fold ? <span className="kx-notepad-fold" aria-hidden="true" /> : null}
      </div>
    </>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to clean up. No listeners, no timers, no animation frames. The hoisted `<style>` is reference-counted by React and removed when the last instance unmounts.

**Reduced motion.** Nothing in this component moves in either state — there is no animation, transition or timer to disable. The surface renders identically with `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` set, including the fold and the edge fade.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Putting the mask on the panel and expecting only the dots to fade. A mask applies to everything the element paints, children included, so text within `--kx-pad-fade` of an edge ghosts out. Content padding must exceed the fade inset — that is why the component has a separate content wrapper for padding rather than padding the panel.
- Reaching for `background-attachment: fixed` to get a parallax grid. The tile origin becomes the viewport, but any ancestor with a `transform`, `filter`, `backdrop-filter` or `will-change` becomes the containing block instead, so the effect silently changes meaning as soon as someone animates a parent. It also repaints the element across its full area on every scroll frame, and iOS Safari has never implemented it usefully.
- Setting `background-attachment: local` on a panel that does not scroll and expecting a difference. `local` and `scroll` are identical until the element itself has overflow — the value is inert, so the "fix" appears to do nothing and gets removed.
- Coincident gradient stops on the dot (`radial-gradient(circle, c 1.1px, transparent 1.1px)`). It looks correct in a screenshot at 100% zoom and turns into a field of tiny squares on a 1.25x or 1.5x display.
- Using the `background` shorthand after setting `background-size`. The shorthand resets `background-size` to `auto`, the tile collapses to the gradient default, and the grid becomes one enormous dot.
- Assuming the fold reads as a hole without matching `--kx-pad-void` to what is actually behind the panel. The first band of the fold gradient is a flat colour pretending to be the page; against a different background it reads as a grey triangle stuck on the corner.

## Notes

- `mask-composite: intersect` needs Safari 15.4+, Chrome 120+ and Firefox 53+. Where it is unsupported only the first mask layer applies, so the grid fades top and bottom but not left and right — a degradation, not a break.
- The dot layer is a real background rather than a pseudo-element so that `background-attachment` has a scroll container to refer to. A decorative absolutely-positioned overlay could not express the `local` behaviour at all.
- The CSS ships inside the component as a `<style href precedence>` element; React 19 hoists it into `<head>` and de-duplicates by `href`, so any number of panels contribute one rule set.

## Definition of done

The dot grid is crisp at 100% and at 150% browser zoom — individual dots stay round, not square. All four edges dissolve rather than ending on a line, and the interior is perfectly even. With `scrollable` and `attachment="local"`, scrolling the panel moves the dots with the text; with `attachment="scroll"` the dots stay put while the text slides over them. With `fold`, the corner reads as turned paper with a single sharp crease and no blur.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Drag with a Dead Zone and Pointer Capture

A deliberate click moves the pointer one to three pixels; a tap on a phone moves five or more. A drag handler with no dead zone calls all of them drags, so the track lurches on every click and the code that suppresses the post-drag click starts suppressing clicks the user meant. This hook captures the pointer on `pointerdown` — so a fast throw that leaves the element keeps delivering moves — and only commits to a drag once the pointer is further than the threshold from the press point. Every one of the four ways a gesture can end funnels through a single exit, because the path you forget is the one that leaves the track welded to a pointer that is no longer there.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Captures the pointer on press but only commits to a drag past a distance threshold, so a shaky click stays a click.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. `pointerdown` records the press point and calls `setPointerCapture(e.pointerId)` immediately, before any distance test. Capture first, commit second: at the moment the threshold is crossed the pointer may already be outside the element, and `setPointerCapture` on a pointer that has since ended throws `NotFoundError`. Inside its own `pointerdown` the pointer is guaranteed active, so it cannot throw there.
2. `pointermove` computes `distance = Math.hypot(clientX - startX, clientY - startY)` and returns early while it is under the threshold — 8 px for mouse and pen, 16 px for touch, read from `pointerType` on the live pointer rather than from a media query. Until it commits, no callback fires and nothing moves.
3. At the moment of commitment the delta origin is re-based to the current point (`lastX = clientX`). A consumer that integrates `deltaX` therefore starts from zero at the commit point instead of receiving the entire dead zone as the first frame's delta, which would snap the track 8 px the instant it engaged. `dx` still measures from the true press point, so the distance maths stays honest.
4. With `axis` set to `x` or `y` the threshold test becomes directional: if the cross axis clears the dead zone first *and* dominates the main axis, the gesture is abandoned as cancelled so the browser can scroll. Combined with `touch-action: pan-y`, a horizontal dragger and vertical page scrolling coexist on a phone.
5. One `finish(clientX, clientY, cancelled)` handles `pointerup`, `pointercancel`, `lostpointercapture` and the returned `cancel()`. It releases the capture if still held, nulls `pointerId`, and calls `onDragEnd(state, { moved, cancelled })`. The `pointerId === null` guard at the top makes the second arrival for one gesture a no-op — `lostpointercapture` always follows a release, so without it every drag would end twice.
6. The effect sets `touch-action` (from `axis`) and `user-select: none` on the element and restores the previous inline values on cleanup, and it cancels HTML5 `dragstart` so a press on an image does not turn into a native file drag.
7. `moved` is the whole output that matters downstream: false means the gesture was a tap and the consumer should treat it as a click; true means a click that arrives next should be swallowed.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `THRESHOLD = 8`
  Dead-zone radius in pixels for mouse and pen. A deliberate trackpad click slips one to three pixels, and a click while the hand is moving toward the target slips more, so below about 6 the dead zone stops catching real clicks. Above about 14 the beginning of a genuine drag feels glued down — the pointer has visibly moved and the track has not.
- `TOUCH_THRESHOLD = 16`
  Dead-zone radius for touch. A finger pad rolls as it presses and the reported point moves with it, typically 5-10 px on a tap; 8 px would classify a large share of taps as drags. Chrome's own touch-slop for scroll arbitration is in the same range, so this roughly matches what the platform already considers a tap.
- `touch-action (axis 'x') = 'pan-y'`
  Not `none`. `none` gives the element every gesture, including the vertical swipe that was meant to scroll the page, and a horizontal carousel that eats vertical swipes makes a phone page feel broken. `pan-y` hands vertical panning back to the browser, which then fires `pointercancel` when it claims the gesture — which is exactly why `pointercancel` has to be handled.

## API

```ts
function useDragDeadzone(ref: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>, options?: { threshold?: number; touchThreshold?: number; axis?: 'both' | 'x' | 'y'; primaryOnly?: boolean; manageStyles?: boolean; enabled?: boolean; onPress?: (state: DragDeadzoneState) => void; onDragStart?: (state: DragDeadzoneState) => void; onDrag?: (state: DragDeadzoneState) => void; onDragEnd?: (state: DragDeadzoneState, end: { moved: boolean; cancelled: boolean }) => void }): { dragging: RefObject<boolean>; pressed: RefObject<boolean>; distance: RefObject<number>; cancel: () => void }
```

- `threshold: number` — default `8`
  Dead-zone radius in pixels for mouse and pen input.
- `touchThreshold: number` — default `16`
  Dead-zone radius for touch, which needs roughly double.
- `axis: 'both' | 'x' | 'y'` — default `'both'`
  A single axis adds a directional lock and narrows `touch-action` to the other one.
- `primaryOnly: boolean` — default `true`
  Ignore secondary touches and any mouse button but the left one.
- `manageStyles: boolean` — default `true`
  Set `touch-action` and `user-select` on the element, restoring inline values on cleanup.
- `enabled: boolean` — default `true`
  Detach every listener when false. Any live capture is released as it detaches.
- `onPress: (state: DragDeadzoneState) => void`
  An accepted `pointerdown`, before any commitment. Kill in-flight settle tweens here.
- `onDragStart: (state: DragDeadzoneState) => void`
  The dead zone was cleared. At most once per gesture.
- `onDrag: (state: DragDeadzoneState) => void`
  Every move after commitment. `deltaX/deltaY` are re-based to the commit point.
- `onDragEnd: (state: DragDeadzoneState, end: DragEnd) => void`
  The single exit. `moved: false` means treat the gesture as a click.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * Dead-zone radius for a mouse, in pixels. Below ~6 a normal click's own
 * tremor clears it and every click becomes a two-pixel drag; above ~14 the
 * start of a deliberate drag feels glued down.
 */
const THRESHOLD = 8;
/** Dead-zone radius for touch. A finger rolls further than a mouse slips. */
const TOUCH_THRESHOLD = 16;

/**
 * Pointer drag that captures immediately and commits on distance.
 *
 * Deliberately does not swallow the trailing `click` — that is a separate
 * concern with its own edge cases (see `capture-phase-click-swallow`). What
 * this reports is the fact the swallow needs: whether the gesture moved.
 */
export function useDragDeadzone(
  ref: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>,
  options: UseDragDeadzoneOptions = {},
): DragDeadzoneHandle {
  const {
    threshold = THRESHOLD,
    touchThreshold = TOUCH_THRESHOLD,
    axis = 'both',
    primaryOnly = true,
    manageStyles = true,
    enabled = true,
  } = options;

  const dragging = useRef(false);
  const pressed = useRef(false);
  const distance = useRef(0);
  const abort = useRef<() => void>(() => {});

  const config = useRef({ threshold, touchThreshold, axis, primaryOnly, options });
  config.current = { threshold, touchThreshold, axis, primaryOnly, options };

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = ref.current;
    if (!el || !enabled) return;

    /** Non-null exactly while a gesture is live. The guard on every handler. */
    let pointerId: number | null = null;
    let pointerType = '';
    let startX = 0;
    let startY = 0;
    /** Origin for `deltaX/deltaY`. Re-based at commitment. */
    let lastX = 0;
    let lastY = 0;
    /** Previous sample, for the path-length integral. */
    let prevX = 0;
    let prevY = 0;
    let travel = 0;
    let committed = false;

    const previousTouchAction = el.style.touchAction;
    const previousUserSelect = el.style.userSelect;
    if (manageStyles) {
      // Without this, the first touch on a drag surface is arbitrated by the
      // browser: it starts a pan, fires `pointercancel`, and the drag never
      // happens. `pan-y` on a horizontal dragger keeps vertical page
      // scrolling working, which `none` would break.
      el.style.touchAction = axis === 'x' ? 'pan-y' : axis === 'y' ? 'pan-x' : 'none';
      el.style.userSelect = 'none';
    }

    const stateAt = (clientX: number, clientY: number): DragDeadzoneState => {
      const dx = clientX - startX;
      const dy = clientY - startY;
      return {
        dx,
        dy,
        deltaX: clientX - lastX,
        deltaY: clientY - lastY,
        clientX,
        clientY,
        distance: Math.hypot(dx, dy),
        travel,
        pointerId: pointerId ?? -1,
        pointerType,
      };
    };

    /**
     * The single exit. `pointerup`, `pointercancel`, `lostpointercapture` and
     * `cancel()` all arrive here, and the `pointerId` guard makes the second
     * arrival for one gesture a no-op — `lostpointercapture` always follows a
     * release, so without the guard every drag would end twice.
     */
    const finish = (clientX: number, clientY: number, cancelled: boolean) => {
      if (pointerId === null) return;
      const state = stateAt(clientX, clientY);
      const moved = committed;

      if (el.hasPointerCapture(pointerId)) el.releasePointerCapture(pointerId);
      pointerId = null;
      committed = false;
      travel = 0;
      dragging.current = false;
      pressed.current = false;
      distance.current = 0;

      config.current.options.onDragEnd?.(state, { moved, cancelled });
    };

    const onPointerDown = (e: PointerEvent) => {
      const cfg = config.current;
      // A second finger is not a new gesture. Overwriting `pointerId` here
      // orphans the first pointer's capture, which is then never released.
      if (pointerId !== null) return;
      if (cfg.primaryOnly && !e.isPrimary) return;
      // Right and middle button, and the second click of a double-click drag.
      if (e.pointerType === 'mouse' && e.button !== 0) return;

      pointerId = e.pointerId;
      pointerType = e.pointerType;
      startX = lastX = prevX = e.clientX;
      startY = lastY = prevY = e.clientY;
      travel = 0;
      committed = false;
      pressed.current = true;
      distance.current = 0;

      // Inside its own `pointerdown` the pointer is guaranteed active, so this
      // cannot throw. Deferring it to the commit is where it can: by then the
      // pointer may have ended, and `setPointerCapture` throws NotFoundError.
      el.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);
      cfg.options.onPress?.(stateAt(e.clientX, e.clientY));
    };

    const onPointerMove = (e: PointerEvent) => {
      if (pointerId !== e.pointerId) return;
      const cfg = config.current;

      travel += Math.hypot(e.clientX - prevX, e.clientY - prevY);
      prevX = e.clientX;
      prevY = e.clientY;

      const dx = e.clientX - startX;
      const dy = e.clientY - startY;
      distance.current = Math.hypot(dx, dy);

      if (!committed) {
        const limit = pointerType === 'touch' ? cfg.touchThreshold : cfg.threshold;

        if (cfg.axis === 'both') {
          if (distance.current < limit) return;
        } else {
          const main = cfg.axis === 'x' ? dx : dy;
          const cross = cfg.axis === 'x' ? dy : dx;
          // Whichever axis clears the dead zone first owns the gesture. A
          // horizontal dragger that skips this eats every vertical flick that
          // happens to start on it, and the page will not scroll.
          if (Math.abs(cross) >= limit && Math.abs(cross) > Math.abs(main)) {
            finish(e.clientX, e.clientY, true);
            return;
          }
          if (Math.abs(main) < limit) return;
        }

        committed = true;
        dragging.current = true;
        // Re-base the delta origin at the commit point. Without this the first
        // `onDrag` carries the whole dead zone as its delta, and a consumer
        // integrating deltas sees the track snap 8 px the instant it commits.
        lastX = e.clientX;
        lastY = e.clientY;
        cfg.options.onDragStart?.(stateAt(e.clientX, e.clientY));
        return;
      }

      cfg.options.onDrag?.(stateAt(e.clientX, e.clientY));
      lastX = e.clientX;
      lastY = e.clientY;
    };

    const onPointerUp = (e: PointerEvent) => {
      if (pointerId !== e.pointerId) return;
      finish(e.clientX, e.clientY, false);
    };

    /** Browser took the gesture: its own pan, a long-press menu, a stylus lift. */
    const onPointerCancel = (e: PointerEvent) => {
      if (pointerId !== e.pointerId) return;
      finish(e.clientX, e.clientY, true);
    };

    /**
     * Capture ended without a release — an OS window switch, a disconnected
     * device, another element calling `setPointerCapture`. Omitting this is
     * how a carousel ends up stuck to a pointer that left the building:
     * `dragging` stays true and no further event will ever clear it.
     */
    const onLostCapture = (e: PointerEvent) => {
      if (pointerId !== e.pointerId) return;
      finish(e.clientX, e.clientY, true);
    };

    /** HTML's own drag-and-drop. Left alone it hijacks any press on an image. */
    const onNativeDragStart = (e: Event) => e.preventDefault();

    abort.current = () => finish(lastX, lastY, true);

    el.addEventListener('pointerdown', onPointerDown);
    el.addEventListener('pointermove', onPointerMove);
    el.addEventListener('pointerup', onPointerUp);
    el.addEventListener('pointercancel', onPointerCancel);
    el.addEventListener('lostpointercapture', onLostCapture);
    el.addEventListener('dragstart', onNativeDragStart);

    return () => {
      // Release first, while `pointerId` still says which pointer. An element
      // that unmounts holding a capture leaves the browser routing pointer
      // events at a detached node, and the pointer stays captured until the
      // next `pointerdown` anywhere in the document.
      if (pointerId !== null && el.hasPointerCapture(pointerId)) {
        el.releasePointerCapture(pointerId);
      }
      pointerId = null;
      committed = false;
      dragging.current = false;
      pressed.current = false;
      distance.current = 0;
      abort.current = () => {};

      el.removeEventListener('pointerdown', onPointerDown);
      el.removeEventListener('pointermove', onPointerMove);
      el.removeEventListener('pointerup', onPointerUp);
      el.removeEventListener('pointercancel', onPointerCancel);
      el.removeEventListener('lostpointercapture', onLostCapture);
      el.removeEventListener('dragstart', onNativeDragStart);

      if (manageStyles) {
        el.style.touchAction = previousTouchAction;
        el.style.userSelect = previousUserSelect;
      }
    };
  }, [ref, enabled, manageStyles, axis]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The cleanup releases the pointer capture first, while `pointerId` still records which pointer holds it, then nulls the gesture state, removes all six listeners (`pointerdown`, `pointermove`, `pointerup`, `pointercancel`, `lostpointercapture`, `dragstart`), neuters the `cancel()` closure, and restores the element's previous inline `touch-action` and `user-select`. There is no timer and no rAF. Under React 19 StrictMode the first effect has fully released its capture before the second attaches.

**Reduced motion.** Nothing changes, and that is the correct behaviour rather than an omission. Every position this hook reports is one the user is currently holding under their own finger — direct manipulation, one to one, with no animation of its own to shorten or remove, which is why the reduced-motion guidance explicitly exempts it. Reduced motion belongs to whatever happens after release: the settle, the snap, the momentum. Note that the dead zone is deliberately not widened either; a tremor threshold and a motion preference are different user needs and conflating them would degrade dragging for people who never asked for it.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- No dead zone at all. Every click becomes a two-pixel drag, so the track twitches on each press, and any click suppression built on "did it drag" now eats clicks the user intended. This is the failure that makes drag carousels feel untrustworthy.
- Capturing the pointer at the moment of commitment rather than on press. Two bugs at once: the moves that happened during the dead zone are lost, and if the pointer has already ended, `setPointerCapture` throws `NotFoundError` and the drag silently never starts.
- No pointer capture. Throw the track quickly and the pointer leaves the element; `pointermove` stops arriving, the track freezes mid-throw with the button still down, and the eventual `pointerup` lands somewhere else entirely, so the gesture never ends.
- Handling only `pointerup`. `pointercancel` fires whenever the browser claims the gesture for scrolling or a long-press menu — routine on touch — and `lostpointercapture` fires when the capture is dropped without a release. Miss either and `dragging` stays true forever: the next `pointermove` from an unrelated hover keeps driving the track.
- Not guarding against the second end event. `lostpointercapture` always follows a release, so a naive implementation runs its end logic twice per drag — two snap tweens, two velocity readings, and a click-swallow flag set and then cleared.
- Ending the drag without re-basing the delta origin at commitment. The first `onDrag` then reports the full dead-zone offset, and the track jumps by the threshold the moment it engages — small, but it is exactly the wrong 8 px because it lands on the frame the user is watching for feedback.
- Overwriting `pointerId` when a second finger lands. The first pointer's capture is then never released, so the element holds a capture for a pointer that has ended and the next gesture on it behaves unpredictably.
- Forgetting `touch-action`. On touch the browser arbitrates the gesture, decides it is a pan, and fires `pointercancel` before the dead zone is even cleared. The drag works perfectly on a desktop and does nothing at all on a phone, which is a hard bug to find without a device.
- Setting `touch-action: none` on a horizontal dragger. The element swallows vertical swipes too, so the page cannot be scrolled by dragging anywhere over the carousel — on a phone that is often most of the screen.
- Unmounting while the capture is held. The browser keeps routing pointer events to a detached node, and the pointer stays captured until the next `pointerdown` anywhere in the document, so the rest of the page appears to ignore the mouse.
- Using cumulative path length instead of straight-line distance for the dead zone. A hand tremor that wobbles back and forth over the same three pixels accumulates past any threshold without the pointer ever leaving the press point, so the click is classified as a drag — the tremor case the dead zone existed to catch.
- Calling `preventDefault()` on `pointerdown` to stop text selection. It also prevents focus, so the element can no longer be reached or activated from the keyboard. Setting `user-select: none` costs nothing and breaks nothing.

## Notes

- Pairs with `capture-phase-click-swallow`: this hook decides whether the gesture moved, that one suppresses the resulting click. They are separate because the swallow has its own edge cases — one click and no more, and keyboard activation must pass through — and because plenty of consumers want the classification without wanting to intercept clicks at all.
- Both `distance` and `travel` are reported. `distance` is what the dead zone tests; `travel` is the path integral, and their ratio is a cheap measure of how straight the gesture was, which is useful if you want to distinguish a flick from a scribble.
- The returned `cancel()` exists so a host can abort a gesture on Escape, on a route change, or when a modal opens. It runs the same single exit, so the capture is released and `onDragEnd` reports `cancelled: true`.
- Momentum, snapping and rubber-banding are deliberately absent. This is the input layer; what the position does after release belongs to whatever integrates the deltas.

## Definition of done

Press and release without moving: the row does not shift by even a pixel and the readout says the gesture was a tap. Press, wobble a few pixels inside the dead-zone ring, release: still a tap, and the ring never fills. Push past the ring and the row starts following the pointer from where it committed, with no initial jump. Drag fast off the side of the panel and keep going — the row keeps tracking, because the capture holds. Release outside the panel and the gesture ends there. On a phone, swipe horizontally and the row moves; swipe vertically and the page scrolls while the readout reports a cancelled gesture. Right-click on the row: nothing starts. Drag with a second finger already down: the first gesture keeps control. Unmount mid-drag and the rest of the page still responds to the mouse.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Drag Marquee

One unwrapped accumulator carries the idle drift, the drag and the throw; the wrap happens once, in the follow tween's `modifiers`, as `mod(x, period) - period`. Because that is a true modulo it is total — a delta of four periods in one frame lands correctly — and because it is the identity for `x` already inside `[-period, 0)` it never shows a seam. Pressing scatters the cards on a single paused timeline that is played forwards and reversed, and releasing hands the row over to a plugin-free inertial throw.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

An endless row that drifts, takes a drag and a throw, and scatters its cards while your hand is down.

- Category: layout
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. The row is `N` copies of the children inside a `w-max` flex track. `period` is the measured width of one copy — `getBoundingClientRect().width`, not `offsetWidth`, because the latter rounds and half a pixel of error is half a pixel of gap that only ever shows at the seam. The copy count is `clamp(ceil(hostWidth / period) + 1, 2, 8)`, which is exactly enough that a translation bounded by one period can never expose the end of the track.
2. Everything that moves the row adds to one number that is never corrected: the drift subtracts `speed * dt`, each `pointermove` adds `dx`, the release adds the throw distance. It walks off to -50000 and nothing cares, because the only consumer of it applies a modulo.
3. That modulo lives in `gsap.quickTo`'s `modifiers`, which post-processes the value on its way to the target. It cannot feed back: `resetTo` advances the tween's start from its own `s + ratio * c` rather than re-reading the target, so the wrapped value is output-only. Wrapping in `onUpdate` instead makes the next retarget interpolate from a value the tween does not believe in, and the row lurches a whole period.
4. For `x` in `[-period, 0)`, `mod(x, period) === x + period`, so `mod(x, period) - period === x`. The wrap is therefore the identity across the entire range the row normally occupies and only bites when the accumulator leaves it — the two sides of the boundary paint identical pixels, so there is nothing to snap.
5. The gap is a trailing `margin-right` on each tile *inside* a copy rather than `gap` on the track. A track-level gap sits between copies too, so the measured copy width would no longer equal the wrap period and the seam would gain one gap of drift every lap.
6. Release velocity is measured over a rolling ~70 ms window of `(accumulator, time)`, then projected with the `power3.out` identity: `p(t) = 1 - (1 - t)^3` has `p'(0) = 3`, so a tween of duration `D` covering `delta` departs at `3 * delta / D`. Retargeting by `v * D / 3` continues the gesture at exactly the speed the hand left, with the core library and no `InertiaPlugin`.
7. The press scatter is one paused timeline built once and stored in a ref, `play()` on `pointerdown` and `reverse()` on the release path. Per-tile rotation and offset come from a seeded generator indexed by position *within* a copy, so every copy of a tile scatters identically and the duplication stays invisible while the cards move.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `copies = clamp(ceil(hostWidth / period) + 1, 2, 8)`
  The `+ 1` is the copy that covers the wrap: with the translation bounded to one period, the window can start one full period into the track and still needs `hostWidth` of content after it. Drop it and the tail of the row shows background for part of every lap. The floor of 2 is the minimum that can hide a seam at all; the ceiling of 8 stops a one-word tile in a wide hero from producing hundreds of nodes.
- `POWER3_OUT_SLOPE = 3`
  The initial derivative of `power3.out`, and the divisor in `delta = v * D / 3`. Exact, not tuned: change the follow tween's ease and this changes with it — `power2` needs 2, `power4` needs 4. Leave it at 3 against a different ease and every throw is off by a constant factor.
- `smoothing = 0.5`
  Seconds the row takes to catch up with the pointer, and the `D` in the throw projection. Under ~0.2 s the row is welded to the finger and the throw is over before it registers; over ~0.8 s the lag between hand and content is large enough to read as dropped frames rather than as weight.
- `speed = 60`
  Idle drift in px/s. Below ~20 the row looks frozen at a glance and the affordance is lost; above ~120 the text is unreadable at rest, which defeats the point of putting words in it. At 0 the ticker is never registered at all, so a parked marquee costs nothing per frame.
- `VELOCITY_WINDOW = 0.07`
  Seconds of gesture history the release speed is averaged over. Shorter is effectively the last delta, which is noisy at 120 Hz and gives visibly different throws for identical gestures; much longer averages away a deliberate slow-down before release, so the row flies off when the user meant to place it.
- `MAX_VELOCITY = 4000`
  px/s the measured speed is clamped to. A coalesced pointer batch, a tab switch mid-drag or a synthetic event can report tens of thousands; without the clamp one bad sample throws the row several periods, and the wrap makes the result look random rather than fast.
- `MAX_THROW = 1200`
  Pixels one throw may carry. Roughly a screen and a half — far enough that a hard flick feels unbounded, close enough that the content the user was looking at is still findable when it stops.
- `DRAG_THRESHOLD = 5`
  Pixels of travel before a press becomes a drag. Below ~3 the tremor in a normal tap counts as a drag and every tap on a card is swallowed; above ~10 a small deliberate nudge does nothing at all.
- `scatter / spin = 6 (percent) / 10 (deg)`
  Half-ranges for the per-tile offset and rotation on press. The offset is a percentage of each tile's own size, so mixed tile widths scatter proportionally instead of the small ones flying off. Past ~15% and ~25° the tiles overlap their neighbours and the row stops reading as a row; below ~3% and ~5° the press produces no visible acknowledgement.
- `ease: back.inOut(3) = 3`
  The overshoot of the scatter, applied at both ends because the same timeline is played and reversed. It is what makes the cards spring apart and spring back rather than easing politely; at 1 the overshoot is invisible, past ~5 the return visibly overshoots the resting layout and the row wobbles after release.

## API

```ts
function DragMarquee(props: { children: ReactNode; speed?: number; gap?: number; smoothing?: number; scatter?: number; spin?: number; pressScale?: number; scatterDuration?: number; seed?: number | string; className?: string; tileClassName?: string; 'aria-label'?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  One tile per child. The whole set is duplicated as many times as the width needs.
- `speed: number` — default `60`
  Idle drift in px/s. Positive drifts left; 0 parks the row and skips the ticker entirely.
- `gap: number` — default `24`
  Pixels between tiles, applied inside a copy so the spacing also spans the seam.
- `smoothing: number` — default `0.5`
  Seconds the row takes to catch up with the pointer. Doubles as the throw duration.
- `scatter: number` — default `6`
  Scatter distance on press, as a percentage of each tile's own size.
- `spin: number` — default `10`
  Half-range of the per-tile rotation on press, in degrees.
- `pressScale: number` — default `0.95`
  Tile scale while the pointer is down.
- `scatterDuration: number` — default `0.5`
  Seconds for the scatter out, and the same again back.
- `seed: number | string` — default `'drag-marquee'`
  Seeds the scatter. The same seed gives the same arrangement on server and client.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the drag surface.
- `tileClassName: string`
  Merged onto every tile. Size the items here.
- `aria-label: string` — default `'Marquee'`
  Label for the focusable row, which also takes left and right arrow keys.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** The only place the track's transform is written. */
const paint = useCallback(() => {
  const track = trackRef.current;
  if (!track) return;
  track.style.transform = `translate3d(${proxyRef.current.x.toFixed(2)}px, 0px, 0px)`;
}, []);

/**
 * Move the accumulator to `value`. With motion allowed this retargets the
 * follow tween — `quickTo` reuses one tween and one `PropTween` rather than
 * allocating a tween per frame — and the wrap happens in its modifier. With
 * reduced motion there is no tween, so the wrap is applied here instead.
 */
const push = useCallback(
  (value: number) => {
    rawRef.current = value;
    const xTo = xToRef.current;
    if (xTo) {
      xTo(value);
      return;
    }
    const period = periodRef.current;
    proxyRef.current.x = period < 1 ? 0 : mod(value, period) - period;
    paint();
  },
  [paint],
);

/**
 * One follow tween for the life of the component. The wrap lives in
 * `modifiers`, which post-processes the value on its way to the target and
 * never feeds back: `resetTo` advances the tween's start from its own
 * `s + ratio * c`, not by re-reading `proxy.x`. Put the wrap anywhere else
 * — in `onUpdate`, say — and the next retarget interpolates from a value the
 * tween does not believe in, and the row lurches a full period.
 */
useEffect(() => {
  const proxy = proxyRef.current;
  if (reduced) {
    xToRef.current = null;
    return;
  }

  const xTo = gsap.quickTo(proxy, 'x', {
    duration: smoothing,
    ease: 'power3',
    modifiers: {
      // Reads the ref, so a resize changes the period without rebuilding
      // the tween — rebuilding mid-throw would restart the ease from rest.
      x: (value: number) => {
        const period = periodRef.current;
        return period < 1 ? 0 : mod(value, period) - period;
      },
    },
    onUpdate: paint,
  });
  xToRef.current = xTo;

  return () => {
    xToRef.current = null;
    gsap.killTweensOf(proxy);
  };
}, [reduced, smoothing, paint]);

useEffect(() => {
  const host = hostRef.current;
  if (!host) return;

  let pointerId: number | null = null;
  let lastX = 0;
  let pressX = 0;
  let pressY = 0;
  let moved = false;
  let swallowClick = false;
  /** Rolling window: the accumulator and clock at the start of the window. */
  let sampleRaw = 0;
  let sampleTime = 0;

  const now = () => performance.now() / 1000;

  const onPointerDown = (e: PointerEvent) => {
    // One pointer owns the row. A second finger arriving mid-throw would
    // otherwise reset the origin and the row would jump.
    if (pointerId !== null || !e.isPrimary) return;
    if (e.pointerType === 'mouse' && e.button !== 0) return;

    pointerId = e.pointerId;
    lastX = e.clientX;
    pressX = e.clientX;
    pressY = e.clientY;
    moved = false;
    sampleRaw = rawRef.current;
    sampleTime = now();
    pressedRef.current = true;

    // Capture on press, not once the threshold is crossed: by then the
    // pointer may already have left the element and `pointermove` would have
    // stopped arriving.
    host.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);
    // Scatter on press, like a physical stack of cards being pinned — the
    // press, not the drag, is what the eye reads as "I have hold of this".
    scatterRef.current?.play();
  };

  const onPointerMove = (e: PointerEvent) => {
    if (pointerId !== e.pointerId) return;

    const dx = e.clientX - lastX;
    lastX = e.clientX;

    if (!moved) {
      if (Math.hypot(e.clientX - pressX, e.clientY - pressY) < DRAG_THRESHOLD) return;
      moved = true;
    }

    push(rawRef.current + dx);

    // Retire the velocity window once it is full. Measuring over a window
    // rather than off the last delta is what stops "drag, pause, lift" from
    // throwing the row: with no movement there are no events, the window
    // never advances, and the measured speed decays toward zero on its own.
    const t = now();
    if (t - sampleTime > VELOCITY_WINDOW) {
      sampleRaw = rawRef.current;
      sampleTime = t;
    }
  };

  /**
   * Idempotent. Called from `pointerup`, `pointercancel` and
   * `lostpointercapture`, all three of which can be the last event a gesture
   * produces, and at least one of which always arrives — including when the
   * pointer is released outside the window or the OS takes it away for a
   * gesture of its own. Guarding on `pointerId` makes the extra calls no-ops
   * instead of a double throw, and it is what stops a drag that ended
   * off-screen from leaving the row stuck mid-throw with the cards still
   * scattered.
   */
  const finish = (e: PointerEvent) => {
    if (pointerId !== e.pointerId) return;
    const id = pointerId;
    pointerId = null;
    pressedRef.current = false;

    const elapsed = now() - sampleTime;
    const velocity =
      moved && elapsed > 0
        ? clamp((rawRef.current - sampleRaw) / elapsed, -MAX_VELOCITY, MAX_VELOCITY)
        : 0;

    swallowClick = moved;
    moved = false;

    if (host.hasPointerCapture(id)) host.releasePointerCapture(id);
    scatterRef.current?.reverse();

    if (velocity !== 0) {
      // v·D/3 is the distance a `power3.out` of duration D covers when it
      // departs at v. Retargeting by exactly that hands the row over from
      // the finger without a change of speed.
      push(
        rawRef.current +
          clamp((velocity * smoothing) / POWER3_OUT_SLOPE, -MAX_THROW, MAX_THROW),
      );
    }
  };

  // Capture phase, ahead of any child's own handler. A drag ends with a
  // `click` on whatever happens to be under the pointer, so without this the
  // gesture that scrolls the row also activates a card.
  const onClick = (e: MouseEvent) => {
    if (!swallowClick) return;
    swallowClick = false;
    e.preventDefault();
    e.stopPropagation();
  };

  const onKeyDown = (e: KeyboardEvent) => {
    const direction = e.key === 'ArrowRight' ? 1 : e.key === 'ArrowLeft' ? -1 : 0;
    if (direction === 0) return;
    e.preventDefault();
    const step = perCopy > 0 ? periodRef.current / perCopy : periodRef.current;
    push(rawRef.current + direction * step);
  };

  host.addEventListener('pointerdown', onPointerDown);
  host.addEventListener('pointermove', onPointerMove);
  host.addEventListener('pointerup', finish);
  host.addEventListener('pointercancel', finish);
  host.addEventListener('lostpointercapture', finish);
  host.addEventListener('click', onClick, true);
  host.addEventListener('keydown', onKeyDown);

  return () => {
    host.removeEventListener('pointerdown', onPointerDown);
    host.removeEventListener('pointermove', onPointerMove);
    host.removeEventListener('pointerup', finish);
    host.removeEventListener('pointercancel', finish);
    host.removeEventListener('lostpointercapture', finish);
    host.removeEventListener('click', onClick, true);
    host.removeEventListener('keydown', onKeyDown);
    if (pointerId !== null && host.hasPointerCapture(pointerId)) {
      host.releasePointerCapture(pointerId);
    }
    pointerId = null;
    pressedRef.current = false;
  };
}, [push, smoothing, perCopy]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Removes `pointerdown`, `pointermove`, `pointerup`, `pointercancel`, `lostpointercapture`, the capture-phase `click` and `keydown`; releases pointer capture if a gesture is still live at unmount; removes the drift callback from `gsap.ticker`; kills the tweens on the proxy object so an in-flight throw cannot call `onUpdate` against a detached track; and reverts the `gsap.context` holding the scatter timeline, which also restores the tiles' inline transforms. Both shared resize observers and the shared intersection observer unregister.

**Reduced motion.** Dragging is unchanged — it is the user's own motion, and tracking it is the component. Everything the component would have animated by itself is dropped: the idle drift is never registered on the ticker, the follow tween is never created (so the row is written straight to the wrapped position, one-to-one with the pointer, and a release does not throw), and the scatter timeline is not built, so pressing moves nothing but the row. Arrow keys still step one tile, instantly.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Correcting the offset with `if (x < -period) x += period` instead of a modulo. It only ever undoes one period, so a fast flick, a coalesced pointer batch, or a tab that was backgrounded for a second leaves the row several periods out and it jumps to the wrong tile. `mod` is total: any magnitude, one step, right answer.
- Applying the wrap in `onUpdate` rather than in `modifiers`. The tween then interpolates from a start value it computed internally toward a target the wrap has already moved, so the next retarget travels a whole extra period. `modifiers` is post-processing on the way out and never feeds back into the tween's own bookkeeping.
- Putting the gap on the track with `gap` or `space-x`. It lands between copies as well as between tiles, so the measured copy width no longer equals the wrap period; the seam gains one gap per lap and slowly slides out of register. The gap belongs inside the copy, as a trailing margin on every tile.
- Measuring the period with `offsetWidth`. It rounds to whole pixels, and a sub-pixel error in the period is a permanent sub-pixel misalignment at the seam that shows as a hairline flicker once per lap.
- Hard-coding two copies. Two is enough only while one copy is at least as wide as the container; a short tile set in a wide hero runs out of content mid-lap and the row ends in empty space. The count has to come from the measured width.
- Randomising the scatter per DOM node. The duplicates are the whole trick, and the instant the cards move with different rotations the eye reads them as different content — the seam becomes obvious. Index the seed by position within a copy, so copy 3 tile 5 matches copy 1 tile 5.
- Rebuilding the scatter timeline per press, or putting the pressed flag in the `useGsap` deps. `revert()` strips the inline transforms GSAP wrote, so the reverse starts from the untouched stylesheet values and animates nowhere — the cards stay scattered. One paused timeline, `play()` and `reverse()` from the pointer handlers.
- Leaving the idle drift running during a drag. The row creeps out from under the finger, which is precisely what one-to-one tracking exists to prevent; over a slow careful drag the divergence is several tiles.
- Calling `setPointerCapture` only after the drag threshold is crossed. A fast gesture has already left the element by then, `pointermove` stops arriving, and the row sticks at the offset it had when the pointer crossed the boundary.
- Handling only `pointerup`. Release outside the window, or let the OS claim the gesture, and no `pointerup` arrives: the row stays captured, the drift never resumes, and the cards stay scattered mid-throw. `pointercancel` and `lostpointercapture` route to the same idempotent finish, guarded on the stored `pointerId` so the duplicate is a no-op rather than a second throw.
- Letting the click through after a drag. The gesture ends with a `click` on whichever card is under the pointer, so dragging the row also opens a project. It is swallowed in the capture phase, once, and only when the gesture actually moved.

## Notes

- The follow tween is retargeted, not recreated: `gsap.quickTo` keeps one tween and one `PropTween` alive and calls `resetTo` on it, so a marquee dragged for ten seconds allocates nothing per frame.
- The drift is registered on `gsap.ticker` rather than a second rAF loop, so the target and the tween that chases it advance in the same tick. On separate loops the row is one frame stale every other frame, which reads as a faint shimmer at speed.
- Because the drift keeps retargeting the same tween after release, the throw decays exponentially with a time constant of `smoothing / 3` rather than tracing a literal `power3` curve. The departure speed is still exactly the hand's, which is the part the eye judges.
- Only the first copy is exposed to assistive technology; the rest carry `aria-hidden`, so a screen reader reads the list once rather than four times.

## Definition of done

The row drifts on its own. Grab it and it follows your hand exactly, with no creep in the drift direction, and the cards tilt and shrink apart the instant you press — then settle back when you let go. Flick and release: it coasts on at the speed you left, slows, and rejoins the drift with no visible seam or jump. Drag several screens' worth in one fast swipe and the tiles stay in order — nothing teleports. Watch one tile go off the left edge and it reappears on the right at the same spacing as every other gap. Release the pointer outside the browser window and the row keeps drifting instead of freezing scattered. Release over a card and no click reaches it; tap without moving and it does. Resize the container narrower and wider — the seam never appears. Scroll it out of view and the drift stops until it is back.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
