# Build: Drag-Throw Scroll

A third input modality bolted onto a scroll position that already has two. Wheel, pointer drag and arrow keys all write to one place, so they cannot disagree — press stops whatever was coasting exactly where it looks, the drag maps 1:1 from the press point, and release converts the last 100 ms of hand movement into a decaying throw. Pointed at the document it drives the shared Lenis instance; pointed at a box it drives `scrollTop` through the same physics.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Grab the page and pull it; let go mid-move and it coasts on, decaying, as far as the flick earned.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: lenis@^1.3.11

## How it works

1. On `pointerdown` the surface calls `setPointerCapture` and records `startY` plus `startScroll = lenis.scroll` — the animated position, not `targetScroll`, so grabbing a coasting page stops the content where the eye sees it rather than where the throw was headed.
2. Every `pointermove` recomputes the scroll target absolutely: `clamp(startScroll - (clientY - startY) * gain, 0, limit)`. Gain is `multiplier` for mouse and pen and hard-wired to 1 for touch, because a finger is physically on the content and any other value slides the content out from under it.
3. Positions are pushed into a 5-entry ring of `{ y, timeStamp }`. On release, velocity is `(newest.y - oldest.y) / (newest.t - oldest.t) * 1000` px/s using only samples inside a 100 ms window, so the number describes the hand rather than the event rate.
4. The throw target is `target + (-velocity * gain) * throwSeconds`, clamped to the scroll limit. Below `MIN_THROW_SPEED` nothing is issued at all, so a careful release parks instead of drifting.
5. The decay is one curve expressed twice: `lenis.scrollTo(y, { lerp: 0.05 })` for the page, and `damp(scrollTop, y, perFrameToSmoothing(0.05), dt)` on the shared rAF for a box scroller, which stops writing once it is within 0.5 px of target.
6. `ArrowUp` / `ArrowDown` on the focused surface step by `keyStep` px through `scrollTo(y, { duration: 0.2 })`, so keyboard, wheel and hand all mutate the same single position.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `multiplier = 2`
  Scroll px per mouse px. At 1 a long page needs a grab per viewport, because the cursor runs out of window; above ~3 the content outruns the hand and the gesture stops reading as direct manipulation. Touch ignores this entirely and uses 1.
- `throwSeconds = 0.65`
  Coast distance is velocity × this, so it is the time constant of the flick. Under ~0.3 a hard flick barely outruns the release and the throw is invisible; over ~1 a flick crosses the whole document and lands somewhere the user did not aim.
- `THROW_LERP = 0.05`
  Per-frame fraction of the remaining gap, i.e. a long slow settle — the point of a throw is that it decays visibly. At 0.2 it arrives in a few frames and reads as a jump; `perFrameToSmoothing` converts the same number for the `damp` path so the two sinks decay identically.
- `SAMPLE_WINDOW_MS = 100`
  Only samples newer than this count toward the release velocity. Without the window, a drag that travels fast and then stops dead for a second still throws, because the fast samples are still in the buffer — the page launches from a hand that was holding still.
- `SAMPLE_COUNT = 5`
  Ring length. One sample is pure jitter, and more than about five spans long enough that the window filter is doing all the work anyway; five covers roughly 80 ms at 60 Hz, which is one flick.
- `MIN_THROW_SPEED = 120 px/s`
  Below this no throw is issued. At 0.65 s of coast, 120 px/s is a 78 px slide — around the point where a deliberate stop stops feeling deliberate. Lower and the content creeps after every release.
- `SETTLE_EPSILON = 0.5 px`
  An exponential never actually arrives. Without a floor the box sink writes a sub-pixel `scrollTop` every frame forever, so the rAF subscription never idles and the scroll event never stops firing.
- `KEY_STEP_SECONDS = 0.2`
  Arrow-key travel time. Instant is disorienting because nothing connects the two positions; beyond ~0.35 s holding the key queues steps faster than they complete and the page falls behind the keyboard.

## API

```ts
function DragThrowScroll(props: { children?: ReactNode; scroller?: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>; multiplier?: number; throwSeconds?: number; keyStep?: number; enabled?: boolean; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  The draggable content. The surface is `position: relative` and nothing else.
- `scroller: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>`
  Box to scroll. Omit to drive the document through the shared Lenis instance.
- `multiplier: number` — default `2`
  Scroll px per pointer px for mouse and pen. Touch is always 1.
- `throwSeconds: number` — default `0.65`
  Time constant of the release throw; distance is velocity × this.
- `keyStep: number` — default `100`
  Arrow-key step in px while the surface has focus.
- `enabled: boolean` — default `true`
  False removes every listener and restores native scrolling.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the drag surface.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * Lenis's per-frame lerp for the throw, and the same curve expressed for
 * `damp` so a box scroller decays identically to the page. One number, two
 * sinks — tuning it in one place cannot desync them.
 */
const THROW_LERP = 0.05;
const THROW_SMOOTHING = perFrameToSmoothing(THROW_LERP);

const SAMPLE_COUNT = 5;
const SAMPLE_WINDOW_MS = 100;
const MIN_THROW_SPEED = 120;
const SETTLE_EPSILON = 0.5;
const KEY_STEP_SECONDS = 0.2;

/** Presses on real controls belong to those controls, not to the drag. */
const NO_DRAG = 'a,button,input,select,textarea,label,[data-no-drag]';

function scrollBoxOf(scroller?: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>): Element | null {
  if (scroller) return scroller.current;
  return typeof document === 'undefined' ? null : document.scrollingElement;
}

export function DragThrowScroll({
  children,
  scroller,
  multiplier = 2,
  throwSeconds = 0.65,
  keyStep = 100,
  enabled = true,
  className,
}: DragThrowScrollProps) {
  const surface = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  /* Lenis owns the document and nothing else. A component pointed at its own
     box must not build one — and under reduced motion nobody wants smoothing
     at all, so the page sink degrades to direct `scrollTop` writes. The hook
     is refcounted: several of these on one page share the single instance
     rather than stacking `wheel` handlers that each call `preventDefault`. */
  const viaLenis = enabled && !reduced && scroller === undefined;
  const lenis = useLenis({ enabled: viaLenis });

  /** Coast target for the box sink. `null` means nothing is in flight. */
  const glide = useRef<number | null>(null);

  useRaf(
    (dt) => {
      const to = glide.current;
      const box = scrollBoxOf(scroller);
      if (to === null || !box) return;
      const next = damp(box.scrollTop, to, THROW_SMOOTHING, dt);
      // Snap and stop. An exponential never arrives, so without a floor this
      // writes a sub-pixel delta every frame forever and the loop never idles.
      if (Math.abs(to - next) < SETTLE_EPSILON) {
        glide.current = null;
        box.scrollTop = to;
        return;
      }
      box.scrollTop = next;
    },
    // Only the box sink needs a loop: Lenis animates its own scrollTo, and
    // reduced motion has nothing to animate.
    enabled && !reduced && scroller !== undefined,
  );

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = surface.current;
    if (!el || !enabled) return;

    let pointerId: number | null = null;
    let startY = 0;
    let startScroll = 0;
    let target = 0;
    let gain = 1;
    const samples: Sample[] = [];

    /* -- the sink: Lenis when it exists, the raw box otherwise -------------- */

    const read = (): number => {
      const l = lenis.current;
      // `scroll`, not `targetScroll`. This is read on press, and grabbing a
      // coasting page has to stop it where the content LOOKS, not where it was
      // headed — otherwise the first pixel of the drag jumps forward by
      // whatever the throw had left to run.
      if (l) return l.scroll;
      return scrollBoxOf(scroller)?.scrollTop ?? 0;
    };

    const limitOf = (): number => {
      const l = lenis.current;
      if (l) return l.limit;
      const box = scrollBoxOf(scroller);
      return box ? Math.max(0, box.scrollHeight - box.clientHeight) : 0;
    };

    /** Direct manipulation: the content is under a finger, so no smoothing. */
    const jump = (y: number) => {
      glide.current = null;
      const l = lenis.current;
      if (l) {
        l.scrollTo(y, { immediate: true });
        return;
      }
      const box = scrollBoxOf(scroller);
      if (box) box.scrollTop = y;
    };

    /** Release: an exponential decay toward the thrown target. */
    const coast = (y: number) => {
      const l = lenis.current;
      if (l) {
        l.scrollTo(y, { lerp: THROW_LERP });
        return;
      }
      glide.current = y;
    };

    const step = (y: number) => {
      const l = lenis.current;
      if (l) {
        l.scrollTo(y, { duration: KEY_STEP_SECONDS });
        return;
      }
      glide.current = null;
      scrollBoxOf(scroller)?.scrollTo({ top: y, behavior: reduced ? 'auto' : 'smooth' });
    };

    /* -- velocity ---------------------------------------------------------- */

    /**
     * Pointer velocity in px/s, measured from the oldest sample still inside
     * the window to the newest. Time-based rather than per-event, so the
     * number describes the hand rather than the display.
     */
    const velocityAt = (now: number): number => {
      let oldest: Sample | undefined;
      for (const sample of samples) {
        if (now - sample.t <= SAMPLE_WINDOW_MS) {
          oldest = sample;
          break;
        }
      }
      const newest = samples[samples.length - 1];
      if (!oldest || !newest) return 0;
      const span = newest.t - oldest.t;
      if (span <= 0) return 0;
      return ((newest.y - oldest.y) / span) * 1000;
    };

    /* -- pointer lifecycle ------------------------------------------------- */

    const onPointerDown = (e: PointerEvent) => {
      if (pointerId !== null || !e.isPrimary) return;
      if (e.pointerType === 'mouse' && e.button !== 0) return;
      if (e.target instanceof Element && e.target.closest(NO_DRAG)) return;

      pointerId = e.pointerId;
      // A finger is physically on the content: any gain but 1 slides the
      // content out from under it. A mouse is an indirect device with a
      // window-height of travel available, so it gets the multiplier.
      gain = e.pointerType === 'touch' ? 1 : multiplier;
      startY = e.clientY;
      startScroll = read();
      target = startScroll;
      jump(startScroll);
      samples.length = 0;
      samples.push({ y: e.clientY, t: e.timeStamp });
      // Captured on press, not on some later threshold: by the time a
      // threshold would trip, the pointer may already be off the element.
      el.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);
      el.dataset.dragging = 'true';
    };

    const onPointerMove = (e: PointerEvent) => {
      if (e.pointerId !== pointerId) return;
      // Absolute, from the press point. Accumulating per-event deltas onto the
      // live scroll position loses whatever the sink has not applied yet, and
      // the content drifts behind the hand over a long drag.
      target = clamp(startScroll - (e.clientY - startY) * gain, 0, limitOf());
      jump(target);
      samples.push({ y: e.clientY, t: e.timeStamp });
      if (samples.length > SAMPLE_COUNT) samples.shift();
    };

    const release = (e: PointerEvent, thrown: boolean) => {
      if (e.pointerId !== pointerId) return;
      pointerId = null;
      el.dataset.dragging = 'false';
      if (el.hasPointerCapture(e.pointerId)) el.releasePointerCapture(e.pointerId);

      if (!thrown || reduced) {
        samples.length = 0;
        return;
      }
      samples.push({ y: e.clientY, t: e.timeStamp });
      const velocity = velocityAt(e.timeStamp);
      samples.length = 0;
      const scrollVelocity = -velocity * gain;
      if (Math.abs(scrollVelocity) < MIN_THROW_SPEED) return;
      coast(clamp(target + scrollVelocity * throwSeconds, 0, limitOf()));
    };

    const onPointerUp = (e: PointerEvent) => release(e, true);
    // Both of these are aborts, so neither throws. `pointercancel` is the OS
    // taking the gesture; `lostpointercapture` is the catch-all — capture
    // revoked with no `pointerup` at all, which is the one path that would
    // otherwise leave the surface stuck believing a finger is still down. It
    // also fires immediately after a normal release, where the `pointerId`
    // guard above has already made it a no-op.
    const onPointerCancel = (e: PointerEvent) => release(e, false);
    const onLostCapture = (e: PointerEvent) => release(e, false);

    // Native HTML5 drag on any image or link inside would hijack the gesture
    // and hand back a ghost image instead of a scroll.
    const onDragStart = (e: Event) => e.preventDefault();

    const onKeyDown = (e: KeyboardEvent) => {
      const dir = e.key === 'ArrowDown' ? 1 : e.key === 'ArrowUp' ? -1 : 0;
      if (dir === 0) return;
      e.preventDefault();
      step(clamp(read() + dir * keyStep, 0, limitOf()));
    };

    el.addEventListener('pointerdown', onPointerDown);
    el.addEventListener('pointermove', onPointerMove);
    el.addEventListener('pointerup', onPointerUp);
    el.addEventListener('pointercancel', onPointerCancel);
    el.addEventListener('lostpointercapture', onLostCapture);
    el.addEventListener('dragstart', onDragStart);
    el.addEventListener('keydown', onKeyDown);

    return () => {
      el.removeEventListener('pointerdown', onPointerDown);
      el.removeEventListener('pointermove', onPointerMove);
      el.removeEventListener('pointerup', onPointerUp);
      el.removeEventListener('pointercancel', onPointerCancel);
      el.removeEventListener('lostpointercapture', onLostCapture);
      el.removeEventListener('dragstart', onDragStart);
      el.removeEventListener('keydown', onKeyDown);
      if (pointerId !== null && el.hasPointerCapture(pointerId)) {
        el.releasePointerCapture(pointerId);
      }
      el.dataset.dragging = 'false';
      glide.current = null;
    };
  }, [scroller, lenis, multiplier, throwSeconds, keyStep, enabled, reduced]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** All seven listeners are removed, any pointer still captured is released, the coast target is cleared so the shared rAF idles, and `data-dragging` is reset. The Lenis instance is refcounted by `useLenis`: the last consumer to unmount destroys it, earlier ones only detach.

**Reduced motion.** Dragging still works and is still 1:1 — pulling content with a finger is direct manipulation, not motion someone asked to be spared. What is removed is everything that keeps moving on its own: no Lenis instance is built, so the page scrolls natively, release stops exactly where the hand stopped, and arrow keys jump rather than travel.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Constructing a second Lenis instance instead of sharing one. Both bind `wheel`, both call `preventDefault`, and the page scrolls at exactly double speed — which looks like a badly tuned multiplier and gets "fixed" by halving the multiplier instead.
- Measuring velocity as the mean of per-event deltas. That is px per event, not px per second: the identical physical flick throws half as far on a 120 Hz display, because each event covers half the distance. Divide by real elapsed time.
- Not expiring old samples. Drag fast, hold still for a second, release — the buffer still holds the fast samples and the page launches from a stationary hand.
- Accumulating `scrollTo(current + delta)` per move. `current` is the animated position, which lags the target, so every event throws away the part the sink has not applied yet and the content drifts behind the hand over a long drag. Track the press point and compute the target absolutely.
- Omitting `setPointerCapture`. Drag past the edge of the surface and `pointermove` stops arriving, so the content freezes mid-gesture and then teleports when the pointer comes back.
- Treating `pointerup` as the only terminator. Capture can be revoked with no `pointerup` — the OS claims the gesture, the element is detached, another finger lands — and the surface is left believing a finger is still down, ignoring every later press. `pointercancel` and `lostpointercapture` both have to end the drag.
- Leaving `touch-action` at its default. The compositor claims the touch gesture, `pointermove` stops, and the drag dies in a `pointercancel` on the first frame while the page scrolls natively underneath.
- Forgetting that a host stylesheet with `scroll-behavior: smooth` fights a direct `scrollTop` write on the box sink, which shows up as a rubbery lag under the finger. Set `scroll-behavior: auto` on the scroll container.

## Notes

- The surface takes `tabIndex={0}` and binds `keydown` on itself rather than on `window`, so arrow keys still belong to a search field elsewhere on the page.
- Presses that land on `a, button, input, select, textarea, label` or anything marked `[data-no-drag]` are left alone, so a link inside the draggable area is still a link.
- `dragstart` is prevented on the surface: native HTML5 drag on an inner image or link would otherwise hand back a ghost image instead of a scroll.

## Definition of done

Press and pull upward: the content follows the pointer and stops the moment the pointer does. Flick and release: it coasts on and decays to a stop. Grab it mid-coast and it stops dead under your hand with no forward jump. Start a drag, run the pointer off the edge of the window and release there — the content stops instead of sticking, and the next press still works. Focus the surface and hold ArrowDown for stepped travel. With reduced motion on, release stops instantly.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Drag Mapped To Pin Progress

A drag surface laid over a pinned horizontal section. Instead of a tuned drag multiplier it reads the pin's live geometry — the scroll span it occupies and the pixels the strip travels — and converts one into the other, so a pixel of thumb is a pixel of track regardless of panel widths or zoom. Release throws it, and the throw decays in wall-clock time rather than per frame.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Drag a pinned horizontal strip and it moves exactly one pixel per pixel, then throws and settles.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. The conversion is `ratio = (trigger.end - trigger.start) / getDistance()`: scroll pixels the pin occupies, divided by horizontal pixels the strip travels. Both are read on every use because ScrollTrigger recomputes `end` on each refresh.
2. During a drag the scroll position is set absolutely — `scrollTop = pressScrollTop - dx * ratio` — using the offset from the press point, never an accumulation of per-move deltas.
3. Velocity is sampled as `(clientX - lastX) / dt` in seconds and clamped to ±4000 px/s, so a single stuttering event pair cannot record an implausible throw.
4. On release the velocity decays with `damp(v, 0, friction, dt)` and the scroll advances by `-v * ratio * dt` each frame, so a 144 Hz display and a 60 Hz display travel the same distance in the same wall-clock time.
5. The loop self-parks: below 20 px/s the velocity is zeroed and the callback returns immediately on subsequent frames, so an idle component costs one comparison per frame.
6. `trigger.progress` is rounded to three decimals and written to a `--pin-progress` custom property on the surface only when it changes, so a progress rail can be pure CSS with no per-frame React render.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `friction = 0.002`
  Fraction of throw velocity remaining after one second. 0.002 lands a hard flick in roughly half a second. Near 0.1 the throw stops dead and the release feels like hitting a wall; above ~0.05 it coasts long enough that the user reaches for the scrollbar to stop it.
- `THROW_FLOOR = 20`
  Pixels per second below which the throw is cut and the loop parks. Exponential decay never reaches zero, so without a floor the component writes a sub-pixel scroll change forever and never idles.
- `MAX_THROW = 4000`
  Velocity clamp in px/s. Two pointer events 2 ms apart produce an enormous instantaneous velocity; unclamped, a single jittery sample launches the track across its entire range.
- `release timeout = 80 ms`
  Hold still for longer than this before letting go and the release is not a throw. Without it, pausing mid-drag and releasing fires the stale velocity from the last movement.
- `progress quantisation = 3 decimals`
  Below this the custom property is rewritten on nearly every frame with a change no one can see; above it the progress rail visibly steps.

## API

```ts
function DragToPinProgress(props: { children: ReactNode; scroller: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>; trigger: ScrollTrigger | null; getDistance?: () => number; friction?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  The pinned section and anything overlaying it.
- `scroller: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>`
  The scroll container whose `scrollTop` the drag writes.
- `trigger: ScrollTrigger | null`
  The pinned trigger being scrubbed. Dragging is disabled while null.
- `getDistance: () => number`
  Live horizontal travel of the strip in px. Omit for a 1:1 scroll mapping.
- `friction: number` — default `0.002`
  Fraction of throw velocity left after one second.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the drag surface.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function DragToPinProgress({
  children,
  scroller,
  trigger,
  getDistance,
  friction = 0.002,
  className,
}: DragToPinProgressProps) {
  const surface = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const startScroll = useRef(0);
  const throwVelocity = useRef(0);
  const lastMoveX = useRef(0);
  const lastMoveTime = useRef(0);
  const lastProgress = useRef(-1);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  // Scroll pixels per pixel of horizontal track travel. Read live, because
  // `end` is recomputed on every ScrollTrigger refresh and the panel widths
  // change with the container.
  const ratio = () => {
    if (!trigger) return 1;
    const span = trigger.end - trigger.start;
    const travel = getDistance?.() ?? span;
    return travel > 0 ? span / travel : 1;
  };

  const applyScroll = (value: number) => {
    const el = scroller.current;
    if (!el) return;
    const max = el.scrollHeight - el.clientHeight;
    el.scrollTop = clamp(value, 0, max);
  };

  useDrag(surface, {
    enabled: trigger !== null,
    onDragStart: (state) => {
      throwVelocity.current = 0;
      startScroll.current = scroller.current?.scrollTop ?? 0;
      lastMoveX.current = state.clientX;
      lastMoveTime.current = performance.now();
    },
    onDrag: (state) => {
      // Absolute, from the press point — not an accumulation of deltas.
      // Accumulating drifts, because every clamp at the ends silently eats
      // part of a delta and the track never returns to where the hand is.
      applyScroll(startScroll.current - state.dx * ratio());

      const now = performance.now();
      const dt = (now - lastMoveTime.current) / 1000;
      if (dt > 0) {
        const instant = (state.clientX - lastMoveX.current) / dt;
        throwVelocity.current = clamp(instant, -MAX_THROW, MAX_THROW);
        lastMoveX.current = state.clientX;
        lastMoveTime.current = now;
      }
    },
    onDragEnd: (_state, moved) => {
      // A tap is not a throw. Without this, releasing after a pause launches
      // the track at whatever velocity the last move happened to record.
      if (!moved || reduced || performance.now() - lastMoveTime.current > 80) {
        throwVelocity.current = 0;
      }
    },
  });

  useRaf((dt) => {
    const el = surface.current;

    // Publish the pin's own progress as a CSS variable rather than state:
    // a progress rail must not cost a React render per frame.
    if (el && trigger) {
      const p = Math.round(trigger.progress * 1000) / 1000;
      if (p !== lastProgress.current) {
        lastProgress.current = p;
        el.style.setProperty('--pin-progress', String(p));
      }
    }

    if (throwVelocity.current === 0) return;

    // Exponential decay in wall-clock time, so the throw travels the same
    // distance on a 60 Hz panel as on a 144 Hz one.
    throwVelocity.current = damp(throwVelocity.current, 0, friction, dt);
    if (Math.abs(throwVelocity.current) < THROW_FLOOR) {
      throwVelocity.current = 0;
      return;
    }

    const current = scroller.current?.scrollTop ?? 0;
    applyScroll(current - throwVelocity.current * ratio() * dt);
  });
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useDrag` removes its pointerdown/move/up/cancel and capture-phase click listeners and releases any outstanding pointer capture; `useRaf` unsubscribes from the shared loop. The `--pin-progress` property dies with the element, and no timers or tweens are created that could outlive it.

**Reduced motion.** Dragging still works and still maps one pixel to one pixel — it is an input method, not decoration. The inertial throw is suppressed, so the strip stops the instant the pointer is released instead of coasting.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Inventing a drag multiplier. It is correct for exactly one panel count and one container width; change either and the strip either outruns the hand or lags behind it, and the number gets re-tuned by eye forever.
- Accumulating per-move deltas instead of using the offset from the press point. Every clamp at the ends of the range silently swallows part of a delta, so the track drifts away from the hand and never comes back.
- Caching `trigger.end - trigger.start`. ScrollTrigger recomputes it on every refresh — a font swap or a resize — and a cached span makes the drag mapping wrong for the rest of the session.
- Decaying the throw with a per-frame constant (`v *= 0.95`). The throw travels less than half as far on a 120 Hz display, so the component feels different on different hardware.
- Setting `touch-action: none` on the drag surface. It kills native vertical scrolling over the whole pinned section, so on a phone the page appears frozen; `pan-y` keeps vertical scroll and hands over only the horizontal gesture.
- Not swallowing the click after a drag. Releasing over a panel fires that panel's click handler, so throwing the track opens whatever happened to be under the finger.

## Notes

- Designed to sit around `pinned-horizontal-track`, whose `onTrack` payload supplies both `trigger` and `getDistance`.
- Because the drag writes `scrollTop`, ScrollTrigger updates through its normal scroll listener — no manual `ScrollTrigger.update()` call, and no second source of truth for position.

## Definition of done

Press and drag left: the strip follows the pointer exactly, and a panel edge under your thumb stays under your thumb. Flick and release: it coasts and settles smoothly. Drag to either end and it stops flush with no rubber band. The progress rail matches the strip at all times, including while throwing. With reduced motion on, release stops it dead.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Drifting Smoke Layers

An absolutely-positioned atmosphere layer for the back of a hero or a card. Three oversized elements, each painting two soft radial gradients, blurred and drifting on periods that never line up. It looks like a rendered volumetric pass and costs three composited transforms.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Slow volumetric fog built from blurred radial gradients on three coprime cycles. No texture, no canvas.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. Each layer is `position: absolute; inset: -25%`, making it 150% of the container in both axes with the excess hanging off every side. The layer can then translate by ±10% of its own box and scale to 1.55 without ever bringing an edge into the container — an exactly-fitting layer shows a hard corner the moment it moves.
2. A layer paints two `radial-gradient(W% H% at X% Y%, tint, transparent E%)` ellipses at different centres and different alphas. Two overlapping ellipses per layer, six across the stack, produce density variation that a single gradient cannot: the visible boundary between clouds is where two soft fields disagree, not where a gradient stops.
3. `filter: blur(40px | 55px | 70px)` erases the elliptical shape entirely and leaves only the density field. The three different radii are what separate the layers in apparent depth — identical blur reads as three copies of one cloud sliding over each other.
4. One `@keyframes kx-smoke-drift` block serves all layers. Its two poses read `translate(var(--kx-smoke-x0), var(--kx-smoke-y0)) scale(var(--kx-smoke-s0)) rotate(0deg)` and the matching `…-x1/-y1/-s1/-r`; custom properties resolve per element, so each layer walks a different path through the same cycle without a keyframe block of its own.
5. The periods are 16s, 22s and 29s. The combined pattern only repeats at lcm(16, 22, 29) = 5104 seconds, roughly 85 minutes, so no viewer will ever see it loop. Equal periods repeat every cycle and the fog reads as a looping video.
6. Only `transform` and `opacity` are animated. The blurred result of each layer is rasterised once and composited thereafter, so a 70px blur is paid for at paint time, not sixty times a second.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `inset = -25%`
  Makes each layer 150% of the container. Worst case is scale 1.55 plus a 10% self-relative translate plus an 11deg rotation; 25% of overflow on each side covers all three with room left. At -10% the corner of the largest layer swings into view during the rotation.
- `periods = 16s / 22s / 29s`
  Chosen so lcm(16, 22, 29) = 5104s. Any pair sharing a factor collapses the combined period — 16/24/32 repeats every 96 seconds and is clearly a loop. 29 is prime, which is what pushes the total past an hour.
- `blur radii = 40px / 55px / 70px`
  Different radii are the depth cue. Below ~25px the elliptical shape of the gradient survives the blur and the fog reads as coloured blobs; above ~90px the layer flattens into an even wash with no internal structure and the drift stops being visible.
- `layer opacities = 0.55 / 0.40 / 0.30`
  Descending with distance. The three layers composite multiplicatively against the background, so equal opacities stack to an opaque haze; the falloff keeps total coverage under about 0.75 and preserves whatever sits behind.
- `scale range = 1.25 to 1.55`
  The breathing. Under about 1.15 the scale change is imperceptible next to the translation; over about 1.8 the browser re-rasterises the blurred layer at the new scale, which shows as a visible sharpness pop mid-cycle.
- `gradient edge stops = 60% to 70%`
  Where each ellipse reaches full transparency, relative to its own size. Below ~50% the falloff is steep enough that the blur cannot hide the ellipse; at 100% the gradient never fully clears and the layer becomes a flat tint with a bright spot.

## API

```ts
function DriftingSmokeLayers(props: { layers?: 1 | 2 | 3; tint?: string; intensity?: number; speed?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `layers: 1 | 2 | 3` — default `3`
  How many layers to render. Fewer layers, less depth and less fill-rate.
- `tint: string` — default `'var(--smoke-tint, currentColor)'`
  Any CSS colour. Mixed down per blob with `color-mix`.
- `intensity: number` — default `1`
  Multiplies every layer opacity. Below 1 for fog behind text.
- `speed: number` — default `1`
  Multiplies every period. 2 is half speed; the periods stay coprime under any multiplier.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the wrapper via `cn`. Use it to change the inset or add a mask.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/* Hand-tuned rather than seeded-random: these are the poses, not samples from
   a distribution, and a PRNG here would only make them harder to adjust. */
const LAYER_SPECS: readonly LayerSpec[] = [
  {
    durationS: 16,
    blurPx: 40,
    opacity: 0.55,
    fromX: '-8%',
    fromY: '-6%',
    fromScale: 1.25,
    toX: '10%',
    toY: '8%',
    toScale: 1.45,
    rotateDeg: 8,
    blobs: [
      { w: 40, h: 50, x: 70, y: 30, alpha: 55, edge: 60 },
      { w: 45, h: 55, x: 30, y: 65, alpha: 40, edge: 62 },
    ],
  },
  {
    durationS: 22,
    blurPx: 55,
    opacity: 0.4,
    fromX: '6%',
    fromY: '4%',
    fromScale: 1.3,
    toX: '-9%',
    toY: '-7%',
    toScale: 1.5,
    rotateDeg: -11,
    blobs: [
      { w: 55, h: 45, x: 25, y: 35, alpha: 45, edge: 64 },
      { w: 50, h: 60, x: 75, y: 70, alpha: 32, edge: 66 },
    ],
  },
  {
    durationS: 29,
    blurPx: 70,
    opacity: 0.3,
    fromX: '-4%',
    fromY: '7%',
    fromScale: 1.35,
    toX: '8%',
    toY: '-9%',
    toScale: 1.55,
    rotateDeg: 6,
    blobs: [
      { w: 60, h: 60, x: 50, y: 20, alpha: 38, edge: 68 },
      { w: 48, h: 52, x: 20, y: 80, alpha: 28, edge: 70 },
    ],
  },
];

const SMOKE_CSS = `
/* One keyframe block for every layer. The transform endpoints are read from
   custom properties, which are resolved per element, so each layer follows a
   different path through the same two-pose cycle. */
@keyframes kx-smoke-drift {
  0%, 100% {
    transform:
      translate(var(--kx-smoke-x0), var(--kx-smoke-y0))
      scale(var(--kx-smoke-s0))
      rotate(0deg);
  }
  50% {
    transform:
      translate(var(--kx-smoke-x1), var(--kx-smoke-y1))
      scale(var(--kx-smoke-s1))
      rotate(var(--kx-smoke-r));
  }
}

.kx-smoke {
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  overflow: hidden;
  pointer-events: none;
  /* Cuts the layers out of the page's paint and layout tree entirely. Without
     it the browser considers the oversized blurred children when computing
     the ancestor's ink overflow on every frame. */
  contain: paint;
}

.kx-smoke-layer {
  position: absolute;
  /* 150% of the container in both axes. A layer that exactly fits would show
     a hard edge the instant it translates. */
  inset: -25%;
  background: var(--kx-smoke-bg);
  filter: blur(var(--kx-smoke-blur));
  opacity: var(--kx-smoke-opacity);
  animation: kx-smoke-drift var(--kx-smoke-dur) ease-in-out infinite;
  will-change: transform;
}

/* Reduced motion parks every layer on its 50% pose rather than its 0% pose.
   The 50% pose is the fuller, more composed frame; 0% is where the layers are
   most nearly stacked, which reads as a single flat wash. */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .kx-smoke-layer {
    animation: none;
    will-change: auto;
    transform:
      translate(var(--kx-smoke-x1), var(--kx-smoke-y1))
      scale(var(--kx-smoke-s1))
      rotate(var(--kx-smoke-r));
  }
}
`;

/** Two offset ellipses per layer. Percentages keep it resolution-independent. */
function backgroundFor(spec: LayerSpec, tint: string): string {
  return spec.blobs
    .map(
      (b) =>
        `radial-gradient(${b.w}% ${b.h}% at ${b.x}% ${b.y}%, ` +
        `color-mix(in oklab, ${tint} ${b.alpha}%, transparent), transparent ${b.edge}%)`,
    )
    .join(', ');
}

export function DriftingSmokeLayers({
  layers = 3,
  tint = 'var(--smoke-tint, currentColor)',
  intensity = 1,
  speed = 1,
  className,
}: DriftingSmokeLayersProps) {
  return (
    <>
      <style href="kinetic-drifting-smoke-layers" precedence="medium">
        {SMOKE_CSS}
      </style>
      <div className={cn('kx-smoke', className)} aria-hidden="true">
        {LAYER_SPECS.slice(0, layers).map((spec) => {
          const style: StyleWithVars = {
            '--kx-smoke-bg': backgroundFor(spec, tint),
            '--kx-smoke-blur': `${spec.blurPx}px`,
            '--kx-smoke-opacity': spec.opacity * intensity,
            '--kx-smoke-dur': `${spec.durationS * speed}s`,
            '--kx-smoke-x0': spec.fromX,
            '--kx-smoke-y0': spec.fromY,
            '--kx-smoke-s0': spec.fromScale,
            '--kx-smoke-x1': spec.toX,
            '--kx-smoke-y1': spec.toY,
            '--kx-smoke-s1': spec.toScale,
            '--kx-smoke-r': `${spec.rotateDeg}deg`,
          };
          return <span key={spec.durationS} className="kx-smoke-layer" style={style} />;
        })}
      </div>
    </>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to clean up. No listeners, no timers, no animation frames, no observers. Unmounting removes the elements and the CSS animations with them; React removes the hoisted `<style>` when the last instance unmounts.

**Reduced motion.** A `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block sets `animation: none` and applies each layer's 50% pose as a static transform, so the fog is still there, still layered, still at full density — it simply stops drifting. `will-change` is reset to `auto` in the same block so the three large blurred layers are not held in compositor memory for an animation that is not running.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Animating `filter: blur()` itself, or animating the gradient stops. Both force the layer to be re-blurred every frame — a 70px blur over a 150%-size layer is tens of milliseconds of GPU work per frame and the whole page drops to single-digit FPS. Animate the transform of an already-blurred layer instead.
- Giving the layers the same duration with different delays. A delay does not decorrelate anything: after the first cycle every layer is at the same phase offset forever, and the stack visibly repeats on the shared period. The periods themselves have to be coprime.
- Sizing the layers to the container. At `inset: 0` the blur samples transparent pixels beyond the element box, so the fog fades out at exactly the container edge and the effect reads as a rectangle of smoke rather than smoke seen through a window.
- Omitting `overflow: hidden` on the wrapper. The layers are 150% of the container by design and will paint over neighbouring content, including through a parent with its own background.
- Leaving off `pointer-events: none`. The layer covers the whole container, so every button underneath stops being clickable and the cause is invisible in the DOM inspector unless you notice the transparent sibling on top.
- Setting `will-change: transform` and leaving it set under reduced motion. `will-change` promotes the element to its own compositor layer permanently; with the animation switched off that is three large blurred textures held in GPU memory for nothing. The reduced-motion block resets it to `auto`.

## Notes

- The component is `position: absolute; inset: 0`, so it expects a positioned ancestor and contributes nothing to layout. Put it as the first child of the section it should sit behind and give that section `position: relative`.
- `contain: paint` on the wrapper keeps the oversized blurred children out of the ancestor ink-overflow calculation, which otherwise runs on every frame of the drift.
- The tint reads `var(--smoke-tint, currentColor)` and is mixed with `color-mix(in oklab, …)`, so the fog inherits the text colour by default and can be re-themed by setting one property on any ancestor. `color-mix` needs Safari 16.2+, Chrome 111+, Firefox 113+.
- Fill-rate is the real cost: three full-container layers at 150% size, blurred. On a low-end phone drop to `layers={2}` — the depth reads almost as well and it removes the widest blur.

## Definition of done

Watch for a full minute: the density pattern never obviously repeats, and no layer edge or gradient ellipse becomes visible at any point in the cycle. Content behind the smoke stays clickable. In a performance profile the frames show composite work only — no repaints of the blurred layers. With reduced motion on, the fog is still present and completely still.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Dual-Canvas Depth Split

Two stacked canvases render the same instanced particle system with opposite `uZSign`, and the page content is a DOM sibling between them. Particles with negative depth pass behind the text and positive ones pass in front. Because size, parallax rate, brightness and softness are one continuous ramp across the depth axis, the plane where the split happens cannot be seen — the effect is that the copy is embedded in the field, and it stays live, selectable text throughout.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

One particle field rendered twice with the depth sign flipped, so the text sits inside the field rather than on top of it.

- Category: webgl
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: ogl@^1.0.11

## How it works

1. `aDepth` is the camera axis, not a distance: -1 is far behind the content plane, +1 is close to the viewer, 0 is the content plane itself. The SIGN chooses which canvas draws a particle; the magnitude drives everything else, which is why the two layers look like one field.
2. Both layers share the same typed arrays, so the two contexts hold identical particles rather than two independent fields. Only the attribute descriptor objects are per-layer, because ogl writes the buffer handle and element count into the object it is given.
3. A particle on the wrong side of the plane is rejected in the VERTEX shader by writing `gl_Position = vec4(2.0, 2.0, 2.0, 1.0)` — outside the frustum on every axis, so all four vertices are clipped before rasterisation and it costs no fragments. The vertex cost doubles across the two layers; the fragment cost, which is the only cost that mattered, does not.
4. Near particles are bigger (`mix(minSize, maxSize, depth01)`), drift further per second (`0.35 + 0.65 * depth01`), are brighter, and have a softer edge — a defocus that stops the front layer reading as dirt on the screen. Four cues from one number.
5. The back canvas is opaque and blends additively (`ONE, ONE`), which is order independent so nothing needs sorting. The front canvas sits over live text and must be transparent, which rules additive out — there is nothing on the GPU to add to — so it blends premultiplied source-over (`ONE, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`). One fragment shader emits premultiplied colour and serves both.
6. The population is derived from container area — `clamp(round(megapixels * density), 250, maxCount)` — and applied with `setInstancedCount` on both layers. Buffers are allocated once at `maxCount`, so a resize never reallocates.
7. Drift is a pure function of `elapsed` and the per-particle seed, with `fract` wrapping the field vertically and `uFadeBand` fading alpha to zero at both ends so the wrap seam is never visible. No per-particle state, so a still frame is drawable from one number.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `split = 0.38`
  Fraction of the population placed in front of the content. Under a half on purpose: dust in front of body copy is a legibility cost, and at 0.5 the text reads as fogged rather than embedded.
- `FRONT_OPACITY = 0.55`
  Extra alpha scale on the front layer only. Depth already brightens near particles, and the front layer is entirely near particles, so without this the layer that overlaps the text is the brightest thing on screen.
- `DEPTH_FLOOR = 0.05`
  Dead zone around the content plane. A particle at exactly 0 is rejected by both layers — `aDepth * uZSign <= 0.0` is false for neither sign — so it would silently never render.
- `sizeRange = [3, 34]`
  Disc diameter at the far and near ends of the ramp. The span is what sells the depth; at 8-to-14 the field is flat, and above ~40 the near particles are large enough that their own softness becomes the dominant texture of the page.
- `parallax factor = 0.35 + 0.65 * depth01`
  Near particles travel about three times as far per second as far ones. A larger ratio makes the far layer look frozen; a smaller one and the field moves as a single sheet, which removes the only depth cue that survives in a static screenshot.
- `MAX_DPR = 1.5`
  Two layers of soft additive discs is a fill-rate problem and fill scales with the square of the pixel ratio. Dust has no detail a third sample per axis would resolve, so a 3x phone renders at 1.5x and pays a quarter of the fragments.
- `FADE_BAND = 0.14`
  Fraction of the field height the wrap fade occupies at each end. Larger than a single-layer field needs, because the near particles are up to 34px across and their radius alone is a few percent of a short container.
- `size jitter = 0.7 .. 1.3`
  Multiplier on top of the depth ramp. Without it the depth ordering is perfectly readable from size alone, which reads as a diagram of a depth field rather than a depth field.

## API

```ts
function DualCanvasZSplit(props: { children?: ReactNode; density?: number; maxCount?: number; split?: number; sizeRange?: readonly [number, number]; speed?: number; wander?: number; opacity?: number; colorA?: string; colorB?: string; background?: string; seed?: number | string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Content rendered between the two particle layers. Ordinary DOM, fully interactive.
- `density: number` — default `850`
  Particles per megapixel of container area. The count is derived from this, not fixed.
- `maxCount: number` — default `1600`
  Population ceiling, and the size the shared buffers are allocated at.
- `split: number` — default `0.38`
  Fraction of the population placed in front of the content.
- `sizeRange: readonly [number, number]` — default `[3, 34]`
  Disc diameter in CSS pixels at the far and near ends of the depth ramp.
- `speed: number` — default `1`
  Multiplier on the whole drift, including the upward march.
- `wander: number` — default `0.05`
  Sinusoidal wander amplitude in field units, where 1 is the container.
- `opacity: number` — default `0.6`
  Overall alpha multiplier. The front layer takes 0.55 of it.
- `colorA: string` — default `'#8ea6c4'`
  First tint. Any value ogl's `Color` accepts.
- `colorB: string` — default `'#e6d9c4'`
  Second tint; each particle mixes between the two by a seeded amount.
- `background: string` — default `'#06080c'`
  Opaque clear colour of the back canvas. The front canvas is transparent.
- `seed: number | string` — default `'dual-canvas-z-split'`
  Seeds the scatter. Same seed, same field on every reload and on the server.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
function createLayer(
  host: HTMLElement,
  data: FieldData,
  opts: {
    zSign: number;
    opaque: boolean;
    background: Color;
    colorA: Color;
    colorB: Color;
    speed: number;
    wander: number;
    opacity: number;
    minSize: number;
    maxSize: number;
  },
): Layer {
  const renderer = new Renderer({
    dpr: pixelRatio(MAX_DPR),
    // The back layer owns its pixels, so it is opaque and can blend
    // additively. The front layer sits over live DOM text and must be
    // transparent, which rules additive out — there is nothing on the GPU to
    // add to. It blends premultiplied source-over instead.
    alpha: !opts.opaque,
    premultipliedAlpha: !opts.opaque,
    // Nothing occludes anything in either layer; the depth ORDER is expressed
    // by which canvas a particle lands on, not by a z-buffer.
    depth: false,
    antialias: false,
    powerPreference: 'low-power',
  });

  const gl = renderer.gl;
  const canvas = gl.canvas;

  if (opts.opaque) gl.clearColor(opts.background.r, opts.background.g, opts.background.b, 1);
  else gl.clearColor(0, 0, 0, 0);

  // Each layer needs its own attribute descriptors — ogl writes the buffer
  // handle and the element count into the object it is handed — but the
  // underlying typed arrays are shared, so the two contexts hold identical
  // particles rather than two independent fields.
  const geometry = new Geometry(gl, {
    index: { data: data.index },
    position: { size: 2, data: data.quad },
    aOrigin: { size: 2, data: data.origins, instanced: 1 },
    aDepth: { size: 1, data: data.depths, instanced: 1 },
    aSeed: { size: 4, data: data.seeds, instanced: 1 },
  });

  const uniforms: Uniforms = {
    uResolution: { value: [1, 1] },
    uPixelRatio: { value: renderer.dpr },
    uElapsed: { value: 0 },
    uZSign: { value: opts.zSign },
    uDrift: { value: opts.speed },
    uRise: { value: RISE },
    uFlowScale: { value: FLOW_SCALE },
    uWander: { value: opts.wander },
    uFadeBand: { value: FADE_BAND },
    uMinSize: { value: opts.minSize },
    uMaxSize: { value: opts.maxSize },
    uColorA: { value: opts.colorA },
    uColorB: { value: opts.colorB },
    uOpacity: { value: opts.opacity },
  };

  const program = new Program(gl, {
    vertex: DUAL_CANVAS_Z_SPLIT_VERT,
    fragment: DUAL_CANVAS_Z_SPLIT_FRAG,
    uniforms,
    transparent: true,
    depthTest: false,
    depthWrite: false,
    // ogl defaults `cullFace` to BACK, and a culled particle is absent with no
    // error anywhere. Nothing here has a back face worth culling.
    cullFace: false,
  });
  if (opts.opaque) program.setBlendFunc(gl.ONE, gl.ONE);
  else program.setBlendFunc(gl.ONE, gl.ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA);

  const mesh = new Mesh(gl, { geometry, program });

  host.appendChild(canvas);
  canvas.style.display = 'block';

  return { renderer, geometry, program, mesh, uniforms, canvas };
}

export function DualCanvasZSplit({
  children,
  density = 850,
  maxCount = 1600,
  split = 0.38,
  sizeRange = [3, 34],
  speed = 1,
  wander = 0.05,
  opacity = 0.6,
  colorA = '#8ea6c4',
  colorB = '#e6d9c4',
  background = '#06080c',
  seed = 'dual-canvas-z-split',
  className,
}: DualCanvasZSplitProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const backHost = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const frontHost = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const stage = useRef<Stage | null>(null);
  const [unsupported, setUnsupported] = useState(false);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const size = useRef({ width, height });
  size.current = { width, height };

  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const visible = useVisibility();
  const { inView } = useInView(host, { rootMargin: '10%' });
  const ready = width > 1 && height > 1;

  const [minSize = 3, maxSize = 34] = sizeRange;

  useEffect(() => {
    const back = backHost.current;
    const front = frontHost.current;
    if (!back || !front || !ready) return;

    if (!hasWebGL()) {
      setUnsupported(true);
      return;
    }

    const total = Math.max(MIN_COUNT, Math.round(maxCount));
    const data: FieldData = {
      quad: new Float32Array([-0.5, -0.5, 0.5, -0.5, 0.5, 0.5, -0.5, 0.5]),
      index: new Uint16Array([0, 1, 2, 0, 2, 3]),
      origins: new Float32Array(total * 2),
      depths: new Float32Array(total),
      seeds: new Float32Array(total * 4),
    };

    const rng = createRng(seed);
    const frontShare = clamp(split, 0, 1);
    const lo = Math.max(1, Math.min(minSize, maxSize));
    const hi = Math.max(lo + 0.5, Math.max(minSize, maxSize));

    for (let i = 0; i < total; i += 1) {
      data.origins[i * 2] = randRange(rng, X_MIN, X_MAX);
      data.origins[i * 2 + 1] = rng();

      // The sign picks the canvas, the magnitude drives size, parallax,
      // brightness and softness. A particle exactly at 0 would be on the
      // content plane and belongs to neither layer, so the range excludes it.
      const inFront = rng() < frontShare;
      data.depths[i] = inFront
        ? randRange(rng, DEPTH_FLOOR, 1)
        : -randRange(rng, DEPTH_FLOOR, 1);

      data.seeds[i * 4] = rng() * Math.PI * 2;
      data.seeds[i * 4 + 1] = rng() * Math.PI * 2;
      data.seeds[i * 4 + 2] = rng();
      // Size jitter on top of the depth ramp. Without it the depth ordering is
      // perfectly legible from size alone, which reads as a diagram.
      data.seeds[i * 4 + 3] = randRange(rng, 0.7, 1.3);
    }

    const colA = new Color(colorA);
    const colB = new Color(colorB);
    const bg = new Color(background);
    const shared = {
      background: bg,
      colorA: colA,
      colorB: colB,
      speed,
      wander,
      minSize: lo,
      maxSize: hi,
    };

    const layers = [
      createLayer(back, data, { ...shared, zSign: -1, opaque: true, opacity }),
      createLayer(front, data, {
        ...shared,
        zSign: 1,
        opaque: false,
        opacity: opacity * FRONT_OPACITY,
      }),
    ];

    const resize = (w: number, h: number) => {
      // Population from area, not a fixed number, so one density reads right in
      // a 320px card and a 2000px hero. The buffers already hold `total`
      // particles in scattered order, so a prefix is still an even field —
      // nothing is reallocated.
      const megapixels = (w * h) / 1_000_000;
      const count = clamp(Math.round(megapixels * density), MIN_COUNT, total);

      for (const layer of layers) {
        layer.renderer.setSize(w, h);
        // `setSize` writes literal px into the canvas's inline style, which
        // beats any class. Re-asserting percentages keeps it fluid.
        layer.canvas.style.width = '100%';
        layer.canvas.style.height = '100%';
        layer.uniforms.uResolution.value = [
          layer.renderer.gl.drawingBufferWidth,
          layer.renderer.gl.drawingBufferHeight,
        ];
        layer.uniforms.uPixelRatio.value = layer.renderer.dpr;
        layer.geometry.setInstancedCount(count);
      }
    };

    const draw = (elapsed: number) => {
      for (const layer of layers) {
        layer.uniforms.uElapsed.value = elapsed;
        layer.renderer.render({ scene: layer.mesh });
      }
    };

    resize(size.current.width, size.current.height);
    stage.current = { layers, resize, draw };
    draw(STATIC_ELAPSED);

    return () => {
      stage.current = null;
      for (const layer of layers) {
        // ogl has no `dispose()`: `remove()` deletes the VAOs and every buffer,
        // then the program and its shaders, and only `WEBGL_lose_context` gives
        // the context itself back. This component holds two of them.
        layer.geometry.remove();
        layer.program.remove();
        loseContext(layer.renderer.gl);
        layer.canvas.width = 0;
        layer.canvas.height = 0;
        layer.canvas.remove();
      }
    };
  }, [
    ready,
    density,
    maxCount,
    split,
    minSize,
    maxSize,
    speed,
    wander,
    opacity,
    colorA,
    colorB,
    background,
    seed,
  ]);

  // Resize is its own effect: a reflow costs two `setSize` calls and an
  // instanced-count change, never a rebuild of the shared buffers.
  useEffect(() => {
    stage.current?.resize(width, height);
    if (reduced) stage.current?.draw(STATIC_ELAPSED);
  }, [width, height, reduced]);

  useRaf(
    (_dt, elapsed) => stage.current?.draw(elapsed),
    ready && inView && visible && !reduced && !unsupported,
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Per layer: `geometry.remove()` deletes the VAOs and every buffer, `program.remove()` deletes the shaders and the program, `loseContext(gl)` hands the context back through `WEBGL_lose_context` — ogl has no `dispose()` and nothing else releases a context — then the canvas backing store is zeroed and the node removed. Both layers are torn down in the same cleanup, so the component never holds one context after the other has gone.

**Reduced motion.** The rAF subscription is never made and both layers are drawn once at `elapsed` 0. That is a complete frame, not a collapsed one: the scatter, depths, sizes, tints and wrap fade are all per-particle seeds that already vary at t=0, so the still shows the same depth split, in front of and behind the same text, with only the drift absent. Resizing redraws the same still in both layers.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Trying to do this with one canvas. A canvas is a single stacking-context leaf, so DOM content cannot be interleaved with parts of it. Two contexts is not an inefficiency here, it is the requirement — and it is two of the roughly sixteen a Chromium renderer process allows, which is exactly why both are released on unmount.
- Making the front canvas additive. With `alpha: true` the destination is zero, so an additive particle over text is a flat colour patch: the layer stops looking like light and starts looking like a sticker.
- Forgetting `pointer-events: none` on the front layer. It covers the content by construction, so every link and button underneath it stops responding, and nothing about the failure looks graphical.
- Letting a particle sit at depth exactly 0. `aDepth * uZSign <= 0.0` rejects it in BOTH layers, so it is uploaded, transformed and never seen — a silent leak of the population.
- Rejecting with `discard` in the fragment shader instead of parking the vertex. `discard` still rasterises the quad and runs the shader per fragment; a clip-space position outside the frustum throws the primitive away after four vertex invocations.
- Writing `gl_Position = vec4(2.0)` for the rejection. w is then 2, the perspective divide brings it back to exactly 1.0 on every axis, and the vertex survives clipping at the frustum boundary — a row of specks in the corner.
- Giving both layers the same attribute descriptor objects. ogl mutates them with a buffer handle belonging to the first context, and the second layer then renders from a buffer its context has never heard of.
- Assuming `renderer.setSize` leaves the CSS alone. ogl writes literal px into the canvas inline style, which beats any class, so the percentages must be re-asserted after every call in both layers.

## Notes

- The content is a DOM sibling, not a texture. It stays selectable, focusable and available to a screen reader while particles pass on both sides of it — which is the entire reason to accept two contexts instead of drawing the text into the field.
- ogl rather than three: two contexts, two instanced meshes, no lights, no cameras and no scene graph. `renderer.render` is called without a camera, so ogl skips frustum culling and the matrix uniforms — the shader writes clip space itself.
- `depth: false` on both contexts. The depth ORDER is expressed by which canvas a particle lands on, so a z-buffer would be memory plus a clear per frame for no result.
- Sizes are authored in CSS pixels and scaled by the pixel ratio in the shader, so the field is identical across a dpr change and nothing rebuilds when one happens.
- GLSL ES 1.00 with no derivative functions — the anti-aliasing floor is `1.0 / sizePx`, exact for a quad of that pixel size — so the same source compiles under a WebGL1 fallback context.

## Definition of done

Particles visibly pass both behind and in front of the text, and the text is still selectable with the mouse while they do. There is no horizontal line anywhere in the container where the field changes character. Near particles are larger, softer and move further per second than far ones. Links inside the content still respond to hover and click. Resize narrow and wide: discs stay circular and the population changes without a stutter. Two contexts per instance, both released on unmount — mount and unmount six instances and none of the earlier ones go black.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Dual-Direction Scrub Entrance

Two elements arrive on the same scrubbed trigger from different directions — the copy rises 60px, the panel slides in from the side by 55% of its own width. Because both tweens sit at position 0 of one timeline, their progress is identical at every scroll position, so the pair reads as one composed arrival. The 0.6s scrub lets them keep moving briefly after the wheel stops, which is the difference between weighted and welded.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Copy rises while a panel slides in from the side, both on one scrub with 600ms of lag.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. A single `gsap.timeline` is created with `scrollTrigger: { trigger: root, start: "top 82%", end: "top 38%", scrub: 0.6 }`. One trigger drives both elements, so there is exactly one progress value in the system.
2. The primary element gets `fromTo({ autoAlpha: 0, y: 60 }, { autoAlpha: 1, y: 0 })` at position 0. `autoAlpha` rather than `opacity`: it also flips `visibility`, so the invisible element is not a click target on the way in.
3. The secondary gets `fromTo({ autoAlpha: 0, xPercent: ±55 }, { autoAlpha: 1, xPercent: 0 })`, also at position 0. `xPercent` is a share of its own width, so the entrance distance scales with the layout instead of being tuned per breakpoint.
4. Both tweens use `ease: "none"`. Under a scrub the ease is applied to timeline time, so easing here means the two elements travel at different rates through the same scroll range and stop looking like one gesture.
5. The secondary is wrapped in an `overflow-hidden` cell. At `xPercent: 55` it begins more than half its width outside the grid column, which without the clip is a horizontal scrollbar on the whole document.
6. `scrub: 0.6` gives ScrollTrigger 0.6s to catch the timeline up to the scroll position, so the elements decelerate into place after the wheel stops rather than freezing with it.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `scrub = 0.6`
  Seconds of catch-up. `true` (zero lag) welds the animation to the wheel and reads as dragging a slider. Past about 1.5s the section is still arriving long after you have stopped, which reads as lag rather than weight. 0.6 is the point where it feels like mass.
- `start / end = 'top 82%' / 'top 38%'`
  The section begins arriving just as it clears the bottom edge and is fully composed while still in the lower half of the screen. Ending at `top 38%` means the entrance completes before the content reaches the reading position — an animation that is still resolving under the eye is unreadable.
- `rise = 60`
  Pixels of vertical travel for the copy. Enough to register as arriving; small enough that the text is legible for most of the transit, which matters because the user is reading during it.
- `slide = 55`
  Percent of the secondary's own width. Above ~60% it starts entirely outside its column and the first half of the scrub shows an empty cell; below ~30% it reads as a nudge rather than an entrance.

## API

```ts
function DualDirectionScrubEntrance(props: { primary: ReactNode; secondary: ReactNode; from?: "left" | "right"; rise?: number; slide?: number; scrub?: number; start?: string; end?: string; scrollerRef?: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `primary: ReactNode`
  Rises from below. The reading anchor — usually the copy.
- `secondary: ReactNode`
  Slides in horizontally. Usually the card, figure or panel.
- `from: "left" | "right"` — default `'right'`
  Which edge the secondary enters from. Also flips the grid order.
- `rise: number` — default `60`
  Pixels the primary rises through.
- `slide: number` — default `55`
  Secondary travel as a percentage of its own width.
- `scrub: number` — default `0.6`
  Seconds of catch-up behind the scroll position.
- `start: string` — default `'top 82%'`
  ScrollTrigger start.
- `end: string` — default `'top 38%'`
  ScrollTrigger end.
- `scrollerRef: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>`
  The scroll container that owns the scroll position. Omit for the document.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the grid container via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function DualDirectionScrubEntrance({
  primary,
  secondary,
  from = 'right',
  rise = 60,
  slide = 55,
  scrub = 0.6,
  start = 'top 82%',
  end = 'top 38%',
  scrollerRef,
  className,
}: DualDirectionScrubEntranceProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const primaryRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const secondaryRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  useGsap(
    gsap,
    () => {
      const container = root.current;
      const a = primaryRef.current;
      const b = secondaryRef.current;
      if (!container || !a || !b || reduced) return;

      const tl = gsap.timeline({
        scrollTrigger: {
          trigger: container,
          scroller: scrollerRef?.current ?? undefined,
          start,
          end,
          // The number, not `true`. `true` welds the timeline to the wheel and
          // the section stops moving in the same millisecond the wheel does.
          scrub,
          invalidateOnRefresh: true,
        },
      });

      // `fromTo`, deliberately, and not `from`. A `from` tween on a scrubbed
      // trigger renders its start state immediately at build time and then
      // treats the element's *current* values as the destination — so a second
      // tween, a resize, or React re-applying a style mid-scroll silently
      // rewrites where the animation is heading. Stating both ends makes the
      // timeline idempotent.
      tl.fromTo(
        a,
        { autoAlpha: 0, y: rise },
        { autoAlpha: 1, y: 0, ease: 'none', duration: 1 },
        0,
      );

      tl.fromTo(
        b,
        { autoAlpha: 0, xPercent: from === 'right' ? slide : -slide },
        { autoAlpha: 1, xPercent: 0, ease: 'none', duration: 1 },
        // Position 0: both tweens share one progress value. Offsetting them
        // would make the pair read as a queue instead of a single arrival.
        0,
      );
    },
    root,
    [from, rise, slide, scrub, start, end, reduced],
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useGsap` builds the timeline inside a `gsap.context` and reverts it on unmount or any prop change. The revert kills the ScrollTrigger and restores the inline `transform`, `opacity` and `visibility` the tweens wrote — without it an unmount mid-scrub leaves the panel permanently half-slid and invisible if React reuses the node.

**Reduced motion.** No timeline and no trigger are created, so both elements render in their final layout position at full opacity on first paint. Nothing is hidden waiting for a scroll that the user may never make.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- `gsap.from()` on a scrubbed trigger. It renders the start state immediately at build time and treats whatever the element's values happen to be as the destination — so any later style change silently rewrites the target and the element ends up somewhere other than where the layout says. `fromTo` states both ends and is idempotent under a scrub.
- Two separate ScrollTriggers, one per element. Their start positions are computed from their own bounding boxes, so on a tall screen the copy is already finished before the panel has begun, and the composition falls apart at exactly the viewport heights you did not test.
- Easing a scrubbed tween. The ease is applied to timeline time, so the two elements move at different rates through the same scroll window and the pair stops reading as one gesture. Use `ease: "none"` and let the scrub supply the smoothing.
- No `overflow-hidden` around the sliding element. At `xPercent: 55` it sits outside its column at the start of the scrub, which extends the document width and adds a horizontal scrollbar that appears and disappears as you scroll.
- Using `opacity` instead of `autoAlpha`. The invisible element still receives pointer events, so a link inside a panel that has not arrived yet is clickable and focusable.
- Omitting `invalidateOnRefresh`. `xPercent` and the trigger boundaries are both derived from measurements taken at build time; after a resize the panel travels the wrong distance and starts at the wrong scroll position.

## Notes

- `from="left"` also reverses the grid order, so the panel enters from the side it visually occupies rather than crossing the copy on its way in.
- The `will-change-transform` hints sit on the two moving wrappers rather than on their contents, so the promoted layer is created once and the children are not each given their own.

## Definition of done

Scroll the section up from the bottom: the copy rises and the panel comes in from the right at exactly the same rate, both finishing together before the section reaches the middle of the screen. Stop the wheel mid-entrance and they keep moving for about half a second before settling. Scroll back down and the entrance reverses. No horizontal scrollbar appears at any point. With reduced motion on, the section is composed and static from the start.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
