# Build: Eased Number Counter

A number tweens from one value to another on `power2.inOut` rather than linearly, so it reads as loading rather than as a progress meter — slow to commit, quick through the middle, easing onto the final figure. The thing being tweened is a plain numeric object; the string on screen is formatted from it on every update and written with `textContent`, so React never re-renders while the count runs. A transparent sizer reserves the width of the wider endpoint, so nothing after the counter moves as digits are added.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A statistic that counts up on an eased curve and settles on its exact final figure without shifting the layout.

- Category: text
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. A local object `{ v: from }` is the tween target. `gsap.to(counter, { v: to, duration, ease })` interpolates the number; the DOM is not the tween target at all.
2. `onUpdate` calls a `write()` closure that does `el.textContent = prefix + format.format(counter.v) + suffix`. Writing `textContent` rather than React children means the tween never touches the reconciler.
3. The `Intl.NumberFormat` is built once in a `useMemo` keyed on `[locale, decimals, grouping]` — three primitives, so the memo actually holds. `minimumFractionDigits === maximumFractionDigits` also performs the rounding, so no `Math.round` or `toFixed` is needed in the tick.
4. `onComplete` assigns `counter.v = to` and writes once more. Tween interpolation lands on values like 99.999999997, and a headline number stopping one unit short of itself is a real bug report.
5. Before the tween starts, `write()` runs once with `v = from`, so the live node is never empty on the first frame and the element does not pop into existence when the tween begins.
6. The width reservation compares `format.format(to).length` against `format.format(from).length` and renders the longer of the two as a `text-transparent` cell stacked under the live node in an `inline-grid`, both at `col-start-1 row-start-1`.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `DURATION = 1.6`
  Seconds. Under ~1s the eye cannot track the digits and the effect is just a flicker before the answer; past ~2.5s the reader has finished the sentence around it and is waiting on a number that has stopped being interesting.
- `EASE = 'power2.inOut'`
  The in-out pair is what separates a counter from a progress bar. `none` reads as a machine metering out a value; `power2.out` starts at full speed and looks like it began before you looked. The slow start is the part that reads as "committing".
- `VIEW_THRESHOLD = 0.6`
  60% of the element visible before counting. A stat that starts at 1% visibility has finished before it clears the fold, so the reader arrives at a static number and never sees the effect.
- `decimals = 0`
  Also the rounding rule, via matched `minimumFractionDigits`/`maximumFractionDigits`. Leaving them unmatched lets `Intl` vary the digit count between frames, so the string length oscillates and the number jitters horizontally.

## API

```ts
function EasedNumberCounter(props: { to: number; from?: number; duration?: number; ease?: string; delay?: number; locale?: string; decimals?: number; grouping?: boolean; prefix?: string; suffix?: string; startOnView?: boolean; className?: string; onComplete?: () => void }): JSX.Element
```

- `to: number`
  The value to land on.
- `from: number` — default `0`
  The value to start from.
- `duration: number` — default `1.6`
  Seconds of counting.
- `ease: string` — default `'power2.inOut'`
  Any GSAP ease string. `none` makes it read as a meter.
- `delay: number` — default `0`
  Seconds to wait after the trigger before counting.
- `locale: string`
  BCP 47 tag. Omitted uses the runtime default locale.
- `decimals: number` — default `0`
  Fixed fraction digits. Also the rounding.
- `grouping: boolean` — default `true`
  Thousands separators.
- `prefix: string` — default `''`
  Literal text before the number, e.g. a currency sign.
- `suffix: string` — default `''`
  Literal text after the number, e.g. a percent sign.
- `startOnView: boolean` — default `true`
  Count when scrolled into view rather than on mount.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the outer span via `cn`.
- `onComplete: () => void`
  Fired once the final figure is written.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const DURATION = 1.6;
const EASE = 'power2.inOut';
const VIEW_THRESHOLD = 0.6;

export function EasedNumberCounter({
  to,
  from = 0,
  duration = DURATION,
  ease = EASE,
  delay = 0,
  locale,
  decimals = 0,
  grouping = true,
  prefix = '',
  suffix = '',
  startOnView = true,
  className,
  onComplete,
}: EasedNumberCounterProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLSpanElement>(null);
  const live = useRef<HTMLSpanElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const { inView } = useInView(root, { threshold: VIEW_THRESHOLD, once: true });

  // Held in a ref so an inline arrow from the caller does not restart the
  // count on every parent render.
  const complete = useRef(onComplete);
  complete.current = onComplete;

  // One formatter for the whole tween, keyed only on the primitives that
  // change it. An options *object* prop would be a new reference every render
  // and would rebuild the formatter — and restart the tween — continuously.
  const format = useMemo(
    () =>
      new Intl.NumberFormat(locale, {
        minimumFractionDigits: decimals,
        maximumFractionDigits: decimals,
        useGrouping: grouping,
      }),
    [locale, decimals, grouping],
  );

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = live.current;
    if (!el) return;

    const counter = { v: from };
    const write = () => {
      el.textContent = `${prefix}${format.format(counter.v)}${suffix}`;
    };

    // Reduced motion is the final figure, immediately — not a blank slot and
    // not a 0.01s tween that still flickers through every intermediate value.
    if (reduced) {
      counter.v = to;
      write();
      complete.current?.();
      return;
    }

    write();
    if (startOnView && !inView) return;

    const tween = gsap.to(counter, {
      v: to,
      duration,
      ease,
      delay,
      overwrite: true,
      onUpdate: write,
      onComplete: () => {
        // Snap to the exact target. Floating-point tweens land on
        // 99.99999999 often enough that a counter visibly stopping one short
        // of its own headline number is a real bug report.
        counter.v = to;
        write();
        complete.current?.();
      },
    });

    return () => {
      tween.kill();
    };
  }, [
    from,
    to,
    duration,
    ease,
    delay,
    prefix,
    suffix,
    format,
    reduced,
    inView,
    startOnView,
  ]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The effect returns `tween.kill()`. Because the tween target is a local object rather than a DOM node, nothing is left written to the element beyond the final string, and there are no inline styles to clear.

**Reduced motion.** Writes the final formatted figure immediately and fires `onComplete`, with no tween created at all. It is never left blank and never runs a shortened tween that still flickers through intermediate values.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Constructing `new Intl.NumberFormat()` inside `onUpdate`. It costs tens of microseconds and it is being built 60-120 times a second per counter; a page of eight stats spends milliseconds a frame building formatters it throws away.
- Tweening the string, or holding the value in `useState`. A `setState` per frame re-renders the subtree at display refresh rate, and worse, any unrelated parent render snaps the number back to the last committed value mid-count.
- Rendering the live value as React children. React will diff and overwrite whatever the tween wrote, so the count freezes on the first parent re-render.
- Not snapping to the exact target in `onComplete`. Floating-point interpolation lands near, not on, the target — the counter finishes at 99,999 instead of 100,000.
- Letting the box size itself from the current text. Every added digit widens the element and shoves the following copy sideways; the count ends up looking like a layout bug.
- Using `visibility: hidden` for the sizer. That removes it from the accessibility tree as well, and the transparent copy is the only readable text on the element — the live node is `aria-hidden` because it is mid-count garbage.

## Notes

- The `onComplete` callback is held in a ref that is reassigned on every render, so passing an inline arrow from the caller does not restart the count on every parent render.
- A number formatting *options object* prop was deliberately not exposed: an object literal is a new reference every render, which would rebuild the formatter, invalidate the effect, and restart the tween continuously.

## Definition of done

Scroll the stat into view: the number counts from its start value, decelerates, and stops on exactly the stated figure — check the last digit. Nothing to the right of the number moves while it counts. Enable reduced motion, reload, and the final figure is present on first paint. Force a parent re-render mid-count and the number keeps counting rather than snapping backwards.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Exit Warp Before Navigate

Choosing a destination does not navigate. It plays an exit: the DOM chrome lifts and fades, the ring of cards is shoved thirty slots forward while its vertical spacing explodes and its radius collapses, the planes dissolve in index order, and only after one settle frame does the router move. The ease is expo.in, so almost nothing happens for the first half-second and then everything happens at once.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A ring of cards tears itself apart and rushes past the camera, and only then does the route change.

- Category: transition
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1, gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. Four scalars describe the ring — `position`, `spacing`, `hSpacing`, `radius` — and one `layout()` reads them: `angle = wrappedOffset(i, position, count) * (2*PI/count) * hSpacing`, then `mesh.position.set(sin(angle) * radius, offset * spacing * 0.12, cos(angle) * radius - radius)` and `mesh.rotation.y = angle`. Idle and exit both drive the same function, so no second code path can disagree about where a card belongs.
2. Idle rotation is `position += dt * 0.16` inside `setAnimationLoop`, with `dt` in seconds clamped to 50 ms — a per-frame constant would spin twice as fast on a 120 Hz display.
3. On select, a timeline fades the chrome (`opacity: 0, y: -20, 0.5s, power2.out, stagger 0.05`) and a `tl.call` pinned at an absolute 0.4s starts the warp, so the ring begins moving 0.1s before the text has finished leaving.
4. The warp is one `gsap.to` on the scalar object: `position + 30`, `spacing 0.8 -> 10`, `hSpacing 1 -> 3`, `radius 2.3 -> 0.6`, 1.4s, `expo.in`, with `onUpdate` calling `layout()`. Radius shrinking while spacing explodes is what makes the planes leave in different directions instead of receding as a group.
5. Each material tweens `opacity: 0` over 1s with `delay: 0.03 * i`, so the ring dissolves in index order rather than as a single fade.
6. The tween's `onComplete` sets a 50 ms timeout, and only that timeout calls `onNavigate`. Textures are canvas-drawn gradients with the item label baked in, so the component ships without a single image.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `duration = 1.4`
  Seconds of warp. With expo.in the perceived length is roughly half the real one; below ~1.1s the accelerating half is too brief to register and it reads as a cut, above ~1.8s the destination feels withheld.
- `shove = 30`
  Ring slots travelled during the exit. For a six-item ring that is five full revolutions — enough that individual cards stop being trackable and the ring reads as a blur rather than as a carousel scrubbing.
- `WARP_CUE = 0.4`
  Absolute seconds at which the scene warp starts, against a 0.5s chrome fade. The 0.1s overlap fuses two moves into one gesture; at 0.5 they read as sequential steps, and at 0 the ring pulls the eye off the text before it has gone.
- `FADE_STAGGER = 0.03`
  Seconds between per-card dissolves. 30 ms x 6 cards is 180 ms of sweep — visible as a direction, short enough that the last card still fades inside the warp.
- `SETTLE_MS = 50`
  GSAP fires onComplete on the same frame the tween ends, before that frame is presented. Navigating there shows one frame of the un-warped ring. One extra tick guarantees the final layout has been painted.
- `WARP_SPACING / WARP_RADIUS = 10 / 0.6`
  Vertical gap goes 0.8 -> 10 while radius goes 2.3 -> 0.6. Spreading without shrinking looks like a zoom out; shrinking without spreading looks like a dolly. Both together are the only combination that reads as the ring tearing apart around the camera.
- `IDLE_SPEED = 0.16`
  Ring slots per second at rest. One card takes about six seconds to reach the front — slow enough to read as ambience, fast enough that the ring is never mistaken for a static image.

## API

```ts
function ExitWarpNavigation(props: { items: { id: string; label: string }[]; onNavigate: (id: string) => void; children?: ReactNode; duration?: number; shove?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `items: { id: string; label: string }[]`
  Destinations. One card and one nav button each; the label is drawn into the card texture.
- `onNavigate: (id: string) => void`
  Called after the warp and its settle frame. Do the router push here.
- `children: ReactNode`
  Chrome over the canvas. Descendants marked `data-warp-chrome` fade and lift first.
- `duration: number` — default `1.4`
  Warp length in seconds.
- `shove: number` — default `30`
  Ring slots the drum travels during the warp.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the positioned wrapper.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  const el = host.current;
  if (!el) return;

  // Checked in an effect, never during render: `hasWebGL()` needs `document`
  // and returning different markup on the server than on the client is a
  // hydration mismatch, not a graceful degradation.
  if (!hasWebGL() || reduced) {
    setFallback(true);
    return;
  }
  setFallback(false);

  const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: true, alpha: true });
  renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio(2));
  renderer.setClearAlpha(0);
  el.appendChild(renderer.domElement);
  renderer.domElement.style.cssText = 'display:block;width:100%;height:100%';

  const scene = new THREE.Scene();
  const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(45, 1, 0.1, 60);

  const geometry = new THREE.PlaneGeometry(1, CARD_H / CARD_W);
  const meshes: THREE.Mesh<THREE.PlaneGeometry, THREE.MeshBasicMaterial>[] = [];
  const textures: THREE.CanvasTexture[] = [];

  items.forEach((item, i) => {
    const texture = new THREE.CanvasTexture(drawCard(item.label, i, items.length));
    texture.colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace;
    textures.push(texture);
    const material = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ map: texture, transparent: true });
    const mesh = new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material);
    scene.add(mesh);
    meshes.push(mesh);
  });

  const state: Warp = {
    position: 0,
    spacing: REST_SPACING,
    hSpacing: 1,
    radius: REST_RADIUS,
  };

  /* One layout function, driven by four scalars. The idle loop and the exit
     tween both call it; there is no second code path that could disagree
     about where a card belongs. */
  const layout = () => {
    const count = meshes.length;
    const step = count > 0 ? (Math.PI * 2) / count : 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < count; i += 1) {
      const mesh = meshes[i];
      if (!mesh) continue;
      const offset = wrappedOffset(i, state.position, count);
      const angle = offset * step * state.hSpacing;
      mesh.position.set(
        Math.sin(angle) * state.radius,
        offset * state.spacing * Y_PER_SLOT,
        Math.cos(angle) * state.radius - state.radius,
      );
      mesh.rotation.y = angle;
    }
  };

  const resize = () => {
    const w = el.clientWidth;
    const h = el.clientHeight;
    if (w === 0 || h === 0) return;
    renderer.setSize(w, h, false);
    camera.aspect = w / h;
    // Pull the camera back on narrow boxes so the ring never grows wider
    // than the frame; a fixed z crops the front card on a phone.
    camera.position.z = 3.2 * Math.max(1, 1.35 / camera.aspect);
    camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
  };

  const observer = new ResizeObserver(resize);
  observer.observe(el);
  resize();
  layout();

  let last = 0;
  renderer.setAnimationLoop((time) => {
    const dt = last === 0 ? 0 : Math.min((time - last) / 1000, 0.05);
    last = time;
    const b = bundle.current;
    if (b && !b.exiting) {
      // Seconds, not frames: a per-frame increment idles twice as fast on a
      // 120 Hz display as it does on 60 Hz.
      state.position += dt * IDLE_SPEED;
      layout();
    }
    renderer.render(scene, camera);
  });

  bundle.current = { renderer, scene, camera, geometry, meshes, textures, state, exiting: false };

  return () => {
    observer.disconnect();
    gsap.killTweensOf(state);
    for (const mesh of meshes) gsap.killTweensOf(mesh.material);
    // disposeRenderer stops the animation loop first: a queued frame that
    // renders into a context we just released throws out of cleanup.
    disposeRenderer(renderer);
    for (const mesh of meshes) mesh.material.dispose();
    for (const texture of textures) texture.dispose();
    geometry.dispose();
    renderer.domElement.remove();
    bundle.current = null;
  };
  // `ids` stands in for `items` so a caller passing a fresh array literal
  // every render does not rebuild the whole scene each time.
  // eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps
}, [ids, reduced]);

const start = useCallback(
  (id: string) => {
    const b = bundle.current;
    const chromeEl = chrome.current;

    // Re-entrancy guard. Without it a double click starts two warps that
    // tween the same scalars in opposite directions and the ring jitters.
    if (b?.exiting) return;

    const chromeTargets = chromeEl
      ? Array.from(chromeEl.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-warp-chrome]'))
      : [];

    if (!b) {
      // No GL: the static crossfade. Same shape, no warp.
      const target = chromeTargets.length > 0 ? chromeTargets : chromeEl;
      if (target) {
        gsap.to(target, {
          opacity: 0,
          duration: reduced ? 0.15 : 0.3,
          ease: 'power2.out',
          onComplete: () => navigate.current(id),
        });
      } else {
        navigate.current(id);
      }
      return;
    }

    b.exiting = true;
    const state = b.state;

    const tl = gsap.timeline();
    if (chromeTargets.length > 0) {
      tl.to(chromeTargets, {
        opacity: 0,
        y: -20,
        duration: CHROME_DURATION,
        ease: 'power2.out',
        stagger: CHROME_STAGGER,
      });
    }

    // Absolute position: the warp starts 0.1 s before the chrome finishes
    // leaving, so the two overlap into one gesture instead of reading as
    // "text goes, then something else happens".
    tl.call(
      () => {
        gsap.to(state, {
          position: state.position + shove,
          spacing: WARP_SPACING,
          hSpacing: WARP_HSPACING,
          radius: WARP_RADIUS,
          duration,
          ease: 'expo.in',
          onComplete: () => {
            // One more frame before the route changes. GSAP's onComplete
            // fires on the same frame the tween ends, so navigating here
            // shows a single frame of the un-warped ring.
            const t = setTimeout(() => navigate.current(id), SETTLE_MS);
            timers.current.push(t);
          },
        });
        for (let i = 0; i < b.meshes.length; i += 1) {
          const mesh = b.meshes[i];
          if (!mesh) continue;
          gsap.to(mesh.material, {
            opacity: 0,
            duration: 1,
            ease: 'power2.in',
            delay: FADE_STAGGER * i,
          });
        }
      },
      undefined,
      WARP_CUE,
    );
  },
  [duration, shove, reduced],
);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Disconnects the ResizeObserver, kills the tweens on the scalar object and on every material, clears the pending navigation timeout, calls `disposeRenderer` (which stops the animation loop, disposes, forces context loss and zeroes the canvas), then disposes every material, texture and the shared geometry, and removes the canvas element.

**Reduced motion.** No WebGL context is created. The same cards render as a static CSS-gradient grid, and choosing one fades the chrome over 0.15s before navigating — the transition still covers the swap, it just does not move.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Calling `router.push` in the click handler and animating afterwards. React unmounts the canvas as the route resolves, so the warp plays for two frames and then disappears; the navigation must be the last step, inside the tween's completion.
- No re-entrancy guard. A double click starts two warps tweening the same four scalars from different origins — the ring jitters and the second navigation fires into an already-unmounting tree.
- Navigating in `onComplete` instead of one tick later. The final frame has not been presented, so a single frame of the intact ring flashes just before the route changes.
- Calling `renderer.dispose()` and stopping there. The GL context stays alive; Chromium kills the oldest context once about sixteen exist, so an unrelated canvas elsewhere on the page goes black. `disposeRenderer` also calls `forceContextLoss()` and zeroes the backing store.
- Leaving the exit tweens running through unmount. They keep writing to disposed materials and to a scalar object nobody reads; the material writes throw once the context is gone. Cleanup kills the tweens on the state object and every material before disposing.
- Deciding whether WebGL exists during render. `hasWebGL()` needs `document`, so it returns false on the server and true on the client, and the two renders disagree — the check runs in an effect and flips to the static fallback afterwards.
- Advancing the idle rotation by a per-frame constant. The ring idles at double speed on a 120 Hz laptop, which is exactly the sort of bug that never reproduces on the developer's machine.

## Notes

- App Router wiring: `onNavigate={(id) => router.push(`/work/${id}`)}`. Call `router.prefetch` on hover (see `hover-prefetch-wipe`) so the 1.4s warp is spent downloading the destination rather than waiting after it.
- Reduced motion and no-WebGL share one path: a static grid of the same cards, a 0.3s fade of the chrome, then navigate. No context is ever created in that branch.
- The ring is index-driven, not raycast-driven. Picking is done with real DOM buttons over the canvas, which keeps the nav keyboard-reachable and screen-reader-legible for free.

## Definition of done

The ring idles at the same speed on a 60 Hz and a 120 Hz display. Choosing a destination fades the caption, then the ring barely moves for about half a second before tearing outward and past the camera; the new route appears only once the frame is empty, with no flash of the intact ring. Unmount mid-warp and the console stays clean.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Font-Safe Text Splitting

Splitting text into lines is a measurement, and measuring before the webfont arrives measures the fallback face. The line boxes are then wrapped in the wrong places and never re-flow when the real font swaps in — with a line mask, the visible symptom is words sliced in half by an invisible edge, and it only reproduces on a cold cache. This component owns the whole lifecycle: gate the first split on `document.fonts.ready`, re-split when a late font finishes loading, and re-split on width change behind a debounce.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Line splitting gated on document.fonts.ready, re-split on late fonts and on width change, debounced.

- Category: text
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. The first split is deferred behind `document.fonts.ready`, so the browser has finished laying out with the real faces before any line box is measured.
2. A `loadingdone` listener on `document.fonts` re-applies the split. Fonts requested after first paint — a lazily mounted section, a second weight, an icon face — trigger another layout pass that moves the line breaks under wrappers that were already fixed.
3. A `ResizeObserver` on the container re-applies the split behind a `debounceMs` timer. Line breaks are a function of container width and nothing else recomputes them; without this, rotating a phone leaves the wrappers describing a layout that no longer exists.
4. The resize guard compares `Math.round(entry.contentRect.width)` against the last value and returns when they match. On iOS the URL bar collapsing changes viewport *height* and fires resize; re-splitting there destroys and rebuilds the DOM mid-scroll for no benefit, on the device least able to spare the frames.
5. `apply()` always tears down first — `ctx.revert()` then `split.revert()` — so a re-split never nests one set of line wrappers inside the previous set. Nesting is what turns three re-splits into a paragraph wrapped nine deep.
6. A `revealed` flag is set by the ScrollTrigger `onEnter`. After the entrance has played, a re-split writes `gsap.set(lines, { yPercent: 0, opacity: 1 })` instead of `gsap.from(...)`, so rotating the device does not replay the entrance from off-screen.
7. `ScrollTrigger.refresh()` runs after every split, because wrapping lines changes this element's height and every trigger positioned below it is now measuring against stale coordinates.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `DEBOUNCE_MS = 200`
  Milliseconds of quiet after the last resize before re-splitting. A split is a full teardown and rebuild of the subtree; running it per resize event during a window drag rebuilds it dozens of times a second. Below ~120ms a drag still triggers repeatedly; past ~350ms the text is visibly broken while the user waits.
- `Y = 110`
  Percent of a line's own height it starts below the mask. Past 100 rather than at it, because the mask clips to the line box and descenders otherwise peek below the mask edge on the first frame.
- `DURATION = 0.9`
  Seconds per line. `power3.out` needs this much room for its deceleration to read; below ~0.5s the curve flattens and lines snap into place.
- `STAGGER = 0.09`
  Seconds between lines. Roughly a tenth of the duration, so several lines are always rising together and the block reads as one mass rather than as a queue.
- `START = 'top 88%'`
  The reveal fires as the block's top edge clears the bottom eighth of the viewport — after it is unambiguously on screen, but before the reader has arrived at it.
- `width comparison = Math.round(contentRect.width)`
  Sub-pixel `contentRect` values differ by fractions on a scrollbar appearing or a zoom level change, so an exact float comparison never matches and the debounce fires forever. Rounding to whole pixels is the smallest unit a line break can actually respond to.

## API

```ts
function FontSafeTextSplit(props: { children: ReactNode; type?: string; mask?: boolean; y?: number; duration?: number; stagger?: number; start?: string; scroller?: Element | null; debounceMs?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Text or markup to split into lines.
- `type: string` — default `'lines'`
  SplitText `type`. Lines are what the mask and the re-split are for.
- `mask: boolean` — default `true`
  Wrap each line in an overflow-hidden box.
- `y: number` — default `110`
  Percent of a line's height it starts below the mask.
- `duration: number` — default `0.9`
  Seconds per line.
- `stagger: number` — default `0.09`
  Seconds between lines.
- `start: string` — default `'top 88%'`
  ScrollTrigger `start` for the reveal.
- `scroller: Element | null` — default `null`
  Scroll container, when the text is not in the document scroller.
- `debounceMs: number` — default `200`
  Milliseconds of quiet after the last resize before re-splitting.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the container via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const Y = 110;
const DURATION = 0.9;
const STAGGER = 0.09;
const START = 'top 88%';
const DEBOUNCE_MS = 200;

export function FontSafeTextSplit({
  children,
  type = 'lines',
  mask = true,
  y = Y,
  duration = DURATION,
  stagger = STAGGER,
  start = START,
  scroller = null,
  debounceMs = DEBOUNCE_MS,
  className,
}: FontSafeTextSplitProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = root.current;
    // Reduced motion never splits. The markup React rendered is the finished
    // state, so the entire font/resize lifecycle below is unnecessary work.
    if (!el || reduced) return;

    gsap.registerPlugin(ScrollTrigger, SplitText);

    let cancelled = false;
    let split: SplitText | null = null;
    let ctx: gsap.Context | null = null;
    let timer = 0;
    // Once the lines have been revealed, a re-split must render them at their
    // final position. Replaying the entrance because the user rotated their
    // phone is the classic symptom of a re-split that forgot it had run.
    let revealed = false;
    // Last measured *width*. Height changes are ignored on purpose.
    let lastWidth = Math.round(el.getBoundingClientRect().width);

    const teardown = () => {
      ctx?.revert();
      ctx = null;
      split?.revert();
      split = null;
    };

    const apply = () => {
      if (cancelled) return;
      teardown();

      const s = new SplitText(el, {
        type,
        mask: mask ? 'lines' : undefined,
        linesClass: 'kinetic-fs-line',
        // SplitText restores the original text for assistive technology.
        // Without it a screen reader announces one fragment per line box.
        aria: 'auto',
      });
      split = s;

      ctx = gsap.context(() => {
        if (revealed) {
          // Already seen. Land the new line boxes in their final state.
          gsap.set(s.lines, { yPercent: 0, opacity: 1 });
          return;
        }
        gsap.from(s.lines, {
          yPercent: y,
          duration,
          stagger,
          ease: 'power3.out',
          scrollTrigger: {
            trigger: el,
            scroller: scroller ?? undefined,
            start,
            once: true,
            onEnter: () => {
              revealed = true;
            },
          },
        });
      }, el);

      // Wrapping lines changes this element's height, so every trigger below
      // it on the page is now measuring against stale coordinates.
      ScrollTrigger.refresh();
    };

    // 1. The first split waits for the fonts the document already knows about.
    void document.fonts.ready.then(apply);

    // 2. A font requested later — a lazy section, a second weight, an icon
    //    face — triggers another layout pass that moves the line breaks.
    const onFontsDone = () => apply();
    document.fonts.addEventListener('loadingdone', onFontsDone);

    // 3. Line breaks are a function of container width. Nothing else
    //    recomputes them, so a resize without a re-split leaves the wrappers
    //    describing a layout that no longer exists.
    const ro = new ResizeObserver((entries) => {
      const entry = entries[0];
      if (!entry) return;
      const width = Math.round(entry.contentRect.width);
      // Width-only. iOS fires resize when the URL bar collapses, which changes
      // height only; re-splitting there rebuilds the DOM mid-scroll for
      // nothing and drops frames on the device least able to spare them.
      if (width === lastWidth) return;
      lastWidth = width;
      window.clearTimeout(timer);
      timer = window.setTimeout(apply, debounceMs);
    });
    ro.observe(el);

    return () => {
      cancelled = true;
      window.clearTimeout(timer);
      ro.disconnect();
      document.fonts.removeEventListener('loadingdone', onFontsDone);
      teardown();
    };
  }, [
    children,
    type,
    mask,
    y,
    duration,
    stagger,
    start,
    scroller,
    debounceMs,
    reduced,
  ]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Sets a `cancelled` flag that closes the async `document.fonts.ready` gap, clears the pending debounce timeout, disconnects the `ResizeObserver`, removes the `loadingdone` listener, then reverts the `gsap.context` and the split in that order. Nothing can re-split or tween after unmount.

**Reduced motion.** The effect returns before registering anything: no split, no font listener, no ResizeObserver. The text React rendered is the finished state and is fully visible on first paint — which also means the entire measurement lifecycle costs nothing for users who asked for less motion.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Splitting synchronously on mount. On a cold cache the fallback face is measured, the line wrappers are fixed at the wrong break points, and when the real font swaps in the masked lines clip words in half. It works perfectly on every reload after the first, which is why it ships.
- Waiting only on `document.fonts.ready` and stopping there. It resolves once for the fonts the document knew about at that moment; a font requested later re-flows the text under wrappers that are already fixed.
- Re-splitting on every resize event. Each split is a full DOM teardown and rebuild, so dragging a window edge rebuilds the subtree dozens of times a second and the page locks up.
- Re-splitting on any resize rather than on width change. iOS fires resize on every URL-bar collapse, so scrolling on a phone continuously destroys and rebuilds the paragraph.
- Comparing raw `contentRect.width` floats. They wobble by fractions of a pixel and the debounce re-arms forever.
- Re-splitting without reverting the previous split first. The new line wrappers nest inside the old ones, and after a few resizes the paragraph is wrapped several layers deep with stale masks at every level.
- Replaying the entrance on re-split. The text drops back below its mask and rises again because the user rotated their phone, which reads as a rendering glitch.
- Skipping `ScrollTrigger.refresh()` after the split. The element's height changed, so every trigger below it on the page fires at the wrong scroll position — usually the bug reported as "the section below animates too early".

## Notes

- This is one of the two components that deliberately use GSAP `SplitText`, because the technique *is* SplitText's lifecycle. `SplitText` ships inside the main `gsap` package and is free to use; it is imported from `gsap/SplitText` rather than vendored, so this is a use grant with no redistribution. The other text components in this set split declaratively in JSX so consumers are not forced into GSAP for effects that do not need it.
- Every other split-based component in the registry inherits this problem. If you split text anywhere — by hand, with `split-type`, or with SplitText — the `document.fonts.ready` gate and the width-only debounced re-split apply just as much.
- GSAP 3.13+ offers `autoSplit` and `onRevert`, which cover part of this. The explicit lifecycle here is kept because it also handles the late-`loadingdone` case and gives you the `revealed` flag, and because it is legible: you can see exactly which of the three triggers fired.

## Definition of done

Hard-reload with the cache disabled and throttled network: the lines break correctly and no word is clipped by a mask edge, on the first load as well as subsequent ones. Drag the window narrower and the lines re-break about 200ms after you stop, once, without replaying the entrance. Scroll on an iOS device and the paragraph never rebuilds as the URL bar collapses. Resize repeatedly and inspect the DOM: line wrappers are exactly one level deep, never nested. A section below the text still triggers at the correct scroll position after a re-split.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: FOV-Derived Row Spacing

A perspective row that never guesses its spacing. Given a vertical field of view and a camera distance, it computes the visible width on the row plane, divides it across the gaps between item centres, and converts to pixels once at the end. The outermost item centres land on the frame edges by construction, at any aspect ratio, with no breakpoint table and no tuned magic number. It is the flat pre-intro layout of a three.js drum, done in the DOM with the identical arithmetic.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A row whose item spacing is solved from a field of view and a camera distance, so it spans the frame exactly at any size.

- Category: layout
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. A pinhole camera at distance d from a plane sees `visibleHeight = 2 · d · tan(fov / 2)` on that plane, and `visibleWidth = visibleHeight · aspect`. Both quantities are in world units; nothing pixel-sized is involved yet.
2. The step is `visibleWidth · spanRatio / (n − 1)` and item centres are `x_i = i · step − rowWidth / 2` where `rowWidth = (n − 1) · step`. The subtraction centres the row on the origin without a second measurement, because the outermost centres are at ±rowWidth/2 by definition.
3. World units become pixels through a single scalar, `pxPerUnit = heightPx / visibleHeight`, applied at the last multiplication. Every intermediate value stays resolution-independent, which is why a resize needs no re-derivation of anything but this one number.
4. CSS `perspective` is set to `cameraZ · pxPerUnit`, which reduces to `heightPx / (2 · tan(fov / 2))` — the cameraZ cancels. That cancellation is the proof that the world-unit scale and the CSS projection describe the same camera: if it did not cancel, the two coordinate systems would disagree and depth would foreshorten by the wrong amount.
5. Items are placed with `translate3d(x · pxPerUnit, 0, z · pxPerUnit)` and the browser performs the perspective divide. An element at world z projects with scale `cameraZ / (cameraZ − z)`, which is exactly what a `PerspectiveCamera` does to a plane at the same depth.
6. The optional bow pushes outer items away on a parabola, `z = −bow · t²` with `t = x / (visibleWidth / 2)`. Depth would shrink their projected x, so the unprojected x is pre-multiplied by `(cameraZ − z) / cameraZ` — the exact inverse of the divide — and the row still spans the frame with the bow at any strength.
7. The four camera scalars are damped rather than assigned, so changing the field of view reads as a dolly. The layout is a pure function of them, so an interruption mid-spread cannot desynchronise anything: there is no accumulated position to corrupt.
8. The frame loop snaps inside an epsilon, writes one final layout, and then returns immediately. Exponential damping never actually arrives, so without that gate the component would rewrite n transforms every frame forever for a row that has visibly stopped moving.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `visibleHeight = 2 · cameraZ · tan(fov / 2)`
  The exact height of the frustum cross-section at the row plane. Half the FOV subtends a right triangle of opposite `visibleHeight / 2` over adjacent `cameraZ`, so `tan(fov / 2) = (visibleHeight / 2) / cameraZ`. The factor of 2 and the half-angle are the two places this is most often written wrong; using `tan(fov)` overstates the span by roughly 3x at 70 degrees.
- `step = visibleWidth · spanRatio / (n − 1)`
  n − 1, not n. The step is the distance between adjacent item CENTRES, and n centres have n − 1 gaps between them. Dividing by n leaves the row one step short, so the last item never reaches the frame edge — the discrepancy is 1/n, which is invisible at twenty items and glaring at four.
- `x_i = i · step − rowWidth / 2`
  Centres the row on the origin arithmetically. With `rowWidth = (n − 1) · step`, item 0 sits at −rowWidth/2 and item n−1 at +rowWidth/2, so the row is symmetric for both odd and even counts without a special case and without measuring the assembled row afterwards.
- `perspective = heightPx / (2 · tan(fov / 2))`
  The CSS perspective distance in pixels that reproduces the same vertical FOV over a box of height H. Derived by asking at what distance the visible height equals H: `H = 2 · P · tan(fov / 2)`. It is `cameraZ · pxPerUnit` with the cameraZ cancelled, which is why the row can be moved nearer or further without touching this value.
- `depthScale = (cameraZ − z) / cameraZ`
  Perspective divides a point's projected x by `(cameraZ − z) / cameraZ`, so pre-multiplying the unprojected x by the same factor leaves the projection exactly where the flat row put it. Omitting it makes any bow pull the outer items inward, which is the bug usually patched by nudging spanRatio above 1 until it happens to look right at one screen size.
- `fov = 70`
  Degrees, vertical. Wide enough that the bow foreshortens visibly rather than reading as a flat scale-down. Above ~90 the near items grow fast enough to clip the frame; below ~40 the perspective is so weak that the depth compensation has nothing to compensate for and the row may as well be 2D.
- `cameraZ = 5`
  World units. It sets nothing visible on its own — it only fixes the unit scale, since a larger distance widens the visible area by the same ratio it shrinks everything on screen. 5 keeps the bow and the item sizes in a range where single decimal digits are meaningful, matching the drum this arithmetic came from.
- `bow = 0.6`
  World units of depth at the frame edge, about 12% of cameraZ. Enough that the outer items read as receding; past ~0.3 · cameraZ they shrink far enough that the row looks like a fisheye rather than a row, and the compensated x starts pushing content beyond the overflow clip.
- `smoothing = 0.0015`
  Fraction of the remaining gap left after one second, so the row is ~99.9% of the way to a new field of view within that second. Frame-rate independent by construction, so a 120 Hz display and a throttled tab converge on the same curve rather than the same per-frame ratio.
- `EPSILON = 0.0005`
  Summed absolute gap across the four scalars below which the layout snaps and the loop stops writing. Small enough to be sub-pixel at any plausible pxPerUnit, large enough that exponential damping crosses it in under a second instead of asymptoting forever.

## API

```ts
function FovDerivedRow(props: { children: ReactNode; fov?: number; cameraZ?: number; spanRatio?: number; bow?: number; smoothing?: number; className?: string; cellClassName?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  One positioned cell per child, laid out on the derived step.
- `fov: number` — default `70`
  Vertical field of view in degrees. Drives both the spacing and the CSS perspective.
- `cameraZ: number` — default `5`
  Camera distance to the row plane in world units. Fixes the unit scale.
- `spanRatio: number` — default `1`
  Fraction of the visible width the row spans. 1 puts the outer centres on the frame edges.
- `bow: number` — default `0.6`
  World units the outermost items recede. Their x is compensated so the span is preserved.
- `smoothing: number` — default `0.0015`
  Fraction of the gap remaining after one second while the row re-spreads.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the stage element.
- `cellClassName: string`
  Merged onto every positioned cell. Size the items here.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function FovDerivedRow({
  children,
  fov = FOV,
  cameraZ = CAMERA_Z,
  spanRatio = SPAN_RATIO,
  bow = BOW,
  smoothing = SMOOTHING,
  className,
  cellClassName,
}: FovDerivedRowProps) {
  const stage = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const cells = useRef<Array<HTMLDivElement | null>>([]);

  const size = useResizeObserver(stage);
  const { inView } = useInView(stage, { threshold: 0 });
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  const items = Children.toArray(children);
  const count = items.length;

  /* The three scalars the layout is a pure function of. They are damped rather
     than assigned so that changing the FOV reads as a dolly, not as a jump —
     and because the layout is a pure function of them, interrupting mid-spread
     cannot desynchronise anything. */
  const live = useRef({ fov, cameraZ, spanRatio, bow });
  const current = useRef({ fov, cameraZ, spanRatio, bow });
  const settled = useRef(false);
  live.current = { fov, cameraZ, spanRatio, bow };

  /**
   * Lay the row out for one set of camera scalars. Pure: same inputs, same
   * transforms, no accumulated state.
   */
  const apply = (params: { fov: number; cameraZ: number; spanRatio: number; bow: number }) => {
    const el = stage.current;
    if (!el || count === 0) return;

    const widthPx = el.clientWidth;
    const heightPx = el.clientHeight;
    if (widthPx < 1 || heightPx < 1) return;

    // Half-angle first: every formula below wants tan(fov/2), never tan(fov).
    const tanHalfFov = Math.tan((params.fov * Math.PI) / 360);
    const visibleHeight = 2 * params.cameraZ * tanHalfFov;
    const visibleWidth = visibleHeight * (widthPx / heightPx);

    // World units to CSS pixels. The whole layout is computed in world units
    // and converted exactly once, here.
    const pxPerUnit = heightPx / visibleHeight;
    // P = H / (2 tan(fov/2)). Independent of cameraZ, which is the sanity
    // check that the world-unit scale and the projection agree.
    const perspectivePx = params.cameraZ * pxPerUnit;

    // n − 1, not n: the step is the distance between adjacent CENTRES, and a
    // row of n centres has n − 1 gaps. Dividing by n leaves the row short by
    // one step and the last item never reaches the frame edge.
    const gaps = Math.max(count - 1, 1);
    const step = count > 1 ? (visibleWidth * params.spanRatio) / gaps : 0;
    const rowWidth = (count - 1) * step;
    const halfSpan = Math.max(visibleWidth / 2, 1e-6);

    el.style.perspective = `${perspectivePx}px`;

    for (let i = 0; i < count; i += 1) {
      const cell = cells.current[i];
      if (!cell) continue;

      const flatX = i * step - rowWidth / 2;

      // Parabolic bow: 0 at the centre, `bow` units back at the frame edge.
      const t = flatX / halfSpan;
      const worldZ = -params.bow * t * t;

      // Depth compensation. Moving a point from z = 0 to z shrinks its
      // projected x by cameraZ / (cameraZ − z), so scaling the unprojected x
      // by the inverse leaves the projection exactly where the flat row put
      // it. Without this line, any bow pulls the outer items inward and the
      // row stops spanning the frame — the bug that gets "fixed" by nudging
      // spanRatio past 1 until it looks right at one screen size.
      const depthScale = (params.cameraZ - worldZ) / params.cameraZ;
      const worldX = flatX * depthScale;

      cell.style.transform =
        `translate(-50%, -50%) translate3d(${worldX * pxPerUnit}px, 0px, ${worldZ * pxPerUnit}px)`;
    }
  };

  // Resize is not an animation: re-derive and write immediately, or the row
  // lags a visible beat behind a window drag.
  useEffect(() => {
    apply(current.current);
    // `apply` closes over refs only; re-running on every render would fight
    // the frame loop for the same transforms.
    // eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps
  }, [size.width, size.height, count]);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!reduced) return;
    // Reduced motion is the resolved layout, not a fast spread: adopt the
    // target scalars outright and lay out once.
    current.current = { ...live.current };
    settled.current = false;
    apply(current.current);
  }, [reduced, fov, cameraZ, spanRatio, bow]);

  useRaf(
    (dt) => {
      const target = live.current;
      const now = current.current;

      const next = {
        fov: damp(now.fov, target.fov, smoothing, dt),
        cameraZ: damp(now.cameraZ, target.cameraZ, smoothing, dt),
        spanRatio: damp(now.spanRatio, target.spanRatio, smoothing, dt),
        bow: damp(now.bow, target.bow, smoothing, dt),
      };

      // Exponential damping never actually arrives, so it would rewrite n
      // transforms forever. Snap inside epsilon, lay out one last time, and
      // then skip the writes entirely until a prop moves again.
      const gap =
        Math.abs(next.fov - target.fov) +
        Math.abs(next.cameraZ - target.cameraZ) +
        Math.abs(next.spanRatio - target.spanRatio) +
        Math.abs(next.bow - target.bow);

      if (gap < EPSILON) {
        if (settled.current) return;
        current.current = { ...target };
        settled.current = true;
        apply(current.current);
        return;
      }

      settled.current = false;
      current.current = next;
      apply(next);
    },
    inView && !reduced,
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useRaf` unsubscribes from the shared loop on unmount and cancels the frame when it is the last subscriber; `useResizeObserver` and `useInView` remove their targets from their shared observers. No listeners, timers or tweens are created directly. Inline transforms are written only to elements this component owns and rendered, so they are removed with them.

**Reduced motion.** The reduced branch adopts the target scalars outright and lays the row out once, so the resolved geometry is on screen rather than a fast spread toward it. The frame loop is not subscribed at all, so no work is scheduled for a user who asked for none, and a later prop change still re-derives the layout immediately through the same code path. Because the layout is a pure function of the four scalars, the reduced render is pixel-identical to the settled animated one.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Spacing a perspective row by `containerWidth / n`. It is wrong twice: it uses n instead of n − 1, and it ignores that the row plane is not the screen plane. It looks correct at one viewport because the error was absorbed into a hand-tuned padding, and it breaks on the first aspect-ratio change.
- Using `tan(fov)` instead of `tan(fov / 2)`. At 70 degrees that overstates the visible extent by about 3x, so the row spreads far past the frame. It survives review because the row still looks deliberate — just wildly too wide — and the fix gets applied as a 0.35 multiplier somewhere else.
- Applying degrees to `Math.tan` directly. `Math.tan(70)` is a perfectly finite number, so nothing throws and nothing warns; the layout is simply nonsense. `(fov * Math.PI) / 360` converts and halves in one step, which is also why that constant is 360 and not 180.
- Bowing items in z without compensating x. Depth shrinks projected x, so the outer items drift inward and the row silently stops spanning the frame. The formula is one multiplication and its absence is normally treated as a spacing problem rather than a projection one.
- Setting `perspective` from a fixed pixel value while deriving the spacing from an FOV. The two then describe different cameras: the arithmetic places items for one frustum and the browser projects them through another, so depth foreshortens by the wrong amount and no amount of spacing tuning fixes it.
- Deriving the layout from `window.innerWidth`. The component is correct on load and wrong the moment it sits in a resizable panel or a grid cell that reflows. Its own `clientWidth` and `clientHeight` are the only inputs that stay true, which is what `useResizeObserver` supplies.
- Letting the damping loop run forever. Exponential approach never reaches its target, so a settled row keeps writing n transforms per frame and the profiler shows a permanent baseline cost for a component that has not moved in a minute. Snap inside an epsilon and return.
- Recomputing on resize only inside the frame loop. A resize is not an animation; deferring it by a frame makes the row visibly lag a window drag by one tick, which reads as jank rather than as smoothing.
- Omitting `transform-style: preserve-3d`, or setting the perspective on an ancestor with its own transform. Either flattens the subtree and every `translateZ` collapses to no effect, leaving a row that is correctly spaced but stubbornly two-dimensional.

## Notes

- The spacing arithmetic is identical to the flat pre-intro row of a three.js drum gallery, which is the point: the formula belongs to the projection, not to the renderer. Porting it means replacing one conversion line, and this component is the DOM half of the pair that `layout-lerp-scalar` interpolates away from.
- With `bow: 0` and `spanRatio: 1` the component has a hands-on correctness test: the outermost item centres sit exactly on the left and right edges of the box, at every viewport, with no tuning. If they do not, one of the formulas above has been mistyped.
- `spanRatio` is the only aesthetic knob here — everything else is determined. Values below 1 inset the row from the frame; above 1 it deliberately overflows the clip, which is useful when the outer items are meant to be cut off.

## Definition of done

Set `bow` to 0 and the leftmost and rightmost item centres sit exactly on the edges of the box — resize the panel from narrow to wide and they stay there, with no jump and no breakpoint. Restore the bow and the outer items recede and shrink while their horizontal positions do not move. Raise the field of view and the row spreads on a smooth dolly rather than snapping. Item counts of 1 and 2 both render without a divide-by-zero or a NaN transform. With reduced motion on, the row is at its final geometry on first paint and the profiler shows no animation frames for it.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Fractional Render Scale

A drifting fog field with a latent grid that develops under the cursor, rendered into a canvas whose backing store is deliberately 0.6x the size of the element it fills. The browser upscales it, and the upscale is invisible because the content was authored for it: no detail finer than a dozen pixels, and the one thing with an edge — the grid — has its line width specified in backing-store pixels rather than CSS pixels. It is a background you can afford, and a demonstration of the cheapest large performance win in WebGL.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A field rendered into a backing store 0.6x its box — 36% of the fragments — with a grid measured in texels so the upscale never shows.

- Category: webgl
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1

## How it works

1. The scale is applied through the pixel ratio: `renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio(maxDpr) * scale)` followed by `setSize(w, h, false)`. three then sizes the backing store to `floor(w * dpr * scale)` while the canvas keeps `width: 100%` from CSS, so one number controls the ratio and there is no second sizing path to keep in sync.
2. The achieved ratio is measured rather than assumed. `setSize` floors, so `getDrawingBufferSize().x / cssWidth` can differ from `dpr * scale` by up to a pixel; that measured value becomes `uScale`, and every length the shader treats as a CSS pixel is `gl_FragCoord.xy / uScale`.
3. The fog is three sines multiplied and added, then pushed through `smoothstep(-0.15, 1.15, fog)`. It is not trying to be fbm — it is trying to contain no feature smaller than roughly a dozen pixels, which is the precondition for a bilinear upscale being undetectable.
4. The grid is drawn from `abs(fract(cell - 0.5) - 0.5) * pxPerCell`, which is the distance to the nearest line expressed in backing-store pixels, and a `smoothstep(width - 0.5, width + 0.5, d)` ramp across exactly one texel. A line specified this way is `1 / scale` CSS pixels wide after the upscale: softer as the scale drops, never thinner, so it cannot fall through the sampling grid.
5. No `fwidth`. The grid is axis-aligned in screen space, so the derivative of the cell coordinate is a constant the shader already holds — `uScale * uGridSize` backing pixels per cell. Computing it directly is exact, is one multiply, and needs no derivatives extension.
6. The geometry is a single triangle with vertices at (-1,-1), (3,-1) and (-1,3). It covers the viewport with three vertices and no diagonal, so the GPU never shades the seam pixels twice as it does where two triangles of a fullscreen quad meet.
7. The pointer is smoothed by `useSmoothPointer` with `perFrameToSmoothing(0.05)`, which reproduces the source's `x += (target - x) * 0.05` at 60 Hz while staying frame-rate independent, and its `nx`/`ny` are flipped to GL's y-up before reaching the uniform.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `renderScale = 0.6`
  Linear, so the saving is quadratic: 0.36 of the fragments, a 64% cut, about 2.8x less fragment work. A 2560x1440 window drops from 3.7 M fragments a frame to 1.3 M. Below roughly 0.5 the grid lines start to look conspicuously soft against crisp DOM text next to them; above 0.8 there is little left to win.
- `MIN_SCALE = 0.25`
  Floor on the prop. At 0.25 a one-texel line is already four CSS pixels wide — a third of a 44 px cell — and the grid stops reading as a grid and starts reading as a plaid.
- `lineWidth = 1 backing pixel`
  The unit is the whole point. One texel is the finest line the buffer can actually hold; asking for one CSS pixel at 0.6 scale asks for 0.6 of a texel, which the rasteriser answers with a dashed line that crawls as the box resizes.
- `gridSize = 44 CSS pixels`
  Authored in CSS pixels so the grid holds its apparent size when the render scale changes — the entire visual difference between 0.6 and 1.0 should be a slight softening, never a different layout.
- `majorEvery = 5`
  A 220 px major cell. Without a second scale the grid is a flat screen door; with one it acquires depth. Its line is 1.6x the minor width, which survives the upscale as a clear hierarchy where a colour difference alone would not.
- `POINTER_ALPHA = 0.05 per frame at 60 Hz`
  The source chose it to be slower than the eye expects, which reads as viscosity: about 330 ms to close 63% of the gap. Passed through `perFrameToSmoothing` so a 120 Hz display gets the same 330 ms rather than half of it.
- `glow exponent = exp(-d * d * 2.2)`
  A Gaussian on distance normalised by the radius, so `glowRadius` is where the glow has fallen to about 11%. A smoothstep here would put a visible circular edge on a field that has no other edges — the one place the upscale would be caught.
- `grid reveal = 0.18 + 0.82 * glow`
  The grid is mostly latent and the cursor develops it. At full strength everywhere it is a background; appearing under the pointer, it is a surface reacting to being touched. The 0.18 floor keeps the structure legible before the pointer arrives.
- `POINTER_EPSILON = 0.0002`
  Under reduced motion the image is a pure function of the pointer, so frames where it has not moved are skipped entirely. The threshold is well under one pixel of an ordinary box, so no real movement is ever swallowed.

## API

```ts
function FractionalRenderScale(props: { renderScale?: number; maxDpr?: number; gridSize?: number; majorEvery?: number; lineWidth?: number; glowRadius?: number; baseColor?: string; fogColor?: string; lineColor?: string; glowColor?: string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `renderScale: number` — default `0.6`
  Backing store size relative to the display pixel ratio. Clamped to 0.25..1.
- `maxDpr: number` — default `2`
  Cap on the device pixel ratio before the render scale is applied.
- `gridSize: number` — default `44`
  Grid spacing in CSS pixels. Floored at 4.
- `majorEvery: number` — default `5`
  Every nth line is drawn as a major one, 1.6x the width.
- `lineWidth: number` — default `1`
  Minor line width in backing-store pixels — not CSS pixels. Floored at 0.5.
- `glowRadius: number` — default `240`
  Cursor glow radius in CSS pixels, at which the glow has fallen to about 11%.
- `baseColor: string` — default `'#080b12'`
  Darkest colour of the field.
- `fogColor: string` — default `'#1d3350'`
  Colour the fog lifts toward.
- `lineColor: string` — default `'#8fb6df'`
  Grid line colour.
- `glowColor: string` — default `'#3f7fd0'`
  Additive colour under the pointer.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function FractionalRenderScale({
  renderScale = 0.6,
  maxDpr = 2,
  gridSize = 44,
  majorEvery = 5,
  lineWidth = 1,
  glowRadius = 240,
  baseColor = '#080b12',
  fogColor = '#1d3350',
  lineColor = '#8fb6df',
  glowColor = '#3f7fd0',
  className,
}: FractionalRenderScaleProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const stage = useRef<Stage | null>(null);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const { inView } = useInView(host, { threshold: 0 });
  const visible = useVisibility();
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const pointer = useSmoothPointer({ target: host, smoothing: POINTER_SMOOTHING });

  const [supported, setSupported] = useState(true);
  useEffect(() => setSupported(hasWebGL()), []);

  /* Read inside resize and draw. Keeping them out of the effect's dependency
     list means dragging a render-scale slider re-sizes the backing store
     rather than tearing down the GL context on every step. */
  const live = useRef({ renderScale, maxDpr, gridSize, majorEvery, lineWidth, glowRadius });
  live.current = { renderScale, maxDpr, gridSize, majorEvery, lineWidth, glowRadius };

  const lastPointer = useRef<{ x: number; y: number } | null>(null);

  const ready = width > 1 && height > 1 && supported;

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = host.current;
    if (!el || !ready) return;

    const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({
      // Nothing in the field has a geometric edge, so MSAA has nothing to
      // sample — and at a fractional scale it would be antialiasing the wrong
      // grid anyway.
      antialias: false,
      // Opaque: the shader covers every pixel, and an alpha channel would make
      // the compositor blend the canvas over the page for no reason.
      alpha: false,
      depth: false,
      stencil: false,
      // The entire point of the component. On a laptop with switchable
      // graphics this keeps a decorative background off the discrete GPU.
      powerPreference: 'low-power',
    });
    renderer.setClearColor(0x000000, 1);
    renderer.domElement.style.display = 'block';
    // CSS size is 1x and fixed to the box; the backing store is set separately
    // by setSize(..., false). The gap between the two IS the render scale.
    renderer.domElement.style.width = '100%';
    renderer.domElement.style.height = '100%';
    el.appendChild(renderer.domElement);

    const scene = new THREE.Scene();
    const camera = new THREE.Camera();

    // One oversized triangle, not a quad. It covers the viewport with three
    // vertices and no diagonal seam for the GPU to shade twice.
    const geometry = new THREE.BufferGeometry();
    geometry.setAttribute(
      'position',
      new THREE.BufferAttribute(new Float32Array([-1, -1, 0, 3, -1, 0, -1, 3, 0]), 3),
    );

    const uniforms: Uniforms = {
      uResolution: { value: new THREE.Vector2(1, 1) },
      uScale: { value: 1 },
      uTime: { value: 0 },
      uPointer: { value: new THREE.Vector2(0.5, 0.5) },
      uGridSize: { value: gridSize },
      uMajorEvery: { value: majorEvery },
      uLineWidth: { value: lineWidth },
      uGlowRadius: { value: glowRadius },
      uBaseColor: { value: new THREE.Color(baseColor) },
      uFogColor: { value: new THREE.Color(fogColor) },
      uLineColor: { value: new THREE.Color(lineColor) },
      uGlowColor: { value: new THREE.Color(glowColor) },
    };

    const material = new THREE.ShaderMaterial({
      vertexShader: FRACTIONAL_SCALE_VERT,
      fragmentShader: FRACTIONAL_SCALE_FRAG,
      uniforms,
      depthTest: false,
      depthWrite: false,
    });

    const mesh = new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material);
    // The triangle's vertices sit outside a unit bounding sphere, and there is
    // no camera transform to cull against in the first place.
    mesh.frustumCulled = false;
    scene.add(mesh);

    const buffer = new THREE.Vector2();

    stage.current = {
      resize(w, h) {
        const state = live.current;
        const scale = clamp(state.renderScale, MIN_SCALE, 1);
        // Scale folded into the pixel ratio: three then multiplies it through
        // setSize for the backing store while the CSS size stays whatever the
        // stylesheet says. One number, no second sizing path to keep in sync.
        renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio(state.maxDpr) * scale);
        renderer.setSize(w, h, false);

        renderer.getDrawingBufferSize(buffer);
        const bw = Math.max(1, Math.round(buffer.x));
        const bh = Math.max(1, Math.round(buffer.y));
        uniforms.uResolution.value.set(bw, bh);
        // Measured, not assumed. setSize floors, so the achieved ratio differs
        // from dpr * scale by up to a pixel — and the grid is authored in CSS
        // pixels, which would then drift against the layout.
        uniforms.uScale.value = w > 0 ? bw / w : 1;

        uniforms.uGridSize.value = Math.max(4, state.gridSize);
        uniforms.uMajorEvery.value = Math.max(1, Math.round(state.majorEvery));
        uniforms.uLineWidth.value = Math.max(0.5, state.lineWidth);
        uniforms.uGlowRadius.value = Math.max(1, state.glowRadius);
      },

      draw(time, pointerX, pointerY) {
        uniforms.uTime.value = time;
        uniforms.uPointer.value.set(pointerX, pointerY);
        renderer.render(scene, camera);
      },
    };

    stage.current.resize(el.clientWidth, el.clientHeight);
    stage.current.draw(0, 0.5, 0.5);

    return () => {
      stage.current = null;
      geometry.dispose();
      material.dispose();
      disposeRenderer(renderer);
      renderer.domElement.remove();
    };
    // eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps
  }, [ready, baseColor, fogColor, lineColor, glowColor]);

  useEffect(() => {
    const current = stage.current;
    if (!current || width < 1 || height < 1) return;
    current.resize(width, height);
    // Resizing a canvas clears its drawing buffer. When time is frozen the
    // loop skips every frame in which the pointer has not moved, so the
    // redraw has to happen here or the field stays blank until it does. When
    // time is running the next frame covers it a few milliseconds later.
    if (reduced) {
      const state = pointer.current;
      current.draw(0, state.nx, 1 - state.ny);
      lastPointer.current = { x: state.nx, y: 1 - state.ny };
    }
  }, [
    width,
    height,
    reduced,
    renderScale,
    maxDpr,
    gridSize,
    majorEvery,
    lineWidth,
    glowRadius,
    pointer,
  ]);

  useRaf(
    (_dt, elapsed) => {
      const current = stage.current;
      if (!current) return;

      const state = pointer.current;
      const px = state.nx;
      // GL's y axis points up; the pointer's does not.
      const py = 1 - state.ny;

      // Reduced motion freezes time at 0 rather than stopping the render, so
      // the fog, the vignette and the cursor glow all survive — only the drift
      // is gone. With time constant the image is a pure function of the
      // pointer, so a frame where the pointer has not moved is skippable.
      if (reduced) {
        const last = lastPointer.current;
        if (
          last &&
          Math.abs(px - last.x) < POINTER_EPSILON &&
          Math.abs(py - last.y) < POINTER_EPSILON
        ) {
          return;
        }
      }

      lastPointer.current = { x: px, y: py };
      current.draw(reduced ? 0 : elapsed, px, py);
    },
    ready && inView && visible,
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nulls the stage ref, disposes the triangle geometry and the ShaderMaterial, then calls `disposeRenderer` for `dispose` + `forceContextLoss` + a zeroed drawing buffer, and removes the canvas from the DOM. The canvas is three's own, created inside the effect and appended per effect run, so a StrictMode remount builds a new context instead of reattaching one that was just force-lost. The pointer listener belongs to `useSmoothPointer` and is removed with it; sizing, visibility and the frame loop are all shared subscriptions that release themselves.

**Reduced motion.** The component reads `useReducedMotion` itself and freezes `uTime` at 0 rather than stopping the render. The fog, the vignette, the grid and the cursor glow are all still drawn — none of them depends on time — so what is lost is exactly the drift and nothing else. With time constant the image is a pure function of the pointer, so the loop skips any frame in which the pointer has not moved by more than 0.0002, and a still page costs nothing beyond the empty rAF callback.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Setting only `canvas.width` and forgetting the CSS size, or the reverse. Either mistake produces a canvas that is simply smaller or simply blurrier than intended; the technique is the deliberate gap between the two sizes, and both have to be set on purpose.
- Putting `image-rendering: pixelated` on the canvas — sometimes inherited from a global rule aimed at sprite art. It replaces the bilinear upscale with nearest-neighbour and the entire effect turns into visible blocks.
- Specifying line widths, glow radii or grid spacing in device pixels via raw `gl_FragCoord`. Everything is tuned on one machine and then renders at 0.6 of that size at 0.6 scale, and a third of it again on a 3x phone. Divide by the measured scale and author in CSS pixels.
- Rendering content with fine detail at a fractional scale. Text, hairlines, high-frequency noise and hard-edged shapes all alias the moment the buffer shrinks. This technique is for soft fields, and content and scale have to be chosen together.
- Listening to `window.resize` instead of observing the element. A sidebar opening, a font loading and reflowing, or a flex sibling changing all resize the box with no window event — and `ResizeObserver` also fires once on observe, which handles the initial size with no separate call.
- Forgetting that resizing the canvas clears its drawing buffer. Any component that skips frames — as this one does when time is frozen — goes blank after a resize unless the resize path redraws explicitly.
- Reading `dpr * scale` back as the achieved ratio. `setSize` floors the backing store, so on most box widths the real ratio is slightly lower; using the nominal value makes the grid drift by a pixel against the layout as the window changes.
- Suppressing the render entirely under reduced motion. Time frozen at 0 still gives the fog, the vignette and the cursor glow, because none of them depend on it — a far better degradation than a flat colour, and the accessibility requirement is about motion, not about the image.
- Assuming `antialias: true` helps. There is no geometric edge to sample: the only visible edges come from the fragment shader, MSAA does not see them, and the request costs a multisampled buffer of the same size as everything just saved.

## Notes

- The renderer is created with `powerPreference: "low-power"`. On a laptop with switchable graphics this keeps a decorative background off the discrete GPU, which is worth more battery than the render scale itself.
- `renderScale` and `maxDpr` are read from a ref inside the resize path, so changing them re-sizes the backing store without rebuilding the GL context — a render-scale slider can be dragged live.
- A useful way to see the technique: set `renderScale` to 1 and then to 0.6 and watch the grid rather than the fog. The lines soften very slightly and nothing else about the image changes, while the fragment count falls by two thirds.
- The colours are individual string props rather than an array, so a caller passing literals does not hand the effect a new identity on every render.

## Definition of done

A soft blue fog drifting behind a faint grid, with the grid brightening into a pool under the cursor that trails a third of a second behind it. Open DevTools and the canvas element reports a backing store of 0.6 of its CSS size — the technique is verifiable, not merely claimed — while the image shows no blockiness and the grid lines stay continuous rather than dashed. Resize the window slowly: the grid keeps its 44 px spacing against the layout and never crawls. With reduced motion the fog stops drifting and everything else, cursor glow included, still works.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
