# Build: Fullscreen Triangle Pass

The smallest possible host for a full-screen fragment shader: a raw WebGL2 context, one buffer, one triangle whose vertices sit at (-1,-1), (3,-1) and (-1,3). The clipped triangle covers the viewport exactly, so there is no diagonal seam and no doubly-shaded band where two triangles would meet. Pass any GLSL ES 3.00 fragment source and it runs against `v_uv`, `u_resolution`, `u_time` and `u_pointer`.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

One 3-vertex triangle covers the viewport and runs your fragment shader. No three, no ogl, no seam.

- Category: webgl
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. A single `Float32Array([-1,-1, 3,-1, -1,3])` is uploaded once as `STATIC_DRAW` and bound into a VAO. The vertex shader is `gl_Position = vec4(a_pos, 0.0, 1.0)` — the positions are already in clip space, so there is no model, view or projection matrix anywhere in the component.
2. `v_uv = a_pos * 0.5 + 0.5` gives uv 0..1 at the visible corners and uv 2.0 at the two overshooting vertices; the rasteriser clips the triangle to the viewport and interpolates the varying linearly, so the surviving fragments carry exactly the uv a two-triangle quad would have produced.
3. The context is requested with `antialias: false, depth: false, stencil: false, alpha: false` — a fullscreen pass has no polygon interiors to multisample and no depth to test, and every one of those buffers costs width x height x DPR bytes plus a resolve.
4. Uniform locations are resolved lazily and memoised in a `Map` keyed by name, because `getUniformLocation` is a synchronous driver round-trip and calling it per frame per uniform is the single most common cause of a raw-GL component being slower than a three.js one.
5. `u_pointer` is fed from `useSmoothPointer` with the y axis flipped (`1 - ny`), so the shader receives the same handedness as `gl_FragCoord`.
6. Resize writes `canvas.width/height` at `pixelRatio(maxDpr)` and calls `gl.viewport`, then draws one frame immediately — which is also the only draw that happens under reduced motion.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `TRIANGLE = [-1,-1, 3,-1, -1,3]`
  The minimum overshoot that still guarantees full coverage. With 1.0 instead of 3.0 you get a half-screen triangle; with 5.0 the uv range widens to 0..3 and any shader that assumes uv is 0..1 at the vertices misinterprets its own derivatives.
- `MAX_DPR = 2`
  Fragment count is quadratic in DPR. A fullscreen shader at DPR 3 costs 2.25x what it costs at 2 for no perceptible gain, and it is the usual reason a hero shader stutters on a phone but not on the laptop it was built on.
- `pointer smoothing = 0.002`
  Fraction of the pointer gap remaining after one second. Raw pointer coordinates arrive in 8-16 ms bursts and pushing them straight into a uniform makes the light jitter one pixel per event.

## API

```ts
function FullscreenTrianglePass(props: { fragment?: string; uniforms?: Record<string, number | readonly number[]>; speed?: number; maxDpr?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `fragment: string` — default `FULLSCREEN_TRIANGLE_FRAG`
  GLSL ES 3.00 fragment source. Must open with `#version 300 es` and declare an `out vec4`. Changing it relinks the program.
- `uniforms: Record<string, number | readonly number[]>`
  Extra uniforms pushed every frame. Numbers become `uniform1f`; arrays of length 2/3/4 become `uniform2f`/`3f`/`4f`.
- `speed: number` — default `1`
  Multiplier applied to `u_time`.
- `maxDpr: number` — default `2`
  Upper bound on device pixel ratio.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/* Two vertices outside the viewport, one at the origin corner. Anything larger
   than 3.0 also works; 3.0 is the minimum that guarantees full coverage. */
const TRIANGLE = new Float32Array([-1, -1, 3, -1, -1, 3]);
const MAX_DPR = 2;

interface Pass {
  gl: WebGL2RenderingContext;
  program: WebGLProgram;
  vao: WebGLVertexArrayObject;
  buffer: WebGLBuffer;
  locations: Map<string, WebGLUniformLocation | null>;
}

function compileShader(
  gl: WebGL2RenderingContext,
  type: number,
  source: string,
): WebGLShader | null {
  const shader = gl.createShader(type);
  if (!shader) return null;
  gl.shaderSource(shader, source);
  gl.compileShader(shader);
  if (!gl.getShaderParameter(shader, gl.COMPILE_STATUS)) {
    // Log rather than throw: a shader that fails to compile should degrade to
    // the static fallback, not take the whole React tree down with it.
    console.error('[fullscreen-triangle-pass]', gl.getShaderInfoLog(shader));
    gl.deleteShader(shader);
    return null;
  }
  return shader;
}

function createPass(gl: WebGL2RenderingContext, fragment: string): Pass | null {
  const vert = compileShader(gl, gl.VERTEX_SHADER, FULLSCREEN_TRIANGLE_VERT);
  const frag = compileShader(gl, gl.FRAGMENT_SHADER, fragment);
  const program = gl.createProgram();
  if (!vert || !frag || !program) {
    if (vert) gl.deleteShader(vert);
    if (frag) gl.deleteShader(frag);
    if (program) gl.deleteProgram(program);
    return null;
  }

  gl.attachShader(program, vert);
  gl.attachShader(program, frag);
  gl.linkProgram(program);
  // Safe to delete immediately after linking — the program holds a reference.
  gl.deleteShader(vert);
  gl.deleteShader(frag);

  if (!gl.getProgramParameter(program, gl.LINK_STATUS)) {
    console.error('[fullscreen-triangle-pass]', gl.getProgramInfoLog(program));
    gl.deleteProgram(program);
    return null;
  }

  const vao = gl.createVertexArray();
  const buffer = gl.createBuffer();
  if (!vao || !buffer) {
    gl.deleteProgram(program);
    return null;
  }

  gl.bindVertexArray(vao);
  gl.bindBuffer(gl.ARRAY_BUFFER, buffer);
  gl.bufferData(gl.ARRAY_BUFFER, TRIANGLE, gl.STATIC_DRAW);
  const attrib = gl.getAttribLocation(program, 'a_pos');
  if (attrib >= 0) {
    gl.enableVertexAttribArray(attrib);
    gl.vertexAttribPointer(attrib, 2, gl.FLOAT, false, 0, 0);
  }
  gl.bindVertexArray(null);

  return { gl, program, vao, buffer, locations: new Map() };
}

/** Uniform locations are stable for the life of a program — look up once. */
function uniformLocation(pass: Pass, name: string): WebGLUniformLocation | null {
  const cached = pass.locations.get(name);
  if (cached !== undefined) return cached;
  const found = pass.gl.getUniformLocation(pass.program, name);
  pass.locations.set(name, found);
  return found;
}

function setUniform(
  gl: WebGL2RenderingContext,
  location: WebGLUniformLocation | null,
  value: UniformValue,
): void {
  // Null means the uniform was optimised out because the shader never reads
  // it. Silently skipping is correct; calling uniform*f with null is a no-op
  // that some drivers log as an error every frame.
  if (location === null) return;
  if (typeof value === 'number') {
    gl.uniform1f(location, value);
    return;
  }
  const a = value[0] ?? 0;
  const b = value[1] ?? 0;
  const c = value[2] ?? 0;
  const d = value[3] ?? 0;
  if (value.length === 2) gl.uniform2f(location, a, b);
  else if (value.length === 3) gl.uniform3f(location, a, b, c);
  else if (value.length >= 4) gl.uniform4f(location, a, b, c, d);
  else gl.uniform1f(location, a);
}

function disposePass(pass: Pass): void {
  const { gl } = pass;
  gl.deleteVertexArray(pass.vao);
  gl.deleteBuffer(pass.buffer);
  gl.deleteProgram(pass.program);
  // dispose alone leaves the context alive; only the extension hands it back.
  loseContext(gl);
}

export function FullscreenTrianglePass({
  fragment = FULLSCREEN_TRIANGLE_FRAG,
  uniforms,
  speed = 1,
  maxDpr = MAX_DPR,
  className,
}: FullscreenTrianglePassProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const canvasRef = useRef<HTMLCanvasElement>(null);
  const passRef = useRef<Pass | null>(null);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const visible = useVisibility();
  const pointer = useSmoothPointer({ target: host, smoothing: 0.002 });
  const [supported, setSupported] = useState(true);

  // Held in refs so a changed uniform object never re-creates the program.
  const uniformsRef = useRef(uniforms);
  uniformsRef.current = uniforms;
  const speedRef = useRef(speed);
  speedRef.current = speed;

  const drawRef = useRef<(elapsed: number) => void>(() => {});
  drawRef.current = (elapsed: number) => {
    const pass = passRef.current;
    if (!pass) return;
    const { gl } = pass;

    gl.useProgram(pass.program);
    setUniform(gl, uniformLocation(pass, 'u_resolution'), [
      gl.drawingBufferWidth,
      gl.drawingBufferHeight,
    ]);
    setUniform(gl, uniformLocation(pass, 'u_time'), elapsed * speedRef.current);
    const p = pointer.current;
    // Flip y: DOM coordinates grow downward, gl_FragCoord grows upward.
    setUniform(gl, uniformLocation(pass, 'u_pointer'), [p.nx, 1 - p.ny]);

    const extra = uniformsRef.current;
    if (extra) {
      for (const name of Object.keys(extra)) {
        const value = extra[name];
        if (value !== undefined) setUniform(gl, uniformLocation(pass, name), value);
      }
    }

    gl.bindVertexArray(pass.vao);
    gl.drawArrays(gl.TRIANGLES, 0, 3);
    gl.bindVertexArray(null);
  };

  useEffect(() => {
    const canvas = canvasRef.current;
    if (!canvas) return;
    if (!hasWebGL()) {
      setSupported(false);
      return;
    }

    // `antialias: false` — a fullscreen pass has no polygon edges to smooth,
    // so MSAA buys nothing and costs a multisample resolve every frame.
    const gl = canvas.getContext('webgl2', {
      antialias: false,
      alpha: false,
      depth: false,
      stencil: false,
      powerPreference: 'high-performance',
    });
    if (!gl) {
      setSupported(false);
      return;
    }

    const pass = createPass(gl, fragment);
    if (!pass) {
      loseContext(gl);
      setSupported(false);
      return;
    }
    passRef.current = pass;
    setSupported(true);

    return () => {
      passRef.current = null;
      disposePass(pass);
    };
  }, [fragment]);

  // Resize and the static frame share one effect: whenever the backing store
  // changes we must redraw, and under reduced motion that redraw is the only
  // one that ever happens.
  useEffect(() => {
    const canvas = canvasRef.current;
    const pass = passRef.current;
    if (!canvas || !pass || width === 0 || height === 0) return;

    const dpr = pixelRatio(maxDpr);
    const w = Math.max(1, Math.round(width * dpr));
    const h = Math.max(1, Math.round(height * dpr));
    if (canvas.width !== w || canvas.height !== h) {
      canvas.width = w;
      canvas.height = h;
    }
    pass.gl.viewport(0, 0, w, h);
    drawRef.current(0);
  }, [width, height, maxDpr, supported, fragment]);

  const running = supported && visible && !reduced && width > 0 && height > 0;
  useRaf((_dt, elapsed) => drawRef.current(elapsed), running);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Deletes the VAO, the vertex buffer and the program, then calls `loseContext(gl)` to hand the WebGL context back to the browser. The rAF subscription unsubscribes with the hook. The effect is keyed on `fragment`, so a source change tears the old program down before building the new one rather than leaking it.

**Reduced motion.** The rAF subscription never starts. The pass still draws exactly one frame on mount and one on every resize, so you get a fully composed still image rather than a blank canvas — `u_time` is pinned to 0 and the pointer light sits wherever it was seeded.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Putting a newline, a comment, or a leading space before `#version 300 es`. The directive must be the first token in the source or the compile fails with "version directive must occur before anything else", and because the shader source lives in a template literal the offending newline is invisible in the diff.
- Drawing a quad out of two triangles. GPUs shade in 2x2 fragment quads, so every quad the shared diagonal crosses is rasterised by both triangles and those fragments are shaded twice — a band of pure waste down the diagonal. It also breaks `fwidth`/`dFdx` across the seam, which shows up as a visible hairline in any analytic-AA shader.
- Calling `gl.getUniformLocation` inside the render loop. It is a driver round-trip, not a hash lookup; the locations are constant for the life of the program, so resolve them once and cache them.
- Passing a uniform that the shader never reads. `getUniformLocation` returns `null` for anything the compiler optimised out, and `gl.uniform1f(null, x)` is a silent no-op that some drivers log to the console 60 times a second. Skip on null.
- Calling `renderer.dispose()` or just dropping the canvas and assuming the context is released. Only `WEBGL_lose_context.loseContext()` hands it back, and Chromium kills the OLDEST live context when a page exceeds roughly 16 — so a leaked context here makes an unrelated component elsewhere on the page go black.
- Throwing on a shader compile error. A syntax error in a user-supplied fragment then unmounts the entire React subtree; logging the info log and falling back to the static poster keeps the page alive and puts the actual error in the console.

## Notes

- WebGL2 only. GLSL ES 3.00 gives `in`/`out`, integer bit operators and core derivatives without an extension dance; WebGL2 is available in every browser that has shipped since 2021 except pre-15.4 Safari, which the `hasWebGL` guard catches.
- Everything else in the WebGL category that does not use three.js is built on this exact pass — it is the shared floor, not a demo.

## Definition of done

The grid fills the frame edge to edge with no lighter or darker band along either diagonal, and the fine grid brightens under the cursor. Resize the container and the grid stays square with hairlines exactly one pixel wide at any DPR. Unmount and `WEBGL_lose_context` fires — mount and unmount twenty times and the twenty-first still renders instead of going black.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: GPU Cubic-Bezier Burst

Concentric rings of dots turning slowly. Fire a sector — by clicking it, or by waiting for the automatic cycle — and its particles burst outward and fade, each one following its own cubic-bezier curve. The curve is the same four numbers CSS takes, but solved per vertex per frame by Newton's method, which is what lets two hundred particles carry two hundred different easings while the CPU only advances a clock.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Rings of dots that burst on click, every particle solving its own cubic-bezier easing in the vertex shader.

- Category: webgl
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1

## How it works

1. A cubic bezier is parametric: for a parameter `t` it gives a point `(x(t), y(t))`. Easing needs `y` at a given *x*, and a cubic has no closed-form inverse, so the shader runs Newton's method — 8 iterations of `t -= (x(t) - target) / x'(t)`, seeded with `t = x` because the curve is monotonic in x — then evaluates `y(t)`.
2. The four control numbers ride in an `aBezier` attribute rather than a uniform. That is the whole reason to solve on the GPU: a uniform would give every particle in the burst one shared easing, and per-particle easing computed on the CPU would mean a buffer upload every frame.
3. Firing writes the current burst-clock time into a contiguous slice of the `aStart` attribute — one sector, one range, one `needsUpdate`. Each particle then computes `age = uBurstTime - aStart - delay` and animates only while `0 <= age <= uBurstDuration`; a start time of 0 means never fired, which is why the clock starts at 1.
4. Resting dots and burst particles live in the same buffer and the same draw call, distinguished by an `isBurst` flag. Burst particles sit invisible on the outer ring until fired, rather than the resting dots being displaced — displacing them would tear a hole in the ring and then pop it shut when the burst ended.
5. There are two clocks. `uRotation` accumulates from delta time only when motion is allowed; `uBurstTime` always accumulates. Under reduced motion the ring freezes at 0.35 rad and the automatic cycle stops, but a click still fires a full burst, and the frame loop is subscribed only for as long as one is in flight.
6. Flight direction is `angle + uRotation`, evaluated live rather than baked, so a burst stays radial to the ring while the ring keeps turning underneath it. Alpha fades linearly against the eased flight, and point size shrinks to 45%, so the particle dissipates instead of blinking out at full size.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `NEWTON_ITERATIONS = 8`
  Newton converges quadratically here, so 4 iterations already land inside a pixel. 8 is cheap insurance for control points near 0 or 1, where the derivative shrinks and convergence slows.
- `MIN_DERIVATIVE = 0.000001`
  Newton divides by the derivative. A curve with a flat segment divides by ~0, `t` becomes NaN, and the NaN propagates into `gl_Position` — the vertex silently disappears rather than erroring.
- `base curve = (0, 0.9, 0.5, 1)`
  A hard ease-out: almost all the distance is covered in the first third. Each particle jitters around it, with x-coordinates clamped to 0..1 because the solver needs monotonicity in x — the same constraint CSS puts on `cubic-bezier()`.
- `MAX_LAUNCH_DELAY = 0.09s`
  Particles all leaving on one frame read as a single expanding ring. Staggering launches over ~90ms reads as a spray, and staying well under `burstDuration` keeps the last launch ahead of the first landing.
- `burstDuration = 0.45s`
  Longer than the 0.25s a click ping wants, because at preview-card size the eye needs the extra frames to actually see the easing differ between particles. Shorten it toward 0.25 when the burst is real button feedback.
- `BURST_END_SIZE = 0.45`
  Particles shrink to 45% over the flight. Constant-size particles read as confetti; shrinking ones read as one thing dissipating.
- `STATIC_ROTATION = 0.35 rad`
  Angle the ring is frozen at under reduced motion. Off-axis, so the field does not look like it snapped to a grid the moment motion was disabled.
- `RING_DOT_SCALE / BURST_DOT_SCALE = 0.7 / 1.15`
  Burst particles are visibly larger than the resting field, so the burst reads as the event rather than as the ring shedding pixels.
- `flight fan = +/- 0.175 rad`
  Jitter added to each particle's radial direction. Pure radial launches leave on rails and the burst looks like a line drawing; more than ~0.3 rad and the sectors start to overlap.

## API

```ts
function GpuBezierBurst(props: { ringCount?: number; ringDots?: number; innerRadius?: number; groups?: number; burstDots?: number; spinSpeed?: number; chordInterval?: number; burstDuration?: number; burstRadius?: number; dotScale?: number; viewScale?: number; opacity?: number; color?: string; burstColor?: string; seed?: number | string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `ringCount: number` — default `4`
  Concentric rings in the resting field.
- `ringDots: number` — default `190`
  Dots on the outermost ring; inner rings scale down to keep density even.
- `innerRadius: number` — default `0.55`
  Radius of the innermost ring as a fraction of the outermost.
- `groups: number` — default `6`
  Sectors that can be fired independently.
- `burstDots: number` — default `34`
  Burst particles per sector.
- `spinSpeed: number` — default `0.18`
  Ambient ring rotation in radians per second.
- `chordInterval: number` — default `1.5`
  Seconds between automatic firings.
- `burstDuration: number` — default `0.45`
  Seconds a single particle's flight lasts.
- `burstRadius: number` — default `26`
  How far a particle travels, in CSS pixels.
- `dotScale: number` — default `1`
  Dot radius multiplier in CSS pixels.
- `viewScale: number` — default `0.4`
  Model-to-pixel scale as a fraction of the container short side.
- `opacity: number` — default `1`
  Multiplier applied to every dot.
- `color: string` — default `'#6f757e'`
  Resting dot colour.
- `burstColor: string` — default `'#ffffff'`
  Colour mixed in at the hot start of a flight.
- `seed: number | string` — default `'gpu-bezier-burst'`
  Seeds every curve, delay and fan angle for a stable, hydration-safe field.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function GpuBezierBurst({
  ringCount = 4,
  ringDots = 190,
  innerRadius = 0.55,
  groups = 6,
  burstDots = 34,
  spinSpeed = 0.18,
  chordInterval = 1.5,
  burstDuration = 0.45,
  burstRadius = 26,
  dotScale = 1,
  viewScale = 0.4,
  opacity = 1,
  color = '#6f757e',
  burstColor = '#ffffff',
  seed = 'gpu-bezier-burst',
  className,
}: GpuBezierBurstProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const stage = useRef<Stage | null>(null);
  const [unsupported, setUnsupported] = useState(false);

  // Gates the frame loop under reduced motion: no ambient animation, but a
  // burst in flight still needs frames until it lands.
  const [burstLive, setBurstLive] = useState(false);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const size = useRef({ width, height });
  size.current = { width, height };

  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  // Read inside the frame loop rather than closed over, so toggling the OS
  // setting does not tear down and rebuild the GL context.
  const reducedRef = useRef(reduced);
  reducedRef.current = reduced;

  const ready = width > 0 && height > 0;

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = host.current;
    if (!el || !ready) return;

    if (!hasWebGL()) {
      setUnsupported(true);
      return;
    }

    const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: false, alpha: true });
    renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio());
    renderer.setClearAlpha(0);

    const scene = new THREE.Scene();
    const camera = new THREE.OrthographicCamera(-1, 1, 1, -1, 0.1, 10);
    camera.position.z = 1;

    const rng = createRng(seed);

    const positions: number[] = [];
    const burstData: number[] = [];
    const bezier: number[] = [];

    /* ------------------------------------------------------------------
       Resting rings. Dot count scales with radius so the inner rings are
       not visibly denser than the outer ones — constant dots-per-ring is
       the classic tell of a generated field.
       ------------------------------------------------------------------ */
    for (let r = 0; r < ringCount; r += 1) {
      const t = ringCount === 1 ? 1 : r / (ringCount - 1);
      const radius = innerRadius + (1 - innerRadius) * t;
      const count = Math.max(8, Math.round(ringDots * radius));

      for (let i = 0; i < count; i += 1) {
        const angle = (i / count) * Math.PI * 2 + rng() * 0.01;
        positions.push(Math.cos(angle) * radius, Math.sin(angle) * radius, 0);
        // isBurst 0: these never move, so flight angle, delay and curve are unused.
        burstData.push(0, angle, RING_DOT_SCALE, 0);
        bezier.push(0, 0, 1, 1);
      }
    }

    /* ------------------------------------------------------------------
       Burst particles, grouped into contiguous sectors so firing one is a
       single contiguous write into the start-time buffer. They sit on the
       outer ring invisible until fired: displacing the resting dots
       instead would leave a hole in the ring, then pop them back.
       ------------------------------------------------------------------ */
    const groupRanges: { start: number; end: number }[] = [];
    const restingDots = positions.length / 3;
    const sector = (Math.PI * 2) / groups;

    for (let g = 0; g < groups; g += 1) {
      const start = positions.length / 3;
      const centre = g * sector;

      for (let i = 0; i < burstDots; i += 1) {
        const angle = centre + (rng() - 0.5) * sector * 0.9;
        const radius = 0.94 + rng() * 0.06;
        positions.push(Math.cos(angle) * radius, Math.sin(angle) * radius, 0);
        burstData.push(
          1,
          // Flight direction fans slightly off pure radial, so the burst
          // spreads instead of leaving on rails.
          angle + (rng() - 0.5) * 0.35,
          BURST_DOT_SCALE,
          rng() * MAX_LAUNCH_DELAY,
        );

        /* Each particle gets its own curve, jittered around an ease-out
           (0, 0.9, 0.5, 1). x-coordinates are clamped to 0..1 because the
           solver needs the curve monotonic in x — exactly the constraint
           CSS puts on cubic-bezier(). y is free to overshoot. */
        bezier.push(
          Math.min(1, Math.max(0, rng() * 0.25)),
          0.9 + (rng() - 0.5) * 0.3,
          Math.min(1, Math.max(0, 0.5 + (rng() - 0.5) * 0.4)),
          0.95 + rng() * 0.1,
        );
      }
      groupRanges.push({ start, end: positions.length / 3 });
    }

    const total = positions.length / 3;
    const starts = new Float32Array(total);

    const geometry = new THREE.BufferGeometry();
    geometry.setAttribute('position', new THREE.BufferAttribute(Float32Array.from(positions), 3));
    geometry.setAttribute('aBurstData', new THREE.BufferAttribute(Float32Array.from(burstData), 4));
    geometry.setAttribute('aBezier', new THREE.BufferAttribute(Float32Array.from(bezier), 4));

    const startAttribute = new THREE.BufferAttribute(starts, 1);
    // The only buffer that changes at runtime, and only on a firing.
    startAttribute.setUsage(THREE.DynamicDrawUsage);
    geometry.setAttribute('aStart', startAttribute);

    const uniforms: Uniforms = {
      uBurstTime: { value: 0 },
      uRotation: { value: STATIC_ROTATION },
      uViewScale: { value: 1 },
      uPixelRatio: { value: renderer.getPixelRatio() },
      uDotScale: { value: dotScale },
      uOpacity: { value: opacity },
      uBurstDuration: { value: burstDuration },
      uBurstRadius: { value: burstRadius },
      uColor: { value: new THREE.Color(color) },
      uBurstColor: { value: new THREE.Color(burstColor) },
    };

    const material = new THREE.ShaderMaterial({
      vertexShader: GPU_BEZIER_BURST_VERT,
      fragmentShader: GPU_BEZIER_BURST_FRAG,
      uniforms,
      transparent: true,
      depthTest: false,
      depthWrite: false,
    });

    const points = new THREE.Points(geometry, material);
    // Vertices are unit-scale and the real placement happens in the shader, so
    // three's bounding sphere does not describe what is on screen.
    points.frustumCulled = false;
    scene.add(points);

    el.appendChild(renderer.domElement);
    renderer.domElement.style.display = 'block';
    renderer.domElement.style.width = '100%';
    renderer.domElement.style.height = '100%';

    /* -- the two clocks ------------------------------------------------ */
    let rotation = STATIC_ROTATION; // ambient; frozen under reduced motion
    let burstTime = 1; // feedback; always runs. Starts at 1 so a start
    //                    time of 0 can mean 'never fired'.
    let nextFire = chordInterval;
    let liveUntil = 0;
    let cursor = 0;

    const fire = (group: number) => {
      const range = groupRanges[group % groupRanges.length];
      if (!range) return;
      for (let i = range.start; i < range.end; i += 1) starts[i] = burstTime;
      startAttribute.needsUpdate = true;
      liveUntil = burstTime + burstDuration + MAX_LAUNCH_DELAY + 0.05;
      setBurstLive(true);
    };

    const render = () => renderer.render(scene, camera);

    const step = (dt: number) => {
      burstTime += dt;

      if (!reducedRef.current) {
        rotation += dt * spinSpeed;
        if (burstTime >= nextFire) {
          fire(cursor);
          cursor += 1;
          nextFire = burstTime + chordInterval;
        }
      } else if (burstTime > liveUntil) {
        // Nothing in flight and no ambient motion to draw: stand the loop
        // down. Idempotent, so this is safe to call every frame.
        setBurstLive(false);
      }

      uniforms.uRotation.value = rotation;
      uniforms.uBurstTime.value = burstTime;
      render();
    };

    const resize = (w: number, h: number) => {
      renderer.setSize(w, h, false);
      camera.left = -w / 2;
      camera.right = w / 2;
      camera.top = h / 2;
      camera.bottom = -h / 2;
      camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
      uniforms.uViewScale.value = Math.min(w, h) * viewScale;
      uniforms.uPixelRatio.value = renderer.getPixelRatio();
      render();
    };

    /* -- pointer: user-initiated, so it fires under reduced motion too -- */
    const onPointerDown = (event: PointerEvent) => {
      const rect = el.getBoundingClientRect();
      const x = event.clientX - rect.left - rect.width / 2;
      // Screen y grows downward, model y grows upward.
      const y = rect.height / 2 - (event.clientY - rect.top);
      // Undo the ambient rotation so the sector under the cursor is the one
      // that fires, not the one that was there before the ring turned.
      const angle = Math.atan2(y, x) - rotation;
      const normalised = ((angle % (Math.PI * 2)) + Math.PI * 2) % (Math.PI * 2);
      fire(Math.round(normalised / sector) % groups);
    };
    el.addEventListener('pointerdown', onPointerDown);

    resize(size.current.width, size.current.height);
    stage.current = { resize, step };

    return () => {
      stage.current = null;
      el.removeEventListener('pointerdown', onPointerDown);
      disposeObject(scene);
      material.dispose();
      disposeRenderer(renderer);
      renderer.domElement.remove();
    };
  }, [
    ready,
    ringCount,
    ringDots,
    innerRadius,
    groups,
    burstDots,
    spinSpeed,
    chordInterval,
    burstDuration,
    burstRadius,
    dotScale,
    viewScale,
    opacity,
    color,
    burstColor,
    seed,
  ]);

  useEffect(() => {
    stage.current?.resize(width, height);
  }, [width, height]);

  useRaf((dt) => stage.current?.step(dt), ready && !unsupported && (!reduced || burstLive));
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Removes the pointerdown listener, nulls the stage ref so a queued frame cannot touch a dead renderer, disposes the geometry via `disposeObject(scene)`, disposes the material, calls `disposeRenderer` for `dispose` + `forceContextLoss` + a zeroed backing store, and removes the canvas. `useRaf` unsubscribes on unmount, so a StrictMode double-invoke leaves no orphaned context.

**Reduced motion.** The ambient rotation freezes at 0.35 rad and the automatic firing cycle stops, so nothing moves unprompted. A pointer press still fires a full burst, because that is feedback for something the user did rather than decoration. The frame loop is subscribed only while a burst is actually in flight and unsubscribes as soon as the last particle lands, so the idle cost is zero.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Freezing the burst along with the ambient rotation under reduced motion. The component then stops answering clicks, which is a broken interface, not an accessible one — feedback for a user action is not decoration, hence the two separate clocks.
- Leaving the frame loop running under reduced motion to keep the burst alive. It burns a GPU-backed rAF forever for a static image; subscribe only while a burst is in flight and stand down when it lands.
- Passing the control points as a uniform. It compiles, it animates, and every particle in the burst moves identically — the effect collapses into one expanding ring and the GPU solve buys nothing.
- Omitting the derivative guard in the Newton loop. Certain control points produce a near-zero derivative, `t` goes NaN, and the affected vertices vanish with no error anywhere — the symptom is a burst that is missing particles at some curves and not others.
- Displacing the resting ring dots instead of using dedicated burst particles. The ring develops a gap for the duration of the burst and snaps shut at the end.
- Baking the flight direction at fire time. The ring keeps rotating during the 0.45s flight, so the particles visibly drift off-radial and appear to curve away from their launch point.
- Sizing burst radius in model units. It then scales with the container, and the burst that felt right on a large canvas barely leaves the ring on a small preview card — pixels are the right unit for an effect this small.

## Notes

- One draw call and one buffer for the resting field and every burst particle. The only runtime upload is the start-time attribute, written once per firing rather than once per frame.
- Clicking maps the pointer angle back through the current rotation, so the sector under the cursor is the one that fires.
- The automatic cycle exists so the component reads as alive in a preview grid; drop `chordInterval` handling if the burst is wired to real user actions.

## Definition of done

Concentric rings of dots turn slowly. Roughly every 1.5 seconds one sector throws a spray of brighter particles outward that fade as they travel, and the particles visibly do not move in lockstep — some shoot ahead and settle, others trail. Clicking a sector fires it immediately. The ring never develops a gap where a burst came from. With reduced motion the ring is still and nothing fires on its own, but a click still produces a full burst.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: GSAP Cursor Follower

A container hides its native cursor and draws its own: a small disc that lags the pointer by a settling tween, and swells into a labelled puck whenever it passes over an element marked `data-cursor-target`. The lag comes from GSAP rather than from a damped rAF loop, which is why the disc comes to rest when the pointer stops instead of asymptoting toward it forever.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A puck that replaces the arrow inside a panel, trailing 0.4s behind and swelling to a label over targets.

- Category: cursor
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. On mount the puck is centred on its own coordinates with `gsap.set(circle, { xPercent: -50, yPercent: -50 })` and the positioning wrapper is parked at `x: -999, y: -999`. From then on the follow tween writes raw x/y and the centring composes into the same matrix, so there is no per-move offset arithmetic and exactly one composited transform per node.
2. Every `pointermove` issues `gsap.to(wrapper, { x: e.clientX - rect.left, y: e.clientY - rect.top, duration, ease: "power2.out", overwrite: "auto" })`. `overwrite: "auto"` retires the previous tween so the ~120 events a second do not accumulate into ~120 concurrent tweens writing the same transform.
3. This is deliberately GSAP smoothing rather than `useSmoothPointer`. A tween re-eases from its current velocity to a *rest* at the target, so the puck decelerates into stillness the instant the pointer stops; an exponential `damp` never actually arrives. Reach for the damped hook when you want a value that is permanently chasing, and for this when you want it to settle.
4. `pointerenter` teleports first (`duration: 0`) and only then fades in, so re-entering the panel does not drag a visible streak across it from wherever the puck was last parked.
5. The hover state is delegated: one handler runs `e.target.closest("[data-cursor-target]")` per move and compares the result with the previous state, tweening `scale` on the disc and `autoAlpha`/`scale` on the label only on the transition. Scale — not width/height — keeps the resize on the compositor with no layout pass.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `PARK = -999`
  Initial x/y. The element exists from first paint but must be *nowhere*; at 0,0 it flashes in the top-left corner for the frames between mount and the first pointer event.
- `duration = 0.4`
  Seconds of catch-up. Below ~0.2 the puck is welded to the pointer and the trailing read disappears; past ~0.7 it feels detached from the hand and users start chasing it.
- `size = 16`
  Resting diameter. Small enough to point precisely with, large enough to see against a busy panel. Applied as `scale: size / targetSize` so only the transform changes.
- `targetSize = 112`
  Diameter over a target. It has to hold a short label at 14px with real breathing room — under ~90 the text touches the circle edge and the puck reads as a broken badge.
- `RESIZE_DURATION = 0.45`
  The swell. With `expo.out` this is almost all its motion in the first 120ms, which is what makes the state change feel like a snap rather than an inflation.
- `FADE_DURATION = 0.3`
  Enter/leave opacity. Fast enough that the puck is present before the user has moved a meaningful distance into the panel.

## API

```ts
function CursorFollower(props: { children: ReactNode; label?: string; duration?: number; size?: number; targetSize?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Panel content. Anything inside carrying `data-cursor-target` triggers the labelled state.
- `label: string` — default `'View'`
  Text revealed inside the puck over a target.
- `duration: number` — default `0.4`
  Seconds of catch-up on the follow tween.
- `size: number` — default `16`
  Resting diameter in px.
- `targetSize: number` — default `112`
  Diameter over a target, in px. Also the disc's laid-out size.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root container via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** Far outside any container, so the puck is nowhere until a pointer exists. */
const PARK = -999;
const FADE_DURATION = 0.3;
const RESIZE_DURATION = 0.45;

export function CursorFollower({
  children,
  label = 'View',
  duration = 0.4,
  size = 16,
  targetSize = 112,
  className,
}: CursorFollowerProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const wrap = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const disc = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const text = useRef<HTMLSpanElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = root.current;
    const point = wrap.current;
    const circle = disc.current;
    const caption = text.current;
    if (!el || !point || !circle || !caption) return;

    // A coarse pointer has no hover state, so the puck could only ever exist
    // between pointerdown and pointerup — and `cursor: none` on a touch device
    // hides nothing while still suppressing the text-selection caret.
    if (!window.matchMedia('(pointer: fine)').matches) return;

    const reduced = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;
    const follow = reduced ? 0 : duration;
    const fade = reduced ? 0 : FADE_DURATION;
    const resize = reduced ? 0 : RESIZE_DURATION;

    // Centre both layers on their own coordinates once. After this the follow
    // tween writes raw x/y and the centring composes into the same matrix —
    // no offset arithmetic per move, and one composited transform per node.
    gsap.set(point, { x: PARK, y: PARK, autoAlpha: 0 });
    gsap.set(circle, { xPercent: -50, yPercent: -50, scale: size / targetSize });
    gsap.set(caption, { xPercent: -50, yPercent: -50, autoAlpha: 0, scale: 0.5 });

    // The puck *replaces* the arrow rather than accompanying it. Set from JS,
    // not from the class list, so a touch device never loses its cursor.
    const previousCursor = el.style.cursor;
    el.style.cursor = 'none';

    let overTarget = false;

    const place = (e: PointerEvent, instant: boolean) => {
      // Live rect: the container can scroll, resize, or be inside a
      // transformed ancestor. A rect cached on mount puts the puck at a
      // constant offset from the real pointer as soon as anything moves.
      const rect = el.getBoundingClientRect();
      gsap.to(point, {
        x: e.clientX - rect.left,
        y: e.clientY - rect.top,
        duration: instant ? 0 : follow,
        ease: 'power2.out',
        // Each move REPLACES the last tween instead of queueing behind it.
        // Without it, ~120 events a second means ~120 live 0.4s tweens all
        // writing the same transform, and the puck visibly stutters.
        overwrite: 'auto',
      });
    };

    const onEnter = (e: PointerEvent) => {
      // Teleport on entry, then fade in. Tweening from wherever the puck was
      // parked draws a visible streak diagonally across the panel every time
      // the pointer re-enters.
      place(e, true);
      gsap.to(point, { autoAlpha: 1, duration: fade, ease: 'power2.out', overwrite: 'auto' });
    };

    const onMove = (e: PointerEvent) => {
      place(e, false);

      const hit =
        e.target instanceof Element ? e.target.closest('[data-cursor-target]') : null;
      const next = hit !== null;
      // Only tween on the transition. Re-firing the same resize tween on every
      // move restarts its ease and the puck never reaches the target size.
      if (next === overTarget) return;
      overTarget = next;

      gsap.to(circle, {
        scale: next ? 1 : size / targetSize,
        duration: resize,
        ease: 'expo.out',
        overwrite: 'auto',
      });
      gsap.to(caption, {
        autoAlpha: next ? 1 : 0,
        scale: next ? 1 : 0.5,
        duration: resize,
        ease: 'expo.out',
        overwrite: 'auto',
      });
    };

    const onLeave = () => {
      gsap.to(point, { autoAlpha: 0, duration: fade, ease: 'power2.out', overwrite: 'auto' });
    };

    el.addEventListener('pointerenter', onEnter);
    el.addEventListener('pointermove', onMove, { passive: true });
    el.addEventListener('pointerleave', onLeave);

    return () => {
      el.removeEventListener('pointerenter', onEnter);
      el.removeEventListener('pointermove', onMove);
      el.removeEventListener('pointerleave', onLeave);
      el.style.cursor = previousCursor;
      // Kill before clearing, or an in-flight tween writes the transform
      // straight back onto a node React has already recycled.
      gsap.killTweensOf([point, circle, caption]);
      gsap.set([point, circle, caption], { clearProps: 'all' });
    };
  }, [duration, size, targetSize]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Removes the three container listeners, restores the container's previous inline `cursor`, calls `gsap.killTweensOf` on the wrapper, disc and label, then `gsap.set(..., { clearProps: "all" })`. Kill precedes clear so no in-flight tween can write the transform back after React has recycled the node.

**Reduced motion.** The puck still appears and still swells over targets — the affordance is preserved — but every duration collapses to 0, so it is welded to the pointer with no trailing lag and the size change is a hard cut. The native cursor stays hidden, because a container with no cursor at all would be worse than one that moves.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Calling `gsap.to` per pointermove without `overwrite: "auto"`. Sixty to a hundred and twenty 0.4s tweens end up live at once, all writing the same transform, and the puck stutters instead of gliding — the single most common way this effect is got wrong.
- Fading in without teleporting first. On every re-entry the puck tweens from its parked coordinates, drawing a diagonal streak across the whole panel before it reaches the pointer.
- Re-issuing the resize tween on every move instead of only on the hover transition. Each call restarts the `expo.out` ease from the beginning, so the puck creeps toward the target size and never gets there while the pointer keeps moving.
- Transitioning `width` and `height` for the swell. That is a layout write per frame on an element the compositor could otherwise leave alone; `scale` on a fixed-size disc is the same picture for free.
- Caching the container rect on mount. The panel scrolls, resizes, and may sit inside a transformed ancestor — a stale rect offsets the puck from the real pointer by a constant amount that never corrects itself.
- Putting `cursor: none` in the class list. It then applies on touch devices too, where it hides nothing but does suppress the text-selection caret; setting it from the effect means it only ever exists where the puck does.

## Notes

- Gated on `(pointer: fine)`. On touch nothing attaches: no listeners, no `cursor: none`, and the puck stays at `autoAlpha: 0` parked off-container, so a tap does not flash a disc at the touch point.
- Mark any element inside with `data-cursor-target` to trigger the labelled state — including elements nested arbitrarily deep, since the check is a `closest()` walk.
- The root sets `isolate`, so the puck stacks above the panel content without needing a page-level z-index.

## Definition of done

Move into the panel: the arrow disappears and a small disc arrives at the pointer without sweeping in from an edge, then trails about 0.4s behind as you move. Pass over a marked target and it swells into a labelled puck; leave and it shrinks back. Stop moving and it comes fully to rest rather than creeping. On a touch device the native cursor and all default behaviour are untouched.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Height-First Media Stage

Almost every media stage on the web is sized width-first: a full-width box with an aspect ratio and whatever height falls out of it. On a short laptop that makes a 3:2 hero taller than the viewport, so the piece built to be seen at a glance has to be scrolled. This inverts the constraint — the height is authored, the width is derived from it through `aspect-ratio`, and `max-width: 100%` is the only escape hatch. The stage always fits vertically, and on a narrow screen it gives up size rather than overflowing. Layers cross-fade on opacity alone; the only JavaScript is the index.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A media stage sized from its height, with the width derived from the ratio, cross-fading layers and a caption that replays per index.

- Category: layout
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The figure gets exactly three sizing declarations: `height` (authored, e.g. `min(80dvh, 100%)`), `aspect-ratio` (which derives the width from that height), and `max-width: 100%`. No width is ever set — setting one would over-constrain the box and `aspect-ratio` would be ignored.
2. When the derived width would exceed the container, `max-width: 100%` clamps it and the ratio then pulls the *height* down to match. That single line is what turns "always fits vertically" into "always fits", with no media query and no measurement.
3. The default height is `min(80dvh, 100%)`: `dvh` so a collapsing mobile URL bar cannot make the stage overflow, and the `100%` term so the same component also behaves inside a bounded parent instead of insisting on a fraction of the viewport.
4. Every layer stays mounted, absolutely positioned in the same stacking context, and only `opacity` changes — from 0 to 1 on the incoming layer and back on the outgoing one, with `pointer-events: none` on the hidden ones so an invisible layer cannot swallow clicks meant for the visible one.
5. The cross-fade transition is `linear`, not eased. Two layers whose opacities are each eased sum to less than 1 halfway through, and the stage visibly dips darker mid-transition; linear keeps the sum at exactly 1 throughout.
6. The caption wrapper carries `key={current}`, so changing index unmounts it and mounts a fresh node. A CSS entrance animation that has never run on a node plays from 0%, which is how the caption re-enters on every change without any JavaScript replay logic.
7. The keyframes live in a scoped `<style href="..." precedence="medium">`. React 19 hoists it into the head and deduplicates by `href`, so ten mounted stages inject one copy and nothing has to be added to a global sheet.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `height = 'min(80dvh, 100%)'`
  80% of the *dynamic* viewport height leaves room for a header and the top of the next section, so the stage reads as part of a page rather than as a takeover. `dvh` rather than `vh` because on iOS Safari `vh` is the URL-bar-collapsed height, so `80vh` overflows the actually visible area at rest. The `min(..., 100%)` term keeps it correct inside a bounded parent.
- `aspectRatio = '3 / 2'`
  Wider than the 80dvh height on any landscape display, so the width clamp is the binding constraint on desktop and the height clamp binds on a phone — both paths are exercised by the default. A ratio taller than the height would make the stage narrower than its own caption row.
- `duration = 500`
  Milliseconds of cross-fade. Under ~250ms the two layers read as a cut and the point of stacking them is lost; past ~800ms both layers are legible at once for long enough to look like a rendering fault.
- `caption entrance = 500ms cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1), translateY(14px)`
  Matched to the cross-fade duration so caption and image resolve together. 14px is roughly one line of the caption type — enough travel to read as arrival, small enough that the text is never legible in the wrong place.
- `cross-fade easing = linear`
  Not a stylistic choice. Any easing applied to both layers makes their opacities sum to less than 1 in the middle of the transition, and the stage flashes darker halfway through every change.

## API

```ts
function HeightFirstMediaStage(props: { children: ReactNode; height?: string; aspectRatio?: string; duration?: number; caption?: (index: number) => ReactNode; index?: number; defaultIndex?: number; onIndexChange?: (index: number) => void; className?: string; 'aria-label'?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  One media layer per child. All layers stay mounted and stacked.
- `height: string` — default `'min(80dvh, 100%)'`
  Authored height as a CSS length. The width is derived from it — never set a width here.
- `aspectRatio: string` — default `'3 / 2'`
  Ratio the derived width follows, as a CSS `aspect-ratio` value.
- `duration: number` — default `500`
  Cross-fade duration in milliseconds.
- `caption: (index: number) => ReactNode`
  Rendered into a node re-keyed on every index change, so its entrance keyframe replays.
- `index: number`
  Controlled index. Omit for uncontrolled behaviour.
- `defaultIndex: number` — default `0`
  Starting index when uncontrolled.
- `onIndexChange: (index: number) => void`
  Called with the wrapped index after either control is used.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the centring wrapper via `cn`.
- `aria-label: string` — default `'Media stage'`
  Accessible name for the figure group.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * Scoped stylesheet. React 19 hoists and deduplicates it by `href`, so the
 * keyframe exists once no matter how many stages are mounted and nothing has
 * to be added to a global sheet.
 *
 * The class exists only so a `key` change can restart it: React unmounts the
 * old caption node and mounts a new one, the animation has never run on that
 * node, so it plays from 0%. Toggling a class on a persistent node would not
 * work — the animation would have to be removed for a frame first.
 */
const STAGE_CSS = `
@keyframes k-hfms-in {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(14px); }
  to   { opacity: 1; transform: translateY(0); }
}

.k-hfms-in {
  animation: k-hfms-in 500ms cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1) both;
}

/* The caption's content is the information; its arrival is decoration. */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .k-hfms-in { animation: none; }
}
`;
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to release. There are no listeners, no rAF, no timers and no observers: the cross-fade and the caption entrance are both CSS on the elements themselves, so they die with the nodes. React 19 reference-counts the hoisted `<style>` and removes it when the last stage unmounts.

**Reduced motion.** The layer transition is set to `none`, so an index change is an instant cut between two fully opaque layers rather than a zero-length fade. The caption entrance is disabled by a `prefers-reduced-motion` block inside the scoped stylesheet, so the caption appears immediately at its final position and full opacity — the information still arrives, only its arrival is dropped. Sizing behaviour is identical either way.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Sizing width-first — `w-full` plus `aspect-ratio` — which is the common shape. On a 13" laptop the derived height exceeds the viewport, so the hero has to be scrolled to be seen and the layout silently breaks on exactly the machines designers use.
- Setting a width as well as the height. The box is then over-constrained, `aspect-ratio` is discarded, and the stage quietly stops being the ratio you asked for while still looking plausible in your own window.
- Using `vh` instead of `dvh`. On mobile Safari `100vh` is the tall viewport with the browser chrome hidden, so a stage sized against it overflows the visible area until the user scrolls — which is the exact failure this layout exists to prevent.
- Easing the opacity transition. Both layers dim toward the middle, their sum drops below 1, and the stage visibly darkens on every change. It looks like a dropped frame and is very hard to attribute to the easing curve.
- Mounting only the current layer. Each change then pays a fresh decode and paint, so the first frame of the incoming layer is empty and the transition starts from blank instead of from the outgoing image.
- Replaying the caption entrance by toggling a class on a persistent node. The animation is already applied, so re-adding the class does nothing — you would have to remove it, force a reflow, then re-add. Changing `key` remounts the node instead, and the animation runs because on that node it never has.
- Wrapping the index with `%`. In JavaScript `-1 % 5` is `-1`, so pressing Previous on the first item indexes past the start and the stage goes blank. `wrapIndex` uses a true modulo.
- Leaving hidden layers hittable. At `opacity: 0` a layer still receives pointer events and sits on top of the visible one, so links and buttons in the current layer stop responding.
- Putting the keyframes in a plain inline `<style>` with no `href`. Every mounted stage then injects its own copy of the same rule into the document.

## Notes

- Uncontrolled by default via `defaultIndex`, controlled when `index` is passed — in controlled mode the internal state is never written, so the parent stays the single source of truth.
- The figure is marked `role="group"` with `aria-roledescription="carousel"`, and non-current layers are `aria-hidden`, so a screen reader is offered one media layer at a time rather than all of them stacked.
- The only content this component draws itself is the counter and the controls; the layers are children, so it composes with a canvas, a video, a CSS gradient, or a Lottie without knowing which.

## Definition of done

Shorten the viewport to about 600px tall and the stage shrinks with it — no vertical scrollbar appears and no part of the media is cut off. Narrow the window until the derived width would exceed the container and the stage gives up height instead of clipping sideways. Press Next and the layers cross-fade with no dark dip halfway through, and the caption rises 14px into place on every change including the wrap from the last item back to the first. Press Previous on the first item and it lands on the last, not on a blank stage. Enable reduced motion and the change becomes an instant cut with the caption already in place.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Hinged Container Intro

A page-enter that tips its container up from below the fold like a lid rather than sliding it in. The panel starts at 120% of its own height, rotated -45deg in X about its bottom edge, and lands over 1.4s on expo.out; captions inside it stagger in starting 0.6s before it arrives. A cue fires at 0.8s so an expensive scene can start while the panel is still in flight.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

The page body swings up from below the fold, hinged on its own bottom edge, with captions following it in.

- Category: transition
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. A wrapper carries `perspective: 1200px` and the panel inside it gets `transformOrigin: "center bottom"` plus `transformPerspective`, so the rotation pivots on the edge the panel is about to rest on and the top edge sweeps a much longer arc than the bottom.
2. The panel tween is `fromTo(el, { yPercent: 120, rotateX: -45, opacity: 0 }, { yPercent: 0, rotateX: 0, opacity: 1, duration: 1.4, ease: "expo.out" })`. `yPercent` rather than a viewport unit means the same component works inside a 320px card and a full-bleed layout without re-tuning.
3. Elements matching `detailSelector` are collected with `querySelectorAll` on the panel and appended at `"-=0.6"`, so their 0.9s stagger overlaps the tail of the flight and the two moves read as one gesture.
4. A `tl.call(cue, undefined, 0.8)` sits at an absolute timeline position, so the cue stays at 0.8s even if either tween is retimed. That is where a WebGL scene, a video `play()`, or a data fetch is kicked off — mid-flight, while the eye is on the moving panel.
5. The whole timeline is built inside `useGsap`, keyed on `routeKey`; a key change reverts the previous context (restoring the inline styles GSAP wrote) and builds a fresh timeline from frame zero.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `duration = 1.4`
  Panel flight in seconds. Under ~1.1s the expo.out tail is too short to read as deceleration and the panel appears to snap; over ~1.8s the visitor is waiting on chrome before they can read anything.
- `tilt = -45`
  Degrees of X rotation at the start. At -20deg the perspective foreshortening is barely visible so it looks like a plain slide; past about -70deg the panel is nearly edge-on and its content is an unreadable sliver for most of the flight.
- `travel = 120`
  Percent of the panel's own height it starts below rest. 100 would put its top edge exactly at the bottom of its box, but the rotation lifts the top edge upward, so 100 lets a corner peek in at frame zero. The extra 20% covers the rotated bounding box.
- `perspective = 1200`
  Pixels. Around 600 the lens is wide enough that the panel visibly skews toward one corner; above ~2000 the projection is near-orthographic and the hinge stops reading as depth.
- `DETAIL_OVERLAP = 0.6`
  Seconds the caption stagger starts before the panel lands. At 0 the two moves read as two separate events with a dead beat between them; beyond ~0.9 the captions are moving while the panel is still steeply rotated and the text shears.
- `DETAIL_STAGGER = 0.1`
  Seconds between captions. Fast enough that three to five items finish inside the panel tween, slow enough that each is individually perceptible.
- `sceneCue = 0.8`
  Seconds into the timeline before the heavy cue fires. Late enough that the panel has visually committed to arriving (so a first-frame stall is hidden by motion), early enough that a 1.6s scene intro finishes about 1s after the panel lands rather than long after.

## API

```ts
function HingedContainerIntro(props: { children: ReactNode; routeKey?: string; duration?: number; tilt?: number; travel?: number; perspective?: number; detailSelector?: string; onSceneCue?: () => void; sceneCue?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Page body. Rendered inside the hinging panel.
- `routeKey: string`
  Change to replay. Pass `usePathname()` in an App Router layout.
- `duration: number` — default `1.4`
  Panel flight time in seconds.
- `tilt: number` — default `-45`
  Starting X rotation in degrees.
- `travel: number` — default `120`
  Starting offset as a percentage of the panel's own height.
- `perspective: number` — default `1200`
  Perspective on the wrapper, in pixels.
- `detailSelector: string` — default `'[data-hinge-detail]'`
  Descendants that stagger in behind the panel.
- `onSceneCue: () => void`
  Called `sceneCue` seconds in. Start expensive work here.
- `sceneCue: number` — default `0.8`
  Absolute timeline position of the cue, in seconds.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the perspective wrapper.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function HingedContainerIntro({
  children,
  routeKey,
  duration = 1.4,
  tilt = -45,
  travel = 120,
  perspective = 1200,
  detailSelector = '[data-hinge-detail]',
  onSceneCue,
  sceneCue = 0.8,
  className,
}: HingedContainerIntroProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const panel = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  // Held in a ref so a caller passing an inline arrow does not have to
  // memoise it to avoid replaying the whole intro on every parent render.
  const cue = useRef(onSceneCue);
  cue.current = onSceneCue;

  useGsap(
    gsap,
    () => {
      const el = panel.current;
      if (!el || reduced) return;

      const details = Array.from(el.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>(detailSelector));
      const tl = gsap.timeline({ defaults: { ease: 'expo.out' } });

      // transformOrigin bottom + negative rotateX is the whole trick: the
      // panel pivots on the edge it is about to sit on, so the top edge
      // travels much further than the bottom and the move reads as a hinge
      // instead of a translation with a tilt bolted on.
      tl.fromTo(
        el,
        {
          yPercent: travel,
          rotateX: tilt,
          opacity: 0,
          transformOrigin: 'center bottom',
          transformPerspective: perspective,
        },
        { yPercent: 0, rotateX: 0, opacity: 1, duration },
      );

      // Guarded: GSAP logs "target not found" for an empty array, and a
      // component that warns on every mount trains people to ignore the
      // console.
      if (details.length > 0) {
        tl.fromTo(
          details,
          { opacity: 0, y: 30 },
          { opacity: 1, y: 0, duration: DETAIL_DURATION, stagger: DETAIL_STAGGER },
          `-=${DETAIL_OVERLAP}`,
        );
      }

      // A number position is absolute on the timeline, so the cue stays at
      // 0.8 s no matter how the two tweens above are retimed.
      tl.call(
        () => {
          cue.current?.();
        },
        undefined,
        sceneCue,
      );
    },
    root,
    [routeKey, reduced],
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useGsap` reverts the `gsap.context` on unmount and on every `routeKey` change, which kills the timeline and restores the inline styles GSAP wrote to the panel and captions. The cue callback lives in a ref that React discards with the component, so a call queued at 0.8s cannot reach a stale closure.

**Reduced motion.** No timeline is built. A `prefers-reduced-motion` rule in the component's own stylesheet cancels the `opacity: 0` start state, so the panel and its captions render in their final position immediately, and `onSceneCue` fires on mount so anything it gates still loads.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Setting the start state only inside the effect. `useEffect` can run after the browser has painted, so the finished page flashes for one frame and then jumps below the fold. The start state is a CSS rule on `[data-hinged-panel]`; the reduced-motion branch of that same rule is what keeps the content from depending on JS at all.
- Rotating without `transformOrigin: "center bottom"`. About the centre the panel appears to tumble through its own resting position, and the bottom edge dips below the fold on the way in.
- Putting `perspective` on the panel instead of an ancestor. Then any transformed child gets its own vanishing point and the parallax between panel and captions is wrong at the edges.
- Positioning the cue with a relative `"-=0.6"` string. Retiming the panel tween silently moves the cue with it; a numeric position pins it to 0.8s absolute.
- Firing the cue only in the animated branch. Reduced-motion users then never get the scene, the video or the fetch it was gating — the cue is content delivery, not decoration.
- Passing an inline arrow as `onSceneCue` and putting it in the effect deps. Every parent render rebuilds the timeline and the intro restarts mid-flight; the callback is held in a ref instead.

## Notes

- App Router wiring: render this inside `app/layout.tsx` around `{children}` and pass `routeKey={usePathname()}`. The component itself never imports a router, so the same file works in Pages Router, Remix, or a modal keyed on a record id.
- The cue is not a substitute for a load event. If the thing it starts can fail, give it its own timeout — see `safe-preloader` for the ceiling pattern.

## Definition of done

On mount the panel rises from below with its top edge visibly further away than its bottom, settles without overshoot, and the captions land about a third of a second later. Switching route replays it from frame zero with no flash of the previous content. With reduced motion on, the panel is simply there, and the cue still fires.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
