# Build: Hover List Image Trail

Each row entered adds a plate to a column beside the list, and the column follows the pointer vertically with `quickTo`. Every plate is a masked-reveal pair — a clipping wrapper sliding up while the canvas inside slides down — and the stack is bounded by culling the oldest node rather than by pooling.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Hovering a row stacks a plate into a column that follows the pointer; the oldest is culled past twenty.

- Category: cursor
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. The spawn is two elements on one tween, moving in opposite directions. The wrapper animates `yPercent` from 100 to 0 while the canvas inside it animates from -100 to 0, on the same duration and the same ease. Because the wrapper clips, the two motions cancel and the plate is uncovered in place instead of flying in — the difference between a card arriving and a card being developed.
2. The cancellation only holds if both tweens share duration and ease exactly. Any mismatch and the plate visibly slides inside its own frame, which reads as a parallax bug rather than a reveal.
3. A node is created per hover and the stack is bounded by a cull, which is the deliberate opposite of `pooled-image-trail`. That is affordable here because hover entry is bounded by how fast a human can cross rows — roughly ten a second at worst — where a pointermove trail is bounded by the display refresh rate. The choice between pooling and culling follows from the event arrival rate, not from taste.
4. Every spawn drops the oldest node once the stack holds twenty, so the DOM has a hard ceiling at all times rather than a ceiling per interaction. Tweens are killed before removal so GSAP cannot write to a node the DOM has already released.
5. The column is centred on the pointer once with `gsap.set(stack, { yPercent: -50 })`, so the follow tween writes a raw `y` and never subtracts a half-height it would have to re-measure. A single `quickTo` at 0.5s with `power4` gives a long, heavy tail: `power4` spends most of its time near the destination, so the column snaps toward the pointer and then settles.
6. Plates are painted once into offscreen canvases at mount and blitted with a single `drawImage` on spawn, so no gradient, sheen or text work lands on the frame where a tween starts — the one frame that cannot afford it. There are no image assets and nothing allocated through `createObjectURL`, so nothing needs revoking.
7. `pointerover` bubbles, so one listener covers every row however React re-renders the list, but it also fires again for each descendant crossed inside the same row. The spawn is therefore gated on `relatedTarget` being outside the row, which turns "the event fired" into "the pointer actually changed rows".

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `MAX_PLATES = 20`
  Hard ceiling on live plates. Enough that a quick scan down a list leaves a visible stack with depth; low enough that twenty composited layers of 168x116 stay trivial. Remove this and an idle user running the pointer up and down the list allocates for as long as the page is open.
- `REVEAL_DURATION = 0.6`
  Seconds for the masked pair. Long for a hover response, deliberately: the reveal is the content of the interaction, not feedback about it. Below ~0.35 the opposite-direction pair is too fast to read as a reveal and just looks like a fade.
- `ease: 'expo.inOut' = expo.inOut`
  The most extreme standard curve, and the reason the reveal reads as mechanical rather than soft. Nearly all the travel happens in the middle third, so the plate is still at the start of its move, then has arrived, with very little visible in between.
- `followDuration = 0.5`
  Seconds of catch-up on the column. Longer than a cursor follow because the column is a heavy object carrying several plates; at 0.2 it is welded to the pointer and the stack stops feeling like it has mass.
- `follow ease 'power4' = power4 (in-out)`
  A very late curve, so the column covers the gap early and creeps the last few pixels. quickTo remutates the end value on every event, so an in-out curve absorbs direction changes instead of restarting an outward ramp each time.
- `PLATE_SCALE = 2`
  Backing-store multiplier for the offscreen plates. Fixed rather than `devicePixelRatio` so the drawn output is byte-identical on every machine and a screenshot diff of this component is meaningful.
- `hue step = 137.508 degrees`
  The golden angle. Consecutive plates are always far apart in hue and the sequence never repeats a near-duplicate, so a fast scan down the list never stacks two plates that read as the same colour.
- `monotonic zIndex = order += 1, never reset`
  A later plate must always sit above an earlier one. Reusing or resetting the counter lets two live plates tie, and tied z-indices resolve by DOM order, which changes as the cull removes nodes — the observable symptom is a plate flickering behind one that arrived before it.

## API

```ts
function HoverListImageTrail(props: { rows: TrailRow[]; tileWidth?: number; tileHeight?: number; followDuration?: number; seed?: string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `rows: TrailRow[]`
  List rows. `{ id, label, meta? }`; one plate is painted per row at mount.
- `tileWidth: number` — default `168`
  Plate width in CSS px.
- `tileHeight: number` — default `116`
  Plate height in CSS px.
- `followDuration: number` — default `0.5`
  Seconds of catch-up on the column follow.
- `seed: string` — default `'hover-list-image-trail'`
  Seeds the plate palette. Same seed, same colours, every render.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root container via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const PLATE_SCALE = 2;
/** Hard ceiling on live plates. Every spawn past this drops the oldest. */
const MAX_PLATES = 20;
const REVEAL_DURATION = 0.6;

/**
 * Plates are painted once into offscreen canvases and blitted on spawn. No
 * image assets, and — more importantly — no gradient, text or shadow work on
 * the frame where a tween starts, which is exactly the frame that cannot
 * afford it.
 */
function paintPlate(
  ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D,
  w: number,
  h: number,
  index: number,
  seed: string,
) {
  // Seeded, never `Math.random()`: the plate colours must be identical on the
  // server and the client, and identical across reloads so a visual diff of
  // this component means something.
  const rng = createRng(`${seed}-${index}`);
  // Golden-angle hue walk: consecutive plates are always far apart in hue, so
  // a fast scan down the list never stacks two similar colours.
  const hue = (index * 137.508 + rng() * 18) % 360;

  const bg = ctx.createLinearGradient(0, 0, w, h);
  bg.addColorStop(0, `hsl(${hue} 46% 26%)`);
  bg.addColorStop(1, `hsl(${(hue + 44) % 360} 52% 13%)`);
  ctx.fillStyle = bg;
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, w, h);

  // A soft off-centre sheen so the plate has a light direction rather than
  // reading as a flat swatch.
  const sheen = ctx.createRadialGradient(w * 0.3, h * 0.22, 0, w * 0.3, h * 0.22, h * 1.15);
  sheen.addColorStop(0, 'rgba(255,255,255,0.22)');
  sheen.addColorStop(1, 'rgba(255,255,255,0)');
  ctx.fillStyle = sheen;
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, w, h);

  ctx.strokeStyle = 'rgba(255,255,255,0.14)';
  ctx.lineWidth = 1;
  ctx.strokeRect(0.5, 0.5, w - 1, h - 1);

  ctx.fillStyle = 'rgba(255,255,255,0.82)';
  ctx.font = `500 ${Math.round(h * 0.19)}px ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, monospace`;
  ctx.textBaseline = 'alphabetic';
  ctx.fillText(String(index + 1).padStart(2, '0'), w * 0.07, h * 0.88);
}

export function HoverListImageTrail({
  rows,
  tileWidth = 168,
  tileHeight = 116,
  followDuration = 0.5,
  seed = 'hover-list-image-trail',
  className,
}: HoverListImageTrailProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const column = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const plates = useRef<HTMLCanvasElement[]>([]);

  // Paint one plate per row, once. Re-running only when the geometry or the
  // row count actually changes — not on every render.
  useEffect(() => {
    const bw = tileWidth * PLATE_SCALE;
    const bh = tileHeight * PLATE_SCALE;
    const made: HTMLCanvasElement[] = [];

    for (let i = 0; i < rows.length; i += 1) {
      const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
      canvas.width = bw;
      canvas.height = bh;
      const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
      if (!ctx) continue;
      ctx.scale(PLATE_SCALE, PLATE_SCALE);
      paintPlate(ctx, tileWidth, tileHeight, i, seed);
      made.push(canvas);
    }

    plates.current = made;
    return () => {
      // Plain canvases: nothing was allocated through `createObjectURL`, so
      // there is nothing to revoke. Dropping the references is the disposal.
      plates.current = [];
    };
  }, [rows.length, tileWidth, tileHeight, seed]);

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = root.current;
    const stack = column.current;
    if (!el || !stack) return;

    // A trail that follows a cursor has no meaning without a cursor. On touch
    // `pointerenter` fires on tap, so every tap would stack a plate under the
    // finger and leave it there.
    if (!window.matchMedia('(pointer: fine)').matches) return;
    if (window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches) return;

    /* Centring the column on the pointer once, so the follow tween writes a
       raw `y` and never has to subtract half a height it does not know. */
    gsap.set(stack, { yPercent: -50 });
    const yTo = gsap.quickTo(stack, 'y', { duration: followDuration, ease: 'power4' });

    let seeded = false;
    let order = 0;

    const onMove = (e: PointerEvent) => {
      const rect = el.getBoundingClientRect();
      const y = e.clientY - rect.top;
      if (seeded) {
        yTo(y);
      } else {
        seeded = true;
        // Second argument is quickTo's START value, so the column teleports on
        // entry instead of sweeping down the list from wherever it was left.
        yTo(y, y);
      }
    };

    const onLeave = () => {
      seeded = false;
    };

    const spawn = (index: number) => {
      const plate = plates.current[index];
      if (!plate) return;

      /* The wrapper is the mask. `overflow: hidden` plus a fixed size is what
         makes the opposite-direction pair read as a reveal instead of two
         elements sliding past each other. */
      const wrap = document.createElement('div');
      wrap.style.position = 'absolute';
      wrap.style.left = '0';
      wrap.style.top = '0';
      wrap.style.width = `${tileWidth}px`;
      wrap.style.height = `${tileHeight}px`;
      wrap.style.overflow = 'hidden';
      wrap.style.borderRadius = '4px';
      wrap.style.willChange = 'transform';
      // Monotonic, never reset: a later plate is always above an earlier one,
      // with no possibility of two plates tying and flickering.
      order += 1;
      wrap.style.zIndex = String(order);

      const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
      canvas.width = plate.width;
      canvas.height = plate.height;
      canvas.style.width = `${tileWidth}px`;
      canvas.style.height = `${tileHeight}px`;
      canvas.style.display = 'block';
      canvas.style.willChange = 'transform';
      const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
      if (!ctx) return;
      // One blit. All the expensive drawing happened at mount.
      ctx.drawImage(plate, 0, 0);

      wrap.appendChild(canvas);
      stack.appendChild(wrap);

      /* The masked-reveal pair: wrapper up from +100%, canvas down from -100%,
         on the same duration and ease so they cancel exactly. Any mismatch in
         either and the plate visibly slides inside its own frame. */
      gsap.fromTo(
        wrap,
        { yPercent: 100 },
        { yPercent: 0, duration: REVEAL_DURATION, ease: 'expo.inOut', overwrite: 'auto' },
      );
      gsap.fromTo(
        canvas,
        { yPercent: -100 },
        { yPercent: 0, duration: REVEAL_DURATION, ease: 'expo.inOut', overwrite: 'auto' },
      );

      /* The cull. Not a nicety — without it the stack grows for as long as the
         page is open, and a user idly running the pointer up and down the list
         builds thousands of composited layers. Killing tweens before removal
         stops GSAP writing to a node React and the DOM have both let go of. */
      while (stack.children.length > MAX_PLATES) {
        const oldest = stack.firstElementChild;
        if (!oldest) break;
        gsap.killTweensOf(oldest);
        gsap.killTweensOf(oldest.firstElementChild);
        oldest.remove();
      }
    };

    const onOver = (e: Event) => {
      const target = e.target;
      if (!(target instanceof Element)) return;
      const row = target.closest('[data-trail-row]');
      if (!row) return;
      /* `pointerover` bubbles and fires again for every descendant crossed
         inside the same row, so the spawn is gated on actually changing rows
         rather than on the event firing. `relatedTarget` still inside the row
         means the pointer never left it. */
      const from = (e as PointerEvent).relatedTarget;
      if (from instanceof Node && row.contains(from)) return;
      const index = Number(row.getAttribute('data-trail-row'));
      if (!Number.isInteger(index)) return;
      spawn(index);
    };

    el.addEventListener('pointermove', onMove, { passive: true });
    el.addEventListener('pointerleave', onLeave);
    el.addEventListener('pointerover', onOver);

    return () => {
      el.removeEventListener('pointermove', onMove);
      el.removeEventListener('pointerleave', onLeave);
      el.removeEventListener('pointerover', onOver);
      gsap.killTweensOf(stack);
      // Every live plate is a node this effect created and React does not know
      // about, so this effect has to remove them itself.
      while (stack.firstElementChild) {
        const child = stack.firstElementChild;
        gsap.killTweensOf(child);
        gsap.killTweensOf(child.firstElementChild);
        child.remove();
      }
      gsap.set(stack, { clearProps: 'all' });
    };
  }, [followDuration, tileWidth, tileHeight]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Removes all three container listeners, kills tweens on the column and on every live plate and its canvas, then removes each plate node — these were created imperatively, so React will not clean them up — and clears the column transform. The offscreen plate canvases are released by nulling the ref array; they are plain canvases, never object URLs, so there is nothing to revoke.

**Reduced motion.** No listeners attach and no plates are ever created. What remains is the list itself — real links, real hover colour — which loses nothing functional. There is no meaningful static version of a trail, so the component removes itself rather than pretending.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- No cull. The stack grows for the lifetime of the page; a user idly running the pointer across the list builds thousands of composited layers and the tab degrades with no single frame that looks like the culprit.
- Culling by index or on a timer instead of on spawn. The ceiling then applies per interaction rather than at all times, and a burst of hovers still spikes the node count.
- Removing a node without `killTweensOf`. GSAP keeps writing transforms to a detached element, which is wasted work per frame forever and, in dev, a confusing set of live tweens for nodes that no longer exist.
- Mismatched duration or ease between the wrapper and the canvas. The cancellation breaks and the plate slides inside its own frame — it looks like a parallax effect nobody asked for, and reads as a bug.
- Putting `overflow: hidden` on the column instead of on each wrapper. Every plate is then clipped by one shared box, so plates offset from the column are cut off and the reveal only works for the newest one.
- Spawning on `pointerover` without checking `relatedTarget`. The event refires for every descendant crossed inside the same row, so a single hover over a row containing a number, a label and a date spawns three plates.
- Using `pointerenter` per row instead. It does not bubble, so it needs a listener on every row plus re-subscription whenever React re-renders the list — the bookkeeping is the bug surface.
- Letting the column receive pointer events. Plates then intercept the very moves that drive the follow, and the column stalls whenever it catches up with the pointer.
- `Math.random()` for the plate colours. The server and client disagree, React reports a hydration mismatch, and every reload produces a different set of plates so no visual regression is ever detectable.

## Notes

- Gated on `(pointer: fine)`. On touch nothing mounts: `pointerenter` fires on tap, so every tap would stack a plate directly under the finger and leave it there with no way to dismiss it, and the vertical follow has nothing to follow.
- Reduced motion disables the component entirely rather than shortening it. The plates and the column exist only as motion — there is no static state that still communicates anything — so the honest reduction is the plain list, which is fully functional on its own.
- The column is `aria-hidden`. The rows are real links and remain the accessible content; the plates are decoration with no text equivalent.
- Compare with `pooled-image-trail`, which solves the same visual problem for a pointermove-rate event by reusing a fixed ring of nodes. Neither approach is correct in general; the arrival rate of the event decides.

## Definition of done

Move down the list and each row entered drops a plate into the column, uncovered from the bottom rather than sliding in — watch the numeral in the corner and it should not move relative to the plate edge. The column follows your vertical position with a long settle. Hover a row, move within it across the number and the date, and exactly one plate appears. Run the pointer up and down the list for ten seconds and inspect the column in DevTools: it holds at most twenty children. On touch, or with reduced motion, the list is plain and no plates appear.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Prefetch-On-Hover Wipe

Two halves of one idea: spend the gap between "the visitor has decided" and "the visitor has clicked" making the next page free. `pointerenter` on any link inside the container prefetches it — 200 to 800 ms of warm-up nobody paid for — and the click covers the screen with a wipe, navigating only once the wipe has genuinely finished covering. Both halves are delegated from a single container, and the same predicate that decides what to intercept decides what to prefetch, so a download link or a cross-origin link is left entirely alone by both.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Warms the next page on hover, wipes the screen on click, and navigates once the wipe has actually covered.

- Category: transition
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. One container holds both delegated listeners. The click listener bubbles normally; the `pointerenter` listener cannot, because `pointerenter` does not bubble at all — so it is registered with `{ capture: true }`. The capture phase runs root-to-target for every event whether it bubbles or not, which makes it the only way to delegate the pointer-enter family.
2. `resolveLink` walks up from the event target with `closest('a[href]')` and returns null for anything the browser must handle itself: a `target` other than `_self`, a `download` attribute, `rel="external"`, a different origin, or a hash pointing at the current document. It gates both halves — a link you must not intercept is a link you must not prefetch either, and a cross-origin prefetch leaks the visitor's intent to a third party.
3. The prefetch is `onPrefetch(href)` if a callback was supplied, otherwise an injected `<link rel="prefetch" as="document">`. `as="document"` matters: without it the browser cannot pick a cache partition or a priority and will report the hint as unused even when the navigation follows immediately. A module-scope `Set` of already-hinted hrefs means a nav that remounts on every route change does not re-hint its whole link set each time.
4. The click calls `preventDefault()`, stores the resolved href in a ref, and flips `data-leaving` on the overlay, which runs a `transform: scaleX(0) -> scaleX(1)` transition from the anchored edge. Navigation waits for `transitionend`, filtered on both `event.target === overlay` and `event.propertyName === "transform"`, because `transitionend` fires once per property and also for descendants.
5. `transitionend` never fires for an element that is not being rendered — a `display: none` ancestor, a tab backgrounded mid-wipe — so a `duration + 120 ms` timer races it and a `fired` flag makes whichever wins the only one that navigates. A navigation that silently never happens is a dead link, which is strictly worse than an early one.
6. A `pageshow` listener clears the wipe. Back-navigation out of the browser's back/forward cache restores the DOM exactly as it was left, including the wipe mid-cover, with no script running to undo it — and `pageshow` is the only event dispatched on a bfcache restore. `load` is not, and neither are React's mount effects. `data-instant` suppresses the transition for exactly one frame so the restore snaps rather than playing a reveal of a page the visitor already saw.
7. The base rule carries an ease-out curve and the `[data-leaving="true"]` rule overrides the timing function with an ease-in, so covering accelerates away and retracting decelerates into place. One declaration, and it is the difference between a page transition and a garage door.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `duration = 0.3`
  Seconds to cover. This is dead time the visitor pays for on every click, so it is priced against the prefetch: roughly 300 ms is what a warm document needs to parse and paint, which is why the wipe and the fetch finish together. Past ~0.5 s the wipe is the slowest part of the navigation it was added to hide.
- `SAFETY_MS = 120`
  Milliseconds past the duration before navigation is forced. Long enough to lose the race with a real `transitionend` under load — a frame or two of jank costs more than 16 ms — short enough that a wipe which genuinely never rendered does not strand the visitor.
- `cover ease = cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1)`
  Ease-in, no ease-out. The wipe must be at its fastest as it reaches full coverage: the last sliver of uncovered page is the part that reads as sluggishness, and an ease-out spends its longest stretch there.
- `retract ease = cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0.2, 1)`
  Ease-out, the mirror. Arriving should settle rather than snap. Reusing the cover curve for the retract makes the wipe linger and then flick away, because a reversed transition traverses the same curve in the same direction.
- `zIndex = 190`
  Above a custom cursor (150) and a scroll progress bar (120), both of which must be hidden while the screen is covered, and below a preloader (200), which owns first load outright.

## API

```ts
function HoverPrefetchWipe(props: { children: ReactNode; onNavigate: (href: string) => void; onPrefetch?: (href: string) => void; pageKey?: string; duration?: number; color?: string; direction?: "left" | "right" | "up" | "down"; zIndex?: number; position?: "fixed" | "absolute"; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Anything containing anchors. Every `<a href>` inside is handled by delegation.
- `onNavigate: (href: string) => void`
  Runs once the wipe has fully covered. Receives `pathname + search + hash`, which is what a router expects.
- `onPrefetch: (href: string) => void`
  The framework-specific half. Omitted, a `<link rel="prefetch" as="document">` is injected instead.
- `pageKey: string`
  Identity of the current page; a change retracts the wipe. Leave undefined for a full document navigation so the cover holds.
- `duration: number` — default `0.3`
  Seconds to cover, and to retract.
- `color: string` — default `'#fff'`
  Any CSS colour. Must be opaque or the swap shows through.
- `direction: "left" | "right" | "up" | "down"` — default `"left"`
  Edge the wipe grows from.
- `zIndex: number` — default `190`
  Above a custom cursor and a progress bar, below a preloader.
- `position: "fixed" | "absolute"` — default `"fixed"`
  `absolute` to scope the wipe to a bounded box; `fixed` for a real page transition.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the container via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * Hrefs already hinted to the browser. Module scope, so it is shared across
 * instances and survives remounts: a nav that remounts on every route change
 * would otherwise re-hint its entire link set on every navigation.
 */
const prefetched = new Set<string>();

/**
 * Milliseconds past the wipe duration before the navigation is forced.
 * `transitionend` is the accurate signal but it never fires if the overlay is
 * not being rendered — a `display: none` ancestor, a tab backgrounded mid-wipe
 * — and a navigation that silently never happens is a dead link.
 */
const SAFETY_MS = 120;

const WIPE_CSS = `
.kinetic-wipe {
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  background: var(--kx-wipe-color, #fff);
  transform: var(--kx-wipe-from, scaleX(0));
  transform-origin: var(--kx-wipe-origin, left center);
  /* Base curve is the RETRACT: ease-out, so arriving decelerates. */
  transition: transform var(--kx-wipe-duration, 0.3s)
    cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0.2, 1);
  will-change: transform;
  /* Transparent and idle: must not eat the click it is waiting for. */
  pointer-events: none;
}
.kinetic-wipe[data-fixed='true'] {
  position: fixed;
}
.kinetic-wipe[data-leaving='true'] {
  transform: var(--kx-wipe-to, scaleX(1));
  /* Cover curve: ease-in, so leaving accelerates away. Asymmetry is the
     difference between a page transition and a garage door. */
  transition-timing-function: cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1);
  /* Covering: now it SHOULD eat clicks. The outgoing page is still live
     underneath and a second click on a nav item would queue a second
     navigation behind an opaque surface. */
  pointer-events: auto;
}
/* Set for exactly one frame after a bfcache restore, so the overlay snaps back
   to rest instead of playing a reveal of a page the visitor already saw. */
.kinetic-wipe[data-instant='true'] {
  transition: none;
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  /* Removed entirely rather than zero-duration: a zero-duration wipe is still
     one painted frame of full-bleed colour, which is a flash. The click
     handler navigates synchronously in this mode, so nothing is lost. */
  .kinetic-wipe { display: none; }
}
`;

/** Per-direction geometry: the two transforms and the anchored edge. */
const GEOMETRY = {
  left: { from: 'scaleX(0)', to: 'scaleX(1)', origin: 'left center' },
  right: { from: 'scaleX(0)', to: 'scaleX(1)', origin: 'right center' },
  up: { from: 'scaleY(0)', to: 'scaleY(1)', origin: 'bottom center' },
  down: { from: 'scaleY(0)', to: 'scaleY(1)', origin: 'top center' },
} as const;

export type WipeDirection = keyof typeof GEOMETRY;

export interface HoverPrefetchWipeProps {
  /** Anything containing anchors. Every `<a href>` inside is handled. */
  children: ReactNode;
  /**
   * Runs once the wipe has fully covered. Receives the app-relative href —
   * `pathname + search + hash` — which is what a router expects.
   */
  onNavigate: (href: string) => void;
  /**
   * The framework-specific half. Next.js: `(href) => router.prefetch(href)`.
   * Omitted, a `<link rel="prefetch" as="document">` is injected instead,
   * which is the right hint for a plain multi-page site.
   */
  onPrefetch?: (href: string) => void;
  /**
   * Identity of the current page — `usePathname()` in Next.js. A change
   * retracts the wipe. Left undefined the wipe stays up after `onNavigate`,
   * which is correct for a full document navigation: the browser keeps
   * painting the old page until the new one is ready, so lowering the curtain
   * early re-reveals the page you just left.
   */
  pageKey?: string;
  /** Seconds the wipe takes to cover, and to retract. */
  duration?: number;
  /** Any CSS colour. Must be opaque or the swap shows through. */
  color?: string;
  /** Edge the wipe grows from. */
  direction?: WipeDirection;
  zIndex?: number;
  /** `absolute` to demo inside a bounded box; `fixed` for a real page. */
  position?: 'fixed' | 'absolute';
  className?: string;
}

/**
 * The anchor a delegated event belongs to, or null if the browser should be
 * left alone. Every clause is a link that would break if intercepted — and the
 * same predicate gates both halves, because a link you must not intercept is a
 * link you must not prefetch either.
 */
function resolveLink(event: Event, root: HTMLElement): HTMLAnchorElement | null {
  const target = event.target;
  if (!(target instanceof Element)) return null;

  const anchor = target.closest('a[href]');
  if (!(anchor instanceof HTMLAnchorElement)) return null;
  if (!root.contains(anchor)) return null;

  // Opens elsewhere, downloads, or is explicitly marked as leaving the site.
  if (anchor.target !== '' && anchor.target !== '_self') return null;
  if (anchor.hasAttribute('download')) return null;
  if (anchor.rel.split(/\s+/).includes('external')) return null;

  // Cross-origin: prefetching leaks the visitor's intent to a third party and
  // intercepting breaks the navigation outright.
  if (anchor.origin !== window.location.origin) return null;

  // Same document, different fragment. Nothing to fetch, and covering the
  // screen in order to scroll down the page is absurd.
  if (
    anchor.hash !== '' &&
    anchor.pathname === window.location.pathname &&
    anchor.search === window.location.search
  ) {
    return null;
  }

  return anchor;
}

function hrefOf(anchor: HTMLAnchorElement): string {
  // Resolved and app-relative. `getAttribute('href')` hands a router raw
  // authored text like '../work', which it cannot resolve on its own.
  return `${anchor.pathname}${anchor.search}${anchor.hash}`;
}

export function HoverPrefetchWipe({
  children,
  onNavigate,
  onPrefetch,
  pageKey,
  duration = 0.3,
  color = '#fff',
  direction = 'left',
  zIndex = 190,
  position = 'fixed',
  className,
}: HoverPrefetchWipeProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const wipe = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const pending = useRef<string | null>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  const [leaving, setLeaving] = useState(false);
  const [instant, setInstant] = useState(false);

  // Held in refs so a new handler identity on the parent's render does not
  // re-bind the delegated listeners.
  const navigate = useRef(onNavigate);
  navigate.current = onNavigate;
  const prefetch = useRef(onPrefetch);
  prefetch.current = onPrefetch;

  /* -- halves one and two, both delegated from the same container ------- */
  useEffect(() => {
    const el = root.current;
    if (!el) return;

    const onEnter = (event: Event) => {
      const anchor = resolveLink(event, el);
      if (!anchor) return;

      const href = hrefOf(anchor);
      if (prefetched.has(href)) return;
      prefetched.add(href);

      const custom = prefetch.current;
      if (custom) {
        custom(href);
        return;
      }

      const link = document.createElement('link');
      link.rel = 'prefetch';
      // Without `as`, the browser cannot choose a cache partition or a
      // priority, and logs the hint as unused even when the navigation
      // follows immediately.
      link.as = 'document';
      link.href = href;
      document.head.appendChild(link);
    };

    const onClick = (event: MouseEvent) => {
      // Someone upstream already handled it, or the visitor asked for a new
      // tab, a new window, or a download. Middle and right clicks are not
      // navigations and must reach the browser untouched.
      if (event.defaultPrevented || event.button !== 0) return;
      if (event.metaKey || event.ctrlKey || event.shiftKey || event.altKey) return;

      const anchor = resolveLink(event, el);
      if (!anchor) return;

      event.preventDefault();

      if (reduced) {
        navigate.current(hrefOf(anchor));
        return;
      }

      // A wipe already covering owns the navigation. Without this a second
      // click retargets `pending` mid-cover and the visitor lands on a page
      // they never aimed at.
      if (pending.current !== null) return;

      pending.current = hrefOf(anchor);
      setLeaving(true);
    };

    // `pointerenter` does not bubble, so delegation only works in the capture
    // phase — which runs root-to-target for every event, bubbling or not.
    el.addEventListener('pointerenter', onEnter, { capture: true, passive: true });
    el.addEventListener('click', onClick);

    return () => {
      el.removeEventListener('pointerenter', onEnter, { capture: true });
      el.removeEventListener('click', onClick);
    };
  }, [reduced]);

  /* -- navigate only once the wipe has actually finished covering ------- */
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!leaving) return;
    const overlay = wipe.current;
    const href = pending.current;
    if (!overlay || href === null) return;

    let fired = false;
    const commit = () => {
      if (fired) return;
      fired = true;
      navigate.current(href);
    };

    // `transitionend` fires once per animated property and also for
    // descendants, so both filters are required: without the target check a
    // transition on anything inside the overlay would trigger navigation.
    const onEnd = (event: TransitionEvent) => {
      if (event.target !== overlay || event.propertyName !== 'transform') return;
      commit();
    };

    overlay.addEventListener('transitionend', onEnd);
    const safety = window.setTimeout(commit, duration * 1000 + SAFETY_MS);

    return () => {
      overlay.removeEventListener('transitionend', onEnd);
      clearTimeout(safety);
    };
  }, [leaving, duration]);

  /* -- retract when the destination is on screen ----------------------- */
  const seenKey = useRef(pageKey);
  useEffect(() => {
    if (pageKey === undefined || seenKey.current === pageKey) return;
    seenKey.current = pageKey;
    // Driven by the same render that swapped the content in, so there is no
    // window in which the retracting wipe exposes the page just left.
    pending.current = null;
    setLeaving(false);
  }, [pageKey]);

  /* -- half three: survive the back/forward cache ---------------------- */
  useEffect(() => {
    const onShow = () => {
      pending.current = null;
      setInstant(true);
      setLeaving(false);
    };
    window.addEventListener('pageshow', onShow);
    return () => window.removeEventListener('pageshow', onShow);
  }, []);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!instant) return;
    // One frame is enough for the resting transform to be committed with the
    // transition suppressed. Re-enable any earlier and style has not been
    // recalculated yet, so the snap becomes a fade after all.
    const frame = requestAnimationFrame(() => setInstant(false));
    return () => cancelAnimationFrame(frame);
  }, [instant]);

  const geometry = GEOMETRY[direction];

  return (
    <div ref={root} className={cn(position === 'absolute' && 'relative', className)}>
      <style href="kinetic-hover-prefetch-wipe" precedence="medium">
        {WIPE_CSS}
      </style>

      {children}

      <div
        ref={wipe}
        aria-hidden
        data-leaving={leaving ? 'true' : 'false'}
        data-instant={instant ? 'true' : 'false'}
        data-fixed={position === 'fixed' ? 'true' : 'false'}
        className="kinetic-wipe"
        style={
          {
            zIndex,
            '--kx-wipe-duration': `${duration}s`,
            '--kx-wipe-color': color,
            '--kx-wipe-from': geometry.from,
            '--kx-wipe-to': geometry.to,
            '--kx-wipe-origin': geometry.origin,
          } as CSSProperties
        }
      />
    </div>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Both delegated listeners are removed with the same `{ capture: true }` flag they were added with, or the removal silently fails to match. The `transitionend` listener and the safety timer are torn down together whenever the leaving state changes, the rAF that re-enables the transition after a bfcache restore is cancelled, and the `pageshow` listener is removed on unmount. Injected `<link rel="prefetch">` tags are deliberately left in the head: removing a hint mid-flight cancels the fetch it exists to start.

**Reduced motion.** The overlay gets `display: none` and the click handler calls `onNavigate` synchronously, so navigation is a hard cut with no coloured frame in either direction. Not a zero-duration wipe — that is still one painted frame of full-bleed colour, which is a flash. The prefetch half is untouched, because a warm cache is not motion and is precisely the thing a visitor on a slow connection wants kept.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Delegating `pointerenter` with a normal bubbling listener. It does not bubble, so the handler fires only when the pointer enters the container itself — once — and every link in the nav is silently never prefetched. `{ capture: true }` is not an optimisation here, it is the mechanism.
- Prefetching everything on mount. A nav of twelve links becomes twelve speculative document fetches competing with the page the visitor is actually reading. Hover is the signal that makes it worth the bandwidth.
- Prefetching cross-origin hrefs. Beyond the wasted request, it tells a third party which of its pages this visitor was considering before they chose. `resolveLink` rejects them for both halves.
- Navigating on a timer instead of `transitionend`. Under load the timer fires while the page is still visible through a half-drawn wipe, which is the exact artefact the wipe exists to hide. Under a throttled background tab it fires long after.
- Trusting `transitionend` alone. It never fires for an unrendered element, so a wipe inside a collapsed ancestor turns every link into a no-op. The safety timer is not belt-and-braces, it is the only thing standing between a CSS edge case and a dead nav.
- Filtering `transitionend` on neither target nor property name. It fires once per animated property and bubbles from descendants, so a hover transition on a child inside the overlay triggers the navigation early.
- Forgetting `pageshow`. On a bfcache restore the visitor lands on a full-bleed sheet of colour with nothing running to clear it. This is the single most common way a wipe transition ships broken, because it never reproduces on a hard reload.
- Leaving the overlay `pointer-events: none` while it covers. The outgoing page is still live underneath, so a second click on a nav item queues a second navigation behind an opaque surface. It flips to `auto` only in the leaving state, because at rest it must not eat the click it is waiting for.
- Retracting the wipe immediately after a full document navigation. The browser keeps painting the old page until the new one is ready, so lowering the curtain early re-reveals the page just left. That is why the retract is driven by `pageKey` and why leaving it undefined holds the cover.

## Notes

- Next.js App Router: `onPrefetch={(href) => router.prefetch(href)}`, `onNavigate={(href) => router.push(href)}`, `pageKey={usePathname()}`. Nothing in this file imports `next/link` or `next/navigation` — the prefetch half is the only framework-specific part of the technique, so it is a callback, and `router.prefetch` already dedupes and no-ops in dev.
- React Router: `onPrefetch` can stay omitted and let the injected `<link rel="prefetch">` warm the loader's data URL, or call your own route-module preloader. `pageKey={useLocation().pathname}`.
- Plain multi-page site: omit `onPrefetch` entirely and set `onNavigate={(href) => window.location.assign(href)}`. Leave `pageKey` undefined so the wipe stays up while the browser fetches, and let `pageshow` clear it on Back.
- Wrap the whole layout, not each nav: one container, one overlay, one pair of listeners, and every link on the page is covered including ones rendered later. `position="fixed"` for that; `absolute` only when the transition is scoped to a panel.
- The colour must be opaque. A translucent wipe shows the outgoing page through the swap, which is the one artefact the whole sequence exists to prevent.
- Pairs with `page-reveal-overlay` if you want the inbound half animated too — this component covers and hands off, that one replays a reveal on arrival.

## Definition of done

Hover a nav item and its dot lights — the href has been hinted, once, and hovering again does not re-hint. Click and the panel wipes over from the left in 0.4 s, the content swaps while covered, and the wipe retracts to the same edge with the opposite ease. Cmd-click, middle-click and a `download` link all behave like ordinary links with no wipe. On a real site, navigate away and press Back: the page appears with no leftover overlay and no reveal animation. With reduced motion the content swaps instantly and no coloured surface is ever painted.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Idle-Gated Page States

A page entrance is the one animation guaranteed to run at the worst possible moment: hydration, font swap, image decode and the first layout pass all land in the same few hundred milliseconds. Start a stagger there and it does not look slow, it looks broken — three elements arrive, the thread blocks, the rest snap in. This gates the entrance on two conditions at once, a floor delay resolved on a frame boundary and at least one report of an idle main thread, and starts only when the slower of the two finishes. Enter and leave are one paused timeline played forward and reversed.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A page entrance that will not start until a floor delay has elapsed and the main thread has reported itself idle.

- Category: transition
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. The machine is `preload -> gating -> entering -> settled`, with `leave(commit)` sending it to `leaving` and the exit's completion sending it back to `gating` for the next page. The current phase is written to `data-page-state` on the root so CSS can read it without a second source of truth.
2. `whenIdleAfter(delay, timeout, done)` is the gate. It schedules two independent waits and calls `done` only when both flags are set: a `setTimeout(delay)` whose callback schedules a `requestAnimationFrame`, and either `requestIdleCallback(cb, { timeout })` or — where that is missing — `setTimeout(cb, timeout)`. It returns a canceller that clears the timer, cancels the frame, and releases whichever of the two idle mechanisms was actually used.
3. The floor delay resolves inside the rAF rather than in the timer itself. A timer callback can fire in the middle of a long task; the frame callback after it cannot, so the first tween is handed a fresh frame budget instead of the tail end of somebody else's work.
4. `requestIdleCallback`'s `timeout` option is the safety net — the callback is guaranteed to run within that many milliseconds whether the thread ever goes idle or not — and the `setTimeout` fallback uses the same number as its delay, so both code paths have identical worst-case behaviour.
5. The first entrance uses `preloadDelay` (0.8 s) and every subsequent one uses `routeDelay` (0.15 s), switched by a `firstEnter` ref. Only the first competes with hydration; keeping 0.8 s for route changes would put nearly a second of nothing between every click and its page.
6. The choreography is ONE paused GSAP timeline: `fromTo([data-page-enter], { opacity: 0, y: 24 }, { opacity: 1, y: 0, stagger: 0.08 })`. `state === "entering"` calls `play()`; `state === "leaving"` calls `timeScale(enterDuration / leaveDuration).reverse()`. The timeline's `onComplete` and `onReverseComplete` report back into the machine, so no phase is advanced by a timer that could disagree with what is on screen.
7. The pre-JS hidden state is a stylesheet rule keyed on `[data-page-state="preload"]` and `[data-page-state="gating"]`, not a `gsap.set` in an effect. Effects run after the first paint, so a JS-only hidden state paints the page fully composed and then hides it. The build then applies `gsap.set(targets, from)` immediately, in the same React commit that swapped the page in, which covers every frame after that.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `PRELOAD_DELAY = 0.8`
  Seconds of floor delay before the FIRST entrance — the one competing with hydration, font loading and the initial layout pass. Below ~0.5 s the stagger still lands inside the hydration burst on a mid-range phone; above ~1 s a fast device shows a finished, blank-looking page and waits.
- `ROUTE_DELAY = 0.15`
  Seconds of floor delay for every entrance after the first. Hydration has already happened; the only competing work is the destination subtree's own mount. Long enough that the mount lands inside it, short enough that the click still feels answered.
- `IDLE_TIMEOUT = 1200`
  Milliseconds after which the idle wait gives up, passed both as `requestIdleCallback`'s `timeout` and as the fallback timer's delay. A saturated thread — a WebGL hero, a heavy hydration, a third-party long task — may never report idle, and an entrance that never starts is a blank page. Longer than a typical hydration burst, comfortably shorter than the ~2 s at which a visitor decides the site is broken.
- `ENTER_DURATION = 0.5`
  Seconds for the entrance, matching the source's `enterDuration`. With a 0.08 s stagger over four elements the last one finishes at 0.74 s, which is the upper limit for a page that should feel like it is already there.
- `LEAVE_DURATION = 0.5`
  Seconds for the exit, matching the source's `leaveDuration`. Applied as `timeScale(enterDuration / leaveDuration)` on the reversed timeline rather than as a second set of tweens, so the exit cannot drift from the entrance. Drop it to 0.25 for an exit that feels decisive against a gradual arrival.
- `ENTER_STAGGER = 0.08`
  Seconds between elements. Below ~0.05 s the group reads as one block and the stagger is wasted; above ~0.12 s the last element arrives after the eye has already moved on and the page feels like it is still loading.
- `ENTER_DISTANCE = 24`
  Pixels each element rises through. Small enough that no element crosses another's resting position — which would read as the layout reflowing rather than arriving — and large enough to be legible at the 0.5 s duration.

## API

```ts
function IdleGatedPageStates(props: { controller: IdlePageStates; pageKey: string; children: ReactNode; enterDuration?: number; leaveDuration?: number; stagger?: number; distance?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
function useIdlePageStates(options?: { preloadDelay?: number; routeDelay?: number; idleTimeout?: number; onGateOpen?: () => void }): { state: PageState; ready: () => void; leave: (commit: () => void) => void; entered: () => void; left: () => void }
function whenIdleAfter(delaySeconds: number, timeout: number, done: () => void): () => void
type PageState = "preload" | "gating" | "entering" | "settled" | "leaving"
```

- `controller: IdlePageStates`
  From `useIdlePageStates()`. Supplies the phase and receives the timeline's completions.
- `pageKey: string`
  Identity of the current page. A change rebuilds the timeline against the new `[data-page-enter]` elements. `usePathname()` in Next.js.
- `children: ReactNode`
  The page. Descendants marked `data-page-enter` are staggered in and, reversed, out.
- `enterDuration: number` — default `0.5`
  Seconds for the entrance.
- `leaveDuration: number` — default `0.5`
  Seconds for the exit, applied as a `timeScale` on the reversed timeline.
- `stagger: number` — default `0.08`
  Seconds between staggered elements. Reversed on exit, so the last one leaves first.
- `distance: number` — default `24`
  Pixels each element rises through.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * Seconds of floor delay before the FIRST entrance. The one enter that
 * competes with hydration, font loading and the initial layout pass, so it is
 * the one that needs real headroom. Below ~0.5 s the stagger still lands
 * inside the hydration burst on a mid-range phone; above ~1 s a fast device
 * shows a finished, blank-looking page and waits.
 */
export const PRELOAD_DELAY = 0.8;

/**
 * Seconds of floor delay before every SUBSEQUENT entrance. Hydration has
 * already happened by then; the only competing work is the destination
 * subtree's own mount, which is a fraction of it. Keeping the first-load value
 * here would put nearly a second of nothing between every click and its page.
 */
export const ROUTE_DELAY = 0.15;

/**
 * Milliseconds after which the idle wait gives up. A thread that is genuinely
 * saturated — a WebGL hero, a heavy hydration, a long task from a third-party
 * script — may never report idle, and an entrance that never starts is a blank
 * page. 1200 ms is longer than a typical hydration burst and comfortably
 * shorter than the ~2 s at which a visitor decides the site is broken. It is
 * passed as `requestIdleCallback`'s own `timeout` option, and it is also the
 * fallback timer's delay, so both paths have identical worst-case behaviour.
 */
export const IDLE_TIMEOUT = 1200;

/** Seconds for the entrance. */
export const ENTER_DURATION = 0.5;
/** Seconds for the exit. */
export const LEAVE_DURATION = 0.5;

/** Seconds between staggered elements. */
const ENTER_STAGGER = 0.08;
/** Pixels each element rises through. */
const ENTER_DISTANCE = 24;
const ENTER_EASE = 'power2.out';

const PAGE_CSS = `
/* The pre-JS hidden state. It cannot come from a 'gsap.set' in an effect —
   effects run after the first paint, so the page would flash fully composed
   and then hide itself. Once GSAP is involved it writes 'opacity' to the
   inline style, which outranks this rule in both directions. */
.kx-idle-page[data-page-state='preload'] [data-page-enter],
.kx-idle-page[data-page-state='gating'] [data-page-enter] {
  opacity: 0;
}
/* Reduced motion never runs the gate, so nothing would ever remove the rule
   above before hydration. */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .kx-idle-page[data-page-state='preload'] [data-page-enter],
  .kx-idle-page[data-page-state='gating'] [data-page-enter] {
    opacity: 1;
  }
}
/* Media Queries 5. Where it is unsupported the declaration is simply dropped,
   so this is a bonus rather than the fix — but where it is supported, a
   scripting-disabled visitor gets the page instead of an empty box. */
@media (scripting: none) {
  .kx-idle-page[data-page-state='preload'] [data-page-enter],
  .kx-idle-page[data-page-state='gating'] [data-page-enter] {
    opacity: 1;
  }
}
`;

/**
 * Call `done` once BOTH a floor delay has elapsed and the main thread has gone
 * idle. Returns the canceller — call it from effect cleanup.
 *
 * `requestIdleCallback` is used where it exists and a plain `setTimeout` where
 * it does not: Safari only shipped it in 17.4, so a fallback is not
 * hypothetical, and the two are cancelled with different functions. Exactly one
 * of them is ever scheduled, and the canceller releases whichever it was.
 */
export function whenIdleAfter(
  delaySeconds: number,
  timeout: number,
  done: () => void,
): () => void {
  let cancelled = false;
  let idleReady = false;
  let delayReady = false;

  const join = () => {
    if (cancelled || !idleReady || !delayReady) return;
    done();
  };

  // The floor delay resolves inside a rAF rather than directly in the timer.
  // A timer callback can fire in the middle of a long task; the frame callback
  // after it cannot, so the first tween is guaranteed a fresh frame budget
  // instead of the tail end of someone else's.
  let frame = 0;
  const delayTimer = setTimeout(() => {
    frame = requestAnimationFrame(() => {
      frame = 0;
      delayReady = true;
      join();
    });
  }, delaySeconds * 1000);

  let idleHandle = 0;
  let idleTimer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined;

  const onIdle = () => {
    idleHandle = 0;
    idleTimer = undefined;
    idleReady = true;
    join();
  };

  if (typeof window !== 'undefined' && 'requestIdleCallback' in window) {
    // The `timeout` option is the guarantee: the callback runs within this many
    // milliseconds whether the thread ever goes idle or not.
    idleHandle = window.requestIdleCallback(onIdle, { timeout });
  } else {
    idleTimer = setTimeout(onIdle, timeout);
  }

  return () => {
    cancelled = true;
    clearTimeout(delayTimer);
    if (frame !== 0) cancelAnimationFrame(frame);
    // Whichever branch ran is the one that gets released. Cancelling an idle
    // handle with `clearTimeout` is a silent no-op, which is how a gate leaks
    // into the next page and starts an entrance on a tree that no longer
    // exists.
    if (idleHandle !== 0) window.cancelIdleCallback(idleHandle);
    if (idleTimer !== undefined) clearTimeout(idleTimer);
  };
}

export type PageState =
  | 'preload'
  | 'gating'
  | 'entering'
  | 'settled'
  | 'leaving';

export interface IdlePageStatesOptions {
  /** Seconds of floor delay before the first entrance. */
  preloadDelay?: number;
  /** Seconds of floor delay before every entrance after the first. */
  routeDelay?: number;
  /** Milliseconds after which the idle wait gives up. */
  idleTimeout?: number;
  /**
   * Fired on the frame the gate opens, before the entrance starts. The place
   * for `ScrollTrigger.refresh()` — measure while nothing is moving, or every
   * trigger is offset by the distance the entrance travels.
   */
  onGateOpen?: () => void;
}

export interface IdlePageStates {
  /** Also written to `data-page-state` on the root, so CSS can read it. */
  state: PageState;
  /** Preload finished — fonts resolved, critical images decoded. */
  ready: () => void;
  /** Run the exit, then `commit` — your navigation. */
  leave: (commit: () => void) => void;
  /** Reported by the component when the entrance timeline completes. */
  entered: () => void;
  /** Reported by the component when the exit timeline reaches zero. */
  left: () => void;
}

export function useIdlePageStates(
  options: IdlePageStatesOptions = {},
): IdlePageStates {
  const {
    preloadDelay = PRELOAD_DELAY,
    routeDelay = ROUTE_DELAY,
    idleTimeout = IDLE_TIMEOUT,
    onGateOpen,
  } = options;

  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const [state, setState] = useState<PageState>('preload');

  const commit = useRef<(() => void) | null>(null);
  const firstEnter = useRef(true);
  const gateOpen = useRef(onGateOpen);
  gateOpen.current = onGateOpen;

  // The gate. Scheduled only while gating, and cancelled by returning the
  // canceller — so a route change or an unmount mid-wait releases the idle
  // handle instead of firing an entrance into a tree that has gone.
  useEffect(() => {
    if (state !== 'gating') return;

    // Reduced motion skips the gate entirely rather than waiting it out. The
    // gate exists to protect an animation; with no animation to protect, all it
    // would do is hold a blank page in front of someone who asked for less
    // motion, not more waiting.
    if (reduced) {
      firstEnter.current = false;
      setState('settled');
      return;
    }

    const delay = firstEnter.current ? preloadDelay : routeDelay;
    return whenIdleAfter(delay, idleTimeout, () => {
      firstEnter.current = false;
      gateOpen.current?.();
      setState('entering');
    });
  }, [state, reduced, preloadDelay, routeDelay, idleTimeout]);

  const ready = useCallback(() => {
    setState((s) => (s === 'preload' ? 'gating' : s));
  }, []);

  const entered = useCallback(() => {
    setState((s) => (s === 'entering' ? 'settled' : s));
  }, []);

  const leave = useCallback(
    (next: () => void) => {
      if (reduced) {
        next();
        return;
      }
      // A second click during an exit would queue a second commit and land the
      // visitor one page past where they aimed.
      if (commit.current !== null) return;
      commit.current = next;
      setState((s) =>
        s === 'entering' || s === 'settled' || s === 'gating' ? 'leaving' : s,
      );
    },
    [reduced],
  );

  const left = useCallback(() => {
    const next = commit.current;
    commit.current = null;
    next?.();
    // Straight back to gating, not to preload: the preloader is a first-load
    // state and showing it again on every route change is the classic version
    // of this mistake.
    setState('gating');
  }, []);

  useEffect(
    () => () => {
      commit.current = null;
    },
    [],
  );

  return useMemo(
    () => ({ state, ready, leave, entered, left }),
    [state, ready, leave, entered, left],
  );
}

export interface IdleGatedPageStatesProps {
  /** From `useIdlePageStates()`. */
  controller: IdlePageStates;
  /**
   * Identity of the current page. A change rebuilds the timeline against the
   * new page's `[data-page-enter]` elements. `usePathname()` in Next.js.
   */
  pageKey: string;
  /** The page. Descendants marked `data-page-enter` are staggered in and out. */
  children: ReactNode;
  /** Seconds for the entrance. */
  enterDuration?: number;
  /** Seconds for the exit. Applied as a `timeScale` on the reversed timeline. */
  leaveDuration?: number;
  /** Seconds between staggered elements. */
  stagger?: number;
  /** Pixels each element rises through. */
  distance?: number;
  className?: string;
}

export function IdleGatedPageStates({
  controller,
  pageKey,
  children,
  enterDuration = ENTER_DURATION,
  leaveDuration = LEAVE_DURATION,
  stagger = ENTER_STAGGER,
  distance = ENTER_DISTANCE,
  className,
}: IdleGatedPageStatesProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const timeline = useRef<ReturnType<typeof gsap.timeline> | null>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  const { state, entered, left } = controller;

  // Held in refs so the timeline's completion callbacks are wired once, at
  // build time, and still call the current functions.
  const onEntered = useRef(entered);
  onEntered.current = entered;
  const onLeft = useRef(left);
  onLeft.current = left;

  // Built once per page and held paused. `state` is deliberately NOT a
  // dependency: `useGsap` reverts on every dependency change, and `revert()`
  // strips the inline values GSAP wrote — so a rebuild keyed on the phase would
  // hand the reverse tween the stylesheet default as its start value and the
  // exit would animate from nowhere to nowhere.
  useGsap(
    gsap,
    () => {
      const el = root.current;
      if (!el) return;

      const targets = Array.from(
        el.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-page-enter]'),
      );
      if (targets.length === 0) return;

      const from = { opacity: 0, y: distance };

      // Applied immediately, in the same commit React swapped the page in, so
      // the destination is never painted composed and then hidden. The CSS rule
      // covers the frames before this file has run at all; this covers every
      // frame after.
      gsap.set(targets, from);

      const tl = gsap.timeline({
        paused: true,
        onComplete: () => onEntered.current(),
        onReverseComplete: () => onLeft.current(),
      });

      tl.fromTo(
        targets,
        from,
        {
          opacity: 1,
          y: 0,
          duration: enterDuration,
          ease: ENTER_EASE,
          stagger,
        },
        0,
      );

      timeline.current = tl;
      return () => {
        timeline.current = null;
      };
    },
    root,
    [pageKey, enterDuration, stagger, distance],
  );

  // The phase driver. Separate from the build for the reason above, and it
  // carries `pageKey` so it runs after — never before — a rebuild.
  useEffect(() => {
    const tl = timeline.current;
    if (!tl) return;

    if (reduced) {
      // A seek, not a zero-duration tween: the timeline is parked on its end
      // frame, so opacity, offset and stagger all land correctly because they
      // are all on this one timeline.
      tl.progress(1).pause();
      return;
    }

    if (state === 'entering') {
      tl.timeScale(1).play();
    } else if (state === 'leaving') {
      // One timeline, two speeds. `timeScale` is a ratio, so a 0.25 s exit off
      // a 0.5 s entrance is `0.5 / 0.25 = 2`, and the reversed stagger takes
      // the last element out first.
      tl.timeScale(enterDuration / Math.max(leaveDuration, 0.01)).reverse();
    }
  }, [state, reduced, pageKey, enterDuration, leaveDuration]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The gate's canceller is the effect's cleanup: it clears the floor-delay timer, cancels the pending `requestAnimationFrame`, and releases whichever idle mechanism was scheduled — `cancelIdleCallback` for the handle, `clearTimeout` for the fallback — with a `cancelled` flag so a callback already in the queue cannot fire after teardown. `useGsap` reverts the `gsap.context`, killing the timeline and stripping every inline style it wrote. The pending commit is nulled on unmount so a leave in flight cannot navigate a tree that has gone.

**Reduced motion.** The gate is skipped entirely — holding a blank page would be more waiting, not less motion — so `gating` advances straight to `settled` with no idle callback and no timer scheduled, and therefore nothing to cancel. The timeline is never played: the phase effect parks it with `tl.progress(1).pause()`, so opacity, offset and stagger all land on their end frame together because they are all on the one timeline. `leave()` calls the commit synchronously, and a stylesheet rule inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` keeps `[data-page-enter]` visible for the frames before hydration.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Starting the entrance on mount. Mount is the single busiest moment in the page's life. The stagger runs against hydration and the first layout pass, so the first two or three elements animate and the rest jump — and it only reproduces on the devices you do not test on.
- Waiting for idle ALONE. On a fast machine `requestIdleCallback` fires almost immediately, before the hydration burst has even begun, so the gate opens straight into the work it was supposed to avoid. The floor delay is what makes the idle check meaningful.
- Waiting for a delay ALONE. On a slow machine the timer expires while the thread is still saturated and you are back to a stuttering stagger. Neither condition works without the other.
- Calling `requestIdleCallback` without the `timeout` option. On a page with a long-running rAF loop the callback may never fire, and the entrance never starts — a permanently blank page, on exactly the devices that can least afford it.
- Cancelling the wrong handle. `requestIdleCallback` returns a handle for `cancelIdleCallback`, and a `setTimeout` returns one for `clearTimeout`; passing either to the other is a silent no-op. Exactly one is ever scheduled and the canceller releases the one that was, or the gate outlives the page and fires an entrance into a tree that no longer exists.
- Assuming `requestIdleCallback` exists. Safari only shipped it in 17.4, so `window.requestIdleCallback(...)` throws on a browser that is still in real use — and it throws inside an effect, which takes the whole page down rather than degrading.
- Putting the phase in the `useGsap` dependency list. Every dependency change reverts the context, and `revert()` strips the inline values GSAP wrote — so the reverse tween reads the stylesheet default as its start value and the exit animates from nowhere to nowhere. The timeline is built once per page and driven from a second effect.
- Hiding `[data-page-enter]` from JavaScript only. An effect runs after the first paint, so the destination is painted fully composed and then hides itself — a flash of the finished page immediately before it animates in. The hidden state belongs in a stylesheet rule keyed on the phase.
- Returning to `preload` after a route change. The preloader is a first-load state; showing it again on every click is the classic version of this mistake. The machine goes back to `gating`, which re-runs the gate without re-running the preloader.
- Gating with reduced motion on. There is no animation left to protect, so all the gate does is hold a blank page in front of someone who asked for less motion, not more waiting. That path skips straight to `settled`.

## Notes

- In Next.js App Router: mount once in `app/layout.tsx` with `pageKey={usePathname()}`, call `ready()` from `document.fonts.ready`, and replace nav `<Link>` elements with buttons calling `leave(() => router.push(href))`. Nothing here imports `next/navigation` — the commit is a callback, so the same machine works under React Router or a plain `useState` page switch.
- `onGateOpen` fires on the frame the gate opens, before the entrance starts. That is where `ScrollTrigger.refresh()` belongs: measure while nothing is moving, or every trigger is offset by the distance the entrance travels. The source did the same thing, refreshing after its preload completed and before its enter.
- Neither `requestIdleCallback` nor `requestAnimationFrame` runs in a backgrounded tab, so the gate does not open until the tab is foregrounded. That is the correct behaviour — an entrance nobody can see is wasted work — but it is also why a headless screenshot taken against a background tab captures the pre-entrance state. Foreground the tab, or drive the timeline to `progress(1)` for capture.
- The preloader should stay up for the whole of `gating`, not just `preload`. The wait is dead time only if you show the visitor an empty page during it; behind a preloader it is indistinguishable from loading.
- The `@media (scripting: none)` rule reveals the content for visitors with JavaScript disabled. It is Media Queries 5 and is simply dropped where unsupported, so treat it as a bonus rather than as the fix.

## Definition of done

Load the preview: the preloader holds, then the content staggers up and in as one group with no element jumping ahead of the tween. Throttle the CPU to 6x in DevTools and reload — the entrance still runs as a smooth stagger rather than arriving in two jerks, because it starts later rather than starting on time and stuttering. Click a nav item: the current content staggers out last-element-first, the page swaps, and the next one arrives after a much shorter gate than the first load used. Click two nav items in quick succession and you land on the first one you clicked. With reduced motion the content is present immediately with no gate, no stagger, and no preloader held past the font load.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
