# Build: Instanced Quad Particles

Four vertices and six indices are shared by every particle; three instanced attributes carry position, size, spin, alpha, tint and shape. One `drawElementsInstanced` puts the whole field on screen. Quads instead of `gl_PointSize` because point sprites are capped at 255px on many drivers, cannot be rotated, and are culled whole the instant their centre leaves the viewport — a large sprite disappears while half of it is still visible.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Up to 1800 drifting particles in one draw call — quads rather than point sprites, so each one has its own size, spin and shape.

- Category: webgl
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: ogl@^1.0.11

## How it works

1. The geometry is one unit quad in `position` (-0.5..0.5) plus an index buffer, and three attributes marked `instanced: 1`: `aOrigin` (field-space rest position), `aParams` (size in CSS px, signed spin rate, base alpha, tint mix) and `aSeed` (two flow phases, spin phase, shape mix). Ten floats per particle, 72 KB at the 1800 ceiling.
2. Buffers are allocated once at `maxCount` and never reallocated. The visible population comes from `geometry.setInstancedCount(count)` where `count` is derived from container area — `clamp(round(megapixels * density), 250, maxCount)` — so the same density reads correctly in a 320px card and a 2000px hero. Because the scatter is random, any prefix of the buffer is still a spatially even field.
3. The vertex shader rotates the quad corner in PIXEL space and only then divides by the drawing-buffer resolution to reach clip space. Rotating in clip space would shear the quad by the container aspect ratio, and a square particle would become a lozenge that changes shape as it spins.
4. Drift is a pure function of `elapsed` and the per-particle seed: the field marches upward with `fract(y + t * RISE)`, then two out-of-phase sinusoids sampled at the particle's own position add wander. No per-particle state is stored, so a resize, a tab switch or a reduced-motion still can all be drawn from one number.
5. `fract` teleports a particle from the top edge to the bottom, which is a visible pop. `uFadeBand` smoothsteps alpha to zero within 12% of each end, so the population always arrives and leaves at zero opacity.
6. One rounded-box SDF in the fragment shader covers both shapes. At `shape` 0 the half-extents and the corner radius are both 0.5, which reduces exactly to `length(uv) - 0.5` — a true circle. At 1 it is a narrow shard, and the shard is the only reason per-particle rotation is visible at all.
7. Blending is additive (`ONE, ONE`) onto an opaque clear colour, which is order independent — a thousand overlapping instances need no depth sort, which is what makes one draw call possible. The canvas is opaque rather than transparent because additive blending onto transparency would have to brighten the page background, and the GPU cannot see it.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `density = 900`
  Particles per megapixel. Tuned so a typical card holds 250-400 and a full-width hero approaches the ceiling. Doubling it does not double the perceived density — it doubles the fill rate and flattens the depth cue that comes from having gaps.
- `maxCount = 1800`
  Ceiling and allocation size. Not a performance limit on the vertex side — 1800 quads is 7200 vertices, nothing — but the fill cost of 1800 soft additive quads averaging 12px is roughly one full screen of blended pixels per frame.
- `MAX_DPR = 1.5`
  Additive fill is the entire cost of this component and it scales with the square of the pixel ratio. Dust has no fine detail that a third sample per axis resolves, so 3x phones render at 1.5x and the frame budget drops by a factor of four against an uncapped ratio.
- `SIZE_BIAS = 2.2`
  Exponent on the uniform random used for size. At 1 a quarter of the population lands in the largest quarter of the range, and a hundred 28px blobs is fog rather than dust. At 2.2 the large sizes are rare enough to read as individuals.
- `RISE = 0.045`
  Field heights per second at `speed` 1 — about 22 seconds to cross. Slow enough that the eye reads drift rather than travel; above ~0.15 the field looks like falling snow played in reverse.
- `FADE_BAND = 0.12`
  Fraction of the field height the wrap fade occupies at each end. Below ~0.06 the pop at the seam becomes visible for the largest particles, whose radius alone is a couple of percent of the height. Above 0.2 a quarter of the field is permanently dim.
- `FLOW_SCALE = 1.4`
  Cycles of wander across the field. Under 1 the whole population slides sideways as a sheet; well above 2 adjacent particles move in opposite directions and the motion reads as noise rather than air.
- `X_MIN / X_MAX = -0.08 / 1.08`
  Field-space x range. Seeding wider than the container means horizontal wander can never bare a strip at the left or right edge. The off-screen quads are clipped by the rasteriser and cost nothing — which is exactly what a point sprite could not do.
- `alpha per particle = 1 - 0.78 * sizeT`
  Large particles are dimmed so total emitted light is roughly independent of size. Without it the few big instances dominate every additive overlap and the field looks like it has hot spots.

## API

```ts
function InstancedQuadParticles(props: { density?: number; maxCount?: number; sizeRange?: readonly [number, number]; softness?: number; spin?: number; speed?: number; wander?: number; opacity?: number; colorA?: string; colorB?: string; background?: string; seed?: number | string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `density: number` — default `900`
  Particles per megapixel of container area. The count is derived from this, not fixed.
- `maxCount: number` — default `1800`
  Population ceiling, and the size the buffers are allocated at.
- `sizeRange: readonly [number, number]` — default `[5, 28]`
  Particle size in CSS pixels. The distribution is biased toward the small end.
- `softness: number` — default `0.62`
  Edge width, 0..1. 0 is a hard silhouette, 1 is a pure gradient. Floored at one device pixel.
- `spin: number` — default `0.5`
  Peak spin in radians per second; each particle takes a signed fraction of it.
- `speed: number` — default `1`
  Multiplier on the whole drift, including the upward march.
- `wander: number` — default `0.06`
  Sinusoidal wander amplitude in field units, where 1 is the container.
- `opacity: number` — default `0.55`
  Overall alpha multiplier applied in the fragment shader.
- `colorA: string` — default `'#9fb4cc'`
  First tint. Any value ogl's `Color` accepts.
- `colorB: string` — default `'#e8ddc9'`
  Second tint; each particle mixes between the two by a seeded amount.
- `background: string` — default `'#07090d'`
  Opaque clear colour the additive field is composited onto.
- `seed: number | string` — default `'instanced-quad-particles'`
  Seeds the scatter. Same seed, same field on every reload and on the server.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function InstancedQuadParticles({
  density = 900,
  maxCount = 1800,
  sizeRange = [5, 28],
  softness = 0.62,
  spin = 0.5,
  speed = 1,
  wander = 0.06,
  opacity = 0.55,
  colorA = '#9fb4cc',
  colorB = '#e8ddc9',
  background = '#07090d',
  seed = 'instanced-quad-particles',
  className,
}: InstancedQuadParticlesProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const stage = useRef<Stage | null>(null);
  const [unsupported, setUnsupported] = useState(false);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const size = useRef({ width, height });
  size.current = { width, height };

  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const visible = useVisibility();
  const { inView } = useInView(host, { rootMargin: '10%' });
  const ready = width > 1 && height > 1;

  const [minSize = 5, maxSize = 28] = sizeRange;

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = host.current;
    if (!el || !ready) return;

    if (!hasWebGL()) {
      setUnsupported(true);
      return;
    }

    // ogl creates its own canvas, and it is appended and removed per effect
    // run. Reusing one React-owned canvas would break under StrictMode: the
    // cleanup force-loses the context, and `getContext` on that same element
    // afterwards hands back the dead one rather than a fresh context.
    const renderer = new Renderer({
      dpr: pixelRatio(MAX_DPR),
      // Opaque, so the field owns every pixel and reads the same on a light or
      // a dark page. Additive blending onto a transparent canvas would have to
      // brighten whatever is behind it, which is the page background, which
      // the GPU cannot see.
      alpha: false,
      // Nothing is sorted and nothing occludes anything, so a depth buffer is
      // memory and a clear per frame for no result.
      depth: false,
      antialias: false,
      // The field is fill-bound, not shader-bound. Asking for the discrete GPU
      // on a laptop costs battery and buys nothing.
      powerPreference: 'low-power',
    });

    const gl = renderer.gl;
    const canvas = gl.canvas;

    const bg = new Color(background);
    gl.clearColor(bg.r, bg.g, bg.b, 1);

    // Four vertices, six indices, shared by every instance.
    const quad = new Float32Array([-0.5, -0.5, 0.5, -0.5, 0.5, 0.5, -0.5, 0.5]);
    const index = new Uint16Array([0, 1, 2, 0, 2, 3]);

    const total = Math.max(MIN_COUNT, Math.round(maxCount));
    const origins = new Float32Array(total * 2);
    const params = new Float32Array(total * 4);
    const seeds = new Float32Array(total * 4);

    const rng = createRng(seed);
    const lo = Math.max(1, Math.min(minSize, maxSize));
    const hi = Math.max(lo + 0.5, Math.max(minSize, maxSize));

    for (let i = 0; i < total; i += 1) {
      origins[i * 2] = randRange(rng, X_MIN, X_MAX);
      origins[i * 2 + 1] = rng();

      // Biased toward small: a linear distribution puts a quarter of the
      // population in the largest quarter of the size range, and a hundred
      // 28px blobs is fog rather than dust.
      const sizeT = Math.pow(rng(), SIZE_BIAS);
      params[i * 4] = lo + (hi - lo) * sizeT;
      params[i * 4 + 1] = randRange(rng, -1, 1) * spin;
      // Big particles are dimmer. Alpha per particle rather than per pixel
      // keeps the total light roughly constant as the size scales.
      params[i * 4 + 2] = 1 - 0.78 * sizeT;
      params[i * 4 + 3] = rng();

      seeds[i * 4] = rng() * Math.PI * 2;
      seeds[i * 4 + 1] = rng() * Math.PI * 2;
      seeds[i * 4 + 2] = rng();
      // A third are discs. The rest are shards, and the shards are the only
      // reason per-particle rotation is visible at all.
      seeds[i * 4 + 3] = rng() < 0.34 ? 0 : randRange(rng, 0.55, 1);
    }

    const geometry = new Geometry(gl, {
      index: { data: index },
      position: { size: 2, data: quad },
      aOrigin: { size: 2, data: origins, instanced: 1 },
      aParams: { size: 4, data: params, instanced: 1 },
      aSeed: { size: 4, data: seeds, instanced: 1 },
    });

    const uniforms: Uniforms = {
      uResolution: { value: [1, 1] },
      uPixelRatio: { value: renderer.dpr },
      uElapsed: { value: 0 },
      uDrift: { value: speed },
      uRise: { value: RISE },
      uFlowScale: { value: FLOW_SCALE },
      uWander: { value: wander },
      uFadeBand: { value: FADE_BAND },
      uColorA: { value: new Color(colorA) },
      uColorB: { value: new Color(colorB) },
      uSoftness: { value: clamp(softness, 0, 1) },
      uOpacity: { value: opacity },
    };

    const program = new Program(gl, {
      vertex: INSTANCED_QUAD_PARTICLES_VERT,
      fragment: INSTANCED_QUAD_PARTICLES_FRAG,
      uniforms,
      transparent: true,
      depthTest: false,
      depthWrite: false,
      // ogl defaults `cullFace` to BACK. The quad's index winding is not
      // guaranteed to face the way the driver expects once it is rotated in
      // the vertex shader, and a culled particle is simply absent.
      cullFace: false,
    });
    // Additive, overriding the source-over that `transparent: true` selected.
    // Order independent, so a thousand overlapping instances need no sort —
    // which is what makes one draw call possible in the first place.
    program.setBlendFunc(gl.ONE, gl.ONE);

    const mesh = new Mesh(gl, { geometry, program });

    el.appendChild(canvas);
    canvas.style.display = 'block';

    const resize = (w: number, h: number) => {
      renderer.setSize(w, h);
      // `setSize` writes literal px into the canvas's inline style, which wins
      // over any class. Re-asserting percentages keeps the element fluid
      // between resize notifications.
      canvas.style.width = '100%';
      canvas.style.height = '100%';

      uniforms.uResolution.value = [gl.drawingBufferWidth, gl.drawingBufferHeight];
      uniforms.uPixelRatio.value = renderer.dpr;

      // Population from area, not from a fixed number: the same density looks
      // right in a 320px card and in a 2000px hero. The buffers already hold
      // `total` particles in scattered order, so a prefix of them is still a
      // spatially even field — no rebuild, no reallocation.
      const megapixels = (w * h) / 1_000_000;
      const count = clamp(Math.round(megapixels * density), MIN_COUNT, total);
      geometry.setInstancedCount(count);
    };

    const draw = (elapsed: number) => {
      uniforms.uElapsed.value = elapsed;
      renderer.render({ scene: mesh });
    };

    resize(size.current.width, size.current.height);
    stage.current = { renderer, geometry, program, mesh, uniforms, resize, draw };
    draw(STATIC_ELAPSED);

    return () => {
      stage.current = null;
      // ogl has no `dispose()`: `remove()` on the geometry deletes its VAOs and
      // every buffer, `remove()` on the program deletes the shaders and the
      // program, and only then is the context worth handing back.
      geometry.remove();
      program.remove();
      loseContext(gl);
      canvas.width = 0;
      canvas.height = 0;
      canvas.remove();
    };
  }, [
    ready,
    density,
    maxCount,
    minSize,
    maxSize,
    softness,
    spin,
    speed,
    wander,
    opacity,
    colorA,
    colorB,
    background,
    seed,
  ]);

  // Resize is its own effect: a reflow costs a `setSize` and an instanced-count
  // change, never a buffer rebuild.
  useEffect(() => {
    stage.current?.resize(width, height);
    if (reduced) stage.current?.draw(STATIC_ELAPSED);
  }, [width, height, reduced]);

  useRaf(
    (_dt, elapsed) => stage.current?.draw(elapsed),
    ready && inView && visible && !reduced && !unsupported,
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `geometry.remove()` deletes every VAO and every buffer, `program.remove()` deletes the shaders and the program, then `loseContext(gl)` hands the context back through `WEBGL_lose_context` — ogl has no `dispose()` and nothing else releases a context. The canvas backing store is zeroed and the node removed, so the drawing buffer goes with it rather than waiting for GC.

**Reduced motion.** The rAF subscription is never made and the field is drawn once at `elapsed` 0. That is a complete, correct frame rather than a collapsed one: the scatter, sizes, tints, shapes and spin phases are all per-particle seeds that already vary at t=0, and the wrap fade applies exactly as it does in motion. Resizing redraws the same still.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Reaching for `gl_PointSize`. It is capped — 255px on a great many drivers, and the cap is silent — it cannot be rotated, and the sprite is culled by its centre point, so anything large blinks out while half of it is still on screen.
- Leaving ogl's `cullFace` at its default. `Program` defaults it to `gl.BACK`; once the quad corners are rotated in the vertex shader the winding the driver sees is not the winding you authored, and culled particles are simply absent with no error anywhere.
- Rotating the corner offset after converting to clip space. The container aspect ratio shears it, so a particle is square only when the container is, and it visibly changes shape through a spin.
- Rebuilding the buffers on resize to change the particle count. `setInstancedCount` selects a prefix of what is already uploaded; reallocating 72 KB of GPU memory on every ResizeObserver notification is a stall for no visual difference.
- Wrapping with `fract` and no fade. The seam is a hard teleport, and at 1800 particles something is crossing it constantly, so the field flickers along one edge.
- Compositing an additive field onto a transparent canvas. Additive needs to know what it is adding to; with `alpha: true` the destination is zero, the result is the particle colour flat, and the field looks pasted on rather than glowing.
- Reusing one React-owned canvas across effect runs. Cleanup force-loses the context, and `getContext` on that same element afterwards returns the dead one — under StrictMode's mount / unmount / mount that means every instance is permanently black. ogl creates its own canvas, which is appended and removed per run.
- Assuming `renderer.setSize` leaves the CSS alone. ogl writes literal px into the canvas's inline `style`, which beats any class; the percentages have to be re-asserted after every call or the element stops being fluid.

## Notes

- ogl rather than three: the whole component is one instanced mesh with no lights, no camera and no scene graph, and ogl's `Geometry` exposes instanced attributes directly with `instanced: 1` instead of through an `InstancedBufferGeometry` wrapper.
- No camera is passed to `renderer.render`, which is deliberate. Without one ogl skips frustum culling and the matrix uniforms entirely — the shader writes clip space itself, so a projection matrix would be an identity multiply per vertex.
- `depth: false` on the context. Nothing occludes anything under additive blending, so a depth buffer would be memory plus a clear per frame for no result.
- Sizes are authored in CSS pixels and multiplied by the pixel ratio in the shader, so the field looks identical across a dpr change and nothing needs rebuilding when one happens.
- GLSL ES 1.00 with no derivative functions: the edge anti-aliasing floor is `1.0 / sizePx`, which is exact for a quad of that pixel size, so the same source compiles under a WebGL1 fallback context where `fwidth` needs an extension.

## Definition of done

The field drifts upward and sideways with no visible seam at the top or bottom edge, and no particle ever appears or vanishes abruptly. Individual particles spin, and the shards are visibly rotating rather than shimmering. Resize the container narrow and wide: particles stay square at every aspect ratio, and the population changes without a stutter. One draw call per frame in a frame capture, whatever the count. Mount and unmount a dozen instances and none of the earlier ones go black.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Inverse Scroll Scale

The inverse of the usual scroll-scale. Instead of growing as it rises, the media starts oversized and resolves down to exactly 1.0 over the first 60% of the scroller, so it settles into its frame rather than bursting out of it — and it is at rest for the whole time it is the thing you are actually looking at. No animation library: one rAF callback, gated by an IntersectionObserver.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Media enters oversized at 1.25x and settles to exactly 1.0 as it rises through the first 60% of the scroller.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. Each frame the component reads the frame element's `getBoundingClientRect().top`, converts it to a position inside the scroller by subtracting the scroller's own rect top, and computes `t = clamp((height - top) / (span * height), 0, 1)`.
2. `t` is 0 while the frame's top edge sits on the bottom of the scroller and reaches 1 once it has climbed `span` of the scroller's height — 60% by default, so it is finished long before the element is centred.
3. Scale is a straight linear ramp: `from - (from - 1) * t`. It ends on exactly 1.0 by construction, which matters because a scale below 1 on an element sized to its frame would let the frame show through at the edges.
4. Optional smoothing runs the result through `damp(current, wanted, smoothing, dt)`, which raises the retention factor to the power of elapsed time and so converges at the same rate on 60Hz and 120Hz displays. The naive `x += (target - x) * 0.1` would run twice as fast on the faster display.
5. The frame is rounded to four decimals and compared against what was last written; on the many frames where nothing changed the style write is skipped entirely, so an idle instance costs one rect read.
6. An IntersectionObserver with a 20% rootMargin flips an `active` ref, and the rAF callback returns immediately when it is false. The observer is hand-rolled rather than pooled because it needs the demo's scroller as its `root`.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `from = 1.25`
  Starting scale. Must be at least 1 — anything less shows the frame through the edges of the media, because the media is sized to exactly fill the frame. Past ~1.4 the visible crop at the start is severe enough that the composition changes rather than just the size.
- `span = 0.6`
  Fraction of scroller height over which the scale resolves, measured up from the bottom edge. The whole argument for the effect: at 1.0 the media is still moving while it is centred and being read, which is exactly when it should be still. At 0.6 it lands well before that.
- `smoothing = 0`
  Off by default. The mapping from scroll position to scale is already continuous, so smoothing adds lag with nothing to hide. It exists for the case where the scroll source is itself steppy (a trackpad-free mouse wheel, or a snapped container).
- `rootMargin = '20% 0px 20% 0px'`
  Starts the rAF work a fifth of a scroller height before the frame is visible, so the first painted frame is already at the correct scale. Without the margin the element pops from its authored scale to its computed one on the frame it enters.
- `toFixed precision = 4`
  Below one device pixel of difference on a 4000px-wide element, so the rounding is invisible; its purpose is to make the "unchanged" comparison actually hit, which it never would on raw floats.

## API

```ts
function InverseScrollScale(props: { children: ReactNode; from?: number; span?: number; smoothing?: number; scrollerRef?: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  The media. Sized to fill the frame; this is what gets scaled.
- `from: number` — default `1.25`
  Starting scale. Must be >= 1.
- `span: number` — default `0.6`
  Fraction of scroller height over which the scale resolves.
- `smoothing: number` — default `0`
  Fraction of the remaining gap left after one second. 0 disables smoothing.
- `scrollerRef: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>`
  The scroll container that owns the scroll position. Omit for the document.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the frame via `cn`. Set the frame size here.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function InverseScrollScale({
  children,
  from = 1.25,
  span = 0.6,
  smoothing = 0,
  scrollerRef,
  className,
}: InverseScrollScaleProps) {
  const frame = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const media = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const active = useRef(false);
  const scale = useRef(from);
  const written = useRef(-1);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  // Gate the rAF work on visibility. Hand-rolled rather than `useInView`
  // because the observer needs a custom `root` — the demo's own scroller —
  // and a pooled observer keyed only by threshold would hand back one rooted
  // at the document.
  useEffect(() => {
    const el = frame.current;
    if (!el || reduced) return;

    const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
      (entries) => {
        for (const entry of entries) active.current = entry.isIntersecting;
      },
      { root: scrollerRef?.current ?? null, rootMargin: '20% 0px 20% 0px' },
    );
    observer.observe(el);
    return () => observer.disconnect();
  }, [reduced, scrollerRef]);

  useRaf(
    (dt) => {
      const el = frame.current;
      const target = media.current;
      if (!el || !target || !active.current) return;

      // One read pass, then one write pass. Reading the rect after writing a
      // transform in the same frame forces a synchronous layout.
      const scroller = scrollerRef?.current ?? null;
      const rect = el.getBoundingClientRect();
      const height = scroller ? scroller.clientHeight : window.innerHeight;
      const top = scroller ? rect.top - scroller.getBoundingClientRect().top : rect.top;

      // t is 0 while the frame's top edge is at the bottom of the scroller and
      // reaches 1 once it has risen `span` of the scroller's height.
      const t = clamp((height - top) / (span * height), 0, 1);
      const wanted = from - (from - 1) * t;

      scale.current =
        smoothing > 0 ? damp(scale.current, wanted, smoothing, dt) : wanted;

      // Four decimals is below one device pixel on a 4000px element, and the
      // equality check skips the style write on the many frames where nothing
      // changed — an idle instance then costs a rect read and nothing else.
      const next = Number(scale.current.toFixed(4));
      if (next === written.current) return;
      written.current = next;
      target.style.transform = `scale(${next})`;
    },
    !reduced,
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useRaf` unsubscribes on unmount and drops the shared loop entirely when it was the last subscriber; the IntersectionObserver is disconnected in its own effect cleanup. Without the disconnect the observer holds a reference to a removed element and keeps firing on every scroll of a container the component no longer participates in.

**Reduced motion.** The media renders at scale 1 — its resolved state, filling the frame — and neither the IntersectionObserver nor the rAF subscription is created, so there is no per-frame work at all.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Using `window.innerHeight` when the element scrolls inside a container. Inside a 300px-tall panel on a 1000px-tall window, `t` never exceeds about 0.3, so the media stays visibly oversized for the whole scroll and never resolves.
- Scaling from below 1 up to 1 instead. The media is sized to its frame, so any scale under 1 leaves a gap at the edges and the background shows through as a hairline border that grows and shrinks.
- Reading `getBoundingClientRect()` after writing the transform in the same callback. That is a forced synchronous layout every frame, and it appears in a profile as a long purple bar attached to the rAF, not as anything obviously related to this component.
- Running the rAF callback for every instance on the page. Ten of these in a long article means ten rect reads per frame for elements that are nowhere near the viewport; the IntersectionObserver gate is what keeps the cost proportional to what is on screen.
- A per-frame lerp constant instead of `damp` when smoothing is enabled. On a 120Hz display the media reaches its target in half the scroll distance, so the effect is materially different on a MacBook Pro than on an external 60Hz monitor.
- Omitting `overflow: hidden` on the frame. At 1.25 the media is 25% larger than its box and overlaps whatever is next to it, which is most visible as text from the following section being covered as you scroll.

## Notes

- No animation library. The whole component is one rAF subscription and one IntersectionObserver.
- The transform is written imperatively rather than through React state, so no scroll frame causes a render.

## Definition of done

Scroll the frame up from the bottom of the scroller: the media is visibly cropped and oversized as it appears, and reaches its natural size a little past halfway up — after which it does not move at all while you read it. Scroll back down and it re-expands. No hairline of background is ever visible inside the frame. With reduced motion on, the media is at natural size at all scroll positions.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: IntersectionObserver Reveal

A wrapper that fades and lifts its child into place the first time it enters the scroll container. The transition is one inline string built from four numbers, so nothing is injected into the document and nothing has to load. Every instance that asks for the same root and the same observation box shares one IntersectionObserver, which is what makes it safe to put two hundred of these on a page.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

One element, one fade-and-rise on entry, no stylesheet and no library — with a single observer shared across every instance.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The element renders at `opacity: 0` and `translate3d(0, 28px, 0)` with a transition string of `opacity 0.7s cubic-bezier(0.22,1,0.36,1) {delay}s, transform 0.7s cubic-bezier(0.22,1,0.36,1) {delay}s`. State flips both properties at once, so the browser interpolates on the compositor and the main thread does nothing after the flip.
2. The observer is pooled in a two-level module map: root element first, then a `rootMargin|threshold` string. `null` is a legal Map key, so "the viewport" gets its own bucket without a sentinel. Each bucket holds a `Map<Element, handler>` and the observer callback dispatches by target — one callback for every reveal in a container.
3. The pool is refcounted. Teardown deletes the handler and unobserves, then disconnects and drops the bucket only when the last target has left. Disconnecting per instance would tear the shared observer out from under every other reveal in the same container.
4. The root is resolved as: an explicit `scroller` ref, else the first ancestor whose computed `overflow-x` or `overflow-y` is `auto`, `scroll` or `overlay`, else `null` for the viewport. `window` is never referenced, so the component behaves the same inside a 320 px preview card as on a full page.
5. `threshold: 0.15` with `rootMargin: "0px 0px -8% 0px"` shrinks the observation box 8% up from the bottom, so an element must be genuinely inside the container before it fires rather than merely touching its edge.
6. Staggering is the caller's job and costs one number: give siblings `delay={0}`, `0.08`, `0.16`. There is no group concept and no shared timeline, which is precisely what keeps the component this small.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `duration = 0.7`
  Seconds. Long enough that a 28 px rise reads as a settle rather than a snap; past ~1s a fast scroller has already read the text while it is still moving.
- `distance = 28`
  Pixels of travel. Roughly one and a half line heights — the element stays inside its own block, so the reveal reads as the content arriving rather than as a card flying in from off-screen. Above ~60 px the motion starts to compete with the scroll itself.
- `ease = cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)`
  Ease-out-quint. Most of the travel is spent in the first third, which is what makes a reveal feel like arrival. A symmetric curve on an entrance always reads as sluggish because the slow part happens while the element is still visibly out of place.
- `threshold = 0.15`
  15% of the element must be visible. At 0 a single intersecting pixel fires the reveal, so a tall element finishes animating before it is on screen. Above ~0.4 an element taller than the container can never satisfy it and never reveals at all.
- `rootMargin = 0px 0px -8% 0px`
  The negative bottom is the whole point: it pulls the trigger line 8% up from the container's bottom edge so the element is inside the box, not touching it. A positive bottom margin fires below the fold and the user scrolls onto content that has already finished.

## API

```ts
function IoReveal(props: { children: ReactNode; scroller?: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>; delay?: number; duration?: number; distance?: number; ease?: string; threshold?: number; rootMargin?: string; repeat?: boolean; as?: ElementType; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  The revealed content.
- `scroller: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>`
  Scroll container for the observer. Omit and the nearest scrollable ancestor is found by walking computed overflow.
- `delay: number` — default `0`
  Seconds of delay. Staggering siblings is done by passing 0, 0.08, 0.16.
- `duration: number` — default `0.7`
  Seconds of travel and fade.
- `distance: number` — default `28`
  Starting vertical offset in pixels. Positive rises into place.
- `ease: string` — default `'cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)'`
  Any CSS timing function.
- `threshold: number` — default `0.15`
  Fraction of the element that must be visible before it fires.
- `rootMargin: string` — default `'0px 0px -8% 0px'`
  Observation box inset. Part of the shared-observer pool key.
- `repeat: boolean` — default `false`
  Re-hide when the element leaves. Off by default, which also lets settled targets be unobserved.
- `as: ElementType` — default `'div'`
  Element to render, so the wrapper can be inline or a list item.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the rendered element.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/* --------------------------------------------------------------------------
   The shared observer pool.

   Keyed by root element first, then by the option string. `null` is a legal
   key in a Map, which is what lets "the viewport" share a bucket with itself
   without a sentinel value. Each bucket refcounts its targets and the
   observer is disconnected when the last one leaves, so a route change does
   not leave observers watching detached nodes.
   -------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
type Handler = (entry: IntersectionObserverEntry) => void;

interface Bucket {
  observer: IntersectionObserver;
  handlers: Map<Element, Handler>;
}

const pools = new Map<Element | null, Map<string, Bucket>>();

function bucketFor(root: Element | null, rootMargin: string, threshold: number): Bucket {
  let byOptions = pools.get(root);
  if (!byOptions) {
    byOptions = new Map<string, Bucket>();
    pools.set(root, byOptions);
  }
  const key = `${rootMargin}|${threshold}`;
  const existing = byOptions.get(key);
  if (existing) return existing;

  const handlers = new Map<Element, Handler>();
  const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
    (entries) => {
      for (const entry of entries) handlers.get(entry.target)?.(entry);
    },
    { root, rootMargin, threshold },
  );
  const bucket: Bucket = { observer, handlers };
  byOptions.set(key, bucket);
  return bucket;
}

function release(root: Element | null, rootMargin: string, threshold: number): void {
  const byOptions = pools.get(root);
  if (!byOptions) return;
  const key = `${rootMargin}|${threshold}`;
  const bucket = byOptions.get(key);
  if (!bucket || bucket.handlers.size > 0) return;
  bucket.observer.disconnect();
  byOptions.delete(key);
  if (byOptions.size === 0) pools.delete(root);
}

/**
 * Nearest ancestor that actually scrolls. An `overflow: auto` element that has
 * not overflowed yet still counts: it is the container this reveal will live
 * inside once content arrives. Returning `null` means the viewport, which is
 * the value IntersectionObserver's `root` already uses for that.
 */
function nearestScrollParent(node: Element | null): Element | null {
  let el = node?.parentElement ?? null;
  while (el) {
    const { overflowY, overflowX } = getComputedStyle(el);
    if (/(auto|scroll|overlay)/.test(overflowY + overflowX)) return el;
    el = el.parentElement;
  }
  return null;
}

export function IoReveal({
  children,
  scroller,
  delay = 0,
  duration = DURATION,
  distance = DISTANCE,
  ease = EASE,
  threshold = THRESHOLD,
  rootMargin = ROOT_MARGIN,
  repeat = false,
  as,
  className,
}: IoRevealProps) {
  const ref = useRef<HTMLElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const [revealed, setRevealed] = useState(false);

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = ref.current;
    if (!el || reduced) return;
    if (typeof IntersectionObserver === 'undefined') {
      // A missing API degrades to visible content, never to a blank page.
      setRevealed(true);
      return;
    }

    const root = scroller ? scroller.current : nearestScrollParent(el);
    const bucket = bucketFor(root, rootMargin, threshold);

    const handle: Handler = (entry) => {
      if (entry.isIntersecting) {
        setRevealed(true);
        if (!repeat) {
          bucket.handlers.delete(el);
          bucket.observer.unobserve(el);
        }
      } else if (repeat) {
        setRevealed(false);
      }
    };

    bucket.handlers.set(el, handle);
    bucket.observer.observe(el);

    return () => {
      bucket.handlers.delete(el);
      bucket.observer.unobserve(el);
      // Refcounted: the observer only dies with its last target. Disconnecting
      // per instance would tear the shared observer out from under every other
      // reveal in the same container.
      release(root, rootMargin, threshold);
    };
  }, [scroller, rootMargin, threshold, repeat, reduced]);

  /* Reduced motion is a different render, not a faster one: no transition
     property is emitted at all, and the element is at its resolved end state
     from the first paint. */
  const style: CSSProperties = reduced
    ? {}
    : {
        opacity: revealed ? 1 : 0,
        transform: revealed ? 'translate3d(0, 0, 0)' : `translate3d(0, ${distance}px, 0)`,
        // One string, two properties, one shared delay. Written inline on
        // purpose: this variant ships no stylesheet, so there is nothing for a
        // consumer's CSS to load and nothing to hoist.
        transition: `opacity ${duration}s ${ease} ${delay}s, transform ${duration}s ${ease} ${delay}s`,
        willChange: revealed ? undefined : 'opacity, transform',
      };
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The effect deletes its handler from the shared bucket, unobserves its own element, then calls `release`, which disconnects the observer and drops the bucket only when no handlers remain. No listeners, no rAF, no timers. The pool itself holds no reference to an element once its handler is removed, so nothing keeps a detached node alive.

**Reduced motion.** The reduced branch renders a different element, not a faster one: the style object is empty, so no `opacity`, no `transform` and no `transition` are emitted and the content is at its resolved final state on the first paint. No observer is created either, which also means no work is scheduled for a user who asked for none. `useReducedMotion` reads through `useSyncExternalStore`, so the value lands in the hydration commit and the animated variant is never painted.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Keying the shared observer on `rootMargin` and `threshold` but not on the root. The first instance to mount then decides which container everyone measures against, and every later instance inside a different scroll panel reports "in view" from the start — so an entire panel reveals on mount and never animates again. The root has to be part of the key.
- Calling `observer.disconnect()` in a single instance's cleanup. With a shared observer that stops every other reveal in the same container dead, and the symptom appears only after a route change unmounts one card. Delete the handler, unobserve the one target, and disconnect only when the handler map is empty.
- Constructing an observer per element. It works and it is invisible at ten elements; at two hundred the browser services two hundred separate intersection computations on every scroll of the container and the frame budget goes to bookkeeping.
- One observer for the whole page with `root: null` when the content is inside an `overflow-y: auto` panel. Everything in the panel intersects the viewport from the start, so every reveal fires at mount.
- Animating `top` or `margin-top` instead of `transform`. Both are layout properties: the reveal then triggers layout on every frame for every element currently animating, and a page with a dozen simultaneous reveals visibly stutters.
- Leaving `will-change: opacity, transform` on after the reveal. Every settled element keeps its own compositor layer, and a long page accumulates hundreds of them until scrolling gets slower the further down you go. It is set only while the element is still hidden.
- Treating reduced motion as `duration: 0`. That still emits a transition and still runs the state flip through the compositor. Here the reduced branch emits no `transition`, no `opacity` and no `transform` at all, so the element is simply in its final position from the first paint.

## Notes

- This variant ships zero CSS, which is the trade it makes: the hidden start state is an inline style on the first render, so a document that never executes scripts renders the content hidden. `css-var-stagger-reveal` is the sibling that pays for a hoisted stylesheet and gets a `@media (scripting: none)` escape hatch in return. Choose this one for a component library where injecting global CSS is unwelcome; choose that one for a site where a designer will retune the choreography and no-JS has to look right.
- Compared to a GSAP reveal system, this cannot scrub, cannot be measured against a `containerAnimation`, and has no timeline you can seek. It is deliberately the floor of the feature set: entry, once, with a delay.
- `as` lets the wrapper be a `span` inside a paragraph or an `li` inside a list, so the reveal does not force an invalid nesting or an extra block-level box into the layout.

## Definition of done

Scroll the container and each element rises 28 px and fades in as it comes properly into view, not as it touches the bottom edge. Give three siblings delays of 0, 0.08 and 0.16 and they arrive in sequence. Mount fifty of them and the browser reports one IntersectionObserver, not fifty. Unmount one card and the rest keep revealing. With reduced motion on, every element is already in place and inspecting it shows no inline `transition` at all.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Single Param Object Timeline

A scroll-driven scene written as data instead of as tweens. One mutable object holds every animated quantity, GSAP tweens the object rather than the DOM, and a single onUpdate writes one transform string and two opacities. The story is then an array of rows — section id, point through the section, params to move to — each anchored to where its section actually sits after layout.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

One plain object holds every animated value; the scroll story is a table of keyframes anchored to real sections.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. Every animated quantity lives in one object: `{ scale, spin, driftX, driftY, glow, dissolve }`. No element is a tween target; GSAP tweens the plain object and one `onUpdate` renders it, so the number of tweens is the number of story beats rather than the number of moving parts.
2. Each keyframe is anchored to a real section: `anchor = clamp(0, 1, (el.offsetTop + el.offsetHeight * t - view / 2) / total)`, where `total = container.offsetHeight - view` is the scroll distance the trigger covers.
3. That expression reads as "when the point `t` through this section reaches the middle of the viewport". `t = 0.5` is the section's own middle, so the beat fires when the reader is looking at the copy it belongs to, at any column width.
4. Rows are sorted by anchor and each is given `duration = nextAnchor - thisAnchor`, so the scene is continuously in motion between beats instead of arriving early and sitting still until the next anchor.
5. `ease: "none"` on every row. Under a scrub the ease warps timeline time, not screen time, so an eased row reaches its params before or after the section it is anchored to — which defeats the anchoring.
6. A `useResizeObserver` on the container re-runs the whole build when its height changes, because every anchor is a function of `offsetTop` and `offsetTop` moves whenever a line wraps.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `scrub = 0.8`
  Just under a second of catch-up. Enough that the scene continues to resolve after the wheel stops, which is what makes it read as a film rather than a slider; `true` welds it to the wheel and every scroll jitter shows up in the mark.
- `at = 0.5`
  Default point through a section at which its keyframe lands. 0.5 puts the beat on the section's midpoint crossing the middle of the scroller. Values near 0 fire while the section is still entering, which reads as the scene reacting to copy the reader has not got to yet.
- `REST.glow = 0.35`
  The scene's idle state, not zero. The stage has to be worth looking at before the first keyframe and after the last one; starting at 0 means the reader's first impression of the component is an empty box.
- `total floor = 1`
  Guards `container.offsetHeight - view` against 0 or negative, which happens for one frame during layout and on a short container. Without it every anchor divides by zero, becomes Infinity, clamps to 1, and the whole story collapses onto the last frame.
- `span floor = 0.001`
  Two keyframes anchored to the same point would otherwise get duration 0. GSAP accepts it, but the row then applies as an instant jump, so a carefully anchored beat becomes a snap.
- `section gap = 45vh`
  Spacing between story sections, in scroller heights. Below about 30vh two anchors land close enough that their spans overlap heavily and the beats blur together; well above it the scene is static for long stretches.

## API

```ts
function KeyframeParamObject(props: { sections: { id: string; label: string; title: string; body?: string; at?: number; to: Partial<StageParams> }[]; scrub?: number; scrollerRef?: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `sections: KeyframeSection[]`
  The story. Each row names a section, an optional point through it, and the params to move to.
- `sections[].at: number` — default `0.5`
  Point through the section, 0-1, at which its keyframe lands.
- `sections[].to: Partial<StageParams>`
  Params this beat moves to. Anything omitted holds its current value.
- `scrub: number` — default `0.8`
  Seconds of catch-up behind the scroll position.
- `scrollerRef: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>`
  The scroll container that owns the scroll position. Omit for the document.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the container via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function KeyframeParamObject({
  sections,
  scrub = 0.8,
  scrollerRef,
  className,
}: KeyframeParamObjectProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const mark = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const halo = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  // Rebuild the anchor table whenever the column reflows: every anchor is a
  // function of offsetTop, and offsetTop changes when a line wraps.
  const { height } = useResizeObserver(root);

  useGsap(
    gsap,
    () => {
      const container = root.current;
      const markEl = mark.current;
      const haloEl = halo.current;
      if (!container || !markEl || !haloEl) return;

      // The one mutable object. Cloned per build so a rebuild starts clean
      // rather than inheriting wherever the last scrub left it.
      const params: StageParams = { ...REST };

      const render = () => {
        markEl.style.transform =
          `translate3d(${params.driftX}%, ${params.driftY}%, 0) ` +
          `rotate(${params.spin * 360}deg) scale(${params.scale})`;
        markEl.style.opacity = String(Math.max(0, 1 - params.dissolve));
        haloEl.style.opacity = String(params.glow);
        haloEl.style.transform = `scale(${1 + params.glow * 0.6})`;
      };

      if (reduced) {
        // Land on the last keyframe: the end of the story, statically.
        for (const section of sections) Object.assign(params, section.to);
        render();
        return;
      }

      const scroller = scrollerRef?.current ?? null;
      const view = scroller ? scroller.clientHeight : window.innerHeight;
      // Scroll distance the trigger actually covers. Guarded against 0, which
      // would make every anchor Infinity and stack the whole story on frame 1.
      const total = Math.max(1, container.offsetHeight - view);

      const anchor = (el: HTMLElement, t: number) =>
        gsap.utils.clamp(0, 1, (el.offsetTop + el.offsetHeight * t - view / 2) / total);

      const rows = sections
        .map((section) => {
          const el = container.querySelector<HTMLElement>(`[data-keyframe="${section.id}"]`);
          return el ? { at: anchor(el, section.at ?? 0.5), to: section.to } : null;
        })
        .filter((row): row is { at: number; to: Partial<StageParams> } => row !== null)
        // Authoring order is document order, but a custom `at` can reorder
        // them; the timeline needs them sorted to compute each row's span.
        .sort((a, b) => a.at - b.at);

      const timeline = gsap.timeline({
        scrollTrigger: {
          trigger: container,
          scroller: scroller ?? undefined,
          start: 'top top',
          end: 'bottom bottom',
          scrub,
          invalidateOnRefresh: true,
        },
        onUpdate: render,
      });

      rows.forEach((row, i) => {
        const next = rows[i + 1];
        // Each row travels until the next one begins, so the scene is always
        // in motion between beats and never sits finished waiting for the
        // next anchor.
        const span = Math.max(0.001, (next ? next.at : 1) - row.at);
        // `ease: 'none'` — under a scrub the ease warps timeline time, so an
        // eased row arrives at its params before or after its own section.
        timeline.to(params, { ...row.to, duration: span, ease: 'none' }, row.at);
      });

      render();
    },
    root,
    [sections, scrub, scrollerRef, reduced, height],
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useGsap` reverts the `gsap.context`, which kills the timeline and its ScrollTrigger and drops the reference to the params object. This runs on every reflow as well as on unmount: a surviving trigger would keep scrubbing a timeline built against stale `offsetTop` values while a new one runs alongside it, and the two would write conflicting transforms to the same element on the same frame.

**Reduced motion.** No timeline and no ScrollTrigger are created. Every keyframe is folded into the params object in order and rendered once, so the stage shows the end of the story and the copy is fully readable and correctly laid out.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Hand-tuning keyframe positions as raw timeline fractions. A single line wrap moves every section below it, so the beat that was on the right paragraph at 1440px is a paragraph early at 1280px. Anchoring to `offsetTop` is the fix and is the reason for the whole `anchor` expression.
- Not rebuilding when the container reflows. The anchors are computed once from measurements taken at build time; a font swap, an image load or an orientation change moves the sections and the timeline keeps using the old numbers.
- Tweening the DOM directly instead of the object. With six properties across three elements you get a tween per property per beat, they fight over the same transform string, and the last one to write wins non-deterministically.
- Easing the rows under a scrub. The ease is applied to timeline time, so the params reach their target at a different scroll position than the anchor says — the beat visibly detaches from its heading.
- Reusing one module-level params object across builds. On rebuild the tweens start from wherever the previous scrub left the object rather than from the resting state, so the scene is subtly different after every resize.
- Letting `total` be zero. It happens on the first layout pass and on any container shorter than the viewport; every anchor becomes Infinity, clamps to 1, and the entire story plays in the last pixel of scroll.

## Notes

- The stage is `position: sticky`, not fixed, so it is bounded by the component rather than by the page and works inside any scroll container.
- Pass `sections` as a stable reference (module scope or memoised) — it is a dependency of the build effect.

## Definition of done

Scroll through the column: the mark scales, spins, drifts and dims, and each change lines up with the heading that names it reaching the middle of the panel. Resize the panel so the copy rewraps and scroll again — the beats still land on their headings. Stop mid-scroll and the scene keeps resolving for around a second. With reduced motion on, the stage shows the final state and nothing moves.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Knockout Zoom Pin

A sticky section holds a single word while a manufactured scroll range plays a zoom out: the word starts several screens wide, showing a gradient through its letters, and settles into a normal headline position. No library — the progress is read from the sticky section's own rect, smoothed exponentially in wall-clock time, and written as one composited transform per changed frame.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A word the size of the screen shrinks into a headline as you scroll, with the scene showing through its letters.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The scroll range is manufactured from the scroller's own height: the section is sized `hostHeight * (1 + viewports)` in pixels and the sticky child is sized `hostHeight`, so the leftover is exactly the pin duration. Pixels, not `vh`, because inside a scrollable box viewport units describe the wrong element.
2. Progress is `(hostTop - sectionTop) / (total - hostHeight)`, clamped. It comes from `getBoundingClientRect()` on the frame it is used, so it stays correct through resizes, font swaps and layout shifts with nothing to invalidate.
3. The raw progress is smoothed with `damp(smoothed, target, smoothing, dt)` — `x + (t - x) * (1 - s^dt)` — so the settle takes the same wall-clock time at 60 and 144 Hz. The per-frame form (`x += (t - x) * 0.1`) converges more than twice as fast on a high-refresh display.
4. Scale and position use different curves on purpose. Scale is `cover - (cover - 1) * easeOutCubic(L)`, front-loading the shrink; the recentre is `easeInCubic(L)`, which keeps the word centred until it is small enough for its position to mean anything.
5. The transform is built as a string, rounded to 4 decimals of scale and 0.1 px of translate, and compared with the previous frame's string. Unchanged frames skip the DOM write entirely, which at both ends of the range is most of them.
6. The letters are a window rather than a fill: `background-clip: text` with a transparent colour, so the gradient behind them scales with the word and the section reads as cut out of the page.
7. The word is sized in `cqw` against a `container-type: inline-size` pin box, so the component is identical in a 320 px preview card and a full-bleed page without a single breakpoint.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `cover = 7`
  Scale at progress 0 — enough that only the counters of one or two letters are on screen, so the opening frame reads as texture and the reveal of the word is the payoff. Below ~4 the word is legible immediately and there is nothing to reveal.
- `viewports = 1.6`
  Scroll travel as a multiple of the scroller height. Under ~1 the zoom is over before it registers; past ~2.5 the pin outstays its welcome and users start scrolling hard to escape it.
- `smoothing = 0.0067`
  Fraction of the gap remaining after one second — `e^-5`, i.e. the familiar `1 - exp(-5 * dt)` filter. It removes trackpad and wheel-step judder without the word feeling detached from the hand. At 0.05 the lag is visible as rubberiness.
- `rest = -0.3`
  Final vertical position as a fraction of the pinned box: three tenths above centre, which is where a display headline sits when body copy follows it.
- `veil window = progress 0.45 → 0.95`
  When the content behind fades up. Earlier and it competes with a word still too large to read past; later and it arrives after the motion has stopped, which reads as a second, unrelated event.
- `write quantisation = 4 dp scale, 0.1 px translate`
  Below a tenth of a device pixel nothing changes on screen, so the comparison lets idle frames cost one string build and one comparison instead of a style write and a composite.

## API

```ts
function KnockoutZoomPin(props: { children: ReactNode; behind?: ReactNode; cover?: number; viewports?: number; smoothing?: number; rest?: number; scroller?: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  The word. Kept on one line — it is a display element.
- `behind: ReactNode`
  Content faded up behind the word as it settles.
- `cover: number` — default `7`
  Scale at progress 0.
- `viewports: number` — default `1.6`
  Scroll travel as a multiple of the scroller height.
- `smoothing: number` — default `0.0067`
  Fraction of the gap left after one second.
- `rest: number` — default `-0.3`
  Final vertical position as a fraction of the pinned box height.
- `scroller: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>`
  Scroll container. Omit to auto-detect the nearest scrollable ancestor.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the outer section.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function KnockoutZoomPin({
  children,
  behind,
  cover = 7,
  viewports = 1.6,
  smoothing = 0.0067,
  rest = -0.3,
  scroller,
  className,
}: KnockoutZoomPinProps) {
  const section = useRef<HTMLElement>(null);
  const pin = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const word = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const veil = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);

  const smoothed = useRef(0);
  const lastTransform = useRef('');
  const lastVeil = useRef('');
  const lastHeights = useRef(0);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  useRaf((dt) => {
    const sectionEl = section.current;
    const pinEl = pin.current;
    const wordEl = word.current;
    if (!sectionEl || !pinEl || !wordEl) return;

    const host = scroller?.current ?? nearestScroller(sectionEl);
    const hostIsRoot = host === document.documentElement;
    const hostTop = hostIsRoot ? 0 : host.getBoundingClientRect().top;
    const hostHeight = hostIsRoot ? window.innerHeight : host.clientHeight;
    if (hostHeight === 0) return;

    // The pin range is manufactured from the scroller's own height, not from
    // `vh`: inside a box, viewport units describe the wrong thing entirely.
    const total = Math.round(hostHeight * (reduced ? 1 : 1 + viewports));
    if (total !== lastHeights.current) {
      lastHeights.current = total;
      sectionEl.style.height = `${total}px`;
      pinEl.style.height = `${hostHeight}px`;
    }

    const rect = sectionEl.getBoundingClientRect();
    const travel = total - hostHeight;
    const target = travel > 0 ? clamp((hostTop - rect.top) / travel, 0, 1) : 1;

    // `damp(x, t, s, dt)` is `x + (t - x) * (1 - s^dt)`; with s = e^-5 that is
    // exactly the `1 - exp(-5 * dt)` constant the technique is named for.
    smoothed.current = reduced ? target : damp(smoothed.current, target, smoothing, dt);
    const L = smoothed.current;

    // Ease-out on the scale: most of the shrink happens early, so the last
    // third of the scroll is a slow settle rather than a continued rush.
    const scale = cover - (cover - 1) * easeOutCubic(L);
    // Ease-IN on the recentre: while the word is huge its position is
    // meaningless, so it must not start travelling until it is nearly small.
    const y = lerp(0, rest * hostHeight, easeInCubic(L));

    const transform = `translate3d(0, ${y.toFixed(1)}px, 0) scale(${scale.toFixed(4)})`;
    if (transform !== lastTransform.current) {
      lastTransform.current = transform;
      wordEl.style.transform = transform;
    }

    const veilEl = veil.current;
    if (veilEl) {
      const opacity = easeInCubic(clamp((L - 0.45) / 0.5, 0, 1)).toFixed(3);
      if (opacity !== lastVeil.current) {
        lastVeil.current = opacity;
        veilEl.style.opacity = opacity;
      }
    }
  });
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useRaf` unsubscribes from the shared loop on unmount; the only state is refs. The inline `height` values written to the section and the pin die with the elements, and no observers, listeners or timers are registered.

**Reduced motion.** The manufactured range collapses to one screen and the smoothing is bypassed, so progress tracks scroll exactly. The word passes through at its resting scale with the caption already present — the section becomes an ordinary headline block instead of leaving a screen and a half of empty scrolling behind.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Sizing the range in `vh` inside a scrollable container. The section is then sized against the window while progress is measured against the box, so the zoom finishes early, late, or never — and it looks correct only when the container happens to be full-height.
- Smoothing with a per-frame constant. The zoom lags noticeably further behind the scroll on a 60 Hz display than on a 120 Hz one, and every attempt to tune it makes the other refresh rate worse.
- Using the same easing for scale and for position. Move the word early and it slides around the screen while still too large to locate, which reads as a bug rather than as choreography.
- Animating `font-size` or `width` instead of `transform: scale`. Every frame relayouts and re-rasterises glyphs at a new size — the single most reliable way to turn this effect into a slideshow on a laptop.
- Writing the transform unconditionally each frame. At the top and bottom of the range the value is identical for dozens of frames, and each write still costs a style invalidation and a composite.
- Caching the section rect. A font swap or an image landing above the section moves it, and a cached top makes the zoom finish at the wrong scroll position for the rest of the session.
- Leaving the manufactured range in place under reduced motion. The user gets a screen and a half of scrolling where nothing happens at all; the height must collapse along with the animation.

## Notes

- The scroll container is auto-detected by walking ancestors for a scrollable `overflow-y`, so the component works unchanged on a normal page. Pass `scroller` when the container is ambiguous or created later.
- The knockout is `background-clip: text`, not an SVG mask: no extra element, no viewBox to keep in sync, and the text stays selectable and readable to assistive technology.
- A single word works best. Two lines re-wrap as the scale changes and the knockout stops reading as one shape.

## Definition of done

The word is unreadably large at the top of the section and lands as a normal headline exactly as the section releases. Scrolling backwards reverses it at the same rate. Stopping mid-zoom settles within about a quarter second with no drift. Resizing the window mid-zoom keeps the word at the same progress. With reduced motion on, the section is one screen tall and nothing scales.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
