# Build: Layout Lerp Scalar

One function places every card from seven scalars — radius, spacing, rowSpread, turns, depth, focus, scale — and each named layout is only a set of values for them. Morphing is therefore `gsap.to(params, preset)`: a tween over an object literal, with no per-item choreography anywhere. Crucially it interpolates the *inputs*, `f(lerp(a, b, s))`, not the outputs, so every intermediate frame is a valid member of the same family instead of a set of cards sliding along straight lines through each other.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Row, stack, drum and fan are one placement function of seven numbers. Switching layout is a tween over an object.

- Category: layout
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1, gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. Placement is `offset = wrappedOffset(i, position, n)`, then `angle = (offset / n) * 2PI * turns` and `p = (radius * sin(angle) + offset * rowSpread * step, -offset * spacing, radius * (cos(angle) - 1) - depth * |offset|)`, with `rotation.y = angle`. Setting `radius` and `turns` to 0 leaves a straight line; adding `spacing` makes it a column; adding `turns` and `radius` wraps that column into a drum. There is no branch anywhere in it.
2. Because the parameters are what get tweened, the shape passes through the family rather than across it. `f` is nonlinear in `radius` and `turns`, so `f(lerp(a, b, s))` and `lerp(f(a), f(b), s)` are different animations: the first keeps the cards on a well-formed helix at every `s`, the second sends each card down a chord that cuts through the middle of the drum and through its neighbours.
3. `cos(angle) - 1` rather than `cos(angle)` puts the focused card at z = 0 for any radius. Growing the drum then pushes the far side away instead of pulling the near card into the camera, which is what makes `radius` safe to tween through large values.
4. The `depth` term gives the flat layouts a strictly monotonic z in `|offset|`. That is not a look — it is what lets three's painter sort order the transparent cards correctly. With every card at z = 0 the sort has nothing to rank and the overlap order in a stack is whatever the traversal happened to produce.
5. The row step is derived from the camera: `visibleHeight = 2 * cameraZ * tan(fov / 2)`, `visibleWidth = visibleHeight * aspect`, and `step = visibleWidth * fill / (n - 1)`. Card size comes from the same `visibleHeight`, so the whole layout is defined in fractions of the frustum and holds its proportions at any viewport.
6. Focus is `1 - focus * (1 - exp(-offset^2))` — 1.000 at the centre, 0.368 one step out, 0.018 two — driving both the card scale and a single `uFocus` uniform that desaturates and dims in the fragment shader. `focus` is itself one of the tweened parameters, so a layout can decide how much of a selection it is.
7. The vertex shader is the default transform and nothing else. Everything that moves is a CPU write to `position`, `rotation` and `scale`, which means the bounding sphere three culls against and the view depth it sorts by both describe where the card actually is. A drum that bends its planes in the vertex shader has to disable culling and reconstruct `renderOrder` by hand; this one gets both for free.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `PRESETS.drum = { radius: 2.55, spacing: 0.74, turns: 2, focus: 1, scale: 1 }`
  Two turns across twelve cards puts adjacent cards 60° apart, so the ring reads as a ring rather than as a coil. Below about 1.5 turns the far side is barely behind the near side and the drum flattens into a wheel; above 3 the cards on the back face are edge-on for most of a lap and the set looks half empty.
- `PRESETS.row.scale = 0.42`
  Matched to the derived row step so twelve cards just touch at the reference aspect. Larger and the row overlaps into a fan; smaller and it becomes a sparse dotted line. It is a scalar for exactly this reason — the row layout gets to pick its own card size.
- `depth = 0.35 (column) / 0.1 (row) / 0 (drum, fan)`
  World units of recession per index step. The drum and fan get their z from the radius, so they need none. The flat layouts need a non-zero value or their transparent cards have identical view depth and the sort order is arbitrary — the symptom is a stack whose overlap flickers as the ring drifts.
- `CARD_HEIGHT_RATIO = 0.4`
  Card height as a fraction of the frustum height at z = 0. Above ~0.55 the drum's vertical spacing has to grow to match or the cards intersect; below ~0.25 the whole formation floats in the middle of the frame with nothing at the edges.
- `CAMERA_FOV / CAMERA_Z = 42 / 7.2`
  A matched pair: they set the visible height, and everything else is a fraction of it. A wider FOV exaggerates the perspective divide so the far side of the drum shrinks dramatically — dramatic, but it also makes the row visibly bow. Change one and the layout is unchanged only if the other keeps `z * tan(fov / 2)` the same.
- `ROW_FILL = 0.92`
  Fraction of the visible width the flat row spans. At 1.0 the outermost cards are cut exactly by the frustum edge and their antialiased rims flicker as they cross it; much below 0.85 the row no longer reads as spanning the frame.
- `SCALE_FLOOR = 0.72`
  The scale an entirely out-of-focus card keeps. At 1.0 the focus falloff is only a dimming and the arrangement loses its centre; below ~0.5 the outer cards shrink so fast the drum looks like it is receding into a tunnel.
- `duration / MORPH_EASE = 1.25 / power3.inOut`
  Long enough to read the shape changing rather than snapping, short enough not to feel like a loading state. `inOut` because the morph has no impulse behind it — an `out` ease implies the shape was thrown, and the sudden start looks like a dropped frame.
- `drift = 0.16`
  Index steps per second of idle travel. About six seconds per card: slow enough to read a caption, fast enough that the wrap is visible within a few seconds of arriving. At 0 the ticker still runs but nothing moves, which is the right default for a layout driven by scroll instead.
- `CARD_CORNER = 0.055`
  Corner radius in units of card height, evaluated as an SDF in the fragment shader. Because the mask is drawn rather than sampled it stays crisp at any scale, and one number gives the same physical radius on both axes since the SDF works in height units and multiplies x by the aspect.

## API

```ts
function LayoutLerpScalar(props: { count?: number; layout?: 'row' | 'column' | 'drum' | 'fan'; params?: Partial<LayoutParams>; duration?: number; drift?: number; hueStart?: number; hueStep?: number; opacity?: number; onFocusChange?: (index: number) => void; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `count: number` — default `12`
  How many cards. They wrap, so this is also the ring's period.
- `layout: 'row' | 'column' | 'drum' | 'fan'` — default `'drum'`
  Which preset the parameter vector is tweened toward.
- `params: Partial<LayoutParams>`
  Overrides individual scalars on top of the preset — radius, spacing, rowSpread, turns, depth, focus, scale. Compared by value.
- `duration: number` — default `1.25`
  Seconds of the morph between presets.
- `drift: number` — default `0.16`
  Index steps per second of idle travel. 0 parks the ring.
- `hueStart: number` — default `232`
  First card's hue, 0-360.
- `hueStep: number` — default `17`
  Degrees of hue between adjacent cards.
- `opacity: number` — default `1`
  Alpha multiplier applied before the focus falloff.
- `onFocusChange: (index: number) => void`
  Fires when a different card takes the focus position.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the wrapper. The canvas fills it absolutely.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/* ---- the morph: one tween over an object literal ------------------------ */

useEffect(() => {
  const target: LayoutParams = { ...PRESETS[layout], ...params };
  const current = live.current;

  if (reduced) {
    Object.assign(current, target);
    return;
  }

  // Every parameter eases together, so the shape passes through a continuous
  // family of shapes rather than each card taking its own path. `overwrite`
  // matters: switch layout twice quickly and the second tween must take the
  // parameters from wherever the first one had got to, not fight it.
  const tween = gsap.to(current, { ...target, duration, ease: MORPH_EASE, overwrite: true });
  return () => {
    tween.kill();
  };
  // `params` is compared by value through `overrideKey`; the object literal
  // most callers pass is a new reference on every render.
  // eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps
}, [layout, overrideKey, duration, reduced]);

useEffect(() => {
  const current = live.current;
  return () => {
    gsap.killTweensOf(current);
  };
}, []);

/* ---- the frame ---------------------------------------------------------- */

useRaf(
  (dt) => {
    const current = stage.current;
    if (!current) return;
    const n = current.cards.length;
    if (n === 0) return;

    const p = live.current;
    const speed = reduced ? 0 : drift;
    // Wrapped rather than left to grow: at 0.16 steps/s an unwrapped
    // accumulator is fine for days, but the modulo costs nothing and keeps
    // float precision constant no matter how long the tab stays open.
    position.current = mod(position.current + dt * speed, n);
    const pos = position.current;

    // The one place the camera and the layout meet. `visibleHeight` is the
    // frustum's height at z = 0 — `2 * z * tan(fov/2)` — and the width is
    // that times the aspect. Deriving the row step from it is why the row
    // spans the frame at any viewport instead of being a guessed constant.
    const visibleHeight = 2 * Math.tan((CAMERA_FOV * DEG_TO_RAD) / 2) * CAMERA_Z;
    const visibleWidth = visibleHeight * current.camera.aspect;
    const step = (visibleWidth * ROW_FILL) / Math.max(n - 1, 1);
    const cardHeight = visibleHeight * CARD_HEIGHT_RATIO;
    const cardWidth = cardHeight * CARD_ASPECT;

    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      const card = current.cards[i];
      if (!card) continue;

      // The call that makes a finite array behave like an endless ring:
      // card 0 is one step BEFORE card 11, not eleven steps after it.
      const offset = wrappedOffset(i, pos, n);
      const angle = (offset / n) * TWO_PI * p.turns;

      // The placement function. Seven scalars in, one transform out, and
      // every layout this component has is somewhere in here.
      card.mesh.position.set(
        p.radius * Math.sin(angle) + offset * p.rowSpread * step,
        -offset * p.spacing,
        // cos(angle) - 1 keeps the focused card at z = 0 whatever the
        // radius, so growing the drum pushes the ring back rather than
        // pulling the front card into the camera. The depth term is what
        // gives the flat layouts a strictly monotonic z, which is what lets
        // three sort them back-to-front without any renderOrder fixing.
        p.radius * (Math.cos(angle) - 1) - p.depth * Math.abs(offset),
      );
      card.mesh.rotation.y = angle;

      // exp(-d^2): 1.000 at the focus, 0.368 one step out, 0.018 two,
      // 0.0001 three. Continuous and branchless, and `focus` scales how much
      // of it applies — at 0 every card is lit equally, which is what makes
      // the flat row read as an index rather than as a selection.
      const f = 1 - p.focus * (1 - gaussian(offset));
      const s = p.scale * (SCALE_FLOOR + (1 - SCALE_FLOOR) * f);
      card.mesh.scale.set(cardWidth * s, cardHeight * s, 1);
      card.uniforms.uFocus.value = f;
      card.uniforms.uOpacity.value = opacity;
    }

    const nextFocus = wrapIndex(Math.round(pos), n);
    if (nextFocus !== focusedRef.current) {
      focusedRef.current = nextFocus;
      notify.current?.(nextFocus);
    }

    current.renderer.render(current.scene, current.camera);
  },
  ready && inView && visible,
);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Kills the parameter tween (and any tween of the same object) so GSAP cannot write into a vector nothing reads; removes every mesh from the scene, then `disposeObject` for the materials, `geometry.dispose()`, `prototype.dispose()`, and `disposeRenderer` — which stops the animation loop, disposes, calls `forceContextLoss()` and zeroes the backing store — before removing the canvas from the DOM. The shared rAF unsubscribes, and the shared resize, intersection and visibility observers all unregister. No textures are allocated, so there are none to leak.

**Reduced motion.** The idle drift is set to zero, so the ring holds still and the same card stays in focus. Layout changes still happen — refusing them would leave the component unable to answer its own prop — but the parameters are assigned rather than tweened, so the new arrangement is simply there on the next frame with nothing travelling across the screen. The frame loop keeps running only because it is what draws; with no drift and no tween it writes the same transforms every frame.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Cross-fading two layouts instead of blending their parameters. `lerp(f(a), f(b), s)` moves every card along the straight line between its two homes, so the drum passes through its own axis and the cards slide through one another. Interpolate the inputs and the shape is always a real member of the family.
- Reaching for `if (layout === "drum")` in the frame loop. Branching per layout means each new arrangement is new code and no pair of them can be shown halfway. Every parameter here is a number precisely so it can be tweened, and the presets are data.
- Multiplying a whole layout to zero and calling that a morph. Scaling `radius` to 0 does not produce a flat row — it produces every card stacked on the axis. A second term (`rowSpread * step`) has to take over as the first one leaves, which is why the row and the ring are separate parameters rather than one.
- Letting the transparent cards share a z. three ranks transparent meshes by view depth; with a flat layout at z = 0 the ranking is arbitrary and the overlap in a stack flips as the ring drifts. The `depth` parameter exists to keep the ordering strict.
- Copying the bend-in-the-vertex-shader approach and keeping frustum culling on. That combination blanks planes that are plainly on screen, because the bounding sphere describes the flat geometry at the CPU position. This component avoids the whole class of problem by keeping the layout on the CPU — but the two approaches cannot be mixed carelessly.
- Guessing the row step in world units. Hard-code it and the row overflows a narrow viewport and floats in the middle of a wide one. It has to come from the frustum: `2 * cameraZ * tan(fov / 2) * aspect`, divided across the set.
- Calling `renderer.dispose()` and stopping there. It frees GPU objects but leaves the WebGL context alive, and Chromium kills the oldest context once about sixteen exist — so an unrelated canvas elsewhere on the page goes black. `disposeRenderer` calls `forceContextLoss()`, which is the call that actually hands it back.
- Building the colours with `new THREE.Color(...)` from a hex string and expecting them to match the CSS beside them. Colours have to enter the linear working space (`setHSL(..., THREE.SRGBColorSpace)`) and the fragment shader has to end with `#include <colorspace_fragment>`, because three injects that chunk only into its own materials, never into a `ShaderMaterial`.
- Passing `params` as an inline object literal and putting it straight in the effect deps. It is a new reference every render, so the morph tween is killed and rebuilt on each one and the parameters never arrive. The override is compared by value through a serialised key.
- Rendering every frame regardless. The loop is gated on the element being in view and the tab being visible; a scrolled-past WebGL canvas that keeps drawing is one of the easier ways to halve a page's battery life for nothing.

## Notes

- The four presets are ordinary data — add a fifth by adding seven numbers, with no new code and no new branch. Any two of them can also be blended by hand at a fixed `s` by passing `params`.
- Each card owns a cloned `ShaderMaterial` so it can hold its own colours, but three keys its program cache on the shader source, so all twelve still share one compiled program and the clone costs a uniform bag.
- Nothing is fetched and no image ships: the card face — rounded rectangle, gradient, hairlines, rim — is a signed distance field in the fragment shader, and the shading of a card turning edge-on is one dot product against the transformed normal.

## Definition of done

The cards turn slowly and endlessly — watch one leave the bottom of the drum and come back at the top, at the same spacing. Switch layout: the whole formation unwinds into a row, or collapses into a stack, in one continuous motion, and at every instant it looks like a formation rather than cards travelling to new addresses. Nothing passes through the centre of the drum on the way. Switch layout twice quickly and the second morph starts from wherever the first had reached, with no jump. In the stack, the overlap order is stable while it drifts — nothing flickers in front of its neighbour. Resize the window from narrow to wide: the row still spans the frame and the cards keep their proportions. Scroll the canvas out of view and the GPU goes quiet.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Lenis On The GSAP Ticker

Lenis and ScrollTrigger each work alone and tear together, because each runs its own clock: Lenis advances the scroll position on its rAF, ScrollTrigger samples it on GSAP's, and a pinned section ends up a frame behind the page it is pinned to. Mounted once near the root, this hands Lenis to `gsap.ticker`, updates ScrollTrigger on Lenis's scroll event rather than per frame, and disables lag smoothing so the two agree about how much time passed.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Smooth scroll and ScrollTrigger on one clock, with the lag-smoothing line everyone omits.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0, lenis@^1.3.11

## How it works

1. Lenis is driven by `gsap.ticker.add((t) => lenis.raf(t * 1000))` — seconds to milliseconds — and its own `autoRaf` is switched off. One clock advances the scroll position and the tweens, in that order, every frame.
2. `gsap.ticker.lagSmoothing(0)` is the line that makes it correct rather than merely working. GSAP normally clamps a large `deltaTime` after a stall so tweens do not jump; but that clamped value is now what Lenis integrates, so an under-reported frame leaves Lenis's scroll position permanently offset from ScrollTrigger's idea of it. Nothing resyncs them afterwards.
3. ScrollTrigger is updated from `lenis.on("scroll")`, not from the ticker. It then samples on the same tick the position actually changed, instead of one frame after — the difference is visible as a shimmering seam at the top edge of a pin.
4. `paused` calls `lenis.stop()` and `lenis.start()` rather than tearing the instance down. This is the preloader gate: construct on mount so everything is measured and ready, but refuse wheel input until the intro clears — which is why you cannot scroll during a well-built intro sequence.
5. Coming out of `paused`, and again on `load` and on `document.fonts.ready`, `ScrollTrigger.refresh()` re-measures. Images and fonts change document height after hydration, and every trigger below the fold was computed against the old one.
6. The instance itself is refcounted at module scope in `use-lenis`, so mounting the provider twice — a layout and a page, say — reuses one Lenis instead of creating two that both `preventDefault` on wheel and scroll the page at double speed.
7. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` no instance is constructed at all. The page scrolls natively and ScrollTrigger reads the native position, which is the path it is already correct on.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `duration = 1.05`
  Seconds for a wheel step to settle. Roughly the feel of Lenis's `lerp: 0.09`, which is the value most award-site builds land on: slow enough to read as smooth, fast enough that a trackpad flick does not feel like it is dragging the page through syrup. Past ~1.4 the page feels detached from the hand.
- `easing = 1.001 - 2^(-10t)`
  Lenis's own default — an exponential decay that is ~99.9 percent settled at t=1, so the tail never visibly crawls. The `1.001` guarantees it reaches exactly 1 rather than approaching it forever.
- `lagSmoothing = 0`
  Disabled, not tuned. Any non-zero threshold means GSAP will eventually report a deltaTime that did not happen, and Lenis will integrate it into a scroll position that does not match the document.
- `ScrollTrigger.update trigger = lenis scroll event`
  One update per position change, on the tick it changed. Calling it from the ticker instead costs an update on frames where nothing moved and delivers a stale position on frames where it did.

## API

```ts
function LenisGsapTicker(props: { children?: ReactNode; duration?: number; easing?: (t: number) => number; paused?: boolean; enabled?: boolean }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Rendered as-is; the provider adds no DOM of its own.
- `duration: number` — default `1.05`
  Seconds for a wheel step to settle.
- `easing: (t: number) => number`
  Decay curve. Must be a stable reference — define it at module scope.
- `paused: boolean` — default `false`
  Holds input via `lenis.stop()` without destroying the instance. Releasing it also refreshes ScrollTrigger.
- `enabled: boolean` — default `true`
  False restores native scrolling and constructs nothing.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function LenisGsapTicker({
  children,
  duration = 1.05,
  easing = DEFAULT_EASING,
  paused = false,
  enabled = true,
}: LenisGsapTickerProps) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  // Smooth scrolling is the motion. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the
  // instance is never built at all, so the page scrolls natively and
  // ScrollTrigger reads the native position — which it already does correctly.
  const active = enabled && !reduced;

  const lenis = useLenis({
    duration,
    easing,
    smoothWheel: true,
    enabled: active,
    // One clock. `useLenis` turns off Lenis's `autoRaf` when a ticker is
    // present and calls `lagSmoothing(0)` on it.
    ticker: gsap.ticker,
    // Sampled on scroll rather than every frame: ScrollTrigger then updates on
    // the same tick the position changed, instead of one frame later.
    onScroll: () => ScrollTrigger.update(),
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    const instance = lenis.current;
    if (!instance) return;
    if (paused) {
      instance.stop();
      return;
    }
    instance.start();
    // Whatever was covering the page while paused was almost certainly holding
    // layout at a different height.
    ScrollTrigger.refresh();
  }, [lenis, paused]);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!active) return;
    let cancelled = false;
    const refresh = () => {
      if (!cancelled) ScrollTrigger.refresh();
    };

    // Images and fonts change document height after hydration. Without a
    // refresh here, every trigger below the fold is measured against a height
    // that no longer exists, and they all fire early by the difference.
    if (document.readyState === 'complete') refresh();
    else window.addEventListener('load', refresh, { once: true });
    void document.fonts?.ready.then(refresh);

    return () => {
      cancelled = true;
      window.removeEventListener('load', refresh);
    };
  }, [active]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `use-lenis` removes its scroll listener, removes the update function from `gsap.ticker`, and destroys the instance only when the last consumer unmounts. The provider removes its own `load` listener and guards the `document.fonts.ready` continuation with a cancelled flag, so a refresh cannot land after unmount.

**Reduced motion.** No Lenis instance is constructed when `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` matches, so scrolling is entirely native and the ticker is left alone. ScrollTrigger keeps working against the native position. The query is live: toggling the OS setting takes effect on the next render without a reload.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Leaving lag smoothing at its default. Everything looks right until the first stall — a heavy image decode, a devtools pause — after which pinned sections sit permanently a few pixels off and no interaction resyncs them.
- Letting Lenis keep `autoRaf` while also adding it to the ticker. It then advances twice per frame: scrolling runs at double speed and the smoothing constant no longer means anything.
- Mounting the provider in two places. Two instances both listen on `wheel`, both call `preventDefault`, and the page moves twice as far as the gesture — the refcount in `use-lenis` exists specifically to make the second mount a no-op.
- Calling `ScrollTrigger.update` from the ticker instead of from the scroll event. Triggers lag the smoothed position by exactly one frame, which is most visible as a seam that shivers at the top of a pinned section.
- Skipping `ScrollTrigger.refresh()` after `load` and after fonts settle. Every trigger below the fold is measured against a document height that no longer exists, so they all fire early by the difference.
- Passing an inline arrow as `easing`. It is a new identity every render, so the effect that owns the instance tears Lenis down and rebuilds it on each one — visible as scroll position snapping to the top mid-gesture.
- Smooth-scrolling a subtree by mounting a second window-level Lenis. Lenis attaches to the window unless given an explicit wrapper; a nested instance fights the outer one for the same wheel events.

## Notes

- The preview does not mount an enabled instance. `useLenis` attaches to the window, and a window-level smooth scroll inside a documentation page would take over the page hosting the preview rather than the preview. The demo therefore shows the provider mounted with `enabled={false}` beside a local reproduction: the right-hand column is offset by the same exponential filter Lenis applies, the left is the raw native position, and the bar at the bottom is the instantaneous gap between them. The ticker wiring itself is exactly as shipped.
- The demo derives its filter constant with `perFrameToSmoothing(0.09)` from `lib/damp`, which converts Lenis's per-frame `lerp` into the per-second constant `damp` wants. That conversion is the same one that makes any ported per-frame easing frame-rate independent.
- Mount above everything that registers a ScrollTrigger. Triggers created before the ticker wiring exists still work, but they are measured against a document that has not yet been refreshed.
- Smooth scroll is a preference, not an improvement. Ship the `enabled` escape hatch and honour reduced motion — a real fraction of users find hijacked scrolling nauseating.

## Definition of done

Scrolling is smoothed and a pinned section stays welded to the page with no shivering seam at its top edge. Pause during a stall — hold a devtools breakpoint for a second — and on release the pin is still aligned. Mounting the provider twice does not double scroll speed. With reduced motion on, scrolling is native and ScrollTrigger still fires at the right positions.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Looping Scroll Cue

A short line that falls repeatedly through a clipping tube, the way a hero says "keep going" without saying it. It is pure CSS — one keyframe pair on one transform — so it costs nothing after mount and a dozen of them still emit a single rule. The character is entirely in the easing: the line hangs, dives, and hangs again, and the pause between dives is what reads as an instruction.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

The hairline that dives down a hero. One keyframe pair, a hard ease, and a seamless loop.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. A `span` is the tube: `position: relative`, `overflow: hidden`, `block-size: var(--kx-cue-length)`, `inline-size: var(--kx-cue-thickness)`. Everything visible happens inside its clip.
2. A child span is the line: absolutely positioned at `top: 0`, `block-size: var(--kx-cue-run)` — 40% of the tube — with `background-color: currentColor`, so the cue takes the colour of whatever text it sits beside.
3. One keyframe pair moves it from `translateY(-100%)` to `translateY(250%)`. Percentages on `translateY` resolve against the element's own height, not the tube's, so with the line at 40% the two ends are exactly flush with the outside of the clip: 40% x 1 above the top, 40% x 2.5 = 100% below it.
4. The line's resting transform is set to `translateY(-100%)`, identical to the keyframe start, so the element is already outside the clip before the animation attaches and there is no first-frame flash.
5. The timing function is `cubic-bezier(.76, 0, .24, 1)`, applied over the whole iteration rather than per keyframe — a hard ease-in-out that spends most of the cycle nearly stationary at the two extremes, both of which are off-screen.
6. The stylesheet is a module-level template literal emitted through React 19's `<style href precedence>`, so it is hoisted to the document head once no matter how many cues render.
7. Reduced motion is answered twice: a `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block so the server-rendered first paint is already correct, and `data-static` from `useReducedMotion` so a setting changed mid-session takes effect. Both resolve to `animation: none; top: 50%; transform: translateY(-50%)`.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `travel = -100% to 250%`
  Relative to the line, not the tube. 350% of its own height means it is entirely outside the clip at both ends, so the wrap from the last frame back to the first happens while nothing is visible. Animating 0% to 100% instead makes the line vanish at the bottom edge and reappear at the top in the same frame, which is the visible seam every hand-rolled version has.
- `--kx-cue-run = 40%`
  The line's height as a fraction of the tube, and the number that makes 250% exactly the far edge. At 100% the line fills the tube and the cue reads as a wipe rather than a falling object; below about 20% it is too short to register as travelling at this speed.
- `timing function = cubic-bezier(.76, 0, .24, 1)`
  A hard ease-in-out with almost no linear section. `linear` reads as a loading bar and `ease-in-out` is too soft to punctuate. The steep middle is what compresses the visible part of the cycle into a dive, leaving a deliberate pause between repetitions.
- `--kx-cue-period = 1.8s`
  One dive plus the pause. Under about 1.2s the cue nags; past roughly 2.5s a visitor can land, look, and leave without ever seeing it move, which defeats the point of having it.
- `--kx-cue-length = 3.5rem`
  Long enough that the dive is legible as travel rather than as a blink, short enough to sit under a line of body copy without becoming a design element in its own right.

## API

```ts
function LoopingScrollCue(props: { length?: string; thickness?: string; run?: string; period?: number; delay?: number; paused?: boolean; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `length: string` — default `'3.5rem'`
  Height of the tube. Any CSS length.
- `thickness: string` — default `'1px'`
  Width of the line.
- `run: string` — default `'40%'`
  Height of the travelling segment as a percentage of the tube.
- `period: number` — default `1.8`
  Seconds for one dive plus its pause.
- `delay: number` — default `0`
  Seconds before the first dive. Use it to stagger a row.
- `paused: boolean` — default `false`
  Park the line in the middle of the tube instead of running it.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the tube. Set `text-*` to colour the line.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const CUE_CSS = `
@keyframes kx-scroll-cue-travel {
  from { transform: translateY(-100%); }
  to   { transform: translateY(250%); }
}
.kx-scroll-cue {
  position: relative;
  display: block;
  overflow: hidden;
  flex: none;
  inline-size: var(--kx-cue-thickness, 1px);
  block-size: var(--kx-cue-length, 3.5rem);
  color: currentColor;
}
.kx-scroll-cue-line {
  position: absolute;
  inset-inline: 0;
  top: 0;
  block-size: var(--kx-cue-run, 40%);
  background-color: currentColor;
  /* Matches the keyframe start, so the line is already outside the clip
     before the first frame and never flashes at rest. */
  transform: translateY(-100%);
  animation: var(--kx-cue-period, 1.8s) cubic-bezier(.76, 0, .24, 1) infinite
    kx-scroll-cue-travel;
  animation-delay: var(--kx-cue-delay, 0s);
}
/* Parked, not frozen. 'animation-play-state: paused' stops on whatever frame
   it reached, and for roughly half the cycle that frame is off-screen — the
   cue would simply vanish. */
.kx-scroll-cue[data-static='true'] .kx-scroll-cue-line {
  animation: none;
  top: 50%;
  transform: translateY(-50%);
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .kx-scroll-cue .kx-scroll-cue-line {
    animation: none;
    top: 50%;
    transform: translateY(-50%);
  }
}
`;

export interface LoopingScrollCueProps {
  /** Height of the tube. Any CSS length. */
  length?: string;
  /** Width of the line. Any CSS length. */
  thickness?: string;
  /** Height of the travelling segment, as a percentage of the tube. */
  run?: string;
  /** Seconds for one full dive. */
  period?: number;
  /** Seconds before the first dive. Stagger a row of cues with this. */
  delay?: number;
  /** Park the line in the middle instead of running it. */
  paused?: boolean;
  className?: string;
}

export function LoopingScrollCue({
  length = '3.5rem',
  thickness = '1px',
  run = '40%',
  period = 1.8,
  delay = 0,
  paused = false,
  className,
}: LoopingScrollCueProps) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  return (
    <>
      {/* Hoisted once by React 19 regardless of how many cues are on the page. */}
      <style href="kinetic-looping-scroll-cue" precedence="medium">
        {CUE_CSS}
      </style>
      <span
        aria-hidden
        data-static={reduced || paused ? 'true' : 'false'}
        className={cn('kx-scroll-cue', className)}
        style={
          {
            '--kx-cue-length': length,
            '--kx-cue-thickness': thickness,
            '--kx-cue-run': run,
            '--kx-cue-period': `${period}s`,
            '--kx-cue-delay': `${delay}s`,
          } as CSSProperties
        }
      >
        <span className="kx-scroll-cue-line" />
      </span>
    </>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to release. No timers, no rAF, no listeners, no observers — the only side effect is the hoisted stylesheet, which React reference-counts and removes when the last cue unmounts.

**Reduced motion.** The line stops travelling and parks in the middle of the tube — visible, centred, still a cue. This is enforced both by a `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block in the hoisted stylesheet, which is correct from the first server-rendered paint, and by `data-static` driven from `useReducedMotion`, which catches the setting being changed while the page is open.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Animating `top` or `margin-top` instead of `transform`. Both are laid out on the main thread every frame; the transform runs on the compositor and is the difference between a cue that stays smooth during a heavy hero animation and one that stutters exactly when the page is busiest.
- Animating 0% to 100%. The line disappears at the bottom edge and is already back at the top on the next frame — the loop has a visible seam, and it is the single most common way this effect is got wrong.
- Assuming the percentages are relative to the tube. `translateY` percentages resolve against the transformed element, so changing the line's height silently changes where the travel ends, and a taller line stops exiting the clip.
- Using `animation-play-state: paused` for a paused state. The line stops on whatever frame it reached, and for roughly half the cycle that frame is outside the clip, so "paused" means "gone" about half the time it is used.
- Honouring reduced motion by rendering the animation's end state. The end state here is off-screen, so the cue would correctly render nothing. Park it in the middle instead: the point of a scroll cue is that it is visible.
- Relying on the `useReducedMotion` hook alone. It reads `false` during server render, so the first client paint animates for a frame before the hook corrects it — the media query in the stylesheet is what covers that window.
- Leaving the line's resting transform at its default. Without `transform: translateY(-100%)` matching the keyframe start, the line is briefly visible at the top of the tube between paint and the animation's first frame.

## Notes

- Cost is CSS. Nothing runs after mount, there is nothing to clean up, and a row of cues is one rule plus one custom-property block each.
- Stagger a row with `delay` — the same period at three different offsets reads as a single wave without any coordination.
- The cue is `aria-hidden`. It is a hint, not content, and a screen reader announcing a decorative line is noise.

## Definition of done

The line falls through the tube, disappears, and pauses before falling again — and at no point is it visible in two places or seen jumping back to the top. Watch a full minute: the loop point cannot be identified. Turn on reduced motion and the line is a static hairline in the centre of the tube, not an empty box.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Lottie Ratio Poster

A slot for a Lottie that costs nothing until the slot is nearly on screen. The box is reserved at a provisional ratio and filled with a poster drawn in CSS; an IntersectionObserver on the already-sized box starts the fetch; the resolved JSON reports its own composition size in its `w` and `h` fields, the box takes that exact ratio, the player mounts underneath and the poster crossfades away. The readout prices the provisional guess in pixels of layout shift. No Lottie runtime is imported — loading and playback go through a render prop, so the packaged part is the reservation, not the player.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Reserves the box, holds a drawn poster, fetches the JSON only in view, then corrects the ratio from the animation's own w and h.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The reserved box is a single `aspect-ratio` declaration on a full-width element, applied on first paint from the provisional ratio. That is what makes everything after it possible: a box with height cannot shift when it fills, and a box with height gives the IntersectionObserver something real to test.
2. The intersection test runs on that reserved box, with `once: true` and a 240px root margin, so the fetch starts roughly one flick of the wrist before the box arrives. Observing an unreserved, zero-height element instead is the classic failure — a collapsed box intersects the viewport from almost anywhere on the page, so the lazy load fires immediately and the laziness was decorative.
3. A Lottie JSON carries its composition size at the root: `w` and `h`, alongside `v`, `fr`, `ip`, `op` and `layers`. `w / h` is therefore the exact box before the player has been constructed, let alone measured, so the correction happens on the frame the file lands rather than after a layout pass.
4. The provisional ratio and the real ratio are both kept, and the difference is reported as `Math.abs(width / ratio - width / actual)` — the number of pixels everything below the box moved, at the current width. It is the same quantity that feeds Cumulative Layout Shift, in the units the user actually experienced.
5. The in-flight promise is stored in a ref rather than guarded by a boolean. StrictMode double-invokes the Effect: with a `started` flag the first call is abandoned by its own cleanup and the second is blocked by the flag, so the load silently never completes. Reusing the promise means one request and one subscription per Effect run.
6. The poster is dissolved two animation frames after `ready`, not on the same tick — one frame for React to commit the player and one for the browser to paint it. It is then unmounted on a timer rather than on `transitionend`, because a transition on a subtree that has been hidden never fires the event and the poster would sit over the player permanently.
7. A zero or missing dimension is treated as a failed load rather than divided by. `w / 0` is Infinity, which collapses `aspect-ratio` and takes the reserved box with it — the exact failure the component exists to prevent, arriving through the component itself.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `DEFAULT_RATIO = 16 / 9`
  The provisional ratio, and named as a guess rather than a default so nobody inherits it by accident. Take the real number out of the design file: against the 3:2 composition in the demo, 16:9 costs 47 pixels of shift at 380px wide.
- `ROOT_MARGIN = '240px'`
  About a third of a laptop viewport, or roughly 400ms of ordinary scrolling — enough for a one-megabyte JSON on a decent connection to land before the box arrives. Larger and you are prefetching things the user will never reach; smaller and the poster is still up when the box is centred.
- `FADE_MS = 320`
  Poster crossfade. Long enough to read as a dissolve rather than a cut, short enough that the poster is not still visibly over the first second of the animation.
- `FADE_SLACK = 60`
  Extra milliseconds before the poster is unmounted. The transition is driven by a class change, so the removal timer and the transition clock do not share an origin; without the slack the poster can be pulled at opacity 0.04.

## API

```ts
function LottieRatioPoster<T extends LottieRatioSource>(props: { load: () => Promise<T>; children: (state: { source: T; reduced: boolean }) => ReactNode; ratio?: number; rootMargin?: string; fade?: number; label?: string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `load: () => Promise<T>`
  Fetches the animation JSON. Called at most once, and only once the reserved box is within `rootMargin`.
- `children: (state: { source: T; reduced: boolean }) => ReactNode`
  Render prop for the player. Mounted absolutely inside the reserved box.
- `ratio: number` — default `16 / 9`
  Provisional width / height, used until the JSON reports its own.
- `rootMargin: string` — default `'240px'`
  How early to start fetching, as an IntersectionObserver root margin.
- `fade: number` — default `320`
  Poster crossfade in milliseconds.
- `label: string` — default `'animation'`
  Short text on the poster.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the outer element via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  if (!inView) return;
  let alive = true;

  request.current ??= loadRef.current();
  setPhase((prev) => (prev === 'waiting' ? 'loading' : prev));

  request.current.then(
    (data) => {
      if (alive) apply(data);
    },
    () => {
      if (alive) setPhase('failed');
    },
  );

  return () => {
    alive = false;
  };
}, [inView, apply]);

// The real ratio comes from the JSON's own composition size, so the box is
// exact from the frame the file lands rather than from the frame the player
// finishes measuring itself.
const actual = source ? source.w / source.h : null;
const applied = actual ?? ratio;

// What the guess cost, in the units the user experiences it in. Everything
// below this box moves by exactly this many pixels at the current width.
const shift =
  actual !== null && width > 0 ? Math.abs(width / ratio - width / actual) : 0;
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The intersection subscription is removed by `useInView`, which also unobserves after the first hit because it is used with `once`. Both timers are cleared and both `requestAnimationFrame` handles cancelled on teardown. The load promise cannot be aborted, so it is neutered instead: an `alive` flag in the Effect closure means a late resolution calls no setter after teardown. The promise itself is deliberately retained in a ref across Effect runs, which is what makes the request happen once rather than once per run.

**Reduced motion.** The poster loses its shimmer and the crossfade collapses to a zero-duration swap, so the poster is replaced rather than dissolved. The fetch is unaffected — reduced motion is a request about movement, not about content, and withholding the animation entirely would leave a permanent placeholder where the user expected something. The render prop is handed `reduced: true` so the player itself can park on its last frame, which is the conventional still for a Lottie.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Lazy-loading against an unreserved box. A zero-height element intersects the viewport from nearly anywhere in the document, so the observer fires on mount and the fetch was never deferred. Reserve first, observe second — in that order, in the same element.
- Waiting for the player to report the size. `lottie-web` measures its own SVG after construction, which is after the layout has already happened at the wrong ratio. The JSON's `w` and `h` are available the instant the fetch resolves, before anything is instantiated.
- Guarding a one-shot fetch with a boolean ref. StrictMode runs the Effect, tears it down and runs it again; the first call is discarded by its own cleanup and the second is refused by the flag, so the promise never lands and the poster stays up in development only. Hold the promise itself in the ref.
- Dissolving the poster in the same commit that mounts the player. The player has not painted, so the crossfade runs over an empty box and reads as a flash. Two `requestAnimationFrame` calls put it after the paint.
- Unmounting the poster on `transitionend`. If the subtree is hidden mid-transition — a route change, a tab switch, an `Activity` boundary — no event is delivered and the poster is stranded on top of the player. Use a timer.
- Dividing by a dimension you did not check. A malformed or truncated JSON with `h: 0` produces an Infinite ratio, `aspect-ratio` gives up, and the reserved box collapses to nothing.
- Shipping the Lottie runtime for a decoration. `lottie-web` is around 60KB gzipped before any animation data; if the thing being animated is one badge in a footer, the runtime costs more than the effect is worth, and this component is where you notice.

## Notes

- No Lottie runtime is imported and no `.json` is committed. `load` is any function returning the parsed animation, and `children` is where the player goes, so the same slot works for `lottie-web`, `@lottiefiles/dotlottie-web`, a video, or a canvas.
- Type the resolved JSON yourself and pass it as the generic: `LottieRatioPoster<MyLottie>` gives the render prop the full object rather than only `w` and `h`.
- For reduced motion the render prop receives `reduced: true`. The conventional response with `lottie-web` is to construct it with `autoplay: false` and call `anim.goToAndStop(anim.getDuration(true) - 1, true)` — `getDuration(true)` returns frames, so the last frame is one less than that.

## Definition of done

On load the box already occupies its full reserved height, with a poster in it and a readout reading `reserved 1.78 · waiting for viewport`. Scroll it into view and the readout goes to `fetching json` roughly a scroll-flick before the box arrives. When the JSON lands the box snaps to 1.50, the player fades up under the dissolving poster, and the readout names the shift in pixels. Set the provisional ratio to 1.5 and reload: same sequence, and the readout says `no shift`. With reduced motion the poster does not shimmer and the swap is instant.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Magnetic Pointer Button

The element translates toward the pointer by a fraction of its offset from centre, and the label translates further still, so the text appears to lead the box it sits in. Release is an elastic overshoot rather than a linear return, which is the difference between "springy" and "sliding back".

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A button that leans toward the cursor and springs back, with the label leading the box.

- Category: cursor
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. A window-level pointermove handler measures the pointer against the button's live bounding rect, not a cached one — the element is being translated by this same effect, so a rect captured on mount goes stale immediately.
2. Inside a hit area padded past the border, the offset from centre is scaled by `strength` and pushed into four `gsap.quickTo` setters: x and y for the button, x and y for the label at `labelStrength - 1` so it moves relative to its already-moving parent.
3. Outside that area, a single `gsap.to` with `elastic.out(1, 0.4)` and `overwrite: "auto"` returns both nodes to zero, cancelling any in-flight follow tween.
4. Cleanup kills tweens before clearing transforms, so nothing writes to the node after React releases it.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `strength = 0.35`
  Fraction of pointer offset the button travels. Below ~0.2 the effect is invisible; above ~0.6 the button outruns the cursor and reads as a rendering fault rather than an affordance.
- `labelStrength = 1.6`
  The label moves 0.6x the button offset *on top of* the button's own movement. That parallax between text and border is what makes the surface feel elastic instead of rigid.
- `padding = 24`
  Pixels of grace beyond the border. Without it the effect engages exactly at the edge, and the button visibly jumps as it snaps into the field.
- `FOLLOW_DURATION = 0.35`
  quickTo duration. Short enough to feel attached to the cursor, long enough to smooth the 8-16 ms gaps between pointer events.
- `RETURN_DURATION = 0.6`
  Elastic return. Shorter than this and the overshoot has no room to read as a spring.

## API

```ts
function MagneticButton(props: { children: ReactNode; strength?: number; labelStrength?: number; padding?: number; className?: string; onClick?: () => void; disabled?: boolean }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Button label. Wrapped in the span that receives the parallax offset.
- `strength: number` — default `0.35`
  Fraction of the pointer offset the button travels.
- `labelStrength: number` — default `1.6`
  Label travel relative to the button. 1 disables parallax.
- `padding: number` — default `24`
  Pixels beyond the border that still count as near.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the button element via `cn`.
- `onClick: () => void`
  Standard click handler.
- `disabled: boolean` — default `false`
  Disables the button and skips the effect entirely.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const RETURN_DURATION = 0.6;
const FOLLOW_DURATION = 0.35;

export function MagneticButton({
  children,
  strength = 0.35,
  labelStrength = 1.6,
  padding = 24,
  className,
  onClick,
  disabled = false,
}: MagneticButtonProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLButtonElement>(null);
  const label = useRef<HTMLSpanElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = root.current;
    const text = label.current;
    if (!el || !text || disabled) return;

    // A coarse pointer has no hover state: the effect would only ever fire on
    // touch-down, which reads as a glitch rather than an affordance.
    const fine = window.matchMedia('(pointer: fine)');
    const reduced = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)');
    if (!fine.matches || reduced.matches) return;

    // quickTo builds one reusable tween per property. The naive version calls
    // gsap.to() on every pointermove, which allocates a tween per event (~120
    // a second) and makes each one fight the last for the same property.
    const xTo = gsap.quickTo(el, 'x', { duration: FOLLOW_DURATION, ease: 'power3.out' });
    const yTo = gsap.quickTo(el, 'y', { duration: FOLLOW_DURATION, ease: 'power3.out' });
    const labelXTo = gsap.quickTo(text, 'x', { duration: FOLLOW_DURATION, ease: 'power3.out' });
    const labelYTo = gsap.quickTo(text, 'y', { duration: FOLLOW_DURATION, ease: 'power3.out' });

    const onMove = (e: PointerEvent) => {
      // Read the rect per move, not once on mount: the element is being
      // translated by this very effect, and any scroll or reflow invalidates
      // a cached rect. Stale centres make the button drift away permanently.
      const rect = el.getBoundingClientRect();
      const cx = rect.left + rect.width / 2;
      const cy = rect.top + rect.height / 2;

      const withinX = Math.abs(e.clientX - cx) < rect.width / 2 + padding;
      const withinY = Math.abs(e.clientY - cy) < rect.height / 2 + padding;

      if (withinX && withinY) {
        const dx = (e.clientX - cx) * strength;
        const dy = (e.clientY - cy) * strength;
        xTo(dx);
        yTo(dy);
        labelXTo(dx * (labelStrength - 1));
        labelYTo(dy * (labelStrength - 1));
        return;
      }

      // Release. Overshoot on the way home is what sells the elastic.
      gsap.to([el, text], {
        x: 0,
        y: 0,
        duration: RETURN_DURATION,
        ease: 'elastic.out(1, 0.4)',
        overwrite: 'auto',
      });
    };

    // Listen on the window, not the element. On the element, `pointerleave`
    // fires the moment the button moves out from under the cursor — it
    // chases itself away and stutters at the edge of the hit area.
    window.addEventListener('pointermove', onMove, { passive: true });

    return () => {
      window.removeEventListener('pointermove', onMove);
      // Kill before clearing: an in-flight tween would otherwise write a
      // transform back onto a node React has already handed to something else.
      gsap.killTweensOf([el, text]);
      gsap.set([el, text], { clearProps: 'transform' });
    };
  }, [strength, labelStrength, padding, disabled]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Removes the window listener, calls `gsap.killTweensOf` on both nodes, then clears the transform with `gsap.set(..., { clearProps: "transform" })`. Kill precedes clear so no in-flight tween can restore it.

**Reduced motion.** The effect never attaches when `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` matches. The button keeps its colour transition on hover, so it still responds — it just does not move.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Listening on the element instead of the window. `pointerleave` fires the instant the button translates out from under the cursor, so it chases itself away and stutters along the edge of its own hit area.
- Calling `gsap.to()` per pointermove. That allocates a fresh tween ~120 times a second and each one fights the previous for the same property. `quickTo` reuses one tween per property.
- Caching the bounding rect on mount. The element moves and the page scrolls; a stale centre makes the button drift further away with every pass.
- Skipping `overwrite: "auto"` on the return tween — the follow tween keeps running underneath and the button never actually reaches zero.
- Leaving the transform behind on unmount. Clear it, but kill tweens first, or an in-flight tween writes it straight back.

## Notes

- Gated behind `(pointer: fine)`. On touch there is no hover, so the effect would only fire on press, which reads as a glitch.

## Definition of done

Approach from any side and the button leans toward the cursor with the label leading it. Leave the padded area and it springs back past zero once before settling. Unmount mid-approach and no transform remains on the node. On a touch device it does not move at all.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Manufactured Scroll Range

Some content has no height. A ring of projects, a canvas scene, a stack of captions — one screen of markup that wants to be a page of interaction. The fix is to manufacture the range: a container sized `count x viewports` screens with a sticky viewport inside it, and `scrolled / scrollable` as the single input. One screen of scroll then means exactly one item, with no per-item measurement to keep in sync.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

An empty box N screens tall turns a one-screen scene into a scrollable sequence, with progress as a CSS variable and the index as state.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The container height is written in the scroller's own pixels — `hostHeight * (1 + count * viewports)` — and the sticky child is written at exactly `hostHeight`, so the difference between them is the scroll range and nothing else. Pixels rather than `vh` because inside a scrollable box, viewport units measure a different element entirely.
2. Progress is `(hostTop - containerTop) / (total - hostHeight)`, read from live rects on the frame it is used. Nothing is cached, so a font swap, an image landing above, or a resize corrects itself on the next frame with no invalidation step.
3. The two outputs are separated by cost. Continuous progress goes out as `--range-progress` and `--range-position` custom properties and to an optional `onFrame` callback — sixty times a second, never through React. The discrete index goes through `useState`, and only on the frame it changes.
4. Progress is quantised to four decimals before writing. Below that nothing downstream can render differently, so a stationary scroller performs zero style writes rather than 60 per second.
5. The index uses `floor`, not `round`, so item `i` owns `[i/count, (i+1)/count)` — equal slots, and the last item owns the end of the range instead of a half-slot.
6. A hysteresis band of 0.04 of a slot guards the index commit. A trackpad resting exactly on a boundary otherwise flips the index every frame, and each flip is a full React re-render of the viewport contents.
7. The render prop receives `{ index, count }`, so the child tree re-renders on item change only — the per-frame value is available to the same tree as an inherited custom property.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `viewports = 1`
  Screens of scroll per item. One is the value that makes the range legible: a full flick moves exactly one item, which is the mapping users infer within two gestures. Below ~0.6 items blur past; above ~2 the sequence feels padded.
- `HYSTERESIS = 0.04`
  Fraction of a slot the position must travel past a boundary before the index commits. Sized above trackpad jitter and sub-pixel rect noise, and far below anything a user could intend as a move.
- `progress quantisation = 4 decimal places`
  One ten-thousandth of the range is below the resolution of any downstream transform or colour mix, so comparing the formatted string lets an idle scroller skip the DOM write entirely.
- `range height = hostHeight * (1 + count * viewports)`
  The extra `1` is the sticky viewport's own screen. Without it the last item is only reachable at the exact bottom of the scroller and can never be centred.

## API

```ts
function ManufacturedScrollRange(props: { count: number; viewports?: number; children: (state: { index: number; count: number }) => ReactNode; onFrame?: (state: { progress: number; position: number; index: number }) => void; scroller?: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `count: number`
  How many items the manufactured range represents.
- `viewports: number` — default `1`
  Screens of scroll per item.
- `children: (state: { index: number; count: number }) => ReactNode`
  Rendered inside the sticky viewport; called again only when the index changes.
- `onFrame: (state: ScrollRangeState) => void`
  Per-frame progress, for work that must not go through React.
- `scroller: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>`
  Scroll container. Omit to auto-detect the nearest scrollable ancestor.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the outer container.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function ManufacturedScrollRange({
  count,
  viewports = 1,
  children,
  onFrame,
  scroller,
  className,
}: ManufacturedScrollRangeProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const viewport = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);

  const [index, setIndex] = useState(0);
  const indexRef = useRef(0);
  const lastHeight = useRef(0);
  const lastProgress = useRef('');

  useRaf((_dt) => {
    const rootEl = root.current;
    const viewportEl = viewport.current;
    if (!rootEl || !viewportEl || count <= 0) return;

    const host = scroller?.current ?? nearestScroller(rootEl);
    const hostIsRoot = host === document.documentElement;
    const hostTop = hostIsRoot ? 0 : host.getBoundingClientRect().top;
    const hostHeight = hostIsRoot ? window.innerHeight : host.clientHeight;
    if (hostHeight === 0) return;

    // The range is measured in the scroller's own pixels, not `vh`. Inside a
    // scrollable box, viewport units describe a completely different element.
    const total = Math.round(hostHeight * (1 + count * viewports));
    if (total !== lastHeight.current) {
      lastHeight.current = total;
      rootEl.style.height = `${total}px`;
      viewportEl.style.height = `${hostHeight}px`;
    }

    const travel = total - hostHeight;
    const progress = travel > 0 ? clamp((hostTop - rootEl.getBoundingClientRect().top) / travel, 0, 1) : 0;
    const position = progress * count;

    // Continuous value: out as a custom property, never as state. Quantised
    // so an idle scroller stops writing to the DOM entirely.
    const text = progress.toFixed(4);
    if (text !== lastProgress.current) {
      lastProgress.current = text;
      rootEl.style.setProperty('--range-progress', text);
      rootEl.style.setProperty('--range-position', position.toFixed(3));
    }

    // Discrete value: equal slots, `floor` not `round`, so item i owns
    // [i/count, (i+1)/count) and the last item owns the end of the range.
    const candidate = clamp(Math.floor(position), 0, count - 1);
    if (candidate !== indexRef.current) {
      // Distance past the boundary being crossed — going forward that is the
      // candidate's own edge, going back it is the current item's edge.
      const boundary = candidate > indexRef.current ? candidate : indexRef.current;
      if (Math.abs(position - boundary) > HYSTERESIS) {
        indexRef.current = candidate;
        setIndex(candidate);
      }
    }

    onFrame?.({ progress, position, index: indexRef.current });
  });
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useRaf` unsubscribes from the shared loop on unmount and no other listener, observer or timer is registered. The inline height and the custom properties are written on nodes React owns and disappear with them.

**Reduced motion.** The range is layout, not animation: it is how the sequence is navigated, so collapsing it would remove access to the content rather than remove motion. The component itself animates nothing — it publishes numbers. Consumers should read the discrete `index` under reduced motion and drive cuts, not `--range-progress` and continuous parallax.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Sizing the spacer in `vh` while the component lives inside a scrollable box. The height comes from the window and the progress comes from the box, so the sequence finishes early or never finishes — and it looks correct only when the box happens to be full-height.
- Pushing continuous progress through `setState`. That is a React render per frame for a value that only ever feeds a transform; the tree re-reconciles 60 times a second to move one bar.
- Committing the index with no hysteresis. Resting on a boundary makes the index oscillate, which reads as flicker and, if items fetch anything, as a request storm.
- Using `round` for the index. Items 0 and count-1 get half-width slots, so the first and last feel twice as fast as the middle for no reason the user can see.
- Putting the spacer as a sibling *before* the sticky element. Sticky positioning is bounded by the parent, so the viewport unsticks as soon as the spacer scrolls past and the sequence stops halfway.
- Deriving progress from `scroller.scrollTop / scrollHeight`. That is the whole document's progress, not the section's, so the mapping breaks the moment anything is added above or below.
- Forgetting `overflow: hidden` on the sticky viewport. Content sized to the viewport bleeds over neighbouring sections during the range and paints outside its own box.

## Notes

- The scroll container is auto-detected by walking ancestors for a scrollable `overflow-y`, so the component works unchanged on a normal page; pass `scroller` when the container is created later or ambiguous.
- Custom properties inherit, so anything inside the render prop can read `--range-progress` without prop drilling and without a re-render.
- For a ring rather than a list, replace the `clamp` on the index with `((i % count) + count) % count` and let the position wrap.

## Definition of done

One screen of scroll advances exactly one item. Resting the pointer on a slot boundary does not flip the index back and forth. The progress bar moves continuously while the item title changes in steps. Resizing the scroller keeps the current item on screen. React DevTools shows a render only when the item changes, not per frame.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
