# Build: In-Shader Mouse Bulge

The pointer is a screen-space quantity and the mesh is a world-space one, so something has to convert between them. Instead of unprojecting the pointer on the CPU with a raycaster, every vertex projects ITSELF once, compares its own normalised device position against the pointer, and displaces by the result. Each vertex gets an exact distance, the cost is one extra matrix multiply per vertex, and nothing about it depends on the CPU knowing the mesh's real shape.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A soft lens that follows the cursor, measured by projecting every vertex to screen space instead of raycasting.

- Category: webgl
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1

## How it works

1. The vertex shader runs `projectionMatrix * modelViewMatrix * vec4(pos, 1.0)` twice. The first is a probe: dividing its xy by w gives this vertex's own NDC position, which is the only common space the pointer and the geometry both live in.
2. NDC spans -1..1 on both axes whatever the viewport is, so a raw distance is stretched by the aspect ratio. The x component of the delta is multiplied by `uAspect` before the length is taken, which is what keeps the lens circular on a 16:9 canvas instead of an ellipse 1.78 times too wide.
3. The weight is `exp(-dot(delta, delta) * falloff)`. A Gaussian never actually reaches zero, so there is no radius at which the deformation visibly stops, and its derivative is continuous, so the sheen has no hard edge either — a smoothstep would give both a visible boundary ring.
4. The vertex is lifted by `bulge * uLift` and the weight is passed to the fragment shader, which pushes the centred UV outward by `centered * vBulge * uMagnify`. Lift alone is a bump; lift plus UV magnification is a lens, and that is the difference between a dent in the surface and glass sitting on top of it.
5. The second projection is the one that ships the vertex, evaluated after the displacement the first one made possible. The extra matrix multiply per vertex is the entire cost of the technique.
6. The strength uniform is damped toward the pointer's active state rather than switched, so the lens fades in on enter and out on leave instead of appearing at, and vanishing from, the last known position.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `falloff = 5`
  Tightness of the Gaussian in aspect-corrected NDC units, where the full viewport is 2 wide. At 5 the lens is roughly a third of the height across. Below ~2 it swells to cover the whole plane and reads as a global warp; above ~15 it collapses to a pinpoint that the vertex grid cannot resolve smoothly.
- `lift = 0.5`
  World units the crown rises, against a plane about 2.5 units tall at a camera distance of 3. Above ~1.2 the crown passes the camera's near plane and the lens punches a hole through itself when the cursor is centred.
- `magnify = 0.12`
  UV displacement at the crown. This is what makes it a lens rather than a bump. Above ~0.3 the magnification outruns the geometry, the texture visibly slides across the surface, and the illusion of glass breaks into a smear.
- `sheen = 0.18`
  Extra brightness at the crown. Small on purpose: the eye reads a slight highlight as curvature, and anything past ~0.4 reads as a blown-out light source instead.
- `segments = 128`
  The bulge is per-vertex, so the mesh density is the resolution of the lens. At 16 the Gaussian resolves into a faceted pyramid chasing the cursor; past ~192 the extra vertices land inside a single pixel of the highlight.
- `STRENGTH_SMOOTHING = 0.0008`
  Fraction of the gap left after one second, so the lens fades in over roughly a fifth of a second. Instant switching leaves the lens visible at the last known position for one frame after the cursor leaves, which flickers.
- `pointer smoothing = 0.0008`
  Matches the strength smoothing so the lens grows and moves at the same rate. A pointer smoothed much harder than the strength arrives late and the lens appears to be dragged; much softer and it inherits every jitter in the raw pointer stream.
- `CAMERA_FOV / CAMERA_Z = 45 / 3`
  Sets how much perspective the lift reads against. At a narrow FOV the raised crown barely changes size and the bulge looks flat; at a wide one the plane's own edges keystone enough to compete with the effect.

## API

```ts
function NdcMouseBulge(props: { strength?: number; falloff?: number; lift?: number; magnify?: number; sheen?: number; segments?: number; paint?: (ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D, size: { width: number; height: number }) => void; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `strength: number` — default `1`
  Peak displacement weight. 0 disables the effect.
- `falloff: number` — default `5`
  Gaussian tightness. Higher is a smaller, sharper lens.
- `lift: number` — default `0.5`
  World units the crown of the bulge rises toward the camera.
- `magnify: number` — default `0.12`
  How far the lens magnifies at the crown, in UV units.
- `sheen: number` — default `0.18`
  Extra brightness at the crown.
- `segments: number` — default `128`
  Plane subdivisions per axis. The resolution of the lens.
- `paint: (ctx, size) => void`
  Override the surface. Receives a 2D context for a 1024x1024 canvas.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the wrapper via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function NdcMouseBulge({
  strength = 1,
  falloff = 5,
  lift = 0.5,
  magnify = 0.12,
  sheen = 0.18,
  segments = 128,
  paint,
  className,
}: NdcMouseBulgeProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const stage = useRef<Stage | null>(null);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const { inView } = useInView(host, { threshold: 0 });
  const visible = useVisibility();
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  // Already in NDC, which is exactly the space the shader compares in — no
  // conversion, no cached bounding rect to go stale on scroll.
  const pointer = useSmoothPointer({ target: host, smoothing: 0.0008 });

  const [supported, setSupported] = useState(true);
  useEffect(() => setSupported(hasWebGL()), []);

  const engaged = useRef(0);

  const live = useRef({ strength, falloff, lift, magnify, sheen });
  live.current = { strength, falloff, lift, magnify, sheen };

  const ready = width > 1 && height > 1 && supported;

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = host.current;
    if (!el || !ready) return;

    const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: true, alpha: true });
    renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio());
    renderer.setSize(el.clientWidth, el.clientHeight, false);
    renderer.setClearColor(0x000000, 0);
    renderer.domElement.style.display = 'block';
    renderer.domElement.style.width = '100%';
    renderer.domElement.style.height = '100%';
    el.appendChild(renderer.domElement);

    const scene = new THREE.Scene();
    const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(CAMERA_FOV, 1, 0.1, 100);
    camera.position.z = CAMERA_Z;

    const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
    canvas.width = TEXTURE_SIZE;
    canvas.height = TEXTURE_SIZE;
    const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
    if (ctx) (paint ?? paintSurface)(ctx, { width: TEXTURE_SIZE, height: TEXTURE_SIZE });

    const texture = new THREE.CanvasTexture(canvas);
    texture.colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace;
    texture.wrapS = THREE.ClampToEdgeWrapping;
    texture.wrapT = THREE.ClampToEdgeWrapping;
    texture.anisotropy = Math.min(4, renderer.capabilities.getMaxAnisotropy());

    const uniforms: BulgeUniforms = {
      uTexture: { value: texture },
      uMouseNdc: { value: new THREE.Vector2(0, 0) },
      uAspect: { value: 1 },
      uStrength: { value: 0 },
      uFalloff: { value: falloff },
      uLift: { value: lift },
      uMagnify: { value: magnify },
      uSheen: { value: sheen },
    };

    // Dense. The bulge is evaluated per vertex, so the lens can only be as
    // round as the mesh is fine: at 16 segments the Gaussian resolves into a
    // faceted pyramid that follows the cursor.
    const geometry = new THREE.PlaneGeometry(1, 1, segments, segments);
    const material = new THREE.ShaderMaterial({
      vertexShader: ndcMouseBulgeVertexShader,
      fragmentShader: ndcMouseBulgeFragmentShader,
      uniforms,
    });
    const mesh = new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material);
    // The lift happens after the bounding sphere was computed; leaving culling
    // on lets three blank a plane that is filling the viewport.
    mesh.frustumCulled = false;
    scene.add(mesh);

    stage.current = { renderer, scene, camera, mesh, geometry, material, texture, uniforms };

    return () => {
      stage.current = null;
      scene.remove(mesh);
      // Inside `uniforms`, where `disposeObject` cannot see it.
      texture.dispose();
      disposeObject(scene);
      geometry.dispose();
      material.dispose();
      disposeRenderer(renderer);
      renderer.domElement.remove();
    };
    // eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps
  }, [ready, segments, paint]);

  useEffect(() => {
    const current = stage.current;
    if (!current || width < 1 || height < 1) return;
    const aspect = width / height;
    current.renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio());
    current.renderer.setSize(width, height, false);
    current.camera.aspect = aspect;
    current.camera.updateProjectionMatrix();

    // Cover the frustum exactly at z = 0. Derived from the camera, because the
    // visible extent at this distance has no fixed relationship to the pixel
    // width of the container.
    const visibleHeight = 2 * Math.tan((CAMERA_FOV * Math.PI) / 360) * CAMERA_Z;
    current.mesh.scale.set(visibleHeight * aspect, visibleHeight, 1);
    // The shader corrects its screen-space distance with this, so a stale
    // value turns the lens into an ellipse the moment the container reshapes.
    current.uniforms.uAspect.value = aspect;
  }, [width, height]);

  useRaf(
    (dt) => {
      const current = stage.current;
      if (!current) return;
      const { strength: peak, falloff: tightness, lift: rise, magnify: zoom, sheen: light } =
        live.current;

      // Fade the whole effect in and out with the pointer rather than snapping
      // it. Snapping leaves a lens sitting at the last known position for one
      // frame after the cursor leaves, which flickers.
      const wanted = pointer.current.active && !reduced ? peak : 0;
      engaged.current = damp(engaged.current, wanted, STRENGTH_SMOOTHING, dt);

      current.uniforms.uMouseNdc.value.set(pointer.current.ndcX, pointer.current.ndcY);
      current.uniforms.uStrength.value = engaged.current;
      current.uniforms.uFalloff.value = tightness;
      current.uniforms.uLift.value = rise;
      current.uniforms.uMagnify.value = zoom;
      current.uniforms.uSheen.value = light;

      current.renderer.render(current.scene, current.camera);
    },
    ready && inView && visible,
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Removes the mesh from the scene, disposes the `CanvasTexture` explicitly because it sits inside `material.uniforms` beyond `disposeObject`'s reach, runs `disposeObject` over the scene, disposes the geometry and material, then `disposeRenderer` — `setAnimationLoop(null)`, `dispose()`, `forceContextLoss()` — and removes the canvas from the DOM. The stage ref is nulled first so a frame already queued on the shared RAF loop exits before touching anything. `useSmoothPointer` removes its own listeners on unmount.

**Reduced motion.** The strength target is held at 0, so no vertex is ever displaced, the UV is never magnified and no sheen appears — the surface is a completely static image that ignores the pointer. The value is still damped to zero rather than assigned, so a lens that is on screen when the preference changes retracts smoothly instead of popping flat.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Comparing raw NDC distances. NDC is -1..1 on both axes regardless of the viewport, so on a 16:9 canvas the falloff is 1.78 times wider than it is tall and the lens is a visible ellipse. The x component of the delta is weighted by the aspect before the length is taken.
- Raycasting the pointer against the plane instead. It costs a matrix inversion per frame, returns exactly one hit point, and — decisively — it intersects the CPU-side geometry, which this shader has already moved. Once anything displaces vertices, the raycast answers a question about a surface that is not on screen.
- Projecting once and reusing `gl_Position`. The probe has to happen before the displacement and the final projection has to happen after it, so the two cannot be shared. Displacing after computing `gl_Position` simply has no effect at all.
- Using a linear or smoothstep falloff. Both reach exactly zero at a finite radius, which draws a visible ring on the surface where the deformation stops. The Gaussian is asymptotic and leaves no boundary.
- Lifting the vertex without magnifying the UV. The result is a bump, not a lens — the surface moves but the image printed on it does not, so it reads as a dent in a rigid sheet rather than glass laid over it.
- Leaving `frustumCulled` on. The lift happens after the bounding sphere was computed, so three can decide a plane that is filling the viewport is off screen and blank it.
- Sizing the plane from the container's pixel dimensions. The plane has to cover the frustum at z = 0, which is `2 * tan(fov/2) * distance` tall; a pixel width has no fixed relationship to that and the plane ends up short of the edges or overscaled.
- Forgetting to update `uAspect` on resize. The lens silently turns elliptical the moment the container reshapes, and because it still follows the cursor correctly the bug looks like a design decision.
- Calling `renderer.dispose()` alone on unmount. GPU objects are freed but the WebGL context survives, and Chromium drops the oldest once a renderer process holds about 16. `disposeRenderer` calls `forceContextLoss`.

## Notes

- `useSmoothPointer` already exposes `ndcX` / `ndcY`, so the pointer reaches the uniform without a single conversion and without a cached bounding rect that could go stale on scroll.
- This is the same two-projections-per-vertex trick `cylinder-gallery` uses; there it has to be in-shader, because the CPU geometry is a flat plane and the visible drum exists only on the GPU.

## Definition of done

Move the cursor over the surface and a round highlight follows it, swelling the lattice cells underneath rather than merely brightening them. The highlight is circular at any container aspect — resize from square to wide and it stays round. It has no visible outer edge or ring where the effect stops. Leave the surface and the lens retracts over about a fifth of a second rather than vanishing. Nothing changes when the cursor moves outside the component. With `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` the surface is completely inert and the cursor has no effect at all.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Nested Split With True Restore

Splitting text destroys the markup inside it: a paragraph containing an `<em>` and an `<a>` goes into SplitText as semantic HTML and comes out as a flat pile of divs. This component splits into masked lines that rise into view, preserves each child element's own tag through the split, and on teardown restores the container's `innerHTML` byte-identically to what it was before anything touched it.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Splits rich markup into masked lines and restores the original innerHTML byte-for-byte on teardown.

- Category: text
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. `const originalHTML = el.innerHTML` is captured **before** any pre-processing. This string is the contract — everything else is arranged so it can be reapplied exactly.
2. The nested pre-pass walks the container's element children. Each child is split to lines on its own with a throwaway `new SplitText(child, { type: "lines" })`; the line markup is read while that split is live, the split is reverted, and each line is re-emitted inside a **shallow clone** of the child (`child.cloneNode(false)`) before the child is removed. A shallow clone carries the tag and every attribute and none of the content — `cloneNode(true)` would duplicate the child's entire text into every line.
3. The container is then split for real with `new SplitText(el, { type, mask: "lines", linesClass, aria: "auto" })`, and `gsap.from(split.lines, { yPercent: 110, duration: 0.9, stagger: 0.08, ease: "power3.out" })` runs inside a `gsap.context` scoped to the element.
4. The build is deferred behind `document.fonts.ready`, because line boxes measured against the fallback face break in the wrong places and never re-flow when the real font arrives. A `cancelled` flag closes the async gap so a build cannot start after unmount.
5. Teardown runs in a fixed order: `ctx.revert()` first, so the tween's inline styles are removed while the split nodes still exist; then `split.revert()`; then `if (el.innerHTML !== originalHTML) el.innerHTML = originalHTML`.
6. That last line is the whole point. GSAP's `revert()` restores the string SplitText itself captured at construction time — which, after a nested pre-pass, is the *intermediate* markup, not the original. The explicit restore is what makes the guarantee real.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `Y = 110`
  Percent of a line's own height it starts below the mask. Past 100 rather than at it, because `mask: "lines"` clips to the line box and descenders on the first frame otherwise peek below the mask edge on tall faces.
- `DURATION = 0.9`
  Seconds per line. Long enough that `power3.out` has room for its deceleration; below ~0.5s the ease flattens and the lines read as snapping into place.
- `STAGGER = 0.08`
  Seconds between lines. About a tenth of the duration, so five or six lines are always in motion together and the block reads as one rising mass rather than as a queue.
- `VIEW_THRESHOLD = 0.25`
  Fraction of the block visible before splitting and revealing. A paragraph is tall, so requiring more than about a quarter means it must be nearly centred before anything happens.
- `cloneNode(false) = false`
  Shallow, always. `true` copies the child's descendants, so every line of a five-line paragraph contains the whole paragraph and the block renders five times its own height.

## API

```ts
function NestedSplitRestore(props: { children: ReactNode; type?: string; mask?: boolean; nested?: boolean; y?: number; duration?: number; stagger?: number; delay?: number; startOnView?: boolean; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Markup to split. Element children keep their own tags and attributes through the pre-pass.
- `type: string` — default `'lines'`
  SplitText `type`. Lines are what the mask and the reveal use.
- `mask: boolean` — default `true`
  Wrap each line in an overflow-hidden box so it rises out of nothing.
- `nested: boolean` — default `true`
  Run the per-child pre-pass. Turn off for a single flat paragraph.
- `y: number` — default `110`
  Percent of a line's height it starts below the mask.
- `duration: number` — default `0.9`
  Seconds per line.
- `stagger: number` — default `0.08`
  Seconds between lines.
- `delay: number` — default `0`
  Seconds before the first line moves.
- `startOnView: boolean` — default `true`
  Split and reveal when scrolled into view rather than on mount.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the container via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const Y = 110;
const DURATION = 0.9;
const STAGGER = 0.08;
const VIEW_THRESHOLD = 0.25;

/**
 * Replace each element child of `host` with one shallow clone per visual line.
 * Text nodes sitting directly under `host` are left alone — they have no tag
 * to preserve, so the outer split handles them correctly already.
 */
function flattenChildrenToLines(host: HTMLElement): void {
  for (const child of Array.from(host.children)) {
    if (!(child instanceof HTMLElement)) continue;

    const inner = new SplitText(child, { type: 'lines' });
    // Read the line markup while the split is live, then put the child back
    // exactly as it was. Reading after revert would read the un-split child.
    const lines = inner.lines.map((line) => line.innerHTML);
    inner.revert();

    for (const markup of lines) {
      // cloneNode(false) — the tag and every attribute, none of the content.
      // cloneNode(true) would duplicate the child's entire text into each line.
      const clone = child.cloneNode(false);
      if (!(clone instanceof HTMLElement)) continue;
      clone.innerHTML = markup;
      host.insertBefore(clone, child);
    }
    host.removeChild(child);
  }
}

export function NestedSplitRestore({
  children,
  type = 'lines',
  mask = true,
  nested = true,
  y = Y,
  duration = DURATION,
  stagger = STAGGER,
  delay = 0,
  startOnView = true,
  className,
}: NestedSplitRestoreProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const { inView } = useInView(root, { threshold: VIEW_THRESHOLD, once: true });

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = root.current;
    // Reduced motion never splits at all. The markup React rendered is the
    // finished state, and leaving it untouched is both the accessible answer
    // and the fast one.
    if (!el || reduced) return;
    if (startOnView && !inView) return;

    gsap.registerPlugin(SplitText);

    // Captured before the pre-pass, not after. This string is the contract.
    const originalHTML = el.innerHTML;

    let cancelled = false;
    let split: SplitText | null = null;
    let ctx: gsap.Context | null = null;

    const build = () => {
      if (cancelled) return;

      if (nested) flattenChildrenToLines(el);

      const s = new SplitText(el, {
        type,
        mask: mask ? 'lines' : undefined,
        linesClass: 'kinetic-split-line',
        // SplitText restores the original text to the accessibility tree
        // itself; without this the reveal is read out one line per node.
        aria: 'auto',
      });
      split = s;

      ctx = gsap.context(() => {
        gsap.from(s.lines, {
          yPercent: y,
          duration,
          stagger,
          delay,
          ease: 'power3.out',
        });
      }, el);
    };

    // Measuring line boxes before the webfont arrives measures the fallback,
    // so the lines break in the wrong places and never re-flow. See
    // `font-safe-text-split` for the full resize and late-font lifecycle.
    void document.fonts.ready.then(build);

    return () => {
      cancelled = true;
      // Order matters. The context reverts the tween's inline styles while the
      // split nodes still exist; reverting the split first would leave those
      // styles orphaned on nodes GSAP can no longer find.
      ctx?.revert();
      split?.revert();
      // The true restore. Only writes when something actually differs, so the
      // no-pre-pass case hands React back the very nodes it created.
      if (el.innerHTML !== originalHTML) el.innerHTML = originalHTML;
    };
  }, [
    children,
    type,
    mask,
    nested,
    y,
    duration,
    stagger,
    delay,
    startOnView,
    inView,
    reduced,
  ]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** A `cancelled` flag guards the async `document.fonts.ready` boundary. Teardown then runs `ctx.revert()` (kills the tweens and strips their inline styles while the split nodes still exist), `split.revert()`, and finally an explicit `el.innerHTML = originalHTML` when the two differ — the true restore.

**Reduced motion.** No split happens at all — the effect returns before touching the DOM. The markup React rendered is the finished state, so the text is fully visible and fully semantic on first paint, with every `<em>` and `<a>` intact. This is both the accessible answer and the fast one.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Trusting `revert()` to restore the original markup after a nested pre-pass. SplitText snapshots `innerHTML` at construction, which by then is your intermediate line markup — `revert()` faithfully restores the wrong thing, and the `<em>` and `<a>` are gone for good.
- Splitting before the webfont loads. Lines are measured against the fallback face, so they break in the wrong places and never re-flow; the mask then clips text that has moved outside its line box. See `font-safe-text-split`.
- Using `cloneNode(true)` in the pre-pass. Each line inherits the child's full contents and the block explodes to several times its height.
- Reading the line markup after reverting the inner split. Revert restores the child to its unsplit state, so you read the whole child back and produce one "line" containing everything.
- Reverting the split before the context. GSAP's inline styles are then orphaned on nodes the context can no longer find, so a remount starts from a half-animated state.
- Letting SplitText's line divs into the accessibility tree. Without `aria: "auto"` a screen reader announces one fragment per line, mid-sentence; with it SplitText restores the original text for assistive technology.
- Splitting at all under reduced motion. There is nothing to gain and a whole DOM tree to rebuild — the markup React rendered is already the finished state.

## Notes

- This is one of the two components that deliberately use GSAP `SplitText`, because the technique *is* SplitText: nested splitting and the shortcomings of its `revert()`. `SplitText` ships inside the main `gsap` package and is free to use; it is imported from `gsap/SplitText` rather than vendored, so this is a use grant and no redistribution is involved. The other text components here split declaratively in JSX so consumers are not forced into GSAP for effects that do not need it.
- The acceptance criterion is exact and testable: after teardown, `element.innerHTML` is byte-identical to what it was before the split — tags, attributes and whitespace included, not merely visually equivalent.
- The `nested` prop can be turned off for a single flat paragraph, in which case the pre-pass is skipped and the restore write never fires because the strings already match.

## Definition of done

Record `element.innerHTML` before mounting, unmount, and compare: the two strings are byte-identical, including the `<em>` and `<a>` tags and their attributes. Visually, lines rise from behind their own mask edge, staggered, with no character visible below the mask on the first frame. A screen reader reads the paragraph as continuous prose rather than as one fragment per line. With reduced motion enabled the paragraph is fully rendered on first paint and the DOM is never modified.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Single-Draw Orbit Rings

Five concentric orbits of static path dots, each carrying one brighter dot that travels it. Every dot in the system is a vertex of one `THREE.Points` object, so ring count and dot count cost buffer memory but never a second draw call. The outer rings are dimmer than the inner ones, which reads as depth even though the camera is orthographic and nothing is actually further away.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Concentric rings of dots, one bright marker travelling each ring, all of it in a single draw call.

- Category: webgl
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1

## How it works

1. Each dot packs its whole identity into one attribute, `aPointData = vec4(kind, ringIndex, angle, dotRadius)`, where `kind` is 0 for a path dot and 1 for the orbiting marker. `position` is zeroed for every vertex and carries no information at all.
2. The vertex shader derives the ring radius as `uBaseRadius * scale * uExtent * 0.5` with `scale = 1.0 - (uRingCount - 1.0 - ringIndex) * 0.1`, so rings step 10% apart with the outermost at full radius, and `uExtent = min(width, height)` keeps the structure inside a preview of any aspect.
3. Path dots sit at `vec2(cos(angle), sin(angle)) * ringRadius`; markers use `angle - PI * 0.5 + uElapsed * uSpeed` instead, so the phase offset baked into the attribute becomes a starting position and the clock does the travelling.
4. Depth is faked with a focal length that no camera uses: `alpha = 0.15 + 0.65 * FOCAL_LENGTH / (FOCAL_LENGTH + ringRadius)` dims a ring in proportion to its size, so wider rings recede.
5. `gl_PointSize` is clamped to a 2px floor and the fragment alpha is then divided by the area that clamping invented — `vAlphaScale = unclamped² / clamped²` — so a dot forced twice as wide comes out four times fainter and the field looks identical at 1x and 3x device pixel ratio.
6. The fragment shader turns each square point sprite into a disc with `1.0 - smoothstep(0.43, 0.5, length(gl_PointCoord - 0.5))` and discards anything fully transparent, so the renderer is created with `antialias: false`.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `RING_STEP = 0.1`
  10% radius difference between adjacent rings. Below ~0.06 the rings visually merge into a band at preview size; above ~0.15 the innermost ring collapses to a dot when ringCount is 5.
- `FOCAL_LENGTH = 800.0`
  Not a camera property — the denominator of the alpha falloff. At 800 the outermost ring lands about 30% dimmer than the innermost at typical preview sizes: enough to read as depth, not enough to read as a fade-out. At 200 the outer rings vanish.
- `MIN_POINT_SIZE = 2.0`
  Hardware floor. Below roughly 1px most GPUs rasterise nothing at all, so a 1px dot at DPR 1 would simply be missing on some machines rather than faint.
- `UNCLAMPED_MIN_POINT_SIZE = 1.0`
  The size the dot *would* have had. It is the numerator of the area correction — without a separate constant there is nothing to compare the clamped size against and the compensation cannot be computed.
- `disc edge = smoothstep(0.43, 0.5, d)`
  A soft band 7% of the point radius wide. Narrower and a 2px dot aliases into a square; wider and every dot looks blurred rather than small.
- `baseRadius = 0.75`
  Outermost ring diameter as a fraction of the container short side. At 1.0 the ring touches the edge and the marker clips as it passes; 0.75 leaves a margin the marker can travel through.
- `dotsPerRing = 170`
  Dense enough that the path reads as a continuous line at 320px wide, sparse enough that the innermost ring is not a solid filled circle.
- `speed = 0.3`
  Radians per second — one lap every ~21s. Linear, no easing: a constant angular rate is what makes it read as a mechanism rather than an animation.

## API

```ts
function OrbitRingPoints(props: { ringCount?: number; dotsPerRing?: number; speed?: number; baseRadius?: number; dotRadius?: number; markerRadius?: number; opacity?: number; color?: string; markerColor?: string; seed?: number | string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `ringCount: number` — default `5`
  Concentric rings. Each gets exactly one travelling marker.
- `dotsPerRing: number` — default `170`
  Static path dots per ring.
- `speed: number` — default `0.3`
  Marker angular speed in radians per second.
- `baseRadius: number` — default `0.75`
  Outermost ring diameter as a fraction of the container short side.
- `dotRadius: number` — default `1`
  Path dot radius in CSS pixels, before pixel-ratio scaling.
- `markerRadius: number` — default `3`
  Marker radius in CSS pixels.
- `opacity: number` — default `1`
  Multiplier applied to every dot in the vertex shader.
- `color: string` — default `'#8a8f98'`
  Path dot colour, any value `THREE.Color` accepts.
- `markerColor: string` — default `'#ffffff'`
  Travelling marker colour.
- `seed: number | string` — default `'orbit-ring-points'`
  Seeds the angular scatter, so the ring is identical on server and client.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function OrbitRingPoints({
  ringCount = 5,
  dotsPerRing = 170,
  speed = 0.3,
  baseRadius = 0.75,
  dotRadius = 1,
  markerRadius = 3,
  opacity = 1,
  color = '#8a8f98',
  markerColor = '#ffffff',
  seed = 'orbit-ring-points',
  className,
}: OrbitRingPointsProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const stage = useRef<Stage | null>(null);
  const [unsupported, setUnsupported] = useState(false);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const size = useRef({ width, height });
  size.current = { width, height };

  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const ready = width > 0 && height > 0;

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = host.current;
    if (!el || !ready) return;

    if (!hasWebGL()) {
      setUnsupported(true);
      return;
    }

    // `antialias: false` is deliberate: the fragment shader anti-aliases each
    // disc itself with a smoothstep, so MSAA would pay for a whole extra
    // sample buffer to solve a problem that is already solved.
    const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: false, alpha: true });
    renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio());
    renderer.setClearAlpha(0);

    const scene = new THREE.Scene();
    // Orthographic and 1:1 with CSS pixels, so `gl_PointSize` in the shader is
    // a real pixel count and the ring radii are real pixel radii.
    const camera = new THREE.OrthographicCamera(-1, 1, 1, -1, 0.1, 10);
    camera.position.z = 1;

    const rng = createRng(seed);
    const perRing = dotsPerRing + 1; // path dots + one marker
    const total = ringCount * perRing;

    const positions = new Float32Array(total * 3); // stays all zeros
    const pointData = new Float32Array(total * 4);

    let at = 0;
    for (let ring = 0; ring < ringCount; ring += 1) {
      // Sorting the angles is not cosmetic. Points are drawn in buffer order,
      // and an unsorted ring interleaves near and far dots so the alpha blend
      // stipples along the path instead of reading as one continuous line.
      const angles = new Float32Array(dotsPerRing);
      for (let i = 0; i < dotsPerRing; i += 1) angles[i] = rng() * Math.PI * 2;
      angles.sort();

      for (let i = 0; i < dotsPerRing; i += 1) {
        pointData[at] = 0;
        pointData[at + 1] = ring;
        pointData[at + 2] = angles[i] ?? 0;
        pointData[at + 3] = dotRadius;
        at += 4;
      }

      pointData[at] = 1;
      pointData[at + 1] = ring;
      pointData[at + 2] = rng() * Math.PI * 2;
      pointData[at + 3] = markerRadius;
      at += 4;
    }

    const geometry = new THREE.BufferGeometry();
    geometry.setAttribute('position', new THREE.BufferAttribute(positions, 3));
    geometry.setAttribute('aPointData', new THREE.BufferAttribute(pointData, 4));

    const uniforms: Uniforms = {
      uElapsed: { value: 0 },
      uExtent: { value: 1 },
      uPixelRatio: { value: renderer.getPixelRatio() },
      uOpacity: { value: opacity },
      uRingCount: { value: ringCount },
      uSpeed: { value: speed },
      uBaseRadius: { value: baseRadius },
      uColor: { value: new THREE.Color(color) },
      uMarkerColor: { value: new THREE.Color(markerColor) },
    };

    const material = new THREE.ShaderMaterial({
      vertexShader: ORBIT_RING_POINTS_VERT,
      fragmentShader: ORBIT_RING_POINTS_FRAG,
      uniforms,
      transparent: true,
      depthTest: false,
      depthWrite: false,
    });

    const points = new THREE.Points(geometry, material);
    // Every vertex sits at the origin, so three computes a bounding sphere of
    // radius zero and culls the entire object the moment the camera is not
    // looking straight at (0,0,0). Displacement happens in the shader, which
    // the culler cannot see.
    points.frustumCulled = false;
    scene.add(points);

    el.appendChild(renderer.domElement);
    renderer.domElement.style.display = 'block';
    renderer.domElement.style.width = '100%';
    renderer.domElement.style.height = '100%';

    const resize = (w: number, h: number) => {
      renderer.setSize(w, h, false);
      camera.left = -w / 2;
      camera.right = w / 2;
      camera.top = h / 2;
      camera.bottom = -h / 2;
      camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
      // Ring radii scale off the SHORT side. Off the height alone, a wide
      // preview leaves the rings floating in a sea of empty space; off the
      // width alone, a tall one clips them.
      uniforms.uExtent.value = Math.min(w, h);
      uniforms.uPixelRatio.value = renderer.getPixelRatio();
    };

    const draw = (elapsed: number) => {
      uniforms.uElapsed.value = elapsed;
      renderer.render(scene, camera);
    };

    resize(size.current.width, size.current.height);
    stage.current = { renderer, scene, camera, uniforms, resize, draw };
    draw(STATIC_ELAPSED);

    return () => {
      stage.current = null;
      // Order matters: release the scene graph's GPU objects while the
      // context is still alive, then hand the context back.
      disposeObject(scene);
      material.dispose();
      disposeRenderer(renderer);
      renderer.domElement.remove();
    };
  }, [
    ready,
    ringCount,
    dotsPerRing,
    speed,
    baseRadius,
    dotRadius,
    markerRadius,
    opacity,
    color,
    markerColor,
    seed,
  ]);

  // Resize is its own effect so a container reflow costs a `setSize` call
  // rather than a full teardown and rebuild of the buffer.
  useEffect(() => {
    stage.current?.resize(width, height);
    if (reduced) stage.current?.draw(STATIC_ELAPSED);
  }, [width, height, reduced]);

  useRaf((_dt, elapsed) => stage.current?.draw(elapsed), ready && !reduced && !unsupported);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Clears the stage ref first so no queued frame can touch a dead renderer, then `disposeObject(scene)` for the geometry, `material.dispose()`, `disposeRenderer(renderer)` for `dispose` + `forceContextLoss` + zeroing the drawing buffer, and finally removes the canvas from the DOM. The rAF subscription is released by `useRaf` on unmount.

**Reduced motion.** The rAF subscription is never opened. One frame is drawn at `uElapsed = 0`, which parks every marker at twelve o'clock on its ring, so the full structure is visible and only the orbiting stops. Resizing still redraws that frame.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Leaving `frustumCulled` at its default. Every vertex sits at the origin, so three computes a bounding sphere of radius zero; the displacement is invisible to the culler and the entire object disappears the moment the camera is not pointed exactly at (0,0,0).
- Not sorting the angles within a ring before writing them into the buffer. Points are blended in buffer order with depth testing off, so an unsorted ring stipples — the path visibly breaks into a dotted texture instead of reading as one line.
- Clamping `gl_PointSize` without correcting the alpha. The clamp is invisible at DPR 3 and doubles the covered area at DPR 1, so the same component looks twice as bright on a cheap monitor as on a retina laptop.
- Turning on `antialias: true` to smooth the dots. The fragment shader already anti-aliases each disc; MSAA then allocates a multisample buffer the size of the canvas to solve nothing.
- Rebuilding the renderer on every resize. The buffer is size-independent — only the camera frustum and `uExtent` change — so a container reflow should cost a `setSize` call, not a teardown that drops and re-acquires a GL context.
- Calling `renderer.dispose()` and stopping there. It frees GPU objects but leaves the context alive; `disposeRenderer` also calls `forceContextLoss`, without which a grid of previews silently blacks out the oldest one at around sixteen contexts.

## Notes

- The camera is orthographic and spans the canvas 1:1 in CSS pixels, so `gl_PointSize` is a real pixel count and ring radii are real pixel radii. That is what makes the pixel-ratio compensation expressible at all.
- Ring count and dots per ring are both free at draw time. A hundred rings is one draw call and one buffer upload.

## Definition of done

Five rings of dots with one brighter dot travelling each, all at the same angular rate, the outer rings visibly dimmer than the inner ones. Resize the container and the rings rescale without flicker or a dropped context. Zoom the browser to 200% and the dots stay the same apparent brightness rather than getting denser. With reduced motion on, the rings render fully and the markers sit still at the top.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Key-Replayed Page Reveal

Two opaque layers and one CSS keyframe do the whole job of a route transition. The inbound layer carries `key={revealKey}`, so a route change unmounts it and mounts a new one — and a freshly mounted element runs its animation from frame zero, which replays the fade with no state, no library and nothing to reset. The outbound layer fades up to opaque and the navigation commits at 80% of that, while the screen is already covered, so the two halves hand off invisibly without ever referring to each other.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

An opaque overlay that fades away on every route change, replayed by nothing more than a changed React key.

- Category: transition
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The inbound layer is `<div key={revealKey} className="kinetic-reveal-in" />`. Its animation runs `from { opacity: 1 }` to `to { opacity: 0; visibility: hidden }` over 0.55 s on `cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1)` with `forwards`. Changing `revealKey` is the entire replay mechanism: React sees a different key, discards the node, mounts a new one, and the new node starts its animation at frame zero.
2. `visibility: hidden` in the `to` frame, held by `forwards`, is what retires the layer. At `opacity: 0` alone a full-viewport opaque surface stays composited for the rest of the page's life; `visibility` removes it from the compositor without unmounting anything.
3. `usePageCover(coverDuration)` returns `{ covering, cover }`. `cover(commit)` sets `covering` true — which flips `data-covering` on the outbound layer and runs `opacity: 0 -> 1` over `coverDuration` on `cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1)` — then, after `coverDuration * 0.8` seconds, calls `setCovering(false)` and `commit()` in the same tick.
4. Both calls in one tick matters: React batches them into a single commit, so the cover drops to transparent on the exact frame the re-keyed inbound layer mounts at opacity 1. Split them across two ticks and there is one frame of bare destination content visible between the two halves.
5. The transition property is declared on the `[data-covering="true"]` rule only, never on the base rule, so release is a hard cut rather than a fade. The inbound layer is opaque and stacked above the cover at that instant, so the cut is invisible — and a symmetric fade there would compound two opacities and hold the screen dark past the end of the reveal.
6. The stylesheet is emitted through React 19's `<style href precedence>` hoisting, which dedupes by `href`. Per-instance values — durations, colour, z-index — ride in CSS custom properties set on the root, because there is only ever one copy of the rule block.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `revealDuration = 0.55`
  Seconds for the inbound fade. Under ~0.35 s the reveal reads as a flicker of the wrong colour rather than a curtain lifting; over ~0.8 s the destination is legible through a haze for long enough that people start clicking through it.
- `PAGE_COVER_DURATION = 0.32`
  Seconds for the outbound cover. Deliberately about half the reveal: leaving should feel decisive and arriving should feel gradual. Exported as a constant so the hook that times the commit and the layer that runs the transition cannot be handed two different numbers.
- `COMMIT_FRACTION = 0.8`
  Fraction of the cover the commit waits for. On `cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1)` the layer is roughly 96% opaque at 80% of the way through, so the step to fully covered is imperceptible while a fifth of the perceived navigation latency disappears. At 1.0 every click pays a full 0.32 s of dead time; below ~0.6 the destination is visibly swapped behind a translucent sheet.
- `cover ease = cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1)`
  Ease-in, no ease-out. The cover must be at its steepest as it approaches opaque, which is what makes 80% look like 100%. An ease-out cover crawls through its last 20% and the early commit becomes visible.
- `zIndex = 195`
  Above a custom cursor (150) and a scroll progress bar (120) — both of which must be hidden during a transition — and below a preloader (200), which must be able to sit over a reveal on first load.

## API

```ts
function PageRevealOverlay(props: { revealKey: string; revealDuration?: number; coverDuration?: number; covering?: boolean; color?: string; zIndex?: number; position?: "fixed" | "absolute"; className?: string }): JSX.Element
function usePageCover(coverDuration?: number): { covering: boolean; cover: (commit: () => void) => void }
```

- `revealKey: string`
  Identity of the current page. A change replays the reveal. `usePathname()` in Next.js.
- `revealDuration: number` — default `0.55`
  Seconds the inbound cover takes to fade away.
- `coverDuration: number` — default `0.32`
  Seconds the outbound cover takes to reach opaque. Pass the same value to `usePageCover`.
- `covering: boolean` — default `false`
  Drive from `usePageCover().covering`.
- `color: string` — default `'#000'`
  Any CSS colour. Must be opaque, or the page shows through the handoff.
- `zIndex: number` — default `195`
  Above the site and any custom cursor, below a preloader.
- `position: "fixed" | "absolute"` — default `"fixed"`
  `absolute` inside a bounded container; `fixed` for a real page transition.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * Seconds the outbound cover takes to reach opaque. Shared default so the hook
 * that times the commit and the layer that runs the transition cannot be given
 * two different numbers.
 */
export const PAGE_COVER_DURATION = 0.32;

/**
 * Fraction of the cover the commit waits for. On the `cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1,
 * 1)` cover, 80% of the way through the screen is about 96% opaque, so the
 * step to fully covered is imperceptible — and a fifth of the perceived
 * navigation latency is gone. Waiting for 100% is a fifth of a second of dead
 * time on every single click.
 */
const COMMIT_FRACTION = 0.8;

const REVEAL_CSS = `
@keyframes kinetic-page-reveal {
  from { opacity: 1; }
  to   { opacity: 0; visibility: hidden; }
}
.kinetic-reveal-root {
  /* Never eats a click, not even mid-fade. The layer is opaque and covers the
     whole viewport; one swallowed click on a nav item is a dead site. */
  pointer-events: none;
  z-index: var(--kx-reveal-z, 195);
}
.kinetic-reveal-layer {
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  background: var(--kx-reveal-color, #000);
}
/* Inbound. Starts opaque because it is mounted at the moment the destination
   is mounted, and holds the end frame with 'forwards' so 'visibility: hidden'
   retires the layer from compositing instead of leaving an invisible
   full-screen surface alive for the rest of the page's life. */
.kinetic-reveal-in {
  opacity: 1;
  animation: var(--kx-reveal-duration, 0.55s) cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1)
    forwards kinetic-page-reveal;
}
/* Outbound. Idle is hidden as well as transparent, for the same reason. */
.kinetic-reveal-cover {
  opacity: 0;
  visibility: hidden;
}
/* The transition is declared on the covering state ONLY, so release is a cut.
   That is deliberate: at release the re-keyed inbound layer is already sitting
   at opacity 1 directly above this one, so a second fade here would compound
   two opacities and hold the screen dark past the end of the reveal. */
.kinetic-reveal-cover[data-covering='true'] {
  opacity: 1;
  visibility: visible;
  transition: opacity var(--kx-cover-duration, 0.32s)
    cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1);
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  /* Not 'animation: none' — that would leave the inbound layer parked at its
     opaque from-frame, permanently covering the site. The layers are removed
     entirely, and 'usePageCover' commits synchronously, so navigation is a
     hard cut to the destination with no flash of overlay in either direction. */
  .kinetic-reveal-layer { display: none; }
}
`;

export interface PageRevealOverlayProps {
  /**
   * Identity of the current page. A change replays the reveal. In Next.js App
   * Router this is `usePathname()`; in the demo it is a local state value.
   */
  revealKey: string;
  /** Seconds the inbound cover takes to fade away. */
  revealDuration?: number;
  /** Seconds the outbound cover takes to reach opaque. */
  coverDuration?: number;
  /** Drive from `usePageCover().covering`. */
  covering?: boolean;
  /** Any CSS colour. Must be opaque, or the page shows through the handoff. */
  color?: string;
  /** Above the site, below a preloader. */
  zIndex?: number;
  /** `absolute` to demo inside a bounded box; `fixed` for a real page. */
  position?: 'fixed' | 'absolute';
  className?: string;
}

export function PageRevealOverlay({
  revealKey,
  revealDuration = 0.55,
  coverDuration = PAGE_COVER_DURATION,
  covering = false,
  color = '#000',
  zIndex = 195,
  position = 'fixed',
  className,
}: PageRevealOverlayProps) {
  return (
    <>
      {/* React 19 hoists and dedupes by `href`, so a hundred navigations and
          any number of instances still emit exactly one rule block. Per
          instance values ride in custom properties for that reason. */}
      <style href="kinetic-page-reveal-overlay" precedence="medium">
        {REVEAL_CSS}
      </style>

      <div
        aria-hidden
        className={cn(
          'kinetic-reveal-root',
          position === 'fixed' ? 'fixed inset-0' : 'absolute inset-0',
          className,
        )}
        style={
          {
            '--kx-reveal-duration': `${revealDuration}s`,
            '--kx-cover-duration': `${coverDuration}s`,
            '--kx-reveal-color': color,
            '--kx-reveal-z': zIndex,
          } as CSSProperties
        }
      >
        {/* Cover first, reveal second: later in the DOM paints on top, and the
            inbound layer's opaque first frame is what hides the cover's cut. */}
        <div
          className="kinetic-reveal-layer kinetic-reveal-cover"
          data-covering={covering ? 'true' : 'false'}
        />
        <div key={revealKey} className="kinetic-reveal-layer kinetic-reveal-in" />
      </div>
    </>
  );
}

export interface PageCover {
  /** Feed to `PageRevealOverlay`. */
  covering: boolean;
  /** Raise the cover, then run `commit` — your navigation — under it. */
  cover: (commit: () => void) => void;
}

/**
 * The outbound half. `commit` is a callback rather than a router call so
 * nothing here depends on a routing library.
 */
export function usePageCover(coverDuration = PAGE_COVER_DURATION): PageCover {
  const [covering, setCovering] = useState(false);
  const timer = useRef<ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | null>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  useEffect(
    () => () => {
      if (timer.current !== null) clearTimeout(timer.current);
      timer.current = null;
    },
    [],
  );

  const cover = useCallback(
    (commit: () => void) => {
      // Reduced motion: no cover at all, and the commit is synchronous. A
      // zero-duration cover would still be one frame of opaque colour, which
      // is a flash — the single most unpleasant thing to show someone who has
      // asked for less motion.
      if (reduced) {
        commit();
        return;
      }
      // A second click while a cover is already up would schedule a second
      // commit and navigate twice. The live timer is the lock.
      if (timer.current !== null) return;

      setCovering(true);
      timer.current = setTimeout(
        () => {
          timer.current = null;
          // Both in one tick, so React batches them into a single commit: the
          // cover drops to transparent on the exact frame the re-keyed reveal
          // layer mounts at opacity 1. Split across two ticks and there is one
          // frame of bare destination content between them.
          setCovering(false);
          commit();
        },
        coverDuration * COMMIT_FRACTION * 1000,
      );
    },
    [coverDuration, reduced],
  );

  return { covering, cover };
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The only resource is the commit timer, cleared in an unmount effect and nulled so the lock cannot survive a remount. There are no listeners, no rAF and no tweens; the animations are CSS and die with the nodes React removes.

**Reduced motion.** Both layers get `display: none`, and `usePageCover` calls the commit synchronously rather than starting a timer. Navigation is a hard cut straight to the destination — no cover, no reveal, and crucially not a zero-duration overlay, which would still be one frame of opaque colour.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Animating the overlay with a tween and a timeline. There is nothing to tween: the whole reason this is bulletproof is that a remount restarts a CSS animation, so there is no in-flight animation to kill, no state to reset, and a double navigation cannot leave the overlay half-faded.
- Using `animation: none` for reduced motion. That leaves the inbound layer parked on its opaque `from` frame, permanently covering the site — the failure looks like a blank page. The layers get `display: none` and `usePageCover` commits synchronously instead.
- Committing the navigation after the cover finishes. A fifth of a second of nothing happening after a click is exactly where a visitor decides the link is broken and clicks again.
- Omitting `pointer-events: none`. A full-viewport opaque div swallows the click on whatever the visitor aims at next, and mid-transition that is usually another nav item.
- Letting `cover()` run while a cover is already up. Without the live-timer lock a fast double click schedules two commits and navigates twice, so the visitor lands one page past where they aimed.
- Leaving the finished inbound layer at `opacity: 0` without `visibility: hidden`. It is still a composited full-viewport surface, and on a page that also runs a WebGL hero it costs a measurable slice of fill rate for the rest of the session.
- Fading the cover back out symmetrically. Two opaque layers both mid-fade multiply, not add: the screen stays darker for longer and the reveal appears to stall before it starts.

## Notes

- In Next.js App Router: mount once in `app/layout.tsx` with `revealKey={usePathname()}` and `position="fixed"`, then replace nav `<Link>` elements with buttons calling `cover(() => router.push(href))`. Nothing in this file imports `next/navigation` — the commit is a callback so the same component works under React Router or a plain state switch.
- The overlay colour must be opaque. A translucent colour makes both halves show the wrong page through the handoff, which is the one artefact this technique exists to prevent.
- The root carries `aria-hidden`: it is a purely decorative surface, and a screen reader announcing it on every navigation would be worse than no transition at all.
- Browser back and forward change the key without going through `cover()`, so they get the reveal but not the cover. That is correct — a history navigation has already happened by the time your code hears about it, so there is nothing left to cover.

## Definition of done

Click a nav item: the panel fades to the overlay colour, the destination content swaps while it is covered, and the overlay fades away over roughly half a second. The heading is never visible in an intermediate state, and there is no frame where old and new content are both on screen. Click two nav items in quick succession and you land on the second one, not past it. With reduced motion the content swaps instantly with no coloured frame in either direction.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Staggered Panel Wipe

The counter, the word list and the exit wipe are three parts of a single `gsap.timeline`, not three independent animations racing each other. The number is tweened on a plain object with `power2.inOut`, so it accelerates and settles instead of ticking linearly — the difference between a loading count and a progress bar wearing a costume.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

An eased 0-100 counter, a word list and a five-column wipe, all on one timeline so they cannot drift.

- Category: transition
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. A plain object `{ v: 0 }` is tweened to 100 over `countDuration` seconds. `onUpdate` writes `String(Math.round(count.v)).padStart(3, "0")` into a ref'd span. Tweening the object rather than the DOM keeps the eased value in one place and means the number is interpolated by the same engine, on the same clock, as everything else on the timeline.
2. The words are placed with `tl.set(wordEl, { textContent: w }, i * step)` where `step = countDuration / words.length` — for five words over 1.6 s that is one word every 320 ms. Because they are positioned on the timeline rather than scheduled with `setTimeout`, they stay locked to the counter if the timeline is retimed, paused, or seeked.
3. When the count lands, the content block leaves on `yPercent: -120, opacity: 0` over 0.5 s with `power3.inOut`. -120 rather than -100 clears the block past its own height plus a margin, so a descender never lingers at the top edge.
4. The five columns then retract with `scaleY: 0` and `transformOrigin: "top"`, 0.9 s of `power4.inOut`, staggered 0.08 s apart, inserted at `-=0.2` so the wipe begins while the content is still leaving. `scaleY` is a compositor-friendly transform; animating `height` here would relayout five elements every frame.
5. The whole build runs inside `useGsap`, which wraps it in a `gsap.context` scoped to the root and calls `ctx.revert()` on unmount, so a preloader torn down mid-count leaves no inline transforms behind.
6. Only after the timeline's `onComplete` fires does React set `gone` and return `null`. Unmounting on a timer instead would pull the nodes out from under running tweens.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `countDuration = 1.6`
  Seconds for 0 to 100. Under ~1.2 s the digits change too fast to read as a count and the word list flickers; over ~2.5 s people have already decided the site is slow.
- `CONTENT_DURATION = 0.5`
  Content exit. Long enough to read as a departure rather than a cut, short enough that it is finished before the panels have opened far enough to reveal what is behind it.
- `PANEL_DURATION = 0.9`
  Per-column retract. `power4.inOut` spends most of its time near the ends, so a shorter duration collapses the slow start and the whole wipe reads as a single instant cut.
- `PANEL_STAGGER = 0.08`
  Gap between columns. At 0 the five columns are one panel; past ~0.15 the last column is still standing after the first has finished, which reads as a stuck element rather than a sequence.
- `PANEL_OVERLAP = 0.2`
  Seconds the wipe is pulled back into the content exit. Without the overlap there is a dead beat between the number disappearing and the panels moving, and that pause is where the eye decides something has hung.
- `padStart(3, "0") = 3`
  Fixed three-digit width. Without it the counter changes character count at 10 and 100 and the number visibly jumps sideways twice mid-tween.

## API

```ts
function PanelWipePreloader(props: { words?: string[]; panels?: number; countDuration?: number; onDone?: () => void; position?: "fixed" | "absolute"; className?: string }): JSX.Element | null
```

- `words: string[]` — default `['Assets', 'Type', 'Shaders', 'Layout', 'Ready']`
  Words shown under the counter, spread evenly across the count.
- `panels: number` — default `5`
  Number of collapsing columns.
- `countDuration: number` — default `1.6`
  Seconds the counter takes to reach 100.
- `onDone: () => void`
  Fires from the timeline's `onComplete`, after the last column has collapsed.
- `position: "fixed" | "absolute"` — default `"fixed"`
  Use `absolute` inside a bounded container; `fixed` for a real full-page preloader.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function PanelWipePreloader({
  words = ['Assets', 'Type', 'Shaders', 'Layout', 'Ready'],
  panels = 5,
  countDuration = 1.6,
  onDone,
  position = 'fixed',
  className,
}: PanelWipePreloaderProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const content = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const counter = useRef<HTMLSpanElement>(null);
  const word = useRef<HTMLSpanElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const [gone, setGone] = useState(false);

  const done = useRef(onDone);
  done.current = onDone;

  useGsap(
    gsap,
    () => {
      const el = root.current;
      const contentEl = content.current;
      const counterEl = counter.current;
      const wordEl = word.current;
      if (!el || !contentEl || !counterEl || !wordEl) return;

      const columns = Array.from(el.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-wipe-panel]'));

      if (reduced) {
        counterEl.textContent = '100';
        wordEl.textContent = words[words.length - 1] ?? '';
        setGone(true);
        done.current?.();
        return;
      }

      const count = { v: 0 };
      const tl = gsap.timeline({
        onComplete: () => {
          setGone(true);
          done.current?.();
        },
      });

      tl.to(count, {
        v: 100,
        duration: countDuration,
        ease: 'power2.inOut',
        onUpdate: () => {
          counterEl.textContent = String(Math.round(count.v)).padStart(3, '0');
        },
      });

      // Positioned on the SAME timeline as the counter, at computed times, so
      // the words stay locked to the number no matter how the timeline is
      // retimed, paused or seeked.
      const step = countDuration / Math.max(words.length, 1);
      words.forEach((w, i) => {
        tl.set(wordEl, { textContent: w }, i * step);
      });

      tl.to(contentEl, {
        yPercent: -120,
        opacity: 0,
        duration: CONTENT_DURATION,
        ease: 'power3.inOut',
      });

      if (columns.length > 0) {
        // transformOrigin top + scaleY 0 retracts each column upward like a
        // blind. The -0.2 overlap fuses the wipe with the tail of the content
        // exit so the two read as one gesture.
        tl.to(
          columns,
          {
            scaleY: 0,
            transformOrigin: 'top',
            duration: PANEL_DURATION,
            ease: 'power4.inOut',
            stagger: PANEL_STAGGER,
          },
          `-=${PANEL_OVERLAP}`,
        );
      }
    },
    root,
    [reduced],
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useGsap` runs the whole build inside a `gsap.context` scoped to the root and calls `ctx.revert()` on unmount, which kills the counter tween, the positioned `set` calls and the panel stagger, and restores every property they touched — including the span's original `textContent`.

**Reduced motion.** No timeline is built at all. The counter is written straight to 100, the last word is set, the component unmounts itself and `onDone` fires on the same tick — so a reduced-motion visitor sees the real page immediately rather than a silent panel that still has to be waited out.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Driving the counter with `setInterval` and the panels with GSAP. Two clocks, and on a loaded main thread the number finishes after the wipe has already covered it.
- Tweening a linear counter. It is the ease that sells the count — `power2.inOut` slows near 100, which is the shape of real work finishing.
- Animating panel `height` instead of `scaleY`. Five elements relayouting every frame on a page that is simultaneously mounting its real content is the one place the jank is guaranteed to be visible.
- Unmounting the preloader on a `setTimeout` sized to match the timeline. The two drift under load; unmount from `onComplete` instead.
- Leaving the preloader in the tree with `opacity: 0`. It still swallows every click on the page underneath. This returns `null`.
- Forgetting `transformOrigin: "top"`. The default centre origin makes the columns shrink to a band in the middle of the screen instead of retracting like a blind.

## Notes

- In a Next.js App Router project this mounts once in `app/layout.tsx`, above `{children}`, and calls `onDone` to flip a context flag the hero listens to. It is deliberately not keyed to the pathname — a preloader that replays on every navigation is a bug, not a feature.
- If the real site has an actual load signal (fonts ready, hero image decoded), gate `onDone` on both the timeline and that promise. See `safe-preloader` for the ceiling-and-floor version of that problem.
- The counter is decorative. The root carries `aria-hidden`, so a screen reader is never read a number climbing to 100.

## Definition of done

The number counts 000 to 100 with a visible ease, never changing width. Five words swap under it at even intervals and the last word lands as the number does. The content lifts away and five columns retract upward in sequence, the wipe starting before the content has finished leaving. `onDone` fires once, after the last column. With reduced motion the preloader is gone on the first frame. Unmount mid-count and no transforms or altered text remain.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
