# Build: Pause, Don't Unmount

A rotating stack of slabs mounted twice over: once behind `<Activity mode="hidden">` and once behind a plain conditional, switchable live. Hiding tears the Effects down either way — the WebGL context is released, which is what you want, since contexts are a scarce per-process resource. What Activity keeps is everything React owns: the fiber, the DOM, and every `useState` and `useRef` value inside. So the stack resumes at the angle it left, and the build counter on its fiber survives to be incremented again. Requires React 19.2 or newer.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

React 19's Activity hides a WebGL scene without losing its state. Effects still tear down, so the GL context is genuinely released.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1

## How it works

1. `<Activity mode="hidden">` does three separable things, and conflating them is where the misuse starts: it sets `display: none` on the host children, it destroys the Effects inside — cleanup functions run, in order, exactly as on unmount — and it keeps the fiber alive, so state, refs and DOM nodes are all still there when `mode` goes back to `visible`. Children continue to re-render, at a priority below anything visible.
2. Because Effects are destroyed, the scene's cleanup runs on every hide: materials and geometry are disposed and `disposeRenderer` calls `renderer.forceContextLoss()`. That is the correct behaviour rather than a shortfall — Chromium hands out roughly sixteen WebGL contexts per renderer process and evicts the oldest past that, so a context parked behind `display: none` is the thing that blanks an unrelated canvas three sections down the page.
3. The rotation phase lives in a `useRef` inside the hidden subtree, and the build Effect seeds the slab rotations from it BEFORE the first draw. On re-show the scene is correct on frame one; there is no snap from zero up to the resumed angle. Under the `unmount` arm the same ref is a fresh zero because the fiber it lived on was collected.
4. The build counter is the proof, and it needs both halves to move: it increments inside the Effect, so it only rises if the Effect really re-ran, and it survives between runs only if the fiber was preserved. Under `activity` it climbs 1, 2, 3; under `unmount` it is pinned, because each show starts a new fiber whose counter is new too.
5. Build cost is measured with `performance.now()` from the top of the Effect to the end of the first completed `render`, so it covers context acquisition, program linking and the initial upload — the work Activity does not save. On a desktop GPU it lands in the tens of milliseconds; the point of the readout is that the number is not zero.
6. The size hook re-seeds synchronously from `getBoundingClientRect` on every Effect run, and its state is preserved across the hide as well, so the re-shown scene already knows its dimensions and skips the zero-sized first render that a fresh mount has to pass through. That one saved render round-trip is a second, quieter thing the preserved fiber buys.
7. The renderer creates its own canvas inside the Effect and it is removed in cleanup. A React-rendered `<canvas ref>` cannot work here: with `forceContextLoss()` in cleanup, StrictMode's double-invoke hands the second run a permanently dead element, and Activity turns that from a once-per-mount hazard into a once-per-toggle one.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `GAP = 0.2`
  Vertical spacing between slabs in world units, at a slab height of 1.15. Tight enough that the group reads as one stack rather than seven separate cards, wide enough that the back-to-front transparent sort has visible separation to work with.
- `TWIST = 0.24`
  Radians of rotation between neighbouring slabs — about 14 degrees, so seven slabs fan through 84 degrees, just under a quarter turn. Past a full turn the stack becomes rotationally ambiguous and "it resumed where it left" stops being checkable by eye.
- `count / period = 7 / 24`
  Seven slabs at 24 seconds a revolution: 15 degrees per second. Slow enough that a hide and a show a second apart leaves a gap the eye can measure against the readout, which is the entire experiment.
- `CAM_Y / CAM_Z = 2.05 / 4.4`
  A camera lean of about 25 degrees above the stack. Flatter and the slabs collapse into a single silhouette; steeper and it reads as a plan view where the vertical stacking disappears.
- `opacity ramp = 0.34 to 0.80`
  Bottom slab to top. The ramp is what makes the stack legible through itself; a constant alpha turns seven slabs into one muddy plane.

## API

```ts
function PauseDontUnmount(props: { strategy?: 'activity' | 'unmount'; count?: number; period?: number; color?: string; accent?: string; seed?: number | string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `strategy: 'activity' | 'unmount'` — default `'activity'`
  Which arm the switch starts on.
- `count: number` — default `7`
  Slabs in the stack.
- `period: number` — default `24`
  Seconds for one full rotation.
- `color: string` — default `'#5f6873'`
  Colour of the bottom slab.
- `accent: string` — default `'#e8e4dc'`
  Colour of the top slab. The stack lerps between the two.
- `seed: number | string` — default `'pause-dont-unmount'`
  Seeds the per-slab size jitter.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  const el = host.current;
  if (!el || !ready) return;

  if (!hasWebGL()) {
    setUnsupported(true);
    return;
  }

  // Timed from here to the first completed draw: allocating the context,
  // linking the programs and uploading the geometry are what re-showing
  // actually costs, and the number is the honest counterweight to "Activity
  // makes hiding free".
  const t0 = performance.now();

  // The renderer makes its own canvas inside the effect. Two reasons, and
  // both bite here: StrictMode double-invokes this effect, so a React-owned
  // `<canvas ref>` would be handed back after `forceContextLoss()` killed
  // it; and Activity destroys and re-runs this effect on every show, which
  // is the same hazard once per toggle instead of once per mount.
  const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: true, alpha: true });
  renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio());
  renderer.setClearAlpha(0);

  const scene = new THREE.Scene();
  const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(FOV, 1, 0.1, 100);
  camera.position.set(0, CAM_Y, CAM_Z);
  camera.lookAt(0, 0, 0);

  const geometry = new THREE.PlaneGeometry(SLAB_W, SLAB_H);
  const rng = createRng(seed);
  const base = new THREE.Color(color);
  const tint = new THREE.Color(accent);

  const slabs: Slab[] = [];
  const span = Math.max(count - 1, 1);

  for (let i = 0; i < count; i += 1) {
    const t = i / span;
    const material = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({
      color: base.clone().lerp(tint, t),
      transparent: true,
      opacity: 0.34 + 0.46 * t,
      side: THREE.DoubleSide,
      // The slabs are flat and stacked along Y with nothing between them, so
      // the transparent pass sorted back to front is already correct. Writing
      // depth would let the upper slabs clip the lower ones they overhang.
      depthWrite: false,
    });
    const mesh = new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material);
    const k = 0.66 + rng() * 0.46;
    mesh.scale.set(k, k, 1);
    mesh.position.y = (i - span / 2) * GAP;
    scene.add(mesh);
    slabs.push({ mesh, material });
  }

  el.appendChild(renderer.domElement);
  renderer.domElement.style.display = 'block';
  renderer.domElement.style.width = '100%';
  renderer.domElement.style.height = '100%';

  const resize = (w: number, h: number) => {
    renderer.setSize(w, h, false);
    camera.aspect = w / Math.max(h, 1);
    camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
    dirty.current = true;
  };
  resize(size.current.width, size.current.height);

  // Seed the scene from the PRESERVED phase before the first draw. Under
  // Activity this is wherever the stack was when it went away; under a
  // conditional the ref is new and this reads zero. Doing it before the
  // timed draw also means the resumed frame is correct on frame one, with
  // no snap from zero to the real angle.
  for (let i = 0; i < slabs.length; i += 1) {
    const slab = slabs[i];
    if (slab) slab.mesh.rotation.set(-Math.PI / 2, 0, phase.current + i * TWIST);
  }
  renderer.render(scene, camera);

  builds.current += 1;
  buildMs.current = performance.now() - t0;

  stage.current = { renderer, scene, camera, slabs, geometry, resize };
  report(true);

  return () => {
    stage.current = null;
    for (const slab of slabs) {
      scene.remove(slab.mesh);
      slab.material.dispose();
    }
    geometry.dispose();
    // Not optional. `dispose()` alone leaves the context alive and counting
    // against the per-process budget; only `forceContextLoss()`, which
    // `disposeRenderer` calls, actually gives it back. Every hide runs this.
    disposeRenderer(renderer);
    renderer.domElement.remove();
  };
}, [ready, count, color, accent, seed, report]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The Effect removes each slab and disposes its material, disposes the one shared geometry, calls `disposeRenderer` — which stops the loop, disposes the renderer and calls `forceContextLoss()` — and removes the canvas it appended. This runs on unmount, on a StrictMode double-invoke, and on every Activity hide, so it is exercised constantly rather than once. `useRaf` unsubscribes and the shared loop parks when its last subscriber leaves; the `ResizeObserver` unobserves with its hook. A separate Effect reports the scene as gone on teardown so the readout does not freeze on a stale row.

**Reduced motion.** The stack holds still — the phase is integrated from delta time, so freezing it is a matter of adding nothing — and with nothing marking the frame dirty the renderer draws once per build and then idles. The demonstration survives the loss of motion because it was never really about the motion: the build counter still climbs under `activity` and stays pinned under `unmount`, and the rebuild cost in milliseconds is still charged on every show. Only the resumed rotation angle stops being informative, since both arms sit at zero degrees.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Expecting Activity to keep the WebGL context alive. It does not, by design — Effects are destroyed on hide, so your cleanup runs and the context is released. If you had assumed otherwise and skipped disposal, you leak instead; if you assumed re-showing is free, the rebuild millisecond readout says otherwise.
- Lifting the state you wanted preserved above the boundary. Anything outside the `<Activity>` was never at risk, and anything the parent owns is not evidence of anything. The value has to live on a fiber inside the boundary or the comparison proves nothing.
- Changing the element at the boundary position instead of changing `mode`. Swapping `<Activity>{scene}</Activity>` for `{scene}` reconciles as a different type at that slot, so React unmounts the subtree and every preserved value goes with it. Keep the boundary mounted and toggle `mode`.
- Treating hidden as unrendered. Children keep re-rendering, only at a lower priority, so a parent state update still walks the hidden subtree. Anything expensive in render — not in an Effect — is still paid for while hidden.
- Assuming a ref into hidden DOM behaves the same as a ref into visible DOM. The DOM nodes themselves survive, but ref attachment is part of the layout-effect phase that the offscreen path tears down and replays, and this component does not depend on the answer either way. Do the work in an Effect, which is re-run on show, rather than caching a node in a closure that outlives the hide.
- Handing three's renderer a React-rendered `<canvas ref>`. Cleanup calls `forceContextLoss()`, and the next Effect run — from StrictMode or from a re-show — is given the same dead element. Let the renderer build its own canvas in the Effect and remove it in cleanup.
- Reading the build counter in development and taking the absolute number literally. StrictMode double-invokes Effects on mount, so the first build reads 2, not 1. The claim to check is the shape: climbing under `activity`, pinned under `unmount`.

## Notes

- `Activity` is exported from `react` from 19.2 (verified against 19.2.8: `exports.Activity = REACT_ACTIVITY_TYPE`, typed as `ExoticComponent<ActivityProps>` with `mode?: "hidden" | "visible"`). On anything older the import is undefined at runtime, not a build error, which fails as a blank subtree.
- The strongest real use is not a canvas at all — it is a tab, a route the user is likely to come back to, or a filter panel: scroll offsets, uncontrolled input values and list virtualisation windows are all preserved for free, and none of them cost a GPU context to rebuild.
- Pre-rendering the other direction, `mode="hidden"` on a subtree that has never been visible, mounts it at low priority without running Effects. Useful for warming a route, useless for warming a renderer, for the same reason as above.

## Definition of done

On `activity`: press hide, wait, press show. The stack picks up at the angle the readout froze at, `builds` has gone up by one, and the rebuild cost is a real number of milliseconds. On `unmount`: the same sequence returns the stack to zero degrees and `builds` never moves. Hide on either arm and the canvas is gone from the DOM inspector under `unmount` but present with `display: none` under `activity`. Neither arm accumulates WebGL contexts — toggle twenty times and the other previews on the page stay drawn.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Percent Slide Carousel

The simplest slide carousel that is still correct. A flex track holds one full-width slide per child and translates by `-100% * index`; because a percentage translate resolves against the translated element's own width, and the track is exactly one viewport-box wide, one step is exactly one slide. Nothing is measured, so nothing goes stale on resize.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A flex track translated by -100% per slide. One CSS transition, no measurement, no library.

- Category: layout
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The viewport box is `overflow: hidden`. Inside it a flex track is `h-full w-full`, and every slide is `w-full shrink-0` — full width of the *track*, not of the flex line, so `count` slides overflow the track by `count - 1` widths instead of being compressed into it.
2. The track carries `transform: translateX(-${100 * index}%)`. A percentage in `translateX` is relative to the border box of the element being transformed, which is the track, whose width equals the viewport box, which equals one slide. So `-100%` is one slide exactly, with no numbers taken from layout.
3. That is the whole reason to prefer this over a pixel translate: a pixel offset needs a measured slide width, which needs a resize observer, which needs a re-measure pass that can land a frame late and show a seam. Here a resize changes the meaning of `100%` on the next paint for free.
4. The transition is `transform 600ms cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)` on the track only. Interrupting it mid-flight is handled by the compositor: the browser retargets from the current computed transform, so rapid clicks chain smoothly rather than restarting from the last committed index.
5. Navigation clamps rather than wraps by default. `-100% * index` is a linear function of the index with no modulo in it, so a wrap from the last slide to the first would translate the whole track back across every intermediate slide — a visible rewind. `loop` is offered but honest about that.
6. Each slide is a `role="group"` with `aria-roledescription="slide"` and an `aria-label` of `n of N`, so a screen reader announces position without the component owning any live region.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `duration = 600`
  Milliseconds for a full slide. Under ~350 ms a full-width traversal reads as a cut rather than a move and the eye loses which direction it went; over ~900 ms a rapid click-through feels blocked because each step is still finishing when the next arrives.
- `EASE = cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)`
  An expo-out curve: ~80% of the distance is covered in the first third of the duration. On a full-viewport traversal that front-loading is what keeps a 600 ms move from feeling slow, while the long flat tail hides the exact moment the slide lands.
- `translate step = 100%`
  Locked to the slide width by construction, not by choice. Any other value desynchronises the track from the slides and leaves a permanent sliver of the neighbour visible at rest.
- `shrink-0 on slides = flex-shrink: 0`
  Without it flexbox honours the container width and squeezes every slide to `1/count` of the track. The translate still moves a full track-width, so one click jumps `count` slides — the single most common way this pattern breaks.
- `loop = false`
  Default off. With a linear percentage translate there is no cheap wrap: going from the last index to 0 animates back through every slide. If you need a true loop, reach for the drum instead.

## API

```ts
function PercentSlideCarousel(props: { children: ReactNode; duration?: number; index?: number; defaultIndex?: number; onIndexChange?: (index: number) => void; loop?: boolean; className?: string; slideClassName?: string; "aria-label"?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  One slide per child. Each is wrapped in a full-width, non-shrinking cell.
- `duration: number` — default `600`
  Slide transition duration in milliseconds.
- `index: number`
  Controlled index. Omit to let the component hold its own state.
- `defaultIndex: number` — default `0`
  Starting index when uncontrolled.
- `onIndexChange: (index: number) => void`
  Fires with the resolved index after clamping or wrapping.
- `loop: boolean` — default `false`
  Wrap past the ends. Off by default because the wrap animates backwards through every slide.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the viewport box.
- `slideClassName: string`
  Merged onto every slide cell.
- `aria-label: string` — default `'Carousel'`
  Label for the carousel group.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const trackStyle = {
  // One slide is one track-width, so the step is exactly 100%. This is the
  // only carousel arithmetic that needs no numbers from layout at all.
  transform: `translateX(-${100 * current}%)`,
  // No transition under reduced motion: the slide still changes, it just
  // arrives instantly. Cutting the movement is the point; cutting the
  // navigation would be a bug.
  transition: reduced ? 'none' : `transform ${duration}ms ${EASE}`,
};
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to clean up. No listeners, no timers, no animation frames, no imperative writes to the DOM; the only state is the current index and the browser owns the transition.

**Reduced motion.** The track transition is set to `none`, so the slide changes on the next paint with no traversal. Navigation, focus order and the announced position are untouched — only the movement between slides is removed.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Omitting `flex-shrink: 0` on the slides. Flexbox compresses them to fit the track, the `-100%` step no longer equals one slide, and the carousel advances by the whole set on the first click.
- Putting the transition on the slides instead of the track. Only the track moves; a transition on the children costs a style recalculation per slide per frame and animates nothing.
- Translating in pixels from a measured slide width. It works until the container resizes between the measure and the paint, at which point the track is offset by the difference and every slide sits a few pixels off-centre until the next navigation.
- Wrapping the index with a modulo and expecting a loop. `-100% * 0` after `-100% * (n - 1)` animates the whole track backwards past every slide; users read it as the carousel malfunctioning, not as a wrap.
- Marking off-screen slides `aria-hidden` while they still contain focusable children. Tab lands inside a hidden subtree, which is an accessibility violation and, in practice, scrolls the overflow container sideways and desynchronises it from the transform.
- Forgetting `overflow: hidden` on the viewport box. The overflowing slides remain visible, and inside a page-level container they widen the document and add a horizontal scrollbar.
- Killing the transition under reduced motion but also killing the index change. The slide must still change — reduced motion removes the traversal, not the navigation.

## Notes

- This is the flat, non-3D member of the carousel trio. `wrapping-drum-carousel` fakes depth with scale and `autoAlpha` over a `gsap.utils.wrap` ring and loops infinitely; `perspective-coverflow-scroller` uses real `perspective()` / `rotateY()` / `translateZ()` driven by a native scroll container. This one has no depth, no wrap and no JavaScript in the motion path at all — reach for it when the content is the point and the carousel is not.
- Because the motion is a single compositor-friendly transform on one element, it holds 60 fps on hardware where the other two do not. If you are shipping a hero on a low-end phone, this is the one that survives.
- Controlled and uncontrolled: pass `index` to drive it from outside, omit it and the component keeps its own state. `onIndexChange` fires in both cases.

## Definition of done

Click next and exactly one slide traverses the box in 600 ms with no neighbour visible at rest. Hold the next button down and the slides chain without restarting from the previous index. Resize the container mid-transition and the resting position stays flush with the box edges. At the last slide the next button is disabled unless `loop` is set. With reduced motion the slide changes instantly and the buttons still work.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Perspective Coverflow Scroller

A horizontal `overflow-x-auto` container with `scroll-snap-type: x proximity`. Each panel's distance from the centre of the viewport is normalised to roughly ±1 and mapped onto a per-element `perspective() translateZ() rotateY() scale()`, so panels turn their inside edge toward you as they leave the middle. The scroll position itself is never animated by JavaScript — momentum, rubber-banding and keyboard paging are the browser's.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Panels turn away from the centre in real 3D as you scroll a native container — no tween, no loop.

- Category: layout
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. A measure pass caches each panel's layout centre as `panel.offsetLeft + panel.offsetWidth / 2` and sets the track's left and right padding to `(scroller.clientWidth - endPanel.offsetWidth) / 2`, which is exactly enough runway for the first and last panel to reach the middle of the viewport.
2. On every coalesced scroll frame, the normalised offset is `r = clamp((centre - scrollLeft - half) / half, -1.2, 1.2)` where `half = scroller.clientWidth / 2`. `r = 0` is dead centre, `r = ±1` is one half-viewport out.
3. That single scalar drives four things: `rotateY = -rotation * r` (negative, so a panel on the right turns its left edge toward you — the flip-book read), `translateZ = -depth * |r|` (always receding), `scale = 1 - scaleFalloff * min(|r|, 1)`, and `opacity = 1 - opacityFalloff * min(|r|, 1.2)`.
4. `perspective(1300px)` is written inside each panel's own transform rather than as a `perspective` property on the track. A shared parent perspective gives every panel the same vanishing point, so panels near the edges skew as well as rotate; per-element perspective turns each panel about its own centre.
5. The two clamps differ on purpose — `min(|r|, 1)` for scale and `min(|r|, 1.2)` for opacity — so distant panels keep their proportions while continuing to fade out.
6. A `ResizeObserver` on the track re-runs the measure pass whenever content size changes (a font swap, a child growing), which is the deterministic replacement for the usual pile of `setTimeout(recompute, 300)` calls.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `perspective = 1300`
  Per-element perspective distance in px. Under ~700 the foreshortening is strong enough that a 40° turn hides most of the panel; over ~2000 the rotation flattens out and reads as a skew rather than a turn.
- `rotation = 40`
  Degrees of `rotateY` at the clamp. 40° is the point where the panel is visibly turned but still legible; past ~55° it is close enough to edge-on that text disappears and antialiasing on the near edge gets ugly.
- `depth = 130`
  Pixels of `translateZ`, always negative so off-centre panels recede. Combined with the rotation this is what makes the row read as the inside of a cylinder rather than a fanned deck. At 0 you get a pure hinge; past ~250 the far panels shrink faster than `scaleFalloff` intends and the two cues disagree.
- `scaleFalloff = 0.12`
  A panel at one half-width out renders at 0.88. Kept small because `translateZ` is already shrinking it perspectivally — stacking a large explicit scale on top double-counts the distance.
- `opacityFalloff = 0.35`
  The edge panels land near 0.58, not 0. They must stay readable, because on a proximity-snap track they are the affordance that tells you there is more to scroll to.
- `maxOffset = 1.2`
  Clamp on `r`. Without it, a long track keeps rotating panels past 90° and they flip to their back faces; 1.2 rather than 1.0 leaves a little travel past the half-width mark so the outermost visible panels are not all frozen at an identical angle.

## API

```ts
function PerspectiveCoverflowScroller(props: { children: ReactNode; perspective?: number; rotation?: number; depth?: number; scaleFalloff?: number; opacityFalloff?: number; maxOffset?: number; initialIndex?: number; className?: string; panelClassName?: string; 'aria-label'?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  One panel per child. Each is wrapped in a snap-aligned cell.
- `perspective: number` — default `1300`
  Per-element perspective distance in px.
- `rotation: number` — default `40`
  Degrees of `rotateY` at the clamp.
- `depth: number` — default `130`
  Pixels of `translateZ` at the clamp. Applied negatively, so panels recede.
- `scaleFalloff: number` — default `0.12`
  How much a panel shrinks one half-viewport out.
- `opacityFalloff: number` — default `0.35`
  How much a panel fades one half-viewport out.
- `maxOffset: number` — default `1.2`
  Clamp on the normalised offset, so distant panels stop turning further.
- `initialIndex: number`
  Panel centred on mount. Defaults to the middle of the set.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the scroll container.
- `panelClassName: string`
  Merged onto each snap cell. Size the panels here.
- `aria-label: string` — default `'Gallery'`
  Label for the scrollable region, which is focusable for keyboard scrolling.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * Cache each panel's layout centre and pad the track so the first and last
 * panel can reach the middle of the viewport.
 *
 * `offsetLeft`/`offsetWidth` are *layout* values: unaffected by `scrollLeft`
 * and, critically, unaffected by the transforms this component writes.
 * Reading `getBoundingClientRect()` in the scroll handler instead would feed
 * each panel's own `scale()` back into the next frame's offset.
 */
const measure = useCallback(() => {
  const scroller = scrollerRef.current;
  const track = trackRef.current;
  if (!scroller || !track) return;

  const panels = panelsRef.current;
  const first = panels[0];
  const last = panels[count - 1];

  // Half a viewport minus half a panel. The source of this technique used a
  // fixed `24vw`, which is wrong for any panel that is not ~52vw wide and
  // wrong for every container that is not the viewport.
  if (first) {
    track.style.paddingLeft = `${Math.max(0, (scroller.clientWidth - first.offsetWidth) / 2)}px`;
  }
  if (last) {
    track.style.paddingRight = `${Math.max(0, (scroller.clientWidth - last.offsetWidth) / 2)}px`;
  }

  // Read after the padding write: the padding moves every offsetLeft.
  centresRef.current = panels.map((panel) =>
    panel ? panel.offsetLeft + panel.offsetWidth / 2 : 0,
  );
}, [count]);

/** Write one transform per panel from the current scroll position. */
const update = useCallback(() => {
  const scroller = scrollerRef.current;
  if (!scroller) return;

  const half = scroller.clientWidth / 2 || 1;
  const scroll = scroller.scrollLeft;
  const panels = panelsRef.current;
  const centres = centresRef.current;

  for (let i = 0; i < panels.length; i += 1) {
    const panel = panels[i];
    const centre = centres[i];
    if (!panel || centre === undefined) continue;

    if (reduced) {
      panel.style.transform = '';
      panel.style.opacity = '';
      continue;
    }

    // Signed, normalised distance from the viewport centre: -1 = one half
    // width to the left, +1 = one half width to the right.
    const r = clamp((centre - scroll - half) / half, -maxOffset, maxOffset);
    const away = Math.abs(r);

    // Perspective lives *in the transform*, not on the parent. A shared
    // parent perspective gives every panel the same vanishing point, so
    // edge panels skew as well as rotate; per-element perspective turns each
    // panel about its own centre, which is the coverflow look.
    panel.style.transform =
      `perspective(${perspective}px) ` +
      `translateZ(${(-depth * away).toFixed(1)}px) ` +
      `rotateY(${(-rotation * r).toFixed(2)}deg) ` +
      `scale(${(1 - scaleFalloff * Math.min(away, 1)).toFixed(3)})`;

    // Two different clamps on purpose: scale bottoms out at 1, opacity keeps
    // going to `maxOffset`. Distant panels stay proportionate while fading.
    panel.style.opacity = (1 - opacityFalloff * Math.min(away, maxOffset)).toFixed(2);
  }
}, [reduced, perspective, rotation, depth, scaleFalloff, opacityFalloff, maxOffset]);

useEffect(() => {
  const scroller = scrollerRef.current;
  if (!scroller) return;

  measure();

  // Start centred on a panel, not on the midpoint of the scroll range: with
  // an even count the midpoint falls in the gap between two panels and the
  // component opens looking like nothing is selected.
  if (!centredRef.current && count > 0) {
    const target = initialIndex ?? Math.floor((count - 1) / 2);
    const centre = centresRef.current[clamp(Math.round(target), 0, count - 1)];
    if (centre !== undefined) {
      scroller.scrollLeft = centre - scroller.clientWidth / 2;
    }
    centredRef.current = true;
  }

  update();

  let frame = 0;
  const onScroll = () => {
    // Coalesce: a trackpad fires `scroll` far more often than the compositor
    // paints, and each handler run writes N transforms.
    if (frame !== 0) return;
    frame = requestAnimationFrame(() => {
      frame = 0;
      update();
    });
  };

  scroller.addEventListener('scroll', onScroll, { passive: true });

  return () => {
    scroller.removeEventListener('scroll', onScroll);
    if (frame !== 0) cancelAnimationFrame(frame);
  };
}, [measure, update, count, initialIndex]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Removes the `scroll` listener, cancels any pending `requestAnimationFrame`, and disconnects the track `ResizeObserver`. The shared element observer unregisters the scroller. Inline `transform`/`opacity` written on panels dies with the nodes; no timer or tween outlives the component.

**Reduced motion.** The scroller keeps working exactly as it did — it is a real scroll container, and scrolling is user-driven, not animation. What is removed is the 3D: `transform` and `opacity` are cleared on every panel, so the row renders as a flat, fully opaque filmstrip that still snaps by proximity. Nothing moves that the user did not move.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Computing the offset from `getBoundingClientRect()`. The rect reflects the transform this component just wrote, so each panel's `scale()` feeds back into the next frame's offset and the row slowly drifts to a wrong steady state. `offsetLeft`/`offsetWidth` are layout values — untouched by transforms and by `scrollLeft`.
- Putting `perspective` on the track instead of in each panel's transform. Every panel then shares one vanishing point, so the ones near the edges skew into parallelograms instead of turning.
- Handling `scroll` without coalescing into a frame. A trackpad fires scroll events considerably faster than the compositor paints, and every run writes N style strings for no visible benefit.
- Padding the track with a viewport unit like `24vw`. It is correct for exactly one panel width and one container width; inside a card, a modal or a split layout the end panels can never reach the centre and are permanently unselectable.
- Setting `scroll-snap-type: x mandatory`. Release between two panels and the browser yanks you to one of them, which fights every attempt to scan the row. `proximity` snaps only when you were already close.
- Starting at `scrollLeft = 0`. The first panel is then hard against the left edge with nothing to its left, so the effect is invisible until the user scrolls. Centring on a panel on mount shows the technique in both directions immediately.
- Re-centring on every resize. `scrollLeft` is only assigned once, guarded by a ref — otherwise rotating a phone, or any resize during a scroll, teleports the user back to the middle mid-gesture.

## Notes

- One of three deliberately different carousel techniques here, and the distinctions are the point. This one is **true 3D on a native scroll container**: actual `rotateY` and `translateZ`, and no JavaScript animation drives the scroll at all — the handler only reads a position the browser already set. `wrapping-drum-carousel` is **fake 3D** driven by a tweened JS position with `rotationY: 0, z: 0` pinned, and wraps infinitely via `gsap.utils.wrap`. `percent-slide-carousel` is **flat, bounded, one CSS transition per index change**.
- Choose this one when the set is long, scanning matters more than stepping, and you want native momentum and keyboard support for free. It cannot loop: a native scroll container has real ends.
- Because the panels rotate in 3D, text inside them is composited on a rotated plane and will look softer than flat text. That is inherent to the technique, not a bug to tune away; keep small type out of the panels or accept it.

## Definition of done

On mount a panel sits centred and the ones either side are visibly turned toward it. Drag or trackpad-scroll and the turn follows continuously with no lag and no snap-back; release near a panel and it snaps, release between two and it does not. Scroll to either end and the outermost panel reaches the exact centre of the container. Resize the container and the end padding recomputes so it still can.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Pinned Horizontal Track

A full-height section is pinned by ScrollTrigger while a flex strip inside it translates on x. The pin lasts exactly as many scroll pixels as the strip has to travel, so the mapping is 1:1 and the section releases the moment the last panel lands. The tween and the trigger are handed back to the parent, so reveal systems and drag handles can drive off the same pin instead of building a second one.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A section pins while a strip of panels slides sideways, one scroll pixel per track pixel.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. One measurement backs the whole construction: `distanceOf() = max(0, track.scrollWidth - root.clientWidth)`. It is a function, not a captured number, because fonts, images and container resizes all change it after first paint.
2. `gsap.to(track, { x: () => -distanceOf(), ease: "none" })` uses a function-based end value, so `invalidateOnRefresh: true` re-derives the travel on every refresh rather than replaying a stale target.
3. The ScrollTrigger pins the root with `start: "top top"` and `end: () => "+=" + distanceOf()`. Because the pin duration and the tween distance come from the same call, one scroll pixel always buys one track pixel.
4. `scrub: 1` gives the strip one second of catch-up, so a flicked wheel produces a glide rather than a jump; `anticipatePin: 1` lets ScrollTrigger apply the pin a frame early, which removes the single-frame jitter at high scroll speeds.
5. `document.fonts.ready` triggers `ScrollTrigger.refresh()`. A font swap changes `scrollWidth` after the pin was measured, and without the refresh the pin ends before the track does — the last panel is unreachable.
6. On build the component calls `onTrack({ animation, trigger, getDistance })`; on teardown it calls `onTrack(null)`, so consumers rebuild rather than holding a reverted tween.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `scrub = 1`
  Seconds of catch-up between the scrollbar and the strip. `true` (0) locks the track to the scrollbar and inherits every wheel step as a visible stutter; above ~1.5 the track keeps moving long after the wheel stops and reads as broken input.
- `anticipatePin = 1`
  Applies the pin one frame of predicted scroll early. At 0, a fast flick pins one frame late and the section visibly slips before locking. Above 1 it pins early enough to look premature.
- `end = `+=${max(1, distanceOf())}``
  Pin duration in pixels, equal to the horizontal travel. The `max(1, …)` floor exists because a track narrower than its container yields 0, and an end equal to start makes ScrollTrigger treat the trigger as degenerate and never fire it.

## API

```ts
function PinnedHorizontalTrack(props: { children: ReactNode; scroller?: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>; scrub?: number; onTrack?: (track: PinnedTrack | null) => void; className?: string; trackClassName?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Panels. The track is a flex row, so give each panel a width and `shrink-0`.
- `scroller: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>`
  The scroll container the trigger reads. Omit to use the document.
- `scrub: number` — default `1`
  Seconds of catch-up between scrollbar and strip.
- `onTrack: (track: PinnedTrack | null) => void`
  Receives `{ animation, trigger, getDistance }` on build and `null` on teardown.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the pinned root.
- `trackClassName: string`
  Merged onto the moving strip.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function PinnedHorizontalTrack({
  children,
  scroller,
  scrub = 1,
  onTrack,
  className,
  trackClassName,
}: PinnedHorizontalTrackProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const track = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const onTrackRef = useRef(onTrack);
  onTrackRef.current = onTrack;
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  useEffect(() => {
    const rootEl = root.current;
    const trackEl = track.current;
    if (!rootEl || !trackEl || reduced) return;

    // `undefined` means "the document" to ScrollTrigger. Passing `null` would
    // be read as an explicit scroller and throw on the first refresh.
    const scrollerEl = scroller?.current ?? undefined;

    // The single source of truth. Both the tween's end value and the pin's
    // duration call it, so a refresh that changes one changes the other.
    const distanceOf = () => Math.max(0, trackEl.scrollWidth - rootEl.clientWidth);

    let cancelled = false;

    const ctx = gsap.context(() => {
      const animation = gsap.to(trackEl, {
        // Function-based value: re-evaluated by `invalidateOnRefresh`.
        x: () => -distanceOf(),
        ease: 'none',
        scrollTrigger: {
          trigger: rootEl,
          scroller: scrollerEl,
          pin: true,
          anticipatePin: 1,
          scrub,
          start: 'top top',
          // 1 px of scroll buys 1 px of track. Expressing the end as a
          // percentage of viewport height instead makes the mapping depend
          // on window shape, and the track finishes early on a short screen.
          end: () => `+=${Math.max(1, distanceOf())}`,
          invalidateOnRefresh: true,
        },
      });

      const trigger = animation.scrollTrigger;
      if (trigger) {
        onTrackRef.current?.({ animation, trigger, getDistance: distanceOf });
      }
    }, rootEl);

    // The most-forgotten line in scroll-driven layout. A font swap changes
    // `scrollWidth` after the pin has already been measured, and the last
    // panel becomes unreachable because the pin ends before the track does.
    void document.fonts?.ready.then(() => {
      if (!cancelled) ScrollTrigger.refresh();
    });

    return () => {
      cancelled = true;
      onTrackRef.current?.(null);
      // revert(), not kill(): it also removes the pin-spacer GSAP injected
      // into the DOM and restores the inline transform on the strip.
      ctx.revert();
    };
  }, [scroller, scrub, reduced]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Calls `onTrack(null)` so consumers drop their reference, then `ctx.revert()`, which kills the tween and the ScrollTrigger, removes the injected pin-spacer, and clears the inline transform from the strip. A pending `document.fonts.ready` refresh is gated behind a `cancelled` flag.

**Reduced motion.** No ScrollTrigger and no pin are created. The root becomes a horizontally scrollable row, so the same panels are still read left to right — under the reader's own control, at the reader's own speed.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Measuring `scrollWidth - clientWidth` once into a variable. Fonts swap after first paint and the number grows; the pin then ends before the track has finished travelling and the final panel can never be reached.
- Expressing `end` as a percentage of viewport height (`"+=" + distance * 100 / innerWidth + "%"`). It works on the machine it was tuned on and finishes the track early on a shorter screen, because the mapping now depends on window shape rather than on the travel itself.
- Passing `scroller: null` when the component sits on the page rather than in a box. ScrollTrigger reads `null` as an explicit scroller element and throws on the first refresh; omit the option instead, which is why the code coalesces to `undefined`.
- Calling `kill()` instead of `revert()` on unmount. `kill()` leaves the pin-spacer div GSAP injected into the DOM and the inline transform on the strip, so the next mount measures a layout that still contains the last one.
- Forgetting that a pinned element inside a custom scroller needs that scroller passed explicitly. Without it, ScrollTrigger measures the document, the trigger never becomes active inside the box, and the panels sit motionless.

## Notes

- Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` no trigger is created at all and the strip becomes a native `overflow-x-auto` row, so every panel stays reachable by thumb, trackpad and keyboard.
- `gsap.registerPlugin(ScrollTrigger)` runs once at module scope behind a `typeof window` guard, so repeated imports are harmless and prerender never touches the plugin.

## Definition of done

Scroll down: the section locks, the panels slide left, and the last panel reaches the right edge at exactly the moment the section unpins. Resize the container mid-pin and the track still ends flush. With reduced motion on, the section never pins and the panels can be swiped sideways instead.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Pointer Palette Sampling

A surface you paint into a 2D canvas, plus a pointer that reads the pixel underneath it and snaps that read to the nearest entry in a named palette. The colour comes out as a CSS custom property on the root and as a throttled callback, so a chip can follow the cursor with no JavaScript per frame. It turns a palette from a legend you read into something you find by pointing.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Point at the artwork and it names the colour — a clamped pixel read snapped to the nearest palette entry.

- Category: cursor
- Runtime cost: canvas2d
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The canvas is created with `document.createElement` inside the effect and appended to the root, not rendered with a React `ref`. `willReadFrequently` is only honoured on the first `getContext` for a given canvas, so the element and the context have to share one lifecycle — under StrictMode a rendered canvas survives the mount/unmount/remount cycle while the context does not.
2. On resize the backing store is set to `round(cssSize * min(devicePixelRatio, 2))` and the transform re-applied with `setTransform(dpr, 0, 0, dpr, 0, 0)`, in that order, because assigning `canvas.width` resets both the bitmap and the transform. The consumer's `paint` then draws in CSS pixels.
3. A `pointermove` converts client coordinates to bitmap coordinates with the canvas's own backing ratio — `canvas.width / rect.width` — rather than `devicePixelRatio`, so browser zoom and any CSS scale on an ancestor stay correct.
4. A 3x3 box centred on that pixel is clamped to `[0, canvas.width - 1]` and `[0, canvas.height - 1]`, then read in one `getImageData` call. The nine samples are averaged with alpha as the weight, so a dithered or grainy surface produces a stable colour instead of oscillating between two palette entries.
5. The average and every palette hex are converted sRGB → linear → OKLab, and the match is the smallest squared OKLab distance. Nearest-colour in raw RGB is dominated by the green channel and routinely calls a mid blue "black".
6. The match is written to `--kx-sample-color` on the root immediately, along with `--kx-sample-x` / `--kx-sample-y` in CSS pixels, and emitted through `onSample` on a throttle — position is a cursor and must not lag, colour is information and must not spam.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `willReadFrequently = true`
  A default 2D context lives in GPU memory, and each `getImageData` forces a synchronous readback that stalls the pipeline — on a pointermove that is a visible drag on the cursor. The flag moves the surface to a software backing: paint is marginally slower, reads are roughly an order of magnitude faster.
- `SAMPLE_BOX = 3`
  Odd, so the box centres on the pointer's own pixel. One pixel flickers between neighbouring palette entries over any gradient dither; 3x3 is enough to settle it, and 5x5 starts averaging across a real colour boundary so edges read as a colour that is not on screen.
- `MAX_DPR = 2`
  Sampling cost is per read and does not care, but paint cost is per pixel. A 3x display would quadruple the fill work relative to 1.5x for no perceptible gain on a flat-colour artwork.
- `throttleMs = 50`
  Matches the source. Fast enough that dragging across the artwork feels continuous, slow enough that a React consumer re-rendering a swatch on every emission stays under one render per three frames.
- `alpha weight = data[i + 3] / 255`
  Transparent pixels carry no colour but their RGB is usually zero, so an unweighted mean over a partly-transparent box returns something darker than anything visible. Weighting by alpha, and bailing when the total is zero, keeps the answer to what was actually painted.

## API

```ts
function PointerPaletteSampling(props: { palette: readonly PaletteEntry[]; paint: (ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D, size: { width: number; height: number; dpr: number }) => void; paintKey?: string | number; onSample?: (entry: PaletteEntry | null) => void; throttleMs?: number; children?: ReactNode; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `palette: readonly PaletteEntry[]`
  Named colours the read snaps to. `{ name, hex }`, `#rgb` or `#rrggbb`.
- `paint: (ctx, size) => void`
  Draws the surface. Context is pre-scaled and cleared, so draw in CSS pixels. Must not draw a cross-origin image.
- `paintKey: string | number`
  Bump to force a repaint when the painter's inputs change. The painter itself is read through a ref, so an inline arrow is safe.
- `onSample: (entry: PaletteEntry | null) => void`
  Throttled match. `null` when the pointer leaves.
- `throttleMs: number` — default `50`
  Minimum gap between emissions.
- `children: ReactNode`
  Overlay content, rendered in a positioned layer above the canvas.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root. Give it a size.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
function parseHex(hex: string): readonly [number, number, number] | null {
  const raw = hex.trim().replace(/^#/, '');
  const full =
    raw.length === 3
      ? raw
          .split('')
          .map((c) => c + c)
          .join('')
      : raw;
  if (!/^[0-9a-fA-F]{6}$/.test(full)) return null;
  const n = Number.parseInt(full, 16);
  return [(n >> 16) & 255, (n >> 8) & 255, n & 255];
}

function srgbToLinear(channel: number): number {
  const v = channel / 255;
  return v <= 0.04045 ? v / 12.92 : Math.pow((v + 0.055) / 1.055, 2.4);
}

/**
 * sRGB to OKLab. Nearest-colour in raw RGB is the usual shortcut and it is
 * wrong in a way users notice: RGB distance is dominated by green, so a mid
 * blue reads closer to black than to a lighter blue. OKLab is perceptually
 * uniform, so "nearest" means what the eye means.
 */
function rgbToOklab(r: number, g: number, b: number): Oklab {
  const lr = srgbToLinear(r);
  const lg = srgbToLinear(g);
  const lb = srgbToLinear(b);

  const l = Math.cbrt(0.4122214708 * lr + 0.5363325363 * lg + 0.0514459929 * lb);
  const m = Math.cbrt(0.2119034982 * lr + 0.6806995451 * lg + 0.1073969566 * lb);
  const s = Math.cbrt(0.0883024619 * lr + 0.2817188376 * lg + 0.6299787005 * lb);

  return [
    0.2104542553 * l + 0.793617785 * m - 0.0040720468 * s,
    1.9779984951 * l - 2.428592205 * m + 0.4505937099 * s,
    0.0259040371 * l + 0.7827717662 * m - 0.808675766 * s,
  ];
}

export function PointerPaletteSampling({
  palette,
  paint,
  paintKey,
  onSample,
  throttleMs = 50,
  children,
  className,
}: PointerPaletteSamplingProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(root);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  // The canvas is created imperatively rather than rendered with a `ref`.
  // Under StrictMode a rendered canvas is the same element across the
  // mount / unmount / remount cycle, so the second mount inherits a context
  // whose `willReadFrequently` was decided on the first `getContext` — and any
  // teardown that disposes the context leaves the survivor holding a dead one.
  // Owning the element per effect run makes the two lifecycles the same.
  const [surface, setSurface] = useState<{
    canvas: HTMLCanvasElement;
    ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D;
  } | null>(null);

  // Read through refs so an inline painter or handler does not tear the canvas
  // down on every parent render.
  const paintRef = useRef(paint);
  const sampleRef = useRef(onSample);
  useEffect(() => {
    paintRef.current = paint;
    sampleRef.current = onSample;
  });

  /** Palette in OKLab, computed once. Entries with an unparseable hex drop out. */
  const swatches = useMemo(() => {
    const out: { entry: PaletteEntry; lab: Oklab }[] = [];
    for (const entry of palette) {
      const rgb = parseHex(entry.hex);
      if (!rgb) continue;
      out.push({ entry, lab: rgbToOklab(rgb[0], rgb[1], rgb[2]) });
    }
    return out;
  }, [palette]);

  /* Mount the canvas. */
  useEffect(() => {
    const rootEl = root.current;
    if (!rootEl) return;

    const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
    canvas.setAttribute('aria-hidden', 'true');
    canvas.style.cssText =
      'position:absolute;inset:0;display:block;width:100%;height:100%';

    // The one call where the flag counts.
    const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d', { willReadFrequently: true });
    if (!ctx) return;

    rootEl.appendChild(canvas);
    setSurface({ canvas, ctx });

    return () => {
      canvas.remove();
      // Guard the swap: on a StrictMode remount the next effect has already
      // published its canvas by the time this cleanup runs in some orderings.
      setSurface((current) => (current?.canvas === canvas ? null : current));
    };
  }, []);

  /* Size and paint. */
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!surface || width <= 0 || height <= 0) return;
    const { canvas, ctx } = surface;

    const dpr = Math.min(
      typeof window === 'undefined' ? 1 : window.devicePixelRatio || 1,
      MAX_DPR,
    );
    // Assigning width or height resets the bitmap AND the transform, so the
    // scale has to be re-applied after, never before.
    canvas.width = Math.max(1, Math.round(width * dpr));
    canvas.height = Math.max(1, Math.round(height * dpr));
    ctx.setTransform(dpr, 0, 0, dpr, 0, 0);
    ctx.clearRect(0, 0, width, height);

    paintRef.current(ctx, { width, height, dpr });
  }, [surface, width, height, paintKey]);

  /* Sample. */
  useEffect(() => {
    const rootEl = root.current;
    if (!rootEl || !surface || swatches.length === 0) return;
    const { canvas, ctx } = surface;

    let timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | null = null;
    let pendingIsClear = false;

    /**
     * The source's throttle, kept verbatim in behaviour: while an emission is
     * pending, a new colour is DROPPED rather than queued, so the consumer sees
     * one colour per window instead of a burst at the end of one. The single
     * exception is that a pending clear may be replaced — re-entering the
     * canvas within the window cancels the leave instead of flickering to
     * nothing and back.
     */
    const emit = (entry: PaletteEntry | null, isClear: boolean) => {
      if (timer !== null && !pendingIsClear) return;
      pendingIsClear = isClear;
      if (timer !== null) clearTimeout(timer);
      timer = setTimeout(() => {
        timer = null;
        pendingIsClear = false;
        sampleRef.current?.(entry);
      }, throttleMs);
    };

    const sampleAt = (clientX: number, clientY: number): PaletteEntry | null => {
      const rect = canvas.getBoundingClientRect();
      if (rect.width <= 0 || rect.height <= 0) return null;

      // Backing ratio, not devicePixelRatio: this is still correct under
      // browser zoom and under a CSS transform on any ancestor.
      const scaleX = canvas.width / rect.width;
      const scaleY = canvas.height / rect.height;

      const px = Math.round((clientX - rect.left) * scaleX);
      const py = Math.round((clientY - rect.top) * scaleY);
      const half = (SAMPLE_BOX - 1) / 2;

      // Clamp to the bitmap. An unclamped box at the right or bottom edge is
      // padded with transparent black, which pulls the average to black.
      const x0 = clamp(px - half, 0, canvas.width - 1);
      const y0 = clamp(py - half, 0, canvas.height - 1);
      const x1 = clamp(px + half, 0, canvas.width - 1);
      const y1 = clamp(py + half, 0, canvas.height - 1);
      const w = x1 - x0 + 1;
      const h = y1 - y0 + 1;
      if (w <= 0 || h <= 0) return null;

      const data = ctx.getImageData(x0, y0, w, h).data;

      // Alpha-weighted mean over the box. A single pixel flickers between two
      // palette entries on any dithered or noisy surface; nine pixels do not.
      let r = 0;
      let g = 0;
      let b = 0;
      let weight = 0;
      for (let i = 0; i + 3 < data.length; i += 4) {
        const a = (data[i + 3] ?? 0) / 255;
        if (a === 0) continue;
        r += (data[i] ?? 0) * a;
        g += (data[i + 1] ?? 0) * a;
        b += (data[i + 2] ?? 0) * a;
        weight += a;
      }
      // Fully transparent: there is no colour here, and dividing would be NaN.
      if (weight <= 0) return null;

      const lab = rgbToOklab(r / weight, g / weight, b / weight);
      let best: PaletteEntry | null = null;
      let bestDistance = Infinity;
      for (const swatch of swatches) {
        const dl = lab[0] - swatch.lab[0];
        const da = lab[1] - swatch.lab[1];
        const db = lab[2] - swatch.lab[2];
        const distance = dl * dl + da * da + db * db;
        if (distance < bestDistance) {
          bestDistance = distance;
          best = swatch.entry;
        }
      }
      return best;
    };

    const onMove = (event: PointerEvent) => {
      const entry = sampleAt(event.clientX, event.clientY);
      if (!entry) return;

      rootEl.dataset.sampling = 'true';
      rootEl.style.setProperty('--kx-sample-color', entry.hex);
      // The colour is throttled because it is information; the position is not,
      // because it is a cursor. Throttling the position makes the readout lag
      // the pointer by up to a frame budget and feel broken.
      if (!reduced) {
        const rect = canvas.getBoundingClientRect();
        rootEl.style.setProperty('--kx-sample-x', `${event.clientX - rect.left}px`);
        rootEl.style.setProperty('--kx-sample-y', `${event.clientY - rect.top}px`);
      }
      emit(entry, false);
    };

    const onLeave = () => {
      rootEl.dataset.sampling = 'false';
      emit(null, true);
    };

    // Pointer events already carry touch; `touch-action: none` on the root
    // stops a drag over the artwork from scrolling the page out from under it.
    rootEl.addEventListener('pointermove', onMove);
    rootEl.addEventListener('pointerdown', onMove);
    rootEl.addEventListener('pointerleave', onLeave);
    rootEl.addEventListener('pointercancel', onLeave);

    return () => {
      rootEl.removeEventListener('pointermove', onMove);
      rootEl.removeEventListener('pointerdown', onMove);
      rootEl.removeEventListener('pointerleave', onLeave);
      rootEl.removeEventListener('pointercancel', onLeave);
      if (timer !== null) clearTimeout(timer);
      timer = null;
      rootEl.dataset.sampling = 'false';
    };
  }, [surface, swatches, throttleMs, reduced]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The canvas element is removed from the DOM in the same effect that created it, which drops the bitmap and the context with it. The four pointer listeners are removed, any pending throttle timer is cleared so no emission lands after unmount, and `data-sampling` is reset. The shared ResizeObserver unsubscribes through the hook.

**Reduced motion.** Sampling is not motion, so it keeps working: the colour still updates and `onSample` still fires. What stops is the chase — `--kx-sample-x` and `--kx-sample-y` are left parked at their initial 50% so a readout pinned to those properties stays still and simply recolours, instead of flying around the frame after the cursor.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Calling `getContext("2d")` first and adding `{ willReadFrequently: true }` later. The attributes of a canvas context are fixed at creation; the second call returns the first context and silently ignores the options, so the optimisation appears to be applied and is not.
- Reading the box unclamped. A pointer on the right or bottom edge produces a rect that overhangs the bitmap — no exception, the overhang is filled with transparent black — so the average darkens and the match snaps to the palette's darkest entry along every border.
- Letting the clamp collapse the rect. `getImageData` with a zero width or height throws `IndexSizeError`, which is what happens on a 1px-wide canvas if the box is clamped naively to a range instead of to an inclusive index pair.
- Converting with `devicePixelRatio` instead of the backing ratio. Correct at 100% zoom on a static layout, then off by the zoom factor the moment the user hits Cmd-plus, and off by the scale factor inside any transformed ancestor.
- Drawing a cross-origin image into the canvas. The canvas is tainted from that draw onward and every `getImageData` throws `SecurityError` — including for the parts of the surface you painted yourself. Paint procedurally, or serve the image same-origin with CORS.
- Matching in RGB. Euclidean distance in sRGB is not perceptual: green outweighs red and blue roughly six to one, so mid-tones snap to the wrong hue and the palette looks mislabelled rather than the maths looking wrong.
- Rendering the canvas as JSX with a `ref` and disposing the context in cleanup. Under StrictMode the element is reused across the double-invoke while the effect runs twice, so the surviving mount holds a context the first teardown already reset.
- Throttling the pointer position along with the colour. The readout then trails the cursor by the throttle window and the whole interaction reads as laggy, even though the sampling itself is instant.

## Notes

- Everything downstream is CSS. `--kx-sample-color` and `--kx-sample-x` / `--kx-sample-y` mean a chip can follow the pointer and recolour itself with no rAF and no React render.
- `data-sampling` on the root is `true` while the pointer is over the artwork, which is the hook for fading the readout in and out.
- Palette entries with an unparseable hex are dropped at match time rather than throwing, so one bad token in a design-token export does not take the interaction down.

## Definition of done

Move the pointer across the artwork: the readout recolours continuously and names a palette entry, with no stutter under a fast drag. Park the cursor exactly on the right or bottom edge — the name must not jump to the darkest colour in the palette. Zoom the browser to 150% and point at the same region; the answer is unchanged. With reduced motion on, the readout stops following the pointer but still renames itself.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Pointer-Variable Gradient

A radial gradient declared once in CSS reads its centre from `--pointer-x` and `--pointer-y`. The pointer handler does nothing but write those two properties as percentages. There is no animation frame, no tween library and no `background` string assembled in JavaScript.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A soft glow tracks the pointer through two CSS custom properties. No rAF, no tween, no string rebuilding.

- Category: cursor
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The gradient — its size, colour, stops and the layer underneath it — is declared once on the element. The only thing JavaScript ever writes is two custom properties, so the style engine invalidates the paint of one gradient rather than re-parsing a `background` shorthand it has already parsed thousands of times.
2. Values are written as percentages, not pixels. A percentage in a gradient position resolves against the element box, so the glow stays put relative to the panel across a resize with no resize listener and no recomputation — the value that was correct before the resize is still correct after it.
3. There is deliberately no `requestAnimationFrame`. A custom-property write is not a layout read, so there is nothing to batch away from; the browser already coalesces style changes into the next paint. Wrapping this in a frame loop adds one frame of latency and buys nothing measurable.
4. There is deliberately no tween. Smoothing the glow would mean owning a value between the pointer and the gradient, which means a frame loop, which is the cost this component exists to avoid. A 38rem glow is so diffuse that a few pixels of jitter are invisible — the smoothing would be paying for something no one can see.
5. Leaving removes the properties rather than writing the rest position back, so the fallback declared in the inline `style` takes over and the resting position is stated in exactly one place.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `REST_X / REST_Y = '50%' / '38%'`
  Where the glow sits before any pointer has been seen, and where it returns to on leave. Slightly above centre because a glow that sits dead-centre behind a headline reads as a lighting mistake, while one a little high reads as a source above the frame.
- `glowWidth / glowHeight = '38rem' / '30rem'`
  Wider than tall, matching the aspect of most content blocks. Sizing in rem rather than % means the glow keeps its physical size on a small panel instead of shrinking to a hotspot — a percentage-sized gradient in a 320px preview looks like a different effect entirely.
- `intensity = 0.09`
  Peak accent opacity at the centre. Under ~0.05 it is indistinguishable from a gradient banding artefact; over ~0.2 it stops being ambient light and becomes a coloured blob that competes with the text it is behind.
- `transparent 68% = 68%`
  Where the glow reaches zero. Ending short of 100% keeps the falloff inside the gradient box so the edge is never visible as a circle boundary against the panel edge.

## API

```ts
function PointerVarGradient(props: { children?: ReactNode; glowWidth?: string; glowHeight?: string; intensity?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Content rendered over the gradient.
- `glowWidth: string` — default `'38rem'`
  Horizontal radius of the glow, any CSS length.
- `glowHeight: string` — default `'30rem'`
  Vertical radius of the glow, any CSS length.
- `intensity: number` — default `0.09`
  Peak accent opacity at the glow centre, 0..1.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root container via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** Where the glow sits before the pointer has ever been seen. */
const REST_X = '50%';
const REST_Y = '38%';

export function PointerVarGradient({
  children,
  glowWidth = '38rem',
  glowHeight = '30rem',
  intensity = 0.09,
  className,
}: PointerVarGradientProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = root.current;
    if (!el) return;

    /* Fine pointers only. On touch a `pointermove` exists only during a drag,
       so the glow would be pinned under the finger that is scrolling the page
       and then abandoned there on lift — worse than not moving at all. The
       rest position set in the inline style stays, so touch users still get a
       composed gradient. */
    if (!window.matchMedia('(pointer: fine)').matches) return;

    const onMove = (e: PointerEvent) => {
      const rect = el.getBoundingClientRect();
      /* Percentages, not px. The gradient position resolves against the
         element box, so a percentage survives a resize with no listener and
         no recalculation — the glow stays where it was relative to the panel
         even if the panel changes size between moves. */
      el.style.setProperty(
        '--pointer-x',
        `${((e.clientX - rect.left) / rect.width) * 100}%`,
      );
      el.style.setProperty(
        '--pointer-y',
        `${((e.clientY - rect.top) / rect.height) * 100}%`,
      );
    };

    const onLeave = () => {
      /* Removing the property rather than writing the rest value back lets the
         inline `style` fallback take over, so the resting position is declared
         in exactly one place. */
      el.style.removeProperty('--pointer-x');
      el.style.removeProperty('--pointer-y');
    };

    el.addEventListener('pointermove', onMove, { passive: true });
    el.addEventListener('pointerleave', onLeave);

    return () => {
      el.removeEventListener('pointermove', onMove);
      el.removeEventListener('pointerleave', onLeave);
      el.style.removeProperty('--pointer-x');
      el.style.removeProperty('--pointer-y');
    };
  }, []);

  /* The gradient definition lives here and only here. The handler above never
     mentions colours, sizes or stops — it only moves the centre.

     No `transition`: an unregistered custom property is an untyped token, so
     the browser cannot interpolate it and a transition on the gradient would
     silently do nothing. Making the leave ease would mean registering the
     properties with `@property { syntax: '<percentage>' }` in a stylesheet,
     which is a real option but not a free one. The snap back is acceptable
     here because the glow at rest is barely above the background. */
  const style = {
    '--pointer-x': REST_X,
    '--pointer-y': REST_Y,
    backgroundImage: `radial-gradient(${glowWidth} ${glowHeight} at var(--pointer-x) var(--pointer-y), color-mix(in oklab, var(--k-accent) ${Math.round(
      intensity * 100,
    )}%, transparent), transparent 68%)`,
  } as CSSProperties;
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Removes the two pointer listeners and removes both custom properties from the element, so a remount starts from the declared rest position rather than inheriting the last pointer location. Nothing else was ever allocated — no frame loop, no tween, no observer.

**Reduced motion.** Unchanged, and intentionally so. Nothing here animates: the gradient centre tracks the pointer one-to-one with no easing, no inertia and no continuing motion after input stops. Suppressing it would remove a hover affordance rather than a motion effect.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Rebuilding the whole `background` string in JavaScript on every move. The browser re-parses every layer, including the static one, and you have moved a CSS declaration into a hot event handler where it will drift out of sync with the stylesheet.
- Expecting a `transition` on the gradient to smooth the leave. An unregistered custom property is an untyped token and cannot be interpolated, so the transition silently does nothing and there is no warning anywhere. Smoothing requires `@property { syntax: "<percentage>"; inherits: false; initial-value: 50% }` in a real stylesheet.
- Writing pixel values instead of percentages. They are correct only until the element resizes, at which point the glow is offset by however much the box changed and stays wrong until the next pointer move.
- Wrapping the write in `requestAnimationFrame`. It adds a frame of latency to a write that was never the bottleneck. rAF batching is for handlers that read layout; this one does not.
- Setting the properties on `document.documentElement` instead of the element. Every subtree that uses the same variable names then responds to a pointer that is nowhere near it, and two instances on one page fight over the same two globals.
- Reading `getBoundingClientRect()` and caching it. The rect is cheap here because nothing in this component writes layout, so there is no forced reflow to avoid — but a cached rect goes stale on scroll, which is the actual bug people ship trying to optimise this.

## Notes

- Gated on `(pointer: fine)`. On touch no listener attaches at all: `pointermove` only fires mid-drag, so the glow would follow the finger that is scrolling and be abandoned wherever it lifted. The inline rest position remains, so touch users get a composed static gradient rather than a blank panel.
- No reduced-motion branch is needed and none is present. There is no animation to reduce — the glow does not move on its own, does not ease, and does not persist after the pointer leaves. It is a hover state that happens to be continuous.
- The glow colour is `color-mix(in oklab, var(--k-accent) N%, transparent)` so it follows the category accent and the light/dark theme without a second code path.
- This is the cheapest component in the cursor category. If an effect can be expressed this way it should be, and the interesting question about any pointer effect is why it cannot.

## Definition of done

Move across the panel and a soft accent glow follows the pointer exactly, with no lag and no easing. Leave and it snaps back above centre. Resize the panel while the pointer is stationary and the glow stays in the same relative position rather than sliding. Open DevTools and confirm the element has exactly two inline custom properties changing and that no `background` or `background-image` value is being rewritten. On touch the glow never moves.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
