# Build: Pooled Cursor Image Trail

Sweeping the pointer across the panel drops a trail of tiles behind it, each fading up over 220ms, holding, and fading out — total life 520ms. The tiles come from a fixed ring of 22 nodes created once at mount and reused by index, and a new one is only released when the pointer has travelled more than 130px since the last. Those two rules are the component; the tween values are decoration.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Tiles drop behind the cursor from a fixed ring of 22 reused nodes, one every 130px of travel.

- Category: cursor
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. A ring of `poolSize` absolutely-positioned canvases is rendered once, all with `will-change: transform` so layer promotion has already happened before the first spawn. Nothing is ever created or removed after mount.
2. `plateCount` gradient plates are painted into offscreen canvases at mount — the registry ships no image assets, so the "photographs" are drawn. A spawn is then a single `drawImage` blit, which keeps the gradient and text work off the frame where a tween starts.
3. On `pointermove` the handler measures `Math.hypot(x - anchor.x, y - anchor.y)` against the last spawn point and returns early below `threshold`. The very first move only seeds the anchor and spawns nothing, so entering from an edge does not drop a tile before any real movement has happened.
4. A spawn takes slot `spawned % poolSize`, picks a plate with a seeded RNG plus a one-line no-repeat guard (`if (i === last) i = (i + 1) % n`), blits it, then `gsap.killTweensOf(node)` before `gsap.set` reinitialises x, y, rotation, scale 0.92, opacity 0 and `zIndex: spawned`.
5. `zIndex` is the monotonically increasing spawn counter, so the newest tile always paints over older ones with no stacking logic at all. At ten spawns a second it would take roughly 285,000 years to reach `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`.
6. The life is one timeline: in over 220ms with `power2.out`, hold 100ms, out over 200ms with `power2.in`. The pool is sized so a slot's 520ms life always expires before the ring wraps back around to it.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `threshold = 130`
  Pixels of travel per tile, and the single most load-bearing number here. A deliberate sweep across a hero yields 8-10 readable tiles; small jitters yield none. Drop it toward 20 and a flick produces a solid smear of overlapping tiles; raise it past ~250 and normal mouse movement never triggers the effect at all.
- `poolSize = 22`
  The ring must not wrap while a tile is still visible. At 520ms of life you would have to move 22 x 130 = 2860px in 520ms to catch your own tail — a flick nobody performs by accident.
- `plateCount = 17`
  Deliberately coprime with the 22 slots, so the plate-to-slot pairing never settles into a short repeating pattern as the ring advances. Also fewer plates than slots, so the memory cost is bounded independently of pool size.
- `IN_DURATION / HOLD / OUT_DURATION = 0.22 / 0.1 / 0.2`
  520ms total. Fast in with `power2.out` (arrives), a beat of stillness so the tile is actually readable, then a `power2.in` exit (leaves). Collapse the hold and the trail reads as a blur instead of as a sequence of pictures.
- `START_SCALE = 0.92`
  An 8% growth on entry. Enough to read as arriving, small enough not to pop — at 0.7 it looks like a modal opening.
- `TILT = 7`
  Degrees of seeded rotation either way. Perfectly square tiles read as UI panels; a few degrees reads as prints dropped on a table. Past ~12 the corners of successive tiles collide and the trail looks untidy.
- `PLATE_SCALE = 2`
  Backing-store multiplier for the plate canvases. Fixed rather than `devicePixelRatio` so the drawn output is byte-identical on every machine and a visual regression is actually visible.

## API

```ts
function PooledImageTrail(props: { children?: ReactNode; threshold?: number; poolSize?: number; plateCount?: number; tileWidth?: number; tileHeight?: number; seed?: string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Content rendered above the trail layer.
- `threshold: number` — default `130`
  Pixels of pointer travel required before another tile is released.
- `poolSize: number` — default `22`
  Number of reusable nodes in the ring.
- `plateCount: number` — default `17`
  Distinct plates painted at mount. Keep coprime with poolSize.
- `tileWidth: number` — default `236`
  Tile width in CSS px.
- `tileHeight: number` — default `160`
  Tile height in CSS px.
- `seed: string` — default `'pooled-image-trail'`
  Seeds plate choice and tilt so the sequence is deterministic.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root container via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const IN_DURATION = 0.22;
const HOLD = 0.1;
const OUT_DURATION = 0.2;
const START_SCALE = 0.92;
const TILT = 7;

export function PooledImageTrail({
  children,
  threshold = 130,
  poolSize = 22,
  plateCount = 17,
  tileWidth = 236,
  tileHeight = 160,
  seed = 'pooled-image-trail',
  className,
}: PooledImageTrailProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const slots = useRef<Array<HTMLCanvasElement | null>>([]);

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = root.current;
    if (!el) return;

    const nodes: HTMLCanvasElement[] = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < poolSize; i++) {
      const node = slots.current[i];
      if (node) nodes.push(node);
    }
    if (nodes.length === 0) return;

    const bw = tileWidth * PLATE_SCALE;
    const bh = tileHeight * PLATE_SCALE;

    // Paint every plate once, offscreen. A spawn is then a single blit; if the
    // plate were drawn at spawn time the gradient + text work would land on
    // the same frame as the tween start, which is the one frame that must not
    // drop.
    const plates: HTMLCanvasElement[] = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < plateCount; i++) {
      const plate = document.createElement('canvas');
      plate.width = bw;
      plate.height = bh;
      const pctx = plate.getContext('2d');
      if (!pctx) break;
      pctx.scale(PLATE_SCALE, PLATE_SCALE);
      paintPlate(pctx, tileWidth, tileHeight, i);
      plates.push(plate);
    }
    if (plates.length === 0) return;

    const contexts = nodes.map((node) => {
      node.width = bw;
      node.height = bh;
      return node.getContext('2d');
    });

    const reduced = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;
    const fine = window.matchMedia('(pointer: fine)').matches;

    gsap.set(nodes, { xPercent: 0, yPercent: 0, opacity: 0, force3D: true });

    if (reduced || !fine) {
      // Poster fallback: three plates fanned in the middle, drawn once. The
      // panel is composed rather than empty, and nothing ever moves.
      const shown = Math.min(3, nodes.length, plates.length);
      for (let i = 0; i < shown; i++) {
        const ctx = contexts[i];
        const plate = plates[i % plates.length];
        const node = nodes[i];
        if (!ctx || !plate || !node) continue;
        ctx.drawImage(plate, 0, 0);
        gsap.set(node, {
          x: el.clientWidth / 2 - tileWidth / 2 + (i - 1) * tileWidth * 0.42,
          y: el.clientHeight / 2 - tileHeight / 2 + (i - 1) * 14,
          rotate: (i - 1) * 4,
          opacity: 1,
          zIndex: i,
        });
      }
      return () => {
        gsap.killTweensOf(nodes);
        gsap.set(nodes, { clearProps: 'all' });
      };
    }

    const rng = createRng(seed);
    /** Monotonic. Doubles as the ring index and as the z-index. */
    let spawned = 0;
    /** Where the last tile was dropped. `null` until the first move seeds it. */
    let anchor: { x: number; y: number } | null = null;
    let lastPlate = -1;

    const onMove = (e: PointerEvent) => {
      const rect = el.getBoundingClientRect();
      const x = e.clientX - rect.left;
      const y = e.clientY - rect.top;

      // First move seeds the anchor and spawns nothing. Otherwise the initial
      // distance is measured from (0, 0) and entering from the right-hand side
      // of a wide panel drops a tile immediately, before any real movement.
      if (anchor === null) {
        anchor = { x, y };
        return;
      }
      if (Math.hypot(x - anchor.x, y - anchor.y) < threshold) return;
      anchor = { x, y };

      const slot = spawned % nodes.length;
      const node = nodes[slot];
      const ctx = contexts[slot];
      if (!node || !ctx) return;
      spawned++;

      // One-line no-repeat guard. It does not attempt a uniform distribution,
      // because the only thing the eye actually notices is the same picture
      // twice in a row.
      let plateIndex = Math.floor(rng() * plates.length);
      if (plateIndex === lastPlate) plateIndex = (plateIndex + 1) % plates.length;
      lastPlate = plateIndex;
      const plate = plates[plateIndex];
      if (!plate) return;

      ctx.clearRect(0, 0, bw, bh);
      ctx.drawImage(plate, 0, 0);

      // Kill before reuse. A slot recycled while still fading out would carry
      // two competing tweens on `opacity` and visibly flicker.
      gsap.killTweensOf(node);
      gsap.set(node, {
        x: x - tileWidth / 2,
        y: y - tileHeight / 2,
        rotate: randRange(rng, -TILT, TILT),
        scale: START_SCALE,
        opacity: 0,
        // Monotonic z-index: the newest tile always paints over older ones and
        // there is no stacking logic to maintain.
        zIndex: spawned,
      });

      gsap
        .timeline()
        .to(node, { opacity: 1, scale: 1, duration: IN_DURATION, ease: 'power2.out' })
        .to(node, { opacity: 0, duration: OUT_DURATION, ease: 'power2.in' }, `+=${HOLD}`);
    };

    el.addEventListener('pointermove', onMove, { passive: true });

    return () => {
      el.removeEventListener('pointermove', onMove);
      gsap.killTweensOf(nodes);
      gsap.set(nodes, { clearProps: 'all' });
    };
  }, [threshold, poolSize, plateCount, tileWidth, tileHeight, seed]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Removes the single `pointermove` listener, calls `gsap.killTweensOf` on every pool node — which also kills the per-spawn timelines, since they only target those nodes — then `gsap.set(nodes, { clearProps: "all" })`. The offscreen plate canvases are plain locals and are collected with the closure; nothing was allocated that needs revoking.

**Reduced motion.** No listener attaches and nothing animates. Three plates are drawn once into the first three pool slots, fanned across the centre with a few degrees of rotation each, so the panel is a composed still of what the effect produces rather than an empty rectangle.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Creating an element per spawn. A fast sweep across a wide hero allocates a hundred nodes, each forcing a style recalc, a layer promotion and a paint at the exact moment the main thread is busiest — the trail stutters precisely when it is being used hardest.
- Spawning on every `pointermove` instead of on distance travelled. Events fire on sub-pixel movement, so a flick produces a solid smear and a slow drift produces a dense clump; "moved" and "moved enough" are different predicates.
- Measuring the first move against a zeroed anchor. The distance from (0, 0) to wherever the pointer entered is usually well over the threshold, so a tile fires the instant the pointer crosses the boundary, before any movement has happened.
- Reusing a slot without `gsap.killTweensOf(node)` first. If the ring wraps onto a tile that is still fading out, two tweens fight over `opacity` and it flickers rather than restarting cleanly.
- Recomputing z-order from tile ages. A monotonic counter is correct, free, and cannot get out of sync; sorting is a whole class of bug bought for nothing.
- Painting the gradient plate at spawn time. The gradient fill, the radial sheen and the text layout all land on the same frame as the tween start, which is the one frame in the effect that must not drop. Paint once at mount and blit.
- Omitting `will-change: transform` from the pool. The browser promotes the tile to its own layer partway through its 220ms entry, so the first frames of every spawn are visibly cheaper-looking than the rest.

## Notes

- Gated on `(pointer: fine)`. On touch a `pointermove` only exists during a drag, so the trail would appear only under a finger that is already covering it and would then be stranded mid-life on lift. The touch path renders the same static fan as reduced motion.
- The tiles sit behind the content layer (`z-0` under a `z-10` child wrapper) so headline copy stays readable while the trail passes under it.
- Plate choice runs on `createRng(seed)`, never `Math.random()`, so the sequence is identical on every load and across a server render.

## Definition of done

Sweep the pointer slowly across the panel and tiles drop behind it roughly every 130px, each readable for about half a second before fading. Jiggle the pointer in place and nothing spawns. Flick as fast as you can and you get a spaced trail, not a smear, and no tile ever restarts mid-fade with a flicker. Enter the panel from an edge and no tile appears until you have actually moved. On touch or with reduced motion you see three static fanned plates.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Pre-Scatter Horizontal Gallery

A pinned horizontal strip whose media is deliberately off-grid: every item gets a small seeded resting offset, then rides in from ahead of its slot and runs out behind it, rotating through zero on the way past. Two `fromTo` pairs per item — one entry, one exit — measured against the strip's own tween rather than against scroll position, so the choreography is a property of where an item is in the container, not of where the page is.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A pinned strip where each item rests slightly off its slot, flies in from ahead and peels away behind.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. The component owns a `PinnedHorizontalTrack` and captures its `onTrack` payload in state. The strip's tween is built in the child's effect and therefore arrives one commit late, which is why it is state and not a ref — the arrival has to re-run the builder.
2. Every `[data-scatter]` element draws one value from `createRng(seed)`: `rest = (rng() - 0.5) * scatter`, a resting `xPercent` offset. It is applied with `gsap.set` for every item whether or not it animates, so the composition is identical with motion on and off.
3. The entry is `fromTo(el, { xPercent: rest + sweep, yPercent: dir * lift, rotation: dir * rotation }, { xPercent: rest, yPercent: 0, rotation: 0 })` scrubbed over `left 110%` to `left 65%` — the item lags behind its slot and catches up as it crosses the container.
4. The exit is the mirror: `fromTo(el, { xPercent: rest, yPercent: 0, rotation: 0 }, { xPercent: rest - sweep, yPercent: -dir * lift, rotation: -dir * rotation })` over `right 35%` to `right -10%`, with `immediateRender: false` so it does not overwrite the entry's from-state at creation.
5. `dir` alternates by index parity, so odd items throw up and rotate clockwise while even items do the opposite, and the rotation passes continuously through zero between the two ranges.
6. Both triggers take `containerAnimation: track.animation` and horizontal position keywords, so ScrollTrigger measures each item along the strip's timeline instead of down the page.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `scatter = 32`
  Total resting spread as a percentage of the item's own width, i.e. ±16%. Below ~10 the grid still reads as a grid and the effect is invisible; above ~50 items collide with their neighbours' captions and it reads as a layout bug rather than a composition.
- `sweep = 400`
  Horizontal lag on entry and lead on exit, as a percentage of item width. Four widths is enough that the item is genuinely off-stage at the start of its range, so the catch-up is a travel rather than a nudge. Under ~150 the item is already visible when its tween begins and appears to jerk into place.
- `lift = 150`
  Vertical throw as a percentage of item height. At 100 the item starts exactly one height away, so its edge is still touching the frame; 150 clears the frame with margin, which is what makes it read as flying in rather than sliding.
- `rotation = 40°`
  Peak tilt. Under ~15° the rotation is mistaken for a rendering artefact; past ~60° the item is legibly upside-down at the extremes and text inside it becomes unreadable during the travel.
- `ENTER_START / ENTER_END = 'left 110%' / 'left 65%'`
  The item's leading edge, measured along the container. Starting past 100% means the tween begins before the item is visible, so nothing pops in already moving. Ending at 65% leaves the middle third of the crossing settled.
- `EXIT_START / EXIT_END = 'right 35%' / 'right -10%'`
  The trailing edge. Ending below 0% carries the item fully past the left frame before the tween completes, so it never freezes half-visible at the edge. The two ranges cannot overlap for any item narrower than 1.3 containers.
- `item scrub = true`
  Locked to the container animation, not a number. These triggers read the strip's progress, and the strip already scrubs with a second of catch-up, so a numeric scrub here smooths an already-smoothed signal and the items swim behind the panels they belong to.

## API

```ts
function PrescatterHorizontalGallery(props: { children: ReactNode; scroller?: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>; seed?: number | string; scatter?: number; rotation?: number; lift?: number; sweep?: number; scrub?: number; className?: string; trackClassName?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Panels for the strip. Give each a width and `shrink-0`, and mark the media inside `data-scatter`.
- `scroller: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>`
  Scroll container the triggers read. Omit for the document.
- `seed: number | string` — default `'gallery'`
  Anything hashable. The same seed rebuilds the same composition.
- `scatter: number` — default `32`
  Total resting spread as a percentage of item width.
- `rotation: number` — default `40`
  Peak tilt in degrees, alternating by index.
- `lift: number` — default `150`
  Vertical throw as a percentage of item height.
- `sweep: number` — default `400`
  Horizontal lag and lead as a percentage of item width.
- `scrub: number` — default `1`
  Seconds of catch-up on the strip, forwarded to the pinned track.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the gallery wrapper.
- `trackClassName: string`
  Merged onto the moving strip.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * The item's leading edge crosses the container from just off the right
 * (110%) to two thirds in (65%), and its trailing edge leaves from a third in
 * (35%) to just past the left (-10%). The two ranges cannot overlap for any
 * item narrower than 1.3 containers, so every item gets a settled window in
 * the middle where it is simply itself.
 */
const ENTER_START = 'left 110%';
const ENTER_END = 'left 65%';
const EXIT_START = 'right 35%';
const EXIT_END = 'right -10%';

export function PrescatterHorizontalGallery({
  children,
  scroller,
  seed = 'gallery',
  scatter = 32,
  rotation = 40,
  lift = 150,
  sweep = 400,
  scrub = 1,
  className,
  trackClassName,
}: PrescatterHorizontalGalleryProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  // The strip's tween is built in a child's effect, so it arrives one commit
  // late. State, not a ref: the arrival has to re-run the builder below.
  const [track, setTrack] = useState<PinnedTrack | null>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  useEffect(() => {
    const rootEl = root.current;
    if (!rootEl) return;

    const containerAnimation = track?.animation;
    const scrollerEl = scroller?.current ?? undefined;

    const ctx = gsap.context(() => {
      const targets = Array.from(rootEl.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-scatter]'));
      const rng = createRng(seed);

      targets.forEach((el, i) => {
        // Drawn for every item whether or not it animates, so adding motion
        // never shifts the resting composition.
        const rest = (rng() - 0.5) * scatter;
        // Parity, not the generator: alternating up/down and cw/ccw is a
        // rhythm, and a random sign clumps three the same way and looks broken.
        const dir = i % 2 === 0 ? 1 : -1;

        gsap.set(el, { xPercent: rest });
        // The resting scatter is layout. Under reduced motion the composition
        // survives and only the flight is dropped.
        if (reduced || !containerAnimation) return;

        gsap.fromTo(
          el,
          { xPercent: rest + sweep, yPercent: dir * lift, rotation: dir * rotation },
          {
            xPercent: rest,
            yPercent: 0,
            rotation: 0,
            ease: 'none',
            scrollTrigger: {
              trigger: el,
              scroller: scrollerEl,
              containerAnimation,
              start: ENTER_START,
              end: ENTER_END,
              // `true`, not a number. The strip already scrubs with catch-up,
              // and these triggers read the strip's progress rather than the
              // scrollbar, so they inherit that smoothing. A second scrub
              // value smooths the smoothed signal and the items swim.
              scrub: true,
            },
          },
        );

        gsap.fromTo(
          el,
          { xPercent: rest, yPercent: 0, rotation: 0 },
          {
            xPercent: rest - sweep,
            yPercent: -dir * lift,
            rotation: -dir * rotation,
            ease: 'none',
            // The single most important line here. A `fromTo` renders its
            // from-state at creation, so without this the exit immediately
            // overwrites the entry's from-state — every item starts on the
            // grid instead of off-stage, and the entry appears not to exist.
            immediateRender: false,
            scrollTrigger: {
              trigger: el,
              scroller: scrollerEl,
              containerAnimation,
              start: EXIT_START,
              end: EXIT_END,
              scrub: true,
            },
          },
        );
      });
    }, rootEl);

    return () => ctx.revert();
  }, [track, scroller, seed, scatter, rotation, lift, sweep, reduced]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** One `gsap.context` scoped to the root holds the `set` calls and both tweens per item, so `ctx.revert()` kills every tween, kills every ScrollTrigger, and strips the inline transforms back off the media. It runs on unmount and on every dependency change, including the commit where the strip's tween arrives.

**Reduced motion.** The resting scatter is still applied — it is layout, not motion, and the gallery is supposed to look deliberately off-grid. What is dropped is the flight: no entry or exit triggers are created, so every item sits at its offset from first paint. The pinned track also declines to pin, so the strip becomes a horizontally scrollable row and every item stays reachable.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Using `gsap.to` for the exit. A `to` records its start values when it is created, which is after the entry has already rendered its from-state — so the exit animates from `xPercent: rest + sweep` and the item never returns to its slot.
- Using a second `fromTo` for the exit without `immediateRender: false`. A `fromTo` writes its from-state immediately, so the later tween wins and every item starts on the grid: the entry animation exists, runs, and is invisible.
- Keeping vertical position keywords with a `containerAnimation`. `start: "top 110%"` on a horizontal container resolves to a position the element never occupies. No error, no warning, no animation — the items simply arrive pre-placed.
- Measuring the scatter in pixels off the container width. It has to be recomputed on every ScrollTrigger refresh or the composition creeps as the window resizes; expressed as `xPercent` it resolves against the element and never needs invalidating.
- `Math.random()` for the offsets. The server and the client disagree at hydration, and the composition is different on every reload, so nobody can tell a regression from a reroll.
- Building the item triggers before the strip's tween exists. Treating `undefined` as "no container animation" builds a full set of vertical triggers on horizontal content and tears them down on the next commit — a visible flash of items that were already in place.
- Alternating direction from the generator instead of from the index. A random sign lands three items the same way often enough to look like a bug, where parity always reads as rhythm.

## Notes

- Mark the media, not the panel: `data-scatter` on an inner element lets the panel keep the caption on the grid while the image drifts off it.
- ScrollTrigger forbids `pin` on a trigger that has a `containerAnimation`. The strip's section is pinned by `PinnedHorizontalTrack`; the items riding it are never pinned.
- Panels need `overflow: visible` for the sweep to be seen. Clipping happens once, at the pinned section's edge.

## Definition of done

Scroll into the section: it pins, the strip travels sideways, and each item swings in from ahead of its slot, straightens, holds through the middle of the crossing, then tilts the other way and runs out to the left. Scroll back up and every item reverses along the same path. Note that no two items rest exactly on the grid, and that reloading gives the identical composition. With reduced motion on, the items are already at their offsets and the strip can be swiped by hand.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Proximity Snap Track

A scrollable rail whose items may be any width. `scroll-snap-type: x proximity` snaps to an item only when the scroll comes to rest near one, so free scanning stays free. `scroll-snap-stop: always` caps a single fling at one item, so a hard swipe cannot launch the user past six cards. No JavaScript runs during the scroll.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A horizontal rail of variable-width cards that snaps only when you stop near one, and never skips past two at once.

- Category: layout
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The container is `overflow-x: auto` with `scroll-snap-type: x proximity`. `proximity` means the browser only adjusts the resting position when the natural end of the scroll already falls close to a snap point; anywhere else, it leaves the position exactly where the user left it.
2. Each item declares `scroll-snap-align: start` (or `center`) — this is what makes it a snap point at all — and `scroll-snap-stop: always`, which forbids the browser from passing more than one snap point per gesture no matter how much momentum the fling carried.
3. `scroll-padding-inline` is set alongside `padding-inline` to the same gutter. They are different properties: `padding` insets the content, `scroll-padding` insets the *snapport* — the rectangle a snap position is measured against. With padding alone, a `start`-aligned item comes to rest flush against the container border and the inset the design asked for vanishes at every rest position.
4. `overscroll-behavior-x: contain` stops a horizontal fling that reaches the end of the rail from chaining to an ancestor scroller or triggering the browser's back-navigation gesture.
5. `scroll-behavior` is `smooth` normally and `auto` under reduced motion, which affects programmatic and keyboard-initiated scrolls. The snap adjustment itself is the browser's own and already respects the OS setting.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `snapType = 'proximity'`
  The whole argument of this component. With `mandatory`, the browser must always come to rest on a snap point, so on a rail of variable-width items it is physically impossible to stop between two of them — every attempt to park somewhere gets yanked. Worse, on a long rail `mandatory` plus a short flick can leave the user unable to reach a position at all. `proximity` snaps when it helps and gets out of the way when it does not.
- `snapStop = 'always'`
  Without it, a hard fling on a trackpad passes every snap point and lands on whichever item the momentum ran out over — which on a rail of 20 cards means the user has no way to advance by exactly one. `always` turns each item into a gate.
- `snapAlign = 'start'`
  Correct default for variable-width items: their left edges line up at rest, which reads as a column of starts. `center` is right only when items are uniform, because with mixed widths a centred rest position puts every item's left edge somewhere different.
- `gutter = 16`
  Set on both `padding-inline` and `scroll-padding-inline`. The two must match or the resting inset and the visual inset disagree by exactly this many pixels, which looks like a rounding bug.
- `gap = 12`
  Large enough that two adjacent cards read as separate snap targets, small enough that the next card is clearly a continuation of the row rather than a separate section.

## API

```ts
function ProximitySnapTrack(props: { children: ReactNode; snapType?: 'proximity' | 'mandatory'; snapAlign?: 'start' | 'center'; snapStop?: 'normal' | 'always'; gutter?: number; gap?: number; className?: string; itemClassName?: string; 'aria-label'?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  One item per child. Widths may differ.
- `snapType: 'proximity' | 'mandatory'` — default `'proximity'`
  Snap strictness. `mandatory` is exposed so the difference can be felt, not because it is usually right here.
- `snapAlign: 'start' | 'center'` — default `'start'`
  Which edge of an item lines up with the snapport.
- `snapStop: 'normal' | 'always'` — default `'always'`
  `always` caps one gesture at one item.
- `gutter: number` — default `16`
  Inset in px, applied to both `padding-inline` and `scroll-padding-inline`.
- `gap: number` — default `12`
  Gap between items in px.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the scroll container.
- `itemClassName: string`
  Merged onto each item cell.
- `aria-label: string` — default `'Track'`
  Label for the focusable scroll region.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const trackStyle: CSSProperties = {
  scrollSnapType: `x ${snapType}`,
  // `scroll-padding` is what a snap position is measured against, and it is
  // a separate property from `padding`. With padding alone, a `start`-aligned
  // item snaps flush to the container's border and the inset the design asked
  // for silently disappears at every rest position.
  scrollPaddingInline: `${gutter}px`,
  paddingInline: `${gutter}px`,
  gap: `${gap}px`,
  // Programmatic scrolls (anchor jumps, `scrollIntoView`, arrow keys in some
  // engines) animate unless told not to. Snapping itself is not affected —
  // it is the browser's own transition and honours the OS setting already.
  scrollBehavior: reduced ? 'auto' : 'smooth',
};

const itemStyle: CSSProperties = {
  scrollSnapAlign: snapAlign,
  scrollSnapStop: snapStop,
};
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to release. All behaviour is declarative CSS on nodes React owns; the only subscription is `useReducedMotion`, which removes its own `matchMedia` listener on unmount. No listeners, no timers, no rAF.

**Reduced motion.** The rail behaves identically — it is a scroll container, and scrolling is the user moving, not the interface animating. The one change is `scroll-behavior: auto` instead of `smooth`, so keyboard and programmatic scrolls jump rather than glide. The snap adjustment is the browser's own transition and already follows the OS setting without any help.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- `scroll-snap-type: x mandatory` on a track with variable-width items. It makes it impossible to rest between items: every release is pulled to a snap point, so the user cannot park where they want, and on a long rail with wide items they end up fighting the browser for the whole length of the track. `proximity` is the correct choice whenever the items are not uniform or the track is long.
- Setting `padding-inline` without `scroll-padding-inline`. Every rest position then puts the item flush against the container edge, so the gutter appears while scrolling and disappears the instant you let go.
- Omitting `scroll-snap-stop: always`. A single hard swipe lands eight cards along, which makes stepping by one impossible and makes the rail feel slippery rather than mechanical.
- Hiding the scrollbar without making the container focusable. The rail becomes invisible to keyboard users and to anyone who was relying on the scrollbar as the affordance. `tabIndex={0}` and a `role`/`aria-label` restore arrow-key scrolling, and Chrome stops warning about a non-focusable scroll container.
- Leaving `overscroll-behavior-x` at `auto`. Flinging past the end chains into the page or, in Safari and Chrome, triggers the swipe-to-go-back gesture and the user loses the page.
- Reaching for a JS carousel because "the design has arrows". A snap track already has momentum, rubber-banding, keyboard support and accessible scroll semantics; arrows are one `scrollBy` call on top, not a reason to replace the mechanism.

## Notes

- Snap is a layout-level contract, not an animation. Everything here runs on the compositor and continues to work when the main thread is blocked, which is the reason to prefer it over a JS track whenever the interaction is genuinely "a scrollable row".
- Items are `shrink-0`. Without it, flex would compress them to fit the container and the track would never overflow, so there would be nothing to snap.
- `scroll-snap-stop` is ignored during programmatic scrolls in every engine — it only constrains user gestures. Arrows implemented with `scrollTo` can therefore still jump several items at once by design.

## Definition of done

Scroll the rail slowly and stop between two cards — it stays where you left it. Stop just past a card's edge and it eases onto that card. Fling as hard as you can and it advances exactly one card. Tab to the rail and press the arrow keys: it scrolls and snaps the same way. At every rest position the leading card sits inset from the container edge by the gutter, not flush against it.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: quickTo Cursor Preview

Hovering a row fades in a preview panel that then trails the pointer with a full second of catch-up, so it reads as a heavy object being dragged rather than a tooltip pinned to the cursor. Position comes from exactly two `gsap.quickTo` setters created once at mount; the hovered row is the only thing that ever enters React state.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A preview panel drifts a full second behind the pointer, driven by two reused quickTo tweens.

- Category: cursor
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. `gsap.quickTo(box, "x", { duration, ease })` returns a setter backed by ONE tween whose end value is mutated in place. A `pointermove` handler firing 60-120 times a second therefore allocates nothing after the first frame, where the `gsap.to()` equivalent allocates and garbage-collects a tween object per event and leaves each new tween fighting the last for the same property.
2. Hovered row is React state because it changes a handful of times a second and drives real DOM structure (text colour, stroke, offset). Panel position is never state: it changes on every pointer event, and a re-render per move would cost more than the animation it is driving.
3. `duration: 1` is roughly five times a normal cursor follow, and that is the entire design. Under `power3` the panel covers most of the gap early and then creeps, so it always reads as heading for the pointer without ever arriving — which is what makes it feel like mass rather than lag.
4. The first move after entry calls `xTo(x, x)` — quickTo's second argument is the tween's START value, so the panel is teleported rather than eased. Without it, re-entering the list sends the panel sailing diagonally across the whole component over a full second before it becomes useful.
5. Position is centred with `xPercent: -50, yPercent: -50` set once at mount, so `x`/`y` are raw pointer coordinates and no offset arithmetic appears in the hot handler.
6. Every preview is a gradient plate painted into an offscreen canvas at mount — the registry ships no image assets. Switching rows is one `drawImage` blit, so the gradient, band and text work never lands on the frame where the fade-in starts.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `duration = 1`
  Seconds of catch-up, and the whole character of the component. At 0.2 it is an ordinary tooltip that happens to be smooth; at 1 it is an object with weight. Past ~1.6 the panel is still crossing the list when the pointer has already left it, and the effect reads as broken rather than heavy.
- `ease: 'power3' = power3 (in-out)`
  In-out, not `.out`. Because the end value is remutated on every event, the tween is permanently restarting from its own midpoint; the symmetric curve means direction changes are absorbed smoothly instead of snapping to a new outward ramp each time.
- `FADE_DURATION = 0.35`
  Fade and scale on row change. Long enough to register as a cross-fade rather than a cut, short enough that dragging down a list of eight rows does not leave the panel permanently mid-transition.
- `scale 0.94 -> 1 = 0.94`
  A 6% growth on appear. Paired with opacity it reads as arriving from behind the page; without it the fade alone looks like a stuck render.
- `DOCK_INSET = 20`
  Pixels of margin when the panel docks to the right edge on touch or reduced motion. Clamped against `panelWidth / 2` so a panel wider than its container still lands fully inside rather than half off-screen.
- `PLATE_SCALE = 2`
  Backing-store multiplier for the plate canvases. Fixed rather than `devicePixelRatio` so the drawn output is identical on every machine and a visual regression is actually visible in a screenshot diff.

## API

```ts
function QuickToCursorPreview(props: { items: PreviewItem[]; duration?: number; panelWidth?: number; panelHeight?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `items: PreviewItem[]`
  Rows to render. `{ id, title, meta? }`; one plate is painted per item.
- `duration: number` — default `1`
  Seconds of catch-up on the follow. The defining value of the effect.
- `panelWidth: number` — default `260`
  Preview panel width in CSS px.
- `panelHeight: number` — default `180`
  Preview panel height in CSS px.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root container via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const PLATE_SCALE = 2;
const FADE_DURATION = 0.35;
const DOCK_INSET = 20;

/**
 * True when the panel must NOT follow: no fine pointer (a `pointermove` on
 * touch only exists during a drag, so the panel would live under the finger
 * that is dragging it), or reduced motion (a full second of drift is precisely
 * what that user opted out of). One predicate, so the two effects below can
 * never disagree about which mode the component is in.
 */
function docked(): boolean {
  return (
    !window.matchMedia('(pointer: fine)').matches ||
    window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches
  );
}

export function QuickToCursorPreview({
  items,
  duration = 1,
  panelWidth = 260,
  panelHeight = 180,
  className,
}: QuickToCursorPreviewProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const panel = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const surface = useRef<HTMLCanvasElement>(null);
  const plates = useRef<HTMLCanvasElement[]>([]);

  /* Hovered row is React state because it changes a handful of times a
     second. Panel position is never state — it changes 120 times a second and
     a re-render per pointermove would dwarf the animation itself. */
  const [hovered, setHovered] = useState<number | null>(null);
  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(root);

  const count = items.length;

  /* Paint every plate once. Drawing at hover time would put a gradient fill,
     four band rects and a text layout on the same frame as the fade-in. */
  useEffect(() => {
    const bw = panelWidth * PLATE_SCALE;
    const bh = panelHeight * PLATE_SCALE;
    const built: HTMLCanvasElement[] = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
      const plate = document.createElement('canvas');
      plate.width = bw;
      plate.height = bh;
      const ctx = plate.getContext('2d');
      if (!ctx) break;
      ctx.scale(PLATE_SCALE, PLATE_SCALE);
      paintPlate(ctx, panelWidth, panelHeight, i);
      built.push(plate);
    }
    plates.current = built;

    const canvas = surface.current;
    if (canvas) {
      canvas.width = bw;
      canvas.height = bh;
    }
    return () => {
      plates.current = [];
    };
  }, [count, panelWidth, panelHeight]);

  /* Centre the panel on its own coordinates ONCE, at mount. Doing it with a
     negative margin or `left: -130px` instead means the offset and the
     transform fight, and the panel sits half a width off. */
  useEffect(() => {
    const box = panel.current;
    if (!box) return;
    gsap.set(box, { xPercent: -50, yPercent: -50, autoAlpha: 0, scale: 0.94 });
    return () => {
      gsap.killTweensOf(box);
      gsap.set(box, { clearProps: 'all' });
    };
  }, []);

  /* With no fine pointer — or with reduced motion, where a second of drift is
     exactly what the user opted out of — the panel docks to the right edge and
     only cross-fades as rows change. */
  useEffect(() => {
    const box = panel.current;
    if (!box || width === 0 || height === 0) return;
    if (!docked()) return;
    gsap.set(box, {
      x: Math.max(width - panelWidth / 2 - DOCK_INSET, panelWidth / 2),
      y: height / 2,
    });
  }, [width, height, panelWidth]);

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = root.current;
    const box = panel.current;
    if (!el || !box || docked()) return;

    // ONE tween per property, reused for the lifetime of the component.
    const xTo = gsap.quickTo(box, 'x', { duration, ease: 'power3' });
    const yTo = gsap.quickTo(box, 'y', { duration, ease: 'power3' });
    let seeded = false;

    const onMove = (e: PointerEvent) => {
      const rect = el.getBoundingClientRect();
      const x = e.clientX - rect.left;
      const y = e.clientY - rect.top;
      if (seeded) {
        xTo(x);
        yTo(y);
        return;
      }
      // Second argument is quickTo's `start` value: it snaps rather than
      // easing. Without it the panel sails in from wherever it was left,
      // taking a full second to cross the list on every re-entry.
      seeded = true;
      xTo(x, x);
      yTo(y, y);
    };

    const onLeave = () => {
      seeded = false;
    };

    el.addEventListener('pointermove', onMove, { passive: true });
    el.addEventListener('pointerleave', onLeave);

    /* Deliberately NOT clearing props here. `xPercent`, `yPercent` and
       `autoAlpha` belong to the mount effect; wiping them whenever `duration`
       changes would un-centre the panel and pop it to full opacity mid-hover.
       Teardown of those lives in the effect that set them. */
    return () => {
      el.removeEventListener('pointermove', onMove);
      el.removeEventListener('pointerleave', onLeave);
      gsap.killTweensOf(box);
    };
  }, [duration]);

  /* Visibility and content follow the hovered row, not the pointer. */
  useEffect(() => {
    const box = panel.current;
    const canvas = surface.current;
    if (!box || !canvas) return;

    const reduced = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;

    if (hovered !== null) {
      const plate = plates.current[hovered];
      const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
      if (plate && ctx) {
        ctx.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
        ctx.drawImage(plate, 0, 0);
      }
    }

    gsap.to(box, {
      autoAlpha: hovered === null ? 0 : 1,
      scale: hovered === null ? 0.94 : 1,
      duration: reduced ? 0 : FADE_DURATION,
      ease: 'power3.out',
      // Only the fade is overwritten; the quickTo tweens own x and y and must
      // keep running underneath, which is exactly what 'auto' guarantees.
      overwrite: 'auto',
    });
  }, [hovered]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The follow effect removes both listeners and calls `gsap.killTweensOf(box)`, which disposes the two quickTo tweens. The mount effect separately kills tweens and runs `clearProps: "all"`, restoring the centring transform and opacity it set. The offscreen plate canvases are dropped by nulling the ref array; they are plain canvases, never object URLs, so there is nothing to revoke.

**Reduced motion.** No `pointermove` listener attaches. The panel docks to the right edge, vertically centred, and hovering a row swaps its plate with a zero-duration cross-fade. The preview still works; it simply never moves.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Calling `gsap.to()` in the `pointermove` handler. It allocates a tween per event and every new one competes with the still-running previous tween for `x`, so the panel judders under fast movement — exactly when the follow is most visible.
- Putting the panel position in React state. Every pointer event becomes a render of the whole list; the follow gets slower the more rows you add, which is a scaling failure with no obvious cause at the call site.
- Omitting the start value on the first call after entry. The panel eases in from wherever it was abandoned, so re-entering the list gives a full second of a panel flying across the layout before it means anything.
- Centring with a negative margin or `left: -130px` as well as `xPercent: -50`. The two offsets compose and the panel sits half a width away from the pointer — a bug that looks like a follow-lag problem and is not one.
- Running `clearProps: "all"` in the cleanup of an effect that only owns `x` and `y`. Any dependency change then wipes the `xPercent`/`yPercent` centring and the `autoAlpha` state owned by a different effect, and the panel jumps or flashes to full opacity mid-hover. Each effect must tear down only what it set.
- Using `overwrite: true` on the fade tween. It kills the quickTo tweens that own `x` and `y`, and the panel freezes in place the moment you move between rows. `overwrite: "auto"` only claims the properties the fade actually animates.
- Transitioning `all` on the row text. The panel and rows share a stacking context, and a blanket transition catches `transform`, which then fights whatever else is animating it.

## Notes

- Gated on `(pointer: fine)`. On touch there is no hover and a `pointermove` only exists mid-drag, so the panel would live directly under the finger dragging it. The touch path docks the panel to the right edge and cross-fades on row change instead, which keeps the preview useful without pretending there is a cursor.
- Reduced motion takes the same docked path — a second of drift is precisely what that user opted out of — and the cross-fade duration drops to 0.
- Both branches read the same `docked()` predicate, so the follow effect and the dock effect can never disagree about which mode the component is in.
- The panel is `aria-hidden` and `pointer-events-none`: it is decoration for the row title, which remains the accessible content.

## Definition of done

Hover a row and the panel fades up over ~350ms while scaling from 0.94. Move the pointer and it follows with about a second of lag, always heading toward the pointer and never quite catching it. Move fast between rows and the image cross-fades while the follow keeps running underneath — the panel never freezes. Leave and re-enter the list and the panel appears at the pointer, not sailing in from the far side. On touch or with reduced motion the panel sits docked at the right edge and only its contents change.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Radial Mask Spotlight

A stacked layer is masked by a radial gradient whose centre follows the pointer, so content is lit rather than uncovered. The mask string is rewritten once per animation frame from a damped pointer position, and both the prefixed and unprefixed `mask-image` properties are set.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A layer masked to a soft disc follows the pointer, with a flat core that makes it read as a beam.

- Category: cursor
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The gradient stops are the design: solid black to 30% of the radius, then a ramp to transparent at 72%. That flat core gives the beam a lit region with an actual size. A gradient that begins falling off at 0% has no lit area at all — just a bright point that fades, which the eye reads as blur rather than as light.
2. A px radius is used rather than a percentage. A percentage radius in a radial gradient resolves against the element box, so the same declaration produces a beam of a different physical size in every panel it is dropped into, and the effect stops being reusable.
3. Position comes from `useSmoothPointer` with a very low smoothing factor, so the beam has a small amount of drag. `damp` is frame-rate independent — the smoothing constant is the fraction of the gap left after one full second — so the same value produces the same feel at 60Hz and 144Hz rather than the beam arriving twice as fast on a fast display.
4. The mask is written in a `useRaf` callback, not in the pointer handler. Setting `mask-image` invalidates paint for the layer, and a fast pointer delivers two or three events per frame, so a per-event write does the same expensive work several times to produce one visible result.
5. The layer is seeded with a mask parked two radii off-panel, so the first painted frame — before rAF has run once — cannot show the layer unmasked. Nothing is written until `pointer.active` is true, which is what stops the beam flashing at the hook's centre-parked seed position on mount.
6. Both `maskImage` and `WebkitMaskImage` are set. This is not defensive habit: released Safari versions mishandle gradient masks without the prefix, and the failure mode is the layer being fully visible or fully invisible rather than slightly wrong.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `radius = 220`
  Beam radius in px, giving a 132px solid core and a 92px falloff. Below ~120 the core is too small to hold a line of text and the effect becomes a magnifier; above ~350 in a small panel the falloff never completes inside the box and the beam reads as an uneven wash.
- `CORE_STOP = 0.3`
  Where the solid region ends. This is the single number that separates "a light" from "a smudge". At 0 there is no lit area, only a peak; past ~0.5 the edge becomes hard enough that it reads as a cut-out hole instead of illumination.
- `EDGE_STOP = 0.72`
  Where the falloff reaches zero. Short of 100% so the gradient completes inside its own radius and the beam never shows a visible circular boundary at the edge of the declared circle.
- `smoothing = 0.0006`
  Fraction of the remaining distance still uncovered after one second — so the beam is effectively caught up within about 100ms. Enough drag to give the light some weight, not enough for the beam to visibly trail behind the thing you are pointing at, which would make it useless for reading.
- `FADE_MS = 260`
  Enter and leave fade on the whole layer. Long enough that the beam does not blink on and off as the pointer crosses the edge, short enough that leaving does not leave a light hanging in an unhovered panel.
- `rest mask offset = -radius * 2`
  Where the seeded mask sits before the first frame. Two radii guarantees no part of the falloff is inside the box at any panel size, so nothing is lit before the pointer has been seen.

## API

```ts
function RadialMaskSpotlight(props: { children: ReactNode; radius?: number; smoothing?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Content of the lit layer. Should have a transparent background.
- `radius: number` — default `220`
  Beam radius in CSS px. Core is 30% of this, falloff completes at 72%.
- `smoothing: number` — default `0.0006`
  Fraction of the gap remaining after one second. Lower is tighter.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root container via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** Where the solid core ends, as a fraction of `radius`. */
const CORE_STOP = 0.3;
/** Where the falloff reaches full transparency, as a fraction of `radius`. */
const EDGE_STOP = 0.72;
const FADE_MS = 260;

export function RadialMaskSpotlight({
  children,
  radius = 220,
  smoothing = 0.0006,
  className,
}: RadialMaskSpotlightProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const lit = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const enabled = useRef(false);
  const visible = useRef(false);

  const pointer = useSmoothPointer({
    target: root,
    smoothing,
    // Touch is explicitly off: this component is fine-pointer only, and
    // letting touch drags drive the mask would move the beam under the finger.
    touch: false,
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = root.current;
    const layer = lit.current;
    if (!el || !layer) return;

    const fine = window.matchMedia('(pointer: fine)').matches;
    const reduced = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;

    if (!fine) {
      /* No pointer to track. Rather than leaving a masked layer invisible, the
         mask is removed entirely so the lit layer simply shows in full — the
         content stays readable and nothing is hidden behind an effect that
         cannot be operated. */
      layer.style.maskImage = '';
      layer.style.webkitMaskImage = '';
      layer.style.opacity = '1';
      return;
    }

    enabled.current = !reduced;

    if (reduced) {
      /* Reduced motion keeps the spotlight — it is a hover affordance, not
         gratuitous movement — but pins it. A beam that chases the pointer with
         inertia is the part that was objected to, so the mask is written once,
         parked, and never updated again. */
      const rect = el.getBoundingClientRect();
      writeMask(layer, rect.width * 0.5, rect.height * 0.45, radius);
      layer.style.opacity = '1';
      return;
    }

    const onEnter = () => {
      visible.current = true;
      layer.style.opacity = '1';
    };
    const onLeave = () => {
      visible.current = false;
      layer.style.opacity = '0';
    };

    el.addEventListener('pointerenter', onEnter);
    el.addEventListener('pointerleave', onLeave);

    return () => {
      el.removeEventListener('pointerenter', onEnter);
      el.removeEventListener('pointerleave', onLeave);
      enabled.current = false;
      layer.style.maskImage = '';
      layer.style.webkitMaskImage = '';
      layer.style.opacity = '';
    };
  }, [radius]);

  useRaf(() => {
    const layer = lit.current;
    if (!layer || !enabled.current) return;
    const p = pointer.current;
    // `active` is false until a real pointer has been seen. Writing before
    // that would place the beam at the hook's centre-parked seed value, which
    // flashes a spotlight the user never asked for.
    if (!p.active) return;
    writeMask(layer, p.x, p.y, radius);
  });

  return (
    <div ref={root} className={cn('relative isolate overflow-hidden', className)}>
      <div
        ref={lit}
        className="absolute inset-0"
        style={{
          opacity: 0,
          transition: `opacity ${FADE_MS}ms ease-out`,
          // Seeded off-panel so the very first painted frame cannot show an
          // unmasked layer before rAF runs.
          maskImage: restMask(radius),
          WebkitMaskImage: restMask(radius),
        }}
      >
        {children}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

function maskFor(x: number, y: number, radius: number): string {
  /* `circle <radius>px at <x>px <y>px` — an explicit px radius rather than a
     percentage, because a percentage radius in a radial gradient resolves
     against the box and would make the beam a different physical size on
     every panel it is dropped into. */
  return `radial-gradient(circle ${radius}px at ${x}px ${y}px, #000 0%, #000 ${
    CORE_STOP * 100
  }%, transparent ${EDGE_STOP * 100}%)`;
}

function restMask(radius: number): string {
  return maskFor(-radius * 2, -radius * 2, radius);
}

function writeMask(layer: HTMLElement, x: number, y: number, radius: number) {
  const value = maskFor(x, y, radius);
  /* Both spellings. Safari has shipped unprefixed `mask-image` for years but
     still mishandles gradient masks without `-webkit-` in enough released
     versions that dropping the prefix means the layer is either fully visible
     or fully gone on those browsers — a total failure, not a degraded one. */
  layer.style.maskImage = value;
  layer.style.webkitMaskImage = value;
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Removes the enter and leave listeners, flips the enabled flag so any in-flight frame is a no-op, and clears the inline `maskImage`, `WebkitMaskImage` and `opacity`. `useRaf` and `useSmoothPointer` unsubscribe themselves. Nothing was allocated beyond the two strings written per frame.

**Reduced motion.** The spotlight is still drawn — it is a hover affordance and removing it would hide content — but it never moves. The mask is written once at 50% across and 45% down, the rAF loop is left disabled, and no pointer listeners attach.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- A linear falloff from 0%. Without a flat core there is no lit region, just a bright centre that fades continuously, and the result reads as a blurred blob rather than a light. This is the most common way this effect is built and the most common reason it looks cheap.
- Setting only `maskImage`. Released Safari versions mishandle gradient masks without `-webkit-mask-image`, and the failure is total — the layer is either always visible or never visible — so it does not look like a mask bug when reported.
- Writing the mask in the `pointermove` handler. Every write invalidates paint for the layer, and a fast pointer produces several events per frame, so the same paint is thrown away two or three times before anything reaches the screen.
- A percentage radius. `circle 30% at ...` resolves against the element box, so the beam is a different size in every container and the constant that looked right in the design mock is wrong everywhere else.
- Writing the mask before the pointer has actually been seen. `useSmoothPointer` parks at the element centre so the first movement eases out sensibly, but that seed is not a real position — treating it as one flashes a spotlight in the middle of the panel on mount.
- Masking a layer containing interactive elements. `mask-image` does not clip hit testing, so links in the dark region are still clickable while being invisible. Either keep the masked layer non-interactive or accept that the mask is purely decorative.
- Putting the effect on a layer with its own background. The mask reveals the layer, and a masked opaque background is a visible disc of colour, not a light. The lit layer needs a transparent background so the beam shows content, not a shape.

## Notes

- Gated on `(pointer: fine)`. On touch the mask is removed entirely and the lit layer shows in full rather than staying hidden — an effect that cannot be operated must not be allowed to hide content. `useSmoothPointer` is also configured with `touch: false` so a scroll drag can never move the beam.
- Reduced motion keeps the spotlight but pins it: the mask is written once, centred slightly above middle, and never updated. The affordance survives; the chasing does not.
- Scoped to its own container and measured against its rect, so several instances can appear on one page without interfering.
- The masked layer is decorative by construction. If it holds links, remember that a mask hides paint but not hit testing.

## Definition of done

Move across the panel and a soft round beam follows the pointer with a slight drag, lighting the content under it. The centre of the beam is evenly lit rather than brightest at one point — cover the middle third with a finger and the light should look flat, not peaked. Enter and leave and the whole layer fades over about a quarter of a second rather than blinking. On first load, before you move, nothing is lit. Check in Safari that the beam appears at all. On touch the layer is fully visible with no mask.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
