# Build: Radial Ripple Dot Cloud

Several thousand dots in one draw call, with a wave travelling outward from a point left of centre. The displacement is a sine in radius minus a phase in time, attenuated exponentially, so the field is violent near the source and nearly still at the rim — which is what gives the motion an origin rather than making it a screensaver. Dot density along the radius is a hand-placed cubic B-spline, so the rings and gaps in the layout are drawn rather than derived from a formula.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A dot field with a travelling wave running out of one off-centre point, its density drawn by hand as a B-spline.

- Category: webgl
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1

## How it works

1. Rest positions are baked once, in field units, into an `aOrigin` attribute: the field spans ±16/9 horizontally and ±1 vertically. The draw-time uniform `uCover = max(1, aspect / (16/9))` scales that field to cover the camera, so a resize writes one float instead of rebuilding a buffer.
2. Density along the radius comes from a uniform cubic B-spline over eight hand-placed control points — five spans — evaluated in JS at bake time. `bsplineWeights(t)` returns the four basis values `[(1-t)³, 4-6t²+3t³, 1+3t+3t²-3t³, t³] / 6` and `sampleRamp` blends control points `i..i+3`. The curve is C2 and does not pass through its control points, which is what lets a hand-placed sequence stay smooth.
3. Positions are chosen by rejection sampling: a seeded candidate uniform over the field rectangle is kept with probability `ramp(dist / maxRadius)`, where `maxRadius` is the distance from the ripple source to the farthest field corner. That is the only way to realise an arbitrary drawn radial density from a uniform PRNG without inverting the curve analytically.
4. The same ramp value is baked into `aScale` (0.55 + 0.75d) and `aAlpha` (0.3 + 0.7d), so a sparse band is also a dim band. Two independent curves would let them disagree and the field would read as noise with holes in it.
5. The vertex shader computes `dist = length(origin - uCenter)`, `wave = sin(dist * uFrequency - uElapsed * uSpeed)` — a travelling wave, because the time term is subtracted from the radius term — and `attenuated = wave * exp(-dist * uDecay)`, then displaces each dot along its own outward direction by `attenuated * uAmplitude`.
6. The direction is guarded: `dir = dist > 1e-5 ? delta / dist : vec2(0.0)`, because normalising a zero vector at the exact source yields NaN and one NaN vertex takes the whole point with it.
7. `gl_PointSize` is floored at 2 device pixels and the alpha is divided by the area that flooring invented, so the cloud has the same density on a 1x monitor as on a 3x phone. The fragment shader cuts a disc with `1 - smoothstep(0.42, 0.5, d)` and tints toward `uCrestColor` by the signed wave, so only the outgoing crest lights up.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `FIELD_HALF_W = 16 / 9`
  Half-width of the baked field, with the field 2 units tall. Baking at one fixed aspect is what makes a resize a single uniform write; 16:9 is the aspect most containers are near, so `uCover` is usually 1 and nothing is scaled at all.
- `DENSITY_RAMP = [1, 1, 0.34, 0.28, 0.92, 0.5, 0, -0.15]`
  Eight control points, so five spans. Sampled it reads 0.89 / 0.44 / 0.40 / 0.74 / 0.49 / 0.06 — dense core, gap, secondary band at ~60% radius, empty rim. The last point is negative deliberately: a control point is not a value, and pulling it below zero is what makes the tail actually reach zero instead of settling around 0.15.
- `centerX = 0.4`
  Ripple source at 40% of the width rather than 50%. A centred radial wave is bilaterally symmetric and the eye reads symmetry as a screensaver; a source off the axis reads as an impact somewhere in the scene.
- `frequency = 6.5 rad per field unit`
  Wavelength 2π/6.5 ≈ 0.97 units, about half the field height, so roughly two and a half crests fit between the source and the far corner. Past ~12 the rings alias against the dot spacing and the field boils; below ~3 there is only one crest and no ripple to read.
- `speed = 2.4 rad per second`
  Crest speed is speed / frequency = 0.37 field units per second, so a crest crosses the field in about six seconds. Fast enough to be motion, slow enough that the eye can follow a single ring outward.
- `decay = 0.85 per field unit`
  Amplitude is 43% at one unit from the source and 13% at the far corner, which gives the wave a source without a visible boundary. A linear falloff reaches exactly zero at a fixed radius and draws a hard circle there.
- `amplitude = 0.045 field units`
  2.25% of the field height — around 25px on a 1100px-tall field, in the same range as the 18px the technique was observed at. Past ~0.12 dots cross each other and the cloud shears instead of rippling.
- `size = 2.6 CSS pixels`
  Base diameter, scaled 0.55..1.3 per dot. Under ~2 the hardware point-size floor kicks in for most dots and the alpha compensation is doing all the work; over ~5 the dense core fills solid and the ripple stops being legible.
- `count = 6000`
  One interleaved-free buffer, one draw call. At this size the field is vertex-bound rather than fill-bound, and 6000 is roughly where the core reads as continuous without the gaps needing more dots to hide them.
- `MAX_ATTEMPTS_PER_DOT = 24`
  Rejection-sampling budget. The mean of the ramp is about 0.45, so ~2.2 attempts per kept dot; a 24x budget absorbs a much sparser custom curve and still terminates rather than spinning forever if someone authors a ramp that is zero everywhere.
- `STATIC_ELAPSED = 3.4 s`
  The frame drawn under reduced motion. Far enough in that two crests have left the source, so the still frame shows the ripple structure rather than the undisturbed lattice.

## API

```ts
function RadialRippleDotCloud(props: { count?: number; size?: number; frequency?: number; speed?: number; decay?: number; amplitude?: number; centerX?: number; centerY?: number; color?: string; crestColor?: string; opacity?: number; seed?: number | string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `count: number` — default `6000`
  Dots kept after density rejection. One draw call regardless.
- `size: number` — default `2.6`
  Base dot diameter in CSS pixels, before the per-dot density scale.
- `frequency: number` — default `6.5`
  Radians of wave per field unit; wavelength is 2π / frequency.
- `speed: number` — default `2.4`
  Radians of phase per second. Crest speed is speed / frequency.
- `decay: number` — default `0.85`
  Exponential attenuation per field unit of radius.
- `amplitude: number` — default `0.045`
  Peak displacement in field units, where the field is 2 units tall.
- `centerX: number` — default `0.4`
  Ripple source across the field, 0..1. Deliberately not centred.
- `centerY: number` — default `0.5`
  Ripple source down the field, 0..1.
- `color: string` — default `'#5d6b7a'`
  Dot colour in the troughs.
- `crestColor: string` — default `'#eaf2ff'`
  Dot colour on an outgoing crest.
- `opacity: number` — default `1`
  Multiplier applied after the per-dot area compensation.
- `seed: number | string` — default `'radial-ripple-dot-cloud'`
  Seeds rejection sampling, so the layout is stable across reloads and matches the server.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** Uniform cubic B-spline basis at parameter `t` within one span. */
function bsplineWeights(t: number): [number, number, number, number] {
  const t2 = t * t;
  const t3 = t2 * t;
  return [
    (1 - 3 * t + 3 * t2 - t3) / 6,
    (4 - 6 * t2 + 3 * t3) / 6,
    (1 + 3 * t + 3 * t2 - 3 * t3) / 6,
    t3 / 6,
  ];
}

/**
 * Sample the density curve at `u` in 0..1. `n` control points give `n - 3`
 * spans; the curve is C2 and does NOT pass through its control points, which
 * is the property that lets a hand-placed sequence stay smooth.
 */
function sampleRamp(ramp: readonly number[], u: number): number {
  const spans = ramp.length - 3;
  if (spans < 1) return clamp(ramp[0] ?? 0, 0, 1);
  const s = clamp(u, 0, 1) * spans;
  const span = Math.min(Math.floor(s), spans - 1);
  const weights = bsplineWeights(s - span);
  let total = 0;
  for (let k = 0; k < 4; k += 1) {
    total += (ramp[span + k] ?? 0) * (weights[k] ?? 0);
  }
  return clamp(total, 0, 1);
}

export function RadialRippleDotCloud({
  count = 6000,
  size = 2.6,
  frequency = 6.5,
  speed = 2.4,
  decay = 0.85,
  amplitude = 0.045,
  centerX = 0.4,
  centerY = 0.5,
  color = '#5d6b7a',
  crestColor = '#eaf2ff',
  opacity = 1,
  seed = 'radial-ripple-dot-cloud',
  className,
}: RadialRippleDotCloudProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const stage = useRef<Stage | null>(null);
  const [unsupported, setUnsupported] = useState(false);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const size2 = useRef({ width, height });
  size2.current = { width, height };

  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const visible = useVisibility();
  const { inView } = useInView(host, { threshold: 0 });
  const ready = width > 0 && height > 0;

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = host.current;
    if (!el || !ready) return;

    if (!hasWebGL()) {
      setUnsupported(true);
      return;
    }

    const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: false, alpha: true });
    renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio());
    renderer.setClearAlpha(0);

    const scene = new THREE.Scene();
    const camera = new THREE.OrthographicCamera(-1, 1, 1, -1, 0.1, 10);
    camera.position.z = 1;

    // Field-unit centre of the ripple. Baked alongside the origins so the
    // normalised radius each dot stores is measured from the same point the
    // shader will use.
    const cx = (centerX * 2 - 1) * FIELD_HALF_W;
    const cy = 1 - centerY * 2;

    /* The farthest corner from the source. Normalising radius by this is what
       makes the density ramp aspect-independent: the tail of the curve lands on
       the corner of the field rather than at some arbitrary unit distance. */
    const maxRadius = Math.max(
      Math.hypot(FIELD_HALF_W - cx, 1 - cy),
      Math.hypot(FIELD_HALF_W + cx, 1 - cy),
      Math.hypot(FIELD_HALF_W - cx, 1 + cy),
      Math.hypot(FIELD_HALF_W + cx, 1 + cy),
    );

    /* Rejection sampling against the density curve. Candidates are uniform over
       the field rectangle and kept with probability `ramp(r)`, which is the only
       way to get an arbitrary hand-drawn radial density out of a uniform PRNG
       without inverting the curve analytically. Seeded, so the layout is
       identical on the server, on the client, and on every reload. */
    const rng = createRng(seed);
    const wanted = Math.max(1, Math.round(count));
    const origins: number[] = [];
    const scales: number[] = [];
    const alphas: number[] = [];

    let attempts = 0;
    const budget = wanted * MAX_ATTEMPTS_PER_DOT;
    while (origins.length < wanted * 2 && attempts < budget) {
      attempts += 1;
      const x = (rng() * 2 - 1) * FIELD_HALF_W;
      const y = rng() * 2 - 1;
      const density = sampleRamp(DENSITY_RAMP, Math.hypot(x - cx, y - cy) / maxRadius);
      if (rng() > density) continue;
      origins.push(x, y);
      // The ramp is reused for weight as well as for density, so a sparse band
      // is also a dim one. Two curves would let them disagree and the field
      // would read as noise with holes in it.
      scales.push(0.55 + 0.75 * density);
      alphas.push(0.3 + 0.7 * density);
    }

    const kept = scales.length;
    const positions = new Float32Array(kept * 3); // zeros; the shader positions
    const originAttr = new Float32Array(kept * 2);
    const scaleAttr = new Float32Array(kept);
    const alphaAttr = new Float32Array(kept);
    for (let i = 0; i < kept; i += 1) {
      originAttr[i * 2] = origins[i * 2] ?? 0;
      originAttr[i * 2 + 1] = origins[i * 2 + 1] ?? 0;
      scaleAttr[i] = scales[i] ?? 1;
      alphaAttr[i] = alphas[i] ?? 1;
    }

    const geometry = new THREE.BufferGeometry();
    geometry.setAttribute('position', new THREE.BufferAttribute(positions, 3));
    geometry.setAttribute('aOrigin', new THREE.BufferAttribute(originAttr, 2));
    geometry.setAttribute('aScale', new THREE.BufferAttribute(scaleAttr, 1));
    geometry.setAttribute('aAlpha', new THREE.BufferAttribute(alphaAttr, 1));

    const uniforms: Uniforms = {
      uElapsed: { value: 0 },
      uCover: { value: 1 },
      uCenter: { value: new THREE.Vector2(cx, cy) },
      uFrequency: { value: frequency },
      uSpeed: { value: speed },
      uDecay: { value: decay },
      uAmplitude: { value: amplitude },
      uSize: { value: size },
      uPixelRatio: { value: renderer.getPixelRatio() },
      uColor: { value: new THREE.Color(color) },
      uCrestColor: { value: new THREE.Color(crestColor) },
      uOpacity: { value: opacity },
    };

    const material = new THREE.ShaderMaterial({
      vertexShader: RADIAL_RIPPLE_VERT,
      fragmentShader: RADIAL_RIPPLE_FRAG,
      uniforms,
      transparent: true,
      depthTest: false,
      depthWrite: false,
      // Additive, because overlapping dots in the dense core should read as
      // brighter rather than as a flat plate of the same colour.
      blending: THREE.AdditiveBlending,
    });

    const points = new THREE.Points(geometry, material);
    // Every vertex is displaced in the shader, so three's bounding sphere is
    // wrong by construction and culling against it can blank the whole cloud.
    points.frustumCulled = false;
    scene.add(points);

    el.appendChild(renderer.domElement);
    renderer.domElement.style.display = 'block';
    renderer.domElement.style.width = '100%';
    renderer.domElement.style.height = '100%';

    const resize = (w: number, h: number) => {
      if (w <= 0 || h <= 0) return;
      renderer.setSize(w, h, false);
      const aspect = w / h;
      camera.left = -aspect;
      camera.right = aspect;
      camera.top = 1;
      camera.bottom = -1;
      camera.updateProjectionMatrix();

      /* Cover, not contain. Past 16:9 the baked field is narrower than the
         camera, so it is scaled up until it reaches both edges; the alternative
         is a visible vertical seam where the dots stop. The centre is scaled by
         the same factor so the ripple stays put relative to the field. */
      const cover = Math.max(1, aspect / FIELD_HALF_W);
      uniforms.uCover.value = cover;
      uniforms.uCenter.value.set(cx * cover, cy * cover);
      // Re-read: moving a window between displays changes devicePixelRatio
      // without changing the CSS size, and dot sizes are specified in CSS px.
      uniforms.uPixelRatio.value = renderer.getPixelRatio();
    };

    const draw = (elapsed: number) => {
      uniforms.uElapsed.value = elapsed;
      renderer.render(scene, camera);
    };

    resize(size2.current.width, size2.current.height);
    stage.current = { resize, draw };
    draw(STATIC_ELAPSED);

    return () => {
      stage.current = null;
      disposeObject(scene);
      material.dispose();
      disposeRenderer(renderer);
      renderer.domElement.remove();
    };
  }, [
    ready,
    count,
    size,
    frequency,
    speed,
    decay,
    amplitude,
    centerX,
    centerY,
    color,
    crestColor,
    opacity,
    seed,
  ]);

  useEffect(() => {
    stage.current?.resize(width, height);
    // A resize clears the drawing buffer, so the frozen frame has to be
    // redrawn or a reduced-motion visitor sees an empty box after any reflow.
    if (reduced) stage.current?.draw(STATIC_ELAPSED);
  }, [width, height, reduced]);

  useRaf(
    (_dt, elapsed) => stage.current?.draw(elapsed),
    ready && inView && visible && !reduced && !unsupported,
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nulls the stage ref, walks the scene with `disposeObject` to release the geometry and its four attribute buffers, disposes the ShaderMaterial explicitly, then calls `disposeRenderer` — `dispose` plus `forceContextLoss` plus a zeroed drawing buffer — and removes the canvas. The canvas is created inside the effect and appended imperatively rather than being owned by a React ref, so a StrictMode double-mount builds a fresh context instead of handing back the one that was just killed.

**Reduced motion.** The component reads `useReducedMotion` itself and opens no rAF subscription. One frame is drawn at `uElapsed = 3.4`, by which point two crests have left the source — so the still image shows the ripple structure and the drawn density bands, not the undisturbed lattice. The layout, the colours and the crest tinting are all present; only the travel stops. The frame is re-drawn on resize because a canvas resize clears the buffer.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Writing `sin(dist * frequency) * sin(elapsed * speed)`. That is a standing wave: the rings pulse in place and never travel. Subtracting the phase from the radius inside one sine is what makes crests move outward — and adding it instead sends them inward, which reads as a drain rather than an impact.
- Normalising the offset vector without guarding the source. At `dist == 0` the division produces NaN, the vertex is discarded by the rasteriser, and on some drivers the whole primitive goes with it — an intermittently missing dot that is very hard to attribute.
- Attenuating the radius instead of the wave, or using a linear falloff. Linear reaches zero at a fixed radius and draws a visible circle across the field; the exponential never quite reaches zero and has no edge.
- Rebuilding the position buffer on resize. It reallocates hundreds of kilobytes during a window drag and, if the layout is re-sampled, re-randomises every dot mid-motion. Baking in field units and scaling by one `uCover` uniform avoids both.
- Leaving `frustumCulled` at its default. Every vertex is displaced in the shader, so three's bounding sphere — computed from the undisplaced attribute — is wrong, and the whole cloud can vanish when the camera or the container changes.
- Using `Math.random()` for the layout. The server and the client disagree, so React logs a hydration mismatch, and the composition a designer approved is not the one the next visitor sees.
- Treating the B-spline control points as points on the curve. The curve does not pass through them — the value at the start of the first span is `(P0 + 4P1 + P2) / 6`. Authoring the ramp as if it were interpolating produces a flatter, wrong curve and hours of confusion.
- Driving dot brightness from a second curve independent of the density curve. Where they disagree the field reads as random noise with holes in it rather than as drawn bands.
- Forgetting that a resize clears the drawing buffer. Under reduced motion nothing redraws afterwards, so the component is blank after any reflow unless the frozen frame is re-rendered.

## Notes

- The camera is orthographic, ±aspect by ±1, so field units are directly comparable to the container height: 1 unit is half the visible height.
- `uCover` implements cover, not contain. Past 16:9 the baked field would otherwise stop short of the container edge and leave a visible vertical seam where the dots end.
- The ripple runs on absolute elapsed time from the shared rAF clock, so several instances on one page stay in phase with each other.

## Definition of done

Rings of dots visibly travel outward from a point left of centre, roughly two crests visible at a time, brightening as each crest passes and dimming behind it. The rim of the field barely moves. The layout has obvious drawn structure — a dense core, a gap, a second band — and is identical after a reload and after resizing the window. With reduced motion the field renders in full and holds a frozen mid-ripple frame.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Realtime Cube EnvMap

A `CubeCamera` sits inside the reflector and renders the six directions around it every other frame; that cube texture is assigned straight onto the material as its `envMap`. Because the panels supplying the reflection are orbiting, the highlights crawl across the surface instead of being painted on. No HDRI, no loader, no asset — the environment is scene geometry.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A metal knot reflecting panels that are actually orbiting it, captured six faces at a time every other frame.

- Category: webgl
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1

## How it works

1. A `WebGLCubeRenderTarget(resolution, { generateMipmaps: true, minFilter: LinearMipmapLinearFilter })` backs a `CubeCamera(0.1, 60, target)` positioned at the reflector, and `cubeTarget.texture` is assigned to `material.envMap` once at build time — the texture object never changes identity, only its contents.
2. The environment is built from geometry: an inside-out `SphereGeometry(16)` with `side: BackSide` carrying a vertical gradient `CanvasTexture`, plus `panelCount` `PlaneGeometry` emitters on a ring of radius `panelRadius`, each `lookAt(0,0,0)` and lifted by `sin(i * 2.39996) * 0.9` so the reflection has vertical structure to move through.
3. Panels alternate bright and near-black via `color.setHSL(hue + i*26, i%2 ? 0.4 : 0.66, i%2 ? 0.08 : 0.62)`. The dark ones are load-bearing: a uniformly bright environment gives a mirror nothing to contrast against and the metal reads as matte plastic.
4. Each frame the ring and the reflector are rotated from `elapsed`, then — only on frames where `frames % refreshEvery === 0` — the reflector is set `visible = false`, `cubeCamera.update(renderer, scene)` runs, and it is set visible again before the single visible `renderer.render`.
5. Resize lives in its own effect: it sets renderer size, sets `camera.aspect`, moves the camera to `BASE_DISTANCE / Math.min(1, aspect)` so a portrait container does not clip the panel ring off both sides, and forces one capture plus one redraw so a reflow never leaves a stale or black frame on screen.
6. Teardown disposes the shell texture, both geometries, every panel material, the reflector material, then `cubeTarget.dispose()` — the cube target is not in the scene graph, so `disposeObject` never reaches it — and finally `disposeRenderer`, which is what calls `forceContextLoss()`.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `refreshEvery = 2`
  Cube captures per rendered frame. Six faces is six scene renders against the visible pass's one, so this is 6/7 of the component's cost. An env map is sampled by direction, not position, so at these rotation speeds a one-frame-old capture is not observable; at 4 or more the highlights visibly step.
- `resolution = 256`
  Cube face size. Cost is 6 x resolution² fragments plus a mip chain — about 2 MB of GPU memory. At 128 the panel edges alias into the reflection as jagged bands; above 512 nothing improves because roughness immediately blurs the detail away.
- `roughness = 0.08`
  Not 0. A perfect mirror shows the panels as hard-edged rectangles and every seam in the cube map becomes visible; a slight roughness selects a lower mip and softens exactly those seams. Above ~0.3 the reflection stops being readable as a scene at all.
- `envMapIntensity = 1.4`
  Reflected light multiplier. At 1 a dark environment leaves the object nearly invisible against the shell; above ~2 the bright panels clip to flat white and the curvature information in the highlight is lost.
- `panelRadius = 4.2`
  Ring radius against a ~1.4-unit reflector. Closer and the panels enter the camera frustum and read as walls rather than as light sources; further and they subtend too small an angle to produce a highlight worth reflecting.
- `BASE_DISTANCE = 7.2`
  Camera distance at aspect >= 1, chosen against a 34 degree field of view so the reflector fills about two thirds of the frame height. Divided by `min(1, aspect)` on narrower containers.
- `STATIC_POSE = 0.9`
  The `elapsed` value used for the reduced-motion still and for post-resize redraws. Not 0: at zero the knot is axis-aligned and the panels sit on the cardinal directions, which reads as a technical diagram instead of a lit object.
- `lift stagger = sin(i * 2.39996) * 0.9`
  2.39996 rad is the golden angle, so successive panels never repeat a height for any panel count. A constant height puts every panel in one band and the reflection has nothing to travel through vertically.

## API

```ts
function RealtimeCubeEnvmap(props: { shape?: 'knot' | 'icosahedron'; panelCount?: number; panelRadius?: number; spinSpeed?: number; objectSpin?: number; resolution?: number; refreshEvery?: number; roughness?: number; metalness?: number; envMapIntensity?: number; hue?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `shape: 'knot' | 'icosahedron'` — default `'knot'`
  Reflector silhouette. The knot has more curvature and so more reflection per pixel.
- `panelCount: number` — default `7`
  Emitting panels on the ring. Odd counts keep bright and dark panels from pairing off across the object.
- `panelRadius: number` — default `4.2`
  Ring radius in world units.
- `spinSpeed: number` — default `0.18`
  Panel ring rotation, radians per second. This is what makes the reflection move.
- `objectSpin: number` — default `0.32`
  Reflector rotation about Y, radians per second. X spins at 0.55 of this.
- `resolution: number` — default `256`
  Cube face size in pixels. Cost is six faces plus mips.
- `refreshEvery: number` — default `2`
  Capture the cube map every Nth rendered frame. 1 captures every frame.
- `roughness: number` — default `0.08`
  Surface roughness, which selects the env map mip level.
- `metalness: number` — default `1`
  1 is a mirror; 0 is diffuse and lit only by the env map.
- `envMapIntensity: number` — default `1.4`
  Multiplier on reflected light.
- `hue: number` — default `208`
  Base hue in degrees for the panels and the shell gradient.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function RealtimeCubeEnvmap({
  shape = 'knot',
  panelCount = 7,
  panelRadius = 4.2,
  spinSpeed = 0.18,
  objectSpin = 0.32,
  resolution = 256,
  refreshEvery = 2,
  roughness = 0.08,
  metalness = 1,
  envMapIntensity = 1.4,
  hue = 208,
  className,
}: RealtimeCubeEnvmapProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const stage = useRef<Stage | null>(null);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const { inView } = useInView(host, { threshold: 0 });
  const visible = useVisibility();
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  const [supported, setSupported] = useState(true);
  useEffect(() => setSupported(hasWebGL()), []);

  const size = useRef({ width, height });
  size.current = { width, height };

  const ready = width > 1 && height > 1 && supported;

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = host.current;
    if (!el || !ready) return;

    const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: true, alpha: false });
    renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio());
    renderer.setSize(el.clientWidth, el.clientHeight, false);
    renderer.domElement.style.display = 'block';
    renderer.domElement.style.width = '100%';
    renderer.domElement.style.height = '100%';
    el.appendChild(renderer.domElement);

    const scene = new THREE.Scene();
    const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(FIELD_OF_VIEW, 1, 0.1, 60);
    camera.position.set(0, 0.35, BASE_DISTANCE);
    camera.lookAt(0, 0, 0);

    // The shell is the environment's floor and sky in one object: a sphere
    // turned inside out. It is what the cube camera sees in every direction
    // the panels do not cover, so without it the reflection has large holes of
    // clear-colour black and the object reads as unlit rather than dark.
    const shellTexture = new THREE.CanvasTexture(makeShellTexture(hue));
    shellTexture.colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace;
    const shellGeometry = new THREE.SphereGeometry(16, 32, 16);
    const shellMaterial = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({
      map: shellTexture,
      side: THREE.BackSide,
    });
    scene.add(new THREE.Mesh(shellGeometry, shellMaterial));

    // Panels. Their arrangement is a pure function of the index — there is no
    // random scatter here, so there is no seed to keep in step between the
    // server render and the client one.
    const ring = new THREE.Group();
    const panelGeometry = new THREE.PlaneGeometry(1.5, 3.4);
    const panelMaterials: THREE.MeshBasicMaterial[] = [];
    const count = Math.max(2, Math.round(panelCount));

    for (let i = 0; i < count; i += 1) {
      const material = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ side: THREE.DoubleSide });
      // Alternating bright and near-black panels. An environment that is
      // uniformly bright gives a mirror nothing to contrast against and the
      // metal reads as matte plastic; the dark panels are what draw the
      // specular edges.
      const bright = i % 2 === 0;
      material.color.setHSL(
        ((hue + i * 26) % 360) / 360,
        bright ? 0.66 : 0.4,
        bright ? 0.62 : 0.08,
      );
      panelMaterials.push(material);

      const panel = new THREE.Mesh(panelGeometry, material);
      const angle = (i / count) * Math.PI * 2;
      // Golden-angle stagger on the height, so the panels do not sit in a
      // single band and the reflection has vertical structure to move through.
      const lift = Math.sin(i * 2.39996) * 0.9;
      panel.position.set(
        Math.sin(angle) * panelRadius,
        lift,
        Math.cos(angle) * panelRadius,
      );
      panel.lookAt(0, 0, 0);
      ring.add(panel);
    }
    scene.add(ring);

    const reflectorGeometry =
      shape === 'knot'
        ? new THREE.TorusKnotGeometry(0.92, 0.31, 220, 32)
        : new THREE.IcosahedronGeometry(1.35, 2);

    // Mipmaps are not optional here. `roughness` selects a mip level of the
    // env map, so a cube target without them samples level 0 at every
    // roughness and the surface stays a hard mirror no matter what you pass.
    const cubeTarget = new THREE.WebGLCubeRenderTarget(Math.max(16, Math.round(resolution)), {
      generateMipmaps: true,
      minFilter: THREE.LinearMipmapLinearFilter,
    });
    const cubeCamera = new THREE.CubeCamera(0.1, 60, cubeTarget);
    // Co-located with the reflector: an env map is sampled by direction, so
    // the capture point is the only position information it carries. Offset it
    // and the reflections belong to a different object.
    cubeCamera.position.set(0, 0, 0);
    scene.add(cubeCamera);

    const material = new THREE.MeshPhysicalMaterial({
      metalness,
      roughness,
      envMapIntensity,
      // Assigned to the material rather than `scene.environment` on purpose.
      // A live capture belongs to one object at one point in space; sharing it
      // scene-wide would give every reflector the same viewpoint.
      envMap: cubeTarget.texture,
      color: 0xffffff,
    });
    const reflector = new THREE.Mesh(reflectorGeometry, material);
    scene.add(reflector);

    const throttle = Math.max(1, Math.round(refreshEvery));
    let frames = 0;

    const draw = (elapsed: number, forceCapture: boolean) => {
      ring.rotation.y = elapsed * spinSpeed;
      reflector.rotation.y = elapsed * objectSpin;
      reflector.rotation.x = elapsed * objectSpin * 0.55;

      frames += 1;
      if (forceCapture || frames % throttle === 0) {
        // Hide, capture, show — in that order, inside one frame. Skipping the
        // hide is the classic version of this bug: the object captures itself
        // and within a second the surface is a recursive tunnel.
        reflector.visible = false;
        cubeCamera.update(renderer, scene);
        reflector.visible = true;
      }

      renderer.render(scene, camera);
    };

    const resize = (w: number, h: number) => {
      if (w < 1 || h < 1) return;
      const aspect = w / h;
      renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio());
      renderer.setSize(w, h, false);
      camera.aspect = aspect;
      // Pull the camera back on narrow containers. A fixed distance frames the
      // object on height alone, so a portrait preview clips the panel ring off
      // both sides and the reflections lose their source.
      camera.position.z = BASE_DISTANCE / Math.min(1, aspect);
      camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
    };

    resize(size.current.width, size.current.height);
    stage.current = { renderer, scene, camera, cubeTarget, resize, draw };
    // First frame forces a capture: with an empty cube map a metal surface is
    // pure black, and on a throttled refresh that black would be on screen for
    // `refreshEvery` frames.
    draw(STATIC_POSE, true);

    return () => {
      stage.current = null;
      scene.remove(cubeCamera);
      // Order matters: free the scene graph's GPU objects while the context is
      // still alive, then hand the context itself back.
      disposeObject(scene);
      shellTexture.dispose();
      shellGeometry.dispose();
      shellMaterial.dispose();
      panelGeometry.dispose();
      for (const panelMaterial of panelMaterials) panelMaterial.dispose();
      reflectorGeometry.dispose();
      material.dispose();
      // The cube target is not in the scene graph, so nothing above reaches
      // it. It holds six faces plus their mip chain — at 256px that is about
      // 2 MB of GPU memory per instance.
      cubeTarget.dispose();
      disposeRenderer(renderer);
      renderer.domElement.remove();
    };
  }, [
    ready,
    shape,
    panelCount,
    panelRadius,
    spinSpeed,
    objectSpin,
    resolution,
    refreshEvery,
    roughness,
    metalness,
    envMapIntensity,
    hue,
  ]);

  // Resize in its own effect: a container reflow costs a `setSize` and one
  // redraw rather than a rebuild of the geometry and the cube target.
  useEffect(() => {
    const current = stage.current;
    if (!current) return;
    current.resize(width, height);
    current.draw(STATIC_POSE, true);
  }, [width, height, reduced]);

  useRaf(
    (_dt, elapsed) => stage.current?.draw(elapsed, false),
    ready && inView && visible && !reduced,
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `disposeObject(scene)` walks the graph, then the shell canvas texture, shell and panel geometries, every panel material and the reflector material are disposed explicitly, then `cubeTarget.dispose()` releases the six faces and their mip chain, then `disposeRenderer(renderer)` calls `dispose()` and `forceContextLoss()` and zeroes the backing store, and the canvas node is removed. The `CubeCamera` is removed from the scene first so nothing holds a reference to a disposed target.

**Reduced motion.** The rAF subscription is never made, and the scene is drawn once at `STATIC_POSE` with a forced cube capture — a fully reflective still with the panels off the cardinal axes. Reflections, gradient shell and material are all exactly as they are in motion; only the rotation is absent. Resizing redraws the same pose rather than resuming.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Capturing with the reflector visible. It photographs its own previous frame, the next capture includes that photograph, and within about a second the surface is a recursive tunnel of dark shells. Hide it, capture, show it — inside the same frame, so it is never absent from the visible render.
- Creating the cube target without mipmaps. `roughness` picks a mip level of the env map; with only level 0 available the surface stays a hard mirror at every roughness value and the prop appears to do nothing.
- Refreshing the cube map every frame because it looks like the honest thing to do. That is seven scene renders per displayed frame, and it is the difference between a preview grid that holds 60fps and one that does not.
- Rendering the first frame without forcing a capture. An unwritten cube map is black, a metal surface reflecting black is black, and on a throttled refresh that black sits on screen for `refreshEvery` frames as a visible flash.
- Building the environment out of bright panels only. Metal is read entirely from the contrast between light and dark in its surroundings; with no dark panels the highlights have no edges and the material looks like painted plastic.
- Letting `disposeObject(scene)` stand in for cube-target cleanup. The target is not a child of anything, so nothing traverses it, and six faces plus mips leak per mount — which under StrictMode double-invocation is two leaks per page load.
- Leaving the camera distance fixed. Framing on height alone means a portrait container crops the panel ring away entirely, and the object loses the thing it is reflecting.

## Notes

- No lights in the scene. `metalness: 1` with `roughness` near 0 is lit purely by its environment, so a light would contribute almost nothing while adding a uniform to every shader compile.
- `transmission` is deliberately not exposed. Three renders a separate full-scene pass per transmissive object, which on top of six cube faces triples the frame cost for an effect the cube map already implies.
- The panel arrangement is a pure function of the index, so there is no RNG and nothing to seed — server and client markup cannot disagree.

## Definition of done

The bright bands on the object crawl across its surface continuously while it turns, and the same colours are visible on the panels orbiting behind it. There is no dark recursive tunnel anywhere on the surface at any moment. Raising `roughness` toward 0.3 progressively blurs the reflection instead of leaving it a hard mirror. Resize the container and the object stays fully in frame in both landscape and portrait. Mount and unmount a dozen instances and none of the earlier ones go black.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Re-Key Caption Replay

A wrapper that replays a staggered entrance every time its `entryKey` changes. It does it by being a different node: React unmounts the old caption and mounts a new one, and a freshly mounted element starts its CSS animation at frame zero. No forced reflow to restart the animation, no tween to kill, and a fast prev/next cannot leave the block half-entered because the half-entered node no longer exists.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A caption block whose staggered entrance replays on every index change, restarted by a changed React key.

- Category: transition
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The children are wrapped in a single `<div key={entryKey}>`. Changing `entryKey` makes React discard that subtree and mount a fresh one; a new element runs its `animation` from frame zero, which is the entire replay mechanism. The key goes on the wrapper, not on each child — keyed individually, only the children whose own identity changed would replay, which for a caption is usually none of them.
2. One keyframe, `kinetic-rekey-in`, runs `opacity: 0` and `translateY(var(--kx-rekey-from))` to `opacity: 1` and `translateY(0)` over 0.5 s on `cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)`. Because the offset is a custom property rather than a literal, flipping its sign on the root turns a rise into a drop — both directions from one set of keyframes.
3. The stagger is a generated ladder of `:nth-child(n) { animation-delay: calc(var(--kx-rekey-stagger) * (n - 1)) }` rules, built once at module scope for the first eight children. A ninth-and-beyond rule pins the tail to the eighth delay, so an overlong block degrades to "the tail arrives together" rather than "the tail arrives first at delay zero".
4. `animation-fill-mode: both` is what makes the delay usable. Without it a delayed line is painted at its normal full-opacity style for the length of its own delay, then snaps to the from-frame to begin animating — every line flashes before it enters.
5. The stylesheet is emitted once through React 19's `<style href precedence>` hoisting, so duration, stagger and offset are read from CSS custom properties set on the wrapper. Ten captions on a page share one rule block and differ only in their variables.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `duration = 0.5`
  Seconds per line. With the 0.06 s stagger, a four-line block finishes in 0.68 s — under the ~0.7 s where a caption change starts to feel like waiting. Halve it and the ease has no room to decelerate, so the rise reads as a jump.
- `distance = 14`
  Pixels travelled. Roughly one line of leading at caption size: enough for the eye to register direction, small enough that the text is never far from where it lands. Past ~30 px the block reads as flying in from off-panel.
- `stagger = 0.06`
  Seconds between lines. At 0 the block is one object; past ~0.12 s the metadata is still arriving after the title has settled, which reads as a slow network rather than a sequence.
- `ease = cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)`
  An out-quart. It covers about 80% of the distance in the first third of the duration, so the line appears to arrive fast and then settle — which is what hides the fact that nothing is actually decelerating.
- `MAX_STAGGERED_LINES = 8`
  How many nth-child rules are generated. Eight covers eyebrow, title, two metadata rows and a counter with room spare. The number exists because CSS cannot do arithmetic on the child index, so the ladder has to be finite.

## API

```ts
function RekeyCaptionReplay(props: { entryKey: string | number; children: ReactNode; duration?: number; distance?: number; stagger?: number; direction?: "up" | "down"; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `entryKey: string | number`
  Identity of the current caption. Any change replays the entrance.
- `children: ReactNode`
  Direct children each get their own delay, in source order.
- `duration: number` — default `0.5`
  Seconds one line's entrance lasts.
- `distance: number` — default `14`
  Pixels a line travels. Signed by `direction`.
- `stagger: number` — default `0.06`
  Seconds between successive lines. 0 makes the block arrive as one piece.
- `direction: "up" | "down"` — default `"up"`
  `up` enters from below; `down` enters from above, for a step backward.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the keyed wrapper via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * How many direct children get their own delay. Eight covers eyebrow, title,
 * two metadata rows and a counter with room to spare; children past the eighth
 * are pinned to the eighth's delay rather than falling back to zero, so an
 * overlong block degrades to "the tail arrives together" instead of "the tail
 * arrives first".
 */
const MAX_STAGGERED_LINES = 8;

const STAGGER_RULES = [
  ...Array.from(
    { length: MAX_STAGGERED_LINES },
    (_, i) =>
      `.kinetic-rekey > :nth-child(${i + 1}) { animation-delay: calc(var(--kx-rekey-stagger, 0.06s) * ${i}); }`,
  ),
  `.kinetic-rekey > :nth-child(n + ${MAX_STAGGERED_LINES + 1}) { animation-delay: calc(var(--kx-rekey-stagger, 0.06s) * ${MAX_STAGGERED_LINES - 1}); }`,
].join('\n');

const REKEY_CSS = `
@keyframes kinetic-rekey-in {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(var(--kx-rekey-from, 14px)); }
  to   { opacity: 1; transform: translateY(0); }
}
/* One keyframe covers both directions: the offset is a custom property, so
   flipping its sign on the root turns a rise into a drop without a second
   set of keyframes to keep in sync. */
.kinetic-rekey > * {
  animation: var(--kx-rekey-duration, 0.5s) cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)
    both kinetic-rekey-in;
}
${STAGGER_RULES}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  /* The still state IS the destination: full opacity, no offset. Dropping the
     animation re-exposes those as the base values, which is why there is
     nothing to declare here beyond 'none'. A zero-duration animation would
     instead hold whatever 'both' resolved and still fire animationend. */
  .kinetic-rekey > * { animation: none; }
}
`;

export interface RekeyCaptionReplayProps {
  /**
   * Identity of the current caption. Any change replays the entrance — in a
   * slideshow this is the slide index, in a filter it is the active facet.
   */
  entryKey: string | number;
  /** Direct children each get their own delay, in source order. */
  children: ReactNode;
  /** Seconds one line's entrance lasts. */
  duration?: number;
  /** Pixels a line travels. Signed by `direction`. */
  distance?: number;
  /** Seconds between successive lines. 0 makes the block arrive as one piece. */
  stagger?: number;
  /**
   * `up` enters from below — the default, and correct for advancing forward.
   * `down` enters from above, which is what makes a step backward read as a
   * step backward rather than as another step forward.
   */
  direction?: 'up' | 'down';
  className?: string;
}

export function RekeyCaptionReplay({
  entryKey,
  children,
  duration = 0.5,
  distance = 14,
  stagger = 0.06,
  direction = 'up',
  className,
}: RekeyCaptionReplayProps) {
  const from = direction === 'up' ? distance : -distance;

  return (
    <>
      <style href="kinetic-rekey-caption-replay" precedence="medium">
        {REKEY_CSS}
      </style>

      {/* The key is on this wrapper, so every child is a new node on every
          change and every child animation restarts. Putting the key on the
          children individually would replay only the ones whose own identity
          changed, which for a caption is usually none of them. */}
      <div
        key={entryKey}
        className={cn('kinetic-rekey', className)}
        style={
          {
            '--kx-rekey-duration': `${duration}s`,
            '--kx-rekey-stagger': `${stagger}s`,
            '--kx-rekey-from': `${from}px`,
          } as CSSProperties
        }
      >
        {children}
      </div>
    </>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to clean up. There are no listeners, no timers, no rAF and no tweens — the animation is CSS and the nodes running it are removed by React itself on every key change.

**Reduced motion.** `animation: none` on the children, which re-exposes their base styles — full opacity, no offset. The caption is fully rendered on the first frame after the key change, in its final position. This is the one case where dropping the animation is the correct still state rather than a cop-out, because the from-frame is the only thing the animation adds.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Restarting the animation by toggling a class off and on. The browser coalesces both mutations into one style recalculation and the animation never restarts, which is why that approach always ends up with a `void el.offsetWidth` forced reflow wedged between the two lines.
- Tweening the caption with an animation library instead. A fast prev/next leaves two opposing tweens on the same node and the text jitters between them; a remount cannot have that problem because the contended node is gone.
- Omitting `animation-fill-mode: both`. Every delayed line paints at full opacity for the length of its delay, then snaps to invisible to start animating. The block flickers, and it flickers worse the larger the stagger.
- Putting the key on the individual lines. Their identities usually do not change between captions, so React reuses the nodes and nothing replays — the most common way this technique silently does nothing.
- Wrapping anything focusable or stateful. The remount destroys DOM state and moves focus to the body: an input inside this loses its caret and its value on every key change. This is for display content only.
- Animating both directions with a second keyframe block. The two drift apart the first time someone tunes the offset. One keyframe reading a signed custom property cannot.

## Notes

- Pairs with a counter badge and prev/next controls to make a slideshow caption, which is where the technique was observed. The same wrapper works for a filter result header, a hovered-row detail panel, or a step label in a multi-step form summary.
- Direction is a prop rather than something derived internally, because only the caller knows whether an index change was forward, backward, or a jump from a thumbnail strip.
- For the media beside the caption, a CSS `transition` on the background beats a tween: an index change is a discrete event with one start and one end state, which is exactly what a transition is for.

## Definition of done

Step forward and the eyebrow, title and metadata rise into place one after another, roughly 60 ms apart. Step backward and they drop in from above instead. Click next four times as fast as you can and every caption plays its full entrance from the start with no jitter or stuck line. With reduced motion the new caption is simply there, complete, on the first frame.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Relaxed Seeded Scatter

Half the points sit on an exact lattice and half are seeded noise; fifteen relaxation sweeps then push the noisy ones apart until no neighbour pair is closer than 40% of the mean spacing. The result keeps the liveliness of random placement without the clusters that read as a bug. The visualiser leaves a dashed ghost at each point's pre-relaxation angle, so the displacement is legible, and prints the smallest gap before and after.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Seeded angles around a ring, pushed apart until nothing collides. Ghost ticks mark where they started.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. `floor(count * evenRatio)` points are written at `(i / fixedCount) * 2PI` and flagged fixed; the remainder get `rng() * 2PI` from `createRng(seed)`, a mulberry32 stream. The raw array is copied before anything moves so the two states can be compared and interpolated.
2. The target gap is `(2PI / count) * 0.4` — 40% of the mean spacing on the full ring, not on the random subset, so the floor means the same thing regardless of how many points are pinned.
3. Each sweep sorts the nodes by `mod(angle, 2PI)`, then walks consecutive pairs measuring `gap = mod(next.angle - current.angle, 2PI)`. Because `mod` always measures the short way round, the pair that straddles zero needs no special case.
4. When a gap is under target, each free endpoint is moved by `(target - gap) * 0.5` away from the other; if one endpoint is pinned to the lattice the free one absorbs the whole `(target - gap)` instead, or points pile up against the lattice and never separate.
5. Angles are stored unwrapped — a point pushed below zero keeps a small negative value rather than jumping to just under 2PI — so the component can interpolate `raw -> relaxed` linearly and never take the long way round. Only the sort and the gap measurement wrap.
6. The visualiser eases that interpolation over 1.4 s with `easeOutQuart` on the shared rAF loop, writing the `transform` attribute of one `<g>` per point. The SVG uses a `-50 -50 100 100` viewBox, so it resizes with its container and needs no ResizeObserver.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `RELAX_PASSES = 15`
  Each sweep removes about half the remaining overlap, so 15 leaves 2^-15 of the initial error — fully converged for any count up to ~64. At 3 passes the tightest pairs are still visibly paired; past ~20 nothing measurable changes and you are paying O(passes · n log n) for nothing.
- `MIN_GAP_RATIO = 0.4`
  Floor on the neighbour gap as a fraction of the mean, so `targetGap = 0.4 * 2PI / count`. Below ~0.25 clusters survive and the scatter still reads as clumped. Above ~0.6 the relaxation cannot satisfy every pair at once, so it oscillates between passes and converges toward the lattice — which throws away the randomness you asked for.
- `EVEN_RATIO = 0.5`
  Fraction pinned to the exact lattice. At 0 the composition has no skeleton and the eye finds no structure; at 1 it is a clock face. Half and half is the mix that reads as deliberate but not mechanical.
- `PUSH_SHARE = 0.5`
  Each free neighbour absorbs half the deficit, so a pair separates by exactly the deficit per sweep. At 1.0 both move the full amount, overshoot, and the pair oscillates instead of settling.
- `MORPH_DURATION = 1.4`
  Seconds for the raw-to-relaxed sweep. Long enough to follow individual points leaving their ghosts; under ~0.6 s it reads as a single cut and the comparison is lost.
- `seed = 'kinetic'`
  Any fixed value works — what matters is that it is fixed. `hashSeed` turns the string into a 32-bit integer, so a named seed per instance gives every ring its own reproducible composition.

## API

```ts
function relaxedRingAngles(count: number, seed: number | string, options?: { passes?: number; minGapRatio?: number; evenRatio?: number; pushShare?: number }): RelaxedRing;
function RelaxedSeededScatter(props: { count?: number; seed?: number | string; passes?: number; minGapRatio?: number; evenRatio?: number; morph?: boolean; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `count: number` — default `24`
  Points on the ring.
- `seed: number | string` — default `'kinetic'`
  Fixed seed. Strings are hashed with `hashSeed`.
- `passes: number` — default `15`
  Relaxation sweeps.
- `minGapRatio: number` — default `0.4`
  Minimum neighbour gap as a fraction of the mean spacing.
- `evenRatio: number` — default `0.5`
  Fraction of points pinned to an exact lattice.
- `morph: boolean` — default `true`
  Ease from the raw angles to the relaxed ones on first view.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the outer element via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** Sweeps. Each halves the residual overlap; 15 is fully converged for n<=64. */
const RELAX_PASSES = 15;
/** Floor on the neighbour gap, as a fraction of the mean gap. */
const MIN_GAP_RATIO = 0.4;
/** Half the points sit on an exact lattice and never move. */
const EVEN_RATIO = 0.5;
/** Each free neighbour absorbs half the deficit. */
const PUSH_SHARE = 0.5;

type Node = { id: number; angle: number; fixed: boolean };

/** Smallest neighbour gap on the circle, and how many pairs are under `target`. */
function ringStats(values: ArrayLike<number>, target: number) {
  const n = values.length;
  if (n < 2) return { minGap: TAU, crowded: 0 };
  const sorted = Array.from(values, (v) => mod(v, TAU)).sort((a, b) => a - b);
  let minGap = TAU;
  let crowded = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const a = sorted[i] ?? 0;
    const b = sorted[(i + 1) % n] ?? 0;
    const gap = i === n - 1 ? b + TAU - a : b - a;
    if (gap < minGap) minGap = gap;
    if (gap < target) crowded++;
  }
  return { minGap, crowded };
}

export function relaxedRingAngles(
  count: number,
  seed: number | string,
  options: RelaxedRingOptions = {},
): RelaxedRing {
  const {
    passes = RELAX_PASSES,
    minGapRatio = MIN_GAP_RATIO,
    evenRatio = EVEN_RATIO,
    pushShare = PUSH_SHARE,
  } = options;

  const n = Math.max(0, Math.floor(count));
  const angles = new Float32Array(n);
  const raw = new Float32Array(n);
  const targetGap = n > 0 ? (TAU / n) * minGapRatio : 0;
  const fixedCount = Math.floor(n * evenRatio);

  if (n === 0) {
    return { angles, raw, minGap: 0, rawMinGap: 0, crowded: 0, rawCrowded: 0, targetGap, fixedCount };
  }

  // Half order: an exact lattice, so the composition has a skeleton.
  for (let i = 0; i < fixedCount; i++) angles[i] = (i / fixedCount) * TAU;
  // Half chaos: seeded, never Math.random().
  const rng = createRng(seed);
  for (let i = fixedCount; i < n; i++) angles[i] = rng() * TAU;
  raw.set(angles);

  const nodes: Node[] = Array.from({ length: n }, (unused, id) => ({
    id,
    angle: angles[id] ?? 0,
    fixed: id < fixedCount,
  }));

  for (let pass = 0; pass < passes && n > 1; pass++) {
    // Re-sort every sweep. A push can carry a point across zero, which
    // re-orders the ring; a gap computed from stale neighbours pushes the
    // wrong point and leaves a permanent clump at the wrap.
    nodes.sort((a, b) => mod(a.angle, TAU) - mod(b.angle, TAU));

    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      const a = nodes[i];
      const b = nodes[(i + 1) % n];
      if (!a || !b || a === b) continue;

      // mod() measures the gap the short way round, so the pair that straddles
      // zero needs no special case.
      const gap = mod(b.angle - a.angle, TAU);
      if (gap >= targetGap) continue;

      const deficit = (targetGap - gap) * pushShare;
      if (a.fixed && b.fixed) continue;
      // A pinned neighbour cannot absorb its share, so the free one takes all
      // of it. Otherwise points pile up against the lattice and never separate.
      if (a.fixed) b.angle += deficit * 2;
      else if (b.fixed) a.angle -= deficit * 2;
      else {
        a.angle -= deficit;
        b.angle += deficit;
      }
    }
  }

  for (const node of nodes) angles[node.id] = node.angle;

  const after = ringStats(angles, targetGap);
  const before = ringStats(raw, targetGap);

  return {
    angles,
    raw,
    minGap: after.minGap,
    rawMinGap: before.minGap,
    crowded: after.crowded,
    rawCrowded: before.crowded,
    targetGap,
    fixedCount,
  };
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useRaf` unsubscribes on unmount and the shared frame is cancelled when the last subscriber leaves; the loop also unsubscribes itself the moment the morph completes, so a settled ring costs nothing. `useInView` unobserves the root. No timers, no listeners, no retained typed arrays beyond the memo.

**Reduced motion.** The relaxed angles render immediately with no sweep. The dashed ghosts at the raw angles stay, so the before/after comparison the component exists to make is fully readable without anything moving, and the gap readout is unchanged.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- `Math.random()` instead of a seeded generator. The server renders one arrangement and the client another, React reports a hydration mismatch and re-renders the subtree, and the layout is different on every reload so no visual diff is ever reviewable.
- Not re-sorting between sweeps. A push can carry a point across zero, which re-orders the ring; the next sweep then measures the gap to a point that is no longer the neighbour, pushes the wrong one, and leaves a permanent clump sitting exactly on the wrap.
- Measuring the gap as `next - current`. For the pair that straddles zero that is a large negative number, which is always below the target, so the relaxation shoves those two apart on every sweep forever and one point walks all the way around the ring.
- Splitting the deficit evenly when one neighbour is pinned. The free point only ever gets half the correction it needs, so it converges to half the required gap and stays visibly stuck to the lattice tick.
- Wrapping the angles into `[0, 2PI)` on the way out. The interpolation from `raw` to `angles` then sends any point that crossed zero the long way round the ring, and one tick sweeps a full circle during the settle while the rest move a few degrees.
- Rebuilding the ring on every render. `relaxedRingAngles` is O(passes · n log n) and allocates; without `useMemo` keyed on the inputs, every parent render re-runs 15 sweeps and re-allocates two typed arrays.

## Notes

- Relaxing over the full ring with the lattice pinned is a deliberate deviation from the version this was taken from, which relaxed only the random subset against itself. That version lets a random point land exactly on a lattice point, which is the one collision the technique is supposed to prevent.
- `relaxedRingAngles` is the shipped part. Feed the angles into whatever you are placing — CSS `rotate()`, an instanced attribute, a `THREE.Vector3` per item — the visualiser is only here to show what the numbers do.

## Definition of done

On first scroll into view the solid ticks slide off their dashed ghosts and stop; every accent tick stays exactly on its ghost because the lattice is pinned. The "min gap" readout shows a struck-through small number followed by a larger one at or above the target. Reload ten times and the arrangement is byte-identical. Set `evenRatio` to 0 and every tick moves.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
