# Build: Rotary Drag Carousel

Items sit at fixed stations around a circle whose hub is below the frame, so only the top arc is ever visible. The gesture is measured in angle rather than pixels: `atan2(y - cy, x - cx)`, differenced through a shortest-signed wrap, so a hand sweeping the top of the wheel turns it by the amount it actually travelled around the hub. Release and it keeps going at the speed it left at, then stops with a station facing up — one motion, no corrective hop.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A wheel of cards you grab and spin. Angular drag, projected inertia, and it always lands on a station.

- Category: layout
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. Layout is a pure function of one number. For wheel angle `A`, station `i` sits at screen angle `theta = A + i * (360 / count) - 90`, at `(cx + R cos theta, cy + R sin theta)`, rotated by the shortest signed distance to the top, `away = wrapRange(theta + 90, -180, 180)`. `A` is unbounded and may be -4000 without consequence, because `away` is the only value that ever needs wrapping.
2. The radius is floored at `1.25 x containerHeight`, which forces the hub `cy = topInset * height + R` strictly below the box. That is a correctness constraint, not a look: `atan2` about a point the user can touch converts a two-pixel wobble near the hub into a hundred degrees of spin.
3. Each `pointermove` computes the pointer's own angle about the hub and adds `wrapRange(current - previous, -180, 180)` to `A`. The wrap is what keeps a drag across the 180° seam from reading as a 359° jerk backwards.
4. Release velocity is measured over a rolling ~70 ms window of `(angle, time)` rather than off the final delta. Because a stationary finger produces no `pointermove` events, the window never advances while the hand is still, and the measured speed decays toward zero on its own — "drag, pause, lift" therefore does not throw.
5. Inertia without a plugin: `power3.out` is `p(t) = 1 - (1 - t)^3`, so `p'(0) = 3`. A tween of duration `D` covering `delta` degrees departs at `3 * delta / D` deg/s, so setting `delta = v * D / 3` makes a plain `gsap.to` continue the gesture at exactly the speed the hand left.
6. That projected landing angle is rounded to a multiple of the station spacing *before* the tween is created, so the throw and the snap are the same tween. Snapping afterwards is a second animation starting from rest — the small hop that gives away a hand-rolled dial.
7. Pointer capture is taken on `pointerdown`, and the release path is one idempotent `finish` guarded on the stored `pointerId`, wired to `pointerup`, `pointercancel` and `lostpointercapture` alike. A drag that ends off-screen still lands.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `MIN_RADIUS_HEIGHT_RATIO = 1.25`
  Radius floor as a multiple of container height, so the hub is always below the visible box. At 1.0 the hub lands exactly on the bottom edge and a press there divides by a near-zero radius; below 1.0 it is reachable and the wheel spins wildly for a pointer that barely moved.
- `POWER3_OUT_SLOPE = 3`
  The initial derivative of `power3.out`, and the divisor in `delta = v * D / 3`. It is exact, not tuned: change the ease and this number changes with it — `power2.out` needs 2, `power4.out` needs 4. Leave it at 3 with a different ease and the throw either undershoots or overshoots by a constant factor.
- `throwDuration = 1.1`
  Seconds of inertial travel. Under ~0.6 s the wheel stops so abruptly that a fast fling feels like it hit a wall; over ~1.6 s the tail is so slow it reads as broken rather than as momentum, and it delays the settle callback past the point anyone is still watching.
- `maxThrow = 260`
  Degrees one throw may carry, applied to the projected distance before snapping. Without a cap, a 900 deg/s fling projects 330° and the wheel makes most of a revolution from a flick — past about 270° the user loses track of which way it went and which station is coming.
- `VELOCITY_WINDOW = 0.07`
  Seconds of gesture history the release speed is averaged over. Shorter and it is effectively the last delta, which is noisy at 120 Hz and jitters the throw distance between identical gestures; much longer and a deliberate slow-down before release is averaged away, so the wheel throws when the user meant to place it.
- `MAX_VELOCITY = 900`
  Degrees per second the measured speed is clamped to. A pointer that jumps (a tab switch mid-drag, a synthetic event, a coalesced move across the hub) can report thousands of deg/s; clamping keeps one bad sample from spinning the wheel several turns.
- `DRAG_THRESHOLD = 5`
  Pixels of travel before a press becomes a drag. Below ~3 the hand tremor in a normal tap counts as a drag, so every tap is swallowed as a gesture; above ~10 a small deliberate nudge of the wheel does nothing at all.
- `CULL_DEG = 96`
  Stations more than this far from the top are `visibility: hidden`. Just past 90° they are behind the horizontal through the hub and outside the box in every supported aspect ratio, so painting them is pure cost; culling at exactly 90° makes the boundary coincide with the fade reaching its floor and items visibly wink out.
- `radiusRatio = 0.78`
  Radius as a fraction of container width, before the height floor. Larger flattens the arc until the wheel reads as a straight row; much smaller pulls the hub up toward the box and the visible arc bends so hard that only three stations fit.
- `fade = 0.85`
  Opacity lost per 90° off the top. The station one step out stays clearly legible, which is the affordance that says the wheel turns; at 1.0 the neighbours reach zero exactly at the cull angle and the wheel looks like it holds one card.

## API

```ts
function RotaryDragCarousel(props: { children: ReactNode; radiusRatio?: number; topInsetRatio?: number; snapDeg?: number; throwDuration?: number; maxThrow?: number; fade?: number; scaleFalloff?: number; initialIndex?: number; className?: string; itemClassName?: string; onIndexChange?: (index: number) => void; 'aria-label'?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  One item per child. Each gets a station on the wheel.
- `radiusRatio: number` — default `0.78`
  Wheel radius as a fraction of container width, floored against height so the hub stays below the box.
- `topInsetRatio: number` — default `0.08`
  Where the top of the wheel sits, as a fraction of container height.
- `snapDeg: number`
  Degrees the wheel snaps to. Defaults to one station, `360 / count`.
- `throwDuration: number` — default `1.1`
  Seconds of inertial travel after release.
- `maxThrow: number` — default `260`
  Hard cap on how far one throw may carry, in degrees.
- `fade: number` — default `0.85`
  Opacity lost per 90° away from the top station.
- `scaleFalloff: number` — default `0.22`
  Scale lost at 90° away from the top station.
- `initialIndex: number` — default `0`
  Station facing up on mount. Seeded once, never re-applied.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the drag surface.
- `itemClassName: string`
  Merged onto every station. Size the items here.
- `onIndexChange: (index: number) => void`
  Fires with the wrapped index of the station that lands facing up.
- `aria-label: string` — default `'Carousel'`
  Label for the focusable wheel, which also takes arrow keys.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * Write one transform per station from the current wheel angle. A pure
 * function of `angleRef.current` and the box size — nothing accumulates in
 * here, so interrupting the throw tween mid-flight cannot desynchronise it.
 */
const layout = useCallback(() => {
  const host = hostRef.current;
  if (!host || count === 0) return;

  const width = host.clientWidth;
  const height = host.clientHeight;
  if (width < 1 || height < 1) return;

  const radius = Math.max(radiusRatio * width, height * MIN_RADIUS_HEIGHT_RATIO);
  const cx = width / 2;
  const cy = topInsetRatio * height + radius;
  const angle = angleRef.current;

  for (let i = 0; i < count; i += 1) {
    const station = stationsRef.current[i];
    if (!station) continue;

    // Station i's screen angle. `UP_DEG` puts station 0 at the top when the
    // wheel is at 0, so the maths and the visual agree at rest.
    const theta = angle + i * step + UP_DEG;
    // Shortest signed distance to the top, in (-180, 180]. The wheel is a
    // real circle, so this is the only place wrapping is needed at all —
    // `angle` itself may be -4000 without consequence.
    const away = wrapRange(theta - UP_DEG, -180, 180);
    const distance = Math.abs(away);

    if (distance > CULL_DEG) {
      station.style.visibility = 'hidden';
      continue;
    }

    const rad = theta * DEG_TO_RAD;
    const x = cx + radius * Math.cos(rad);
    const y = cy + radius * Math.sin(rad);
    const t = Math.min(distance / 90, 1);

    station.style.visibility = 'visible';
    // Counter-rotating by `-away` would keep the cards upright; leaving the
    // rotation in is what makes it read as one rigid wheel rather than a row
    // of cards travelling along an arc.
    station.style.transform =
      `translate(-50%, -50%) translate(${x.toFixed(2)}px, ${y.toFixed(2)}px) ` +
      `rotate(${away.toFixed(2)}deg) ` +
      `scale(${(1 - scaleFalloff * t).toFixed(3)})`;
    station.style.opacity = clamp(1 - fade * t, 0, 1).toFixed(3);
    station.style.zIndex = String(100 - Math.round(distance));
  }
}, [count, step, radiusRatio, topInsetRatio, fade, scaleFalloff]);

/** Angle at which station `index` faces up: `angle + index * step = 0`. */
const angleForIndex = useCallback((index: number) => -index * step, [step]);

const report = useCallback(() => {
  if (count === 0) return;
  // `angle = -i * step` puts station i up, so `i = -angle / step`.
  const index = wrapIndex(Math.round(-angleRef.current / step), count);
  if (index === reportedRef.current) return;
  reportedRef.current = index;
  notify.current?.(index);
}, [count, step]);

/**
 * Land the wheel. `velocity` is degrees per second at the moment of release;
 * pass 0 for a keyboard step or a tap.
 */
const settle = useCallback(
  (velocity: number) => {
    const projected =
      angleRef.current +
      clamp(
        (velocity * throwDuration) / POWER3_OUT_SLOPE,
        -maxThrow,
        maxThrow,
      );
    // Round to a station BEFORE tweening. Snapping afterwards is a second
    // animation that starts from rest, which is the little hop that gives
    // away every hand-rolled dial.
    const landing = Math.round(projected / snap) * snap;

    gsap.killTweensOf(angleRef);

    if (reduced || Math.abs(landing - angleRef.current) < 0.01) {
      angleRef.current = landing;
      layout();
      report();
      return;
    }

    gsap.to(angleRef, {
      current: landing,
      duration: throwDuration,
      ease: 'power3.out',
      overwrite: true,
      onUpdate: layout,
      onComplete: report,
    });
  },
  [throwDuration, maxThrow, snap, reduced, layout, report],
);

useEffect(() => {
  const host = hostRef.current;
  if (!host) return;

  let pointerId: number | null = null;
  let lastPointerAngle = 0;
  let pressX = 0;
  let pressY = 0;
  let moved = false;
  let swallowClick = false;
  /** Rolling window: the wheel angle and clock at the start of the window. */
  let sampleAngle = 0;
  let sampleTime = 0;

  const now = () => performance.now() / 1000;

  const pointerAngle = (clientX: number, clientY: number) => {
    const rect = host.getBoundingClientRect();
    const radius = Math.max(
      radiusRatio * rect.width,
      rect.height * MIN_RADIUS_HEIGHT_RATIO,
    );
    const cx = rect.left + rect.width / 2;
    const cy = rect.top + topInsetRatio * rect.height + radius;
    return Math.atan2(clientY - cy, clientX - cx) / DEG_TO_RAD;
  };

  const onPointerDown = (e: PointerEvent) => {
    // One pointer owns the wheel. A second finger arriving mid-throw would
    // otherwise reset the origin angle and the wheel would jump.
    if (pointerId !== null || !e.isPrimary) return;
    if (e.pointerType === 'mouse' && e.button !== 0) return;

    pointerId = e.pointerId;
    pressX = e.clientX;
    pressY = e.clientY;
    moved = false;
    lastPointerAngle = pointerAngle(e.clientX, e.clientY);
    sampleAngle = angleRef.current;
    sampleTime = now();

    // Capture on press, not once the threshold is crossed: by then the
    // pointer may already have left the element, and `pointermove` would
    // have stopped arriving.
    host.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);
    gsap.killTweensOf(angleRef);
  };

  const onPointerMove = (e: PointerEvent) => {
    if (pointerId !== e.pointerId) return;

    const current = pointerAngle(e.clientX, e.clientY);
    // Shortest signed step. Without the wrap, dragging across the 180°
    // seam reads as a 359° jerk in the wrong direction.
    const delta = wrapRange(current - lastPointerAngle, -180, 180);
    lastPointerAngle = current;

    if (!moved) {
      if (Math.hypot(e.clientX - pressX, e.clientY - pressY) < DRAG_THRESHOLD) return;
      moved = true;
    }

    angleRef.current += delta;
    layout();

    // Retire the velocity window once it is full. Measuring over a window
    // rather than off the last delta is what stops "drag, pause, lift" from
    // throwing the wheel: with no movement there are no events, the window
    // never advances, and the measured speed decays toward zero on its own.
    const t = now();
    if (t - sampleTime > VELOCITY_WINDOW) {
      sampleAngle = angleRef.current;
      sampleTime = t;
    }
  };

  /**
   * Idempotent. Called from `pointerup`, `pointercancel` and
   * `lostpointercapture`, all three of which can be the last event a gesture
   * produces, and at least one of which will always arrive — including when
   * the pointer is released outside the window, or the OS takes it away for
   * a gesture of its own. Guarding on `pointerId` makes the extra calls
   * no-ops instead of a double throw.
   */
  const finish = (e: PointerEvent) => {
    if (pointerId !== e.pointerId) return;
    const id = pointerId;
    pointerId = null;

    const elapsed = now() - sampleTime;
    const velocity =
      moved && elapsed > 0
        ? clamp((angleRef.current - sampleAngle) / elapsed, -MAX_VELOCITY, MAX_VELOCITY)
        : 0;

    swallowClick = moved;
    moved = false;

    if (host.hasPointerCapture(id)) host.releasePointerCapture(id);
    settle(velocity);
  };

  // Capture phase, ahead of any child's own handler. A throw ends with a
  // `click` on whatever happens to be under the pointer, so without this the
  // gesture that spins the wheel also activates a card.
  const onClick = (e: MouseEvent) => {
    if (!swallowClick) return;
    swallowClick = false;
    e.preventDefault();
    e.stopPropagation();
  };

  const onKeyDown = (e: KeyboardEvent) => {
    const direction =
      e.key === 'ArrowRight' || e.key === 'ArrowDown'
        ? -1
        : e.key === 'ArrowLeft' || e.key === 'ArrowUp'
          ? 1
          : 0;
    if (direction === 0) return;
    e.preventDefault();
    gsap.killTweensOf(angleRef);
    angleRef.current = Math.round(angleRef.current / snap) * snap + direction * snap;
    settle(0);
  };

  host.addEventListener('pointerdown', onPointerDown);
  host.addEventListener('pointermove', onPointerMove);
  host.addEventListener('pointerup', finish);
  host.addEventListener('pointercancel', finish);
  host.addEventListener('lostpointercapture', finish);
  host.addEventListener('click', onClick, true);
  host.addEventListener('keydown', onKeyDown);

  return () => {
    host.removeEventListener('pointerdown', onPointerDown);
    host.removeEventListener('pointermove', onPointerMove);
    host.removeEventListener('pointerup', finish);
    host.removeEventListener('pointercancel', finish);
    host.removeEventListener('lostpointercapture', finish);
    host.removeEventListener('click', onClick, true);
    host.removeEventListener('keydown', onKeyDown);
    if (pointerId !== null && host.hasPointerCapture(pointerId)) {
      host.releasePointerCapture(pointerId);
    }
    pointerId = null;
  };
}, [layout, settle, snap, radiusRatio, topInsetRatio]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Removes `pointerdown`, `pointermove`, `pointerup`, `pointercancel`, `lostpointercapture`, the capture-phase `click` and `keydown`; releases pointer capture if a gesture is still live at unmount; and kills the throw tween on the angle ref via a separate effect so an in-flight `gsap.to` cannot call `onUpdate` against detached nodes. The shared resize observer unregisters. Nothing but inline styles on the stations remains, and those die with the nodes.

**Reduced motion.** Dragging is unchanged — it is the user's own motion, tracked one-to-one, and removing it would remove the component. What goes away is everything the component would have animated by itself: the inertial throw is not created, so release rounds the current angle to the nearest station and assigns it in one frame, and an arrow key moves one station instantly. The wheel never travels further than the hand did.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Driving the rotation from `deltaX` instead of from an angle. A linear delta turns the wheel by the same amount wherever you grab it, so a drag near the left edge feels geared wrong and a drag straight down the middle does nothing at all. Angular input is what makes it feel like a physical wheel.
- Differencing raw `atan2` output. Crossing the ±180° seam gives a delta of about -359° instead of +1°, and the wheel snaps a full turn backwards once per revolution. Every angle difference here goes through `wrapRange(d, -180, 180)`.
- Putting the hub inside the container. Near the hub the pointer's angular change per pixel goes to infinity, so a press within a few pixels of it and a one-pixel jitter spins the wheel a hundred degrees. The radius floor makes that geometrically impossible rather than guarding it after the fact.
- Taking the release velocity from the last `pointermove`. Drag, hold still for half a second, lift, and the wheel flies off at the speed from before the pause, because the last event recorded was the last time the hand moved. A rolling time window measured against `performance.now()` at release decays to zero on its own.
- Snapping after the inertial tween instead of before it. The throw finishes, comes to rest between two stations, and a second tween hops it into place — two eases back to back, and it is instantly recognisable as fake momentum.
- Calling `setPointerCapture` only after the drag threshold is crossed. By then a fast gesture has already left the element, `pointermove` has stopped arriving, and the wheel sticks at the angle it had when the pointer crossed the boundary.
- Handling only `pointerup`. Release outside the window, let the OS claim the gesture, or have the element re-parented mid-drag and no `pointerup` arrives; the wheel stays captured and frozen mid-throw. `pointercancel` and `lostpointercapture` both route to the same idempotent finish, guarded on the stored `pointerId` so the duplicate is a no-op rather than a second throw.
- Letting the click through. A throw ends with a `click` dispatched on whatever card is under the pointer, so spinning the wheel also opens a project. The click is swallowed in the capture phase, once, only when the gesture actually moved.
- Reaching for `InertiaPlugin`. It is a Club GreenSock plugin — not redistributable, and not installable from a public registry — so a component that depends on it fails to build for most consumers. The `v * D / 3` projection reproduces the throw with the free core.
- Re-seeding `initialIndex` on resize. Rotate a phone mid-gesture and the wheel teleports back to its opening station. The seed is guarded by a ref and runs exactly once.

## Notes

- The counter-rotation is deliberately absent: each card is rotated *with* the wheel by `away`, so the whole thing reads as one rigid disc. Cancelling that rotation keeps labels upright but turns it into a row of cards sliding along an arc, which is a different and much weaker effect.
- The snap grid is a multiple of `360 / count`, so a station always lands facing up. The source of this technique snapped to a fixed 10°, which only coincides with item positions when `360 / count` is itself a multiple of 10 — with 7 or 9 items it lands between cards.
- Arrow keys step one station and route through the same settle path, so keyboard and pointer cannot disagree about where the wheel rests.

## Definition of done

Grab anywhere in the box and drag in an arc: the wheel follows your hand around the hub, and a drag near the left or right edge turns it less than the same pixel distance across the top. Fling and release — it keeps going, decelerates, and comes to rest with one card exactly upright, in a single continuous motion with no hop at the end. Drag, hold still for a second, then lift: it settles to the nearest station without throwing. Start a drag, move the pointer off the window, and release outside — the wheel still lands rather than freezing. Release over a card and no click reaches it; tap the same card without moving and the click goes through. Arrow keys step one card at a time.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Preloader That Cannot Hang

Every hand-rolled preloader eventually ships the same bug: a signal that never arrives — a 404 on a font, a decode that fails on iOS, an image behind a dead CDN — and the site is a permanent opaque rectangle nobody can see through or tab past. This inverts the contract. A hard ceiling guarantees the page is visible by a fixed time and the load signal only ever makes it sooner; a floor stops a warm cache turning the overlay into a two-frame flash; a session flag keeps it an introduction rather than a toll booth.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

An intro overlay with a hard ceiling, a minimum visible time and a once-per-session flag, so a stalled load cannot trap the page.

- Category: transition
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. A three-state phase machine — `holding`, `leaving`, `gone` — drives the render. It starts at `holding` on both server and client so the markup matches, and the session check runs in a `useLayoutEffect`, before paint, so a returning visitor never sees a single frame of the overlay.
2. THE CEILING: `setTimeout(reveal, ceilingMs)` is armed in an effect on mount, before anything subscribes to a load signal, and nothing clears it except a successful reveal or unmount. This is not a fallback — it is the actual guarantee, and the load signal is the optimisation.
3. THE FLOOR: when the signal does arrive, the remaining hold is `Math.max(0, floorMs - (performance.now() - started))` and the reveal is deferred by that much. Measured from mount, not from the signal, so the floor overlaps the load instead of being added to it.
4. The signal is `ready` when the prop is passed, otherwise the browser's own: `document.readyState === "complete"` is checked first and only then is a one-shot `load` listener attached, because if the document has already finished the event has been and gone and a listener alone would wait forever.
5. ONCE: on reveal, `sessionStorage[sessionKey] = "1"`, wrapped in try/catch because `setItem` throws in Safari private browsing and a preloader is not worth taking the page down for. Both the read and the write are guarded.
6. `reveal()` guards on a ref, not on state, so the ceiling and the floor firing in the same tick still reveal exactly once. It sets `leaving` — a CSS opacity transition on `[data-leaving="true"]` — and schedules the actual removal `fadeMs` later, so the node is never pulled out of the tree mid-transition. `onDone` fires from that same timer, after the overlay is gone.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `ceilingMs = 4000`
  The reveal deadline. Long enough that a genuinely slow first paint on a cold 3G connection is not cut off mid-load, short enough that a user staring at a broken overlay gives up after it rather than before. Past ~6s people reload, which restarts the same stall.
- `floorMs = 700`
  Minimum visible time. On a warm cache the signal resolves in about 40ms; without a floor the overlay appears and vanishes inside two frames, which reads as a rendering fault rather than an introduction. Below ~400ms the fade has no room to be perceived as deliberate.
- `fadeMs = 420`
  Fade-out duration, passed to CSS as `--k-safe-fade` and used as the removal delay so the two can never disagree. Long enough that the page underneath is already composited and visible through the fade; past ~700ms the user is looking at content they cannot yet click.
- `fade easing = cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)`
  Heavily front-loaded, so most of the opacity is gone in the first third and the perceived wait is shorter than the measured one. A linear fade of the same length feels about twice as long.
- `scan bar = 1.4s cubic-bezier(0.65, 0, 0.35, 1) infinite`
  A determinate progress bar would be a lie — nothing here knows a byte count. This is an indeterminate scan whose cycle is slow enough not to read as urgency and fast enough to prove the page is not frozen. The in-out curve keeps the ends from clipping at the container edges.
- `sessionKey = 'k-preloader'`
  Session, not local, storage. Local storage would mean the introduction plays once ever, so a returning visitor months later gets no reveal and QA can never see it again without clearing site data.

## API

```ts
function SafePreloader(props: { children?: ReactNode; ready?: boolean; ceilingMs?: number; floorMs?: number; fadeMs?: number; sessionKey?: string; once?: boolean; onDone?: () => void; position?: 'fixed' | 'absolute'; className?: string }): JSX.Element | null
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Overlay content. Defaults to a label and an indeterminate scan bar.
- `ready: boolean`
  The load signal. Leave undefined to use the browser's own `load` event and `readyState`.
- `ceilingMs: number` — default `4000`
  Hard ceiling. The reveal happens by this time whether or not the signal ever arrives.
- `floorMs: number` — default `700`
  Minimum time the overlay stays up, measured from mount.
- `fadeMs: number` — default `420`
  Fade-out duration in ms. Also the delay before the node is removed.
- `sessionKey: string` — default `'k-preloader'`
  sessionStorage key used by the once-per-session gate.
- `once: boolean` — default `true`
  Set false to replay on every load, for development.
- `onDone: () => void`
  Fires after the overlay has finished leaving and unmounted.
- `position: 'fixed' | 'absolute'` — default `'fixed'`
  Absolute lets the overlay be scoped to a container instead of the viewport.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the overlay via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const reveal = useCallback(() => {
  if (revealed.current) return;
  revealed.current = true;
  clearTimers();
  if (once) markShown(sessionKey);
  setPhase('leaving');
  // The node is removed only after the fade has actually run, so nothing is
  // pulled out of the tree mid-transition.
  timers.current.push(
    setTimeout(
      () => {
        setPhase('gone');
        done.current?.();
      },
      reduced ? 0 : fadeMs,
    ),
  );
}, [clearTimers, fadeMs, once, reduced, sessionKey]);

useLayoutEffect(() => {
  if (once && wasShown(sessionKey)) {
    revealed.current = true;
    setPhase('gone');
    return;
  }
  started.current = performance.now();
}, [once, sessionKey]);

// THE CEILING. Armed on mount, before any load signal is subscribed to, and
// never cancelled by anything except a successful reveal. If the signal
// never comes, this is what saves the page.
useEffect(() => {
  if (revealed.current) return;
  const id = setTimeout(reveal, ceilingMs);
  timers.current.push(id);
  return () => clearTimeout(id);
}, [ceilingMs, reveal]);

// THE FLOOR. When the signal arrives, wait out whatever is left of the
// minimum so a warm cache does not produce a two-frame black flash.
useEffect(() => {
  if (revealed.current) return;

  const settle = () => {
    const elapsed = performance.now() - started.current;
    const remaining = Math.max(0, (reduced ? 0 : floorMs) - elapsed);
    const id = setTimeout(reveal, remaining);
    timers.current.push(id);
  };

  if (ready !== undefined) {
    if (ready) settle();
    return;
  }

  // No `ready` prop: use the browser's own signal. If the document has
  // already finished loading, the event has been and gone — check first.
  if (document.readyState === 'complete') {
    settle();
    return;
  }
  window.addEventListener('load', settle, { once: true });
  return () => window.removeEventListener('load', settle);
}, [floorMs, ready, reduced, reveal]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Every timeout is pushed into a ref array and cleared on unmount, the ceiling effect clears its own id, and the one-shot `load` listener is removed by its effect. Because the removal timer is cleared, `setPhase` cannot run on a dead component and `onDone` cannot fire for a page that has already gone. No rAF, no observers, no global state beyond the session flag.

**Reduced motion.** The overlay still appears and the ceiling still applies — withholding content is a behaviour, not an animation, so it is not skipped. What goes away is the motion: the floor collapses to 0 so nothing is held longer than it must be, the removal delay drops to 0 and the CSS transition to 1ms, and the scanning bar becomes a static full-width rule via `animation: none; transform: scaleX(1)` rather than a pulsing one. The result is a brief still plate, not a zero-duration version of the animated one.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Having no ceiling at all. One 404 on a font or a decode that fails only on iOS, and the overlay stays up forever: the content is not visible, not scrollable, and not reachable by keyboard, and it happens to a fraction of users you will never hear from.
- Clearing the ceiling when the load signal is subscribed to, or when it fires. Whatever the signal hands off to — a floor timer, a promise chain, a decode — can itself stall, and the one thing that guaranteed a reveal has already been thrown away.
- Attaching a `load` listener without checking `document.readyState` first. On a warm cache or after a client-side navigation the event has already fired, so the listener never runs; the ceiling silently does all the work and you only discover it the day someone shortens the ceiling.
- Shipping without a floor. The overlay appears and vanishes inside two frames on a fast connection, producing a black flash on every load that reads as a broken paint and is nearly impossible to reproduce on a throttled dev machine.
- Starting the floor clock when the signal arrives instead of at mount. The floor is then added to the load time rather than overlapping it, so a 2s load becomes a 2.7s hold for no benefit.
- Using state for the reveal-once guard. The ceiling and the floor can both fire before React re-renders, so `reveal` runs twice and the second call re-arms the fade on a node that is already leaving. A ref flips synchronously and cannot be raced.
- Unmounting the overlay in the same commit that starts the fade. The node leaves the tree before the transition can run a single frame, so the overlay simply disappears and the fade you wrote never happens.
- Reading `sessionStorage` in `useEffect` instead of `useLayoutEffect`. The overlay gets one painted frame before the effect runs, so a returning visitor sees a flash of it on every single navigation.
- Initialising state from `sessionStorage` during render. The server has no session storage, so it renders `holding` while the client renders `gone`, and React logs a hydration mismatch and re-renders the tree.
- Calling `sessionStorage.setItem` unguarded. It throws in Safari private browsing, and an unhandled throw inside the reveal path leaves the overlay up permanently — the exact failure the component exists to prevent.
- Replaying it on every visit. A preloader is an introduction; on the fourth arrival in the same session it is a toll booth, and the fix is one flag rather than a shorter animation.
- Leaving timers pending on unmount. The removal timer fires after the route has changed, so `setPhase` runs on a dead component and `onDone` fires for a page that is no longer mounted.

## Notes

- `position` defaults to `fixed` for real page use and can be switched to `absolute` so the overlay can be demonstrated, or used, inside a bounded container.
- The overlay is `role="status"` with `aria-live="polite"`, so a screen reader announces the loading state once rather than reading a decorative bar, and the announcement is not interrupted by the reveal.
- `once={false}` exists for development and for the demo. In production the default keeps the overlay to one appearance per tab session.

## Definition of done

Simulate a signal that never arrives and the page is nonetheless visible and interactive at the ceiling. Reload with a warm cache and the overlay is visible for at least the floor — never a single-frame flash. Reload again in the same tab and no overlay is painted at all, not even one frame. Watch the reveal and the overlay fades rather than vanishing, with the content already composited underneath. Navigate away mid-hold and no state update warning appears and `onDone` never fires. With reduced motion on, the plate appears static and leaves immediately.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Scroll Deformation Wave

Signed, smoothed scroll velocity drives a single scalar, and that scalar scales two sine displacements in the vertex shader. Because the velocity keeps its sign, scrolling up bends the surface the opposite way from scrolling down, which is the direction cue that makes the effect read as momentum rather than as noise. Everything else — the wave shape, the shading, the crop — is a pure function of that one number.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

An image that ripples with scroll speed and bends the other way on the way back, from two sine terms.

- Category: webgl
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1

## How it works

1. The depth term is `pos.z += sin(position.y * frequency + phase) * deform * amplitude`, and the shear term is `pos.y += sin(position.x * frequency) * deform * shear`. Both are sampled from `position` — the original flat attribute — not from the running `pos`.
2. That distinction is the whole technique. Sampling `position` fixes the wave to the picture, so a given pixel always sits at the same point on the sine and the image appears to flex. Sampling the already-displaced `pos` would make each term feed the next, so the wave travels through the surface and reads as a glitch.
3. The phase constant breaks the symmetry. Without it, `sin(y * f)` is odd about the plane's centre line and the top and bottom halves mirror each other exactly, which looks like a crease rather than a wave.
4. The slope, not the height, drives the shading: `vBend = cos(position.y * frequency + phase) * deform` is the analytic derivative of the depth term, so crests brighten and troughs darken with one cosine and no recomputed vertex normals.
5. `useScrollVelocity` supplies a two-stage smoothed signal — a low-pass on the raw delta, then a damped approach — and the component damps once more on top of it with a 0.0025 smoothing factor, so the ripple eases out for a beat after the scroll stops instead of snapping flat.
6. The fragment shader cover-fits the source into the quad and divides the sampled window by an overscan factor, which is what keeps the displaced vertices from sampling past the texture edge at the crest of every wave.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `amplitude = 0.07`
  World units of depth at full deflection, against a plane roughly 2.5 units tall. Below ~0.02 the ripple is lost in the perspective foreshortening; above ~0.2 the crests swing far enough toward the camera to cross the near plane and punch holes in the image.
- `shear = 0.04`
  Deliberately about half the amplitude. Its only job is to break the perfectly horizontal banding so the surface reads as cloth; raise it toward the amplitude and the two waves beat against each other into a visible moire.
- `frequency = 3`
  Radians per world unit, so roughly one and a half crests across the visible plane. Below ~1.5 there is less than a full wave on screen and the image just tilts; above ~8 the crests fall closer together than the vertex spacing and the wave aliases into flicker.
- `phase = 100`
  An arbitrary large offset whose only purpose is to be nowhere near a multiple of pi. At phase 0 the sine is odd about the plane's centre, the halves mirror, and the ripple looks like a fold down the middle.
- `maxDeform = 1.5`
  Ceiling on the signed scalar, so a trackpad flick cannot drive the displacement past the point where the surface self-intersects. Everything downstream multiplies by this, so it is the one number that bounds the entire effect.
- `reference = 900 px/s`
  Scroll speed that counts as full deflection. The hook defaults to 1500, which is tuned for whole-page parallax; a component-sized scroller rarely reaches it, so the wave would never appear.
- `DEFORM_SMOOTHING = 0.0025`
  Fraction of the gap remaining after one second. Slower and the wave lags visibly behind the scroll; much faster and it snaps flat the instant scrolling stops, losing the ease-out that makes it feel like momentum.
- `overscan = 1.12`
  Twelve percent crop held in reserve. At exactly 1.0 the displaced vertices sample past the edge of the texture at every crest and the clamped border pixel smears across the top and bottom of the image.
- `segments = 96`
  The wave is evaluated per vertex, so subdivision is its resolution. Below ~32 the sine renders as a polyline and the shading term steps in visible bands; above ~160 the vertices land inside a single pixel and only cost transform time.
- `shade = 0.22`
  How far the slope term swings brightness. At 0 the ripple is nearly invisible on a busy image; above ~0.5 the crests blow out to white and read as a lighting bug rather than as a surface.

## API

```ts
function ScrollDeformWave(props: { scrollTarget?: HTMLElement | null; amplitude?: number; shear?: number; frequency?: number; phase?: number; maxDeform?: number; reference?: number; shade?: number; overscan?: number; segments?: number; paint?: (ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D, size: { width: number; height: number }) => void; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `scrollTarget: HTMLElement | null` — default `null`
  Element whose scrollTop drives the wave. null reads window.scrollY.
- `amplitude: number` — default `0.07`
  Depth of the ripple in world units at full deflection.
- `shear: number` — default `0.04`
  Vertical shear, which breaks up the horizontal banding.
- `frequency: number` — default `3`
  Spatial frequency of the sine, in radians per world unit.
- `phase: number` — default `100`
  Phase offset, so the wave is not symmetric about the plane centre.
- `maxDeform: number` — default `1.5`
  Clamp on the signed deform scalar.
- `reference: number` — default `900`
  Pixels per second of scroll that count as full deflection.
- `shade: number` — default `0.22`
  How far the slope term brightens crests and darkens troughs.
- `overscan: number` — default `1.12`
  Crop held in reserve so displaced vertices never sample past the edge.
- `segments: number` — default `96`
  Plane subdivisions per axis. The resolution of the wave.
- `paint: (ctx, size) => void`
  Override the image. Receives a 2D context for a 1024x1024 canvas.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the wrapper via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function ScrollDeformWave({
  scrollTarget = null,
  amplitude = 0.07,
  shear = 0.04,
  frequency = 3,
  phase = 100,
  maxDeform = 1.5,
  reference = 900,
  shade = 0.22,
  overscan = 1.12,
  segments = 96,
  paint,
  className,
}: ScrollDeformWaveProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const stage = useRef<Stage | null>(null);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const { inView } = useInView(host, { threshold: 0 });
  const visible = useVisibility();
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  // Signed and already smoothed. Raw scroll deltas are spiky enough that
  // feeding them straight into a geometry parameter produces visible stutter.
  const scroll = useScrollVelocity({ reference, target: scrollTarget });

  const [supported, setSupported] = useState(true);
  useEffect(() => setSupported(hasWebGL()), []);

  const deform = useRef(0);

  const live = useRef({ amplitude, shear, frequency, phase, maxDeform, shade, overscan });
  live.current = { amplitude, shear, frequency, phase, maxDeform, shade, overscan };

  const ready = width > 1 && height > 1 && supported;

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = host.current;
    if (!el || !ready) return;

    const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: true, alpha: true });
    renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio());
    renderer.setSize(el.clientWidth, el.clientHeight, false);
    renderer.setClearColor(0x000000, 0);
    renderer.domElement.style.display = 'block';
    renderer.domElement.style.width = '100%';
    renderer.domElement.style.height = '100%';
    el.appendChild(renderer.domElement);

    const scene = new THREE.Scene();
    const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(CAMERA_FOV, 1, 0.1, 100);
    camera.position.z = CAMERA_Z;

    const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
    canvas.width = TEXTURE_WIDTH;
    canvas.height = TEXTURE_HEIGHT;
    const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
    if (ctx) (paint ?? paintImage)(ctx, { width: TEXTURE_WIDTH, height: TEXTURE_HEIGHT });

    const texture = new THREE.CanvasTexture(canvas);
    texture.colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace;
    texture.wrapS = THREE.ClampToEdgeWrapping;
    texture.wrapT = THREE.ClampToEdgeWrapping;
    texture.anisotropy = Math.min(4, renderer.capabilities.getMaxAnisotropy());

    const uniforms: WaveUniforms = {
      uTexture: { value: texture },
      uTextureAspect: { value: TEXTURE_WIDTH / TEXTURE_HEIGHT },
      uPlaneAspect: { value: 1 },
      uOverscan: { value: overscan },
      uShade: { value: shade },
      uDeform: { value: 0 },
      uFrequency: { value: frequency },
      uPhase: { value: phase },
      uAmplitude: { value: amplitude },
      uShear: { value: shear },
    };

    // A unit plane, rescaled on resize rather than rebuilt. The wave is
    // measured in world units, so the plane keeps a fixed subdivision and the
    // mesh scale carries the aspect.
    const geometry = new THREE.PlaneGeometry(1, 1, segments, segments);
    const material = new THREE.ShaderMaterial({
      vertexShader: scrollDeformWaveVertexShader,
      fragmentShader: scrollDeformWaveFragmentShader,
      uniforms,
      transparent: true,
    });
    const mesh = new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material);
    // The bend happens after the bounding sphere was computed, so a plane at
    // the edge of the frustum blinks out mid-ripple if this stays on.
    mesh.frustumCulled = false;
    scene.add(mesh);

    stage.current = { renderer, scene, camera, mesh, geometry, material, texture, uniforms };

    return () => {
      stage.current = null;
      scene.remove(mesh);
      // Lives inside `uniforms`, which `disposeObject` never walks.
      texture.dispose();
      disposeObject(scene);
      geometry.dispose();
      material.dispose();
      disposeRenderer(renderer);
      renderer.domElement.remove();
    };
    // eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps
  }, [ready, segments, paint]);

  useEffect(() => {
    const current = stage.current;
    if (!current || width < 1 || height < 1) return;
    const aspect = width / height;
    current.renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio());
    current.renderer.setSize(width, height, false);
    current.camera.aspect = aspect;
    current.camera.updateProjectionMatrix();

    // Cover the frustum exactly at z = 0, in world units derived from the
    // camera — not from `window.innerWidth`, which has no fixed relationship
    // to the visible extent at this distance.
    const visibleHeight = 2 * Math.tan((CAMERA_FOV * Math.PI) / 360) * CAMERA_Z;
    current.mesh.scale.set(visibleHeight * aspect, visibleHeight, 1);
    // The shader fits the texture into the QUAD, so this is the quad's aspect.
    current.uniforms.uPlaneAspect.value = aspect;
  }, [width, height]);

  useRaf(
    (dt) => {
      const current = stage.current;
      if (!current) return;
      const {
        amplitude: depth,
        shear: skew,
        frequency: freq,
        phase: offset,
        maxDeform: limit,
        shade: light,
        overscan: zoom,
      } = live.current;

      // Signed on purpose. Taking the magnitude would make scrolling up and
      // scrolling down produce an identical wave, and the direction cue — the
      // surface bending the other way — is most of the effect.
      const target = reduced ? 0 : clamp(scroll.current.normalized, -1, 1) * limit;
      deform.current = damp(deform.current, target, DEFORM_SMOOTHING, dt);

      current.uniforms.uDeform.value = deform.current;
      current.uniforms.uAmplitude.value = depth;
      current.uniforms.uShear.value = skew;
      current.uniforms.uFrequency.value = freq;
      current.uniforms.uPhase.value = offset;
      current.uniforms.uShade.value = light;
      current.uniforms.uOverscan.value = zoom;

      current.renderer.render(current.scene, current.camera);
    },
    ready && inView && visible,
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Removes the mesh from the scene, disposes the `CanvasTexture` by hand because it lives inside `material.uniforms` where `disposeObject` does not look, runs `disposeObject` over the scene, disposes the geometry and the material, then `disposeRenderer` for `setAnimationLoop(null)` / `dispose()` / `forceContextLoss()`, and removes the canvas element. The stage ref is nulled first so a queued frame is a no-op. `useScrollVelocity` unsubscribes with the shared RAF loop it was registered on.

**Reduced motion.** The deform scalar is forced to 0 regardless of scroll velocity, and it is still damped there, so a component that is mid-ripple when the preference changes eases flat rather than snapping. The image then stays perfectly still while scrolling — the cover fit and the resize handling continue to work, but no vertex is ever displaced and no shading swing occurs.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Sampling the wave from the running `pos` instead of the original `position`. Each term then feeds the next, the ripple travels through the surface as it deforms rather than staying pinned to the image, and the effect looks like a rendering fault instead of the photograph flexing.
- Taking the magnitude of the velocity. `abs(velocity)` makes scrolling up and scrolling down produce an identical wave, which throws away the direction cue that carries most of the effect. The scalar stays signed all the way into the uniform.
- Using a phase of 0. `sin(y * f)` is odd about the plane's centre, so the top and bottom halves mirror each other exactly and the ripple reads as a crease down the middle rather than a wave.
- Feeding raw scroll deltas into the uniform. A wheel emits discrete steps and a trackpad emits bursts; either drives the geometry into visible stutter. The signal is low-passed, damped, and damped again before it reaches the shader.
- Leaving `frustumCulled` on. The bounding sphere was computed for the flat plane, so when the component sits at the edge of the viewport three culls it against geometry the shader has already moved and the image blinks out mid-ripple.
- Fitting the plane with `window.innerWidth`. The plane has to cover the camera's frustum at z = 0, which is `2 * tan(fov/2) * distance` tall — a pixel width has no fixed relationship to that, so the image ends up letterboxed or overscaled depending on the viewport.
- Skipping the overscan. Displaced vertices sample outside [0,1] at the crest of every wave, and the texture's clamped border smears along the top and bottom edges exactly when the wave is at its most visible.
- Passing a ref to `scrollTarget`. The hook takes an `HTMLElement | null`, not a ref object, so a scroller inside the component has to be captured with a callback ref into state before it can be handed over — a plain ref would still be null on the render that matters.
- Calling `renderer.dispose()` alone. That frees GPU objects and leaves the context alive; a page with several WebGL components then hits Chromium's per-process cap and the oldest canvases go blank. `disposeRenderer` calls `forceContextLoss`.

## Notes

- `scrollTarget` defaults to `null`, which reads `window.scrollY`. Pass the scrolling element when the component lives inside its own `overflow-y-auto` container, as the demo does.
- The plane is a unit quad rescaled on resize rather than rebuilt, so a container resize never reallocates a 96x96 vertex buffer.

## Definition of done

Scroll the container and the image ripples in horizontal bands, with the crests catching a little more light than the troughs. Scroll the other way and the bands bow the opposite direction. Stop and the surface eases flat over about half a second rather than snapping. Flick hard and the ripple deepens but never folds through itself or shows a smeared edge. The image keeps its own proportions at any container aspect, and scrolling the page while the component is off screen costs nothing because the loop is gated on visibility. With `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` the image is completely still at every scroll speed.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Scroll-Scrubbed Video

The hard part of a scroll-scrubbed hero is never the playback — it is the mapping and the throttle. Scroll becomes a smoothed progress value that snaps when it arrives; progress becomes a quantised frame index; the frame is only ever requested when that index changes; and the loop unsubscribes once the two agree. This component ships all four and draws its frames procedurally onto a canvas, so the technique can be read without a video file in the way.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

The scroll-to-frame mapping a scrubbed hero actually needs: smoothing, a snap, a frame quantiser and a loop that parks itself.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. Progress is `(hostTop - sectionTop) / (total - hostHeight)` against a manufactured range, read from live rects each frame. The range height is written on mount and on resize as well as from the loop, so a section still below the fold already occupies its full height instead of shifting the page when it arrives.
2. The playhead follows with `damp(current, target, smoothing, dt)`, the per-second form of the familiar `current += (target - current) * 0.12`. `perFrameToSmoothing(0.12)` performs that conversion, so the feel is preserved and the settle no longer runs at double speed on a 144 Hz display.
3. A snap threshold ends the approach. Exponential smoothing is asymptotic: without `if (|target - current| < 0.0002) current = target` the value never arrives, and any loop that waits for arrival runs forever.
4. The frame index is `round(progress * (frames - 1))`, and the draw call is guarded by `index !== drawnIndex`. This is the same guard as the `Math.abs(video.currentTime - t) > 0.003` test in a real player: asking the decoder to seek to the frame it is already showing is what makes a scrubbed video judder.
5. The loop parks itself. Once the value has snapped, `useRaf` is disabled and the subscription dropped; a scroll listener on the container wakes it. A settled hero therefore costs nothing, rather than 60 wasted frames a second over a still image.
6. Work is gated on `useInView` with `rootMargin: 200px`, so the first frame is painted just before the section enters rather than just after — the difference between arriving on a picture and arriving on a blank box.
7. The canvas backing store is sized in device pixels and the element in CSS pixels, with the ratio clamped at 2. Assigning `width`/`height` also clears the canvas, so the resize path forces a redraw by resetting the drawn index to -1.
8. Smoothed progress is published as `--scrub-progress` on the section, so a scrubber bar can move continuously in CSS while the frame behind it advances in steps.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `frames = 96`
  Steps the range quantises to. Around three seconds of 30 fps footage. Fewer than ~48 and the stepping is visible as stutter; many more and consecutive frames differ by less than the smoothing can resolve, so decode work is spent on frames nobody perceives.
- `smoothing = perFrameToSmoothing(0.12)`
  The classic `0.12` per frame at 60 Hz expressed per second (~0.0004). It absorbs wheel steps without the playhead feeling detached from the gesture. The conversion is the point: the raw 0.12 would settle more than twice as fast at 144 Hz.
- `SNAP = 0.0002`
  Progress delta below which the playhead is considered arrived. Two ten-thousandths of the range is well under one frame at any sane frame count, so snapping is invisible — and it is what allows the loop to terminate at all.
- `rootMargin = 200px`
  Starts work just before the section enters. Enough lead time to decode and paint the first frame at typical scroll speeds, small enough that scrolling past does not warm up work that is never seen.
- `viewports = 2`
  Scroll travel as a multiple of the scroller height. Two screens over ~96 frames is roughly one frame per 15 px of scroll, which reads as a continuous shot rather than a flipbook.
- `MAX_DPR = 2`
  Backing-store cap. Past 2x the extra pixels are invisible on the phones that report 3x and 4x, but the per-frame fill cost scales with their square.

## API

```ts
function ScrollScrubbedVideo(props: { frames?: number; draw?: (ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D, frame: ScrubFrame) => void; viewports?: number; smoothing?: number; children?: ReactNode; scroller?: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `frames: number` — default `96`
  Discrete frames the scroll range quantises to.
- `draw: (ctx, frame: ScrubFrame) => void`
  Called only when the frame index changes or after a resize. Replace with a `currentTime` write for real footage.
- `viewports: number` — default `2`
  Scroll travel as a multiple of the scroller height.
- `smoothing: number` — default `perFrameToSmoothing(0.12)`
  Fraction of the progress gap left after one second.
- `children: ReactNode`
  Overlaid on the canvas — captions, a scrubber, a title.
- `scroller: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>`
  Scroll container. Omit to auto-detect.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the outer section.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function ScrollScrubbedVideo({
  frames = 96,
  draw = defaultDraw,
  viewports = 2,
  smoothing = DEFAULT_SMOOTHING,
  children,
  scroller,
  className,
}: ScrollScrubbedVideoProps) {
  const section = useRef<HTMLElement>(null);
  const pin = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const canvas = useRef<HTMLCanvasElement>(null);

  const current = useRef(0);
  const drawnIndex = useRef(-1);
  const lastProgress = useRef('');
  const lastHeight = useRef(0);
  const palette = useRef<ScrubPalette | null>(null);
  const drawRef = useRef(draw);
  drawRef.current = draw;

  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const size = useResizeObserver(pin);
  // Work starts 200 px before the section enters, so the first frame is
  // already painted when it arrives rather than after it.
  const { inView } = useInView(section, { rootMargin: '200px' });

  // A self-parking loop. Once the smoothed value has reached the target there
  // is nothing left to compute, so the subscription is dropped entirely; a
  // scroll on the container wakes it. Without this, a settled hero keeps a
  // core busy re-deriving the same frame index sixty times a second.
  const [awake, setAwake] = useState(true);

  const render = (index: number, progress: number) => {
    const el = canvas.current;
    const ctx = el?.getContext('2d');
    if (!el || !ctx || size.width === 0 || size.height === 0) return;
    if (!palette.current) palette.current = readPalette(el);

    drawnIndex.current = index;
    ctx.save();
    const dpr = Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio || 1, MAX_DPR);
    ctx.setTransform(dpr, 0, 0, dpr, 0, 0);
    drawRef.current(ctx, {
      progress,
      index,
      frames,
      width: size.width,
      height: size.height,
      palette: palette.current,
    });
    ctx.restore();
  };

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = canvas.current;
    if (!el || size.width === 0 || size.height === 0) return;
    // The backing store is sized in device pixels and the element in CSS
    // pixels; assigning width/height also clears it, so a redraw is forced.
    const dpr = Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio || 1, MAX_DPR);
    el.width = Math.round(size.width * dpr);
    el.height = Math.round(size.height * dpr);
    palette.current = readPalette(el);
    drawnIndex.current = -1;
    setAwake(true);
  }, [size.width, size.height]);

  useEffect(() => {
    const sectionEl = section.current;
    if (!sectionEl) return;
    const host = scroller?.current ?? nearestScroller(sectionEl);
    const target = host === document.documentElement ? window : host;
    const wake = () => setAwake(true);
    target.addEventListener('scroll', wake, { passive: true });
    return () => target.removeEventListener('scroll', wake);
  }, [scroller]);

  // The manufactured range is layout, so it is written on mount and on resize
  // rather than only from the loop — a section still below the fold must
  // already occupy its full height, or entering it shifts everything below.
  useEffect(() => {
    const sync = () => {
      const sectionEl = section.current;
      const pinEl = pin.current;
      if (!sectionEl || !pinEl) return;
      const host = scroller?.current ?? nearestScroller(sectionEl);
      const hostHeight =
        host === document.documentElement ? window.innerHeight : host.clientHeight;
      if (hostHeight === 0) return;
      const total = Math.round(hostHeight * (reduced ? 1 : 1 + viewports));
      if (total === lastHeight.current) return;
      lastHeight.current = total;
      sectionEl.style.height = `${total}px`;
      pinEl.style.height = `${hostHeight}px`;
      setAwake(true);
    };
    sync();
    window.addEventListener('resize', sync);
    return () => window.removeEventListener('resize', sync);
  }, [reduced, viewports, scroller]);

  useRaf((dt) => {
    const sectionEl = section.current;
    const pinEl = pin.current;
    if (!sectionEl || !pinEl) return;

    const host = scroller?.current ?? nearestScroller(sectionEl);
    const hostIsRoot = host === document.documentElement;
    const hostTop = hostIsRoot ? 0 : host.getBoundingClientRect().top;
    const hostHeight = hostIsRoot ? window.innerHeight : host.clientHeight;
    if (hostHeight === 0) return;

    const total = Math.round(hostHeight * (reduced ? 1 : 1 + viewports));
    if (total !== lastHeight.current) {
      lastHeight.current = total;
      sectionEl.style.height = `${total}px`;
      pinEl.style.height = `${hostHeight}px`;
    }

    const travel = total - hostHeight;
    const target = reduced
      ? 0.5
      : travel > 0
        ? clamp((hostTop - sectionEl.getBoundingClientRect().top) / travel, 0, 1)
        : 0;

    // Smooth, then snap. Without the snap the value approaches the target
    // asymptotically and the loop can never decide it has arrived.
    current.current = reduced ? target : damp(current.current, target, smoothing, dt);
    let settled = false;
    if (Math.abs(target - current.current) < SNAP) {
      current.current = target;
      settled = true;
    }

    const text = current.current.toFixed(4);
    if (text !== lastProgress.current) {
      lastProgress.current = text;
      sectionEl.style.setProperty('--scrub-progress', text);
    }

    // The seek throttle. A real player writes `video.currentTime` here, and
    // only when the frame actually changed — re-seeking to the frame already
    // displayed makes the decoder stall and the playhead judder.
    const index = clamp(Math.round(current.current * (frames - 1)), 0, frames - 1);
    if (index !== drawnIndex.current) render(index, current.current);

    if (settled) setAwake(false);
  }, awake && inView);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useRaf` unsubscribes on unmount and again whenever the loop parks. The scroll and resize listeners are removed with their effects, `useInView` unobserves through its pool, and `useResizeObserver` disconnects. The canvas holds no timers and no decoded resources.

**Reduced motion.** The manufactured range collapses to a single screen and the playhead is pinned to the middle frame with no smoothing, so the section becomes a still image with its caption rather than several screens of scroll that scrub something. The loop parks immediately and never redraws.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Writing `video.currentTime` on every frame. The decoder is asked to seek to the position it is already at dozens of times a second, and on Safari in particular the playhead visibly stalls and jumps. Quantise to a frame and guard the assignment.
- Smoothing without a snap. The playhead approaches the target forever, the "is it settled" test never passes, and a loop written to park itself never does.
- Using a per-frame smoothing constant. The scrub lags noticeably further behind the scroll at 60 Hz than at 144 Hz, and there is no single value that feels right on both.
- Encoding the source with long GOPs. Seeking then lands on the nearest keyframe and decodes forward, which is why a scrub built on a normal web encode stutters no matter how good the JavaScript is — an all-intra encode is a prerequisite, not an optimisation.
- Running the loop while the section is off screen. The whole point of a scrubbed hero is that it costs nothing until it is on screen; without an IntersectionObserver gate it costs a decode loop for the entire page lifetime.
- Sizing the canvas in CSS only. The backing store stays at its default 300x150 and the image is stretched — the resize path must assign `width` and `height` in device pixels.
- Ignoring the device pixel ratio cap. A 4x phone quadruples the fill area for pixels nobody can see, and the scrub drops to single-digit frame rates.
- Leaving the manufactured range in place under reduced motion. The user gets several screens of scroll during which nothing at all changes.

## Notes

- No video file is shipped. `draw(ctx, frame)` renders each frame procedurally so the mapping, the quantiser and the throttle can be read on their own. A real implementation replaces the body of that call with a single assignment — `video.currentTime = frame.progress * (video.duration - 0.05)` — keeping the surrounding `index !== drawnIndex` guard exactly as it is, and draws the video element instead of the canvas.
- The other things a production version needs, none of which are part of the mapping: an all-intra encode (`-g 1`), several responsive encodes selected by width with the playhead position preserved across the swap, and a decode prime on Safari — `play()` followed immediately by `pause()` — because a video that has never played will not seek.
- The `frames` value should match the source: with a video, use `duration * fps` so one index step is one real frame.
- The default draw reads its colours from the `--k-*` custom properties on the canvas, so the placeholder footage follows the theme.

## Definition of done

Scrolling advances the frame counter smoothly and reverses exactly. Stopping settles within a few frames, after which a performance profile shows no rAF activity until the next scroll. Scrolling the section off screen stops all work. Resizing redraws at the correct resolution with no stretching. The settle takes the same wall-clock time at 60 and 144 Hz. With reduced motion on, one static frame is shown and the section is one screen tall.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Scrubbed Character Colour Reveal

A paragraph sits at 16% strength and resolves character by character as it crosses the viewport, with the reveal position pinned to the scrollbar rather than to a clock. Scroll back up and the characters ghost out again in reverse, because a scrubbed timeline is a function of position, not a playback. The stagger and durations are ratios of the scroll range rather than seconds, so the pacing per character is unchanged whether the paragraph is thirty words or three hundred.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A dim paragraph resolves character by character as it crosses the viewport, tied to scroll position not a clock.

- Category: text
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. The text is split in JSX — `text.split(" ")` for word boxes, `Array.from(word)` for one `inline-block` span per character — so React owns every node and nothing mutates the tree behind its back.
2. One `gsap.to(chars, { opacity: 1, stagger, duration, ease: "power1.out", scrollTrigger: {...} })` does the whole reveal. GSAP builds the stagger internally as a single tween whose total length is `duration + (n - 1) * stagger`.
3. ScrollTrigger maps that total length onto the distance between `start` and `end`, which is why `stagger: 0.1` and `duration: 0.35` are ratios, not seconds: each character begins 0.1/total of the way through the scroll range and takes 0.35/total to resolve. Change the paragraph length and the pacing per character is identical; change the scroll range and everything rescales together.
4. The resting opacity is written as a JSX inline style on each character, so the pre-scroll frame — including the server render and the no-JS render — is already the dim state, and GSAP has a real DOM value to tween away from.
5. The paragraph carries `aria-label={text}` and the character spans are inside an `aria-hidden` wrapper, so assistive technology reads one paragraph rather than two hundred single letters.
6. `ease: "power1.out"` applies *within* each character's own resolve, not across the stagger. The stagger itself remains linear against scroll, which is what keeps the sweep pinned to the scrollbar.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `DIM = 0.16`
  Resting strength as opacity on `currentColor`. Below ~0.1 the unread text is illegible and the block reads as a loading skeleton; above ~0.3 the contrast between resolved and unresolved is too weak for the sweep to be visible while scrolling.
- `STAGGER = 0.1`
  Timeline units between adjacent characters. Combined with `CHAR_DURATION` it sets the width of the resolve front: roughly 3-4 characters are mid-transition at any moment. Larger and the front narrows to one character at a time, which reads as a typewriter rather than a wash.
- `CHAR_DURATION = 0.35`
  3.5x the stagger, so several characters are always resolving together. Equal to the stagger it becomes a hard edge sweeping the paragraph; much larger and the front is so soft the reveal has no direction.
- `SCRUB = 0.75`
  Seconds of catch-up. `scrub: true` welds the reveal to the scrollbar exactly, which on a trackpad exposes every jitter in the input. Three quarters of a second smooths it without ever feeling like the text is animating on its own.
- `START / END = 'top 78%' / 'bottom 55%'`
  The reveal begins when the paragraph top is a little above the fold and completes when its bottom passes just past the middle. Ending at `bottom top` means the last characters only resolve as the paragraph leaves the screen, so the reader never sees the finished text.

## API

```ts
function ScrubCharColorReveal(props: { text: string; dim?: number; stagger?: number; charDuration?: number; scrub?: number; start?: string; end?: string; scroller?: Element | null; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `text: string`
  Body copy. Split to words then characters in JSX.
- `dim: number` — default `0.16`
  Resting strength of an unrevealed character, 0-1.
- `stagger: number` — default `0.1`
  Timeline units between adjacent characters.
- `charDuration: number` — default `0.35`
  Timeline units for one character to resolve.
- `scrub: number` — default `0.75`
  Seconds of catch-up between the scrollbar and the reveal.
- `start: string` — default `'top 78%'`
  ScrollTrigger `start`.
- `end: string` — default `'bottom 55%'`
  ScrollTrigger `end`.
- `scroller: Element | null` — default `null`
  Scroll container, when the text is not in the document scroller.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the paragraph via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const DIM = 0.16;
const STAGGER = 0.1;
const CHAR_DURATION = 0.35;
const SCRUB = 0.75;
const START = 'top 78%';
const END = 'bottom 55%';

export function ScrubCharColorReveal({
  text,
  dim = DIM,
  stagger = STAGGER,
  charDuration = CHAR_DURATION,
  scrub = SCRUB,
  start = START,
  end = END,
  scroller = null,
  className,
}: ScrubCharColorRevealProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLParagraphElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = root.current;
    if (!el || reduced) return;

    gsap.registerPlugin(ScrollTrigger);

    const chars = Array.from(el.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-char]'));
    if (chars.length === 0) return;

    const ctx = gsap.context(() => {
      gsap.to(chars, {
        opacity: 1,
        duration: charDuration,
        ease: 'power1.out',
        stagger,
        scrollTrigger: {
          trigger: el,
          scroller: scroller ?? undefined,
          start,
          end,
          scrub,
        },
      });
    }, el);

    return () => ctx.revert();
  }, [text, dim, stagger, charDuration, scrub, start, end, scroller, reduced]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `ctx.revert()` on the `gsap.context` scoped to the paragraph. That kills the staggered tween, disposes the ScrollTrigger instance so it stops measuring a detached node, and strips the inline `opacity` GSAP wrote — leaving React's own inline dim value intact.

**Reduced motion.** The resting opacity collapses to 1 in the JSX, so the paragraph renders fully resolved, and the effect returns before registering ScrollTrigger. The text is never left dim waiting for a scroll that will not drive it.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Splitting text before the webfont has loaded. Character boxes are measured against the fallback face, so widths and line breaks are wrong and never re-flow when the real font arrives — see `font-safe-text-split` for the `document.fonts.ready` gate and the debounced re-split this needs at scale.
- Treating `stagger` and `duration` as seconds. Under `scrub` they are proportions of the scroll range; a value tuned as "0.35 seconds" behaves completely differently the moment the trigger distance changes.
- Building a separate tween per character. That is one ScrollTrigger per character on a paragraph of two hundred, and refresh cost becomes visible on resize. A single staggered tween is one trigger.
- Leaving the character spans exposed to assistive technology. A screen reader announces every letter individually — `aria-label` on the paragraph plus `aria-hidden` on the spans is not optional here.
- Setting the resting opacity from `gsap.set` in the effect. The first paint then shows the paragraph at full strength before dimming it, which is a visible flash on every load.
- Splitting straight to characters with no word boxes. Line breaks land inside words and the paragraph becomes unreadable at narrow widths.
- Forgetting `scroller` when the paragraph lives in an `overflow-y-auto` panel. ScrollTrigger measures the window instead and the reveal fires at the wrong scroll position or not at all.

## Notes

- The split is declarative JSX, deliberately: GSAP `SplitText` is reserved for the two components whose subject *is* SplitText (`nested-splittext-restore`, `font-safe-text-split`). Here a React split gives the same per-character targets with no DOM mutation and no extra dependency for the consumer.
- Opacity on `currentColor` rather than a literal colour tween, so the component is correct in any theme without a per-context variant.

## Definition of done

Scroll the paragraph up through the viewport: characters brighten in a soft front sweeping left to right and top to bottom, and the front position tracks the scrollbar rather than a clock. Scroll back up and it reverses. Turn on a screen reader and the paragraph is announced once as whole sentences, not letter by letter. With reduced motion enabled the paragraph is at full strength on first paint.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
