# Build: Scrub Timeline Spine

A vertical rule that fills with scroll while entries alternate either side of it. Entries rest at 50% opacity rather than 0, so the animation adds emphasis to content that is already readable, and each one reverses as it leaves — so scrolling back up replays the sequence instead of showing a column of finished animations.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A rule that fills as you scroll, with entries alternating either side and reversing on the way back.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. The rule is two elements: a faint full-height track, and a fill of the same height scaled with `gsap.fromTo(fill, { scaleY: 0 }, { scaleY: 1, ease: "none" })` on a `scrub: 0.6` trigger running `top 55%` → `bottom 75%`.
2. `transformOrigin: "top center"` is passed to the tween, not just set in CSS. GSAP writes its own transform string, and without it the fill grows from the centre and the rule appears to unroll in both directions at once.
3. Every entry gets its own trigger with `toggleActions: "play reverse play reverse"` — the four slots are onEnter, onLeave, onEnterBack, onLeaveBack. Reversing on leave is what makes the column scrubbable upward as well as downward.
4. Entries animate `fromTo({ opacity: 0.5, scale: 0.9 }, { opacity: 1, scale: 1, duration: 0.6, ease: "power2.out" })`. The rest state is 0.5, not 0, so nothing is gated behind a scroll event.
5. `transformOrigin` per entry follows the side it hangs off — `left center` on the left column, `right center` on the right — so each card grows outward from the spine. A centre origin makes both columns creep toward the middle and the rule looks squeezed.
6. Alternation is decided from the measured container width. Below `alternateAbove` px, entries stop alternating and stack to the right of a left-hand rule, and every origin becomes `left center`.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `restOpacity = 0.5`
  The resting state of an entry. Zero is the obvious choice and the wrong one: it makes the animation a gate on the content, so a failed script or a skipped trigger leaves a blank column, and a screen reader meets text that is visually absent. At 0.5 the animation is emphasis, not access.
- `restScale = 0.9`
  Paired with the opacity change so the entry gains presence rather than just brightness. Below ~0.85 the text visibly reflows as it scales and becomes hard to read mid-transition.
- `scrub = 0.6`
  Catch-up on the fill only. The rule keeps advancing for about half a second after the wheel stops, which reads as the timeline settling. `true` makes it feel welded to the mouse.
- `fillStart / fillEnd = 'top 55%' / 'bottom 75%'`
  The fill begins once the section is past halfway up the scroller and completes before its bottom clears. Ending at `bottom top` instead would leave the rule still filling while the last entry is already being read, which makes the last item feel unreached.
- `entryDuration = 0.6`
  Not scrubbed — this one plays on its own clock, so it must be short enough to finish before the next entry enters at normal scrolling speed.
- `alternateAbove = 420`
  Container width in px below which a half-width column cannot hold a title and a line of body. Measured from the element, not the window, because the spine is usually inside an article column narrower than the page.

## API

```ts
function ScrubTimelineSpine(props: { entries: { label: string; title: string; body?: string }[]; scrub?: number; restOpacity?: number; restScale?: number; entryDuration?: number; fillStart?: string; fillEnd?: string; entryStart?: string; alternateAbove?: number; scrollerRef?: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `entries: { label: string; title: string; body?: string }[]`
  Ordered entries. Rendered as an `<ol>` either side of the rule.
- `scrub: number` — default `0.6`
  Seconds of catch-up on the fill.
- `restOpacity: number` — default `0.5`
  Resting opacity of an inactive entry. Do not set 0.
- `restScale: number` — default `0.9`
  Resting scale of an inactive entry.
- `entryDuration: number` — default `0.6`
  Seconds for one entry to reach full emphasis.
- `fillStart: string` — default `'top 55%'`
  ScrollTrigger start for the fill.
- `fillEnd: string` — default `'bottom 75%'`
  ScrollTrigger end for the fill.
- `entryStart: string` — default `'top 78%'`
  ScrollTrigger start for each entry.
- `alternateAbove: number` — default `420`
  Container width in px above which entries alternate sides.
- `scrollerRef: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>`
  The scroll container that owns the scroll position. Omit for the document.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the wrapper via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function ScrubTimelineSpine({
  entries,
  scrub = 0.6,
  restOpacity = 0.5,
  restScale = 0.9,
  entryDuration = 0.6,
  fillStart = 'top 55%',
  fillEnd = 'bottom 75%',
  entryStart = 'top 78%',
  alternateAbove = 420,
  scrollerRef,
  className,
}: ScrubTimelineSpineProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const fill = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const { width } = useResizeObserver(root);
  const alternate = width >= alternateAbove;

  useGsap(
    gsap,
    () => {
      const container = root.current;
      const line = fill.current;
      if (!container || !line) return;

      const items = Array.from(container.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-spine-entry]'));
      const scroller = scrollerRef?.current ?? undefined;

      if (reduced) {
        gsap.set(line, { scaleY: 1 });
        gsap.set(items, { opacity: 1, scale: 1 });
        return;
      }

      gsap.fromTo(
        line,
        { scaleY: 0 },
        {
          scaleY: 1,
          ease: 'none',
          // transformOrigin is set in CSS too, but GSAP writes its own
          // transform string; without stating it here the fill grows from the
          // centre and the rule appears to unroll in both directions.
          transformOrigin: 'top center',
          scrollTrigger: {
            trigger: container,
            scroller,
            // Starts filling once the section is just past halfway up and
            // completes before its bottom leaves — so the rule is never still
            // filling while the last entry is already being read.
            start: fillStart,
            end: fillEnd,
            scrub,
            invalidateOnRefresh: true,
          },
        },
      );

      items.forEach((item, i) => {
        gsap.fromTo(
          item,
          { opacity: restOpacity, scale: restScale },
          {
            opacity: 1,
            scale: 1,
            duration: entryDuration,
            ease: 'power2.out',
            // Scale from the edge the entry hangs off, so it grows outward
            // from the spine. A centre origin pulls both columns toward the
            // middle and the rule looks like it is being squeezed.
            transformOrigin: alternate && i % 2 === 1 ? 'right center' : 'left center',
            scrollTrigger: {
              trigger: item,
              scroller,
              start: entryStart,
              // onEnter, onLeave, onEnterBack, onLeaveBack. Reversing on the
              // way out is what makes the column scrubbable upward as well as
              // downward.
              toggleActions: 'play reverse play reverse',
            },
          },
        );
      });
    },
    root,
    [
      scrub,
      restOpacity,
      restScale,
      entryDuration,
      fillStart,
      fillEnd,
      entryStart,
      alternate,
      reduced,
      entries.length,
    ],
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useGsap` reverts the `gsap.context`, killing the fill tween, all per-entry tweens and all of their ScrollTriggers, and restoring the inline transform and opacity. This matters more than usual here because the alternation flip rebuilds every trigger on resize: a surviving trigger would keep writing a right-edge `transform-origin` to a card now laid out on the left.

**Reduced motion.** The fill is set to `scaleY: 1` and every entry to full opacity and scale during the first effect, with no triggers created. The spine renders as a completed timeline — the rule is drawn, every entry is emphasised, and nothing changes with scroll.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- `toggleActions: "play none none none"`. The default-feeling choice, and it means scrolling back up shows a column of already-completed animations with no motion left in them. Reversing on leave is what makes the direction of travel legible.
- Resting entries at `opacity: 0`. The animation becomes a gate: any trigger that fails to fire — a mis-set scroller, a refresh during a resize, a JS error elsewhere — leaves the content permanently invisible while still occupying layout and still being read by assistive technology.
- Setting `transform-origin` only in CSS. GSAP writes a complete transform and its own `transform-origin`, so the CSS value is overwritten and the fill grows from the middle of the rule instead of the top.
- A single centre `transform-origin` for both columns. Cards then scale toward the spine, so the whole layout appears to pinch inward as you scroll instead of each entry growing outward from the rule.
- Scaling the same element that is the track. The fill needs to be a second element; scaling the visible track means the "remaining" portion disappears and the reader loses the sense of how much is left.
- One shared ScrollTrigger for all entries. The emphasis then depends on the section's progress rather than each entry's own position, so on a tall screen three entries brighten at once and none of them reads as current.

## Notes

- The fill uses the accent token, so it inherits the category accent when placed inside a `data-category` subtree.
- Entries are a real `<ol>`, so the sequence is conveyed structurally and not only by the drawn rule.

## Definition of done

Scroll down: the accent rule fills from the top and each entry brightens and grows outward from its own side of the rule as it arrives. Scroll back up and each entry dims again as it leaves the top, and the rule retreats. Stop mid-section and the fill continues for about half a second. Disable JavaScript and every entry is still readable at half opacity. Narrow the container and the entries stack to the right of a left-hand rule.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Pixels-Per-Second Marquee

A looping strip of content whose speed is expressed in pixels per second and whose duration is derived from it, never the other way round. A fixed `duration` means a 900px strip crawls while a 4000px strip sprints, so two marquees on the same page visibly disagree about how fast scrolling is — and adding one word to either changes its speed. The loop distance is exactly one content set plus its gap, so the wrap frame is pixel-identical to the frame before it and the seam is invisible.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A marquee whose duration is derived from measured width and a px/second speed, so every strip moves at the same rate.

- Category: text
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. A `ResizeObserver` on the first content copy gives `copyWidth`; the repeating unit is `setWidth = copyWidth + gap`, because the gap that follows a copy is part of the unit — omit it and the rhythm at the seam is one gap tighter than everywhere else, which reads as a stutter once per cycle.
2. Duration is `setWidth / speed` — seconds = px / (px per second). Every marquee on the site then moves at the same rate regardless of how much content is in it.
3. The number of copies is `Math.max(2, Math.ceil(rootWidth / setWidth) + 1)`, from a second `ResizeObserver` on the container. The `+1` covers the gap that the translation itself opens up; with the exact ceiling a blank wedge appears at the right edge on the last frame of every cycle.
4. The tween is `gsap.fromTo(track, { x: 0 }, { x: -setWidth, duration, ease: "none", repeat: -1 })`. `ease: "none"` is mandatory — any easing makes the strip accelerate and decelerate once per cycle, which turns the seam into a visible pulse.
5. Pausing lives in a *separate* effect that calls `tween.paused(!(visible && inView))`, driven by `useVisibility` (tab hidden) and `useInView` (scrolled away). Rebuilding the tween on a visibility flip would snap the strip back to x = 0.
6. Hover ramps the timeScale rather than toggling paused: `gsap.to(tween, { timeScale: 0 | 1, duration: 0.35, overwrite: true })`. The tween object is itself a valid GSAP target, so the strip glides to a stop instead of stopping dead.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `SPEED = 60`
  Pixels per second. Around 60px/s a 12px word takes a fifth of a second to cross its own width — readable while moving. Past ~120px/s the copy is decorative texture; below ~30px/s viewers assume it is stuck.
- `GAP = 48`
  Pixels between items and between the last item and the next copy. It must be identical in both places or the seam is visibly a different rhythm from the interior. Below ~24px adjacent items read as one phrase.
- `HOVER_RAMP = 0.35`
  Seconds to ramp `timeScale` between 1 and 0. Zero (a hard pause) reads as a broken animation; past ~0.6s the strip keeps drifting long enough that a user trying to read an item has to chase it.
- `copies = max(2, ceil(rootWidth / setWidth) + 1)`
  The floor of 2 covers content wider than the container, where the ceiling alone yields 1 and there is nothing to wrap into. The `+1` covers the width the translation itself vacates.

## API

```ts
function SeamlessMarquee(props: { children: ReactNode; speed?: number; direction?: 'left' | 'right'; gap?: number; pauseOnHover?: boolean; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  One content set. Cloned as many times as the container width requires.
- `speed: number` — default `60`
  Pixels per second. Identical for every marquee whatever its width.
- `direction: 'left' | 'right'` — default `'left'`
  Travel direction.
- `gap: number` — default `48`
  Pixels between items and between copies.
- `pauseOnHover: boolean` — default `true`
  Ramp `timeScale` to 0 on pointer enter and back to 1 on leave.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the clipping container via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const SPEED = 60;
const GAP = 48;
const HOVER_RAMP = 0.35;

export function SeamlessMarquee({
  children,
  speed = SPEED,
  direction = 'left',
  gap = GAP,
  pauseOnHover = true,
  className,
}: SeamlessMarqueeProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const track = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const copy = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const tween = useRef<gsap.core.Tween | null>(null);

  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const visible = useVisibility();
  const { inView } = useInView(root);
  const { width: rootWidth } = useResizeObserver(root);
  const { width: copyWidth } = useResizeObserver(copy);

  // The loop distance is one copy *plus* the gap that follows it — the gap is
  // part of the repeating unit. Leave it out and the rhythm of the seam is one
  // gap tighter than the rhythm everywhere else, which reads as a stutter.
  const setWidth = copyWidth + gap;
  const measured = copyWidth > 0;
  const copies =
    reduced || !measured ? 1 : Math.max(2, Math.ceil(rootWidth / setWidth) + 1);

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = track.current;
    if (!el || reduced || !measured) return;

    const duration = setWidth / speed;
    const t = gsap.fromTo(
      el,
      { x: direction === 'left' ? 0 : -setWidth },
      {
        x: direction === 'left' ? -setWidth : 0,
        duration,
        ease: 'none',
        repeat: -1,
      },
    );
    tween.current = t;

    return () => {
      tween.current = null;
      // Kill the hover timeScale tweens too — they target the tween object
      // itself, so killTweensOf(el) would not reach them.
      gsap.killTweensOf(t);
      t.kill();
      gsap.set(el, { clearProps: 'transform' });
    };
  }, [setWidth, measured, speed, direction, reduced]);

  // Separate effect so a visibility flip pauses in place instead of rebuilding
  // the tween, which would snap the strip back to its start position.
  useEffect(() => {
    const t = tween.current;
    if (!t) return;
    t.paused(!(visible && inView));
  }, [visible, inView, setWidth, measured, speed, direction, reduced]);

  const ramp = useCallback(
    (to: number) => {
      const t = tween.current;
      if (!pauseOnHover || !t) return;
      gsap.to(t, { timeScale: to, duration: HOVER_RAMP, overwrite: true });
    },
    [pauseOnHover],
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The build effect clears the tween ref, calls `gsap.killTweensOf(tween)` to catch in-flight hover `timeScale` ramps that target the tween object, then `tween.kill()`, then `gsap.set(track, { clearProps: "transform" })`. Both `ResizeObserver` instances are disconnected by their hooks.

**Reduced motion.** Renders a single, un-cloned content set with no tween created at all. The content is fully visible and static — the strip is not left mid-translation and nothing is clipped out of view.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Specifying `duration` instead of a px/second speed. Two marquees on one page then move at different rates, and editing the copy silently changes the speed of the one you edited.
- Translating by the copy width and forgetting the gap. The seam arrives one gap early every cycle — a small, regular hitch that is very hard to diagnose from the code.
- Hardcoding the clone count at 2. On a wide viewport with short content the strip runs out and a blank band sweeps through once per cycle.
- Any ease other than `none`. The strip speeds up and slows down once per loop, so the seam that is geometrically invisible becomes obvious from the velocity change alone.
- Rebuilding the tween when visibility or hover changes. The `fromTo` restarts at x = 0 and the strip teleports backwards.
- Killing only `killTweensOf(trackElement)` on unmount. The hover ramps target the *tween object*, not the element, so they survive and keep writing `timeScale` to a dead tween — `gsap.killTweensOf(t)` before `t.kill()` is what catches them.
- Leaving the cloned copies exposed to assistive technology. A screen reader reads the same six items three times; every clone past the first is `aria-hidden`.

## Notes

- Reduced motion renders exactly one copy with no tween and no transform, so the content sits statically at the left edge and remains fully readable.
- No text splitting is involved — the marquee moves whole content sets, so no split library dependency is imposed on consumers.

## Definition of done

Watch the seam for a full cycle: no jump, no blank wedge, no change in spacing as one copy hands over to the next. Put two marquees with very different content lengths side by side and both move at visibly the same speed. Hover and the strip glides to a stop over about a third of a second rather than halting. Switch browser tabs and back, and the strip resumes from where it was rather than restarting. With reduced motion the content is static and readable.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Self-Parking RAF

An eased value never arrives. Closing 12% of the remaining gap each frame closes it 100% never — the distance decays asymptotically and `current !== target` stays true for the life of the page, so a loop conditioned on that comparison never stops. One line fixes it: below a threshold, assign the target outright. The equality test can now succeed, the loop reaches its own stopping condition, and it unsubscribes itself. The frame callback exists only while something is genuinely moving.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

An epsilon snap lets a damped value reach its target exactly, so the frame loop hits its exit test and dies.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The damped step is `damp(current, target, smoothing, dt)`, which is `current + (target - current) * (1 - smoothing^dt)`. The exponent is what makes it frame-rate independent: the naked `* 0.12` from the source converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz, so the same code feels different on different hardware and visibly speeds up whenever the browser drops frames.
2. After the step, `Math.abs(target - next) < epsilon` assigns `next = target` exactly. This is the entire technique. Without it the loop's exit condition — `next === target` — is unreachable, because exponential decay produces 1e-8, then 1e-9, then a denormal, and never a clean zero.
3. Parking is expressed as React state, not as a local flag: `setRunning(false)` drops the `useRaf` subscription, and when the last subscriber leaves the shared loop calls `cancelAnimationFrame` and stops scheduling frames at all. The saving is the whole callback plus the paint it would have dirtied, not merely the arithmetic.
4. Waking is driven by a `target` change in an effect, guarded by `value.current === target`. The guard is load-bearing: without it any unrelated re-render that happens to pass the same target restarts a loop that had already parked, which is how "self-parking" quietly degrades back into an always-on loop.
5. Because `perFrameToSmoothing(0.12)` is `0.88^60 ≈ 0.00047`, the value retains 0.047% of its gap after a second — so the settle time is a few hundred milliseconds and the epsilon is crossed within roughly twenty frames rather than being an escape hatch from a genuinely long tail.
6. A hidden tab and reduced motion both take the same short path: `park()` assigns the target, emits one `onFrame`, and never starts a loop. No observer means no reason to interpolate, and the value stays correct either way.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `per-frame rate = 0.12`
  Fraction of the remaining gap closed per frame at 60fps, converted through `perFrameToSmoothing`. It settles in about 300 ms — fast enough that a scrubber feels attached to the click, slow enough to read as motion. Above ~0.3 the damping is barely visible and the loop may as well be a jump; below ~0.05 the tail is long enough that a user beats it with the next click.
- `EPSILON = 0.0002`
  Snap threshold, in the units of the value. For the 0-1 normalised scrub position of the source this is a fifth of a pixel on a 1000 px track — invisible. Set it to 0 and the loop never parks, which is the exact bug this component exists to fix. Set it far too large and the last visible fraction of the travel is skipped as a jump.
- `MAX_DT = 0.1`
  Inherited from `useRaf`. A tab returning from the background delivers a multi-second delta; unclamped, `smoothing^dt` underflows to 0, the damp closes the entire gap in one frame, and the "settle" is a teleport.

## API

```ts
function useSelfParkingRaf(target: number, options: { smoothing?: number; epsilon?: number; onFrame: (value: number) => void }): { running: boolean; value: RefObject<number>; park: () => void }
```

- `target: number`
  The value to settle toward. Changing it wakes the loop; it is the only trigger.
- `smoothing: number` — default `perFrameToSmoothing(0.12)`
  Fraction of the gap remaining after one second. Smaller is snappier.
- `epsilon: number` — default `0.0002`
  Distance below which the value snaps to the target and the loop parks. Must match the unit of the value.
- `onFrame: (value: number) => void`
  Called with the damped value every frame while running, and once when it parks. For DOM writes.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * `0.12` of the gap per frame, measured at 60fps, expressed as the retention
 * factor `damp` wants. Using the raw 0.12 with a per-frame multiply would run
 * twice as fast on a 120 Hz display; this converges in the same wall-clock
 * time on any refresh rate.
 */
const SMOOTHING = perFrameToSmoothing(0.12);
/** The snap threshold. This single line is what allows the loop to end. */
const EPSILON = 0.0002;

/**
 * A damped value that runs a frame loop only while it is moving.
 *
 * `target` is a plain prop: changing it wakes the loop, and the loop parks
 * itself once it arrives. There is no `start`, and there is no
 * `requestAnimationFrame` running when the value is at rest.
 */
export function useSelfParkingRaf(
  target: number,
  options: SelfParkingOptions,
): SelfParkingValue {
  const { smoothing = SMOOTHING, epsilon = EPSILON } = options;
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const visible = useVisibility();

  const value = useRef(target);
  const [running, setRunning] = useState(false);

  const config = useRef({ smoothing, epsilon, target, options });
  config.current = { smoothing, epsilon, target, options };

  const park = useCallback(() => {
    const cfg = config.current;
    value.current = cfg.target;
    cfg.options.onFrame(value.current);
    setRunning(false);
  }, []);

  // Waking the loop is the only thing a target change does. The guard matters:
  // without it, any unrelated re-render that happens to pass the same target
  // restarts a loop that had already parked.
  useEffect(() => {
    if (value.current === target) return;
    // Nothing to interpolate: reduced motion wants the end state, and a hidden
    // tab has no observer, so both arrive in one write instead of a loop.
    if (reduced || !visible) {
      park();
      return;
    }
    setRunning(true);
  }, [target, reduced, visible, park]);

  useRaf((dt) => {
    const cfg = config.current;
    let next = damp(value.current, cfg.target, cfg.smoothing, dt);

    // The whole technique. Asymptotic approach means `next` would otherwise
    // never equal `cfg.target`, so the exit test below could never pass.
    if (Math.abs(cfg.target - next) < cfg.epsilon) next = cfg.target;

    value.current = next;
    cfg.options.onFrame(next);

    // Parking flips `running`, which drops the `useRaf` subscription. When the
    // last subscriber goes, the shared loop cancels its frame entirely.
    if (next === cfg.target) setRunning(false);
  }, running);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useRaf` removes the subscription when `running` goes false or the component unmounts, and cancels the shared frame when it was the last subscriber — so an unmount mid-settle leaves nothing scheduled. The visibility and media-query listeners belong to `useVisibility` and `useReducedMotion`, which detach their own. No timers and no direct `requestAnimationFrame` handles are held.

**Reduced motion.** No loop is started at all. A target change calls `park()`, which assigns the target and emits a single `onFrame`, so the value lands on its final position in one write. That is the still, correct state rather than a zero-duration animation: `onFrame` still fires, so the DOM the consumer writes is identical to the end of a full settle, and `running` never goes true.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Omitting the epsilon snap. The value approaches the target forever, the exit test never passes, and one hover or one scrub leaves a rAF running for the rest of the session. It is invisible in a demo and shows up as a battery complaint.
- Expressing epsilon in the wrong unit. The threshold is compared against the value, so 0.0002 is correct for a 0-1 progress value and absurd for a pixel offset — at pixel scale it costs dozens of extra frames to cross, and the loop appears not to park.
- Keeping the loop alive to "avoid the cost of restarting it". Subscribing to a shared rAF is a `Set.add`; a frame callback plus the paint it dirties is orders of magnitude more. Restarting is free, running is not.
- Using `current += (target - current) * 0.12` directly. Frame-rate dependent: the same settle takes 300 ms at 60 Hz and 150 ms at 120 Hz, and speeds up mid-motion whenever a long task drops frames — the animation gets faster precisely when the page is struggling.
- Waking the loop without comparing against the current value. Every re-render that re-supplies the same target restarts the loop, which parks on its first frame and restarts on the next render — a loop that thrashes instead of resting.
- Calling `setState` from `onFrame`. That re-renders on every frame of the settle, which costs far more than the loop being parked ever saved. `onFrame` is for DOM writes.
- Reading the returned `value` ref during render. It changes between renders without notifying React, so the rendered output and the ref disagree; read it inside a frame callback or an event handler only.
- Forgetting that the loop is asleep when the target is set imperatively. Anything that mutates the underlying source without changing the `target` prop leaves the value stale, because nothing is polling — the trade for not running a loop is that changes must be declared.

## Notes

- The natural pairing is with an invalidate-driven renderer: a WebGL scene that renders only on demand plus a value that only moves on demand gives a page that is genuinely idle at rest, not merely cheap.
- The `park()` escape hatch exists for handoffs — a drag that takes over the value, or a route change that should not animate the old position. It emits one final `onFrame` so the DOM is left in the correct end state rather than mid-travel.
- `running` is exposed because parking is otherwise unobservable, and a component that claims to park should be able to prove it. The demo prints it beside a frame count that freezes.
- For several values settling together, one hook per value is fine — they all share the single `useRaf` loop, and the last one to park is the one that stops it.

## Definition of done

Click a timecode. The bar and the readout race to it and stop, and the status line goes from "rAF live" to "rAF parked" with the frame count frozen at roughly twenty — not climbing. Leave it alone for a minute: the count does not move. Open DevTools performance and record while idle after a seek; there are no animation frames. Click the timecode that is already active and nothing wakes. Switch tabs mid-settle and come back — the bar is already at its target with no catch-up sweep. With reduced motion on, a seek moves the bar in one step, the count reads 1, and the status never leaves "parked".

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Slab Page Transition

The outgoing page slides one screen height up and out while a solid slab rises from below to take its place. The route commits under the slab, the slab holds for a beat with the destination name on it, then the slab keeps travelling up and out while the new page follows it in from below. Nothing reverses direction at any point, which is the whole difference between a slab and a curtain: a curtain that drops and lifts reads as an interruption, a slab that passes through reads as travel.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

An opaque slab rises through the frame, the route changes under it, and it keeps going — nothing ever reverses.

- Category: transition
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. One paused GSAP timeline, played from zero on every navigation, covers the whole gesture. `to(content, { y: -H })` and `fromTo(slab, { y: +H }, { y: 0 })` both start at 0 and run for `duration`; a `.call()` at `duration` fires the caller's commit; `set(content, { y: +H })` on that same frame teleports the page below the frame; then `to(slab, { y: -H })` and `to(content, { y: 0 })` both start at `duration + hold`. Total length is `2 * duration + hold`.
2. The midpoint commit and the content teleport happen while the slab is exactly covering the frame, so neither is ever visible. That is the only reason the page can jump from -H to +H without a flash: there is an opaque surface in front of it for the whole of that frame.
3. Each half eases `power3.inOut` on its own rather than one tween covering the full 2H. An `inOut` across the whole travel is at its FASTEST in the middle — precisely where the slab has to look like it stopped. Two `inOut` halves meet at zero velocity, so the slab lands, holds, and leaves.
4. Travel is measured in pixels per run — `window.innerHeight` when `position="fixed"`, `root.getBoundingClientRect().height` when `"absolute"` — through GSAP function-based values. `yPercent: -100` would be 100% of the CONTENT element's own height, which on a long page is the whole document, so the page would fly thousands of pixels instead of one screen.
5. `tl.invalidate().play(0)` starts each run. `invalidate()` re-evaluates every function-based value, so a resized container or a flipped direction is picked up without rebuilding the timeline; without it the slab travels whatever height the box had when the component mounted.
6. Direction is a sign read from a ref inside those function values, and the ref is written in `run()` before `play(0)` rather than during render. `play(0)` renders the timeline synchronously, so a direction that only landed on the next React commit would be read one frame late and the two halves would disagree about which way is out.
7. The slab's parked position — `transform: translateY(100%)` — is declared in an injected stylesheet, not set from an effect. Effects run after the first paint, so a slab parked from JS is one frame of full-frame colour on mount. GSAP's inline transform outranks the rule while a transition runs, and when `useGsap` reverts it strips that inline value, which re-parks the slab with no extra code.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `SLAB_DURATION = 0.8`
  Seconds for ONE half; the full gesture is twice this plus the hold. The source ran 1 s per half and 0.8 keeps the weight while taking 0.4 s off the round trip. Under ~0.5 s the slab stops reading as a physical object and becomes a colour flash; over ~1.1 s the hold in the middle turns into a wait and people click a second nav item.
- `SLAB_HOLD = 0.12`
  Seconds the slab sits still at full cover. Two jobs: it is the beat in which the label is legible, and it is the margin in which React commits the destination — the commit fires at the start of the hold, so a page whose first layout costs two or three frames still finishes laying out before the slab moves off it. At 0 a heavy destination visibly settles while it is sliding in.
- `SLAB_EASE = 'power3.inOut'`
  Applied to each half separately. `inOut` is the only family that starts and ends at zero velocity, which is what makes the midpoint a stop rather than a peak. `power3` specifically: `power2` does not hold still long enough at the ends for the hold to read as deliberate, and `power4` spends so long near stationary that the 0.8 s feels like 1.2 s.
- `zIndex = 190`
  Above a custom cursor (150) and a scroll progress bar (120), both of which must be hidden during a transition, and below a preloader (200), which has to be able to sit over a slab on first load.

## API

```ts
function SlabPageTransition(props: { controller: SlabNavigation; children: ReactNode; duration?: number; hold?: number; direction?: "up" | "down"; color?: string; labelClassName?: string; position?: "fixed" | "absolute"; zIndex?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
function useSlabNavigation(): { host: RefObject<SlabRunner | null>; navigate: (commit: () => void, options?: { label?: string; direction?: "up" | "down" }) => void }
```

- `controller: SlabNavigation`
  From `useSlabNavigation()`. The component registers its runner on it.
- `children: ReactNode`
  The current page. Swapped by the `commit` you hand to `navigate`.
- `duration: number` — default `0.8`
  Seconds for ONE half. The full gesture is `2 * duration + hold`.
- `hold: number` — default `0.12`
  Seconds the slab holds at full cover, between the halves.
- `direction: "up" | "down"` — default `"up"`
  Default travel. Overridable per navigation via the options argument.
- `color: string` — default `'#000'`
  Any CSS colour. Must be opaque, or the swap shows through the slab.
- `labelClassName: string`
  Applied to the label span, so the caller owns its typography.
- `position: "fixed" | "absolute"` — default `"fixed"`
  `absolute` inside a bounded container; `fixed` for a real page transition.
- `zIndex: number` — default `190`
  Above the site and any custom cursor, below a preloader.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * Seconds for one half. The source ran 1 s per half; 0.8 keeps the weight and
 * takes 0.4 s off the round trip. Under ~0.5 s the slab stops reading as a
 * physical object and becomes a colour flash; over ~1.1 s the hold in the
 * middle turns into a wait, and people click a second nav item.
 */
export const SLAB_DURATION = 0.8;

/**
 * Seconds the slab sits still at full cover, between the two halves. Two jobs:
 * it is the beat in which the slab's label is legible, and it is the margin in
 * which React commits the destination. The commit fires at the start of the
 * hold, so a destination whose first layout costs two or three frames still
 * finishes laying out before the slab starts moving off it. At 0 a heavy page
 * visibly settles while it is sliding in.
 */
export const SLAB_HOLD = 0.12;

/** Both halves. `inOut` on each is what makes the midpoint a stop, not a peak. */
const SLAB_EASE = 'power3.inOut';

const SLAB_CSS = `
.kx-slab-panel {
  /* An opaque full-frame surface must never eat a click, not even while it is
     covering. Mid-transition the pointer is usually already aimed at the next
     nav item. */
  pointer-events: none;
  z-index: var(--kx-slab-z, 190);
  background: var(--kx-slab-color, #000);
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  overflow: hidden;
}
/* The parked position lives in CSS, not in an inline style and not in a
   'gsap.set' inside an effect. Effects run after the first paint, so a slab
   parked from JS is one frame of full-frame colour on mount. GSAP's inline
   'transform' outranks these rules while a transition runs, and when
   'useGsap' reverts it strips that inline value — which parks the slab again
   with no extra code. */
.kx-slab-park-up { transform: translateY(100%); }
.kx-slab-park-down { transform: translateY(-100%); }
`;

export interface SlabNavigateOptions {
  /** Written into the slab, legible during the hold. */
  label?: string;
  /** Overrides the component's `direction` for this one navigation. */
  direction?: 'up' | 'down';
}

/** What the component registers on the controller. Internal. */
export interface SlabRunner {
  run: (commit: () => void, options?: SlabNavigateOptions) => void;
}

export interface SlabNavigation {
  /** Pass straight to `<SlabPageTransition controller>`. Do not read it. */
  host: RefObject<SlabRunner | null>;
  /**
   * Raise the slab, run `commit` — your navigation — under it, then lower the
   * page in behind it.
   */
  navigate: (commit: () => void, options?: SlabNavigateOptions) => void;
}

/**
 * The caller's half. `commit` is a callback rather than a router call, so
 * nothing here depends on a routing library.
 */
export function useSlabNavigation(): SlabNavigation {
  const host = useRef<SlabRunner | null>(null);

  const navigate = useCallback(
    (commit: () => void, options?: SlabNavigateOptions) => {
      const runner = host.current;
      // No mounted component — the caller wired the hook up but rendered the
      // transition conditionally, or this fired during the first commit.
      // Navigate anyway. A transition that swallows navigations is worse than
      // no transition.
      if (!runner) {
        commit();
        return;
      }
      runner.run(commit, options);
    },
    [],
  );

  return useMemo(() => ({ host, navigate }), [navigate]);
}

export interface SlabPageTransitionProps {
  /** From `useSlabNavigation()`. */
  controller: SlabNavigation;
  /** The current page. Swapped by the `commit` you hand to `navigate`. */
  children: ReactNode;
  /** Seconds for ONE half. The full gesture is `2 * duration + hold`. */
  duration?: number;
  /** Seconds the slab holds at full cover between the halves. */
  hold?: number;
  /**
   * Default travel. `up` sends everything upward; `down` mirrors it, which is
   * what a back navigation wants. Overridable per navigation.
   */
  direction?: 'up' | 'down';
  /** Any CSS colour. Must be opaque, or the swap shows through the slab. */
  color?: string;
  /** Applied to the label span so the caller owns its type. */
  labelClassName?: string;
  /** `absolute` to demo inside a bounded box; `fixed` for a real page. */
  position?: 'fixed' | 'absolute';
  /** Above the site, below a preloader. */
  zIndex?: number;
  className?: string;
}

export function SlabPageTransition({
  controller,
  children,
  duration = SLAB_DURATION,
  hold = SLAB_HOLD,
  direction = 'up',
  color = '#000',
  labelClassName,
  position = 'fixed',
  zIndex = 190,
  className,
}: SlabPageTransitionProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const content = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const slab = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const labelEl = useRef<HTMLSpanElement>(null);

  const timeline = useRef<ReturnType<typeof gsap.timeline> | null>(null);
  const pending = useRef<(() => void) | null>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  // Read inside the tweens' function-based values, so flipping direction
  // between navigations needs no rebuild — and therefore no `revert()`, which
  // would strip the transform GSAP is mid-way through writing. Set in `run`,
  // never during render: `play(0)` renders the timeline synchronously, so a
  // value that only lands on the next React commit would be read one frame
  // too late and the two halves would disagree about which way is out.
  const dir = useRef<'up' | 'down'>(direction);
  const defaultDir = useRef(direction);
  defaultDir.current = direction;

  // Built once and held paused. `direction` is deliberately NOT a dependency:
  // `useGsap` reverts on every dependency change, and revert removes the
  // inline transform, so a rebuild during a transition drops the slab back to
  // its CSS park mid-cover and the swap is visible.
  useGsap(
    gsap,
    () => {
      const rootEl = root.current;
      const contentEl = content.current;
      const slabEl = slab.current;
      if (!rootEl || !contentEl || !slabEl) return;

      // Travel in pixels, measured per run. `yPercent: -100` would be 100% of
      // the CONTENT's own height — on a long page that is the whole document,
      // so the page would fly thousands of pixels instead of one screen. The
      // original wrote `y: '-100vh'` for exactly this reason; measuring the
      // real box also gets the bounded case right, where one screen is the
      // container and not the viewport.
      const travel = () =>
        position === 'fixed'
          ? window.innerHeight
          : rootEl.getBoundingClientRect().height;
      const sign = () => (dir.current === 'down' ? -1 : 1);

      const tl = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });

      tl.to(contentEl, { y: () => -travel() * sign(), duration, ease: SLAB_EASE }, 0)
        .fromTo(
          slabEl,
          { y: () => travel() * sign() },
          { y: 0, duration, ease: SLAB_EASE },
          0,
        )
        // Midpoint. The slab is exactly covering the frame for the whole of
        // this and the `set` below, so neither is ever seen.
        .add(() => {
          const commit = pending.current;
          pending.current = null;
          commit?.();
        })
        .set(contentEl, { y: () => travel() * sign() })
        .to(
          slabEl,
          { y: () => -travel() * sign(), duration, ease: SLAB_EASE },
          duration + hold,
        )
        .to(contentEl, { y: 0, duration, ease: SLAB_EASE }, duration + hold)
        // Re-park the slab below the frame at the very end, so `progress(0)`
        // and `progress(1)` describe the same rest state and a second run
        // starts from a known place rather than from wherever it stopped.
        .set(slabEl, { y: () => travel() * sign() });

      timeline.current = tl;

      return () => {
        timeline.current = null;
        // A dependency change reverts and kills this timeline. If it happened
        // mid-transition the commit had not fired yet, so fire it here: the
        // visitor clicked a link and must end up on that page whatever the
        // animation did.
        const commit = pending.current;
        pending.current = null;
        commit?.();
      };
    },
    root,
    [duration, hold, position],
  );

  const run = useCallback(
    (commit: () => void, options?: SlabNavigateOptions) => {
      const tl = timeline.current;
      const span = labelEl.current;
      if (span) span.textContent = options?.label ?? '';
      dir.current = options?.direction ?? defaultDir.current;

      // Reduced motion: no slab and a synchronous commit. Not a zero-duration
      // slab — that is still one frame of full-frame colour, which is the
      // single most unpleasant thing to show someone who asked for less
      // motion. `pause(0)` suppresses callbacks, so the midpoint `.call()`
      // cannot fire a second commit.
      if (!tl || reduced) {
        tl?.pause(0);
        commit();
        return;
      }
      // A second click while the slab is in flight would queue a second commit
      // and land the visitor one page past where they aimed.
      if (tl.isActive()) return;

      pending.current = commit;
      // `invalidate()` before replaying re-evaluates every function-based
      // value: the box may have been resized, and `direction` may have
      // flipped, since the timeline was built. Without it the slab travels the
      // height the container had on mount.
      tl.invalidate().play(0);
    },
    [reduced],
  );

  useEffect(() => {
    const host = controller.host;
    host.current = { run };
    return () => {
      if (host.current?.run === run) host.current = null;
    };
  }, [controller, run]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useGsap` reverts the `gsap.context`, which kills the timeline and strips every inline transform it wrote — restoring the slab to the parked position its stylesheet rule specifies and the page to `y: 0`. The cleanup also flushes any commit that had not fired yet, so a prop change mid-transition cannot lose a navigation. The runner registration is removed from the controller on unmount, and it is removed only if it is still the current one, so a remount cannot null out the live handle.

**Reduced motion.** The timeline is never played. `navigate()` calls the commit synchronously and `tl.pause(0)` resets the slab to its rest position — deliberately not a zero-duration slab, which is still one frame of full-frame colour. `pause()` suppresses callbacks, so the midpoint `.call()` cannot fire a second commit. Navigation is a hard cut straight to the destination in both directions.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Using `yPercent: -100` on the page wrapper. Percentage transforms resolve against the element's OWN height, so on a 6000 px page the wrapper travels 6000 px in 0.8 s and the screen just goes blank a frame in. The travel has to be one screen — measured in pixels, or written as the original did with an explicit `vh` unit.
- Reversing the slab instead of driving it through. `tl.reverse()` after the commit sends the slab back down the way it came, and the eye reads the whole thing as a mistake being undone rather than as a move. The second half is a separate forward tween to `-H`.
- One `power3.inOut` across the full 2H travel. That ease is at maximum speed at its own midpoint, which is exactly the frame the route changes on, so the slab appears to accelerate straight through the cover and the label is unreadable.
- Putting the direction flag in the `useGsap` dependency list. Every dependency change reverts the context, and `revert()` strips the inline transform GSAP is mid-way through writing — so flipping direction during a transition drops the slab back to its CSS park while it is meant to be covering, and the content swap is visible. Direction is read from a ref by function-based values instead.
- Parking the slab with `gsap.set` in an effect. Effects run after the first paint, so the first frame of the page is a full-frame slab. The rest position belongs in a stylesheet; GSAP overrides it from the inline style the moment it is needed.
- Setting the slab label through state. `setLabel()` inside the navigate handler re-renders the subtree React is about to hand to GSAP on the exact frame the timeline starts. The label is one `textContent` write on a ref, and the slab is off-frame when it happens.
- Letting a second click start a second run. Without the `tl.isActive()` guard a double click queues two commits and the visitor lands one page past where they aimed.
- Dropping the commit when the timeline is destroyed. If a prop change reverts the context mid-transition, the `.call()` never fires and the route never changes — the visitor clicked a link and stayed put. The `useGsap` cleanup flushes any pending commit.
- Leaving the slab clickable. A full-frame opaque div swallows the pointer for the length of the transition, and mid-transition the pointer is usually already aimed at the next nav item. It carries `pointer-events: none` and `aria-hidden`.

## Notes

- In Next.js App Router: mount once in `app/layout.tsx` with `position="fixed"`, then replace nav `<Link>` elements with buttons calling `navigate(() => router.push(href), { label })`. Nothing in this file imports `next/navigation` — the commit is a callback, so the same component works under React Router or a plain `useState` page switch.
- The content wrapper stays in normal flow. A transform moves an element without taking it out of flow, so the page keeps its own height and the document still scrolls — which an `absolute inset-0` wrapper would break on any real page.
- The colour must be opaque. A translucent slab shows the content teleport at the midpoint, which is the single artefact this technique exists to hide.
- Browser back and forward change the route without going through `navigate()`, so they get no slab. That is correct: by the time your code hears about a history navigation it has already happened, and there is nothing left to cover.
- Set `direction: "down"` per navigation for anything that reads as going back — an up-nav click, a breadcrumb, a close button — and the site acquires a sense of which way the visitor is travelling for the cost of one ternary.

## Definition of done

Click a nav item: the page slides up out of frame while a coloured slab rises from below, the slab pauses at full cover with the destination name on it, then continues up and out while the new page follows it in from below. The slab never travels downward on a forward navigation, and there is no frame in which old and new content are both visible. Click a nav item to the left of the current one and the whole gesture mirrors — everything travels down. Click two items in quick succession and you land on the first one you clicked, not past it. Resize the preview and navigate again: the slab still travels exactly one frame height. With reduced motion the content swaps instantly with no coloured frame in either direction.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Slow Idle Float

The ambient motion you put on a hero image, a floating card or a badge so the page does not feel frozen. Fourteen pixels over five seconds is under the threshold at which the eye tracks it as movement — you read it as presence. Because it animates `translate` rather than `transform`, the element can still carry a hover scale or a tilt without the two fighting.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A 14px rise and fall over 5 seconds, on the independent translate property so hover transforms still work.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. A two-pose keyframe: `0%, 100% { translate: 0 0 }` and `50% { translate: var(--kx-float-x) var(--kx-float-y) }`. Both endpoints of the round trip are the resting position, so the loop has no seam and the element always returns to exactly its layout position.
2. The animated property is `translate`, not `transform`. They are separate properties that compose in the order translate, rotate, scale, transform — so a consumer can put `hover:scale-105` (a `transform`) on the same element and both apply. An animation on `transform` would instead override any transition on `transform` for its entire duration, and the hover would appear dead.
3. Direction comes from custom properties rather than separate keyframe blocks: `axis="y"` writes `--kx-float-y: -14px` and leaves X at 0, `axis="x"` does the reverse. One keyframe block covers both axes and any diagonal a consumer wants to set by hand.
4. `phase` is applied as a negative `animation-delay` — `-durationMs * phase`. A negative delay means the animation is treated as having already been running for that long, so an element starts mid-flight on its first painted frame. A positive delay would make it sit dead still until its turn came round, which is exactly what makes staggered idle animations look broken on load.
5. `ease-in-out` is what makes it buoyant. The element decelerates into both extremes and hangs there; `linear` gives constant velocity and reads as a mechanical lift.
6. `will-change: translate` names the property that is actually animating. `will-change: transform` — the reflex — hints at a property this component never touches.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `distance = 14px`
  Peak travel. Average speed works out at roughly 11px per second, which is below the rate at which the eye starts tracking an object instead of just registering it. Under about 6px the motion is invisible on a 1x display; over about 24px it reads as a balloon on a string and pulls focus from the content.
- `durationMs = 5000`
  The round trip. Faster than about 3s and it becomes a pulse that competes with real feedback in the UI; slower than about 8s and the element appears to have simply drifted out of position rather than to be floating.
- `timing function = ease-in-out`
  Buoyancy comes from the hold at the two extremes. `linear` moves at constant velocity, which reads as a machine; `ease-out` alone makes the return leg abrupt and the loop develops a visible tick at 100%.
- `phase sign = negative`
  Negative delay starts the animation partway through its first cycle instead of postponing it. With a positive delay a staggered group is motionless for the first phase*duration milliseconds after mount — on a five-second cycle with four items that is several seconds of a page that looks frozen.

## API

```ts
function SlowFloatIdle(props: { children: ReactNode; distance?: number; durationMs?: number; axis?: 'x' | 'y'; phase?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  What floats. Wrapped in a block-level element that owns the `translate`.
- `distance: number` — default `14`
  Peak travel in pixels, reached at the midpoint of the cycle.
- `durationMs: number` — default `5000`
  Full round trip in milliseconds.
- `axis: 'x' | 'y'` — default `'y'`
  Direction of travel. `y` rises then falls; `x` drifts right then back.
- `phase: number` — default `0`
  Start position in the cycle, 0-1. Applied as a negative `animation-delay`.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the wrapper via `cn`. Safe to use `transform`-based utilities here — the float does not use `transform`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const FLOAT_CSS = `
@keyframes kx-float-idle {
  0%, 100% { translate: 0 0; }
  50%      { translate: var(--kx-float-x, 0px) var(--kx-float-y, -14px); }
}

.kx-float {
  display: block;
  animation: kx-float-idle var(--kx-float-duration, 5s) ease-in-out infinite;
  animation-delay: var(--kx-float-delay, 0s);
  /* Names the property that is actually animating. 'will-change: transform'
     is the reflex here and it hints at the wrong property entirely. */
  will-change: translate;
}

/* No motion: the element rests at its natural layout position, not at the
   midpoint of the float. The hint is released too — a promoted layer for an
   animation that is not running is pure GPU memory. */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .kx-float {
    animation: none;
    will-change: auto;
  }
}
`;

export function SlowFloatIdle({
  children,
  distance = 14,
  durationMs = 5000,
  axis = 'y',
  phase = 0,
  className,
}: SlowFloatIdleProps) {
  const style: StyleWithVars = {
    '--kx-float-duration': `${durationMs}ms`,
    // Negative: the animation is treated as having already run for this long,
    // so a set of floats is out of phase from the very first frame.
    '--kx-float-delay': `${-durationMs * phase}ms`,
    // Rise, not fall: negative Y is up. X drifts right on the positive side.
    '--kx-float-x': axis === 'x' ? `${distance}px` : '0px',
    '--kx-float-y': axis === 'y' ? `${-distance}px` : '0px',
  };

  return (
    <>
      <style href="kinetic-slow-float-idle" precedence="medium">
        {FLOAT_CSS}
      </style>
      <div className={cn('kx-float', className)} style={style}>
        {children}
      </div>
    </>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to clean up. No listeners, no timers, no animation frames. Unmounting removes the element and its CSS animation; React removes the hoisted `<style>` when the last instance unmounts.

**Reduced motion.** A `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block sets `animation: none` and `will-change: auto`. The element rests at its natural layout position — not at the top of the float — so nothing shifts and no gap appears where the animation used to be.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Animating `transform` instead of `translate`. Animations beat transitions on the same property for as long as they run, so a `transition: transform` hover on the same element never has a visible effect — the hover looks broken and the cause is a keyframe elsewhere in the file.
- Animating `top` or `margin-top` for the float. Those are layout properties: the ancestor reflows on every frame and any sibling laid out after it jitters. Only `translate`, `transform`, `opacity` and `filter` stay off the layout path.
- Staggering a group with positive `animation-delay`. Every element holds at its 0% pose until its delay expires, so the group starts as a static row and comes alive one item at a time — most visible right after a page load, which is the worst possible moment.
- Setting `will-change: transform` for an animation on `translate`. The hint names a property that never changes; the browser may still promote the layer for other reasons, so the mistake produces no error and no benefit.
- Leaving `will-change` on when reduced motion is active. The element keeps a dedicated compositor layer for an animation that has been switched off — cost with no motion in exchange.
- Parking the element at the midpoint of the float for reduced motion. The float exists to add life, not to reposition anything; freezing it 14px above its layout position leaves a permanent, unexplained gap under the element.

## Notes

- The independent `translate`, `rotate` and `scale` properties need Chrome 104+, Safari 14.1+ and Firefox 72+. In an older engine the declaration is dropped and the element simply does not float — the layout is unaffected.
- The wrapper is a `div` with `display: block`. To float an inline element, pass `className="inline-block"`; a floated `display: inline` box would have nothing to translate.
- For a group, give each instance a different `phase` — 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 for four items. Equal phases make the group move as one rigid object, which is more noticeable than no motion at all.

## Definition of done

The element rises about 14px, hangs, and settles back over five seconds with no visible tick at the loop point. Add a `hover:scale-110` to the same element and the scale still works while the float continues. Give three instances phases 0, 0.33 and 0.66 and all three are already at different heights on the first painted frame. With reduced motion on, the element sits exactly where the layout puts it.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
