# Build: Wheel Accumulator Stepper

`wheel` is four input devices wearing one event name. A mouse notch is a single event carrying 100 units; a trackpad swipe is forty events of four units each, followed by a synthesised momentum tail that keeps arriving for about a second after the fingers lift; and `deltaMode` decides whether those numbers are pixels, lines, or whole pages. This hook scales the delta by `deltaMode`, sums it, and emits one step per 90 normalised pixels — then latches, and re-arms only when the incoming magnitude stops decaying, which is the one signal that separates a fresh flick from the tail of the last one.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Wheel input normalised by deltaMode and accumulated to a threshold, so one flick of any device moves exactly one step.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. `wheelDelta(e, axis)` picks the axis — `Math.abs(deltaX) > Math.abs(deltaY) ? deltaX : deltaY` for `both`, so a sideways two-finger swipe and a mouse wheel drive the same widget — then multiplies by the scale `deltaMode` implies: 1 for pixel mode, 40 for line mode, 800 for page mode. Everything downstream counts pixels.
2. A signed accumulator sums the normalised deltas. While `Math.abs(units) >= step` it subtracts one signed `step` and calls `onStep(direction, detail)`, capped at `maxPerEvent` iterations. One mouse notch (100 units) clears the 90-unit threshold on its own; a trackpad swipe clears it after roughly a dozen events. No device detection anywhere.
3. After any step the accumulator is zeroed rather than left holding the remainder, and a latch closes. `peak` records the magnitude of the event that fired the step.
4. While latched, an event whose magnitude is below `peak` is absorbed: no accumulation, no step, but `preventDefault` still runs so the page does not scroll underneath the widget. The first event whose magnitude reaches `peak` re-arms. macOS momentum is monotonically decreasing, so a tail can never reach its own peak and is swallowed entirely; the next notch of a mouse wheel has an identical magnitude and re-arms immediately; a second deliberate flick exceeds it on its first event.
5. Two further resets bypass the latch: a gap greater than `gestureGapMs` since the previous accepted event, which means the gesture and its tail are finished, and a change of sign, since no momentum tail reverses direction.
6. `e.ctrlKey` events return before `preventDefault` and before accumulation — that combination is pinch-zoom on a trackpad and page zoom on a mouse, and swallowing it removes the only way to enlarge the page.
7. The listener is registered `{ passive: !preventDefault }`, so it is non-passive exactly when it intends to cancel. The live accumulator is exposed as a `RefObject`, not state, so a gauge can read it every frame without re-rendering the widget forty times per swipe.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `STEP = 90`
  Normalised pixels per step. It has to sit below one mouse notch so a single notch always moves exactly one item — Chrome reports 100 per notch and legacy browsers 120, so anything above 100 makes a mouse feel broken. Going much below ~60 puts it inside the range of a small trackpad twitch and the widget steps when the user meant to scroll past it.
- `LINE_UNITS = 40`
  Pixels assumed per line for `deltaMode === 1`. Firefox reports line mode on several platforms, where `deltaY` is typically 3 — 3 x 40 = 120 units, which matches what the same physical notch reports as pixels in Chrome. Using 1 here (i.e. not normalising at all) makes the stepper need thirty notches per step in Firefox and one in Chrome.
- `PAGE_UNITS = 800`
  Pixels assumed per page for `deltaMode === 2`. Roughly one viewport. The exact figure barely matters because any page-mode event is far past the threshold; what matters is that it is not 1, which would make a full-page wheel event register as almost no movement.
- `GESTURE_GAP_MS = 140`
  Silence that ends a gesture. Momentum tail events arrive at frame rate, so ~8-17 ms apart; sustained finger input is similar. 140 ms is far above both and far below the ~250 ms a person needs to lift, reposition, and flick again, so it never splits one gesture in two and never merges two.
- `MAX_PER_EVENT = 1`
  Steps emitted from a single event. One event should mean at most one step, and with the latch in place the only thing this guards is a single enormous delta — a page-mode wheel worth 800 units, or a synthetic event from an automation script, either of which would otherwise advance eight items in one frame. Raise it to 2 or 3 if a violent flick should travel further; the demo keeps it at 1.

## API

```ts
function useWheelStepper(ref: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>, options: { step?: number; axis?: 'both' | 'x' | 'y'; maxPerEvent?: number; gestureGapMs?: number; preventDefault?: boolean; enabled?: boolean; onStep: (direction: 1 | -1, detail: { index: number; delta: number; deltaMode: number; event: WheelEvent }) => void }): { units: RefObject<number>; latched: RefObject<boolean> }
function wheelDelta(e: WheelEvent, axis?: 'both' | 'x' | 'y'): number
function wheelUnitScale(deltaMode: number): number
```

- `step: number` — default `90`
  Normalised pixels of travel per emitted step. Must stay below one mouse notch (100).
- `axis: 'both' | 'x' | 'y'` — default `'both'`
  `both` uses whichever of `deltaX` / `deltaY` dominates, so horizontal and vertical input both work.
- `maxPerEvent: number` — default `1`
  Ceiling on steps emitted from one event. Guards a single page-mode delta worth 800 units.
- `gestureGapMs: number` — default `140`
  Silence that ends the gesture and clears the latch. Above frame interval, below a human reflick.
- `preventDefault: boolean` — default `true`
  Cancel the page scroll on every accepted event. Also decides whether the listener is passive.
- `enabled: boolean` — default `true`
  Detaches the listener when false — for a widget that only owns the wheel while open.
- `onStep: (direction: 1 | -1, detail: WheelStepDetail) => void`
  Called once per step, synchronously in the wheel handler. `+1` is down or right.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** Normalised pixels per step. */
const STEP = 90;
/** Pixels per line for `deltaMode === 1`. */
const LINE_UNITS = 40;
/** Pixels per page for `deltaMode === 2`. */
const PAGE_UNITS = 800;
/** Milliseconds of silence that end a gesture. */
const GESTURE_GAP_MS = 140;
/** Steps allowed out of one event. */
const MAX_PER_EVENT = 1;

/** The pixel scale implied by `deltaMode`. Unknown modes are treated as pixels. */
export function wheelUnitScale(deltaMode: number): number {
  if (deltaMode === 1) return LINE_UNITS;
  if (deltaMode === 2) return PAGE_UNITS;
  return 1;
}

/**
 * One wheel event as normalised pixels on the chosen axis.
 *
 * `'both'` takes whichever axis dominates, so a two-finger sideways swipe and
 * a mouse wheel drive the same widget and the user never has to discover
 * which axis it wanted.
 */
export function wheelDelta(e: WheelEvent, axis: WheelAxis = 'both'): number {
  const raw =
    axis === 'x'
      ? e.deltaX
      : axis === 'y'
        ? e.deltaY
        : Math.abs(e.deltaX) > Math.abs(e.deltaY)
          ? e.deltaX
          : e.deltaY;
  return raw * wheelUnitScale(e.deltaMode);
}

/**
 * Turn continuous wheel input into discrete steps, one per physical gesture.
 *
 * Attaches to `ref`, so the widget owns the wheel only while the pointer is
 * over it. Nothing is published as state: `onStep` fires on the event and the
 * live accumulator is a ref.
 */
export function useWheelStepper(
  ref: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>,
  options: UseWheelStepperOptions,
): WheelStepperState {
  const {
    step = STEP,
    axis = 'both',
    maxPerEvent = MAX_PER_EVENT,
    gestureGapMs = GESTURE_GAP_MS,
    preventDefault = true,
    enabled = true,
  } = options;

  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  const units = useRef(0);
  const latched = useRef(false);

  const config = useRef({ step, axis, maxPerEvent, gestureGapMs, reduced, options });
  config.current = { step, axis, maxPerEvent, gestureGapMs, reduced, options };

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = ref.current;
    if (!el || !enabled) return;

    /** `timeStamp` of the previous accepted event, for the gesture gap. */
    let lastTime = 0;
    /** Largest magnitude seen since the latch closed. */
    let peak = 0;

    const onWheel = (e: WheelEvent) => {
      // ctrl+wheel is pinch-zoom on a trackpad and page zoom on a mouse.
      // Swallowing it takes away the user's only way to enlarge the page, so
      // it is passed through untouched — no preventDefault, no accumulation.
      if (e.ctrlKey) return;

      const cfg = config.current;
      const delta = wheelDelta(e, cfg.axis);
      // A pure cross-axis event on a single-axis widget, or the zero-delta
      // event some drivers emit at the end of a gesture. Neither is input.
      if (delta === 0) return;

      // Before the latch check, not after: while the widget is absorbing a
      // momentum tail the page must not scroll underneath it instead.
      if (preventDefault) e.preventDefault();

      const magnitude = Math.abs(delta);
      const gap = e.timeStamp - lastTime;
      lastTime = e.timeStamp;

      // Silence long enough to outlast a momentum tail's frame interval means
      // the previous gesture is over in every sense. Start clean.
      if (gap > cfg.gestureGapMs) {
        units.current = 0;
        latched.current = false;
      }

      // A reversal is always deliberate — no momentum tail changes sign — so
      // it clears both the latch and any units banked in the other direction.
      if (units.current !== 0 && Math.sign(delta) !== Math.sign(units.current)) {
        units.current = 0;
        latched.current = false;
      }

      if (latched.current) {
        // The whole technique. A tail decays, so it never reaches the peak it
        // had when the step fired; a new flick or the next wheel notch does,
        // on its first event. Magnitude alone cannot tell them apart and a
        // fixed cooldown either eats the second flick or leaks the tail.
        if (magnitude < peak) return;
        latched.current = false;
      }

      units.current += delta;

      // Reduced motion caps the burst at one step regardless of the option:
      // travelling several items from one flick is the motion-heavy part.
      const limit = cfg.reduced ? 1 : Math.max(1, cfg.maxPerEvent);
      let fired = 0;

      while (Math.abs(units.current) >= cfg.step && fired < limit) {
        const direction: 1 | -1 = units.current > 0 ? 1 : -1;
        units.current -= cfg.step * direction;
        cfg.options.onStep(direction, {
          index: fired,
          delta,
          deltaMode: e.deltaMode,
          event: e,
        });
        fired += 1;
      }

      if (fired > 0) {
        // Zeroed, not left with the remainder: a flick's overshoot belongs to
        // the flick that is now finished, and banking it means the next
        // gesture starts part-way to a step and fires early.
        units.current = 0;
        latched.current = true;
        peak = magnitude;
      }
    };

    // Non-passive only when it actually calls preventDefault. Registering
    // non-passive unconditionally opts the element out of the scrolling fast
    // path for nothing; calling preventDefault inside a passive listener is
    // ignored with a console error, which is the same bug from the other end.
    el.addEventListener('wheel', onWheel, { passive: !preventDefault });
    return () => {
      el.removeEventListener('wheel', onWheel);
      units.current = 0;
      latched.current = false;
    };
  }, [ref, enabled, preventDefault]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The effect removes the `wheel` listener with the same capture flag it was added with, and zeroes both the accumulator and the latch so a remount does not inherit half a gesture. There is no timer, no rAF, and no pointer capture to release. Re-running under React 19 StrictMode is harmless: the second effect attaches a second listener only after the first has removed its own.

**Reduced motion.** Steps still fire — a step is the user's input, not decoration, and suppressing it would leave the widget unresponsive. What changes is the burst: the per-event step count is clamped to 1 regardless of `maxPerEvent`, so a violent flick advances one item instead of travelling several in a single frame. Whatever the consumer animates in response to a step is where a reduced-motion transition belongs.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Reading `deltaY` without reading `deltaMode`. The same physical notch is `deltaY: 100` in pixel mode and `deltaY: 3` in line mode, so a threshold tuned in Chrome needs about thirty notches per step in a line-mode browser. The bug never reproduces on the developer's machine.
- Stepping on every wheel event. A trackpad emits thirty to forty events per swipe, so a carousel jumps thirty slides for one gesture — the single most common wheel bug and the reason the accumulator exists at all.
- Accumulating with no latch. The accumulator fixes the burst but not the tail: macOS keeps synthesising decaying wheel events for about a second after the fingers lift, and a hard flick has enough left in that tail for three or four more thresholds. The carousel takes one step under your fingers and then keeps going on its own.
- Latching with a fixed cooldown instead. A cooldown long enough to outlast the tail (roughly 600-1000 ms) also eats the second of two deliberate flicks, so the widget feels dead when hurried; a cooldown short enough to keep double flicks alive lets the loud part of the tail through. Decay is the only signal that separates the two cases.
- Comparing each tail event against the previous event rather than against the peak. Tail magnitudes jitter, so `39 >= 38` looks like new input and re-arms mid-tail, which is exactly the extra step the latch was added to prevent. Comparing against the peak since the latch closed cannot be fooled by jitter.
- Carrying the leftover units past a step. Zeroing looks lossy but is correct: the overshoot belongs to the gesture that just ended, and banking 80 of 90 units means the next flick fires after a single event of travel.
- Skipping `preventDefault` while the latch is absorbing the tail. The widget correctly refuses to step, and the page scrolls instead — so the carousel holds still and the whole section slides away underneath it.
- Registering the listener non-passive when it never cancels. That opts the element out of the browser's scrolling fast path for nothing. The mirror-image bug is calling `preventDefault` inside a passive listener, where it is silently ignored with a console error and the page scrolls anyway.
- Swallowing `ctrl`+wheel. That is pinch-zoom on every trackpad and page zoom on every mouse; intercepting it means a low-vision user cannot enlarge the page while the pointer is anywhere over the widget.
- Publishing the accumulator as React state. Forty state updates per swipe re-render the whole widget to move a 40 px gauge; a ref plus one CSS custom property write costs nothing and cannot tear.
- Attaching to `window` instead of the element. The widget then steps while the pointer is somewhere else entirely, and a non-passive window-level wheel listener degrades scrolling for the whole document.

## Notes

- The latch makes one gesture mean one step, which is right for a carousel, a chapter list, or anything with discrete positions. For a continuous value — a zoom level, a scrub position — drop the latch and use the normalised delta directly; the `deltaMode` scaling is the part you still need.
- `onStep` is called synchronously inside the wheel handler, so it runs before the frame that would have scrolled. Keep it to a state update or a ref write; layout reads there cost a forced synchronous reflow on every notch.
- A trackpad in a browser that supports it will also fire `gesturestart` / `gesturechange` for pinch, which is a separate event stream. This hook deliberately ignores it rather than trying to reconstruct pinch from `ctrl`+wheel.

## Definition of done

Wheel over the panel with a mouse: every notch moves exactly one item, and a fast spin moves one per notch with no skipping. Flick hard on a trackpad and let go: the index advances exactly once and then holds still while the readout shows the tail arriving and being absorbed. Flick twice in quick succession and it advances twice. Push slowly and continuously and the gauge fills to the threshold before each step, so the accumulation is visible. Reverse direction mid-gesture and it steps back without first having to unwind the units already banked. Hold ctrl and wheel: the browser zooms, and the index does not move. Scroll the outer page with the pointer just outside the panel and the panel ignores it.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Shortest Signed Ring Offset

A ring of items laid out from `wrappedOffset(i, position, count)` — the shortest signed distance around the circle — with the naive `i - position` printed beside each one so the two can be compared while the ring turns. The dots move continuously through the seam; the raw numbers leap by a whole count at it. This is the single function that makes a finite array behave like an infinite one, and the only honest way to teach it is to show the version it replaces failing.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Ten dots on a ring, each showing its wrapped offset and the raw index difference it replaces.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. `wrappedOffset(i, position, count)` computes `mod(i - position, count)` and then subtracts `count` when the result exceeds `count / 2`, producing a signed distance in `(-count/2, count/2]`. Negative means the item is behind the read head.
2. Each item is placed at `angle = (offset / count) * 2PI - PI/2`, so offset 0 sits under the notch at twelve o'clock and the ring is symmetric about it. Because a ±count jump in the offset is exactly one full turn, the dot lands on the same pixel and the seam is invisible.
3. Focus is `gaussian(|offset|, 0.45)` — `exp(-(0.45·d)²)` — driving scale from 0.74 to 1.20 and opacity from 0.30 to 1.00. A continuous falloff with no thresholds is what makes the ring read as analogue rather than stepped.
4. Dragging converts the pointer to an angle about the ring centre with `atan2`, then advances the target position by `shortestAngle(previous, current) / 2PI * count`. `shortestAngle` is required here for the same reason `wrappedOffset` is required for the layout: `atan2` flips from +PI to -PI at nine o'clock.
5. The ring position is eased with `damp(position, target, 0.0015, dt)` on the shared rAF loop, and every frame writes only `transform`, `opacity` and `z-index` — no layout reads, because width and height come from a ResizeObserver rather than `clientWidth`.
6. React re-renders only when `wrapIndex(Math.round(position), count)` changes, which is a couple of times a second; the sixty-times-a-second work is plain style writes on refs.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `count = 10`
  Items on the ring, and therefore the wrap threshold at count / 2 = 5. Ten keeps every raw label at most two characters wide, so the pills fit on a 320 px preview without colliding; above ~16 the labels overlap tangentially and the comparison becomes unreadable.
- `FOCUS_FALLOFF = 0.45`
  Gaussian falloff on |offset|. Yields 1.00 / 0.82 / 0.44 / 0.16 / 0.04 at distances 0-4, so roughly four items read as "near" on a ten-item ring. At 1.0 only the centre item is lit and the ring looks broken; at 0.2 nothing falls off and there is no focus at all.
- `SMOOTHING = 0.0015`
  Fraction of the remaining gap left after one second. Fast enough that the ring feels attached to the pointer, slow enough that releasing mid-drag reads as momentum rather than a cut. This is `damp`'s smoothing argument, not a per-frame lerp constant — a per-frame constant converges twice as fast at 120 Hz.
- `RADIUS_RATIO = 0.36`
  Ring radius as a fraction of the shorter container side. Above ~0.42 the 36 px pills clip the edges of a 16:10 frame; below ~0.30 adjacent pills touch.
- `IDLE_DRIFT = 0.22`
  Ring positions per second before the first interaction, so the seam sweeps past roughly every 45 s and the component demonstrates itself without being touched. Faster than ~0.6 and the raw labels change too quickly to read.
- `threshold (useDrag) = 3`
  Pixels of travel before a press becomes a rotation. Lower than the 8 px a carousel wants, because this ring has no click target to protect — it only has to reject hand tremor.

## API

```ts
function WrappedRingOffset(props: { count?: number; drift?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `count: number` — default `10`
  Items on the ring. The wrap threshold is count / 2.
- `drift: number` — default `0.22`
  Ring positions per second before the first interaction. 0 to sit still.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the outer element via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** Fraction of the gap to the target that survives one second. */
const SMOOTHING = 0.0015;
/** Gaussian falloff on |offset|. At 0.45: 1.00 / 0.82 / 0.44 / 0.16 / 0.04. */
const FOCUS_FALLOFF = 0.45;
const RADIUS_RATIO = 0.36;
const IDLE_DRIFT = 0.22;

export function WrappedRingOffset({
  count = 10,
  drift = IDLE_DRIFT,
  className,
}: WrappedRingOffsetProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const nodes = useRef<(HTMLLIElement | null)[]>([]);

  /** Where the ring is being pulled to. Fractional and unbounded. */
  const target = useRef(0);
  /** Where the ring actually is. Eased toward `target`. */
  const position = useRef(0);
  /** Suppresses the idle drift once a human has touched it. */
  const engaged = useRef(false);
  const grabAngle = useRef(0);
  const shown = useRef(0);

  const [index, setIndex] = useState(0);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(root);

  /** Pointer angle around the ring centre, measured fresh: the page scrolls. */
  const angleAt = useCallback((clientX: number, clientY: number) => {
    const box = root.current?.getBoundingClientRect();
    if (!box) return 0;
    return Math.atan2(clientY - (box.top + box.height / 2), clientX - (box.left + box.width / 2));
  }, []);

  useDrag(root, {
    threshold: 3,
    onDragStart: (s) => {
      engaged.current = true;
      grabAngle.current = angleAt(s.clientX, s.clientY);
    },
    onDrag: (s) => {
      const angle = angleAt(s.clientX, s.clientY);
      // shortestAngle, not `angle - grabAngle`: atan2 flips from +PI to -PI at
      // nine o'clock, and the raw difference there is a full turn of garbage
      // that spins the ring backwards every time the pointer crosses it.
      const step = (shortestAngle(grabAngle.current, angle) / TAU) * count;
      target.current -= step;
      grabAngle.current = angle;
    },
  });

  useRaf((dt) => {
    if (!engaged.current && !reduced) target.current += drift * dt;

    // Reduced motion still moves the ring — it just does not ease into place.
    position.current = reduced
      ? target.current
      : damp(position.current, target.current, SMOOTHING, dt);

    const p = position.current;
    const radius = Math.min(width, height) * RADIUS_RATIO;

    for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
      const el = nodes.current[i];
      if (!el) continue;

      // The one line the whole component exists to demonstrate. `offset` is
      // continuous in `p` even across the seam, because the ±count jump maps
      // to exactly one turn of the circle and lands on the same place.
      const offset = wrappedOffset(i, p, count);
      const angle = (offset / count) * TAU - Math.PI / 2;
      const focus = gaussian(Math.abs(offset), FOCUS_FALLOFF);

      const x = Math.cos(angle) * radius;
      const y = Math.sin(angle) * radius;
      // translate3d places the box origin, translate(-50%,-50%) re-centres it,
      // scale runs about that centre. One string, one composited property.
      el.style.transform = `translate3d(${x.toFixed(2)}px, ${y.toFixed(2)}px, 0) translate(-50%, -50%) scale(${(0.74 + focus * 0.46).toFixed(3)})`;
      el.style.opacity = (0.3 + focus * 0.7).toFixed(3);
      el.style.zIndex = String(10 + Math.round(focus * 40));
    }

    // Labels are integers, so they only need a render when the rounded ring
    // position changes — a couple of times a second, not sixty.
    const next = wrapIndex(Math.round(p), count);
    if (next !== shown.current) {
      shown.current = next;
      setIndex(next);
    }
  });
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useDrag` removes its five pointer listeners and releases any outstanding pointer capture; `useRaf` unsubscribes and cancels the shared frame when it was the last subscriber; `useResizeObserver` unobserves the root. No transforms are left behind because the nodes unmount with the component.

**Reduced motion.** The idle drift never starts and the `damp` easing is bypassed, so the ring tracks the drag one-to-one and stops dead on release. Dragging and the arrow keys still work, and the labels still update — the maths is the content here, so removing it would remove the component.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Using `i - position` for layout. The ring still turns, but item 0 renders nine slots away from item 9 instead of one slot back, so the last item snaps across the entire ring every time the position passes zero. That snap is the seam, and it is the whole reason this function exists.
- Using `%` instead of a true modulo. JavaScript's `%` returns a negative result for negative operands, so scrolling backwards past zero produces offsets outside `[0, count)` and half the ring inverts. `mod(n, m) = ((n % m) + m) % m` is the fix.
- Comparing `offset > count / 2` with `>=`. On an even count that puts the antipodal item at `-count/2` instead of `+count/2`, and the item directly opposite the read head flickers between the two on alternate frames.
- Taking `angle - previousAngle` when converting pointer motion to rotation. `atan2` wraps from +PI to -PI at nine o'clock, so the raw difference there is a full turn and the ring spins backwards once per lap. `shortestAngle` wraps the difference into `(-PI, PI]`.
- Reading `element.clientWidth` inside the rAF callback to compute the radius. The same loop has already written transforms, so every read forces a synchronous reflow — sixty per second, and it only shows up as jank once there are a few of these on a page. The size comes from a ResizeObserver instead.
- Driving the per-item transforms through React state. Sixty commits a second for ten nodes is an order of magnitude more work than writing `style.transform` on refs, and it makes the labels — which change twice a second — re-render at frame rate for nothing.

## Notes

- `wrappedOffset` is the same three lines behind an infinite marquee, a drum carousel, a cylinder of image planes, and any "closest N to the playhead" query. Pair it with a scroll library set to `infinite: true` and the sequence has no beginning and no end.
- The idle drift stops permanently at the first drag or arrow key. An ambient motion that resumes on top of a user's input reads as the component fighting them.

## Definition of done

Leave it alone: the ring drifts and, as each item passes the six o'clock antipode, its struck-through raw label flips sign by the full count while the dot itself does not move. Drag the ring in a full circle past nine o'clock and it keeps turning in the same direction. Press ArrowRight and the position readout increments by one. Resize the frame and the ring re-radiuses without the dots drifting off-centre.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Wrapping Drum Carousel

Cards sit stacked at the centre of the stage and are pushed outward by their signed distance from a fractional carousel position. That distance is wrapped into a ring, so the sequence has no first or last card and the position variable can drift forever. The drum reads as three-dimensional but every transform is flat: `rotationY` and `z` are pinned to zero on purpose.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

An endless carousel that reads as a rotating drum with no 3D at all — only x, scale and fading opacity.

- Category: layout
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. `gsap.utils.wrap(-count / 2, count / 2)` turns `i - pos` into a signed ring offset in `(-count/2, count/2]`. For six cards at `pos = 0`, card 5 resolves to `-1` and renders one slot to the *left* of centre instead of five slots right — this single call is what makes a finite array behave like an endless one.
2. Horizontal placement is `x = offset * step` where `step = min(spacingRatio * stage.clientWidth, maxSpacing)`. Spacing is measured off the stage element, not `window.innerWidth`, so a preview in a grid cell lays out correctly when the grid reflows rather than only when the viewport does.
3. Depth is faked by two curves with deliberately different clamps: `scale = 1 - scaleFalloff * min(distance, 1)` bottoms out one slot from centre, while `autoAlpha = clamp(0, 1, 1.15 - 0.75 * distance)` keeps falling and reaches zero at distance 1.533. Cards therefore fade out *before* they shrink far enough to look wrong, which reads as recession into fog rather than into a vanishing point.
4. `rotationY: 0` and `z: 0` are written on every `gsap.set`. They are not decoration — they stop an ancestor `perspective` or `transform-style: preserve-3d` from turning a deliberately flat drum into a half-broken 3D one that skews at the edges.
5. `zIndex = 100 - round(10 * distance)` is stepped, not continuous, so cards at similar distances do not flicker past each other as `pos` crosses an integer.
6. Drag comes from `useDrag`, which handles pointer capture, an 8 px dead zone and the capture-phase click swallow. `onDrag` divides `deltaX` by the current spacing so the drum tracks the finger 1:1, and `onDragEnd` snaps to `Math.round(pos)` with a 0.7 s `power3.out` tween whose `onUpdate` re-runs the same layout function.
7. The wheel handler accumulates `deltaX` and fires one step per 90 units, capped at 3 steps per event, then discards the remainder — an inertial trackpad flick otherwise keeps queuing steps after the fingers lift.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `spacingRatio = 0.46`
  Card spacing as a fraction of stage width. At 0.46 the neighbours are half-visible at the edges, which is what tells the user there is more to come. Below ~0.3 the cards overlap into a stack; above ~0.6 the neighbours leave the stage and the drum looks like a single card.
- `maxSpacing = 560`
  Upper bound in px. Without it a 3440 px monitor computes 1582 px of spacing and the neighbours are simply gone; the ratio has to stop scaling at roughly the width of one comfortable reading column.
- `scaleFalloff = 0.2`
  Neighbours render at 0.8. Less than ~0.12 and the depth cue disappears; more than ~0.3 and the off-centre cards look like a different component rather than the same one further away.
- `ALPHA_INTERCEPT / ALPHA_SLOPE = 1.15 / 0.75`
  Alpha is `1.15 - 0.75 * distance`. The intercept above 1 keeps the first ~0.2 of travel at full opacity so the centre card does not start dimming the instant you touch it; the slope puts the zero crossing at distance 1.533, comfortably past where scale clamps.
- `SNAP_DURATION = 0.7`
  Seconds for the release snap. Under ~0.45 the settle is abrupt enough that the drum reads as stepped; over ~0.9 a second drag arrives before the first has landed.
- `WHEEL_STEP = 90`
  Accumulated wheel units per index step. Matches roughly one detent on a mouse wheel and one deliberate trackpad swipe; at 40 a single flick advances four cards.
- `MAX_WHEEL_STEPS = 3`
  Ceiling on how many steps one wheel event may fire. A high-resolution trackpad can deliver a `deltaX` of 400+ in one event, which without the cap jumps five cards from a gesture the user read as one.
- `DRAG_THRESHOLD = 8`
  Pixels before a press counts as a drag. Below ~4 a click on a touchpad registers as a drag and the click swallow eats the tap; above ~12 short deliberate flicks are ignored.

## API

```ts
function WrappingDrumCarousel(props: { children: ReactNode; spacingRatio?: number; maxSpacing?: number; scaleFalloff?: number; className?: string; cardClassName?: string; onIndexChange?: (index: number) => void }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  One card per child. Each is wrapped in a positioned cell the component controls.
- `spacingRatio: number` — default `0.46`
  Card spacing as a fraction of the stage width.
- `maxSpacing: number` — default `560`
  Ceiling on spacing in pixels, so wide screens do not fling the neighbours off-stage.
- `scaleFalloff: number` — default `0.2`
  How much a card shrinks by one slot out from centre.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the stage element.
- `cardClassName: string`
  Merged onto every positioned cell. This is where you size the cards.
- `onIndexChange: (index: number) => void`
  Fires on every snap with the wrapped index, always in `0..count-1`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function WrappingDrumCarousel({
  children,
  spacingRatio = 0.46,
  maxSpacing = 560,
  scaleFalloff = 0.2,
  className,
  cardClassName,
  onIndexChange,
}: WrappingDrumCarouselProps) {
  const stageRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const cardsRef = useRef<Array<HTMLDivElement | null>>([]);
  /** Fractional carousel position. Tweened by the snap, driven raw by drag. */
  const posRef = useRef({ pos: 0 });
  /** Integer target index. Unwrapped — it counts up forever. */
  const indexRef = useRef(0);
  /** Last computed spacing in px. Drag divides by this for 1:1 tracking. */
  const stepRef = useRef(1);

  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const size = useResizeObserver(stageRef);

  const items = Children.toArray(children);
  const count = items.length;

  const notify = useRef(onIndexChange);
  notify.current = onIndexChange;

  /**
   * Lay every card out for the current `pos`. Called on mount, on resize,
   * on every frame of the snap tween, and on every pointermove during a drag.
   * It is a pure function of `pos` — there is no accumulated state in here,
   * which is why interrupting the tween mid-flight cannot desynchronise it.
   */
  const layout = useCallback(() => {
    const stage = stageRef.current;
    if (!stage || count === 0) return;

    const step = Math.min(spacingRatio * stage.clientWidth, maxSpacing);
    stepRef.current = step > 0 ? step : 1;

    // Signed ring offset in (-count/2, count/2]. The whole illusion is here.
    const ring = gsap.utils.wrap(-count / 2, count / 2);
    const pos = posRef.current.pos;

    for (let i = 0; i < count; i += 1) {
      const card = cardsRef.current[i];
      if (!card) continue;

      const offset = ring(i - pos);
      const distance = Math.abs(offset);

      gsap.set(card, {
        xPercent: -50,
        yPercent: -50,
        x: offset * step,
        // Explicitly flat. Without these two, a `transform-style: preserve-3d`
        // or a stray `rotateY` on an ancestor turns a deliberately 2D drum
        // into a half-broken 3D one that skews at the edges.
        rotationY: 0,
        z: 0,
        // Scale bottoms out at one slot out; alpha keeps falling and hits 0 at
        // distance 1.533. Cards therefore fade into fog rather than shrink to
        // a vanishing point — that mismatch is what sells the cylinder.
        scale: 1 - scaleFalloff * Math.min(distance, 1),
        autoAlpha: gsap.utils.clamp(0, 1, ALPHA_INTERCEPT - ALPHA_SLOPE * distance),
        zIndex: 100 - Math.round(10 * distance),
        transformOrigin: '50% 50%',
      });
    }
  }, [count, spacingRatio, maxSpacing, scaleFalloff]);

  /** Tween `pos` to an integer index and re-lay out on every frame. */
  const snapTo = useCallback(
    (index: number) => {
      indexRef.current = index;
      notify.current?.(wrapIndex(index, count));

      if (reduced) {
        // Not "duration 0" via the tween: a zero-duration gsap.to does not
        // guarantee an onUpdate call, so the layout would never run.
        posRef.current.pos = index;
        layout();
        return;
      }

      gsap.to(posRef.current, {
        pos: index,
        duration: SNAP_DURATION,
        ease: 'power3.out',
        overwrite: true,
        onUpdate: layout,
      });
    },
    [count, layout, reduced],
  );

  useDrag(stageRef, {
    threshold: DRAG_THRESHOLD,
    onDragStart: () => {
      // Kill the snap first or it keeps writing `pos` underneath the drag and
      // the cards visibly fight the finger.
      gsap.killTweensOf(posRef.current);
    },
    onDrag: (state) => {
      posRef.current.pos -= state.deltaX / stepRef.current;
      layout();
    },
    onDragEnd: (_state, moved) => {
      if (moved) snapTo(Math.round(posRef.current.pos));
    },
  });
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Removes the wheel listener, kills the tween on the internal position object, kills any tween on the card elements and clears every property GSAP wrote with `clearProps: "all"`. `useDrag` releases pointer capture and removes its own five listeners. Ordering matters: tweens are killed before props are cleared, or an in-flight tween writes the transform straight back.

**Reduced motion.** Drag still tracks the finger 1:1 — direct manipulation is not motion the user did not ask for. What changes is the release: instead of a 0.7 s `power3.out` tween, `pos` is assigned the target index and the layout runs once, so the drum arrives in a single frame. Wheel steps land instantly for the same reason.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Reaching for `rotationY` and `translateZ` to get the drum look. This technique is flat on purpose — real 3D needs a shared or per-element perspective decision, correct `transform-style` on every ancestor, and it renders text on a rotated plane, which is where the blurring comes from. Write `rotationY: 0, z: 0` explicitly so an ancestor cannot opt you into 3D by accident.
- Accumulating position instead of recomputing it. If the layout adds a delta to each card's current transform, interrupting the snap tween mid-flight leaves the cards permanently offset from `pos`. Layout must be a pure function of `pos` and nothing else.
- Using `opacity` instead of `autoAlpha`. At `opacity: 0` the wrapped-around cards are still hit-testable, so a click intended for the centre card lands on an invisible one stacked on top of it. `autoAlpha` also sets `visibility: hidden`, which removes them from hit-testing.
- Forgetting to kill the snap tween on `onDragStart`. The tween keeps writing `pos` underneath the drag and the cards visibly stutter against the finger.
- Calling `preventDefault` on every wheel event. A vertical trackpad scroll over the carousel then does nothing and the page appears frozen. Only the horizontal component is claimed here — `Math.abs(deltaX) > Math.abs(deltaY)` gates the whole handler.
- Registering the wheel listener as passive. `preventDefault` is silently ignored on a passive listener and Chrome logs an "Unable to preventDefault inside passive event listener" warning on every event.
- Computing spacing from `window.innerWidth`. The carousel is then correct on load and wrong the moment it sits inside anything narrower than the viewport — a sidebar, a modal, a preview grid.

## Notes

- This is one of three deliberately different carousel techniques in the registry, and they must not be collapsed into one. This one is **fake 3D driven by a JS position variable**: `gsap.utils.wrap` maps a continuous, unbounded index onto the item count, and depth is scale plus `autoAlpha` only. `perspective-coverflow-scroller` is **true 3D driven by a native scroll container** — real `rotateY`/`translateZ`, no JS loop. `percent-slide-carousel` is **flat percentage translation with a CSS transition** and no wrapping at all.
- Choose this one when the sequence must be endless in both directions and the item count is small enough that every item can stay mounted. It cannot virtualise: every card is laid out on every frame of a drag.
- `touch-action: pan-y` on the stage tells the browser that horizontal gestures belong to the carousel and vertical ones to the page. Without it, dragging on a phone either scrolls the page or forces you to `preventDefault` every `touchmove`, which fights the browser instead of cooperating with it.

## Definition of done

Drag left past the last card and the first one arrives from the right without a gap or a jump. Release mid-way and it settles onto the nearest card. Neighbours are visibly smaller and dimmer, and inspecting a card shows a `matrix()` transform with no 3D component. Scroll the page vertically with the cursor over the carousel and the page scrolls normally; swipe horizontally and the drum steps one card.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
